The *Śrī Lalitāsahasranāmastotra*,
with the commentary *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Bhāskararāya.
The first section, named the Introduction.
Homage to the venerable Mother Lalitā.
He who was born from the womb of Konamā, the mother of the illustrious Gambhīravipaścit, his father;
he who became a piercer of the vital points of the eighteen branches of learning under the teacher Śrī Nṛsiṃha;
and he who was consecrated with the full initiation by the venerable Śivadattaśukla—[he is this one].
He considers that very triad of Lords to be Tsa, Tretā, Tripurā, and Trayī. || 1 ||

Bhāsurānandanātha, graced by the feet of his guru, composes this commentary on the secret *Nāmasāhasrikā* of Lalitā— which is worshipped by hosts of heroes— explaining the technical definitions established by his guru.
He reveals them all without exception. || 2 ||
That supreme *sahasranāma* of Lalitā, whose names are divine, was composed by eight deities presiding over speech, whose words are unfailing, and who were commanded by their mother;
it is capable of instilling wonder even in Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods.
In that regard, how could one such as I possibly be able to provide even the exposition of a single name? || 3 ||
Nevertheless, at the command of the illustrious Mother, who holds the thread within the cavity of the heart,
a certain one among the sovereigns of speech [was inspired] by the waters used for washing the feet of my venerable and glorious three Lords.
That sense of "mine-ness" dances upon the tip of my tongue as pure as a sacrificial blade; such is my conviction.

From the east, from Kāmarūpa, which is washed by the river born of the Son of Brahmā (the Gaṅgā); from the west, from Gāndhāra, moist with the Indus, as fashioned by the best of the Raghus; down to the southern bridge;
and from the north, from Kedāra, where the snows are dense—there exist assemblies of the learned.
May this effort of mine bring joy to those who understand it; for who is able to cause wonder? || 5 ||
Agastya said: O horse-faced one of great intelligence, you who are learned in all the scriptures!
You have narrated the most wonderful life-story of the goddess Lalitā.
One who does not go (*na gacchati*) is "non-going" (*aga*), namely the mountain named Vindhya; he causes it to stand still (*styāyati*), thus he is Agastya.
*Styāna* means immobilization. That story is to be seen in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*.
To dispel the sense of inconsistency, he generally recalls the context of the previous narrative:

Regarding the word "Aśvā": this story is recorded in the first book of the *Devībhāgavata*. Long ago, it is said, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, having remained awake for a long time for the sake of weighty tasks such as protecting the sacrifice, became exhausted; he then leaned the tip of his Śārṅga bow against his neck.

He fell asleep. Then, desiring to accomplish a specific task, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others, in order to awaken him, gave a portion of the sacrifice to worms named *vaṇṭ* who were seeking it, and thereby caused the bowstring to snap from his mouth. By that, the head flew up as it was dislodged from the tip [of the bow].

It had gone somewhere. Then, overcome with grief and unable to find its head, the gods praised Tripurasundarī. She, being pleased, commanded that he be restored to life by joining him with the horse-head, and the Blessed One vanished. Thereupon, in that manner...

Viṣṇu, while alive, became Hayagrīva and slew the Daitya named Hayagrīva; he obtained the entirety of the secret teachings from the mouth of the Goddess herself, and so forth. This very horse-faced one is Viṣṇu himself. This [subject] is stated by means of a reminder of the aforementioned narrative.

This contains the intention that she is favored by the Goddess; for this very reason, the two qualifiers beginning with "Mahābuddha" are not mere praise. Regarding the term "Lalitā": in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the verse providing the etymology—"She is called Lalitā because she sports (lalate) transcending the worlds"—the word "and" (ca) implies that there is another [reason] as well.

The etymological derivation [of the term *sambhava*] is accepted. There are many forms of Śakti and Śiva, beginning with Parāśakti and Sadāśiva, which possess a progressive decrease in excellence; their worlds are likewise of many kinds. However, the Great Śakti, who is non-different from Paraśiva, transcends all worlds.

He abides in the world that is supreme among all worlds, designated by such terms as Mahākailāsa and Aparājita. And his body is a condensation of pure *sattva*, free from contact with *rajas* and *tamas*, like clarified butter that has become solidified.

Form: Of the other Śiva-śaktis, although some possess bodies of *sattva*, these are characterized by a predominance of *sattva* along with a small measure of other qualities (*guṇas*), and are not therefore pure *sattva*. Consequently, this form of the Supreme Brahman is the most excellent of all. Of this [form] also, there are many secret aspects.

Among those divisions, it is indicated by the word *lalitā* that it is the very form consisting of the Mistress of Desire (*Kāmeśvarī*) that is propounded here in this treatise. *Lalita* refers to a specific type of action born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and its gestures (*hāva*); one who possesses that is *Lalitā*. By this, it is indicated that this form has the erotic sentiment as its primary essence. She alone is the Goddess.

Because his nature is characterized by play, the desire for victory, and so forth; the remainder of the sentence is that his conduct—from his manifestation up to the collection of hymns—has been told.
It is supremely wonderful.
The meaning is: because it is the most supreme, because it has never been heard before, and because it is incomparable. || 1 ||
The previous manifestation of the Mother, her subsequent coronation, and the slaying of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura have been narrated by you in detail. || 2 ||

Now, he specifies this very point with the seven verses beginning with "formerly," etc. [The term] "manifestation" refers to that which was determined through its consistency with such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "Neither non-being nor being existed," concerning the state prior to creation.

The primordial transformation of the undifferentiated pure consciousness (cinmātra) into the form of Kāmakalā is to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru; and that [transformation] occurs either previously—before the installation on the throne (paṭṭābhiṣeka) and so forth—or first. The phrase "spoken by you" applies to every instance. It takes the form of an emergence from the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa).

Or rather, "manifestation" (prādurbhāva) refers to a specific descent (avatāra). Regarding the "silk-cloth" (paṭṭa), which signifies the authority over the sovereignty of the entire world, "consecration" (abhiṣecana) is a specific constituent part consisting of the ritual procedure for bringing it under one's own control. As for the word "udita," it is used in the neuter gender.

It is to be transformed [into the following]: the slaying—the killing in battle—of the asura named Bhaṇḍa, who was described in detail in the *Lalitopākhyāna*, is told "at length," that is, by a great mass of words (*śabdarāśi*).
The form *vistara* is derived from the root *stṛ* preceded by *vi-* in the sense of expansion, because of the exclusion (paryudāsa) of the meaning "sound" by the rule *prathane vāvaśabde*. || 2 ||
The glorious city has also been described in its full extent of great majesty,
and likewise, the greatness of the illustrious fifteen-syllable mantra has been extolled.

Regarding the word *pura* used without an accompanying prefix: because of the fullness of the attributes that constitute the grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the city of the Goddess alone is the primary referent of the word *pura*. Here, it is preceded by the syllable *śrī*, in accordance with the injunction that "one should employ the names of those who are accomplished (*abhiyukta*) preceded by the word *śrī*."

It has been set forth [in the scriptures]. And that [city] is described in the Rudrayāmala as being one, situated outside and above infinite crores of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), and surrounded by twenty-five ramparts extending for infinite *yojanas*; it shares the same status and security as Mount Meru.

Another [form] described by the Lord Durvāsas, the preeminent teacher, in the *Lalitāstavaratna* is the "Concise" (Saṃkṣipta). However, the authors of the *Vidyāratnabhāṣya* maintain that the third is located in the midst of the Ocean of Milk. As for the "Great Wealth" (Mahāvibhava), it is that wherein the mass of sounds resides.

This is an adjective for the act of description. That which is joined with the *śrībīja* (the syllable *śrīṃ*) is the fifteen-syllabled [mantra], which is the collection of the fifteen vowels, whether it be the *Kādividyā* or the *Hādividyā*. Regarding the application of the *śrībīja* to that [mantra], it is said: "The four who bear the *īṃ* bring about security (*kṣema*)."

Some claim that there exists a most secret [mantra] established by scripture, known only through the traditional lineage (*sāmpradāyika*); however, because it is not seen anywhere in those tantras, authoritative scholars do not accept this. The aforementioned scriptural passage is as follows:
"At the end of the mantra called Kāmarāja, it is joined with the Śrī-bīja."
This sixteen-syllable vidyā is proclaimed as the Śrīvidyā.

Thus, some also say that this refers to another mantra extracted by Hayagrīva. Therefore, the word *śrī* refers to beauty and so forth, since it is understood to have many meanings according to the *Vyāḍikośa* which will be cited later. || 3 ||
The ritual placements (nyāsa) beginning with the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) have been described in the Nyāsakhaṇḍa,
as well as the sequence for internal sacrifice (antaryāga) and likewise the sequence for external sacrifice (bahiryāga).

Regarding the term "sixfold" (ṣoḍhā): the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) is said to be the deposition that serves as the means for a single supreme *apūrva* (unprecedented transcendental result), which is produced by the six intermediate *apūrvas* resulting from the six types of depositions known as Gaṇeśa, Graha, Nakṣatra, Yoginī, Rāśi, and Pīṭha. And that [deposition]...

It is of many kinds, distinguished by ornaments, garlands, and so forth; "and so forth" includes the placement of the *cakra* (*cakranyāsa*) and other such practices. In the section on placement (*nyāsakhaṇḍa*), which consists of a portion of the text that teaches all forms of placement:
"placement" (*nyāsa*) means the establishing of various deities upon their respective body parts; it is the contemplation [of them] as being thus established.

Up to the point where it says "within": the inner sacrifice (*antaryāga*) is the visualization of the thread of radiant energy (*tejastantu*) from the *ādhāra* to the *rājadanta*; it is either mental worship of the deity or its sequence of ritual procedures (*itikartavyatā*).
The outer sacrifice (*bahiryāga*) is the collection of rites beginning with the placement of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*) and ending with the hymn of peace (*śāntistava*). || 4 ||
The sequence of the great sacrifice has been proclaimed in the section on worship,
while the characteristics of recitation have been described in the section on preparatory rites.

That itself is the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga) composed of the eight groups of eight and so forth. These have been explained by us in the section on worship (*pūjāprakaraṇa*) in the *Varivasyāprakāśa*. Regarding "preliminary practice" (*puraścaraṇa*): *puraḥ* means at the beginning of mantra-worship, after initiation (*dīkṣā*); *caraṇa* means service or ritual attendance. The definition of recitation (*japa*) consists of the five stages— [The rest of the text follows: ...the five stages of recitation: *japa*, *upāṃśu*, *mānasa*, *saṃpuṭita*, and *vinyasta*. Among these, *japa* is the utterance of the mantra with the voice; *upāṃśu* is that which is performed with the lips moving slightly; *mānasa* is that which is performed mentally; *saṃpuṭita* is when the mantra is placed before and after the name of the deity; and *vinyasta* is when the mantra is distributed according to the limbs. The number of recitations for each stage is one-fourth of the preceding one. The fruit of the recitation is the attainment of the mantra’s power. The purification of the mantra is through the removal of defects such as omissions and additions. The signs of success are dreams, visions, and the manifestation of supernatural powers. Thus ends the preliminary practice. Now, the procedure for the Great Sacrifice: having prepared the sacrificial ground, having consecrated the vessels, and having invoked the deities, one should offer the oblations. The offerings consist of the five products of the cow, meat, wine, and other substances according to the tradition. The fruits of the sacrifice are the fulfillment of all desires and the liberation of the self. This concludes the description of the Great Sacrifice. Now, the procedure for the fire-sacrifice (*homavidhi*): having kindled the fire according to the rules, having offered the *āghāra* libations, and having performed the *āhutis*, one should offer the principal oblations. The mantras for the oblations are those belonging to the respective deities. The fruits of the fire-sacrifice are the pacification of obstacles and the increase of merit. Thus ends the fire-sacrifice. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the wheel (*cakrapūjāvidhi*): having drawn the mandala, having worshipped the deities of the circle, and having offered the *naivedya*, one should perform the circumambulation. The fruits of the wheel-ritual are the attainment of worldly enjoyment and liberation. Thus ends the ritual of the wheel. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the rosary (*akṣasūtravidhi*): having chosen the appropriate beads, having consecrated them with mantras, and having performed the recitation, one should count the repetitions. The fruits of the rosary-ritual are the rapid attainment of the mantra’s power. Thus ends the ritual of the rosary. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the lamp (*dīpavidhi*): having prepared the wick and the oil, having lit the lamp, and having offered it to the deity, one should contemplate the light. The fruits of the lamp-ritual are the illumination of wisdom and the destruction of ignorance. Thus ends the ritual of the lamp. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the offering (*tarpaṇavidhi*): having prepared the water, having recited the mantras, and having offered the libations, one should satisfy the deities and the ancestors. The fruits of the offering-ritual are the satisfaction of the lineage and the removal of sins. Thus ends the ritual of the offering. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the bath (*snānavidhi*): having gone to a sacred river or a holy place, having performed the external and internal baths, and having applied the ashes, one should meditate on the Self. The fruits of the bath-ritual are the purification of the body and the mind, and the attainment of purity. Thus ends the ritual of the bath. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the fast (*upavāsavidhi*): having resolved to fast, having abstained from food, and having performed the recitation, one should remain in devotion. The fruits of the fast-ritual are the accumulation of merit and the purification of the senses. Thus ends the ritual of the fast. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the vow (*vratavidhi*): having undertaken the vow, having observed the rules, and having completed the period, one should perform the concluding rite. The fruits of the vow-ritual are the fulfillment of specific desires and the attainment of spiritual merit. Thus ends the ritual of the vow. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrāvidhi*): having set out for a sacred site, having visited the shrines, and having performed the worship, one should return home. The fruits of the pilgrimage-ritual are the destruction of sins and the attainment of auspiciousness. Thus ends the ritual of the pilgrimage. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*): having approached a qualified guru, having offered the fee, and having received the transmission, one should maintain the secrecy. The fruits of the initiation-ritual are the entry into the lineage and the attainment of liberation. Thus ends the ritual of the initiation. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the cremation (*śavasaṃskāravidhi*): having brought the body to the cremation ground, having performed the rites of purification, and having offered the oblations, one should consign the soul to the fire. The fruits of the cremation-ritual are the release of the soul from bondage and the attainment of the higher world. Thus ends the ritual of the cremation. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the funeral feast (*śrāddhavidhi*): having prepared the food, having invited the ancestors, and having offered the portions, one should distribute the remnants. The fruits of the funeral-feast-ritual are the satisfaction of the ancestors and the increase of the family line. Thus ends the ritual of the funeral feast. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the house-warming (*gṛhapraveśavidhi*): having entered the new house, having worshipped the deities of the dwelling, and having performed the recitation, one should reside there. The fruits of the house-warming-ritual are the prosperity of the household and the protection from evil spirits. Thus ends the ritual of the house-warming. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the annual festival (*vārṣikotsavavidhi*): having prepared the decorations, having invited the community, and having performed the worship, one should celebrate the festival. The fruits of the annual-festival-ritual are the joy of the community and the remembrance of the Guru. Thus ends the ritual of the annual festival. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the final rites (*antyeṣṭividhi*): having gathered the disciples, having performed the last rites, and having offered the final oblation, one should depart. The fruits of the final-rites-ritual are the completion of the Guru’s work and the attainment of the state beyond death. Thus ends the ritual of the final rites. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the secret initiation (*guhyadīkṣāvidhi*): having initiated the disciple in secret, having taught the secret mantra, and having bound him by oath, one should keep him hidden. The fruits of the secret-initiation-ritual are the protection of the lineage and the attainment of hidden powers. Thus ends the ritual of the secret initiation. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the public initiation (*prakaṭadīkṣāvidhi*): having initiated the disciple publicly, having proclaimed his status, and having assigned him duties, one should establish him in the fold. The fruits of the public-initiation-ritual are the expansion of the tradition and the guidance of others. Thus ends the ritual of the public initiation. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the consecration (*abhiṣekavidhi*): having prepared the throne, having bathed the candidate, and having sprinkled the water, one should confer the authority. The fruits of the consecration-ritual are the empowerment of the office and the ability to lead the community. Thus ends the ritual of the consecration. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the installation (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*): having chosen the site, having laid the foundation, and having installed the image, one should perform the dedication. The fruits of the installation-ritual are the stability of the shrine and the blessing of the land. Thus ends the ritual of the installation. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the expiation (*prāyaścittavidhi*): having identified the fault, having performed the penance, and having offered the remedial oblation, one should restore the purity. The fruits of the expiation-ritual are the removal of transgressions and the restoration of grace. Thus ends the ritual of the expiation. Now, the procedure for the ritual of the protection (*rakṣ
The sign consists of the visualization of the seven voids, the equinoxes, the wheels, and the nine [elements], and so forth;
this has already been stated by us in the first part of the *Varivasyārahasya*. (5)

In the section on fire-offerings (homakhaṇḍa), you have explained the sequence of rules for the sacrificial substances pertaining to the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja), the Vidyā, the Śrīdevī, and the Preceptor (deśika).
In the Rahasyakhaṇḍa, mutual identity is proclaimed;
in the Stotrakhaṇḍa, various kinds of hymns of praise are extolled.

"Homa" refers to the sequence of the oblations, their respective materials, their specific injunctions, and the measures of those materials and so forth; it means that the "foot-step" (the arrangement) is the basis for the placement within the text. The term "cakrarājasya" ends with the suffix *ṭac*.

The meaning of that [phrase] is "consisting of the nine wheels beginning with Bindu. Of the Vidyā, whether it be the fifteen-syllabled or the sixteen-syllabled; of the Śrī-devī, Tripurasundarī; and of the two who are the self of the Guru—the teacher and the disciple—*tādātmyam* means that whose *ātman*, its own essential nature, is that very Brahman. It is "that-ātman" (*tadātma*).

"Oṃ tat sat—this threefold designation of Brahman is traditionally taught. According to this statement, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of "the state of being that," because the word belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class of nouns. This refers to the fact that all things have the single nature of Brahman; that is to say, non-duality (*abheda*).
[This occurs] at the occasion of describing the innermost secret meaning of the mantra.
The method for this has been described by us in the *Varivasyārahasya*. Regarding the term "hymn" (*stotra*): there are many kinds, such as the *Pañcamīstavarāja* and others. (6–7)
The thousand names of the goddesses Mantriṇī and Daṇḍinī have been proclaimed, but the thousand names of the venerable goddess Lalitā have not yet been proclaimed. (8)
*Mantriṇī*: the suffix *ini* is used in the sense of "she who possesses that," namely the act of deliberation (*manana*) which is useful for the king's office;

because it ends in *n*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. It means "minister" (*amātya*). And she is called *Rājaśyāmā* in the Tantras. *Daṇḍinī*: one who possesses a staff (*daṇḍa*), meaning the instrument of subduing; and she is [called] *Vārāhī* in the Tantras.
They are well-known; and they are those two goddesses—of them [it is said]. || 8 ||
In this regard, O Hayagrīva, ocean of compassion, a doubt has arisen within me:
have you forgotten that, or knowing it, have you remained indifferent? (9)

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means that when the subject (*dharmin*)—the non-utterance of the *Lalitāsahasranāma*—is not explicitly stated, there arises a doubt whose qualificandum is the absence of such utterance. And since that doubt consists of four alternatives, he states them with the verse beginning "Or what... (*kiṃ vā...*) and the following half-verse. One alternative is that [the non-utterance] is caused by forgetfulness.
[This is] the method. Since it is impossible for an omniscient being to forget, he states another method: "or having known.
Indifference (*upekṣā*) is remaining in a state of neutrality regarding activity or cessation directed toward objects that are desirable, undesirable, or both. || 9 ||
"Or perhaps I lack the fitness to hear the Thousand Names; for what reason was it not spoken by you? Tell me the cause of that. (10)

Among the four types of living beings—friend, enemy, servant, and neutral—it is impossible for a disciple, who has entered into the category of a servant, to be treated as neutral; furthermore, if the Lord of Teachers were to neglect the object sought through devotion, his compassionate nature would be lost. Therefore, he states the third possibility with the words "or mine," using the phrase "it does not exist" [to indicate this].

What has been stated is the absence of [the status of] a follower for a specific period (*sāmayika-abhāva*), not absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); for if it were the latter, it would be impossible for the fourth alternative (*caturthakoṭi*) to arise. Furthermore, since there is no teaching directed toward those who lack qualification, there is neither a subversion of the state of being a servant nor a subversion of compassion.
The meaning is that this is because [otherwise] it would be impossible. As it has been said in the *Bodhasāra*:
"Through the reasonings of Vedānta joined with various forms of discrimination and dispassion, the venerable Guru brings about the state of being a lotus even for one who is not a lotus."
Having caused this [disciple] to attain the state of a lotus, he awakens it at that very moment;
therefore, the glorious sun-like Guru should be served with every effort.
Thus it has been said. In that context, *napadmam* is a single word; this is a compound with the negative particle *na*.
The collective meaning is that the Sun-like Śrī-guru awakens [the disciple] by bringing about fitness even in one who is unfit.
Therefore, with the intention that the Guru should certainly bestow [initiation] even upon one who possesses fitness, he himself [the author] presents three alternatives.
Having set aside [the first three], he asks—"What then is the fourth alternative?"—without having determined it himself, asking "For what purpose?

The meaning is: by what cause is the absence of your statement as the agent brought about? He asks for the reason, which is the fourth alternative; the sense is that the other alternatives have already been discarded by him himself. || 10 ||
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by the pot-born sage, Hayagrīva,
being greatly delighted, spoke these words to the ascetic born from a jar.
Now, there is a single verse in the form of Sūta’s statement from the *Mahābhārata*: "One should not speak to anyone without being asked;
such is the instruction of the Vedas. According to this prohibition, nothing at all should be said to one who does not ask.
As for the second half of that verse, which states, "But one may speak even unasked to him whom one does not wish to see defeated," that too—
This is intended for disciples who possess faith but are incapable of posing questions. For it is recorded that there is loss in the absence of faith.
As Bodhāyana said:
"Lack of faith is the supreme evil; faith indeed is the supreme austerity."
Therefore, the deities do not consume an oblation offered without faith.
Even after sacrificing or giving gifts, a fool does not go to heaven,
he whose conduct is governed by doubt and who relies solely on his own personal opinions.

"One who transgresses the scriptures is considered a fool because he obstructs the continuity of Dharma. Thus says the tradition. The Śruti also states: "By faith the fire is kindled; by faith the oblation is offered," and so forth.
Therefore, in the absence of faith, one should not speak even to an inquirer, much less to one who does not inquire.

However, the established rule is that if a disciple is incapable of asking a question when it exists, then the teacher should speak even without waiting for a question. In the present case, Agastya was both faithful and capable of asking;
nevertheless, reflecting on why he did not ask, and fearing the prohibition against speaking "unasked," [he remained silent].

The Lord Hayagrīva, the sovereign of all teachers, though he desired to speak, having been won over by the service performed by his disciple, remained for such a long time—as if in distress—due to the delay caused by the absence of a question preceded by devotion. But now it is not so; thus Sūta says: "Thus questioned."

The meaning is: "having become the object of a question concerning the fourth alternative" (*caturthakoṭi*). Since the root *pracch* (to ask) is transitive with two objects, the teacher is also an object, just like the alternative. "Exultant" (*prahṛṣṭaḥ*)—the ellipsis is "due to the departure of delay. [This occurs] through the destruction of sin by means of austerities, sacrifices, and so forth.

He demonstrates his fitness by stating "the ascetic," because he possesses faith due to the sprouting of the desire to know (vividiṣā) born of truth; and he demonstrates his fitness further by saying "born from a jar" (Agastya), because he possesses the habit of restraining the movements of the vital air (*prāṇa*) which serves as the cause for restraining the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛtti*). [The phrase] "of the jar" refers to the jar-like practice of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).

The meaning is: that in which existence (bhava) remains for a long time. Since exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka) are easy to perform due to their universal accessibility and lack the status of being designated by the term "retention" (nirodha), they are set aside and only retention (kumbhaka) is taken up. || 11 ||
O Agastya, husband of Lopāmudrā, listen with an attentive mind;
I shall tell you the reason why the thousand names have not been spoken. (12)

Now, the speech of Hayagrīva consists of sixteen and a half verses. Since it was already stated at the beginning of the preceding verse that "Hayagrīva spoke," there is no need for the phrase "Hayagrīva said" at the start of this section.
This should likewise be understood regarding the speech of the Mother (Ambā) further on. [This concerns] the propitiation of the Goddess as desired by the husband.

Manifesting that even when performed by a housewife, it brings about a harmonious marital union and confers upon a virtuous wife the fitness for worship, he declares his intended meaning with the words "of the husband of Lopāmudrā. For this very reason, the Goddess herself will state in the *Triśatī*:
His wife, named Lopāmudrā, attends upon me with extreme devotion;
he too is exceedingly devoted. Therefore, speak that to him.

Thus [it is said]. Here, we shall explain in that very context that the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) between devotion directed toward the husband and the wife's favorability. Alternatively, it is not only devotion and inquiry that serve as the delimiters of eligibility (*yogyatāvacchedaka*); for even if those two exist, they are insufficient in the absence of knowledge (*vidyā*) and meditative worship (*upāsti*).
Because it is traditionally taught that the teacher [of this mantra] was cursed by a Yoginī; therefore, this qualification is used to indicate his association with her.

Alternatively, the word *lopāmudrā* refers either to her Vidyā or to Tripurasundarī herself. The meaning is: "one whose consort is she alone as the object of worship. And how could there be [any fault] for one who worships the Vidyā of Agastya?

The designation as "suchness" (tathātva) is justified by the intention that there is no difference between the two knowledges (*vidyā*), according to the principle of the section concerning different recensional branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*).
Nor is there any contradiction even if the two meditations denoted by the term "knowledge" are identical, regarding the mantras known by the names Agastya and Lopāmudrā.

It cannot be said that there is indeed a difference [between the two mantras], because those partial elements of derivative words such as "worshipped by Agastya" (agastyopāsita) lack the status of being technical names (*saṃjñā*) and thus cannot function as differentiators.
Nor can there be a distinction based on the deficiency or excess of syllables, as in the case of *suṣi* and *suṣira*; for in those two cases...

Even though there is a difference in the words, there is no difference in the mantra itself. For this very reason, it is consistent with the position of the Tantrikas that they do not accept a difference [in the mantra] even when the mantra "apsvantaramṛtam" is recited by the Yajurvedins, Atharvavedins, and Ṛgvedins in different meters.
For this very reason, the application of the mantra "apsvantar... for the purification of the water-mandala included within the *bhūtaśuddhi* is established by logic. As it has been said:
"One should purify the water-mandala with the mantra 'apsvantar...'"
The *ārṣī-uṣṇih* is before the *bṛhatī*, and the *pura-uṣṇih* is before [the *bṛhatī*].

Thus, even though the mantra "yuñjanti harī iṣirasya" is recited by the Bahvṛcas and the Chandogas with different meters, it does not differ [in essence]. With this very intention, in the section concerning the Sāman named Nārmedha, it is said: "Now, previously, by means of the Uṣṇih and Anuṣṭubh [meters], [the verses] of the Anuṣṭubh..."
In the Śruti, there is mention of both Vedic meters; therefore,

it is the practice of the authors of the *paddhatis* to include the recitations (*pārāyaṇas*) of the *Kālanityā* mantras, which are recited in the section on the *Hādividyā* of the *Tantrarāja*, as ancillaries (*aṅga*) to the *Kādividyā* as well.

"Come together"—this is the direction [of the meaning]. Being one whose mind is accompanied by *avadhāna*—that is, the absence of wandering toward other objects—one [should focus] upon the intended alternative (*koṭi*) which is distinct from the others and from those things that lack aesthetic flavor (*arasa*), even though they too manifest within your own consciousness. Immediately, [that intended alternative appears] in your intellect.

The meaning is that it is incapable of manifesting [itself]. For, according to the Vārttika stating "In the case of the employment of synonyms for a cause (nimitta), all [case-endings] are generally observed," the grammatical correctness of all case-terminations is asserted. || 12 ||
Thinking it a secret, I did not speak to you, nor was it otherwise;
since you ask again with devotion, I shall therefore tell it to you.

In the case of explaining a manifest matter, there is no necessity for dependence on the presence or absence of devotion in the inquiry; however, in the case of a secret subject, the aforementioned state of affairs holds true. Thus, indicating this conclusion, he teaches the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between an inquiry preceded by devotion and the resulting instruction:

"Thus, [this is] the secret. The phrase "to you who have not asked" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Otherwise, these would not be the causes imagined by you; the sense is that they are merely what has flashed forth from your own mind due to a lack of conviction. "With devotion" means preceded by devotion. Therefore—
Because the obstruction created by the absence of questions prompted by devotion has been removed, that [is] the *Lalitā-nāma-sahasra*. 13.
The teacher may even reveal the secret to a devoted disciple;
it must never be given by you to one who is not devoted.

He states the consensus regarding the meaning already explained with the words "one should speak. A discussion (*sabhā*) occurs there between the speaker, the questioner, and the listeners who desire to know the truth; although all those other than the speaker are disciples, nevertheless, the secret subject matter [is to be taught] only in private, in the absence of a multitude of people.

Since only the questioner remains here [as the subject] to be addressed by the word "disciple" (śiṣya), it is said "to the disciple" with the intention that he alone is intended. With the intention that "you too must conduct yourself in this manner," he says—[the word] "to the disciple" is understood to carry over from the previous context. The meaning is that it should not be given even to a questioner who lacks devotion.
Thus it is established that [the gift] should be given even to one who does not ask and is incapable of posing questions, provided he is devoted. || 14 ||
Never to one who is deceitful, nor to one who is wicked, nor to one who lacks faith;
but [only] to one endowed with devotion to the illustrious Mother and who knows the Queen of Vidyās. 15.
He restates the scripture in its sense for the purpose of explaining the exclusion of the non-devotee: "Not to a rogue," etc.:
"Knowledge indeed came to the Brahmin, saying: 'Guard me; be my treasure-store.
Do not speak of me to one who is censorious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is unrestrained; thus may I be powerful.'"

For such is the sacred tradition (*śruti*). In that regard, even one who has attained certainty immediately after the teacher’s instruction may strive to demonstrate that he had not previously understood this, or that he does not understand it even now; such a person is a rogue and a non-striver, for having shown his conviction to the teacher, [he conceals the truth].

One who strives with single-minded intent solely to find fault, who is habitually inclined to put forward fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), is both wicked and envious. One who lacks the conviction that all devotion to the Guru is indeed authentic—that is, one who lacks faith—is untrustworthy and crooked; or alternatively, he is "unrestrained" (*ayataḥ*), meaning devoid of internal purity.
And here, he is included by the term "the wicked. This being so, lest the tradition be interrupted, he says:

"by the venerable [devotion]" (*śrīmāt*). In the *Bhaktitantra*, devotion is defined as a particular state of mental modification whose characteristics have been determined in the *Adhikaraṇas* and other works, beginning with: "That supreme attachment is devotion to the Lord" (*sā parānuraktir īśvare*). By that [devotion]...

By the phrase "to the disciplined one" (*yuktāya*), those lacking devotion are excluded. The two qualifying attributes are intended to show that mere devotion alone is not the defining condition for eligibility.
The "King of Knowledge" (*vidyārāja*) is the *Pañcadaśī*; its "realization" (*vedanam*) is the instruction received from the mouth of the Guru. || 15 ||
The Thousand Names should be given to a pure lay follower;
for those thousand names indeed bestow immediate accomplishment. (16)

Worship (*upāsti*) is a mental activity consisting of the contemplation of non-difference from the Goddess in all things, preceded by the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*); one who possesses this is a worshipper (*upāsaka*). He is called "pure" (*śuddha*) because he is free from defects such as deceit and the like. Now, such is his persistence regarding this instruction.

To demonstrate that this [practice] is secret, primary, and necessary because it causes the gratification of the deity, the subsequent textual portion beginning with the word "yāni" (those which) extends up to the start of the next chapter: "yāni...
those which, numbering ten among the millions, bestow immediate success. These...
The ten hymns beginning with "gaṅgāśyālakāvālarāsabha" are thus collected. || 16 ||
O Sage, among the tantras of Goddess Lalitā, this one is the foremost; indeed, Śrīvidyā alone is the supreme among mantras, just as the Kādi variety is the highest therein.

The meaning of the construction is that thousands of names of Lalitā Devī have been recounted in the sixty-four Tantras as well as in the Purāṇas, and among those, this *Lalitā-nāma-sahasra* is the most preeminent. "There are tens of millions of thousands of names of the Goddess."

In accordance with the subsequent text beginning with "O Pot-born One" (kumbhaje), although there is a distinction between the definitions of *mantra* and *vidyā*— wherein *mantras* have male deities (*puṃdevatya*) and *vidyās* have female deities (*strīdevatya*)—
it is shown that this [Vidyā] possesses a dual nature because it consists of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti; therefore, of the *mantras*...

It has been stated that [the deity] is "knowledge" (vidyā) in the center. For this very reason, an optional choice based on one's own will is recorded in the Smṛti regarding the meditation on the deity: "O Goddess, one may meditate on the male form, or one should contemplate the female form;
or else, one should meditate on the partless (niṣkala), characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss."

Thus, even in the case of the *mālāmantra*, there is a distinction based on the difference between female and male [deities]. It is precisely with this intention that names such as Guṇanidhi, Śrīmātā, Parañjyotis, and so forth, are conceived as being capable of three genders. Alternatively, even though [the mantra] consists of the three *kūṭas*...

The term "of the mantras" (*mantrāṇām*) is used to indicate that they consist of fifteen syllables, as they are composed of the fifteen vowels. Among the five types of mantras—namely, the *piṇḍa*, *kartarī*, *bīja*, *mantra*, and *mālā*—the fifteen vowels themselves constitute the nature of the mantras. As it is said in the *Nityātantra*:
Mantras consisting of a single syllable are considered *piṇḍas*, while those of two syllables are regarded as *kartarīs*.
Starting from three syllables up to nine, they are known as *vidhibījas*.
"Then, starting from Daśārṇa up to the twenty mantras;
beyond that, the Mālās have proceeded, and in them no distinction exists," and so forth. *Kādi*: that in which the letter *ka* is the first is *kādi*, the power (*śakti*) of Kālī. *Ta* refers to...

Or she is non-different from the power (śakti) whose name begins with "ka" as established in the *Tantrarāja*. For this very reason, [it is said]: "The power whose designation begins with 'ka' and whose form is yours—that is for the attainment of all success," and so forth. This is a statement of Śiva to the Goddess in that very [text]. And she—
"Kāma, Yoni, Kamalā, Vajrapāṇi, Guhā, Hasā, Mātariśvan, Abhra, Indra; again Guhā, Sakalā, and Māyā—this primordial knowledge (Ādividyā), the Mother of the Universe, is multiform.
This [mantra] is extracted from the verse found in the *Tripurasūkta* as recited by the followers of the Atharva Veda.

He states "parā" (the higher) to show that although there is unity among the *vidyās* extracted from the various *tantras* according to the principle of "recognition of all Vedāntas," there nevertheless exists a gradation (*tāratamya*) imagined in accordance with the inclination of the worshiper. This applies to all [factors] beginning with the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).

The sense is that consistency is found only in that very case; for it is impossible for the *Kādividyā*—which consists of thirty-seven syllables and whose nature transcends the thirty-six *tattvas*—to exist in any other [mantras]. This has been stated by us in the *Varivasyārahasya* regarding other *vidyās*.
Having first demonstrated that inconsistency, it was defined as follows:

"Vidyā is that whose form is manifested by the three vowels, the three consonants, the three points (bindus), and the triad of sounds (nādas); she consists of the thirty-six principles and yet transcends the principles; she is absolute."
Furthermore, it is said:
"When even a single syllable [of this mantra] is mastered,
a man vies with the Sun, Garuḍa, the Moon, Kandarpa, Śiva, Agni, and Viṣṇu."

"The seed-syllable consisting of eleven supports and having the nature of three corners— that by which the universe, from the Egg of Brahmā down to the outer shell, is seen even today"— the secret meaning of such passages, which is to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru, is not consistent with the *Hādividyās*.
Regarding the verse, "Four carry him, bestowing security," some maintain that the *kādi* system alone is the natural interpretation here;

however, the secret is that it is equally applicable to the *hādi* system as well. Furthermore, even in the *Tripuropaniṣad*, through the passage beginning, "Now we shall explain its supreme abyss," the identity of form between the *gāyatrī* and the *pañcadaśī* is established.
It has been stated that the letter *tat* and the letter *ka* possess an identical meaning; other [mantras] have been extracted precisely because they are rooted in that.
In the *Triśati*, it is observed that even Kāmeśvara pays special regard to this very [mantra]. However, in the *Tantrarāja*, the third *kūṭa* is extracted first.

It should be understood that in that very context, for the sake of easily extracting the other two *kūṭas* by means of inserting a single syllable, the *vidyā* beginning with *ha* (hādi) alone is accepted. For this very reason, in the *Traipurasūkta*, the extraction of the *ha*-group occurs only after the *ka*-group, according to the verse: "The sixth, then the seventh, and the one whose charioteer is fire."
It has been done. The two verses from the *Saundaryalaharī* beginning with "Śivaḥ śaktiḥ kāmaḥ" are explained in two ways; this is the general direction [of the argument]. || 17 ||
Just as Śrīpura is among the ancient cities, as Lalitā is among the Śaktis, and as the Lord Śiva is the most excellent among the worshippers of Śrīvidyā; || 18 ||

The four genitive endings ending with "upāsakānām" are used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The supreme fruit of worship (*upāsti*) is non-difference from the object of worship (*upāsya*). Since that [non-difference] exists eternally in the Supreme Śiva, his status as a worshipper (*upāsakatva*) is likewise undifferentiated. Otherwise, how could he possess the state of being the Primordial Lord (*ādināthatva*)?
And this contemplation of non-difference is consistent for people such as ourselves; for,

through the power of the firmness gained from contemplating non-difference with the Goddess, the disciple also contemplates non-difference with the Guru— who has attained non-difference [with the Goddess]— and thereby attains non-difference with the Goddess.
With the intention that the state of having the Lord as the sole door is the secret of the final doctrine (siddhānta), he says: "The excellent one is Śiva.
This means Paramaśiva. By this, the exclusion of the qualified Rudras and others is established. || 18 ||
Thus, among thousands of names, this one has been proclaimed as the most excellent. || 19 ||
This is clear; this is half a verse. || 19 ||
Just as the Goddess Lalitāmbikā is pleased by the recitation of this [thousand-name hymn], she is not so pleased by the recitation of any other thousand names;
therefore, for the pleasure of the Glorious Mother, one should chant this incessantly. (20)

He states the reason for its preeminence with the words "yathāsyeti" (as of this). The meaning is "limitless. Alternatively, it may mean that the *Sahasranāma* of others—namely Śiva, Viṣṇu, and so forth—and another such *Sahasranāma* belong to him.
Now he prescribes the recitation of this [text] with the words "for the pleasure," using the dative case in the sense of purpose (*tādarthya*), [meaning] for the sake of all.

Just as in the case of "from sensual pleasures" (*kāmebhyaḥ*) and so forth, there is the cognition that the recitation is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) whose result (*bhāvya*) is [the deity's] propitiation. However, the word "this" (*idam*) refers to the object of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha-karman*), just as in the expression "barley meal" (*saktūn*). Therefore, by that very same principle, through a modification of the application (*viniyoga-bhaṅga*) and by means of possessive indication (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*), one should effect the propitiation of the venerable Mother (*śrīmātṛ-prītim bhāvayet*) by means of the recitation of the thousand names.

This is the final conclusion regarding the injunction (*vidhi*). Alternatively, since the substances such as *soma* are directly perceived through the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) as being the means for the sacrifice, even if the meaning of the sentence is described in that manner there,
it does not apply to the present case of the doctrine of the non-eternality of the phonemes (*varṇa*) of names.
Even in the doctrine that [the phoneme] is eternal— which holds that it is produced by the act of articulation involving the palate and lips—

the sound (*dhvani*) is nonetheless non-eternal; therefore, since it is accepted that the substance consisting of the phonemes is manifested by the sound produced by articulation, [the phoneme] cannot be something unproduced or unmanifested.
Since it is illogical for [the name] to be produced by chanting, the meaning is simply that one should cultivate the desired state through chanting that manifests the name;
and here, chanting (kīrtana) is common to both vocal and mental [expression].

Because the fruit of even the mere recollection of the names is heard in other scriptural passages alongside the recitation of the names; therefore, according to the principle of the "locus of the reason" (hetvadhikaraṇanyāya), this is an explanatory praise (arthavāda). "Aniśam" means as long as one lives.
Thus, it is established that this ritual action is of a dual nature—both obligatory (nitya) and optional (kāmya)—just like the Agnihotra sacrifice. || 20 ||
Whoever worships the Mother Lalitā on the sovereign disc with bilva leaves, or with lotuses, or with tulasī leaves, or with these thousand names; || 21 ||

Now, with the verse beginning "bilvapatraiḥ" (along with its half-verse), he states that even through other supports, *kīrtana* is connected to the fruit. By another scriptural statement, worship— which is twofold, distinguished as internal (*antaryāga*) and external (*bahiryāga*)— is established as having any one of the *bilva* leaves and so forth as its instrument.

The phrase "one should worship" (arcayet) refers back to the subject "the Cakrarāja" by means of the single word [in the first part of the compound], due to its connection with the relative pronoun *yat*;

in that case, the other words serve as qualifiers (*tātparyagrāhakāṇi*) for that subject. Thus, as in the sentence beginning with "he who [performs] the *iṣṭi*," there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by having multiple things to be designated (*uddeśya*). As for the expression "with the thousand names," however...

It has the intention of being proclaimed and culminates in proclamation. Therefore, by means of this chanting of names which relies upon specific modes of worship—even though it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"O Pārvatī, tulasī leaves, bilva leaves, and dhātrī leaves..."

Although a prohibition is thus understood— namely, "bilva leaves are by no means suitable for worship of the Arcane Wheel-King"— nevertheless, because bilva leaves are specifically prescribed for worship performed with the Thousand Names, that prohibition is established as referring to worship performed by other means.
There, the Mistress of the Lion-Throne (Siṃhāsaneśvarī) grants immediate grace to one who has worshipped the Sovereign of the Wheel (Cakrādhirāja) and recited the fifteen-syllable mantra.

The meaning is that one should contemplate immediate grace. Now, he specifically summarizes the general time-period delimited by life—which was established by the statement regarding "as long as one lives"—with the words "the sovereign of the wheel. This refers to the period following the worship, during which the obligatory recitation (*nityajapa*) is performed.

The meaning is that one should recite it constantly, once [per day]. This is a conjunction for the purpose of time (*kālārtha-saṃyoga*), similar to the injunction: "Having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma. This is because the acts of worship, recitation, and glorification have already fulfilled their purpose through their respective injunctions regarding specific fruits. For this very reason, [the same applies] to recitation, worship, and so forth.

Because it serves the purpose of indicating the time, [the text] restates the necessity of performing [the rite] even in its absence, according to the maxim: "For the non-disappearance of the time is indeed indicated by the sacrificial cakes" (*anapāyo hi kālasya lakṣaṇaṃ hi puroḍāśāḥ*). Thus it says, "japa," etc.; by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), the inclusion of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other such acts is intended. || 22 ||
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should always proclaim this Thousand Names;
even if one is unable to perform the recitation, worship, and other rites, one should still recite the Thousand Names.
Since recitation (*japa*) and all other such acts are subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the ritual service (*upāsti*),

and since it is an established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the performance of the subsidiaries of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) is bound by one's capacity (*yathāśakti*), there is no requirement for their performance immediately following [the main rite] even when recitation and so forth are not performed due to incapacity.

The meaning is that because the time indicated by that [rite] does not lapse, the recitation of the thousand names must indeed be performed even in a sacrifice consisting of a single puroḍāśa cake, just as in the case of the upāṃśuyāja. || 23 ||
One shall obtain that fruit which comes from worship with its ancillaries and recitation with its ancillaries;
indeed, it is an auspicious advancement to recite other hymns while seated on the seat.

Now, is this *kīrtana* enjoined for one who is capable or for one who is incapable? Not the first, because since it is a compulsory duty (*nityakarman*), it is already established for the capable person; therefore, its restatement would be redundant.
Nor the second, because an injunction itself is impossible for one who is incapable, let alone a mere restatement.
Based on the maxim that "the potency (*śakti*) is the auxiliary factor for verbal roots expressing their meaning," he says:
"together with its limbs" (*sāṅga*). This means accompanied by the limbs;
namely, the worship of the principal deity together with the worship of the *āvaraṇa* (surrounding deities).

The meaning is that one should recite [the Vidyā] even with the specific intention of attaining whatever fruit results from the recitation of the Kullukā, the Setu, the Mahāsetu, and the Vidyā accompanied by recitation, as well as from the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and so forth. This is the underlying idea:
if one is capable of performing only one of these—namely, the ritual depositions (nyāsa), worship (arcana), recitation (japa), or glorification (kīrtana)—then, according to the principle of logic...

When an option (vikalpa) arises, it is precisely the proclamation [of the substitute] that is enjoined by way of an exception (apavāda) to that. Therefore, just as the Viśvajit sacrifice is prescribed for the absence of a Satra in the case of "If those initiated for a Satra should die together, they should divide the Soma and perform the Viśvajit," this [substitute] serves as a proxy; however—

From the force of the scriptural statement, there is also the fruit of worship and so forth. However, the Viśvajit sacrifice does not have the Satra as its fruit, because there is a lack of evidence. Now, he states that recitation (kīrtana) is an optional subsidiary (aṅga) with respect to meditation (upāsanā): "In meditation" (upāsane). By the locative case, there is an understanding of its being the primary element (aṅgin), just as in the passage, "There one should offer the Jaya oblations."

As ancillaries to that [primary rite], there is an excellence in the result—namely, a specific benefit—in reciting other hymns such as the *Trailokyamohana-kavaca* and others; however, if they are not recited, there is no fault arising from a deficiency in the ancillaries. Therefore, those scriptural statements found within their respective contexts which indicate that these [hymns] are ancillaries to the sacrifice [retain their validity].
This statement is decisive regarding the alternative;

therefore, just as with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, the status of the others as auxiliary (*aṅga*) [to this practice] is established by the word "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) in various statements found within their respective contexts, such as: "Even if recited nine million times, his knowledge does not succeed."
There is no fault, for there is another fruit of knowledge, characterized by the prosperity (*abhyudaya*) produced by the recitation of each respective [text]. || 24 ||
One should recite this thousand names as part of one's daily obligatory rite;
the worship of the King of Wheels (cakrarāja), the chanting of the Goddess, and the proclamation of the names [constitute this]. (25)

But this [act] is not such a subsidiary part (*aṅga*); rather, like the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) or the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*), this suffix *-vat* has the sole sense of "incapability of being reduced to a mere conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*) with respect to its natural counter-positive. Consequently, by the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*), the act of recitation (*kīrtana*) possesses a dual nature, serving both as a subordinate element of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and as a means to human welfare (*puruṣārtha*).

It must be considered that even by the context of the section primarily dealing with worship (*arcanā*) and so forth, it confirms that [the mantra] is indeed an auxiliary to meditation (*upāsanā*). The term "of the Goddess's Vidyā" connects to both [contexts] according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). || 25 ||
For a devotee, this much is the duty; they know that anything else is merely for worldly prosperity.
This recitation of the Thousand Names is an absolute necessity for a devotee.

"Of the devotee" means of the worshipper (*upāsaka*). "Prosperity" (*abhyudaya*) means that which brings about prosperity; the suffix *-ac* here has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), meaning "that which causes welfare. Lest one should suspect that [this practice] is merely equal to worship (*arcana*) and so forth because it is read in the same context as worship and the like, he says "of the devotee"—the ellipsis being "even in comparison with recitation (*japa*) and worship (*pūjā*)."
The meaning is that it has already been stated that [the cause] produces that result.
In this regard, I shall declare the cause; listen, O Pot-born One!
Formerly, the goddess Śrī Lalitā, out of a desire for the welfare of her devotees, [acted as follows]. (27)

Having raised the doubt as to how this [stotra] can produce that fruit, the author begins the narrative— starting with the words "Therein" (*tatra*) and so forth— in order to state the cause for that,

by way of demonstrating the supreme excellence of the deity who is the subject of the hymn, through the fact that she is worshipped by the entire host of Śiva’s powers (*śakti*). For it is not the case here that...

The statement "he is about to offer the after-offerings" (*anūyājānyakṣyan bhavati*) is a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) intended to show that, like a statement of reason (*hetuvāda*), it has its own intrinsic purpose and significance, expressed with emphasis as "I shall speak further. For this very reason, in order to indicate that one should not disregard it under the impression that it is merely a descriptive eulogy (*arthavāda*), there is the address "Listen! (*śṛṇu tvam*) to draw the listener's attention toward oneself. [This is said] because [the Lord] has attained all desires.
Because the Goddess has no desire for her own self-interest, he says: "of the devotees" (bhaktānām). || 27 ||
Having summoned the goddesses of speech, headed by Vaśinī, he spoke this:
"O goddesses of speech, Vaśinī and the others, listen to my words. (28)

"Vaśinyādyāḥ" refers to those for whom Vaśinī alone is the primary one to be counted at the beginning—that is, at the outset—and who is the principal. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of the group of seven starting with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Kaulinī.
Regarding their invocation, the following is a qualifying attribute containing a causal reason, expressed through the figure of speech *parikara* (poetic elaboration):

Regarding the term *vāgdevī* (the Goddess of Speech): here, all the meanings of the root *div*—namely, play (*krīḍā*), desire for victory (*vijigīṣā*), brilliance (*dyuti*), praise (*stuti*), worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), joy (*moda*), intoxication (*mada*), and movement (*gati*)—are intended, but not sleep (*svapna*), because deities do not sleep. Alternatively, they are called *vāgdevyaḥ* because they "play with speech," "desire victory through speech," "shine by means of speech," "praise by means of speech," and so forth; that is, they consist solely of speech (*vāṅmaya*).

The sense is that, by virtue of their sovereignty, they themselves are being summoned for the purpose of the hymn (stotra) intended to be recited. This refers to the narrative that is about to be told. Now, with the following three and a half verses, follows the speech of Ambā:
"O Vaśinī and the others! Since you are the deities of speech, therefore listen to my words."
The interpretation (*yojanā*): By virtue of your mastery over speech, it is you alone who have the authority to hear my words; this is the implied encouragement (*vyaṅgya*). || 28 ||
By my grace, O ladies, your splendor of speech has blossomed forth;
you have been appointed to bestow the power of eloquence upon my devotees. (29)

One might object: "Are not even the deities who worship Vaśinī and the others masters of speech (*vāgīśvarī*), and thus already accomplished? Why then would they require hearing your command? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "They become... The word "tataśca" (and then) is to be supplied as an ellipsis and joined with every preceding term. They shine forth with excellence and preeminence.

Those whose speech possesses *vibhūti* (manifestations) and *aiśvarya* (sovereignty)— that is, excellence distinguished from others and preeminence consisting in being the most excellent of all— [are the ones qualified]. For since only that knowledge (*vidyā*) obtained through the grace of the most excellent deity is the most excellent of all knowledges, only those possessing such [knowledge] are qualified to compose this most excellent hymn.

[The word] *dhvaniḥ* [is used]. Now, one might object: "Since Nakulīdevī and others also possess the nature of eloquence and sovereignty obtained through the grace of the Blessed Lady, let them alone be appointed for the composition of this hymn. To this, he says: "Of my devotees" (*madbhaktānām*).

Nakulī, Vāgīśvarī, and the others, however, are employed for the purpose of paralyzing the speech and so forth of others who dispute with the devotees of Lalitā; and since even the *Sahasranāma-stotra* is of the nature of the manifestation of speech (*vāgvibhūti*), it is intended to be given only to the devotees of Mother Lalitā.
It is implied that if Nakulī and the others were employed for that purpose [of creation], it would result in the subversion of the authority of Vaśinī and the rest. || 29 ||
"You who know the secret of the wheel of death and are devoted to my name, therefore I command you to perform a hymn of praise to me. (30)
One might object: "Surely hymns have already been composed by Vaśinī and others; what is the use of this new one? To this he replies:

"They are knowers of the secret of my *cakra*. This means they know the secret of the *cakra*—from the *bindu* to the outer enclosure (*bhūpura*)—which consists of the body of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*). Alternatively: there exists...
One's own self-awareness, whose nature is reflective discernment (*vimarśa*), does not manifest other objects;

its internal vibration consists of the emergence of a flash-like intuition in the form of an instantaneous surging forth, which is termed the "perfect sense of I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāvanā*) and the state of the Fourth (*turyāvasthā*). And of that...

The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are of infinite kinds; their collection is the wheel (*cakra*). The contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of that is a secret obtainable solely from the mouth of the Guru. When that [contemplation] exists, there occurs the reabsorption (*upasaṃhāra*) of everything other than oneself into oneself alone. And thus says the *Śivasūtra*:

"In the contemplation of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), there is the dissolution of the universe," and "to the one whose form is the Guru. They know this very thing; thus [they are described as] such. Consequently, it is implied that while the secret of the wheel has not been revealed in other hymns, it ought to be revealed here, as it is intended to be composed. Now, [one might object]:

One might ask: "Since the secret of the *cakras* (cakrarahasya) has already been revealed in such works as the *Aruṇopaniṣad*, the *Guhyopaniṣad*, and the *Tripuropaniṣad*, what is the purpose of this [present work]? To this, he replies: "Those who have my name as their supreme refuge.
Here, the word *nāma* (name) refers both to the nominal stem denoting the deity and to the mantra itself.
In the *Saundaryalaharī*, in the verse that extracts the mantra— “*Śivaḥ śaktiḥ kāmaḥ*”—

the letters of the mantra are extracted, and at the end, by the usage “*varṇās te tava janani nāmāvayavatām bhajante*,” there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of two types of words. Thus, under the guise of teaching the Name (*nāma*), [it is taught].

The exposition of the secrets of the *cakra* and the extraction (*uddhāra*) of mantras are not found in the Upaniṣads; rather, it is implied that you alone possess the qualification for composing such unprecedented hymns due to your innate wisdom. Therefore, for these five aforementioned reasons, I command you.
The construction is: "there is no other. || 30 ||
Compose a hymn marked with my thousand names, by which, when I am praised by my devotees, supreme delight shall immediately arise within me. (31)
He states the very purpose for which he gives this command: "Perform it.

In the phrase "with the thousand names," the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic (itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe). The syntactical connection is: "Compose my hymn, characterized by the thousand names. He further qualifies the hymn as "marked with my [name]."

The meaning is that it is marked with my name. "Marking" (aṅkana) refers to the insertion of one's name at the end of the final verse, as in the *Rāghavapāṇḍavīya* which is marked by Kāmadeva, and the *Kirātārjunīya* which is marked by Kāvyalakṣmī. And in the present case, although Ambā has infinite [verses],...

Nevertheless, the name "Lalitā" is unique; for although names such as Bhavānī are applied to the consorts of Guṇirudra, Īśvara, and others, those names are common to them all. Furthermore, even the name Tripurasundarī exists in other Tantras as the name of a *pratipad-tithinityā* (the daily goddess of the first lunar day). Therefore:
In the concluding verse of the *Sahasranāma* and in the final verse concerning the declaration of rewards (*phalaśruti*), the name "Lalitāmbikā" is mentioned. || 31 ||
Hayagrīva said:
Thus commanded by the divine mother Śrī Lalitā, the goddesses of speech performed an unsurpassed hymn of praise with divine, secret names.
Then, with nine and a half verses, the speech of Hayagrīva is presented once more.

It is stated in this way because there is no tautology with the preceding half-verse. [The speech is] "together with the secrets of the Cakrarāja," meaning accompanied by the two secrets of the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*); the suffix *-ac* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). || 32 ||
That supreme [text] is renowned as the *Rahasyanāmasāhasra*.
Then, on one occasion, Ambikā sat upon her lion-throne in the assembly hall.
In order to demonstrate that the name of this hymn is etymologically significant, he provides its derivation: "The Thousand Names of the Secret.
The word *param* (supreme) is connected twice;

because it is pregnant with secrets (*rahasyagarbhitatvāt*), it is called the "Thousand Names of the Secret" (*rahasyanāmasahasram*)—that is, supreme (*param*) in the sense of being preeminent (*atiśayena*).
"Renowned" means well-known. His presence upon the lion-throne is for the purpose of being seen by all. || 33 ||
O Agastya (Kumbhasambhava), he granted the opportunity for service to all;
there, ten million Brahmāṇīs arrived for the purpose of service.
The term *sevāvasaraḥ* means an opportunity for service. Regarding the form *brahmāṇī*, this is not derived from the word *brahman* with the feminine suffix *ṅīp*;

for the word *brahman* is not included in the rule beginning with *indravaruṇa* (Pāṇini 4.1.49), and thus such a derivation would be impossible. Rather, it is derived from the root *aṇ* [to sound] applied to *brahma* [the Vedas], meaning "she who sounds the Vedas."

"Śabdāyate" means she speaks; that is to say, she is Brahmā, the speaker of the four Vedas through her four faces. The meaning is "Brahmā. To denote her as his wife, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for feminine nouns derived from masculine ones (*puṃyogalakṣaṇa*). Thus, there is a correspondence with the *Svacchanda-śāstra*.
(Verse): "Brahmāṇī is another Śakti who rests upon the lap of Brahmā.

She is called Brahmāṇī because she brings forth or gives life to Brahmā. Therefore, there is no possibility of applying the *ekaśeṣa* rule (*pumān striyā*) [which would result in the form *brahmāṇau*]. Alternatively, the word *brahmāṇī*...

"Beyond ten million *bhāratīs*. [The compound] "ten million *brahmas* together with that" (*tatsametā brahmakoṭayaḥ*) is a *madhyamapadalopa* (elision of the middle term) compound, following the class of words beginning with *śākapārthiva*.
The plural number indicates a quantity exceeding ten million. Thus, by combining both the base and the suffix, [the total is:]...

A crore multiplied by a crore results in a *koṭikoṭi*. This means that there are as many Brahmāṇīs as there are oceans, and an equal number of Brahmās. For this very reason, it is stated in the Rudrayāmala, in the section on the meditation on Sarvamaṅgalā: "Surrounded..."
It is recorded in the Smṛti: "With crores upon crores of Brahmās accompanied by their Brahmāṇīs," and so forth. || 34 ||
Tens of millions of Lakṣmīs and Nārāyaṇas arrived,
as did tens of millions of Rudras accompanied by tens of millions of Gaurīs.

"Accompanied by ten million Lakṣmīs" means ten millions of Nārāyaṇas. "Of the Rudras" likewise means of ten millions of Rudras. According to the literal reading, it would be understood that each individual Rudra is accompanied by ten billion Gaurīs, along with the two previously mentioned Śaktis.
And there is a discrepancy regarding the number;

for if, on the other hand, the qualification consisting of being equal to ten million Gaurīs is intended with reference to the collective subject— the assembly of Rudras numbering many millions— and not to each individual Rudra.
If it is considered with the intention that [the term] is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then it is correct exactly as it was heard. Furthermore,
all plural forms refer to an infinite number regarding the infinity of the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) among those qualified for the creation of cosmic eggs.
Since there is no dispute regarding the necessity of these three and their infinite number,
the intention behind summoning them simultaneously is to establish his renown throughout all the brahmāṇḍas. || 35 ||
The various forms of Śaktis, headed by Mantriṇī and Daṇḍinī, who have assembled for the purpose of service—their number is beyond reckoning. (36)
"Of various forms" means: "The Supreme Śakti, the Primordial Śakti, Will, Knowledge, Action, Bala, Bālā, Annapūrṇā, Bagalā, Tārā, Vāgvādinī, and Parā."
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Siddhalakṣmī who chooses her own husband,
Nakulī mounted on a horse, Kurukullā, and Reṇukā.
She is the bestower of prosperity, the Fortune of Sovereignty, Padmāvatī, the Auspicious One;
she is Durgā, she of auspicious form, Kālī, Kālarātri, and Subhadrikā.
Chinnamastā, Bhadrakālī, Kālakaṇṭhī, Sarasvatī,

and so forth, are well known in the Rudrayāmala and other scriptures. Although their innumerability was already expressed by the plural term "koṭis" (crores) in the preceding passage, nevertheless here—
For each of these, there are an equal number of similar classes, such as *bālā* and so forth;

since they are infinite even when considered as mutually distinct, it was stated that "no number exists" because it is impossible to specify their names individually. Alternatively, it is called "numberless" (*asaṃkhyā*).
The meaning is "having an incalculable name. The ellipsis is that it is neither found nor can it be spoken.
Alternatively, the meaning is that *saṃkhyā* is that which is correctly known (*samyak khyāti*), namely, the designation of a name. || 36 ||
The divine lineages, the human lineages, and the perfected lineages assembled there;
there, the illustrious Goddess Lalitā granted her vision to all of them.

The divine ones (*divyāḥ*) are the gods such as the guardians of the quarters (*dikpāla*s) and others. The human ones (*mānava*s) are the meritorious ones, such as the Brahman-sages (*brahmarṣi*s) beginning with Viśvāmitra. The perfected ones (*siddha*s) are the yogis, such as Sanaka, Nārada, and others. Their "multitudes" (*ogha*s) refer to specific numerical categories. And so it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"By many millions of world-protectors, by tens of millions of moons, suns, and Vasus, by the lords of yogis beginning with Sanaka, and by tens of millions of the seven ṛṣis."
"Surrounded by tens of millions of great floods (*ogha*) such as Nārada and others.

(19) Thus, the plural form "floods" (*oghāḥ*) refers to many tens of millions (*koṭi*). Although a specific numerical category named "flood" (*ogha*) is not observed in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), it has been stated: [as follows].
Ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, hundred-thousand, million, and ten-million are in successive order;
from that [ten-million] come hundred-million (arbuda), billion (abja), ten-billion (kharva), hundred-billion (nikharva), trillion (mahāpadma), and ten-trillion (śaṅkha).
"The ocean (jaladhi) and the last [term] are the middle and the *parārdha*; these are designations increasing tenfold.

Nor is this stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*. For therein it says: "Listen to the enumeration of the supreme *parārdha* and the subordinate one," and so forth, ending with: "A thousand times ten million times ten million is proclaimed as a *parārdha*."
Having stated everything up to this point as before, it was further said:
"The wise call the supreme number twice the value of a *parārdha*. They say that a hundred is *paridṛḍha*, and a thousand is *paripadmaka*."
Then ten thousand (ayuta), a million (niyuta), ten million (prayuta), and then one hundred million (arbudam).
Nyarbuda, kharbuda, kharva, nikharva, śaṅku, padma,
samudra, madhyama, and then parārdha.
"Thus, these eighteen places [of calculation], when reckoned according to the method of counting, should be known as hundreds, as they have been taught by the wise.
Nevertheless, in the *Yuddhakāṇḍa* of the *Rāmāyaṇa*, it says: "A hundred of hundreds of thousands..."
Beginning with "The wise call [the next] a *koṭi*" and ending with "a hundred thousand oceans are known as a *mahaugha*," there are the names *śaṅku*, *mahāśaṅku*, *vṛnda*, *mahāvṛnda*, *padma*,
*mahāpadma*, *kharva*, *mahākharva*, *samudra*, and *mahaugha*, each ten times greater than the preceding one.

The number ten, multiplied by a hundred thousand times a hundred thousand, has been mentioned there; in that context, the word *ogha* alone was employed according to the maxim "the mention of a part [implies] the whole. Alternatively, there are seven supreme gurus, beginning with Paraprakāśānandanātha.

The three lineages (*oghatrika*) denoted by such terms as "divine" and so forth consist of the eight supreme-and-non-supreme gurus beginning with Gaganānandanātha, and the four non-supreme gurus beginning with Bhogānandanātha; and this has been stated with reference to the lineage of Kāmarāja.

The many triads of lineages (*oghatrika*), such as those beginning with Mitreśānandanātha, which arise through the divisions of the lineage of Lopāmudrā and the divisions of the *vidyā*s, are to be found in the *Jñānārṇava* and other scriptures. However, the sequence of the divine and other gurus must be understood from the oral instruction of the teacher (*gurūpadeśa*). In that regard, "of all" refers to a specific number.
The term "mahaughaparyāya" refers to a cycle of great floods. The plural number also signifies the infinitely infinite.
In the enumeration found in the *Yajurveda*, following the formula "parārdhāya svāhā," there is a series beginning with "uṣase svāhā" and ending with "sarvasmai svāhā."

Eight mantras are heard [in this context]. Furthermore, the words *uṣā* and so forth occurring therein must be stated to denote numbers increasing by a factor of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa-lakṣa*) each, based on their position in the sequence of recitation (*prāyapāṭha*). This is the summary:
"Uṣas, vyuṣṭi, tathā, eṣyantī, udyantī, udita,
and likewise svarga and loka— all these are recorded as names in the Śruti.
These [terms] represent numbers increasing ten-fold beyond a parārdha."

Thus, this being the case, consistency with the *Rāmāyaṇa* is also obtained, because the "Great Śaṅku" mentioned in the *Rāmāyaṇa* is synonymous with a "Parārdha" in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Furthermore, when it is possible [to find a basis], there is no reason to search for another source for a Smṛti. Nor is this so in the case of the word "all" (*sarva*).
There is no failure to attain the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) because it has the form of a name (*saṃjñārūpatva*).

Since the term "pronoun" is etymological (*anvarthaka*), even the word *sarva*—which denotes the final number [one hundred thousand]—is justified as a pronoun by virtue of its denoting a totality (*samasta*). For this very reason, it is stated even in the Śruti:

The substitution of *smāy* for the dative case ending is appropriate; however, it should be understood that since this is a Vedic usage, the *suṭ* augment likewise applies in the present context. || 37 ||
When they had been seen and had sat down in their respective places in due order,
[the others] there were impelled by the casting of the side-glance of the venerable Goddess Lalitā.
Then, having risen, those foremost of self-controlled women, with palms joined in reverence,
praised Mother Lalitāmbikā with thousands of names composed by themselves.

In the *Viśvakarmaśāstra*, it is stated according to the following method: "On the left side of the king, the son of Dakṣa, are the eight ministers," and so forth. "In due order" means without transgressing the sequence. Here, the word *sva* (self) is used in the masculine gender when referring to the self; thus, even though it refers to the self of the Goddess of Speech (*Vāgdevatā*) in the present context, it is used in the form *svakṛtaiḥ* (by her own deeds).
It remains in the masculine gender alone; or, in all types of compound formation (*vṛtti*), there is optionally the substitution of the masculine form for a pronoun.
Having heard the hymn of praise, the supreme goddess Lalitā became gracious,
and all those who were present there in the assembly were filled with wonder.
