All these, beginning with Brahmāṇī as well, [are included]. However, the root of both grace (*prasāda*) and wonder (*vismaya*) is the enrichment of word and meaning through figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) and the absence of defects (*adoṣatā*). For example, in the *Viṣṇusahasranāma* and similar texts, there is no employment of meaningless words in passages such as "He is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) and indeed the Imperishable (*akṣara*)."

In the case of names limited to a hundred, there is a repetition of some twice and a repetition of others thrice or four times; however, here there is no such employment of *stobhas* or mere tautology. Although a difference in meaning was described by the venerable Bhagavatpāda in his commentary (*bhāṣya*) regarding those [names], nevertheless, the acceptance of a distinction between names based on a difference in meaning—
Since there would otherwise be the consequence of the abolition of various meanings and so forth, it cannot be understood otherwise.

Furthermore, even when the meaning is not different, a difference [in the mantra] arises from the difference in pronunciation. Likewise, there are other wondrous secret meanings, such as the extraction of the *cakrarahasya* mantras and so forth.
Although these [meanings] are to be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone, nevertheless,
for the sake of causing wonder in the minds of the learned, we shall occasionally indicate alternative meanings here and there by way of mere direction. (40)
Then Lalitā spoke to the members of the assembly and the hosts of deities:
"By my command alone, the goddesses of speech have composed this unsurpassed hymn."

He spoke to the members present in the assembly—this is the ellipsis—to dispel their astonishment. Now follows the speech of Ambā in six verses. "By my command alone, and not merely by her own intuition"—the sense is that, therefore, no wonder should be felt here. || 41 ||
Marked with my divine names that bestow affection upon me, you should always recite this hymn for the increase of my pleasure. (42)

This is the primary injunction (*vidhi*). However, that which was previously mentioned, although it takes the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*), is nonetheless an injunction due to the distinction between the speaker and the listener. For this very reason, because there is no purpose other than [the injunction] itself in the case of repeated hearing, [it remains an injunction] despite the difference in recensional branches (*śākhā-bheda*).
Just as in the case of those who have heard the injunctions for the Agnihotra, there is no differentiation of the ritual act [by the mere mention of the name]. 42.
Cause this Thousand Names of mine to be recited among my devotees;
that devotee who recites this Thousand Names of mine repeatedly— || 43 ||

He ordains that the tradition must be propagated. He ordains that, among the devotees initiated into the Śrīvidyā who will be mentioned in the context of the optional rites (*kāmyaprayoga*) to be described, the recitation of the hymn (*stotrāvṛtti*) should be performed whenever possible—this is indicated by the words "This" (*idam*). Whoever recites it even once, even a single time... || 43 ||
He should be known as my most beloved; to him I grant all desires, provided he has worshipped me within the Śrīcakra and recited the fifteen-syllable mantra.

"I give desires to him"— by this phrasing, "how much more so many times," even though there is no injunction for repetition (*āvṛtti*) in the performance of rites for specific desires (*kāmyaprayoga*), the intention is nevertheless to enjoin its repetition,
just as in the injunction for the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*. Otherwise, by the rule for the oblation (*homavidhi*), [the result would follow] from the mere falling of the first drop.

The accomplishment of the purpose of the scripture is achieved by a single recitation alone; for there is no authority for repetition, and because the injunction of "once-only" would otherwise result in futility, as it would serve merely to exclude other options (*parisaṃkhyā*).
He states "the Śrīcakra" in order to conclude the perpetual nature that was mentioned in the initial injunction.
He states the meaning obtained through the force of the logical principle that "even when the indicator (upalakṣaṇa) is absent, the indicated (upalakṣya) does not cease to exist": "44-45.
Afterwards, for my satisfaction, one should recite my Thousand Names; whether one worships me or not, or whether one mutters the Vidyā or not."
He states that even for one who is incapable of recitation, worship, and so forth, the fruit is obtained from this very [practice] alone: || 45 ||
One should always recite this Thousand Names for my pleasure;
through my pleasure, one obtains all desires—of this there is no doubt. (46)
This is clear. || 46 ||
"Therefore, recite my thousand names always with devotion.
Hayagrīva said:
Thus did the illustrious Laliteśānī instruct the gods along with their followers.
Then he gave his command for the sake of favoring the world.
Now, the speech of Hayagrīva consists of four and a half verses (*adhyuṣṭa-śloka*).

Although this speech actually extends up to the penultimate verse, it is stated thus because they say that a verse on meditation (*dhyāna-śloka*) has been interpolated in the middle. He concludes Ambā’s speech.

Because she is eternal in her nature as the will of the Bhagavatī, for the purpose of setting in motion the command of the teaching—which is a synonym for the "order of instruction"—the present-tense designation "she teaches" (*śāsti*) is also appropriate; just as it is said: "Even Ajāmila, the sinner, having called out 'Nārāyaṇa' while dying after reviling his son, attained liberation."
By his command, from that time forward, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
along with the powers headed by Mantriṇī, [composed] this thousand names.
He concludes. || 48 ||
They constantly recite this with devotion for the complete satisfaction of Lalitā;
therefore, O Sage, this must necessarily be chanted by a devotee. (49)

In this regard, while concluding the subject matter introduced with the words "I shall state the reason," he makes a formal promise in order to secure the student's attention by first demonstrating the logical connection [of the topics]. || 49 ||
O Lord of Sages, I have now declared the necessity and the reason for this;
now I shall speak the Thousand Names—listen with faith. (50)
Regarding the necessity [of this]: || 50 ||
Now, the verse on meditation:

[I meditate upon her] whose body is crimson like vermilion, who has three eyes, whose crest is the shimmering leader of stars (the moon) upon a crown of rubies, whose face is smiling, and whose breasts are full.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mother, who is gentle, holding in her two hands a jeweled goblet filled with wine and a red lotus, and whose feet rest upon a jeweled vessel.
For this *Śrī Lalitāsahasranāmastotramālāmantra*: salutation to the sages, Vaśinī and the other Goddesses of Speech, on the head; salutation to the *Anuṣṭubh* metre, on the mouth;
salutation to the deity Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable *Ka* (four times), on the navel; salutation to the seed-syllable *Sa* (three times).

To Śakti at the secret place; to the Kīlaka at the feet; for the application (viniyoga) in recitation for the sake of attaining the fourfold aims of human life, [the mantra is applied] to all limbs. Having repeated the three peaks (kūṭas) twice, or with the Bālā [mantra], one performs the two sets of six-limbed rites (ṣaḍaṅga). Now—

"The Sage (ṛṣi) is to be placed on the head because of his gravity; the Deity (devatā) in the heart because he is to be meditated upon; and the Metre (chandas) on the tongue because of its nature as syllables. Thus, by those most skilled in mantra, the locations for the placement of the Sage (ṛṣinyāsa) are to be established according to the methods taught in the *Prapañcasāra*, with their various divisions such as Śaiva, Śākta, and so forth."

The specific mudrās for the ritual placement (nyāsa) have been stated in the *Padārthādarśa*, and their respective meditative impressions (*vāsanās*) have already been explained by us in the section on recitation (*japa*); therefore, they are not written here.

From the word *māṇikya*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*); alternatively, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. And thus:

She whose crest-ornament (*śekhara*)—that is, her head-ornament—is the moon, the leader of the stars, shimmering and radiant upon her crown (*mauli*) which is adorned with rubies (*māṇikya*); or, the word *mauli* may refer to the highest [part] (*uttamapara*).
"Shimmering like the finest ruby," and so forth, as before. [Her breasts are] plump (*pīna*) or well-developed on all sides.
According to the lexicon, "ūdhastu klībamāpīnam," she was one whose breasts were like udders (*ūdhah*).
She held a *caṣaka*—a vessel or bowl made of jewels filled with bees (*alibhiḥ*, i.e., *bhramaraiḥ*).
As it is said: "A *caṣaka*, a *kaṭorī*, a *vāṭikā*, and likewise a *khārikā* [are synonyms for such vessels]."

"Kacolī, gāthikā, and [kaccholikā] are indeed names with the same meaning," according to the statement in the *Ratnasamuccaya*. Because the honey contained therein is fragrant, it is "filled with honey" (*madhupa-pūrṇatā*). Alternatively, as it is said: "An *ali* is one who licks wine and flowers."

The term "mad-malipa" refers to wine from a golden vessel; she is the one whose fifth fluid is such a jewel residing in a jar—one with red feet. Thus, by means of these four verses, the first portion of the *Sahasranāma* has been explained according to this technical convention. May there be auspiciousness. 51.
Thus ends the first digit, Tāpinī, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by the illustrious Bhāsurānanda, consisting of these introductory verses. || 1 ||

Thus [composed] by the worshipper of the feet of the venerable Nṛsiṃhayajvan, who was foremost among those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of the authoritative words and sentences, and who is independent in all systems of philosophy.

In the *Saubhāgyabhāskara*, the commentary on the *Lalitāsahasranāmaparibhāṣāmaṇḍala*, composed by Bhāskararāya— the son of the venerable Gambhīrarāya Dīkṣita, whose surname was Bhārati, and who bore the initiatory name Bhāsurānandanātha.
The first section, titled "The Introduction," is complete.
Now begins the second *tāpinīkalā*, named the First Century:
"In the foot [of Śiva], which possesses the flesh of the fear of the moth-like [insects] on the two pillars of incense, there is the excellent union;
in the dharma of the clarified butter from the courtyard of the manifest Gayā-water, there is the intellect of the commentary on the *mākhakholka*. (7)

Now, the meaning of the names is introduced. Among those, since the names with feminine, masculine, and neuter genders function as adjectives, the words "the conscious self" (*cidātman*), "Brahman," and so forth—which provide the substantive referents—are indicated in their respective order. For the genders follow the words themselves, and not otherwise.
In reality, even though Brahman is one, it possesses no gender; as stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "Neither female, nor neuter, nor male is the Victor.
And: "O Mother, You are neither a man nor a woman, O You whose nature is consciousness, nor even neuter."
"Nor does even your husband possess the three genders; without you, even that would not manifest.
This is also from the words of Kālidāsa. For this very reason, it is recorded in the Smṛti that even in the meditation upon a deity, the choice is indeed optional.
"O Goddess, one should remember Him in male form, or contemplate Him in female form;
or else, one should meditate upon the partless (niṣkala), characterized by Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
Thus, at the beginning [of the practice], the Praṇava—which is common to all three genders—is used solely for the purpose of indicating the substantive.

The practice (*prayoga*): and the meaning of that entire [mantra] is Brahman alone, according to the Lord’s own statement: "The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*.
Through the letters *A*, *U*, *M*, the *Nāda*, and the *Bindu* taken individually, one [attains] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
Or, it may mean that its form consists of those five [vowels] because of the statement beginning with "Āṃ. This has been stated in the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
"The letter *A* is the form of Brahmā; the letter *U* possesses the form of Viṣṇu;
the letter *M* is the form of Rudra; and the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is the Supreme Self (*parātman*)."
"That which is to be expressed is the Supreme Brahman; the Praṇava is traditionally held to be the expresser.
The relationship between these two—the expressed and the expresser—is figurative.
Thus, the word "form" (rūpa) intends non-difference between the expressed and the expresser, meaning they are identical. For this very reason:
The relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*), being constituted by differentiation, is figurative (*aupacārika*) and secondary (*amukhya*);

that is to say, it is conventional (*vyāvahārika*). With this very intention, Puṣpadanta also said: "O Giver of Refuge, the word *oṃ*, both in its entirety and in its parts, praises You. However, in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*:
Various meanings have been described:
"When it ought to be said that an object is known as 'it is known,' yet people in the world say 'om' instead; therefore, *om* is a designator of what is known."
When the meaning is unknown, and the word "thus-known" (tathājñāta) is reached as the designator, this world says "Oṃ"; therefore, Oṃ is the designator of that which is known.
When a word that expresses a doubtful meaning is encountered, people in this world say "Oṃ"; therefore, it is a term used to express doubt.
On this earth, there are words that denote objects such as space;
yet, without all those words, people in the world utter only "Om."
Therefore, due to its frequent application, like the words "jar" or "wall," the *praṇava* is traditionally held to be the designator of categories such as space (*ākāśa*).
He who, being a twice-born, mutters this mantra which illuminates all, is considered equal to Brahman, the illuminator of all.
"He quickly obtains the fruit declared for the recitation of all mantras.
Thus [it is said]. The *Bṛhatpārāśarasmṛti* also states:
"The *praṇava* is indeed the supreme reality; it consists of the three Vedas and is composed of the three qualities (*guṇas*)."
It has three deities, three abodes, three types of wisdom, and is established in three ways.
The wise know it to have three measures, three times, and three genders;
for all this is pervaded by the Praṇava in its threefold form.
Agni, Soma, and Sūrya are proclaimed as the three abodes;
they are described as that which has internal consciousness, external consciousness, and dense (unified) consciousness.
The heart, the throat, and the palate—these are proclaimed as the three locations.
It is said to have three morae (mātrās) by means of the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*.
In all undertakings of action, one should proclaim that three-syllabled [mantra];
for by it all sounds, having been established, are indeed pervaded.
"For without that [Oṃ], no speech whatsoever can proceed.

Thus it is said. Also in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa: "We inquire about the syllable Oṃ: what is its root (*dhātu*), what is its nominal stem (*pratipadika*), what is its noun (*nāman*) or verb (*ākhyāta*), what is its gender (*liṅga*), what is its case-ending (*vibhakti*), and what is its accent (*svara*)?"

Through this extensive section beginning with these words, the determination of its essential nature has been established by the commentators Padmapādācārya in the Praṇava-paṭala of the *Prapañcasāra*, as well as in other works such as the *Praṇavārthadīpikā*; a great deal of detail regarding this should be consulted therein.

In this world, it is well known that when one is in a state of suffering, one remembers one’s mother; yet, the mothers one has actually experienced are not capable of removing the three types of affliction. As it has been said by the learned:
"Due to being born through the occurrence of thousands of various wombs, how many mothers have there been?"
"How many Janakas are renowned? And how many more will arise before me?
There is no counting these; O Treasure of Compassion, protect me, who am utterly terrified of the vast ocean of worldly existence and have no other refuge."

Thus [it is said]. Therefore, among those capable of removing endless suffering, the Mother of the World alone is the most excellent; with the intention that she should be praised as a mother in order to evoke her compassion toward oneself, and also praised for the sake of the fruit consisting of liberation and so forth—which is the purpose of composing this hymn—he says:
The illustrious Śrīmahārājñī, the sovereign of the glorious lion-throne;
"Śrī" means the mother of Lakṣmī (Śrī). Here, "Śrī" is used as a metonym for speech (gīḥ), or it may simply denote that which expresses it.
Thus, the Vyāḍikośa states:
"Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, intellect, the three goals of life (trivarga), prosperity, majesty, and splendor; as well as the sciences of implements, dress, and adornment—in these she is renowned as Śrīvidyā.
And thus, because she is the progenitor of Śrī (Goddess Lakṣmī), this Rudrāṇī does not belong to the same category as her, but rather—

It is said that she is the Supreme Goddess (Parā Bhaṭṭārikā), the consort of Paraśiva, who gives birth to that triad. Alternatively, she "measures" or delimits (māti) Śrī, that is, Lakṣmī; since a delimitation must necessarily exceed that which is delimited, the meaning is that liberation consists of the form of infinite Śrī.

For it is well known from the Śruti that "She is indeed the immortal glory of the virtuous. She measures the Trayī (the three Vedas), awakens Brahmā, or emits them through her own limitation, according to the Śruti: "He who first created Brahmā and who indeed sent forth the Vedas to him. She is the form of the primordial manifestation.

The meaning is "in the form of Vyāsa. Alternatively, because it measures (māti) prosperity (śrī) or poison (viṣa) by placing them in the throat, the name is masculine in gender in these two cases. Due to the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti, either *prakāśa* (light) or *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) is the substantive. This is [the case] in the mantra "Obeisance to Śrīmātā."

Even in the absence of a specific distinction, there is a distinction in the contemplation of the meaning. Alternatively, it is "Mātā" (Mother) because of the well-known usage of experts, according to the rule: "One should employ the name of those who are eminent preceded by the word 'Śrī', as in Śrīcakra, Śrīśaila, Vidyāśrī, Phalāśrī, and so forth."

The meaning is that [the Lord] is the producer of even a single word. This is because, due to the absence of a specific determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), it follows that [the Lord is the cause] of all things;

and because of the non-specific scriptural statement: "From which indeed these beings are born. For this very reason, the words *Īśvara*, *Īśāna*, and so forth, when used without any qualifying adjuncts, denote Paraśiva. And thus, "Īśāna... [and so on].
Just as in the case of "bhūtabhavyasya" and so forth, even when there is a mention of a correlative term such as "jaganmātā" (Mother of the World),
the fact that the word "mātṛ" alone denotes Tripurasundarī is not impaired. Alternatively,
when the six consonants *ha-sa-ka-la-ra-ḍa* of Bālā are joined at the end with her three vowels (*ai-au-a*), [the result is the mantra].

The mantra that arises as consisting of the three peaks (kūṭas) is called the Mother (Mātṛ). This is because, in the verse from the *Mantrapārāyaṇoddhāra* which reads "Māyā, Kuṇḍalinī, Kriyā, Madhumatī," the word "Mother" has been explained in such a manner by the elders; thus, the commentary devoted to the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) should be understood.

From the word *rājan*, because it ends in *n*, when the suffix *ṅīp* is applied and subsequently compounded with the word *mahat*, the form *śrīyuktā mahārājñī* arises through the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopa-samāsa*) and the substitution of *ā* by the rule "ānmahataḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.46). It does not, however, derive from the word *mahārāja* with the suffix *ṅīp*; for if that were the case, the undesirable form *mahārājī* would result.
The meaning is that she is authorized for the protection of the entire multitude of phenomenal existence (*prapañca*).
This is because protection is included within the category of "kingship" (*nṛpatva*), which is the delimitor of the denotation of the word "king.
Thus, the Śruti says: "By whom all beings live."

Herein is the extraction of the three secret syllables within the Śrīvidyā. Among them, one is called the "sixteenth digit" (ṣoḍaśīkalā). According to the statement, "That digit should be taught to a good disciple who is devoted to the guru," it has likely been learned from the mouth of the guru by many modern practitioners. And that [digit] is "Śivaḥ..."

In the verse on the extraction of the Vidyā (*vidyoddhāra*) from the *Saundaryalaharī*, it is revealed that among the four *lakṣmī* mantras, this is the first; the other two consist of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). This has been stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*:
"The letter *a* is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme light, the absolute Śiva;
the final letter *ha*, which is the form of the *kalā*, is proclaimed as being called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).
Because of its extreme secrecy, [this is stated] by means of this [verse] above—

The essential nature [of the Goddess] has been extracted in the *Yoginīhṛdaya* through verses of such hidden meaning as: "In the supreme state consisting of the abode within the visarga at the central point, her counterpart is the form of Kuṭilā, a digit of the void. Thus, by means of these very verses of concealed significance, the true form has been revealed.

The exposition of that has already been performed by us in the *Varivasyārahasya-setubandha*, and thus it is not elaborated upon here. By the word "Queen" (*rājñī*), the extraction of the *Māyārājñī* mantra is intended; for this very reason, it is not used with the feminine suffix *-tad*.

A throne presided over by a king is called a *siṃhāsana*. Regarding the compound *siṃhāsana*, the word *siṃha* (lion) is placed first according to the rule for *rājadanta*-type compounds, in the sense that "among seats, the lion is the best.
That is the *siṃhāsana*, and she is its sovereign (*īśvarī*), possessing the splendor of the sovereignty over the entire manifested universe (*prapañca*).

The term *īśitrī* (the Sovereign) refers to the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*), or rather, it signifies that the Goddess is seated upon a lion-throne. As it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*, in the chapter on the etymology of names:
"Having mounted a lion while still a maiden, Mahiṣa was slain by her."
"Then there is the Goddess Mahiṣaghnī, as well as Siṃhāsaneśvarī.

Alternatively, the word *siṃha* has the sense of "to injure. As it has been stated by the grammarians: "The word *siṃha* is derived from the root *hiṃs* (to injure); *śiva* is traditionally remembered [as derived] from the root *vaś* (to desire)."
"In the case of establishing [the meaning] through the transposition of syllables, one sees it as in the case of Kaśyapa.

By that lion, there is *āsana*, which means casting away (*kṣepaṇa*) or rejection; this is from the root *asu* in the sense of "casting," with the suffix *lyuṭ*. The collective meaning is "destruction" (*saṃhāra*). In that regard, the Goddess is capable. And so:
The Śruti says: "That into which they enter when they depart. Alternatively, the letter *ma* signifies the number five.
There are [the goddesses] known as Siṃhāsanas, beginning with Caitanyabhairavī and ending with Bhairavī, who bestow the perfections (*sampat*).
There are eight mantras. Among them, three are in pairs and two are single; thus, five lion-thrones are described in the *Jñānārṇava* according to the divisions of the directions and the center:
"How is that supreme Tripurā seated upon the five lion-thrones?"
When asked, "O Maheśāna, tell me how the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) comes to be," [He replied]:
"First listen, O Goddess of gods: when Brahmā was the creator of the world..."
Then, being unconscious, he [beheld] the Goddess of Gods, Tripurasundarī.
O Supreme Goddess,
O Beloved, having propitiated Brahmā through great austerity, he became the creator of the universe.
"Śakra became this king of the gods, the protector in the eastern direction;
then Tripurā, being pleased, was seated upon the eastern throne," and so forth. By the phrase "the sovereign lady of those five thrones," the extraction of the mantra is indicated.

Thus, having defined Brahman by means of three names through its agency in creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and while for the most part following the sequence of narratives such as the manifestation of the Mothers as described in the Purāṇa under discussion, [the author] also elaborates upon [Brahman] as the bestower of bondage and liberation— which are respectively synonymous with concealment and grace.
He begins to characterize her:
"Born from the fire-pit of consciousness, she is intent upon the work of the gods. (52)

From the passage beginning with "The fire of consciousness" (cidagni) and ending with "the form of the unity of Śiva and Śakti," [it is explained as follows]: Consciousness alone is Brahman; that itself is the sacrificial fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa), because it is the adversary of the darkness characterized by ignorance (avidyā). As it is said: "Blazing within, without interval or fuel, it is the enemy of the darkness of delusion."
This is because we observe the use of the metaphor of the fire of consciousness (*cidvahnirūpaka*) in such passages as *saṃvidagnāv* and others. The *Śaktisūtra* also states:
"The fire of consciousness, though concealed in the stage of descent (*avarohapada*), nourishes the fuel of the objects of knowledge through pure consciousness alone.
And its commentary explains: "Consciousness itself is the fire, because it has the nature of devouring the universe. In that regard, correctly...
It exists as the nature of the attribute called consciousness (caitanya) residing in the elements (bhūta) without distinction, but it is not "born" (jāta).

This is because Pāṇini mentions the roots *bhū* and *jan* separately in the rule "tatra jātaḥ, tatra bhavaḥ," and because there is no difference between power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimat). As it was said by the teacher of the Saṃkṣepaśārīraka:

"The pure power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) of the Supreme Lord is called consciousness itself. Alternatively, the term "fire-pit" (*agnikuṇḍa*) may refer to what is well-known as such; or rather, there is a metaphorical compound (*upamitasamāsa*) between the words "consciousness" (*cit*) and "fire" (*agni*), as in such passages as: "O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes."
Because of the observation of the form (*rūpaka*). The meaning is that he was born from, emerged from, or produced by that vessel (*kuṇḍa*).
This is because the verb *bhavati* is used even in the sense of "origination" (birth), as in such passages as "From him Dhundhumāra came into being.
This is stated in the *Reṇukā-purāṇa*, beginning with: "A son named Reṇu was born, who increased the Ikṣvāku lineage," and so forth.

Having described his asceticism and the boon from the Goddess, [he said]: "In the meantime, at that sacrifice, a woman endowed with a divine form and adorned with celestial ornaments slowly emerged from the sacrificial fire-pit, O twice-born ones."
Beginning thus:
"From the fire, there suddenly emerged outside a radiance resembling the orb of the cool-rayed moon;
she alone is the sole sustainer of the world, and there is no second whatsoever."

Thus [ends the passage]. In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* as well, after describing Śakra being tormented by the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, it is stated—beginning with "Having properly fashioned a most beautiful sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) one *yojana* in extent"—that the gods performed their respective offerings of flesh into the sacrificial pit of the fire of consciousness (*cidagni-kuṇḍa*). Then it was said:
While the gods were desiring to consume that unsurpassed body,
there appeared a great mass of supreme splendor consisting of a vast heap of light.
Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons,
there arose from the midst of that an incomparable form in the shape of a wheel.
"From the midst of that [group], the Great Goddess, possessing a radiance like the rising sun... beginning thus, up to:
"Having beheld that Great Goddess, all the gods, together with Indra..."
"...bowing down again and again with joyful hearts to her who is the soul of all.
Thus ends [the passage]. Anticipating the objection that the birth of the Eternal One is impossible, he provides the resolution: "For the sake of the work of the gods" (*devakārya*).
This refers to the works of the gods, such as the slaying of the demons Bhaṇḍāsura and Mahiṣāsura; she is intent upon those purposes.

She has manifested. Although a compound with a word ending in the dative case expressing "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is generally not permitted when there is no relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), here a compound is formed with the genitive case of the "residual" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) type. As it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"When she manifests for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods..."
When it has arisen in the world, it is then designated as "eternal," even though it is not.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the Blessed Lady said to Himavat:
"I was indeed entreated by the gods and remembered because of the gravity of the task; having censured my father Dakṣa, who reviles Maheśvara."
For the sake of establishing the Dharma and as a means of propitiating you,
she was born from the body of Menā and has taken refuge in you alone as her father.
And so forth. || 52 ||
Having thus described the nature of light as consisting of the essence of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), he speaks of the nature consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*):
"She has the luster of a thousand rising suns and is endowed with four arms.
Regarding the word "rising": she is one whose [luster] is like a thousand *bhānus*, that is, a thousand rays.

The sun; its rising is the qualifier. Its meaning is the state of possessing a rising occurring at the present time, because the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed for the present tense (*laṭ*). By this, its crimson hue is suggested. The "thousand" of rising suns—that is, of red suns—is their infinity.
Or, it means "equal to that. The realized meaning is "exceedingly red. For it is said in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"One's own self alone is declared to be the deity, Lalitā, whose form is the universe;
its redness is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and the contemplation of this is the worship."

Thus it is said. Also in the Vāmakeśvaratantra: "The goddess Tripurā herself is the redness (lauhitya), which is its reflective awareness (vimarśana). Of this Goddess, who has attained the state of equilibrium between such Light (prakāśa) and Reflective Awareness (vimarśa), there are three forms: the gross (sthūla), the subtle (sūkṣma), and the supreme (para).

The gross [form] is distinguished by hands, feet, and so forth; the subtle consists of mantra; and the supreme consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). As it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*:
"O sinless one, know that my forms are twofold: the common and the supreme."
That universal which is associated with hands and other limbs, which the deluded worship;
"The supreme form, which is without beginning or end, unique and free from affliction—
this is expressed by such terms as Brahman, Ātman, and Paramātman," and so forth. "The universal (sāmānya) is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as gross and subtle."

The same applies elsewhere as well. As for the form of the Gaṅgā and other rivers consisting of water and so forth, that is the fourth [form], which is the grossest. Furthermore, the subtle [form] will also be described as being threefold. Among those, he points out the gross one with the word "four. This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the mantras of the limbs mentioned in the meditation (dhyāna).
Or [the cord] may be only as long as an arm;
it is enriched with nooses in the form of passion and radiant with hooks in the form of wrath. (53)
In connection with the discussion of weapons, he describes their threefold form in four verses beginning with "rāga" (attachment).

*Rāga* is a specific modification of the mind characterized by passion, or simply desire itself. It is "rich" (*āḍhyā*) with that gross noose whose own nature consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

"In the lower left hand" has been stated. "Krodha" (anger) refers to the mental state known as aversion (*dveṣa*). From the word *ākāra*, by adding the suffix *ac* (as in *ādyac*), the meaning is "cognition having an object," i.e., knowledge accompanied by its objective content. This is because the word *ākāra* is used in such expressions as "the cognition having the form 'this is a jar'" (*ghaṭo'yam ityākārakam jñānam*) with reference to the object. Only the word *krodha* [is used here].

However, some claim that "jñāna" means "supreme. This is incorrect, because it contradicts the scriptural statement "the goad of his wrath," and because the word "jñāna" can only be understood as referring to "wrath" within the *smṛti* passage that is about to be cited. Therefore:
Her lower right hand is radiant and beautiful with a goad (*aṅkuśa*) consisting of both hatred and knowledge.

As it is stated in the *Pūrvacatuḥśatīśāstra*: "His noose and goad are traditionally held to consist of attachment and hatred. And also in the *Tantrarāja*, in the chapter on latent impressions (*vāsanāpaṭala*):
"The mind is said to be the bow, passion the noose, hatred the goad, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) the flower-arrows. Thus it is stated. However, in the *Uttaracatuḥśatīśāstra*:

"It bears the noose consisting of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and the goad in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*), while holding the radiant bow and arrow consisting of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
Thus it has been said. (53)

She whose bow is made of sugarcane has the mind as its form; that mind, consisting of volition and conceptualization, is her very form, and she possesses a sugarcane bow— that is, a bow made of *puṇḍra* sugarcane— whose arrows are the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

She is thus described as having that [form] in her upper left hand. The five *tanmātras*—sound and the others—are the objects (*viṣaya*). The meaning is that each of those *tanmātras* is the very form of the five elements.
As it is said in the *Mahāsvacchandasaṃgraha*:
The nature of the elements consists merely of the [five] bhūtas, which define specific objects;
whereas words consist of the sound-tanmātra, as is determined by the softness or heat [of the utterance].
That which is characterized by specific touch is designated as the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra), and likewise,
form itself is characterized by blueness, yellowness, and whiteness.
That which is called the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra) is endowed with sweetness and acidity;
however, that known as the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra) is distinguished by qualities such as fragrance.

"Smell shall be the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra), and from those [subtle elements] indeed arises the pentad of gross elements. These very subtle elements (tanmātras) are the shafts (sāyakas) or arrows of her right upper hand;
she is thus described. As it is said in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra: "Sound, touch, and the others are the arrows..."
"His mind became a bow. Also, in the Kādima-tantra:
"Arrows are said to be of three kinds, according to their being gross, subtle, or supreme. The gross arrows consist of flowers; the subtle ones are declared to be of the nature of mantra."
Furthermore, O beloved, the secondary latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been described; now hear of the gross ones:
the lotus, the white water-lily, the red lotus, the *kahlāra*, and the blue lotus.
"O Īśvarī, know that the five flowers are called the Sahakāraka," it is said.
Their names, however, are given in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"Harṣaṇa, the one called Rocana, Mohana, and likewise Śoṣaṇa."
"And this slaying—these arrows cause even sages to fall into delusion.
But in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Goddess, [the powers] known as agitating, liquefying, and likewise attracting..."
"O Supreme Goddess, Vaśya and Unmāda are indeed the names [of the first two], followed by Mohana and Dīpana," as stated in the *Tantrarāja*.
However, in the *Tantrarāja* it says:
"Madana and Unmādana, and then likewise Mohana and Dīpana."
"And the withering one—thus are the five arrows previously mentioned.

Now follows the extraction of the weapon-mantras: *ra* and *aga* and *svam*; the collection of these is *rāgasvam*. By the word *aga*, *sthāṇu* (the immovable one), meaning the letter *ha*, is intended; for it is said: "Ha is Śiva, the sky, and Sthāṇu."

From the *kośa*: "One's own" refers to the vowel *ī* together with the bindu (*ṃ*). Thus, the form of the *pāśa* consists of the combination of the letters *ra*, *ha*, *i*, and the bindu; and so forth. Here, according to the oral tradition (*sampradāya*), the letter *ra* is to be understood as following the letter *ha*. *Kro* and *dha* and *ā* are the *krodhas*. Above that...
The suffix *kāra*, being heard [in the compound], is connected with each member because it occurs at the end of a dvandva;

the meaning is "the letter *kra*, the letter *dha*, and the letter *ā*. These are "resplendent with the goad" (*aṅkuśa*), meaning they shine with the *anusvāra*. As for "goad": one who lies in the earth (*kau śete*) is *kuśa*; a goad is a *kuśa* that is non-different from the letter *aṃ*.

*Mana* is the technical name for the letter *tha*, according to the lexicon which states under the section on *tha*: "The lord of the left nostril is *mana*. *Kodaṇḍa* is the anusvāra, according to the lexicon which states: "The syllable *aṃ* is the beak and the bow (*kodaṇḍa*).
Thus, the bow in the form of *mana* is the letter *u*, which is non-different from the letter *tha*, as seen in names such as "the form of Krodha" and so forth.

The letters *da*, *ra*, *ka*, *la*, *ya*, *sa*, and *va*, together with the vowels *ā*, *ī*, *ū* and the nasal bindu (*m*), are intended [to be used]; the others are not intended. Through their application according to tradition, the seed-syllables of the arrows (*bāṇabīja*) are perfected. However, the specific division of the weapon-seed syllables (*āyudhabīja*) should be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
The circle of the universe was submerged in the flood of her own ruddy radiance.
She is one in whose [light] the spheres of the universes— appearing as non-different from it— are immersed within the flood, that is, the stream, of her own innate, crimson radiance;
[she who shines thus] at dawn during the specific ritual installations (nyāsa) such as Saubhāgya and others.
The meaning is that she possesses a form exactly corresponding to the kind of meditation that has been prescribed. || 54 ||

Her hair is fragrant with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṇnāga*, and *saugandhika* flowers. Now, at the moment of the manifestation of the gross form derived from the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*), because it is the first [part] of the head, there is the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*, which is non-different from the face of the Goddess, in the fifteenth [syllable].

And because it is the first [member], he begins the description starting from the head down to the lotus-feet. Although words such as *campaka* have their primary denotation (*śakti*) for the tree, they are also conventionally established as having a figurative meaning (*nirūḍhalākṣaṇika*) for those respective flowers, according to the *Agnipurāṇa* lexicon which states: "All [names] are applied to the fruit, but two [are applied] to the blossom. Thus, "and the *campakas*" and so forth.

A copulative compound (*dvandva*). She is one whose hair—her locks—is radiant and beautiful with *saugandhika* flowers, that is, white water-lilies (*kahlāra*). Alternatively, the word *lasat* may have the sense of the causative (*ṇic*) inherent within it; by this, the result is that her own hair imparts its fragrance to the flowers. As it has been said:
"O bee, you know the scents of flowers; tell me the truth:
with what can the fragrance in the braid of hair of the Goddess be compared? Thus [it is said].
She is "rich" (āḍhyā) by means of that bond (pāśa) whose nature is desire (icchā); and [the form] "to the rich one" (āḍhyāyai) is also used.
She is adorned with a crown whose tips are bent by a row of Kuruvinda gems glowing with wrath.

Kuruvinda gems, known as padmarāgas, are red and possess many qualities such as the power to fulfill desires and inspire passion; they are a specific class of jewels. As it is stated in the *Ratnādhyāya* chapter of the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:

"On its banks there are gems of brilliant and beautiful hue, and in its waters there are *padmarāga* rubies; those originating from *saugandhika*, those born of *kuruvinda*, and those produced from crystal are of great quality.
These refer to the various types of stones such as *saugandhika*, *kuruvinda*, and crystal found within its interior.

The origin of ruby gems (*padmarāga-maṇi*) occurs specifically among those produced in Kuruvinda. "They possess a splendor equal in color to the *bandhūka* flower, the *guñjā* berry, a fragment of an *indragopa* insect, the *japā* flower, rabbit's blood, or cow's blood;
some are radiant with the color of pomegranate seeds, while others have the luster of the *kiṃśuka* flower."
Thus [it is said]. Here, the phrase "of her" (tasyāḥ) means "of the Rāvaṇagaṅgā":
"Those rubies (kuruvindakas) which are born in the Rāvaṇagaṅgā are red lotus-gems (padmarāgas) possessing a dense form and clearly radiant rays."
Because of this introductory statement, the excellence of its qualities is also described in that very same place:
"The passion of desire for those [gems] born of the *kuruvinda* is not quite like that for those arising from crystal;
endowed with auspiciousness, they grant devotion to Hari and bestow prosperity through mere remembrance."

Thus: she is adorned with a crest-jewel (*koṭīra*) that shines, gleaming in rows and lines of such [gems]. The implied meaning (*dhvani*) is that for those who meditate upon the Goddess endowed with such specific attributes, there occurs an increase in devotion and other virtues. Furthermore, *kuruvinda* refers to rubies (*maṇi*).
However, some say it is a *dvandva* compound; this is because there is no knowledge of its origin. 55.

She is adorned by a forehead-region shining like the moon of the eighth day (*aṣṭamīcandra*). That lunar day on which the eighth digit (*kalā*) of the moon either waxes or wanes is called the eighth day; the moon associated with that [day] is the one endowed with eight digits.

That is to say, "level with the half-moon. Likewise, she is adorned by a forehead (alikasthalena)—the region of the brow—that shines resplendently; for the *Agni Purāṇa* lexicon states, "The forehead is called *alika*, *godhi*, and so forth.
She possesses a decorative mark made of musk that resembles a spot on the moon of her face. 56.

"Her face is indeed the moon"—this is a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification). She is described as such because she has a decorative mark (*viśeṣaka*) made of musk (*mṛganābhi*), which is equal to the spot (*kalaṅka*) [of the moon].

Thus, there exists a relationship of similarity between the spot and the decorative mark, wherein one serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the other as the object of comparison (*upameya*). || 56 ||
Her creeper-like eyebrows are the archway for the auspicious house of the face of Smara.
Her face itself is the auspicious house of Smara, the King of Love;
its archway is the outer gate, and the "cillikā" refers to her creeper-like eyebrows. As it is said: "The word *cillikā* may denote a creeper-like eyebrow."

The *Nāmakalpadruma* and the *Lalitāstavaratna*, which begins with the verse "ābhugnamasṛṇacillī," contain a series of metaphors (*paramparitarūpaka*). Based on the usage in ancient readings, it should be understood that the word *cillī* itself refers to the eyebrow.
Her eyes were like the pupils of fish moving in the overflow of the beauty of her face.

Her eyes are like two moving, flickering fish in the overflow—the flood of water—of the beauty of her face; or rather, her gaze is like that of a fish. For by the mere sight of a fish, children grow, but not otherwise.
"By means of giving breast milk and so forth" is well known; thus, the meaning is that she nourishes her devotees by a mere glance.
She was resplendent with a nose-bridge shining like a fresh campaka flower,
and radiant with a nose-ornament that eclipsed the luster of the stars.

A fresh, newly blossomed *campaka* flower—not merely a bud, but one slightly opened, which is to say a *gandhaphalī*—is like that with which her nose-bridge (*nāsā-daṇḍa*) is adorned; by means of that, the goddess Tārā shines forth.
Or, it may refer to two specific star-goddesses named Maṅgalā and Śuklā; [the verse describes] their radiance.
"Surpassing" means she conquers; thus, she is radiant and beautiful with such a nose-ornament fashioned from rubies, pearls, and other gems. || 58 ||
Charming with an ear-ornament fashioned from a *kadamba* cluster:

she is beautiful and delightful because of that ear-ornament (*karṇapūra*)— a crest (*śekhara*) placed upon the upper part of the ear— which was fashioned (*klpta*), that is, prepared, from a *kadamba* cluster, namely a sprig of the *nīpa* tree.
The orbs of the sun and moon have become her pair of earrings.

A pair of earrings (*tāṭaṅkayugala*), meaning a pair of ear-ornaments made of gold or similar materials—since such [materials] are absent in the present context—the suffix *cvi* is used here in the sense of "becoming what it was not. She is one whose [earlobes] have thus become the orbs of the sun (*tapana*) and the moon (*uḍupa*). As it has been said:
The sun and moon are the two breasts of the Goddess, and they alone are remembered as her two eyes;
both together constitute her pair of earrings—such is the Vedic revelation.
Thus [ends the verse]. 59.
The region of her cheek surpasses—that is, it excels even—a mirror made of ruby stone;
for, due to its extreme purity and its capacity to reflect images, it treats that very mirror as inferior. It surpasses it by an even greater degree.

Because it captures the reflection of the Lord of Desire (Kāmeśvara) and because it is crimson, her cheek— the wall of her face— is such that her lip eclipses the beauty of fresh coral and the bimba fruit. (60)
She whose lips— resembling fresh coral and the bimba fruit, surpassing and eclipsing their beauty and luster due to their superior excellence— she is Śuddhavidyā.

Because it is stated that there is a cognition of non-difference between "this-ness" (idantā) and "I-ness" (ahaṃtā), and because in the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā* and other texts Śrīvidyā is explained as being intent upon such non-difference, she alone is called Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
Resplendent with two rows of twice-born [teeth] whose form is like the sprouts of pure knowledge; that is,
by means of those two rows of twice-born [teeth] whose nature is like the sprouts of that sixteen-fold knowledge which rivals the impurity of ignorance.
Resplendent and beautiful with her two rows of teeth, the Śrīvidyā—

having emerged from the Mūlādhāra and other centers through the sequence of Parā, Paśyantī, and so forth, in the form of Vaikharī— issued from the mouth of the Mother; subsequently, it was transmitted from ear to ear by oral instruction.
It became expanded. Therein, the state of swelling of the seed which is the nature of the Śabdabrahman is Parā;
the state of bursting open is Paśyantī; the two petals, still unmanifest and folded like a bud, are Madhyamā;
and the two petals, fully blossomed, spread out, and joined at their mutual roots, are Vaikharī.
That very thing is what is denoted by the term "sprout" (*aṅkura*). In that state, there is indeed a similarity to teeth;
for since the sixteen-syllable sprouts each consist of two petals, the total number of thirty-two teeth is also achieved. Therefore, those very sprouts are the embodied forms.

The intended meaning is "having the form of teeth. Furthermore, through the pun on the word *dvija* (twice-born) and the figure of speech *samāsokti* (speech of compendium), another meaning is also conveyed: the sciences, such as the Vedas, indeed abide only by relying upon the Brāhmaṇa, as it is said, "Knowledge, indeed, came to the Brāhmaṇa."
According to the Śruti, being without a fixed foundation, they [the truths] attain expansion elsewhere.

For this reason, the Brāhmaṇas alone are the sprouts of knowledge (*vidyā*). Consequently, that which is pure, stainless, and in the form of the sprout of knowledge exists within the twice-born Brāhmaṇas.

The row [of teeth] shines with those two; the intended meaning is that even for the Brahmins, because they have issued from the mouth of Ambā, they themselves are her very teeth personified. Alternatively, [the sequence] proceeds up to Anuttara according to the order beginning with "Śuddhavidyā, Bālā, Dvādaśārdhā, Mataṅginī," and so forth.

The thirty-two initiations (*dīkṣā*) well-known in the Tantras are expressed by the term "the row of the twice-born" (*dvijapaṅkti*), because initiation also has the nature of a birth and because it is the second [birth] in relation to the *upanayana*. This is in accordance with the scriptural statement: "Initiation shall be the third birth."

There is no contradiction, as it intends to express the union [of the seed-syllable] with birth from the mother's womb. *Śuddhavidyāṅkurā* refers to that whose sprout (*aṅkura*)—the beginning—is the three-syllabled *Śuddhavidyā*.

In the word *akāra*, by eliding the vowel *a* after the prefix *aṅ*, it denotes the inclusive limit (*abhividhi*) of both the sprout (*aṅ*) and the vowel (*kāra*), signifying the Unsurpassed (*Anuttara*).

The meaning is that it extends up to the supreme limit of the veins (*vena*). It is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of "she who is the sprout of pure knowledge" (*śuddhavidyāṅkurā*) and "she who is the row of twice-born [letters]" (*ākārā dvijapaṅktiḥ*); following this, the analysis of the phrase is: "shining and manifesting by means of the duality of that [row].
[She is perceived] by those whose internal organs have been initiated through the thirty-two [initiations] transmitted through the lineage of tradition.
The meaning is that she is to be attained only by the foremost of men, and not by others;
[she] who draws the fragrance of camphor-rolls into the very quarters of the sky. 61.
"With cardamom, cloves, camphor, musk, saffron, and the like;
with nutmeg, jasmine petals, betel nuts, betel leaves, long pepper, and ginger."

Those ten directions— the deities of the east and so forth— who draw toward themselves and spread forth the fragrance and scent of the betel-leaf characterized by such features as being prepared with powders of *khadira* heartwood and camphor boluses.
She whose lower garment was thus;
by those goddesses— who, though longing to partake of the mouthfuls of betel-leaves trickling from Ambā’s lotus-face—
were unable to obtain them, [the fragrance] of that very first emission was seized simultaneously and with a scramble of "I first, I first."

She is seized by all [the senses] after being drawn in; for it is with the very desire for her that they stand surrounding her in invisible guise—this is the suggested meaning (*tātparyagati*). Thus, through the suggestion of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāradhvani*) based on a fact (*vastunā*), there is the suggestion of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣādhvananāt*). Alternatively, [it may refer to her] whose betel-roll fragrance, that is, the excellence of its scent...

She [is she] who draws in the quarters of space with her fragrances. Regarding "fragrance" (*āmoda*): it is that which is intensely pervasive; its grammatical gender varies according to the quality [it describes]. However, "attracting" (*samākarṣī*) is that which is pervasive, while "sugandhi" (*surabhi*) is that which gratifies the sense of smell.
Thus ends Amara [Kośa], verse 61.
Completely surpassing the lute by the sweetness and charm of her own conversation—
that is, by the sweetness and loveliness of her own, inherently beautiful speech concerning Brahman, consisting of articulated sounds.
She by whom the *kacchapī*—meaning a lute (*vīṇā*)—was reviled and insulted.

Because the rule for forming compound endings is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*), the suffix *kap* is not applied here according to the rule *na ṛtaśca*. However, some maintain that *kacchapī* means "the female of a tortoise" (*kacchapa*), based on the observation of lexicons such as: "That *kacchapī* is a large lute," and so forth.
The *Amarakośa-śeṣa* also speaks concerning the lute (*vīṇā*):
"That [lute] of Viśvāvasu is the *bṛhatī*; that of Tumburu is the *kalāvatī*;
that of Nārada is the *mahatī*; and that of Sarasvatī is the *kacchapī*."

Thus it is said. For in the world, even in the absence of the manifestation of phonemes (*varṇa*), there is the experience that "the sound of the lute is pleasing" simply by means of the manifestation of notes such as *ṣaḍja*, having inferred the very same phonemes already known [from other sources], and desiring merely their pleasantness. As for the *kacchapī* [lute], however, it is [so called] precisely because of its connection with Sarasvatī.
There is indeed a manifestation of phonemes that is slightly clear, as in the case of parrots, starlings, and the like;

however, there is no dispute regarding the fact that conversation characterized by a more distinct manifestation of phonemes and a greater degree of sweetness possesses a superiority that transcends all others. For this very reason, it is said in the *Saundaryalaharī*:
When you began to sing in detail the various exploits of Paśupati, nodding your head at his words of praise,
the sweetness of those [words] eclipsed the melodious sound of the lute strings.
"she silently covers her own lute, Vāṇī, with her garment (cola). Thus [it was said].
Her mind, the Lord of Love (Kāmeśa), was submerged in the flood of light from her gentle smile. 62.

A "smile" is a slight laugh; that [smile] is "slow" (manda). It is "sinking" (majjat) because it sinks into the flood of his radiance, which is a stream of loveliness; however, it is not "submerged" (magna). For if it were submerged in one place, the movement of other limbs would necessarily be lost. This...

It is implied by the present tense that [the practitioner] exerts himself for the sake of moving to another part of his own body and does not desire to emerge from it. Kāma is the *bindu* which constitutes the body of the *kalā*, known as the Sun (*ravi*) consisting of Agni and Soma. As it is said in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"The *bindu* is the essence of ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the sun is the form of this couple in their state of aesthetic union (*samarasa*).
Kāma is so called because of his loveliness, and the *kalā* is the *bindu* whose form consists of fire and the moon.
Thus, she is so described as one whose mind is that of the Lord, the Sovereign of the Lords of Kings (*rājarājeśvara*).
By describing the submergence of even the all-pervading mind according to the Mīmāṃsaka school, the boundless superiority of the flood of light is suggested. || 62 ||
Adorned by the splendor of a chin whose likeness has never been grasped—
since poets have begun to describe it today, starting from the Goddess of Speech, they have not grasped it (an-ākalita),
meaning it has not been fully encompassed, nor has it been conceived, nor has it been properly attained.
Because no [suitable] simile could be found; rather,
she is resplendent with the beauty of her chin, which possesses a likeness that has almost been attained through some slight point of comparison, such as the form of a mirror-handle for the face.
Her neck is adorned with an auspicious thread bound by the Lord of Desire.

Her neck— that is, her nape— is adorned with that auspicious thread (māṅgalyasūtra) which was tied by Kāmeśvara Paramaśiva, serving as the cause for the revival of Kāma and acting as an ornament of good fortune. || 63 ||
She possesses arms made beautiful by golden armlets (*aṅgada*) and bracelets (*keyūra*).

The term *aṅgada* means "that which gives the limb," signifying a constituent part of the body. [The phrase] "by those whose very bodies are gold" refers to those whose limbs are exclusively of gold. [She is adorned] with four bracelets, which are ornaments for the arms.

She is endowed with, or possessed of, arms that are desirable and beautiful; or, by relying on the difference in form between the armlet (*aṅgada*) and the bracelet (*keyūra*), it may be explained as referring to two types of ornaments. For this very reason, it is stated in the seventh chapter of the *Brahmottara-khaṇḍa*:
The application [of this] in the section on the meditation on Śiva is:
"wearing serpent-bracelets, armlets, bangles, and finger-rings. Elsewhere as well:
"resplendent with ornaments such as armlets, bangles, necklaces, and bracelets."
The *Agnipurāṇa*, however, states "keyūramaṅgadaṃ dorbhūṣe" (the keyūra and aṅgada are arm-ornaments),
intending to describe them as ornaments of the upper arms; since Amarasiṃha follows that [text], he too intends that very same thing, and thus there is no fault.
Adorned with a jeweled necklace, a wish-fulfilling gem, a crest-jewel, and pearls.

It was adorned with a neck-ornament (*grīvābharaṇa*)— a *cintāka* [necklace] made of gold, as implied by its context— which was studded with jewels and accompanied by dangling, flickering pearls that had attained the state of a *hāra* (long necklace). The jewel-encrusted *cintāka* related to the neck was arranged in a horizontal row below.
Or, it may refer exclusively to an ornament consisting of hanging pearls.

It is well known as *cintāka* in the Andhra country; however, some claim it is a synonym for *lalāṭikā* (a forehead ornament), which is questionable given the descriptions in such lexicons. [The term] refers to those whose *cintā*—that is, meditation (*dhyāna*)—is fixed solely upon the neck.

Those who possess the contemplation of the neck-jewel (graiveyacintā) are those who practice meditation merely by falling repeatedly upward; they are not capable of stabilizing the deities within the small space (dahara). This means they are practitioners of intermediate capacity (madhyamādhikārī). Those who are "fickle" (lolāḥ), meaning full of craving, are practitioners of inferior capacity (adhamādhikārī).

According to the *Amarakośa* following the *Agnipurāṇa*, "lola" means "unsteady" or "possessing thirst. The meaning is that "muktāḥ" refers to those of the highest qualification (*uttamādhikāriṇaḥ*). Of these three [types of practitioners], there are those which are like jewels—those with no fruit, those with small fruit, and those with great fruit.
According to the lexicon [Amarakośa], "āṅ" is used in the sense of "slightness" (īṣadartha) and "pervasion" (abhivyāpti). Thus, "endowed with those" means "intent upon giving them.
This constitutes a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) concerning both the relevant and the irrelevant subjects. || 64 ||
Her breasts serve as the counter-bet for the jewel-gem of Kāmeśvara’s love.

The "jewel-gem" (ratnamaṇi) is the very love of Kāmeśvara, the most excellent of gems; her breasts are the counter-bets (pratipaṇa) in the matter of that wager. Here, the word *maṇi*, while referring to a gem, applies specifically to the breasts.
Or it may be taken as an adjective. The sense is that she has sold her "jewel of breasts" (stanaratna) and purchased the "jewel of love" (premaratna).

By this act of buying and selling at a double price, there is an even greater loss of mutual ownership, ensuring that there can be no reversal of their love and attesting to the excellence of her wifely devotion (pātivratya).
Through the figure of exchange (vinimaya-alaṅkāra), there is a suggestion of a fact (vastudhvani):
"The navel is the basin for the creeper of the line of body hair, and the two breasts are its fruit. (65)
Her navel is the basin for watering, and her line of body hair is the trench for the creeper; she is one whose two breasts are the fruit of that creeper which is not distinct from her hair-line.
This is a *paramparita-rūpaka* (successive metaphor), as well as a combination (*saṅkara*) of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), *sambandha-atiśayokti* (hyperbole of connection), and so forth. || 65 ||
The middle [part of the body] is to be inferred from its being the locus of the line of hair (*romalatā*);

it is "perceptible" (*lakṣyā*), meaning it is fit to be characterized, that is to say, it is being made known. This is because only that which is itself being known serves as the cause for inference, and not the mere cognition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*).

Even in the theory that [the cognition] is the cause, since there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanā*) regarding the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the mark (*liṅga*) and the cognition, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that causality belongs to both.
This is because even future objects and the like exist as mental forms (*bauddhākāra*). And thus says the Sūtra of Gautama:

"The establishment of the cognition [is as follows]: 'that [middle part] does not exist'. The intended referent (*lakṣya*) is the state of being the locus of the line of hair—that is, the status of being the site for the planting of the creeper in the form of the line of hair.

The point is that the line of hair itself is the logical mark (*liṅga*) by virtue of its relation as a locus. By means of that [mark], the middle part is to be correctly inferred; it is the object of a valid inferential cognition (*pramānumiti*).

The application [of the term] is as follows: that whose lower abdominal region possesses a dense part called the "waist" (madhyama) because it is like a creeper of hair. Since the waist is supported by the presence of a creeper-like line of hair, there is the poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality). Although [it is said], "the supportless... [hā...]

Just as in the verse beginning "I weep; tell me, before whom today? (*rodimi kathaya kasyādya purataḥ*), where the correctness of a vowel situated between two words—consisting of multiple phonemes—is established only by its dependence on a semivowel (*antastha*) at the end of a word such as *samudra*, so too is the case for a vowel at the end of a foot (*pādānta*). [Therefore, one should] bow down...

Just as in the phrase "The pair of lotus-feet of Nārāyaṇa, which bestows bliss, for the destruction of the afflictions that bind one to existence," the term *ādhāratā* (the state of being a locus) lacks grammatical correctness when placed in the middle; nevertheless, [it is used] by sages such as Rāta and Māṇḍavya.
According to the opinion of the ancient masters who established the science of prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*),

since the term *yati* (caesura) is not considered a constituent part [of the verse], its grammatical correctness is established in that manner. Furthermore, we have demonstrated in the *Chandobhāskara* that the *Paiṅgala* treatise refers exclusively to works belonging to the Kali Yuga.
Her waist, burdened by her breasts, displays three folds from the binding of her silk sash.

With the weight and heaviness of her breasts, as if her waist were about to burst, she has bound it with a cloth-band made of golden strips; this very binding constitutes the three folds [of her waist].
This is a combination of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) and hyperbole (atiśayokti). || 66 ||
Her hips were radiant with saffron-colored garments as crimson as the dawn;

"aruṇāruṇa" means exceedingly red, for the repetition (vīpsā) of the word emphasizes the intensity, as in the expression "red-red" (*raktarakta*) meaning "reddened by the glow of the beloved’s palms. Alternatively, it means "as red as the dawn" (*aruṇavat*) or "as red as the thighless one" (*anūruvat*).
She whose hip-region is radiant and shining with a garment dyed with safflower, which is called *kausumbha*.
She was adorned with a girdle-string made of beautiful strings of jeweled bells.
She was adorned with jeweled tinkling bells, small bells,
and a beautiful girdle consisting of a cord of golden waistbands.
She is endowed with two thighs that possess the good fortune and softness known only by Kāmeśa,
who alone is their witness; that is, she is possessed of two thighs whose auspiciousness and tenderness, as well as their beauty and delicacy, are known solely by Kāmeśa.
She is resplendent with her two knees shaped like ruby crowns. || 68 ||
She is resplendent with two knees and two shanks that possess the form of a *māṇikya-mukuṭa*— a crown made of unbroken rubies, a head-covering known as a *ṭopikā* which is inverted. || 68 ||

Her shanks resemble the quivers of Smara, the King of Love, which are encrusted all around with indragopa insects; indragopas are specific types of extremely red worms that appear during the rainy season. Her shanks are like those two quivers, being studded on all sides by them.

She whose shanks are like those of an antelope; if they were inlaid with jewels by them [the gods], then a simile might be possible—thus there is a suggestion (*dhvani*) of the "becoming" aspect (*abhūtatva-aṃśa*) regarding the simile.
Her ankles are hidden, and her forefeet are endowed with qualities that surpass even the back of a tortoise. (69)

Her ankles are hidden and fleshy, and her heels are such that they conquer the backs of tortoises; she is endowed with forefeet—the tips of the feet—which are victorious. The word *jayiṣṇu* ends with the suffix *iṣṇuc*, and not [the suffix] *ksnu* as in the rule "glājisthaścaksnu."

The form *jiṣṇu* would result from the suffix *kṣnu*; however, the prescription of the suffix *iṣṇuc* is established because the author of the *Vṛtti* explains that the particle *ca* in the rule *bhuvaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.138) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. Furthermore, one should not apply the term *chandasī* (in the Vedic language) to that rule, as the *Amarakośa* states: "bhūṣṇu, bhaviṣṇu, and bhavitṛ."
Because of usage; according to the maxim that "grammarians rely upon usage," therefore *viṣṇu*, *bhrājiṣṇu*, and likewise *jayiṣṇu* are indeed correct. || 69 ||
She whose quality of darkness—
the ignorance of those who bow down, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and other beings— is completely covered and dispelled by the rays of her nails, which are like moons upon her feet.
The sense is that ignorance is destroyed through meditation on her feet. Alternatively, since there is no distinct manifestation of the rays of this pair of feet—
which are moons of nails— due to the profusion of reflections from the shadows of the clusters of gems in the crowns of those bowing down,
[it is for the sake of] destroying darkness by means of those [rays].

The poet imagines that [the Lord] has entered the interior of her heart; this is the intended meaning. And likewise, there is the speech of Nārada in the *Matsya Purāṇa* and the *Padma Purāṇa*, having observed the marks of Pārvatī’s body according to the science of physiognomy (*sāmudrika*):
"O blessed lady, her husband has not yet been born; she is devoid of auspicious marks, with hands perpetually turned upward and feet that wander astray."
"I shall be [endowed] with my own reflection; what more need be said?"—
to this reply from Menā, Himavān, being deluded into thinking that these were merely ill-omened signs, questioned [the sage] with great sorrow.
Nārada said:
"O great mountain, even when there is a cause for great joy, you express sorrow; because you have not grasped the meaning of my words, you fall into delusion."
Having thus explained the meaning of such statements as "her husband has not been born," he concluded by saying:
"As for what was said by me— that my two feet do not deviate from my own shadow— "
O best of mountains, hear now the meaning of these words of mine as well.
Her feet, resembling lotuses and radiant with clear nails,
were illuminated by the luster of the jewels in the crowns of the gods and asuras bowing before her.
"With their reflections of various colors, they will cast out her own radiance;
having entered within, they will destroy the quality of darkness (tamas) in their hearts. Thus [it was said].
With the mass of light from her two feet, she eclipsed the lotus. (70)

She is one by whom the lotuses have been surpassed—that is, set aside—by the mass of radiance belonging to her two feet, that pair of feet, which consists of a collection of qualities such as elegance. || 70 ||
Her glorious lotus-feet are adorned with tinkling jeweled anklets;
"tinkling" means producing a specific sound arising from ornaments, and she is "adorned" by those two anklets which possess such jeweled foot-rings.
In whose lotus-feet such glory resides—

regarding the word *śrī*, even though the suffix *kap* would have been optional by the rule "nadī-ṛtaś-ca," it does not occur precisely because the prohibition of the designation *nadī* for the word *śrī* applies; furthermore, the shortening [of the final vowel] by the rule "hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya" does not occur here, because a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñā-pūrvaka*) is not invariably obligatory.
Or it may be a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she whose lotus-feet are adorned and endowed with glory";
she whose gait is as slow and graceful as that of a female swan, and who is a treasure-trove of great loveliness. (71)

A *marāla* is a swan, slow-moving by its very nature; even among those, it is specifically a female one that is intended here. She whose gait is as slow as that of such a bird. She is a treasure-trove (*śevadhi*), a storehouse of great loveliness—that is, of surpassing beauty. [Note: *Nidhiḥ* is masculine.]

This is because the *Agnipurāṇa* states, "It is a treasure-trove (*śevadhi*). For this very reason, according to Pāṇini’s sūtra, "The gender of a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa* compound follows that of the final member," this name is masculine. Consequently, the usage "Obeisance to Śevadhaye" (*śevadhaye namaḥ*) is the only correct form; the alternative form "Obeisance to Śevadhye" (*śevadhye namaḥ*) is not optional. || 71 ||

She whose every limb is entirely ruddy and faultless, adorned with all ornaments; she whose everything— her garments, ornaments, flowers, luster, and so forth— is indeed ruddy, and whose limbs and members are "faultless," meaning they are not blameworthy but possess auspicious characteristics.
She is adorned with all the ornaments, beginning with the crest-jewel and ending with the toe-rings, as described in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, the *Kalpasūtra*, and other sources— namely, forty in number.
Having thus described the gross form, he states the locations where she resides:
"Śivā, whose beloved is under her own control, dwells upon the lap of Śiva-Kāmeśvara. (72)

By the words "Śivakāma" and so forth: he is called *kāma* because he is desirable, according to the statement, "Kāma is so called due to his desirability. Alternatively, he is called *kāma* because his form (*rūpa*) is according to desire (*kāma*), i.e., as one wishes. It is precisely through this etymological derivation that the application of the word *kāma* to Manmatha is demonstrated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*.
"In all the worlds, there is none equal to you in the power to assume any form at will;
therefore, O Manobhava, become renowned by the name of Kāma.
Or rather, desire (*kāma*) is simply consciousness (*prajñāna*). And thus says the Śruti: "That which is this heart..."

"And this mind— consciousness, non-consciousness, discernment, wisdom, intelligence, vision, fortitude, thought, deliberation, speed, memory, volition, determination, life-force, desire, and will— all these are indeed names of consciousness. Herein:
By the word *prajñāna*, Śiva alone is meant; for such an expansion is seen in the *Brahmagītā* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"That which is called Śaṅkara, namely consciousness (*vijñāna*), is designated in many ways by the wise."
"Some say it is the heart"— starting from this point up to—
"some believers say it is the *vaśa*; all these [are] eternal."
"these are undoubtedly the names of this Śiva, who is consciousness"—thus it ends. The Lord (Īśvara), desiring to emit the world, is denoted by the word *kāma*.
And so it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only."

The passage beginning with "He desired" and ending with "this much indeed is desire" [is cited]. The term *śivakāmeśvara* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "He who is Śiva, and He who is Kāma, and He who is Īśvara. The three words are used to exclude Guṇirudra and Madana. In His lap...

She remains seated upon the left lap; for this very reason, she is called Śivā. [The root] *śvi* is used in the sense of "desire" (*kānti*), and thus *śiva* is traditionally understood as desire. The meaning is that she is of the nature of the will of the Supreme Śiva. The implication is that power (*śakti*) in the form of will has Śiva as its substratum. Alternatively, she is called Śivā because she is non-different from Śiva. In that regard:
The etymological derivation of the word *Śiva* is given in the Śaiva Āgama: "He who abides as the witness of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), of the prior non-existence of those modifications,
of the desire to know, and likewise of the object of initial cognition such as 'I am the knower'."

He is real because he has no unreal object; he is real for all insentient beings because he is their means of accomplishment; and he is of the nature of consciousness because he is always the object of love.
He whose nature is bliss, by virtue of being the accomplisher of all aims,
and by virtue of possessing all connections, is complete and designated as Śiva.

"He is Śiva alone, devoid of the nature of being the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), and so forth. Alternatively, the word *śivā* is derived from the root *śiv* with the suffix *ṇic* according to the rule "that which makes it so" (*tatkaroti*), followed by the suffix *ac* and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Or else, it means "in whom everything rests," according to the rule beginning with "sarvanighṛṣvariṣva... [which applies the suffix *ka*] in the sense of something other than the agent.

[The word *śivā*] is derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Alternatively, it means "she in whom auspicious (*śiva*) qualities exist," using the suffix *ac* according to the rule for the *arśas-ādi* group. In the Jainendra Vyākaraṇa, however, there is the rule: "And *śiva*, etc. This was explained by Subhūticandra: [the word] *śiva* is derived from the root *śam* with the suffix *kvun*.
Thus, the elision of the *maṅgala* vowel is applied by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
"Because he constantly promotes the undertaking of all goals for human beings through the word 'Śiva,' therefore he is remembered as Śiva."
Thus it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:
"All the Dānavas and the immortals are equal to me; I am the bringer of welfare to all beings, and for that reason, O gods, I possess the nature of Śiva."
And thus: "He who, being one, presides over every womb, in whom this entire universe comes together and dissolves"—so says the Śruti.
And also: "The three-eyed, blue-throated, and tranquil one. All of this has been summarized by us in our commentary on the *Śivāṣṭottaraśatanāma*.

O Supreme Śiva, because of Your natural purity, Your association with stainless qualities, Your tranquility, Your being the support of the world, and Your bestowing of immortality upon those who worship You, as well as Your power of will such as strength and so forth, You are [the goal] according to the multitude of Vedāntas.
"By virtue of being non-different from *rasa*, you have come to be designated as 'Śiva'.
Or, *śivā* may mean "non-different from Śiva. And that non-difference is the cause for engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), as shown in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*:
"As Śiva is, so is the Goddess; as the Goddess is, so is Śiva.
Therefore, with the very understanding of non-difference, they call Umā 'Śiva.
In that same work, in another place:

"In ultimate reality, there is no difference whatsoever between Umā and Śaṅkara; having assumed two forms, he alone exists as one—of this there is no doubt. And: "The Supreme Self is declared to be Śiva, and she (Umā) is likewise proclaimed to be Śivā."

Also in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*: "O best of the twice-born, that consciousness which, being non-conceptual and self-luminous, has entered into the form of the power of Māyā which rests upon pure consciousness (cinmātra)..."
"Always sixfold in aspect, supreme bliss, the destroyer of saṃsāra—
she is the goddess Śivā, the supreme, non-different from Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness.
Beginning thus...

"Whatever desired object is not accomplished for one who worships this Śāṅkarī, who is an ocean of compassion, by her very grace? Thus ends [the passage]. Alternatively, Vāyu’s wife is named Śivā; and it is stated in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
"Pervading all worlds and the sustainer of all embodied beings,
the god whose nature is wind is celebrated by the wise as Īśāna."
"The wise have declared that Śivā is the wife of the Lord Īśāna, the creator of the universe, the Supreme Self; and his daughter is Manojava.
And also in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "O beautiful one, Śiva is the wind, whose crest-jewel is the young moon."
"The fourth form of Īśāna is remembered as Vāyu;
his wife is named Śivā, and his son is Manojava.
Alternatively, she is called Śivā because she bestows *śiva*, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). As it is said in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Liberation is declared to be auspicious (*śivā*), bestowing release upon yogis;
because the Goddess is born for the sake of Śiva, she is therefore remembered as *Śivā* in the world.
Thus it is said in the Āgama.
"This Śivā is innate to Śiva, like heat to fire, like radiance to the sun, and like moonlight to the moon. Thus,
he says that even though she consists of attributes such as will (icchā) and the rest, she is not subordinate to the substratum (dharmin).
Regarding the term *svādhīna*: she whose husband, the beloved Lord of Desire (*Kāmeśvara*), is dependent upon and subject to her own self.
