Since Śiva’s very acquisition of selfhood is dependent upon Śakti, the meaning is that he is like a husband who is dependent upon his wife. As it is said in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"Even there he dwells eternally with Pārvatī, engaging in playful dalliance;
the temple of the Goddess is in the center, and Śaṅkara is subject to her authority.
Thus it is stated in the Āgama as well.
"I bow with my whole being to that primordial one, whose nature is consciousness, by whom Śambhu is empowered for the enjoyment and liberation of this multitude of bound souls (paśu).
Thus it is said; and also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O best of sages, even that Śiva who has become the cause of the universe possesses that power; devoid of it, he is purposeless.
Thus it was also said by the venerable teacher, the Blessed Ācārya:

"If Śiva is joined with Śakti, he is able to exercise his power; if it were not so, the Lord would indeed not be capable of even a single movement. Or, [the name may mean] "she by whom her beloved is under her own control. [This refers to] Sukanyā, the daughter of Śaryāti.

In the seventh book of the Devībhāgavata, the following story is recorded: not knowing that her husband had been transformed by the Aśvins into a form identical to their own, she propitiated the Blessed Goddess and thereby brought him under her control.
"O Mother of the World, I have come to you for refuge, being deeply distressed;
protect my virtue today! I bow at your feet.
Following such prayers as these—

As it is said: "When the Goddess Tripurasundarī was thus praised by her, she bestowed upon her heart that knowledge by which her husband became subject to her will. In this same way, Śacī’s attainment of Indra should also be cited as described in the Sixth Skandha.

Although in the *Bhaktimīmāṃsā*, under the sūtra "tatpratiṣṭhā gṛhapīṭhavat" (its establishment is like that of a house or a seat), it is stated that because there is no difference in usage— such as "it stands in the house" and "it stands on the seat"— the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) belongs primarily to both, and not...
It has been stated that even the foundational ground of the hierarchy— consisting of forms such as direct connection, indirect succession, and so forth—

is included within the "house" (the body); nevertheless, because no expectation arises as to where [the deity] resides within the house, one must consider the other substrates in relation to the *pīṭha*.
The gradation [of these locations] is indeed established by experience. By that same principle, having first mentioned the lap of Kāmeśvara’s consort because of its primacy, he speaks of other sites:
"The Mistress of the Glorious City resides on the central peak of Sumeru."

Regarding the phrase "situated on the central peak of Sumeru," and so forth: she is *tatsthā* because she dwells on the central peak (*madhyaśṛṅga*) of Sumeru, the Golden Mountain; or alternatively, she is on the beautiful central peak of Meru. For on Mount Meru there are three peaks shaped like the triangle of Śiva, and among them there is a fourth peak.
Thus it has been said by the great sage Durvāsas in the *Lalitāstavaratna*:
"Victorious is that Golden Mountain, whose form is composed of the entire circle of the worlds,
where the manifold songs of the celestial nymphs sprout forth from the groves and gardens of its golden thickets."
We praise his three peaks, which rest upon the ends of the directions of Indra, Nairṛta, Vāyu, and Varuṇa,
and which serve as the foundation for the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
"In its center, moreover, I worship that preeminent peak, four hundred yojanas high, which delights the horizons with clusters of rays from enchanting jewels.
Thus [he spoke]. That city, possessing glorious fortune (*lakṣmī*), is such that the word "city" (*nagara*) alone, without any further qualification, [suffices].
The one who speaks of the City of Knowledge (Vidyānagara) is its presiding deity, the Sovereign (Adhipati). And that city is of two kinds;
first, it is situated upon the peak of Mount Meru in the center. As it is said in the *Lalitāstavaratna*:
"There, [the city] has an extent of four hundred yojanas and was fashioned by the divine architect."
"I bow to the city of Ādividyā, delightful with various *sāla* trees.
There, regarding the phrase "four hundred" (*catvāri śatāni*) on the middle peak, the analysis is as follows:
it means four hundred, but not "one hundred plus four," as in the *Piṅgala-sūtra* rule "four hundred is *utkṛti*. This is evident from the following verse.
This is because it would contradict the statement regarding the measurement [of the city], namely that the first enclosure wall measures one thousand six hundred *yojanas*.
Its meaning is that there are twenty-five enclosure walls with various galleries. Furthermore—
It is situated on a jewel-island in the midst of the ocean of nectar, at the uppermost part outside the entire cosmic egg. As it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"Above and outside of many millions of millions of cosmic eggs..."
In the midst of the ocean of nectar, which is ten billion leagues in extent, [is it].
In the Jewel Island, the island of the world, extending for a hundred koṭis,
there are twenty-five ramparts consisting of the twenty-five principles.

"The auspicious city of Śrīvidyā is three hundred thousand yojanas high," and so forth. In the *Vidyāratnabhāṣya*, however, it is stated that there is also a city in the midst of the Ocean of Milk; nevertheless, it has been repeatedly stated that it possesses twenty-four walls.

In that regard, the deficiency of one enclosure (prākāra) is to be investigated. Alternatively, the term "Śrīnagara" refers to the Śrīcakra, according to the statement in the Viśvaprakāśa: "Cakra, pura, sadana, agāra, nagara, and guhā [are synonyms]. Furthermore, in the Gauḍapādīya-sūtra beginning with "ka-ga-ja-da-śāre," there is mention of the "Śrīpura."

Furthermore, this is because it is explained as such in its commentary (*bhāṣya*), and because we observe the use of words such as "city" (*nagara*) in reference to the *cakra* in Vedic texts, such as: "One should not enter the city without knowing this seer," "Ayodhyā is the foremost city of the gods," and "The city enveloped in immortality. Thus, [the term refers to] the "city-cakra" (*nagaracakra*).
Thus from the Rudrayāmala:
"She resides within the palace of the Cintāmaṇi jewel, seated upon the throne of the five Brahmans. (73)
But mine is of very small dimensions:
"May my abode— the dwelling of all the gods, constructed from clusters of wish-fulfilling gems, and situated to the north of the rampart of the color of love— dispel my anxiety."

Thus it is from the *Lalitāstavaratna*. However, in the *Gauḍapādīya-sūtra-bhāṣya*, after stating that the very same [lotus] is the place of manifestation for all mantras that grant the objects of one's thoughts— thereby describing its nature as a "wish-fulfilling gem house" (*cintāmaṇigṛha*)— the manner of its manifestation is described in detail.
There she is seated upon a throne in the form of a couch, fashioned from the five Brahmans.
This is stated in the *Bahurūpāṣṭaka-tantra* and the *Bhairavayāmala-tantra*:
"Therein is the supreme palace of the Goddess, composed of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*)."
Upon the great couch whose essence is Śiva, with Maheśāna as its pillow.
On that exceedingly beautiful surface, Sadāśiva was the bed-clothing,
the four-legged animals were the attendants, and Mahendra was the spittoon.

"Therein dwells the Supreme Sovereign, Mahātripurasundarī. The term *bhṛtakāḥ* means servants; that is to say, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara. In the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (Āgneya) and ending with the northeast (Īśāna), these [deities] such as Brahmā and the others exist in the form of pillars above and below.

In the center, although they have the form of persons, they have attained the state of Śakti through meditation on Śrī; that they have closed eyes and are motionless, and so forth, is to be understood from the Purāṇas. || 73 ||
She resides in the Mahāpadma forest and dwells in the Kadamba grove;
she stands perfectly within such a forest where there are great lotuses.
She is the very embodiment of the Padmāṭavī forest above.

One [description] is as stated in the *Rudrayāmala*: "It is surrounded by a great lotus forest (*mahāpadmavana*) three hundred thousand *yojanas* in length. Another is stated in the *Lalitāstavaratna*:
"In the middle of the jeweled mansion and the palace, [there are trees] as tall as ten palm trees (*tāla*)."
It was endowed with full stalks the color of white clouds, each a yojana in height.
[She is] joined by five-fold tālī measures and united with clusters of filaments,
while a multitude of bees emerges from the continuous stream of nectar flowing forth.
"Let us resort to the lotus-forest, which is turned tawny by the pollen rising from the gusts of wind through the young *pāṭīra* trees, and whose edges are fringed with the ripples of fragrance.
The thousand-petaled lotus situated at the *brahmarandhra* is also called a "lotus-forest. And it has been said:

In the *Svacchandatantra*, beginning with the passage: "Above that is the Kula-lotus, thousand-spoked and facing downwards," it continues: "And this Great Lotus Forest is equal to that and situated above it. This is also because of the identity in form between the Egg of Brahmā (the macrocosm) and the Egg of the Body (the microcosm). This...
In the *Cāruṇopaniṣadbhāṣya*, this was clarified during the commentary on the sentence "āṇḍībhavajamāmuhuḥ":
[He] dwells in a forest of *kadamba* and *nīpa* trees; thus [he is so called]. [It is] a house made of *cintāmaṇi* gems.
Surrounding that jeweled pavilion is a grove of *kadamba* trees. As it is stated in the *Bhairavayāmala*:
"The station of the Bindu, the ocean of nectar, the five wombs (*pañcayoni*), and the celestial trees;
right there is a row of *nīpa* trees, and in their midst is the jeweled pavilion."
"In that place, [there is] a ground made of wish-fulfilling gems...
and so forth. It is also established in the Purāṇa that the ground within the golden and silver walls is seven yojanas [in extent], and that there are *kadamba* trees rising two yojanas high from it.
Situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar, Kāmākṣī is the bestower of all desires.

There is one ocean of nectar (*sudhāsāgara*), white as ambrosia (*pīyūṣavarṇa*), situated above, which is well-known from the Vedic scripture: "The city enveloped in nectar. Another is located within the *piṇḍāṇḍa*, in the place of the *bindu*, in the center of the moon at the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*). It is also known as Aparājita.

In the city attained through the meditation on Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahmopāsanā), there are two sons named Ara and Kya, who are full of nectar and resemble the ocean. They are mentioned in the Śārīrakabhāṣya under the sūtra "anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt" (non-return [to this world] is declared by scripture). Since there is no distinction made, all of them are included here. Of these—
She stands in the center; thus [she is called] "Tathā.

She is one whose eyes are fixed upon *kāma*, that which is desirable; the suffix *ṭac* is applied at the end of the compound. Alternatively, she is one whose eye is *Kāmeśvara* himself. Because he is the object of her vision, the status of being an "eye" is metaphorically attributed to him.
This is the unique name of the presiding deity of the Kāñcīpīṭha. As it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Being omniscient, she fulfills various desires by acting as a witness."
Having seen that conduct of the goddess, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [spoke].
"Then she gave her the name Kāmākṣī, and [the Lord] Kāmeśvara [gave her the name] Kāmeśvarī.

She is called Kāmadāyinī because she grants desires—that is, mental longings—or because she bestows Kāmeśvara himself upon her devotees, with the intention of granting non-difference from Śiva; thus she is Kāmadāyinī. [She is also] Kāma...
Or, she is "Kāmada" because she tears (*dyati*) or shatters *manmatha* (the god of love); thus, she is "Ayinī," one who possesses the auspicious method (*aya*) [of Śiva].

According to Amara, "aya" means an auspicious method. Alternatively, *dāya* refers to property inherited through the lineage of one's father and so forth; therefore, she is "Dāyavatī," possessing such inheritance from the Lord of Desire (*Kāmeśvara*).
The meaning is that it possesses an unoriginated, eternally established nature non-different from that [reality]. || 74 ||
Now, while clearly describing the functions of the Goddess’s gross form, he begins to describe her supreme, secret form through secret expressions alone:
"Her own majesty is being praised by the multitude of hosts of gods and sages."

By the words "devarṣi" and so forth: she whose majesty (*vaibhava*) consists of that essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is being praised by the assembly—the great collective—of both the hosts of gods and the hosts of sages; [alternatively,] she whose pervasive self-nature (*ātmano vyāpakatvam*) is being praised.

Or rather, it means being praised in many ways by the hosts of celestial sages (*devarṣi*) in groups; or else, "in groups" (*saṃghāta*) refers to a particular hell, and [the phrase] "being praised" and so forth is for the purpose of dispelling that. Of evil...
In passages such as *prāyaścitta* ("atonement"),

since the genitive case is seen to signify a relationship of the "destroyed" and the "destroyer," here too it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Alternatively, it may mean "that which is praised for the sake of the complete destruction (*samyaṅghāta*), namely the slaying of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura."

For this very reason, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, there is the description of the effort to slay [the demon] that occurred subsequent to that. For this same reason, in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, after the gods, who were oppressed by the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, had performed a hymn of praise to the Goddess beginning with "Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World," Ambā granted a boon.

When she said, "Choose," the gods spoke these words: "O auspicious lady, if you are pleased with us, we have been oppressed by the lord of the Daityas; our very lives are difficult to preserve, and thus we have come to you seeking refuge."
And so forth. Also elsewhere:
"Then, on one occasion, the venerable sage Nārada, having arrived and bowed to the Supreme Śakti, spoke with humility."
Beginning thus: "O Goddess, this demon Bhaṇḍa oppresses the three worlds;
he must be conquered by you alone, for he cannot be defeated by other gods."
Thus far. In reality, however, the "gods" (devāḥ) are Brahmā and others; the "sages" (ṛṣayaḥ) are Vasiṣṭha and others;
the "divine sages" (devarṣayaḥ) are Nārada and others. The compound is analyzed as "the divine sages and the divine sages. The "hosts" (gaṇāḥ) are the Ādityas and others.
"Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Tuṣitas, Ābhāsvaras, Nīlas,
Mahārājikas, Sādhyas, Rudras, and the Gaṇadevatās"—
thus from the Agni Purāṇa. Their "saṃghāta" is their assembly or collective group.

The meaning is that [the Lord] is being praised by those described in the *Rudrayāmala*, beginning with the words "by many tens of millions of world-protectors, and by tens of millions of moons, suns, and Vasus.
Therefore, one should not suspect a redundancy between the two terms *gaṇa* and *saṃghāta*. Now, regarding the position that it refers to the supreme form (*pararūpa*):

By the qualification "being praised by gods and others," it is implied that the true nature of the self, as taught in the Śaiva scriptures, is consciousness alone— which is all-pervading, known by all, and the object of all love. This is also stated in the Agni Purāṇa:
"His consciousness is the Self—this is declared as the first aphorism; 'Bondage is knowledge'—this, however, is the second aphorism of the Lord.
And thus, while being praised and recognized by the gods and others, [he perceives] his own Self. "The Self alone..."

The description should be as follows: she is the one whose majesty (*vaibhava*), sovereignty (*vibhutva*), and power (*prābhava*)—consisting in being enveloped by infinite powers—belong to that deity who is non-different from the self, as stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "The deity Lalitā is said to have a universal form. Furthermore, [she is described as] "ready for the work of the gods."
He elaborates upon that which was stated as the effect of her gross form:
"Accompanied by the army of Śaktis, she was intent on slaying the demon Bhaṇḍa. (75)
The asura named Bhaṇḍa and that battle and so forth are very well known in detail in the Lalitopākhyāna. That is stated in that very Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, introducing the burning of Manmatha:
"Then, having observed that ash, Citrakarmā, the lord of the Gaṇas,
fashioned a man of variegated form out of that very ash.
Beginning thus...
"Having seen this conduct, the Creator called out 'Bhaṇḍiti-bhaṇḍiti';
therefore, he is known by the name Bhaṇḍa among the worlds.
This is the end [of the passage]. His nature as an Asura is also stated in that very same place:

"Since Bhaṇḍa, who possessed great strength, was born from the fire of Rudra’s wrath, he therefore became a Dānava of a fierce nature. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the female deities (śaktis), who were intent upon the slaying—that is, the killing—of that Daitya:

"Endowed with armies" means being joined with the army through the proper formation of battle arrays (*vyūha*), or alternatively, being endowed with complete non-differentiation (*abhedena*). Thus, there is a *sūtra* by Gauḍapāda:
"For the sake of slaying the demon Bhaṇḍa, she who is one indeed becomes many. Or else, *bhaṇḍa* refers to one who is shameless, and he—

In this context, the embodied being has attained the state of a *jīva*. Regarding this, they say: "Though your nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccitsukhātman*), you suffer through insentience, instability, pain, and so forth; this is the delusion (*bhaṇḍimā*) of Māyā. He takes away (*rāti*) its vital breaths (*asūn*); that is to say, he takes all that belongs to it—the attributes residing within it—which is what is meant by "delusion" (*bhaṇḍima*). This is the bondage of ignorance (*jñānabandha*).

Thus, the meaning is that "bondage" (bandha) is what is stated in the Sūtra. Regarding the two Sūtras, "His self is knowledge" and [the subsequent one], through the presence or absence of the elision of the vowel *a* (*sandhau akāra-śleṣāśleṣābhyām*), the absence of the cognition of selfhood in the Self and the cognition of selfhood in the non-Self are well known by the designation of the term *āṇavamala* (the atomic impurity), which constitutes bondage.

This is the meaning stated in its *bhāṣya* and *vārttika*. Its "slaughter" (*vadha*) is that from which [it arises]; "exertion" (*udyukta*) means effort (*udyama*). The secret meaning is that it is "endowed with a host (*senā*), that is, a collection, of those powers (*śakti*), that is, capacities. And thus are the *Śivasūtras*: "Exertion..."

Bhairava says: "In the contemplation of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), there is the dissolution of the universe; in the contemplation of power (śakti), there is the arising of the body; in the contemplation of the elements (bhūta), there are the distinctness of the elements and the conjunction of the universe," and so forth.
These are its explanatory verses (vārtika), as follows:
"This [state] consists of the sudden emergence of the manifestation of the form of surging forth, belonging to one's own consciousness as it flows out in the form of reflective awareness."
Exertion is the internal vibration consisting of the realization of the full sense of "I";
it arises from the complete integration of all powers.

Because he completely fills all things, such that even the devouring of the diverse conceptual constructions is rendered superfluous, he is called Bhairava by virtue of this very etymological meaning.
This exertion of self-awareness which has been described is of the nature of Bhairava;
it possesses a great power that transcends both sequence and non-sequence.
Eager to invade the entire army of one's own innate consciousness-power,
this supreme [power] is distinct from both the empty and the non-empty forms, yet it is that which subdues them.
In the very same way, upon the wall of one's own conscious self, beginning from the manifestation of objects of knowledge,
there occurs a vibration whose nature extends up to the final repose in the supreme subject.
Through the expansion of its power, the light known as creation, maintenance, dissolution,
and the end [of the cycle] manifests the fivefold activity that vibrates throughout the realm of phenomenal diversity.

Furthermore, that which is the reintegration of this wheel of powers once it has been projected by her, occurring in the interval, is Māyā; she is the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the aforementioned sequence.

When that [state] exists, there occurs the withdrawal of this entire universe— from the fire of time (kālāgni) up to the limit of the kalās— characterized by the true presence of the fire of one's own self-awareness.

When the yogi performs contemplation on that [Supreme Lord] who consists of that power— namely, the power described in the sūtras beginning with "icchāśaktir umā" (the will-power is Umā)— during the process of unification;
By virtue of that [desire], the arising of bodies appropriate to each respective desire is admitted for those elements—
which, though devoid of body, intellect, and breath, possess the nature of perceivers.
The joining together and nourishing of those things to be grasped, whether stationary or otherwise;
as well as their separation and liberation from the bonds of afflictions such as disease and the like.
Furthermore, the convergence of all things— however remote in space, time, and so forth— and their being made perceptible by the senses, such as the eyes and others;

"All this occurs for the yogin when there is the stabilization of power (śakti)," and so forth. Just as the power of virility, though concealed in childhood, manifests in youth, so too the various multitudes of powers existing within the individual soul (jīva) remain concealed by the force of ignorance.
But when there is effort, all of them shine forth; this is the collective meaning. || 75 ||
There is a certain deity named Sampatkarī, who is served by a multitude of mounted elephants and brings about prosperity. Regarding her, it is stated in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"There is a certain Vidyā named Sampatkarī, whose majesty is inconceivable," and so on, up to: "Thus, that Vidyā consists of three syllables."

The procedure is described up to the end of the passage beginning with "And now the ritual is told. For it is well known in the *Lalitopākhyāna* that she is appointed over the elephants of Tripurasundarī; starting from "The goddess named Sampatkarī emerged from the goad-weapon (*aṅkuśāstra*) of the Supreme Goddess Lalitā," and continuing through "the tumult of battle... [the text proceeds].
Having spoken thus, beginning with "O elephant,

mount [me]," and ending with "ten million excellent elephants followed her," she [mounted] them properly, having restrained them by means of the methods prescribed in the treatises on elephants, such as mounting and so forth.

[The city] is served by a multitude of elephants (*hāstika*) belonging to the Sindhu region—elephants distinguished by various types such as the *bhadra*, *mandra*, and *mṛga*. Alternatively, "prosperity" (*sampat*) refers to a state of mind (*cittavṛtti*) consisting of the attainment of happiness; [the city is served] by multitudes of elephants that have become objects of perception for those mounted upon such prosperity.
It is served by the collection of objects such as sound and the rest. Thus, it is stated in the *Kādimata*:

"One should first worship the sense organs, their objects, and the [deities] born of them, using their respective names. It is the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) consisting of the knowledge of the relationship, having analytically distinguished the triad (*tripuṭī*)—which has become the object within a single act of cognition.
It brings about the perfection of happiness. As it is said in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"In the commonality of the consciousness of the grasped and the grasper among all embodied beings, this is the distinction for yogins: their attentiveness toward that relationship."

Thus, this has been made clear in the commentary on the *Śivasūtra*: "The bliss of the worlds is the bliss of samādhi. Furthermore, it was stated by Varadarāja regarding the sūtra: "In the reconnection with one's own cognition, there is the resurrection of that which was lost": "By the measure (*mātrā*), through the continuous contemplation of one's own cognition, there is the resurrection of that which had perished."

The "measurements" (*mātrā*) consist of the forms and other qualities of objects; through these sense organs, such as the eyes, there arises what is called self-cognition, and from that follows the perception of the ungraspable.
Reintegration, however, is the complete synthesis of "I" with that [object];
this being present, there is the recovery of what was lost from the aforementioned category.
"Furthermore, there may be the re-arising or resurfacing of the Fourth state for that lord of yogis; it is taught that this brings about the perfection of oneness.
Thus it is said.
She was surrounded by tens of millions upon tens of millions of horses, each mounted and presided over by [a deity].
A certain deity known as Aśvārūḍhā is well-known in the Tantra; she possesses a thirteen-syllable mantra and is presiding over horses. As it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Now, [the mantra] of the venerable Laliteśānī, which originated from her noose-weapon..."
"Moving with extremely rapid strides, mounted upon a horse with its front parts swaying," beginning thus, [the text continues] "...he went forth, having mounted the horse named Aparājita."
"Many horses, swift as the wind, followed after her.
Thus ends [the passage]. For this very reason, the etymology of the name is given in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*:
"And because of her steadiness upon the horses, she is celebrated as 'Aśvārūḍhā' (Mounted on Horses). [She is the one] presided over by her, who has brought them under her own control.

It is surrounded by many horses, numbering in the millions multiplied by ten million, as numerous as the oceans; or else, according to the statement in the *Kādimata*, "The senses are in the form of horses; there, I worship from the west," the word "horses" refers to the senses, and the mind is that which is mounted upon them. Of the mind...

Because the modification (vṛtti) issues forth through the very door of the sense-faculties; and thus, by means of a single mind, having presided over innumerable sense-faculties, one enjoys their respective pleasures—this is the meaning.
[This is] in the analysis of the compound using the plural ending in "aśvārūḍhaiḥ" (by those mounted on horses).
The meaning is that [the yogi] becomes the presiding deity over infinite sense organs simultaneously by means of many minds.
If the yogi, who is of the nature of the deity called the Self,
possesses the aforementioned exertion and practice, he becomes the possessor of the conceit of all bodies merely through his will.
That which comes into being is "bhāva" (existence). And thus say the Śiva-sūtras: "Astonishment is the stages of yoga;
the power of will is Umā Kumārī; the visible world is the body. And their commentaries (*vārttikas*) state:
"Just as there might arise in him a cognitive astonishment toward that unsurpassed bliss..."
Likewise, for this yogin, there is a constant perception of each respective object of knowledge.

When the senses are stilled by the experience of the supreme bliss that is beyond all commonality, the wonder that arises from a lack of satiety within one's own supreme self is what is called astonishment (*vismaya*).
Indeed, these very stages of yoga, which takes the form of the supreme reality,
indicate the successive ascent and the ultimate state of rest.
For one whose mind has ascended to the stage of the union of such wonder and knowledge,
and who practices the state of Supreme Bhairava through this method, [there arises] the eternal [state].
The power of will belonging to that very yogin becomes Umā;
she is the Supreme Bhaṭṭārikā, and she is celebrated as Kumārī.
Through the play of creating the universe, from Sadāśiva down to the earth, she is Kumārī; furthermore, as the Great Māyā, she is called Kumbhūmimāraṇī because she destroys the earth.
The maiden belongs to the yogin who is to be enjoyed as the self of Bhairava;
the maiden does not belong to one who is to be enjoyed by another, for she abides in identity with the enjoyer alone.
Umā Kumārī, having abandoned all attachments, was intent on the worship of Maheśvara;
likewise, the Power of Will (icchā-śakti) is devoted to the worship of the Yogin.
This very method has been seen as the clear means by the teachers of the Unsurpassed [Tantra].
Thus it is for a yogin endowed with such power and the will-power (*icchā-śakti*).
Whatever is entirely invisible is the body of that yogin,
because it appears as non-different from the "I," like a reflection.

"Thus, for this yogin, everywhere—both within the body and externally—the visible object becomes the body, and the body also becomes the visible object. And another aphorism states: "As it is there, so it is elsewhere."
"Wherever natural sovereignty has become manifest in one's own body,
in that same way it occurs for the yogin in another body."
"For one who is disciplined, that which consists of the nature of full *hantā* becomes manifest.

Mounted upon the chariot of the king of wheels (cakrarāja-ratha) and equipped with all weapons, various types of chariots—such as the Cakrarāja, Kiricakra, Geyacakra, and others—are described in the treatises on chariots (rathaśāstra) and in the Lalitopākhyāna: The Cakrarāja is a chariot that possesses a wheel made of gold, adorned with jewels, and is yoked to eight horses; it is capable of conquering all enemies. The Kiricakra is a chariot that possesses a wheel made of silver, adorned with pearls, and is yoked to six horses; it is capable of conquering all hostile armies. The Geyacakra is a chariot that possesses a wheel made of coral, adorned with lapis lazuli, and is yoked to four horses; it is capable of conquering all adversaries. And so forth.
Joined with the banner of bliss and endowed with nine joints,
it rose ten yojanas high and was four yojanas wide.
The great queens shone as they moved upon the sovereign chariot of the wheel-king;
[the Mothers] were consecrated in the Great Wheel, the Song-Wheel, the most excellent of chariots.
Seven joints have been mentioned there; hear now of those goddesses who reside upon the five joints of the great chariot of Kiricakra.
And listen, O wise one, to the names of the deities; victory belongs to those who hear them.
Wherever the king of chariots, the Cakrarāja, is present, there the supreme singing chariot is found.
"Where there is the Geyaratha, there is the Kiricakrarathottama;
these three chariots are like the three worlds moving together.
And so forth. [It was filled] by all those mounted upon the chariot known as the Cakrarāja, equipped with every kind of weapon.

The Goddess is adorned and embellished at the time of battle; the meaning is that all the weapons of the Goddess have been filled and placed upon the chariot of the King of Wheels (cakrarājaratha). Alternatively, it means those all-weapons which have mounted the chariot that is the King of Wheels—the Śrīcakra itself.

"All the means for the knowledge of the Self" and so forth; for in such passages as "he gathers the sacrificial implements," we observe the use of the word *āyudha* (implement) in the sense of a means (*sādhana*). The *āṇavopāya*, *śāktopāya*, *śāmbhavopāya*, and others are specific means taught in the Śaiva scriptures.
The meaning is that those [channels] mentioned in the Yogaśāstra are not distinct from the Śrīcakra. And thus says the Sūtra:
"By performing *saṃyama* on the tip, middle, and end of the nose, what need is there for the left, right, or *sauṣumna* [channels]?
The meaning is that once the *cakra* is mastered, nothing further remains to be accomplished on the path of Yoga. Or else:

The chariot has the Wheel-King itself as its support; that is to say, it is the accomplishment known as "sovereignty over the wheels. Mounted upon that [chariot] is that which is authorized for the bestowing of it—the "all-weapons," meaning that in which all weapons, i.e., all means consisting of ritual actions and so forth, reside. [As stated: "All action in its entirety..."
"Knowledge is completed in Pārtha"—from this statement it follows that [Pārtha] is knowledge; the meaning is that he is Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā).
He is adorned by that. And thus says the Śivasūtra:
"From the arising of Pure Knowledge, there is the attainment of mastery over the circle (cakreśatva). The Vārtikas also state:
When, no longer desiring limited accomplishments, he again desires the supreme accomplishment which consists in manifestation as the Self of the universe, then indeed for him—
Through the arising of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), one attains the state of being the sovereign of the wheel (cakrarāja) and achieves perfection;
desiring the manifestation of the universal self (vaiśvātmya), he unites his own power (śakti).
When the yogi touches the state of Sadāśiva, then for him,
Īśvara is the external unfolding (unmeṣa) and Sadāśiva is the internal closing (nimeṣa).

And according to the principle that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the cognition of "Being-knowledge" (*sad-vidyā*) and the cognition "I am this," the realization arises that "I alone am the entire world."
That pure and stainless knowledge, through its manifest arising— that is,
its emergence— he should perpetually contemplate as his own power of consciousness (cicchakti).

"When the yogi [is thus], then his unsurpassed status as the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśatva) is accomplished for the yogi through the excellence of immersion (samāveśa) into Māheśvarī. Thus it is said. She is mounted upon the chariot of the Geya-cakra and attended by the Mantriṇīs. 77.

She is attended on all sides by the queen Śyāmalā, who is a minister and is mounted upon a chariot called Geyacakra; or else, [she is attended] by that solar orb which possesses such a chariot whose wheel (cakra) is renowned as Geya.
There she is attended by female mantra-practitioners (*mantriṇī*), female practitioners of *vidyā* (*vidyopāsikā*), and female yogis (*yoginī*) who have ascended [to that state].
Alternatively, she is Tripurasundarī, whose primary vehicle (*geya*) is the chariot (*ratha*) known as the *cakra*.
"Ascended" (*ārūḍha*) refers to the act of mounting; that is to say, making it an object of the intellect (*buddhi*) and maintaining a continuous mental connection (*anusandhāna*). By means of that—
"Mantriṇīḥ" refers to those who possess mantra (*mantra*); that which possesses mantra is "mantrin," meaning one who brings forth or makes manifest the potency of mantra (*mantravīrya*).
She is "served" (*parisevitā*) by means of that experience. When one practices the contemplation of oneself as non-different from Tripurasundarī, as it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
The meaning is that the application of the potency of mantra, which is to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru, becomes an experience for him. And thus says the Sūtra:
"From the contemplation of the Great Lake [of consciousness], there is the experience of the potency of mantra."
"The Supreme Goddess Śakti is called the Great Lake (Mahāhrada);
contemplation (anusandhāna) is said to be the reflective awareness of identity with that."
"The potency of mantra is said to be the reflective awareness of the full I-consciousness;
its experience is the clear manifestation of one's own Self.
And this was stated by the Lord in the aphorism: "The secret of mantra is the throbbing of the body of Vidyā."
This has been clearly elucidated in detail by Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 77 ||
[She] was preceded by Daṇḍanātha, who had mounted a chariot whose wheels were shaped like or drawn by boars (*kiri*).

According to Amara, "boar" (*kiri*) is synonymous with *varāha*, *kola*, *potrī*, and *kiṭiri*. [The compound thus refers to] one who has ascended a chariot possessing wheels of that shape or drawn by them.

She is preceded by and served by the Goddess known as Vārāhī. According to the *Tripurāsiddhānta*, the name Daṇḍanātha is etymologically explained as: "Because she always holds a staff (*daṇḍa*) in her hand, she is sung as Daṇḍanāthā.
Alternatively, *kira* means rays (*kiraṇāḥ*), which is to say, emanations (*sṛṣṭayaḥ*). This is an elliptical expression for [the three functions of] creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

Their "wheel" is indeed their collective assembly, which is the chariot; even when mounted upon it, they have not been brought under subjection by the Lord of Punishment, Kṛtānta. Even though a yogi has fallen within the scope of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, he is not an object of the torments of time (*samaya*). This means that his continuous contemplation (*anusandhāna*) remains unimpaired. And thus says the Sūtra:
"Even when those [states] are active, there is no cessation because of the existence of the self-cognizer. And it was explained by the venerable Kṛṣṇadāsa:
"Even during the continuous activity of those states such as creation and so forth..."
Even upon emerging, he remained possessed of the support of unwavering yoga.
"There is no rejection [of anything], because there is no falling away from one's own innate state of self-awareness;
this is due to the wonder of the emerging fourth state (turya), by virtue of its nature as pure perception.
Thus, she stands in the midst of a circle of fire cast forth by Jvālāmālinikā. (78)

The fourteenth lunar day, Jvālāmālinī, is the daily deity (tithinityā). For by her, a wall consisting of fire was constructed all around the venerable Mother. Of that constructed wall consisting of fire which was thus projected—
"Situated in the middle of Varaṇa" means she stands in its central part. And likewise, in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*, there is a statement by the Goddess concerning Jvālāmālinī:
"O child, you are the form of fire, your appearance consisting of garlands of flames."
"Let protection be provided by you for this most excellent child."

"Encompassing the surface of the earth for a hundred *yojanas* in width, it rises thirty *yojanas* high and takes the form of a rampart of flames," and so forth. Or rather, [one might ask]: "But how can a knower (*jñānin*) be encompassed by a creation and so on that is mutually distinct?"
To the question, "How is there no loss of continuity in the investigation of non-duality? he says: "The flame...

[etc. The *mālinikās* are garlands of flames; and those which are projected, as well as those produced at that very moment—the ramparts (*prākārāḥ*), types (*prakārāḥ*), sparks (*sphulliṅgāḥ*), and so forth—[the mind] stands in their midst as the perceiver thereof.

And by virtue of being their creator, she stands as an intermediate witness—like a mediator between two disputing parties—and is changeless; that is to say, although there is change in those [entities] due to her being the agent of creation and so forth, she herself remains unchanging. As it is said in the *Spanda-śāstra*:
And here, there is a pair of states designated as "the state of being an effect" and "the state of being an agent.

Thus: in this context, the "sons of Bhaṇḍa" are the impurities (mala) such as the āṇava and others; "viṣaṅga" means hostile attachment or the longing for sense-objects, or alternatively, that which goes toward poison (*viṣa*), meaning it is of the nature of poison. The accomplishment of sound (*śabdasiddhi*). The meaning is this: when the identification with that [body]—which arises from the verbal designation "living being"—is destroyed by the knowledge of one's own true nature, namely the knowledge of the Lordship over the *puryaṣṭaka*, there occurs an absence of the qualified [entity] caused by the absence of the qualifier. having entered into the nature of reality, which consists of a mass of consciousness and bliss.

"From the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*: 'Those beginning with Rudra and ending with the Piśācas are proclaimed as the bound souls (*paśu*); because he is their lord, Bhava is considered Paśupati, the Lord of all. This [system] belongs to Paśupati, the Lord Sadāśiva; hence it is called Pāśupata."

The city called Śūnyakā was rendered empty by the weapon of Kāmeśvara, which utterly consumed the Asura Bhaṇḍa along with his equipment.

She went to his city; and so it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:

"That city named Śūnyaka was indeed empty in reality.

Or alternatively: having, through this much of the composition, described the state of one who has attained liberation through union (sāyujya-mukti) with the deity called Ātman while still in the state of a living being—a status equal to that of Śiva—now [the author proceeds].

He states that for one who remains under the influence of *prārabdha* karma, the appearance of duality—which resembles a burnt cloth—is destroyed along with its counterpart, the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) and so forth, by means of self-knowledge; thus he declares that only Śiva remains. The weapon of Kāmeśvara is the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*); it belongs to the conscious Self alone.

Because she is the Mistress of Desire (*kāmeśvarī*) by virtue of being desired by all; for the Śruti declares, "Everything becomes dear for the sake of the Self's desires. The demon Bhaṇḍa is the state of being a limited individual (*jīvabhāva*), which causes the appearance of duality.
The meaning of the word *śūnyakā* is the appearance of duality resembling a burnt cloth.

Or rather, it is emptiness itself as accepted by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*). When the state of emptiness, which is accompanied by the state of being a living soul (*jīva*), is removed by the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*), pure consciousness alone remains; thus it is established.

Thus, having been praised by the gods who were oppressed by the demon Bhaṇḍa, and having accomplished the task of the gods ending with the slaying of Bhaṇḍa, she was praised once more by the gratified deities; regarding this, he says:

"Brahmā" means she whose majesty and prowess are perfectly praised by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śakra.

Thus, from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), she is that deity whose nature is the Self (*ātmarūpa*), whose sovereignty (*vibhutva*)—meaning familiarity with or the state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmatva*)—is praised by Brahmā and is unlimited (*aparicchinna*).

She is the life-restoring medicine for Kāma, who was completely consumed and reduced to ashes by the fire residing in Hara’s third eye; she is the very means of revival for Manmatha, even though he was the Lord of Desire who had become utterly detached.

"Indeed, one is consoled by the mother alone"—this maxim is also supported by this very intention.

For it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "When Hari is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no protector at all. One should not suspect that it must be stated that Paramaśiva alone is the limit of the lineage of gurus, and not the reverse; for since even Paramaśiva is a worshipper of Śrīvidyā, and since worship is impossible without a guru, there is a dependence on him, and in that regard, [the lineage] belongs to Tripurasundarī herself.
Because its gravity has been accepted [by tradition]. For this very reason, it was said by Śiva himself to Pārvatī in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:

Thus, since desire is the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*), it is established that the Blessed Lady alone is the impeller of Śiva; therefore, her status as the Guru is proven. Since the *Tantras* enumerate Ādinātha as none other than Paraśiva— distinguished by the power of will (*icchāśakti*)— as in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*, there is no objection that it would follow that Tripurasundarī should be enumerated or worshipped prior to Ādinātha within the circle of gurus (*gurumaṇḍala*).
There is scope for this; and so it is said in the Mahāsvacchandatantra:
"Abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, Sadāśiva himself brought down the Tantra through sentences consisting of questions and answers."

Thus, by the phrase "by herself," the relationship of teacher and disciple between the two aspects of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is indicated. The roles of initiator and questioner reside in the Goddess, while the roles of speaker and one being impelled to act reside [in Śiva].
Since the limiting factors (*avacchedaka*) for the states of being a teacher and a disciple are fixed by devotion to Śiva, there is no contradiction due to their difference.

To illuminate this very point, there is the qualification "in the form of my will" and the address with the word "Lord" (*prabhu*). In reality, however, [the lineage] from Ādinātha downwards is known by the name Ādiśakti-ambā.
Since it is indeed counted in the second position, there is no recurrence of counting it prior to that.

Because Ādinātha, as delimited by the primordial power (Ādi-śakti), is the very guruhood with respect to the third guru named Sadāśiva, he must be counted in the second position alone; thus, there is no question of priority or posteriority between those two.

The lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) is also [to be understood] as the direction [of the argument]. Alternatively, *hara* means taking away; it is the deprivation of one's own essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*).

Or, *harāḥ* refers to those who take away, namely the stealers of the self; their leader (*netā*) or guide is he alone, the fire that pervades everywhere (*āsamantād vyāptaḥ*), because he effects a transformation of one's own essential nature. This is the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

Up to this point: because of the predominance of his fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), that desire which has attained the state of a living soul (*jīva*) is completely burnt away; thus, for the Self—which is the very nature of Kāmeśvara—there follows the attainment of its own true nature during its "living" state, preceded by the complete reversal of its concealment (*āvaraṇa*).

The meaning is that the herb is the root [of knowledge]; through the worship of this [herb] in the form of wisdom, ignorance is removed, and liberation—characterized by the attainment of one's own true nature—is realized. This is because, just as Manmatha was seen to exist later without a body even while still living after his burning [by Śiva], so too is it with the Self.
It is implied that although Brahman alone existed previously, by virtue of ignorance it remained as if possessed of a body;

upon the cessation of that [ignorance], the attainment of oneness with Brahman preceded by bodilessness is indicated. And this very point has been stated in the final chapter of the Śaiva scriptures: "There shall again be the proclaimed union."

In the Vārttika as well: "Furthermore, for the supreme yogin who is firmly established through the higher yoga and so forth, there occurs that which consists of the union with the nature of consciousness already described."
The intention of the statement "it may become even more so" is quite clear:
that which has been described as the state of Śiva for this [yogin] is not something new for him.
That very nature [of the Self], as it were, appears to be defeated by itself due to the wretchedness of various conceptual constructions projected by its own power of illusion (māyā-śakti).

This has been indicated by the word *nija* (intrinsic) within the portion of the aphorism, "the attainment of lordship over the circle of deities of one's own consciousness. By this much of the treatise, the supreme form of the Goddess [has been described].
Because it is subtler than the subtle and higher than the highest, it ought to be spoken of last;

yet, because it is the subject of secret discourse, it was mentioned earlier along with the coarse form—the slaying of the demon Bhaṇḍa—in order to achieve a wordplay (*śleṣa*). Now, the subtle form, which follows in due order, [is described].
He describes her as non-different from the gross form:

By the passage beginning with "Śrīmadvāgbhava," etc., it is shown that even the subtle form is threefold— subtle, subtler, and most subtle— due to the divisions of the fifteen-syllable Vidyā,
the syllable Kāmakalā, and Kuṇḍalinī. Among these, the first is expressed by three names.

His lotus-face is such that its primary and inherent form is the *kūṭa* (syllabic cluster) named Vāgbhava— which, by etymology, means "speech arises from this"— and which possesses the character of majesty such as being the bestower of glorious knowledge. This *kūṭa* is indeed the collection of five syllables.
Of her [it is said]: "The emergence of the letters of the eyes, lips, and the region below the throat within speech is called the 'mouth,' which is the peak-syllable known as Vāgbhava. || 85 ||
She whose nature is that of the central peak extending from below the throat to the waist:
that middle portion which begins below the throat and ends at the waist is itself the own (sva) or innate [nature] of the six-syllable collection known as Kāmarāja situated in the center.

Her form [is such]; the possessive suffix is applied even after a karmadhāraya compound, as in the example "her eyes are sharp and luminous. She bears the lower part of her waist, which has attained a state of unity with the peak of power (śakti). || 86 ||

Because she possesses the power of creation (*sarjana-śakti*), she holds the lower part of Kaṭi, which has attained non-duality (*ekatvam-abhedam*) with the *kūṭa* named Śakti—a collection of four syllables; thus she is so described.
As it has been said:
"O Mother, because He dwells in Your heart as desire, He is the King of Desire (Kāmarāja); and because of His creative power, thereafter follows Your Peak of Power (Śaktikūṭa). || 86 ||

She whose essence is the root-mantra (mūlamantra) and whose body consists of the three root-syllables (kūṭa), is called "the Root" (mūla) because she is the fundamental cause of the fourfold aims of human existence (puruṣārtha). That very [mantra] of fifteen syllables is a "mantra" because it protects through contemplation (manana). Her "self" (ātman) is her own essential nature (svarūpa). As it has been said:

"Mantra is said to be that which consists of the contemplation of full I-consciousness, which, by its nature of manifesting through reflection, brings about the destruction of transmigratory existence through its nature of protection.
Thus, she whose body is the gross form consisting of the three *kūṭas* of the root [mantra] according to the aforementioned method—

Alternatively, it means that whose body is the subtle form consisting of the three *kūṭas* themselves. In reality, however, by the two words "root" (*mūla*) and "sound" (*śabda*), the syllable *Kāmakalā* is expressed; whereas by the term "three *kūṭas*" (*kūṭatraya*), the constituent parts forming the aggregate of three are expressed, because the suffix *tayap* is prescribed [by Pāṇini] in the sense of a part of a whole.
In the *Kāmakalā*, there is one upper bindu, below it two transverse bindus,
and below those the "half-and-a-half" (*sārdhakalā*)— these three constituent parts are to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru.
These very parts, in sequence, transform into the form of the *Vidyākūṭa* and into the nature of the gross forms, such as the face and other limbs.

Thus, the two names—*sūkṣmatara* (the subtler) known as Kuṇḍalinī and *sūkṣmatama* (the subtlest), the supreme form of the best—are distinguished by the difference between the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*); this is the detailed account in the tradition of the Guru’s feet (*nāthacaraṇāgama*).
Having thus described the form within the macrocosm (*brahmāṇḍa*), [he now describes] that which resides within the microcosm (*piṇḍāṇḍa*).

He begins to describe the form known as Kuṇḍalinī: for she, sleeping in the wheel called Mūlādhāra in the shape of three and a half coils, is awakened by yogins; piercing the six wheels and the knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, she is led to the thousand-spoked [lotus].
It causes nectar to flow from the lunar mandala in the form of its pericarp.
Even by non-yogins, this entire process is accomplished through mere meditation;
he now states the names [of the deities] dedicated to that process:
She delights solely in the nectar of the Kula and protects the conventions of the Kula. || 87 ||

By the words "the nectar of the *kula*," and so forth: *Kula* is a collection of things belonging to the same genus (*sajātīya*). And that [collection] consists of a triad—the knower, the known, and the knowledge—having attained a commonality in the form of being objects of a single cognition, because the form of cognition is precisely "I know the jar."

If the manifestation of knowledge were dependent upon a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), it would entail the absurdity of a lamp requiring another lamp for its own manifestation. And as it has been stated by the venerable Ācārya Bhagavatpāda: "This entire world shines only after that [Self] which shines, thinking 'I know'. Consequently, that is the triad (*tripuṭī*).

It is called *kula*. As it is stated in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*: "The *kula*, characterized by the object of knowledge (*meya*), the knower (*mātṛ*), and the act of knowing (*miti*), reaches its ultimate rest therein. This refers to the thirty-two lotuses described in works such as the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*, which exist in an arrangement of upper and lower positions.
The lotus at the very bottom is called *akula* because it lacks connection with the *tripuṭī*;

those situated above it are connected to *kula*. Alternatively, *ku* refers to the earth element (*pṛthvītattva*), and that in which it dissolves is *kula*, namely the *ādhāra-cakra*; by association, the term also metaphorically denotes the path of the *suṣumṇā*.

Therefore, the nectar flowing from the thousand-spoked [cakra] is the *kulāmṛta*. According to the statement in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*, "The body is called *kula*," it is the *kulāmṛta* because of its connection with the body. In that regard, the *rasikā* is primarily intent on tasting that flavor. [She is] the "flowering one" (*puṣpitā*) whose abode is the *kula*.

Because of the application [of the term] in the *Kālītantra*: "The man who, having seen [it], mutters [the mantra]," and because the entire collection of objects consisting of the worshipped and the worshipper are of the same nature (*sājātya*) due to being of the nature of consciousness (*cittva*), the scripture that expounds that collection is also called *kula*. Thus it is said in the *Kalpasūtra*:
The application [of the term] is as follows: "One should guard the family scriptures," and in the Āgama: "Indeed, all philosophical systems enter into the family alone.

Furthermore, because of the statement in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "They do not call family by the word 'family'; conduct is called family," conduct (*ācāra*) is also the family; these are the conventions regarding those two.

It is so because it protects the secrets therein, does not reveal them to the uninitiated (paśus), and, having revealed them for the sake of the traditional lineage, sets the thread of the tradition in motion;
thus it is said: "The convention of the *cakra* and the conventions of mantra and worship."

"O Supreme Goddess, the convention of the goddess Tripurā is threefold," so it is said in the Āgama. "Then, having entered the royal streets, this noble lady [arrives] within the houses of convention."
This same point is established in the *Cintāmaṇistava*: "Having rested repeatedly and having united with the Supreme Person, [the Goddess] brings forth the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). || 87 ||
She is a noble woman (*kulāṅganā*), established within the *kula*, a *kaulinī*, and a *kulayoginī*.

"Kula" refers to a lineage whose character consists of a mass of virtues such as devotion to one's husband; just as a woman belonging to such a lineage is protected [from public view], so too is she a "noble woman" because she is concealed by the curtain of ignorance (*avidyājavanikā*).
As it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"All other sciences are manifest like jewels,
but this Śāmbhavī science is hidden like a woman of noble family."
Thus [it is said]. The Blessed Paraśurāma also said: "Other sciences are like courtesans, excessively exposed," and so forth.

She resides within the *kula*—that is, between the mother (*mātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*meya*)—in the form of the means of knowledge (*miti*). Or, she resides within the *Kula-śāstra* as the object to be known (*jñeya*). In every house and in every region...

It remains as an object of worship for every body or every lineage. Regarding the word *kula*, the *Viśva* lexicon states: "In a country, a house, a group of those belonging to the same caste, a clan (*gotra*), and even in the body—it is called *kula*.
This has also been stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"The Goddess is to be worshipped by people in every place, in every city, in every house by those devoted to Śakti, in every village, and in every forest.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the red thousand-petaled lotus situated below is also the *kula*; in its pericarp...
The *Svacchanda Tantra* provides a detailed exposition on this point, stating that the *Kuladevis* and the *Kulaśaktis* reside upon the petals [of the lotus].
From the word *kula* in this sense, the derivative *kaula* is formed by adding a suffix in the sense of a general relationship (*sambandha-sāmānya*).
It is said: "Kula is declared to be Śakti, while Akula is called Śiva."

"The connection between the *akula* and the *kula* is designated as *kaula*," so it is stated in the Tantras. Alternatively, *kaula* refers to the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti; that which possesses this is *kaulinī*.
Having drawn a *cakra* within the space of the external sky, the worship and other rites performed therein constitute *kaula*.

Some say it is so called by convention (*rūḍhi*). She is a *kulayoginī* because she possesses a connection (*yoga*), that is, a relationship, with the *kula* whose meaning has already been explained. Regarding the statement by the authors of the *Chalākṣara-sūtra* that the eight syllables [of the mantra] constitute a single name—namely, *Kaulinī* and *Kulayoginī*—the justification for this is given in the tenth [chapter].
We shall explain this in the *Śataka*.
She who is without lineage (*akula*), who abides within the *samaya*, and is devoted to the conduct of the *samaya*—[she is the consort]. (88)

The thousand-petaled lotus situated at the upper end of the *suṣumṇā* is called *akula*. Thus it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "Beginning from [the description] 'below and above the *suṣumṇā*, joined with a thousand petals'... [it continues] 'O Īśānī, these two lotuses consist of *kula* and *akula*.'"

Up to the word "śubham" [the mantra is recited]. It is called *akulā* because it has that as its form (*tadrūpatvāt*) or because it is established therein (*tanniṣṭhatvāt*), or because it possesses no *kula*—such as body, lineage, and so forth. Having visualized the wheel within the space of the *dahara-ākāśa*, the ritual worship and other rites performed there are conventionally designated by the term *samaya*. And this is unanimously agreed upon by all yogis.

Because it is a convention (*saṅketa*) in the sense that its meaning has been definitively determined (*nirṇīta*), it is called *samaya*. Furthermore, because it expounds that [meaning], the pentad of tantras known as the *Vasiṣṭha*, *Śuka*, *Sanaka*, *Sanandana*, and *Sanatkumāra* is also designated by the term *samaya*. It exists within that [pentad] as that which is to be expounded. Alternatively, *sama* means equality (*sāmya*).

"Śiva is *samaya* because he goes (*yāti*); [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*. Śakti is *samayā*, and there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of these two. Furthermore, the mutual equality (*sāmya*) of Śiva and Śakti is fivefold:
equality of substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), equality of practice (*anuṣṭhāna*), equality of state (*avasthāna*), and equality of name (*nāma*)."
And "similarity of form" (*rūpasāmya*) refers to the following: the *adhiṣṭhāna* (substratum) is the locus of worship, such as the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth;

the *anuṣṭhāna* (performance) is the ritual activity of emanation and so forth; the *avasthāna* (state) is the action of dancing and so forth; the *nāman* (name) is Bhairava and so forth; and the *rūpa* (form) is the reddish hue and so forth. And the detailed expansion of this [is as follows]:

In the commentary on the *Vāsanāsubhagodaya* composed by Lalla, it is said that [the deity] abides in their end (*anta*) as their essential nature (*svarūpa*). Regarding the word "end" (*anta*), the *Viśvakośa* states: "End (*anta*) means limit, proximity, destruction, and essential nature (*svarūpa*); it is most enchanting. In the *Rudrayāmala*, the conduct taught in ten chapters is called *samayācāra*. Alternatively:
When, for the initiated disciple, through the power of the Guru’s glance,
there arises on the Mahānavamī day both the firmness of contemplation upon either of the sixfold or fourfold unities and the purificatory rite known as the "Great Piercing" (mahāvedha).
Afterwards, the Goddess, having risen from the *mūlādhāra*, becomes manifest in the *maṇipūra*.
Having worshipped her there with the services beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with ornaments, and having led her to the *anāhata* center,
worshipped her up to the end of the betel offering (*tāmbūla*), and then led her to the *viśuddhi* center, [one should worship] the digit of the moon located there—

Having filled [the vessel] with forms and jewels, having led it to the *ājñācakra* and performed the *nīrājana* rite, he united it with Sadāśiva in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasradalakamala*) amidst the honey of the bees; then, having drawn the curtain (*tiraskariṇī*) and stationed himself within the nearby temple, he remained there until the Goddess emerged once again.

The manner in which she enters the pit of the *mūlādhāra* and waits for the appointed time (*samaya*) right there is the practice of the observance (*samayācāra*), to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru. Devoted to both of these two modes, she is intent upon them,
her sole abode is the *mūlādhāra*, and she pierces the knot of Brahmā (*brahmagranthi*).

In the center of the pericarp of the four-petalled lotus called Mūlādhāra, within the point known as Kulakuṇḍa, Kuṇḍalinī remains perpetually asleep, having covered her mouth. Therefore, because it is the foundation of this and the root of the Suṣumṇā, it is called Mūlādhāra.

Thus it is said. She is she whose sole primary abode (*nilaya*)—that is, her place of residence—is that very [state]. In the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), there are two knots (*granthi*) at the beginning and end of each wheel. Among these, she is so called because she specifically pierces the two Brahma-knots belonging to the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by the venerable Bhāsurānanda, the second digit, Tāpinī, has been [expounded] by means of the first hundred [verses]. (100)
Thus ends the second part, named the first century, in the *Paribhāṣā-bhāṣya* on the *Lalitāsahasranāma*, composed by the venerable Bhāskararāya, author of the *Padavākyapramāṇa* and other works. 2.
The third digit, called the Second Hundred, is the Smoky (dhūmrikā) kalā; arisen within the Maṇipūra, it pierces the knot of Viṣṇu. || 89 ||

In the ten-petaled lotus at the navel, during the conventional (sāmayika) worship, the Goddess is filled with and adorned by jewels and gems; thus, that wheel is designated by the term "Maṇipūra. Having pierced the knot situated below it, she has arisen and become manifest, having specifically distinguished [and pierced] the Viṣṇu-knot situated above that.

It is "thus" because it pierces [the knots]. Because the Maṇipūra-cakra is situated in Viṣṇu, the two knots there are designated as the "Viṣṇu-knots. In the same way, those designated as the "Brahma-knots" and "Rudra-knots" are also to be understood. (89)
Situated within the center of the *ājñācakra*, it pierces the *rudragranthi*.
The name *ājñācakra* is derived from the abiding of the venerable Guru, the bestower of command (*ājñāpakas*), in the two-petaled lotus between the eyebrows; [the channel] extends up to that point.
Or, it means that through the practice of mental conflict (*manovigraha*), there arises a slight emergence of knowledge; the prefix *ā-* here signifies "slightness.

It remains in the interval between those two. It is so called because it pierces the two Rudra-knots located in the heart within the Anāhata-cakra. In the case of ritual application (*anuṣṭhāna*), the reverse of this should be inferred.

This is because the sequence of meaning is more powerful than the sequence of recitation, according to the rule from the fifth book [of Pāṇini]: "On account of the sense" (arthāt). Alternatively, in the Śrīvidyā there are four sections known as Āgneya, Saura, Saumya, and Candrakalā; these are also known as Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, Śakti, and Turya.

Among those four, there are three knots known as *hṛllekhā*. These three are, respectively, named Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. He pierces that triad and enters into its interior; this is the meaning of "designated by that. In reality, however, [this is stated] in the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*:
This group of six names is the supreme Kaulika meaning as taught in the *Ṣaḍarthaprakaraṇa*. As it is said in that very work:
"The group of six cakras beginning with the Mūlādhāra is known as *kula*; therein lies the triple knot, O Goddess, which contains within it the triad of cakras."

"The two wheels of earth and water, arising from the location of the *brahmagranthi*, consist of fire and sun; they are a great, radiant pair of wheels. The wheel described by the term *viṣṇugranthi* is composed of light and bestows all spiritual accomplishments."
The two supreme wheels have the dual nature of wind and space.
"The great abode of auspiciousness has been described by the term 'Rudragranthi,'" and so forth.
Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus, she rains down a stream of nectar. (90)
She has ascended that lotus whose petals (or spokes) number one thousand,
situated below the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
[she is] a downpour of nectar from its pericarp, which is connected to the moon.

She whose nature it is to rain down upon him a continuous stream [of grace], according to the Vedic revelation: "May the stream of nectar, being milked in many ways, establish our conduct firmly placed in the world. (90)

She possesses a luster equal to a streak of lightning and is situated above the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*). "A streak of lightning" refers to *saudāminī*, which is a creeper (*latā*); thus, she has a luster—meaning a radiance—equal to that. This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "Shining like a streak of lightning. The term "six wheels" (*ṣaṭcakrāṇi*) refers to those consisting of six parts.
This is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*). Consequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not apply according to the rule for *dvigu* compounds.
These [centers] are named Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā-cakra; she is perfectly situated above them in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*).
The great power Kuṇḍalinī is thinner than a lotus fiber. || 91 ||
She whose attachment—that is, her devotion—is to the *mahotsava*, which consists of the union (*samāyoga*) of Śiva and Śakti there;

according to Amara, "maha" means "uddhava" (exaltation) or "utsava" (festival). Or, she whose attachment is to the splendor of fire (*vahnitejas*); according to Viśva, "maha" means "festival" or "splendor. Or, she whose great (*mahatī*) and all-pervasive (*ā*) attachment—that is, her union—is [with Him].
She is called Kuṇḍalinī because she possesses earrings (kuṇḍala), or because she is a female serpent by her form. And her essential nature is described in the Tantrarāja:
"She is situated in the midst of the fire-like light located at the Mūlādhāra."
The power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), known as Kuṇḍalinī, is of the nature of vital breath (prāṇa) and is luminous (taijasī).
Having the form of a sleeping serpent, with three coils and great splendor,
she whose head is Māyā roars incessantly as she rises into the sky.
"When that [sound] in the middle of the *suṣumṇā* is not heard by one who has closed both ears, then death occurs for him," and so forth. Also, in the *Yogavasiṣṭha*, in the *Cūḍālā-upākhyāna*:
"Know Kuṇḍalinī to be the life-principle within the mind—which is otherwise called the *puryaṣṭaka*—just as a flower-cluster is the life-principle within a fragrance.
And the etymology of her name is given in the Devīpurāṇa: "Because she has the form of a *śṛṅgāṭaka* (a triangle)..."
"Then she is called Kuṇḍalinī"—or rather, "Kuṇḍalinī" is the name for the seed-syllable *vāgbhava*.

She is of the form of a lotus-fiber (*bisatantu*); like that very fiber of a lotus stalk, she is exceedingly slender, having an extremely thin form. This is according to the Śruti: "She is as thin as the awn of a grain of wild rice (*nīvāra*), yellow, radiant, and comparable to an atom."
The entire process of liberation, beginning with the words "those who delight solely in the nectar of the Kula" and ending here,
has been clearly elucidated in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
"Residing in the Mūlādhāra in the form of a coiled serpent..."
The power named Kuṇḍalinī is auspicious and resembles a lotus fiber.
Holding the root-tuber with the tip of her hood like a lotus-root held by its tusk,
she joins her tail to the mouth and unites it with the *brahmarandhra*.
Seated on a lotus posture and established in composure, the practitioner, contracting the anus and fixing his mind upon the kumbhaka, causes the vital air to move upward.
By the force of the impact of the wind, the fire situated in its own locus blazes;
and by the impacts of that blazing fire and the wind, the sovereign serpent is awakened.
Then, having pierced the Brahma-knot, one pierces the Viṣṇu-knot;
and having indeed split the Rudra-knot, one pierces the six lotuses.

"In the thousand-petaled lotus, Śakti rejoices together with Śiva; that state is to be known as the supreme (parā), and it alone is the cause of bliss. Thus it is said. It is also heard in the Aruṇopaniṣad:
"Arise, do not sleep; seek Agni, O Bhāratas!
Satiated by King Soma, you shall be united with the splendor of the Sun.
And this entire Upaniṣad is devoted solely to the Blessed Goddess, as is seen from the supporting corroborative texts (upabṛṃhaṇa).
This is because she is mentioned in the *Śyāmalāsahasranāma* as "the song of the Aruṇopaniṣad. This is a mutual utterance among the practitioners named Pṛśni;
it refers to Bhāratī, Sarasvatī, and Vidyā. Those related to her are the Bhāratas. O [Bhārati]!
O worshippers of Śrīvidyā, arise and proceed with the sequence of worship! Do not sleep;

do not be negligent! Alternatively, these two verbal roots may be understood as having an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), with Kuṇḍalinī as their object. [Arouse] Agni, who consists of the fiery splendor located in the Svādhiṣṭhāna.

Desire the Kuṇḍalinī; having struck her with the staff of will (icchā-daṇḍa), raise her up by means of that fire which is conjoined with the Sun—that is, together with the Sun situated between the Viśuddha and Anāhata cakras. [Raise her] from the Moon—meaning from the Moon that has been burnt and liquefied—accompanied by Umā, the Sovereign of the Kings of Kings (Rājarājeśvarī).

Of the King, the Lord of the Kings of Kings, who resides within the thousand-spoked lunar disc—or, by implication, being satisfied by the nectar—may you become satisfied; may you be satiated. Having raised up the fire-cuṇḍalinī and joined it with the sun-cuṇḍalinī, by means of those two...

The meaning is that, having caused [the body] to melt through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the lunar orb, the auspicious Śiva and Śakti, one should become satiated by filling the paths of the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) with the streams of nectar arising therefrom. In the word *tṛptāsaḥ*, the augment *asu* is applied according to the rule *ājjaseḥ*. Likewise—
"Whatever a maiden utters, whatever a woman [utters], whatever a devoted wife [utters], and whatever auspicious act is performed—Agni penetrates all that.
*Ku* is the earth-element (*pṛthvītattva*); that in which one dies—that is, dissolves—is the *kula-kuṇḍa*, the "youthful" (the womb).

The maiden associated with that is the *kulakuṇḍalinī*. She "mandrayate," meaning she resounds with a deep, low tone (*mandrasvara*). Precisely because she is accompanied by the state of weeping (*rodana*) and because her arousal from the *kulakuṇḍa* constitutes her very nature as an emergence, she is called the "newly born maiden" (*sadya-utpannā kumārī*). She is a young woman.

Because she is united with the sun characterized by youth in the upper region of the unstruck (*anāhata*) [cakra], the devoted wife (*pativratā*) "vows" (that is, enjoys) her husband, Kāmeśvara, who resides in the *brahmarandhra*. This is according to the usage seen in such expressions as "the milk-vow (*payovrata*) of a Brāhmaṇa. Thus, through the enjoyments of childhood and youth, [she attains] the state of immortality (*ariṣṭa*).

Whatever else there may be, such as auspicious acts in the form of raining down nectar, all that is performed or accomplished by Agni residing in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, who kindles it; the sense is that [this occurs] precisely through the blazing of Agni from the melting of the lunar orb (*candramaṇḍala*). This is corroborated in the *Sanatkumāra-tantra*:
"The sages named Pṛśnis, who are devotees of the Śrīvidyā, have come together and are instructing one another: 'Awaken her; do not delay!'"
"O descendants of Bharata, you desire fire as the presiding deity upon the pericarp;
having driven away the Sun, King Soma is satisfied," and so forth, ending with: "In the case of a devoted wife (*pātivratya*), fire alone is her companion. Thus...
The mantra, "The radiant, pure gate of the world— luminous, shining, and glorious;

yielding manifold streams of immortality— may it establish us in a well-placed station in the world," also refers to the gate, that is, the means of access, to the world, namely the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
The words *arcis*, *jyotis*, and *mahaḥ* denote the digits of fire, the sun, and the moon, respectively.

The word *caraṇa*, derived from the etymology "that which moves" (*carati*) or "performs coming and going" (*yātāyātaṃ karoti*), refers to Kuṇḍalinī. It is neuter in the general sense. [The word] *sudhitān* means "satisfied. [This concerns] the letter *ha*.

The substitution of the letter *dh* for the word *arciḥ* and the elision of the letter *s* are Vedic (chāndasa). The meaning is: may Kuṇḍalinī, having reached the locus of fire and the other elements, cause us to be satisfied by raining down nectar (*sudhā*). This very point is further elaborated [in the following verse]:
In the Śukrasaṃhitā: "The stream of nectar, being milked by the flame of fire, the light of the sun, and the splendor of the moon, flows in seventy-two thousand ways."
"May that Kuṇḍalinī, whose conduct is secret, grant satisfaction to us.

Here, the meaning of the word *caraṇa* (conduct) is "she who moves in a manner that is hidden (*guptam*). In this way, corroborative passages (*upabṛṃhaṇāni*) should also be sought in the Vasiṣṭha-tantra and other scriptures. || 91 ||
Bhavānī is accessible through meditation; she is the axe that cuts down the forest of worldly existence (*bhava*).
She is called Bhavānī because she brings about (*ānayati*) and sustains (*jīvayati*) *bhava*—whether understood as Mahādeva, *saṃsāra*, or *kāma*.
As it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*, in the chapter on etymologies (*nirvacanādhyāya*): [text follows]

"Rudra, Bhava, Bhava, Kāma, Bhava, and the ocean of saṃsāra—because she is the life-force (prāṇana) of all these, this Goddess is celebrated as Bhavānī. Alternatively, "Bhava" is the name of the Supreme Lord in his watery form; she is his consort.
The mother is named Uṣā, and the son is known as Śukra. As it is stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"He is called Bhava by the gods and the exponents of the Vedas, because he brings beings into existence (bhava) through the life-sustaining power of the Supreme Self."
"Uṣā is proclaimed as his wife, and Śukra as his son by the wise. Also, in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"That which is the second body of Bhava is indeed remembered as Water (Āpaḥ)."
"His wife was named Uṣā, and his son is remembered as Uśanas.
The derivation of the word *bhava* is also given in that same place:
"Because beings arise from them, and because they cause [beings] to flourish (*bhāvayanti*)."
"Because of existing (*bhavana*) and because of causing to exist (*bhāvanā*), he is remembered as *Bhava* among living beings.

Here, the word "from them" (*tābhyaḥ*) means "from the waters" (*adbhyaḥ*), according to the reading that begins with, "Therefore, the waters are remembered as *Bhava*. He brings even the water that constitutes life—that is, he causes [beings] to live.

Bhavānī. Alternatively, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied in the sense of "the wife of Bhava" according to the rule for feminine nouns derived from masculine names (*puṃyogalakṣaṇa*). The augment *ānuk* is added by the rule beginning with "indravaruṇa...
(*Pāṇini 4.1.49*). She is the presiding deity of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) known as Sthāneśvara. As it has been said:
In the *Pādma Purāṇa*, in the chapter on the "Garland of One Hundred and Eight Tīrthas of the Goddess," it says:

"At Sthāneśvara she is named Bhavānī, and at Bilvaka she is named Nāmapatrakā. Having thus described these five forms, he speaks of the means for attaining them through several names. First, regarding *bhāvanā* (meditative cultivation):

There are two kinds: verbal *bhāvanā* (śābdī bhāvanā) and objective *bhāvanā* (ārthī bhāvanā). Among these, the verbal [bhāvanā] resides in Vedic words and shares the same status as the intention of a teacher; indeed, we have already established in our discussion on the curiosity regarding the Mīmāṃsaka doctrine that it is simply the will of God (*īśvarecchā*). The objective [bhāvanā], however, consists in the form of activity (*pravṛtti*).

It has also been explained in that very same place that [meditation] consists of the mutual relationship between the factors of action (*kāraka*). The meaning is that it is either unattainable or attainable by those two, being outside the scope of the path of ritual action (*karmamārga*), or else it is of the nature of the purification of the mind produced thereby.
