Alternatively, meditation (*bhāvanā*) is threefold; as it has been said:
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "O twice-born ones, the three contemplations— the Brāhmī, the Māheśvarī, and likewise the Akṣarabhāvanā— constantly abide in Rudra."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, elsewhere:
"O Brahman, understand from me the threefold meditation as it is being described:
one among them has me as its object, and the second has the Unmanifest as its support."
"But the last one, the Brāhmī, should be known as possessing three qualities and being of three kinds.

This is the statement of the Lord in his Kūrma incarnation addressed to Indradyumna. Furthermore, the extraction of the definition of this [Brāhmī] has been made by the Dīkṣitas in the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā*. From that...
This is how it should be understood: "Everything up to the level of Ājñā is called Sakala (with parts); beyond that is Sakalaniṣkala (partially without parts).
At the end of Unmanī is the supreme state, which is Niṣkala (without parts), existing in three ways."
Thus, there are three meditations (*bhāvanā*) characterized as described in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*; she is to be reached and known through them.

Existence (*bhava*), which is transmigratory existence itself, is a forest because of its extreme density and because it sprouts again and again. She is like an axe for that [forest]; the feminine gender is used because the lexicon states, "the word *kuṭhāra* [is used] in two genders."
The meaning is "she who cuts that [bond]";
she is the beloved of the auspicious, the embodiment of auspiciousness, and the bestower of good fortune upon her devotees. 92.

She for whom auspiciousness (*bhadra*), blessing (*maṅgala*), and endearment (*priya*) exist; or, she for whom the *bhadra*—a specific type of elephant—and elephants of that breed are dear. She whose form and nature (*mūrti-svarūpa*) are auspicious (*bhadrā*, i.e., excellent).
As stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "They know that Brahman is auspicious" (*maṅgala*). And [as it is said]: "Of all auspicious things..."

And from the *Mahābhārata*: "It is auspicious (*maṅgalam*). According to the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the meanings of the word *bhaga* are "fortune, beauty, desire, majesty, heroism, effort, the sun, and fame.
That which possesses these auspicious qualities is *subhagā*; she is indeed *lalitā*, and her state is [the quality of being so].
Good fortune (*saubhāgya*) means non-difference from that [the Supreme Reality]. As for what is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Sugarcanes, the king of trees (the *tāla*), flat beans, and *jīradhānyaka* grains;
likewise, cow's milk that has undergone transformation, and safflower as well as its flower."
And salt as the eighth—thus the "eightfold fortune" (*saubhāgyāṣṭaka*) is described.

Even that which is enumerated in this statement is indeed "fortune" (*saubhāgya*), because it is useful for auspicious rites and because it brings prosperity (*śrīkara*). It is excellent fortune (*suṣṭhu bhāgyaṃ*).
The state of one for whom there is destiny is "fortune" (saubhāgya); he is so called because he bestows those [fortunes] upon his devotees.

In this regard, the following should be understood: these nine names, beginning with *mahāśakti* and ending with this [last one], are indicated by the *chalākṣara-sūtra* as "baḍaṇ. For instance, it is stated in the *Vararuci-saṅketa*: "The group of *ya* [consonants] consists of eight here, but it is designated as nine," namely: *ka, ā, jñā, dvāḥ, ṭa, ya, au*.

The meaning of these two sūtras is that there are nine doors starting from the letter *ka* and extending up to the letter *jha*; the *ṭa*-class and *ya*-class are likewise [nine each]. *Piṣuḥ*: the term *pa*-class is a designation for the five [consonants] beginning with *pa*.
She who is fond of devotion, accessible through devotion, subject to devotion, and the remover of fear.

Devotion is of two kinds: primary (mukhyā) and secondary (gauṇī). Among these, the primary devotion is a specific modification of the mind (cittavṛttiviśeṣa) characterized by attachment toward the Lord. And so it is said:

The *Bhaktimīmāṃsāsūtra* states: "It is supreme attachment to the Lord. The meaning of the term *tat* (that) is the devotion (*bhakti*) introduced by the sūtra: "Now, therefore, the desire to know devotion. Regarding this, "supreme" (*parā*) is its qualification. With reference to that specific type of devotion which is supreme—that is, primary—attachment is prescribed as its defining characteristic.
That is its meaning. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* states that the word "para" (supreme) excludes the secondary (*gauṇī*) [form of devotion].
In the sūtra, "But through the secondary, the perfection of concentration," secondary devotion is described as being in the form of service (*sevā*).
And so it is said in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"The root *bhaj* is indeed proclaimed to mean service (*sevā*);
therefore, service has been declared by the wise to be the primary means for attaining devotion (*bhakti*).
Its various forms include remembrance (*smaraṇa*), chanting (*kīrtana*), and so forth. By this—
"Indeed, this eightfold devotion exists even in an outcaste;
he is a lord of Brahmins, an ascetic, a glorious one, a sage, and a scholar."

Thus says the statement from the *Āditya-purāṇa* and the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*. "O King, devotion is of nine kinds," and so forth, is the statement from the *Bhāgavata*. And there is the passage establishing its tenfold nature: "Devotion is to be known as tenfold, like a forest fire to the wilderness of sin."
Other such statements from the *Bṛhannāradīya* are merely reiterative (anuvāda) by way of partial extraction (*avayutya*).
She is one for whom such a category of devotion (*bhakti*) is dear. And so it is said in the *Śivapurāṇa*:
"What can be done for me by men, who am fulfilled and satisfied?"
"Whether external or internal, indeed my being (bhāva) is grasped.

Here, by the word *bhāva*, both the external activity in the form of service and the internal intention are grasped. [She is] reachable through devotion and propitiation; she is directly perceptible. And thus says the Śruti:
"The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore, people look outward and not at the inner self.
Only some wise man, desiring immortality, looks within at the inward self with his eyes turned back.
Thus [it is said]. Smṛti also says: "Yogis behold that eternal Blessed Lord."

The same is stated in the *Yogasūtra*: "Or, from devotion to the Lord" (*īśvarapraṇidhānād vā*). This is because the term *praṇidhāna* is explained in the *Rājamārtaṇḍa* as being synonymous with *bhakti*. Furthermore, the *Brahmasūtra* also states:
"Moreover, through intense devotion (*saṃrādhana*), [the unmanifest Brahman is known] by means of perception and inference. Thus, even the unmanifest Brahman is [attained] through devotion.
The meaning of this is that it becomes directly perceived, because it is understood as such from both Śruti and Smṛti:
"But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, am I— such as I am—
capable of being known in truth, seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of foes."
This is also the word of the Blessed One. Here, by the phrase "to enter," liberation known as the state of Brahman is expressed;

the meaning is that even this is obtained through devotion alone. Therefore, in the context [of the verse], the term *gamyapada* (the goal to be reached) should be explained as referring to that which is to be attained. As it is said in the Śruti: "Established in Brahman, one attains immortality."

This is because it is established as such by the word *saṃsthā*, which denotes devotion (*bhakti*) as a synonym for finality (*niṣṭhā*). For this very reason, there is the sūtra in the *Bhaktimīmāṃsā*: "Because immortality is taught for one who is established in that" (*tatsaṃsthasyāmṛtatvopadeśāt*);
and likewise, the sūtra in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*: "Because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon that" (*tanniṣṭhasya mokṣopadeśāt*).
In the *Nityātantra* as well, after first describing the characteristics of devotion,
its quality of bestowing all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) has been stated: "In a Guru endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, and likewise in [the teachings] proclaimed by him..."
It is the destroyer of doubt for one whose mind is steadfast in both knowledge and practice.
"Devotion, which bestows all goals when practiced with vigilance and as a savior, has been described;
devoid of it, one is certainly miserable both in this world and the next.
Alternatively, "devotion" (*bhakti*) is used in its secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*), meaning that [the goal] is to be reached or understood through it by those possessing specific capacities.

Because words such as "truth" (*satya*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) cannot denote a Brahman devoid of attributes; for this very reason, it will be stated in the *Triśatī*: "The indicated meaning is that which is to be reached through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And: "According to Aitiśāyana, all [the priests] share the same mantra, because the purifying power of devotion belongs to the entire assembly."
In the *Jaimini-sūtra*, the term *bhakti* is used in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*). In our own hymn to Śiva as well:
"I have no power even to praise a single atom of Your glorious majesty."
Nevertheless, having relied upon some measure of devotion to you, I have performed this;
for it is not the platforms that cry out, yet the proclamation proceeded just as it does in the world through devotion, O Supreme Śiva, and not by one's own inherent power.
Thus, she is "subdued" (*vaśyā*), meaning dependent upon devotion characterized by the aforementioned definition; or alternatively, "subdued by devotion," according to the statement:
"Though independent, she attains dependence through devotion to Śiva. She is the "remover of fears" (*bhayāpahā*), for she destroys all fears arising from water, land, and so forth. [She is] bliss...
"From the Vedic scripture: 'The knower of Brahman fears nothing whatsoever. Likewise, in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
'Whether in a forest, in a wilderness, in water, or even on land—especially in places of fear from tigers, crocodiles, or thieves.'"
"And in all the [protective] amulets as well, one should recite the names of the goddesses:
Śāmbhavī, Śāradārādhyā, Śarvāṇī, and Śarmadāyinī. (93)
She is the consort of Śambhu, the mother of the Śāmbhavas, or Śāmbhavī;
this is the name of a specific *mudrā* in the Yogaśāstra. Its definition is given in that very same work:
"The gaze is fixed externally while the internal object of focus remains, free from both closing and opening the eyes."

"This is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, hidden in all Tantras. However, in the Kalpasūtra, there are three initiations (dīkṣās)—Śāktī, Śāmbhavī, and Māntrī—and their characteristics are explained in detail; in the Devībhāgavata, it is stated: "And the eight-year-old [initiation] is Śāmbhavī."

The name of a particular maiden has been mentioned; the meaning is that she possesses such a form. She is to be worshipped by Śāradā (Sarasvatī) and the goddesses of speech; or, she is to be worshipped in the autumn season (*śarad*), at the beginning of the rains, etc., for according to Amara: "Now, *śaratsamāḥ* [is] a year. And: "In the autumn season, the Great Worship (*mahāpūjā*) is performed."

Regarding the phrase "and that which is annual" (*vārṣikī*), it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* that "annual" means occurring at the beginning of the year. Furthermore, from the *Rudrayāmala*: "One should worship Raktadantikā during the Navarātra in spring. [This is understood] by autumnal, proficient scholars.

She was worshipped by those whose character conforms to the specific stage of life known as *śālīna*. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The term *śārada* may refer to one with yellow seals (*pītamudra*), to one who is modest (*śālīna*), or to one who is brilliant. Furthermore, it is said: "The letter *a* is Vāsudeva, while the letter *ā* is Pitāmaha (Brahmā)."

Since this has been stated in the *Itthanekārthadhvanimañjarī*, the meaning is established through the pun (*śleṣa*) on the two syllables "ārādhyā" [meaning both "to be worshipped" and "Śāradā"]; thus, there may also be a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she who is Śāradā and is to be worshipped. Regarding the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the portion "Śāradā," it is given in the *Kālīpurāṇa*:
"Because she was formerly awakened by the gods on the ninth day of the autumn season (śaratkāla), she is known as Śāradā by name, both in the sacred seat (pīṭha) and in the world.
Thus, the name of Paramaśiva, whose form is the earth, is Śarva; [the following term] is used in the sense of his wife.
In the sense of connection with a male, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied along with the augment *ānug*. This means she is the mother of Maṅgala, named Sukeśī. As it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"The sustainer of all beings, moving and unmoving, whose nature is that of the supporter of the universe..."
The God is called Śarva by those who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures.
"Of that Śarva, the supreme lord whose self is the sustainer of the universe (Viśvambhara), Sukeśī is said to be the wife, and Aṅgāraka is remembered as his son.
Thus it is stated; and also in the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]:
"That which is the third [form] of Śarva is known as Bhūmitanu;

his wife is named Sukeśī, and Aṅgāraka is considered his son. [The word *śarman* means "happiness," for it is her nature (*śīla*) to grant happiness (*sukha*); thus, *śarma* refers to peace and joys.]
This is the definition from the *Agnipurāṇa-kośa*. Furthermore, according to the *Devībhāgavata*: "She bestows happiness upon her devotees; therefore, she is the giver of bliss (*śarmadāyinī*). (93)

*Śāṅkarī* means "belonging to Śaṅkara. [The term] *kara* is derived from the root *kṛ* (to do/make) with the suffix *ac* according to the rule for the *pacādi* group; alternatively, it takes the suffix *ṭa* according to the rule "after *kṛ*, when meaning cause or habit" (*kṛño hetutācchīlye*).
Thus, *śaṃkara* is one who makes (*kara*) happiness (*śam*). Alternatively, *śaṃkara* is one in whom happiness resides; his wife is *śāṅkarī*.

And so it is said in the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Having obtained a body from Dakṣa, I shall follow Śambhu— the one who is undisturbed throughout the beginning, middle, and end of every cycle of creation— in the form of a woman."

"Then the inhabitants of heaven shall praise me, who am Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the Yoganidrā, and the essence of the universe, as 'Śāṅkarī' and 'Rudrāṇī. [The term] *karī* means "one who acts"; thus, *śrīkaro* refers to Viṣṇu, the "bringer of prosperity. [As it is said: "He is Śrīdhara, he is Śrīkara."
Or, because it is recited among the *Viṣṇusahasranāma* as "Śrīmān," this [mantra] is its "glory-bestowing" (*śrīkarī*) counterpart.
A virtuous woman, her face resembling the autumnal moon;

a virtuous woman who is devoted to her husband. According to the *Amarakośa*: "A *satī* is a virtuous woman, one devoted to her husband. Because she has no connection with another husband even throughout the three periods of time, her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*) is unique and unsurpassed. As it has been said:
By the venerable Śrīmad-Ācārya-Bhagavatpāda:
"How many poets do not resort to the wife of Brahmā?
Or who does not become the husband of the goddess Śrī by means of whatever riches?"
"O Satī, the foremost among virtuous women, having abandoned Mahādeva, even the embrace of the *kurabaka* tree by your breasts is difficult to obtain.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Devībhāgavata*: "You are celebrated as a virtuous wife (*sādhvī*) because of your extraordinary devotion to your husband (*pātivratya*)."
She whose face is comparable to the autumn moon;
she who has a tranquil belly, who is peaceful, supportless, and stainless. 94.

The root *śo* means "to thin. *Śātam* means "thin. By the rule *ādeca upadeśe'śitī*, there is the substitution of *ā*. She whose belly (*udara*) is thin is *śātodarī*. Alternatively, it means she is the daughter of Himavat, the "Hundred-Bellied" (*śatodara*) or "Infinite-Caverned" (*anantaguhā*), thus *haimavatī*. She who possesses tranquility (*śānti*) is *śāntimatī*.
Because there is an absence of agitation (*auddhatya*) toward devotees. "Emerging from the support" means risen from the *mūlādhāra*.

The compound is formed according to the rule: "Words beginning with *nir-* [form a compound] with words meaning 'gone beyond' (*krānta*), etc., when used with the fifth case. Alternatively, it means that for her, the support—the other substratum—has departed; for she is the substratum of the entire universe.
Because, in its nature as reality (*satyatva*), it cannot have another substratum. Alternatively, its essential form is the worship known as "without a substratum" (*nirādhāra*).

Thus, in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*, after beginning with the statement, "The worship of the Supreme Śakti is proclaimed to be of two kinds," and having stated the twofold division according to the distinction between external and internal, [it continues:]
Having described the two-fold nature of the external [worship]— distinguished as Vedic and Tantric— along with their characteristics, it is said:
"That which is internal worship is also proclaimed to be of two kinds."
It is both with support and without support; being without support, it is most great.
She who has a support rests upon a support, but she who is without support rests in pure consciousness;
[I worship] the Supreme Goddess in the support whose form is composed of phonemes.
One should propitiate [the Guru] with great affection by following the path taught by the Guru;
that which is called worship in the context of consciousness is indeed the dissolution of the mind within it.
In the ultimate sense, supreme consciousness alone is the power, and nothing else;
therefore, for the destruction of saṃsāra, one should [meditate upon] her who is the witness and whose nature is the Self.
One should propitiate the Supreme Śakti, who is devoid of the manifestation of phenomenal expansion,
the Great Goddess who has become one's own self, directly realized through one's own experience.
"One should worship with great reverence; that worship bestows the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).

Now, [the text proceeds] with the essential negation, affirmation, and refutation of the opponent's views regarding the nature of consciousness, which is the object of the supportless (nirādhāra) rite of worship.

Having first established [the nature of the goal], he describes the means for attaining it and the essential nature of the fruit produced thereby through eight verses beginning with "Nirañjana. For indeed, there are three kinds of bound souls (paśus).

In this regard, there is a distinction: one who is joined with the *āṇavamala* alone, which consists of the cognition of selfhood in what is not-self, is a *vijñānakevala*; one who possesses the *kārmaṇamala*, consisting of the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) that initiates the body, is a *pralayākala*; and one who possesses the *māyīyamala*, known as *māyā*, which generates the notion of duality, is a *sakala*. Thus they are distinguished.

Among these, each subsequent impurity pervades each preceding one; this and more has been explained by us in the *Setubandha*. In that context, he speaks for the purpose of excluding the *sakala* bound souls (*paśu*): "The stainless ones" (*nirañjanāḥ*).

"Staining" (*añjana*) means blackness (*kālimā*), which is to say, association with *māyā*. This is because [the *sakala*] consists of darkness (*tamas*) and possesses the quality of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*).
Because of their similarity. Thus it is said in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*:

"O Rāma, that which causes the fluctuations of joy and anger regarding the existence or non-existence of objects is called 'impure latent impression' (*vāsanā*), by which the term 'attachment' (*saṅga*) is expressed."

Thus: she from whom the "añjana" (tint/impurity) has departed is "Nirañjanā. This is according to the Śruti: "The stainless is without taint" (*niravadyaṃ nirañjanam*). The meaning is that she is devoid of contact with ignorance (*avidyā*), because false ignorance does not exist in its own substratum (*svādhiṣṭhāna*)—that is, within the locus as it is actually apprehended (*pratipannopādhau*).

Because falsity consists precisely in being the counter-positive of a negation at all three times; or else, it is that in which there is intense coloring (*rāga*), meaning redness or satisfaction. 94.

Untainted, stainless, eternal, formless, and undisturbed, she dispels excessive pervasion at the time of dissolution. She is freed from "taint," which is the attachment resulting from the connection with karma, according to the Smṛti: "Actions do not taint me. Or else:
"Smearing" (lepa) refers to the connection with karma; that from which this has departed through knowledge is "unstained" (nirlepā). As it is said in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*:
"Even by all actions, the foremost knower of Brahman is not smeared in any way."
"Ah, the majesty of the most eminent knower of the Supreme Brahman is like a lotus leaf by water!
As it is said in the Gītā: "He is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
[The author] avoids over-extension [of the definition] to the *vijñānakevala* [liberated souls] by stating that they are "immaculate," meaning they are devoid of the innate impurity (*āṇavamala*).
Impurity is either that [state] whose nature is that [impurity], or it is that which possesses its absence. The liberated soul (*muktajīva*), however, is precisely what is to be characterized.

Alternatively, by the term "eternally liberated" (*nityamukta*), that [liberated soul] is excluded. Or rather, since ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is impurity because it causes the delusion of impurity in that which is eternally pure, she is "stainless" (*nirmalā*) due to the absence of that [ignorance].
Because impurity is false, its substrate is not so; thus he says:

"Eternal" means uncontradicted even throughout the three periods of time. By this, the [proposition] that the self is merely momentary consciousness is refuted, as is the [view of] external [objects] held by the Utpātivādins, in accordance with the Vedic revelation: "O, this self is indeed indestructible."
The *tithinityā* is the *kālanityā* in the form of mantra.

To refute the proponents of cognition with forms (*sākāra-vijñānavādin*) and the Mādhyamikas, he says: she is "formless" (*nirākārā*) because form—that is, the nature endowed with qualities—is merely conceptualized. As it is said in the *Viṣṇubhāgavata*:
"He indeed is neither god, nor asura, nor mortal, nor animal; neither female, nor neuter, nor male, nor a living being;
he is neither quality, nor action, nor existent, nor non-existent—the remainder of negation, may he be victorious in his entirety.
Here, the term "ākula" (confused) is a designation where the abstract state is the primary referent.

"Nirākulā" means being undisturbed even in contact with ignorance (*avidyā*), or that from which those with agitated minds have departed. This refers to those who are far [removed from such states]. "Agitation" (*ākulatva*) is the absence of everything or emptiness (*śūnya*). By this, the profound doctrine of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*)—a non-Buddhist view—is refuted. He now refutes the position of the logicians (*tārkika*).
She is devoid of qualities, partless, tranquil, free from desire, and undisturbed. || 95 ||

She is "without qualities" (nirguṇā) because She is devoid of qualities; for the Śruti declares, "The Witness, the Conscious One, alone and without qualities," and because qualities are attributes of the body and not attributes of consciousness. This was stated by Nārada to Himavat in the Matsya and Padma Purāṇas:
"And as for what was said by me— that the queen is devoid of auspicious marks—
listen to the correct meaning of those words through careful reflection."

"A characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is a quality (guṇa) that has the body as its sole locus and is marked by millions of divine signs; however, this Goddess is devoid of qualities (nirguṇā) and is not at all capable of being characterized.
Thus he speaks in order to refute the view that Brahman possesses parts (sāvayava): "The parts (kalāḥ), meaning portions, have departed [from her]."

The one whose [nature] is real is referred to by the Sūtra: "A portion [of Me], because of various designations," and by the Smṛti: "A portion of My very Self is the world of living beings. These are not contradictory, as they intend a conceptualized portion. Alternatively, meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) is called "without parts" (niṣkala). As it was said by the venerable Vijñānabhairava Bhaṭṭārakas:
"Meditation (*dhyāna*) is that thought which is partless (*niṣkalā*), without support, and without basis;

meditation is not the conceptualization of the body, such as the face, hands, and so forth. Here, "partless" means beyond parts (*kalātītā*). It is peaceful (*śāntā*), possessing tranquility. [As it is said: "Partless, actionless..."

"Śāntam" (the peaceful) refers to the *Tripuropaniṣad*. It means that whose end (*anta*) is the letter *śa*; that is to say, it consists of the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*). Alternatively, by the analysis as "ā-śānta," there is a rejection of those who maintain the soul's finitude (*paricchinnatā*)—such as the Digambaras—through the statement of its pervading the ends of the quarters (*diganta-vyāptatva*). [As stated: "He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true."

By such scriptural passages as these, he refutes the view that Brahman is of such [a qualified] nature. That from which desire—that is, longing—has departed is "niṣkāmā" (desireless). As stated in the *Devībhāgavata*: "For her who has attained all desires, what object could there be for thirst? And from the Śruti: "The Self is 'not this, not this'," and "That is full, this is full."

The sense is that other scriptural passages concerning qualities are intended to be merely figurative (*aupādhika*). Alternatively, it means "whose pride has departed" (*niṣkramamati*), from the root *ama* meaning "to go" and so forth; that from which delusion (*upaplava*)—meaning destruction—has departed.
Or, it means that in the very vicinity (*upa*), that is, within the physical body (*piṇḍāṇḍa*) itself, there is an overflow (*plava*) of nectar in its entirety and with excellence.

By this [prefix *ni-*], it is free from disturbance (*nirupaplavā*). This is because the prefix *nir-* is used in the sense of "excess" (*atiśaya*) and so forth in words such as *nirbandha* (insistence).
Thus, it is said in the Āruṇopaniṣad: "Plunge! Float away! Become an egg! Do not perish repeatedly!"

She is eternally liberated, changeless, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and without support. She is "eternally liberated" because her devotees are eternally liberated; or, she is liberated in such a way that it is eternal; or, she eternally releases [others] or is herself eternally released; or, it is the state (*bhāva*) or the essence (*tattā*) of one who is eternally liberated. The meaning is that she is the very form of liberation (*mokṣarūpā*).

To exclude both primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the mind (*manas*), he says: "That from which the twenty-three transformations well-known in Sāṃkhya—beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*)—have departed. This has been stated in the *Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī*:
"Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolutes;
the group of sixteen is the evolute alone; and the Spirit (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolute.
That [Prakṛti] from which the manifestations (prapañca)—the expansions and extensions of the accumulation of earth and the other elements—have emerged.
It is "niṣprapañcā" (free from conceptual proliferation). Regarding the term *prapañca*, the Viśvaprakāśa lexicon states: "Prapañca is said to mean accumulation, expansion, and deception.
Furthermore, it is so called because of the Vedic scripture: "They consider the fourth [state] to be the cessation of *prapañca*, auspicious, and non-dual.
Thus, the Cārvāka position—that Brahman is dependent upon the body—is refuted.

Because it is impossible for that which is the support of all things to have another support, it is without support; as it is said: "Where could that upon which the universe is established itself be established?
It is eternally pure, eternally awakened, faultless, and uninterrupted. (96)

It is eternally pure because there is an absence of impurity even throughout the three periods of time, according to the Vedic revelation: "And the Great One is untouchable and pure. And according to the Smṛti: "The body is exceedingly impure, but the embodied self is exceedingly pure. Also: "For there is no loss of the consciousness of the knower."

Having in mind the sacred scripture (*śruti*), he says: "The eternally awakened one is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpā*). Alternatively, it means that she is the one by whose grace those two—Śuddha and Buddha—are specific Victors (*jinaviśeṣau*) who are eternal. This is because, in the *Ṣaḍdarśanapūjā*, the Goddess is seen to be worshipped as the object of veneration for the Jaina system as well.

That is to say, she is in the form of the Goddess named Tārā who is to be worshipped. She is "Niravadyā," from whom all that is blameworthy—the entire collection of transformations born of ignorance (avidyā)—has departed; as the Śruti declares: "Without blemish, stainless.
Alternatively, she is so called because by her grace one has emerged from *avadya*, which is to say, from hell. And thus it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Therefore, if a person should constantly remember the Goddess day and night, he shall not go to the blameworthy hell, his sins being entirely exhausted.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*:
And in those [hells] beginning with Māyānta and Ghorādi, numbering twenty-eight crores,
sinners are cooked in those blameworthy hells.

"Unattached to Bhavānī’s lord, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita," and so forth— [the term *nirantara* means] devoid of those internal entities which are the distinctions and apertures that serve as the limits of space; thus, she is "without interval" (*nirantara*).

"Interval, space, limit, enclosure, disappearance, division, purpose, hole, one's own, absence, outside, opportunity, middle, and the inner self—these are the meanings of *antara*," according to Amara. "He who perceives even a slight difference in this [Reality], then for him there is fear. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7)
This is because of the Vedic revelation. By this, the view that Brahman possesses the threefold distinctions such as those of its own kind (sajātīya) and so forth is refuted. || 96 ||
She is without cause, stainless, without limiting adjuncts, and without a lord.

She is "without cause" because there is no other cause for the Cause of all; as the Śruti declares: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; yet there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any lord over Him."
Alternatively, it means that in whom the primary cause exists without remainder; the sense is that she possesses the bliss born from that [cause], according to the statement:
"She who dwells within the forest of the great lotus, whose form is the bliss of the cause.
She is stainless (*niṣkalaṅkā*) due to the absence of blemish (*kalaṅka*), which is sin, according to the Vedic scripture: "Pure, unpierced by evil. Upa...
An *upādhi* (limiting adjunct) is that which, by its proximity, imposes its own property; [this is derived] from the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*.

A hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) is an *upādhi* because, through mere proximity, it imparts its own redness (*lauhitya*) to a crystal. In the same way, [it functions] through a distinction from consciousness (*cit*).
In the case of manifestation, ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); that which is devoid of it is "without adjunct" (*nirupādhi*).

Alternatively, when the uncommon attributes such as stainlessness are to be proven, the Goddess's being the cause through identity (*tādātmya*) constitutes "being without adjunct," which means the absence of the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), i.e., a valid reason (*saddhetu*).
Or, it means "devoid of both kinds of attributes—those with parts (*sakhaṇḍopādhi*) and those without parts (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).
Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsā and Sāṅkhya systems are each of two kinds: with a Lord (*seśvara*) and without a Lord (*nirīśvara*).
Because she possesses the nature of both these forms, she is *nirīśvarā*. [She is so called] because she is the sovereignty (*īśvaryā*) of all.
Or because there is no other Lord;
she is free from passion, the crusher of passion; she is free from pride, the destroyer of intoxication. || 97 ||

Now, in order to refute the notion that the various internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are the Self, and to demonstrate that the abandonment of the sixfold group of enemies is the means [to liberation], [it is said]: "Passion" (rāga) is desire;
because all her desires have been attained, she is "passionless" (nīrāgā). Alternatively—

The meaning is that she has emerged from "rāga," because in the *Śāṇḍilya-sūtra* it is stated that devotion (bhakti) is also denoted by the word "rāga" due to its being the antidote to hatred (*dveṣa*) and because of the term "rasa. Alternatively, "nīra" means water and "aga" means a mountain; thus, she takes the form of both. By bestowing dispassion (*vairāgya*) upon her devotees, she removes their passion (*rāga*).

She is called *rāgamathanī* because she "crushes passion" (*mathnāti*). Regarding the suffix *lyuṭ*, its application even in the active sense (*kartari*) has been established in the *Mahābhāṣya* by the passage beginning with: "The suffix *lyuṭ* is not stated [in Pāṇini’s rules] only for the two causes [the instrument and the locus]. Here, "passion" (*rāga*) refers to that which is mentioned in the *Yogasūtra*: "Passion, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions" (*kleśāḥ*). She is *nirmadā* (free from intoxication) because she is devoid of pride; she destroys pride.
Or she is called Madanāśinī because she eats the madana and dhattūra plants. || 97 ||
Free from anxiety, free from egoism, free from delusion, and the destroyer of delusion.

Although the word *cintā* (anxiety) is generally expressive of memory (*smṛti*) in its primary sense, it is here used in a conventional figurative sense (*nirūḍhalākṣaṇika*) to denote a specific kind of memory that produces suffering.
"Thought (cintā) should be known as equal to a funeral pyre (citā); indeed, thought is superior to the pyre by virtue of the bindu [the anusvāra].

A pyre burns the lifeless; thought burns the living. This is according to such usage. Furthermore, based on the *Viśvakośa* stating "cintā means deception (chale) and a hearth (cullikā)," "deception" is also a meaning.

She is "free from anxiety" because she is devoid of both [ego and delusion]. She is "without ego" because of her absence of that threefold ego, according to the statement: "Ego is threefold: Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Bhūtādi. She is "free from delusion" because of the absence of delusion, which is mental confusion. She destroys delusion by bestowing the knowledge of unity.
She is the destroyer of delusion, according to the Vedic scripture: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?
She is free from possessiveness, the slayer of the sense of "mine," sinless, and the destroyer of sin. 98.
The word *mama* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that resembles a case-ending;

it refers to the cognition in the form "this is mine" (*mamedam*). And that cognition naturally takes as its object a relationship constituted by difference (*bheda*). Because such [a relationship] is absent in what is non-different from oneself, one is "without *mama*" (*nirmama*). Of such a *mamatā*...
She is the destroyer by means of wisdom. She is sinless because she is free from sin;

likewise, she destroys the sins of her devotees through the recitation (*japa*) and other practices of her own knowledge, according to the Śruti: "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is completely consumed, even so are his sins consumed. And thus:
The Vasiṣṭha-smṛti states:
"Sin does not attach itself even to one who performs sinful deeds, provided he is a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and austerity and devoted to the constant recitation of sacred texts."

"Sins do not dwell with those who recite prayers, those who perform fire-sacrifices, those who practice meditation, those who reside at sacred fords, and those who have bathed while observing the vow of the head," thus it is said in the Puṣkara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa.
And so forth. Also in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"Having cut through, pierced, and destroyed all these elements and this entire world, one who bows his head to the Goddess is not defiled by sins."
"Even if one has reached any state whatsoever, or is joined with all sins, a man who beholds Durgā becomes purified and goes to the supreme abode," and so forth. Also, in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Even for those most sinful men who are devoid of caste and stage of life,
by the mere meditation upon His form, their evil deeds turn into meritorious ones. (98)
She is free from anger and the pacifier of anger; she is free from greed and the destroyer of greed.

She is "free from anger" because there is no one to be hated, according to the Lord’s words: "To Me, none is hateful and none is dear. She pacifies the anger that belongs to the group of six internal enemies (ṣaḍvarga) within her devotees.

It is called *krodhaśamanī* because it destroys anger. Regarding the wickedness of anger, Āpastamba has said: "If one who is possessed by anger performs a sacrifice, offers oblations, or worships, he takes away all the merit of that act, just as a broken jar [holds no water]."
Thus [it is said]. Because of her extreme magnanimity, she is free from greed (*nirlobhā*). Since greed destroys all virtues, she destroys that censured greed for her devotees; thus she is so called.
She is free from doubt (*niḥsaṃśayā*), meaning she is the destroyer of doubt (*saṃśayaghnī*).

In the *Tantrarāja*, within the section explaining the characteristics of the Guru, it is stated: "One who is free from doubt, who has severed all doubts, and who is independent is considered a Guru. Having said this, the definition of those two qualifying attributes is given: "Free from doubt means one who knows reality (*tattva*)."

"Because it establishes that cutting [of doubt]" means that these two names arise from such non-difference from the Guru. "Niḥsaṃśayā" (Free from Doubt) and "Saṃśayaghnī" (Destroyer of Doubt), because of the Śruti and Smṛti: "All doubts are cut asunder."
She is free from existence and the destroyer of worldly becoming. || 99 ||

She is *nirbhavā* because she is devoid of origination, according to the Vedic revelation: "Brahman is without beginning and supreme. She is likewise so called because she destroys *bhava*, that is, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). And thus it is said in the *Śaktirahasya*:
"O King, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight, one should duly worship Caṇḍikā..."
Listen now to the meritorious fruit of him who bathes [the image] with clarified butter.
"Having rescued ten ancestors, ten descendants, and especially himself, from the ocean of worldly existence, one is glorified in the world of Durgā. Thus it is said;
and also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"This very [knowledge] is the sustainer and the creator for those desiring supreme bliss,
destroying all the miseries of saṃsāra under the name of the Lord.
Thus it is stated in the Devībhāgavata as well.
"I indeed rescue those devotees who are intent on me and have resorted to the yoga of the Lord from this ocean of worldly existence without delay"—
this is the word of the Blessed One. Or else, she went to Nṛsiṃha on the banks of the Bhavanāśinī.
The Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad takes the form of a well-known specific river. || 99 ||

It is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpā*), unimpeded (*nirābādhā*), undifferentiated (*nirbhedā*), and the destroyer of differentiation (*bhedanāśinī*). Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a cognition produced by words whose object is empty [of the thing itself]. Thus, the *Yogasūtra* states: "Conceptual construction is that which follows only the word and is devoid of the real object. Also, in the *Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya*:

For it is said: "Indeed, verbal cognition produces knowledge even regarding an object that is absolutely non-existent. Furthermore, in the *Phalaparīkṣā*, there is a sūtra of Gautama: "That [object] is established by cognition, though it does not exist [externally]. [The term] *tanniṣkrāntā* means "free from conceptual construction" (*nirvikalpā*). The compound is formed according to the rule:
"Words such as *ati* [form a compound] with a word in the second case when they have the sense of 'transcending' and so forth. And its transcendence is as follows:

Regarding the aspect of being produced by words (*śabdajanyatva*): by this, it is established that [the nature of the final state] consists of an eternal cognition devoid of an object (*nirviṣayaka-nityajñāna*). Alternatively, *vikalpa* refers to a "mode" (*prakāra*); thus, it is that form in which no such mode exists in the final cognitive transformation (*caramavṛtti*).
Or else, *vikalpa* is a contradictory conceptualization or alternative position (*pakṣa*); [the state] is that which is devoid of such.

Because there is no other category opposed to itself, and because everything is non-different, the ultimate meaning is that it is "without distinction. This is established in the third chapter of the Brahmamīmāṃsā, in the section [sūtra 14] stating, "For that [Brahman] is indeed formless, because it is the primary subject," which demonstrates that Brahman possesses only the single characteristic of being free from conceptual differentiation (*nirvikalpa*).
Because its reality has been established, even when silver is sublated by the cognition "this is not silver," the object denoted by "this" remains unsublated; thus, it is uncontradicted.

This is because mutual absence stands in the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) with respect to that [silver], and in the relation of sub-stratum (*anuyogitva*) with respect to this [object].
And because of the absence [of differentiation], She is without division. As it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"For You are that supreme Śakti, infinite and most excellent;
liberated from all distinctions and the destroyer of all distinctions."

Thus it is said. In another passage of that very same work: "Yogins who contemplate reality declare that there is a difference between power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimat) from a non-ultimate perspective, yet they perceive their non-difference."
Thus, it is so because the cognition of difference, or indeed difference itself, which is merely conventional, is destroyed by the knowledge of reality.
She is indestructible, the destroyer of death, actionless, and without possessions. 100.

"End" (*anta*) means destruction; because that [destruction] is absent, she is "destructionless" (*nirnāśā*). This is according to the Vedic revelation: "Truth, knowledge, infinite. She is likewise called so because she grinds away the death of her devotees. Furthermore, it is asked: "Why is she called *Māmṛtāditya*? Because she causes one to attain immortality (*amṛtatva*), and because she causes one to attain imperishability (*akṣayatva*) and eternal end.
This is because of the statement in the *Traipura Upaniṣad*: "He attains [it] and becomes Rudra himself.

It is "actionless" (*niṣkriyā*) due to the absence of actions consisting of both prescribed and prohibited forms, as stated in the Śruti: "Indeed, pleasure and pain do not touch one who exists as bodiless. Alternatively, it is actionless even without any connection to action.
She has attained the state of being a grammatical factor (kāraka), such as the agent (kartṛ) and so forth. As it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Just as fragrance causes agitation by its mere presence and not by acting as an auxiliary, so too is this Supreme Lord."
Thus [it is said]. "She whose possession has departed" (*nirgataparigrahā*); according to the *Medinī*, "possession" (*parigraha*) refers to "attendants, a wife, acceptance, or a source. (100)
"Matchless, with dark tresses, free from misfortune, and free from calamity;
matchless because of the absence of comparison, devoid of cause and illustration"—thus says the *Tripuropaniṣad*.
She is one whose tresses—meaning her locks of hair—are dark blue (*nīla*). She is devoid of misfortune (*apāya*), which is to say, calamity (*atyaya*) or destruction.
According to the Viśvakośa, which states that "atyaya" means transgression, punishment, destruction, fault, or difficulty, she is *niratyayā*, being free from transgression and the like.
She is difficult to attain, difficult to traverse, the invincible one (*durgā*), the destroyer of suffering, and the bestower of happiness. (101)

She is "difficult to attain" (*durlabhā*) because she is unattainable even for yogins; for this very reason, she is "hard to traverse" (*durgamā*), meaning she cannot be reached. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *adurgamā*; the meaning is that she for whom no obstacle exists. That is to say, she is the one who instigates the slaying of the demon named Durgama; for this very reason, she is *Durgā*. As it has been said:
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, the Pāñcarātra, and the Lakṣmītantra, it is stated by the Blessed One herself:
"And right there I shall slay the great asura named Durga;
my name shall become renowned as Durgā-devī."

Thus [it is said]. In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* as well, the entire chapter beginning with "The great Daitya named Durga" is devoted solely to this [subject]. Furthermore, regarding the etymology of the word "Durgā," the *Devī-purāṇa* states that she dwells in the Sannati-kṣetra on the banks of the Bhīmarathī.

"She by whom the gods, Śakra and the others, were delivered from fear of Subāhu and the like, from difficult terrain, and from the perils of enemies, is therefore proclaimed as Durgā. And she was requested by that king Subāhu through the granting of a boon in Vārāṇasī.
The goddess Satī remains well-known by this name. As it is stated in the *Devībhāgavata*, following the granting of the boon, in the section concerning her request:
"O Mother Śivā, you must always remain here in this city."

"By the name Durgādevī, you indeed abide here as Śakti. A nine-year-old girl is also called Durgā; this too is stated in that very same place: "She who is nine years old shall be Durgā," by which it is meant that she possesses that form. She is the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence.
"Final liberation is absolute release from that," according to the *Gautama-sūtra*;
and "He moves about completely liberated from suffering," according to the *Śruti*.
She is the Bestower of Happiness (*sukhapradā*), for she grants excellently all forms of happiness—those pertaining to this world, the next, and the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).

"Having attained this, he indeed becomes one who rejoices," according to the Śruti. A detailed exposition of this is to be found in six chapters in the final section of the Puṣkara-khaṇḍa in the Pādya-purāṇa. || 101 ||
She who is far from the wicked, the pacifier of misconduct, and free from defects;

she is *dūrā*, unattainable by the wicked and the faulty. As stated in the *Devībhāgavata*: "Those who rely on fallacious reasoning do not worship the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe, the Auspicious One. [She is the remover of] *durācāram* (misconduct).

It is so called because it pacifies conduct that contradicts the scriptures; as will be stated further on: "Whatever sin arises for men from the non-performance of obligatory duties and from the performance of prohibited acts, all of that is quickly destroyed."
Thus: she is free from defects such as attachment and aversion; she is omniscient, possesses intense compassion, and is devoid of equals or superiors. (102)

She is "all-knowing" (*sarvajñā*) because she knows everything, according to the Vedic revelation: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and also from the *Devīpurāṇa*: "All-knowing, because of her state of knowing all. She is one whose compassion is "dense" (*sāndrā*), meaning thick or intense; for the Vedic revelation—"No one is seen equal to Him, nor superior"—prohibits the perception [of any other being] as His equal.
Because the negation applies only to those two objects, it is excluded from [the case where] they share the same substratum (samānādhikaraṇa). 102.
She who consists of all powers and is the embodiment of all auspiciousness—now, assuming a qualified form (*saguṇarūpa*), he says:
she "consists of all powers" because she is non-different from all powers such as Bālā, Bagalā, and others; she is composed of Brahman.
Just as in the passage beginning with "the world" (*jagat*), the suffix *mayaṭ* also signifies non-difference (*abheda*).

She is "consisting of all powers" (*sarvaśaktimayī*) because she is the very form of the aggregate of all the powers of the gods. This has been stated by the Goddess herself to Indra in the *Pāñcarātra* and *Lakṣmītantra*:
"O Śakra! I am Mahālakṣmī; furthermore, in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, for the welfare of all the gods, I was born as Mahiṣamardinī."
Those fragments of my power which reside in the bodies of various deities,
having come together, became my most beautiful form.
"And whatever weapons belong to the gods, O Lord of the Suras,
my powers (śaktis) then became weapons of those same forms.
This matter should be seen described in detail in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

"Whatever powers belong to the meanings of words, the wise know them all as Gaurī"—from this *Laiṅga* [Purāṇa], it follows that the word "all" (*sarva*) has an unrestricted meaning; or else, she is the one in whom all auspicious things reside.
However, in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"Because she bestows all auspicious and virtuous things that reside in the heart, as well as all desired objects, she is therefore called Sarvamaṅgalā."
"And because this Goddess, O Hari, bestows auspicious and most excellent things upon her devotees and removes their distress, she is therefore known as Sarvamaṅgalā.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Śrī Bhāsurānanda.
By the second hundred [of breaths], the third digit, Dhūmrikā, arose. || 200 ||
Thus ends the third digit, named the second century, in the commentary on the *Lalitāsahasranāma* composed by the venerable Bhāskararāya, author of the *Padavākyapramāṇa* and other works. || 3 ||
The fourth digit, named Marīcī, is called the Third Hundred;
she bestows the good states of existence (*sadgati*). "Good states" refers to those beginning with heaven and ending with liberation, as well as the realization or knowledge of the True Brahman.
Or, it is so called because she grants the goal of the virtuous; for as the learned have said: "You are the goal, you are the intellect, you alone are Bhavānī. And in the Padma Purāṇa:
"O King, he who worships her at the three times of day on the fourteenth lunar day..."
"He goes to the supreme abode where the Goddess resides," beginning thus, [it continues]:
"The materials for the worship of Durgā, whether they be few or many..."
Having performed [this] according to one's wealth, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.

These words, which establish the attainment of all worldly states through the four chapters ending with this verse— prescribing the specific benefits for each ritual service (*pratyupacāra*)— should be applied here as supporting evidence.
She is the sovereign of all, consisting of all, and the very embodiment of all mantras. || 103 ||

For this very reason, because she possesses sovereignty over all, she is the Sovereign of All (*sarveśvarī*). She states that uncontracted sovereignty cannot be sustained without non-duality: "She consists of all" (*sarvamayī*), meaning she is non-different from the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva.
As it is said in the *Kāmika*:
The path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), which consists of two hundred and twenty-four worlds,
should be contemplated as being of the nature of the multitude of hairs of the all-pervading Lord.
By praising him in the form of the fifty phonemes,
this conceptualization of the path of phonemes is the inconceivable nature of the skin of the trident-bearing God of gods.
The path of mantra (mantrādhvan) of the Lord of Pārvatī is to be contemplated as that very Self which is the junction, consisting of seventy million great mantras arising from the root-vidyā.
The collection of words of mantras, divided into many varieties, is called the path of words (padādhvan), O gentle one; it exists in the form of veins and flesh.

"The twenty-six principles beginning with Earth, known by those who know the Āgamas, are declared to be the 'path of principles' (tattvādhvan); this [path] assumes the form of semen, marrow, and bone. This very [point] is restated in three [verses] by way of analysis: "All mantras, numbering seventy million..."
This is its essential nature. And it is heard in the *Sundarītāpinī*:

"Many forms of the Vidyā have been fashioned from the preceding and the succeeding [sections]. This is even more clearly stated by Gauḍapāda in seven aphorisms beginning with: "From the preceding and succeeding [sections], many [forms] of the Vidyā were born."

The fact that [the Lord] is the essence of all mantras has been described [therein], and it is elaborated upon in its commentary; in that very same work, under the aphorism "likewise the yantras and tantras," he states the object of knowledge as it was described. || 103 ||
She is the nature of all yantras, the form of all tantras, and *manonmanī*.

She is "of the nature" (*ātmikā*) of all yantras, such as the *ghaṭa* and *argala*, because her very essence is their self-nature; [the substitution of *i* for *ya*] occurs by the rule *pratyayasthāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.44).
All the Tantras, such as the Vāmakeśvara and others, are her very form, that is, her body; or rather, she is to be defined by all the Tantras. As it has been said:
"The paths that cause accomplishment, though divided in many ways by the Āgamas..."
"These [qualities] fall upon you alone, like rivers into the ocean.
Regarding the body as well, it is said in the *Kāmikāgama*:
"The lotus-feet are the *kāmika* [tattva], and the pair of ankles is the *yogaja* [tattva]."
In the form of the two feet and their toes, they are called the "extended causes."
The pair of knees of the Lord is Ajitā, his two radiant thighs are Dīptā,
the region of his back is Aṃśumatī, and his navel is Śrīsuprabhedakā.
They say Vijaya is the belly, Niḥśvāsa is the essence of the heart,
Svāyambhuva is the pair of breasts, and Anala is the three eyes.
The Vīrāgama is the region of the throat, the Rurutantra is the two ears,
the Makuṭatantra is the crown of the head, and the Vimalāgamas are the arms.
The Candrajñāna is said to be the chest, the Bimba the lotus-face,
the Prodgītatantra the tongue, and the Lalita the pair of cheeks.
The forehead-plate is perfected, as are the lineage-mark and the two earrings;
the radiance is the jewel-ornament, and the wind-whirl is the nature of the garment.
"The limbs, the secondary limbs, the body hairs, and all other constituent parts—thus, O Mahādeva, one should contemplate the form consisting of the principles (tattvas).
Thus [it is said]. The eighth station from the middle of the eyebrows is that which is below the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
She is said to be *Manonmanī* because she has that as her form. Her essential nature is described in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
"That power which exists as the cause is known as *Unmanī* beyond that;
herein there is no measure of time or its divisions, no *tattva*, and no deity."
"Perfectly extinguished (sunirvāṇa), supremely pure—that is called the face of Rudra.
It is renowned as Śiva-Śakti, free from conceptual construction and stainless.
For this very reason, [it refers to] that which is well-known in the Śruti: "Salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Jyeṣṭha... and so forth.

And it is said that she is the power (śakti) of Śiva known as Manonmanā. Also in the Tripuropaniṣad: "When the mind, having withdrawn its attachment to objects, is completely restrained within the heart and attains the state of Unmanī, then that is the supreme state."
Thus [it is said]. This is the designation for a specific *mudrā* in the Yogaśāstra. Its definition is given in that very same work:

"May that Manonmanī be present within me—she by whom the eyes are freed from opening and closing, by whom the breath is devoid of exhalation and inhalation, and by whom the mind is emptied of conceptualization and discursive thought."
Thus it is said; and also in the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
"When one perceives intensely the state consisting of meditation, the meditator, and the object of meditation, then the state of *unmanā* arises from partaking of the nectar of knowledge."

Thus [it is said]. "Manāṃsi unmanyante" means "make the minds possessed of superior knowledge"; the *sandhi* (euphonic combination) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). She is Māheśvarī, the Great Goddess, Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Mṛḍa. || 104 ||

"He who is the sound proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda and established at the end of the Veda— He who is beyond that [sound] which is dissolved into primordial nature (prakṛti), He is Maheśvara.
Thus, the state of transcending the three qualities (triguṇātītatva) belongs to the term Maheśvara as it is well-known from such scriptural passages.
This is the delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). As it has been stated in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*:

"By means of *tamas* he is called Kālarudra; by means of *rajas* he is the one born from the golden egg; by means of *sattva* he is the all-pervading Viṣṇu; and by means of being beyond the qualities (*nirguṇya*) he is Maheśvara."

Thus [it is said]. Here, "uninterruptedness" (*avicchinnatva*) is the meaning of the instrumental case. There is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *maheśvara* for its denoted object, in accordance with the introductory statement "known as Kālarudra. Therefore, Maheśvara is delimited by that [time].
"By means of truth and celibacy, his *liṅga* remains as it is."
"Those worlds who worship him are called Maheśvara.
And in the *Bhārata*: "He is Maheśvara because he is the lord (īśvara) of great beings (mahat).
He whose twenty-five-fold manifestation (*vyūha*) is set forth in the *Vātulaśuddha* is also [Maheśvara].
She belongs to Maheśvara, thus she is Māheśvarī. She is both great (*mahatī*) and a goddess (*devī*), hence Mahādevī.
Her greatness (*mahattva*) consists in having a body that is inaccessible to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Her body is vast, being immeasurable by any standard of measurement."
"Because she is great (mahā) in worship (pūjā), she is therefore remembered as Mahādevī.

Alternatively, the meaning is that she is the wife of Śiva—who is designated as Mahādeva because he possesses the form of the moon—and the goddess named Rohiṇī, the mother of Budha. And so it is stated in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
Renowned as the primordial source of all gentle things,
the God whose nature is Soma is remembered by the wise as Mahādeva.
"Rohiṇī is declared by the wise to be the beloved of the god Mahādeva, whose essence is Soma, and Budha is his son born of her body.
Thus it is said; and also in the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]:
"The eighth body of the great god by name is Candramas (the Moon);
Rohiṇī is his wife, and his son is known as Budha.
This very deity is the presiding goddess of Cakratīrtha on the Gaṇḍakī river. [In Śālagrāma...]

She is called "Mahādevī" because she is enumerated among the Devī-tīrthas in the Puṣkarakhaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa. In that very same text, she is listed as "Mahālakṣmī" at Karavīra. Thus, the text refers to the Goddess who has been so enumerated as Mahālakṣmī;
she is both great (*mahatī*) and Lakṣmī. She is the wife of Mahāviṣṇu. [In] the Kali age, [she resides at] Karavīra.
It is renowned as Kolāpura; or rather, she is indeed a portion of Ambikā. As it is said in the Mailāratantra:
"She devours—that is, destroys—the demon named Mahāla."
She became renowned as Mahālasā and Mahālakṣmī.
"At the foot of the Sahya mountain, on the shore of the western ocean.
Thus it is said. Also, in the Śiva Purāṇa, introducing Śiva:
"The supreme Māheśvarī Śakti is seated upon the circle of his lap."

"She is renowned as Mahālakṣmī, dark-complexioned, and captivating to all. Furthermore, in the *Āyuṣyasūkta*, in the verse "Śriyam lakṣmīm ambikām aupalāṅgām," the word *lakṣmī* alone is used for Pārvatī. By that term...

The compound *pūjyavācimahatpadasya* is formed by the rule *asanmahatparama-* and so forth. Furthermore, the *Mākaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states: "The primordial Mahālakṣmī, composed of the three qualities (*triguṇā*), is established as the beginning of everything. Alternatively, she may be in the form of a maiden (*kanyā*) consisting of thirteen years.

Regarding the maiden, Dhaumya stated, "In the thirteenth year, she is Mahālakṣmī. Furthermore, from the verbal root *mṛḍ* (meaning "to gladden" or "to grant happiness"), the name *Mṛḍa* is applied to Śiva, who maintains the universe and possesses the quality of *sattva*. As it is said:
"Salutations again and again to Mṛḍa, who brings happiness to people and in whom *sattva* predominates."
From the *Mahimnastava*: "His beloved. || 104 ||
She possesses a great form, is worthy of great worship, and is the destroyer of great sins.
Her form is superior in comparison to the four great forms. As it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O twice-born one, the Puruṣa is the first form of the supreme Brahman;
likewise, the Manifest and the Unmanifest are other forms, as is Time, which is the highest."
That which is the supreme among primordial matter, the individual soul, the manifest, and time—
that pure state which the wise perceive is the highest step of Viṣṇu.
"Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Vyakta, and Kāla, according to their respective divisions,
are the causes of the existence of the forms [of the world]— namely, maintenance, creation, dissolution, and manifestation.
She is "Mahāpūjyā" (Greatly Worshipful) because she is worthy of worship even by those who are themselves worshipful, such as Śiva and others.

The meaning is "to be worshipped. Accordingly, in the *Pādma* and *Devībhāgavata* [Purāṇas], there is a distinction of the forms of the Goddess to be worshipped according to their respective [deities]— such as Śiva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Kubera, the Viśvedevas, Vāyu, the Vasus, Varuṇa, Agni, Śakra, Sūrya, Soma, the planets, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, the hosts of Mothers (Mātṛgaṇa), and so forth— within the mantra.
It has been shown in detail that [the images] take the form of transformations of emerald, gold, silver, brass, bell-metal, crystal, ruby, pearl, coral, lapis lazuli, tin, lead, diamond, and iron.
Among these, Agni, Śakra, and Sūrya worship only the image made of ruby.

The others should be applied according to their respective order. It is so called because it destroys great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). And likewise, in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "Of all committed sin, whether done knowingly or even unknowingly..."
"Recollection of the feet of Parāśakti is declared to be the supreme expiation.
Also, in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa: "What is the use of saying much here? I shall speak in half a verse:"
"Even a hundred killings of Brahmins shall be destroyed by the worship of Śiva.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Artharatnāvalī* that "by the term *mahāpātaka* (great sin), the killing of a hero (*vīra*) alone is meant.
In this very context, within the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta*) in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara* and other works, according to the gradation of sins—
The statements regarding the relative gradations in the number of recitations for the fifteenth day should be applied as supporting evidence:
"Mahāmāyā, Mahāsattvā, Mahāśakti, and Mahārati. (105)
She is called Mahāmāyā because she causes even Brahmā and the other gods to be deluded. As it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Indeed, that divine Goddess [deludes] even the minds of the wise."
"Having forcibly drawn it out, Mahāmāyā delivers it to delusion.
Also in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*: "Endowed with the knowledge within the womb, it is impelled by the winds of birth."
She who continuously renders whatever has arisen devoid of knowledge;
Having directed [the mind] through the conditioning of successive prior aggregates,
one should then [remove] delusion, the sense of "mine," ignorance, and doubt regarding the elements beginning with earth.
Having repeatedly cast [the mind] into anger, obstruction, and greed again and again,
one should afterwards quickly join it with desire, remaining engaged in contemplation day and night.

"She who makes a living being endowed with fragrance yet attached to calamity is called Mahāmāyā; therefore, she is the Sovereign of the World. Alternatively, according to the lexicon which states "māyā means deceit and compassion," she is abundant in compassion (*kṛpābahulā*). The state of being good (*sadbhāva*)...

*Balam* means quality (*guṇa*). And *prāṇinaḥ* refers to sentient beings (*sattva-padārthāḥ*). According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *sattva* [denotes] a quality, a piśāca and the like, strength, a substance, and inherent nature. She whose *sattvas* (beings) are great—greatness consisting in her being the sustainer of the entire universe and so forth.

She whose power (*śakti*)—meaning capacity or capability—is extensive and manifold. Regarding this, Yādava states: "The word *śakti* denotes strength, capability, as well as a type of weapon. Here, the meanings of "strength," "weapon," and "wing" are all applicable. And it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide,
so too is this entire universe the power (śakti) of the Supreme Brahman.
Even in that case, there is multiplicity and minuteness due to proximity and distance.
"O Maitreya, just as there is a distinction in the moonlight, so too does that power exist.

Regarding the statement "the Great Power is Kuṇḍalinī," if it is certain that the third syllable belongs to the *tālavya* (palatal) class, then an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā* must be made here; thus, there is no tautology. Not [otherwise].

It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in relation to which there exists a great power. This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which states: "Neither one equal to Him nor one superior to Him is seen. [This is mentioned] in the *paribhāṣā* of the *Chalākṣara-sūtra*.

Furthermore, because it is stated that these two consist of four syllables each and because they are found in certain manuscripts, we have explained them accordingly by accepting a distinction between them, similar to the pair of terms *mahāsanā* and *mahāśanā*. For this [text] is not, like the *Viṣṇusahasranāma* and other such works, beset by hundreds of repetitions.
By this, it is intended that one should accept a mere difference in meaning while tolerating identity in terms of the word.
She is called Mahāratī because she possesses a great delight (*rati*) or affection (*prīti*) toward the objects of knowledge that exceeds [ordinary] pleasure;
or else, she is called Mahāratī because she is exceedingly beautiful due to her great passion (*kāma*). || 105 ||

She possesses great enjoyment (*mahābhoga*), great sovereignty (*maheśvarya*), great heroism (*mahāvīrya*), and great strength (*mahābala*). "Great enjoyment" refers to her vast extension (*vistāra*) consisting of the earth and other elements, or it may mean that she possesses great pleasure (*sukha*) or wealth (*dhana*). Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) refers to both lordship (*īśvaratā*) and majestic power (*vibhūti*).

She whose [qualities] are great; she whose heroic powers (*vīrya*), such as semen (*śukra*) and so forth, are great—according to the *Viśva* lexicon, "heroic power" (*vīrya*) refers to semen, influence (*prabhāva*), splendor (*tejas*), and capability (*sāmarthya*). She whose strengths (*bala*), such as fragrance (*gandha*) and so forth, are great.
"Strength (*bala*) is found in smell, taste, form, stability, stoutness, and armies;

*Bala* [is the name] of Halāyudha, a type of Daitya, and a strong person; *vāyasa* [is the name] of a crow," so says the Viśva-kośa. Regarding the case of the crow, it is said that Bhusuṇḍa and others became great through his grace.
This is to be applied accordingly. Thus, in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*, there is the speech of the crow named Bhusuṇḍa addressed to Vasiṣṭha:
"My brothers, the sons of Caṇḍa, are twenty-one crows."
Likewise, the divine Brāhmī was there with her brothers and the female swans.
Having been propitiated by us for a long time, the Blessed Lady herself then, at the proper time when we had ceased from meditative absorption, became intent on showing her grace.
"In this very way we have been favored, by which we remain liberated," and so forth.
She is of great intellect, of great perfection, and the sovereign of the lords of great yoga. (106)

She is both great and intelligence, thus "Mahābuddhi. That intelligence in which, once arisen, nothing remains to be known is "great," according to the Vedic scripture: "When that is known, all this becomes known. Alternatively, she is so called because from her proceeds great intelligence.

In this very way, the state of the great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhipada*) is to be explained in two ways. The accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* and so forth are well known; others also have been mentioned in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The spontaneous manifestation of the essences (*rasa*) is declared to be the first accomplishment."
And invincibility by the pairs of opposites is called the second accomplishment.
The third supreme accomplishment is the absence of inferiority or superiority;
the fourth is their equality in terms of lifespan, happiness, and suffering.

The fifth stage, named Viśokā, consists of an abundance of splendor and strength; it is characterized by devotion to the Supreme Self and steadfastness in austerity, meditation, and other such practices.
"The sixth is moving at will; the seventh is called accomplishment (siddhi);
and the eighth is likewise declared to be sleeping wherever one may be.
Thus she is the Mistress of the great Lords of Yoga (yogeśvara). (106)
The great tantras, the great mantras, and the great yantras are the great seats.
The "great" refers to the tantras that bestow abundant fruits, such as the *Kulārṇava* and the *Jñānārṇava*; the "mantras" refer to Bālā, Bagalā, and others; and the "yantras" [are likewise great].
She is such because she possesses the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*), the lotus-circle (*padmacakra*), the nectar-pitcher (*amṛtaghaṭa*), the Meru-linga, and so forth; or else,
because she possesses the *Tantra* known as the *Svatantra*, the *Mantra* known as the *Śrīvidyā*, and the *Yantra* known as the *Siddhivajra*, which is great and supreme among all.
Its greatness consists in its independence, as it does not depend on anything else. As it is said in that very same [text]: "O Blessed One, all the Tantras were indeed spoken by you in the past;
however, due to their mutual dependence, a confusion of thought arises."
"Therefore, O Lord, tell me that independent tantra of theirs.
To this question, [the reply is]:
"Listen to the Kādimata Tantra, which is complete and independent of others."
"It must be guarded with every effort; such is the concealment enjoined by the Tantras.
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Saundaryalaharī*, it is stated:
"Having encompassed the entire world through the sixty-four Tantras..."
Paśupati remained dependent upon the production of various supernatural powers (siddhis);
however, due to your persistent request, he brought down to the surface of the earth this independent *tantra* of yours, which accomplishes every human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

Thus it is said. Regarding the subject of mantras, however, one should consult the descriptions found in the *Kulārṇava* and *Śaktirahasya*, numbering more than a thousand verses, beginning with "The Śrīvidyā alone [is the foremost] among mantras. Furthermore, concerning the yantra known as Siddhivajra, it is recorded in the *Nityātantra*:

"He who considers another mantra to be equal to the Lalitā-vidyā, or another yantra to be equal to this [yantra], is one of deluded intellect. Her "great seat" (mahadāsana) consists of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), beginning with earth. This...
"The Blessed Lady abides by relying upon all principles," according to the *Devībhāgavata*.
She is to be propitiated through the sequence of the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*) and is worshipped by Mahābhairava. (107)

The Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga) is accompanied by the worship of the sixty-four yoginīs, beginning with Akṣobhya, who constitute the portions of [the goddesses] Brāhmī and the others; that alone is the true sequence (krama), because everything other than that is not a sequence (akrama) since it yields results only after a long delay. Therefore, she is to be propitiated through this [sequence]. [The word *krama* applies] both to power (*śakti*) and to a regular order (*paripāṭī*).

According to Śāśvata, the term *krama* refers to "a row of moving [steps]. Alternatively, it refers to the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*), which is a more profound secret sacrifice expounded in the *Bhāvanopaniṣad*, achievable solely by one fit for Śiva. That has been clarified by us in its commentary and in the manual for its performance (*prayogavidhi*), and thus is not discussed here.
He who performs the acts of supporting, delighting, and subduing, and who effects creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—that very Supreme Śiva is Bhairava;
she is worshipped by that Great Bhairava. As it is said in the *Pādma*:
"Śambhu worships the auspicious Goddess, who consists of the power of mantra."
"Holding a rosary in his hand, Bhavodbhava [performed] the ritual placement (nyāsa).
It is well known in the *Lalitopākhyāna* that Mahāśambhunātha caused Lalitā to manifest from the fire-pit of consciousness (*cid-agnikuṇḍa*) through a great sacrifice (*mahāyāga*). || 107 ||
She is the witness of Maheśvara’s great *tāṇḍava* dance during the *mahākalpa*.

During the *mahākalpa*, that is, the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), there occurs the great *tāṇḍava* of Maheśvara, which arises from the joy produced by the withdrawal of the universe and the resulting state where only the Self remains; at that time, no other [being] exists.
Since there is no other [witness], this very [consciousness] is the witness. As it is said in the *Pañcadaśī-stava*:
"Of the Lord Khaṇḍaparaśu, the Supreme Bhairava, who performs the cosmic dance at the dissolution of the aeon..."
"With the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow, and the flower-arrows—your single form stands victorious as the witness.
Thus it is said: "Having withdrawn the entire universe, she sports at the time of dissolution."

"And having placed the marks (liṅgas) of all living beings within one's own body," so it is said in the *Devībhāgavata*. Also, in the eighty-first canto of the latter half of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* in the *Mahāvāsiṣṭha*, there is [an account] consisting of more than a hundred verses that is most wonderful and extremely terrifying.
Having observed the dance of both, it was concluded:
"Ḍimbaṃ ḍimbaṃ suḍimbaṃ, cook, cook! Suddenly jhamyajhamya, prajhamya!
As she dances to the accompaniment of sound and instruments, [she wears] a garland upon her breast and a crest on her head made of the feathers of Garuḍa."
"Holding in his hand the great horn of Yama’s buffalo, filled with red wine, may Bhairava protect you as he is being saluted by Kālarātri, who rejoices at the dissolution of the world.
Thus [ends the description of] Mahātripurasundarī, the consort of the Great Lord of Desire. 108.

She is the consecrated queen—the wife—of the Great Lord (Mahat), who is the Sovereign (Īśa) non-different from Supreme Śiva; she is the embodiment of the city consisting of the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; and she is likewise both "Great" (Mahatī) and "Beautiful" (Sundarī). 108.
Rich with sixty-four modes of service (*upacāra*) and consisting of the sixty-four arts (*kalā*),
the sixty-four— namely, sixty plus four— are enumerated as such services by the venerable Paraśurāma in the *Kalpasūtra*. There are also eight others mentioned in another Tantra:
The wearing of the flowers from the feet of Śiva, the planting [of the seed] within oneself,
the dismissal of the retinue, and likewise the worship of those devoted to the Guru.
Then follows the worship of the Śaiva scripture, the sacrifice to the fire of Śiva,
the receiving of the water from Śiva’s feet, and the Prāṇāgnihotra together with its ancillaries.
"These are the seventy-two services augmented by sixty-four.

Thus, sixty-four is sixty plus four; the services numbering that amount were described by us in the section on worship (*pūjā*). She who is enriched (*āḍhyā*) by them—that is, one whose wealth and character are inseparable from them—is so called.
The sixty-four arts (*catuḥṣaṣṭikalā*) as enumerated with specific distinctions in the *Śārṅgadharīya*, the *Kathākośa*, and the *Lakṣmīpīṭhikā* of Śrīdhara are extracted and written here:
"Knowledge of the eighteen scripts, writing them, and rapid reading— this is the marvelous art (*citram*)."
Knowledge of many kinds of languages, as well as poetry, learning, and eloquence, constitute gambling.
The Vedas and the four Upavedas, the two groups consisting of the six auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) and the [six] systems of philosophy (śāstra),
the triad of Tantra, Purāṇa, and Smṛti, and the two categories beginning with poetry, poetics, and drama.
Pacification, subjugation, attraction, causing enmity, expulsion, and killing—these six;
as well as the sevenfold obstruction of movement, water, sight, fire, weapons, speech, and the front—constitute the art of sorcery.
The training of elephants, horses, chariots, and men; palmistry, wrestling, cooking, and snake-charming;
various types of musical instruments—hollow, struck, and solid—as well as magic, dance, song, and instrumental music.

"The examination of gems, theft, and the examination of minerals, as well as invisibility—thus the sixty-four arts have been extracted and stated by the wise poet Bhāskara. It is "abounding in" these [arts]. Alternatively, the word *kalā* refers to the *tantras*; those too [are included].
Sixty-four [tantras] are enumerated in the Vāmakeśvaratantra;
these have been explained by us in the Setubandha, and we shall analyze them in its commentary (ṭīkā).
"Consisting of that" means having that as its primary focus.
She is served by a host of sixty-four million great yoginīs. || 109 ||
