Among the eight [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī, there are eight powers (śakti) for each, such as Akṣobhyā and the others; thus, there are sixty-four yoginīs. Furthermore, each of these has individual retinues (gaṇas) numbering in the tens of millions, which are served by those great ones.
In reality, only those [mantras] taught in the *Tantrarāja* should be adopted here. As it is said:
"O Dear One, in each of the nine *lalitā*-cakras, there are sixty-four crores of Śaktis."

Thus, when these are totaled, they amount to five padmas, seven arbudas, and six koṭis. Since there are sixty-four koṭis of Yoginīs— both distinct and non-distinct— in each of the nine cakras, beginning with the Trailokyamohana-cakra, when these are all added together:

Five hundred million, seven hundred million, and sixty million make up the total. To illustrate this, the term "great" (*mahat*) is used as a qualification for "ten million" (*koṭi*) itself; and its greatness consists in being multiplied by nine. || 109 ||
She is the knowledge of Manu, the knowledge of Candra, and she dwells in the center of the lunar disc.
Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, and Manmatha;
Agasti, Agni, Sūrya, Indra, Skanda, and likewise Śiva.
"In the statement, 'Krodhabhaṭṭāraka, the Goddess, and these twelve Upāsakas,' the twelve-fold Śrīvidyā-prastāra is included;
its extraction is to be seen in the Jñānārṇava. Among those—
The two names are a restatement by way of analytical distinction (*avayutya-anuvāda*) of the dual nature of Manu as both Moon and Knowledge (*vidyā*).
They are so called because they go to the center of the lunar orb, since the Kuṇḍalinī pierces the moon at the pericarp of the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*).
Because she is to be meditated upon in the moon-maṇḍala during the evening twilight worship and in practices for the prolongation of life;
as stated by Śiva to the Goddess in the Śiva Purāṇa:
"I am established in the head of Agni, while you reside in the head of Soma."
"The entire universe, whose nature is Agni and Soma, is presided over by us two.
This is the secret: that the lunar orb is non-different from the Śrīcakra.
She is of beautiful form, with a lovely smile, and she bears the beautiful digit of the moon. (110)

She whose form is beautiful and lovely, and whose smile is full of grace—as it is said: "The moon is but a drop of your gentle smile. However, some have explained this by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as: she whose nature is the bestower of supreme bliss, a particular state of awakening known solely from the mouth of the Guru. [This refers to] the one who is beautiful (*cārvyā*).

She is the support (*dhara*) of the digit of the moon known as *Sādākhya*, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and free from increase or decrease; or else, she is the princess named Candrakalā, well-known in the *Devībhāgavata*.
In a dream, you [saw] her [attended by] a prince named Sudarśana, a practitioner of the *Kāmarāja-bīja* mantra.
"It is to be chosen," so said Ambā; therefore, "as is fitting" means that she became the support (dharā) for Candrakalā. As it was stated in that very same work, in the third skandha:
"At this time, the excellent daughter of the King of Kāśī..."
"Named Śaśikalā, divine, and endowed with all auspicious marks"— beginning thus, [it continues]:
"In the middle of the night, the Mother of the World approached her in a dream."
Having comforted her, she spoke these words as she stood at ease:
"O lady of beautiful hips, choose a boon; O beautiful woman, by my word, let Sudarśana, who is devoted to me, be the granter of all your desires. And so forth. (110)
She is the sovereign of the moving and unmoving world, whose abode is the king of wheels (cakrarāja).
She is the supreme mistress of the universe consisting of both the mobile and the immobile;
she whose dwelling place is precisely the nine kings of wheels, beginning with the Trailokyamohana.
Pārvatī has lotus-like eyes and a radiance equal to that of a ruby.

Pārvatī is so called because she is the female offspring of the Himavat mountain. Some say that there is an absence of the suffix *iñ* because the general rule (*utsarga*) applies even in cases where an exception (*apavāda*) might otherwise be expected. However, it is more reasonable to hold that here, as in the expression "Let Māthilī be given to the son of Daśaratha," only a general relationship is intended, not a specific one.

She whose eyes are like lotuses is *padmanayanā*. She whose radiance or luster is equal to—that is, similar to—the deep red of the gem called *padmarāga*; or alternatively, she who is endowed with the color, the redness, of a specific kind of lotus, the *kokanada*. "Protect me, O Kuṇḍalinī!"
"Red as saffron paste"—according to the words of Kalyāṇācārya, this is the supreme name of Amṛtakuṇḍalinī. 111.
Seated upon the throne of the five *pretas*, she is the embodiment of the five *Brahmās*.

Since even the five beginning with Brahmā are incapable of action in the absence of their respective powers (*śaktis*)—Vāmā and the others—they are *pretas* by virtue of their leftward (*vāma*) aspect; she sits upon the couch (*mañcaka*) fashioned by them as a throne.
She sat [and asked]. As it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Maheśāna, tell me about the five pretas; what is their cause?
Tell me, how is it that they are lifeless, indestructible, and of eternal form?"
Thus questioned by the Goddess with these words, the Lord said: "Well asked by you, O blessed one, is the matter of the five thrones of the deceased (pañcapretāsana).
[They are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva."
O lady of beautiful hips, those five pretas are always indeed motionless;
O Supreme Goddess, the agency of Brahmā consists of the form of creation.
"She is to be known as the power Vāmā; Brahmā is the corpse, there is no doubt.
For Śiva has no instrument (karaṇa), whereas the power possesses an instrument.
Beginning thus...
"O Dear One, Sadāśiva is the great preta, solitary and motionless;
O Goddess, deprived of Śakti, he is not capable of anything whatsoever.
Thus ends [the passage]. [This applies] to all five, from Brahmā up to Sadāśiva.
Because she is included within the ten million Brahmās (*brahmakoṭi*), her essential nature consists of the five Brahmās. As it is stated in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*:
"Although Brahman is devoid of distinctions, through the play of its own *māyā* within itself..."
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
"Thus, by virtue of its names, [it] exists as the fivefold Brahman.

Alternatively, the five Brahmans are those known as Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta. And so it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "The individual soul (*kṣetrajña*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*)..."

Having stated that the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and generative organ, as well as the five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with sound, are of the nature of Brahman, it is further declared that they are the generators of the five gross elements beginning with space.
The meaning is that she possesses such a nature. It is also stated in the Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa:
"Śiva alone is the manifest reality, characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth;
free from modification and pure, he exists in five ways through his own power."

Thus, the meaning is that he has arisen in five forms, beginning with Sadyojāta, through the powers of the fivefold cosmic functions (pañcakṛtya) such as creation, maintenance, and so forth. Also in the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
"Viṣṇu is the benefactor of the worlds and the destroyer of all the wicked."
In the form of Vāsudeva as well as Saṅkarṣaṇa.
"He exists in five ways as non-dual: in the form known as Pradyumna, in the form known as Aniruddha, and in the form of Nārāyaṇa. Thus it has been said by the Teachers as well:
"The five male deities are the play of the masculine principle, while the three Vedas are their spontaneous discourse;
O Mother, the sun is but a tiny particle of your eye, and the moon is but a drop of your gentle smile. Thus [it is said].
She is composed of consciousness, supreme bliss, and the very embodiment of the mass of pure knowledge. (112)

She is composed of consciousness (*cinmayī*) because she is non-different from consciousness. Her essential nature is supreme, most excellent bliss (*paramānanda*), according to the Vedic scripture: "That which is plenitude (*bhūmā*) is happiness. Her form is a mass of pure awareness—consciousness itself, dense and thick, having that as its sole flavor—according to the text: "It is indeed a mass of consciousness alone [arising] from these..."

For in the Śruti passage, "Having arisen from the elements," we see that the term *vijñānaghana* (mass of consciousness) is explained as referring to that which has consciousness as its sole essence (*cidekarasa*). Alternatively, the word *vijñāna* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), as is seen in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa: "He who, dwelling in consciousness, controls consciousness from within," and so forth.

Because of the [scriptural] explanation. Its form is "dense" (ghana) with them, meaning it consists of Hiraṇyagarbha who identifies with the collective totality (samaṣṭi). This is because the term "jīva-ghana" in the scriptural passage, "From this mass of living beings," is explained in that very way. || 112 ||
She has the nature of meditation (*dhyāna*), the meditator (*dhyātṛ*), and the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), and is devoid of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).

[The root] *dhyai* means "to contemplate. Contemplation is mental cognition; as stated in the *Yoga Sūtra*: "Meditation is the one-pointedness of the mental process" (*pratyayaikatānatā dhyānam*). The meaning is that she has the form of the triad known as knowledge (*jñāna*), the knower (*jñātṛ*), and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Dharma and adharma are the two types of action that bring about desirable and undesirable results, respectively. As it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"The verbal root *dhr* signifies 'sustaining' (*dhāraṇa*), and it indeed attains the sense of 'greatness' (*mahattva*). Through sustaining and through greatness, it is defined as *dharma* itself."
"117) Therefore, the Dharma that leads to the attainment of what is desired is taught by the teachers;
however, that which yields undesirable results is likewise taught by the teachers. Thus also says the Saṃvarta-smṛti:
"In every region, that custom which has come down through a traditional succession and is not contradicted by the sacred scriptures (āmnāyas) is proclaimed to be Dharma.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Of the acts of sacrifice, ritual conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and Vedic study, this indeed is the supreme duty: the perception of the Self through yoga.
Thus [it is said]. Jaimini also states: "Dharma is a purposeful matter characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā). In this very context, [he defines] adharma...

By the elision of the vowel *i* (*it-i-akāra-praśleṣeṇa*), the definition of those [actions] is to be understood as consisting in being prescribed or prohibited acts. She is devoid of both of these. This is because, according to the logic of the section on animals (*tiryag-adhikaraṇa-nyāya*), deities lack eligibility for ritual action;
or else, because the scripture has as its subject matter only those possessed of ignorance (*avidyāvat*). Alternatively, dharma and adharma refer to bondage and liberation.

Because such an interpretation is seen in the *Nityāhṛdaya* verse—"of dharma and adharma, which are to be expressed, and which consist of poison and nectar"—she is devoid of both. And thus it is heard in the *Tripuropaniṣad*:
"There is no opposition, no origination, no bondage, and no seeker."

"Neither one who desires liberation nor liberation itself exists; this is the ultimate truth. Alternatively, by means of a *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* (indication based on possession), the word *dharma* refers to the substratum (*dharmī*); the word *adharma*, through a *bahuvrīhi* compound, refers to that which possesses qualities. [The world] is devoid of the relationship between substratum and quality. Of the world...
The meaning is that it is absolutely non-different from them. The words *dharma* and *adharma* denote the syllables *Śakti* and *Śiva*;
the secret meaning, however, is that the fifteenth [digit] is devoid of those two.
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, "devoid" (*varjita*) signifies "increased" (*abhivṛddhi*). And those two syllables—
It is stated in the *Nityāhṛdaya*:
"Furthermore, she resides in the space of vibration (*spanda*), which is the manifestation of the central vital breath (*madhyaprāṇa*);
then again, in the middle mantra-cluster, and then again in the third cluster."
"The two peaks of Rāhu flash forth...

[as it says]. The meaning of this should be understood from the mouth of the Guru; or else, it has been explained by us in the *Varivasyā-rahasya* or the *Setubandha*, so it should be understood from those.

Now, distinguishing the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) by means of nineteen names, he begins to praise the Goddess as being identical with them, starting with the words "Viśvarūpā" and so forth. For in the order of creation, there is first the creation of *tamas*, then the creation of the Great Principle (*mahat*), and then that of the threefold ego (*ahaṅkāra*).
From that, there arise the subtle elements—sound and the rest—which are synonymous with the five *tanmātras*.
Within these reside five powers of cognition and five powers of action.
Of these, the former, in their individualized aspect (*vyaṣṭi*), produce the pentad of cognitive organs beginning with the ear.

In their collective form (*samaṣṭi*), however, they produce the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Even the final [elements], in their individual form (*vyaṣṭi*), produce the pentad of organs of action such as speech, while in their collective form, they produce *prāṇa*.
As for the objects, sound and so forth, which serve as the substrata (*dharmin*), they produce the pentad of gross elements beginning with space.

This is the actual state of things. In that regard, consciousness (caitanya), when conditioned respectively by the gross elemental adjuncts (upādhi) constituting the individual (vyaṣṭi), the subtle elemental adjuncts, and the causal adjuncts,
becomes designated by the terms Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña.

The reality (tattva) conditioned by those [entities] in their collective totality is indeed designated, in sequence, by the terms Vaiśvānara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Īśvara. The Supreme Self (paramātman) conditioned by the cause of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is Hiraṇyagarbha; that conditioned by the cause of the vital breaths (prāṇa), however, is the Sūtrātman.
The Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is said to be that which is established by following after both these inseparable causes.
These three alone are respectively denoted by the terms Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. And this—

This was stated by relying on the Upaniṣadic doctrine that the individual self (*jīvātman*), the collective self (*samaṣṭijīvātman*), and the supreme self (*paramātman*) each possess a threefold nature. At their conclusion [are mentioned] the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
This is because [in other systems] only three of each [set of five] functions are accepted; however, in the view of the Tantrikas,

there is an increase of two for each pair of states— namely, the fourth (turya) and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta)— as well as for the two functions of concealment (tirodhāna) and grace (anugraha).
Because the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), having entered into those respective states,
also possess an additional fivefold nature each, there is no contradiction in this;
for it is like the distinction between the gross and subtle perspectives regarding the processes of *trivṛtkaraṇa* (triplication) and *pañcīkaraṇa* (quintuplication).
Because this systematic arrangement is logically consistent. However, it is only during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) that the *prājña* attains the state of Brahman;

thus, for the Self that has entered those two transcendent states, there is no longer the status of a transmigrating individual (*jīva*). Yet, because a trace of ignorance (*avidyā-leśa*) persists, it does not possess the status of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) either. For this very reason, regarding the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul situated in the state of deep sleep...

Just as there is a conventional designation of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the *jīva* who has entered the fourth state (*turya-daśā*) as the "causal body" (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), so too, according to the *Śivasūtra*, "he becomes equal to Śiva and intent upon that," such a one is designated as being "equal to Śiva.
Its meaning is that he is called "Half-Śiva" (*ardha-śiva*) due to partial equality. And for this very reason:

Furthermore, in the scriptural passage, "The stainless one attains supreme equality," the mention of non-difference (*abheda*) by means of the term "supreme equality" is logically consistent. With this very intention,
it is understood that in that state, neither the status of a full individual soul (*pūrṇajīvatā*) nor the prior state of Śiva exists.

The Upaniṣadic [commentators] count them separately. For this very reason, in the section concerning the state of fainting (*mūrcchāvasthā*), they have presented this same reasoning as the ground for not counting it separately under the heading "In the case of the fainting person, there is partial attainment, because of the remainder. Or rather, they do indeed count it.

Since the fivefold adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) are seen to be designated by the term "five sheaths" (*pañcakośa*), and because the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) possesses as its adjunct the capacity to bestow bondage and liberation— which are synonymous with concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*)— He is the Lord (*īśvara*).

In accordance with the definition stated in the Śaiva Tantra, "The external unfolding is the *unmeṣa* (opening), and the internal [folding] is *nimeṣa* (closing) in Sadāśiva," two further divisions beyond Rudra remain intact. This being so, the "entirety" (*viśva*) consists of those whose nature is consciousness established in the waking state, conditioned by gross elements.

The meaning is that she is "Viśvarūpā" (the Universal-formed), because her form—viewed from the perspective of consciousness—is indeed the Vaiśvānara who is the collective totality of those individual souls (*jīvas*). Alternatively, since it was previously stated that she is devoid of the relationship between attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*), he says this to establish the non-difference of the world [from her]: [The verse continues: *viśvākārā viśvanirvāhikā ca viśvātmikā viśvasamuddhṛtikarī |* *viśveśvarī viśvahṛdisthitā ca viśveśvaraprāṇanikā viśvarūpā || 12 ||* She is the one whose form is the universe, the sustainer of the universe, the soul of the universe, and the one who effects the upliftment of the universe; she is the Sovereign of the universe, residing in the hearts of all, the vital breath of the Lord of the universe, and the Universal-formed. (12) She is the one whose form is the universe, meaning she is the universal form itself. She is the sustainer of the universe, meaning she is the cause of its maintenance. She is the soul of the universe, meaning she is the inner self of the universe. She is the one who effects the upliftment of the universe, meaning she is the cause of its creation. She is the Sovereign of the universe, meaning she is the mistress of the universe. She resides in the hearts of all, meaning she dwells within the hearts of all beings. She is the vital breath of the Lord of the universe, meaning she is the life-force of Śiva. She is the Universal-formed, meaning she is the form of the entire universe. (12) Furthermore, she is the one who bestows the fruit of liberation upon the devotees of Śiva, the one who grants the fruit of enjoyment to the devotees of Viṣṇu, the one who bestows the fruit of worldly prosperity upon the devotees of Brahmā, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Goddess. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Sun, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of Gaṇeśa, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Mothers, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Planets. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Yakṣas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Rākṣasas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Gandharvas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Kinnaras. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Siddhas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Vidyādharas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Cāraṇas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Apsarases. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Nāgas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Piśācas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Bhūtas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Pretas. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Asuras, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Dānavas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Daityas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Danujas. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Sādhyas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Rudras, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Vasus, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Maruts. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Pitṛs, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Manus, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Yugas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Kalpas. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Manvantaras, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Caturyugas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Tithis, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Nakṣatras. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Muhūrtas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Kṣaṇas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Lavas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Truṭis. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Nimeshas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Āvalis, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Ghaṭīs, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Praharas. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Ahorātras, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Pakṣas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Māsas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Ṛtus. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Ayanas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Saṃvatsaras, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Yugas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Manvantaras. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Kalpas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Mahākalpas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Brahmalokas, and the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Vaikuṇṭhas. She is the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Kailāsas, the one who grants the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life to the devotees of the Śvetadvīpas, the one who bestows the fruit of the attainment of the four aims of human life upon the devotees of the Puṣkaradvīpas, and the one who grants
She is the multiformed one, the wakeful, the sleeping, and the one whose nature is the Taijasa state.

Regarding the term *viśvarūpā*: the meaning is that her very form is the universe itself, and there is no other form existing as a substratum (*dharmibhūta*) that serves as the support for the universe. As it is said in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Just as in the case of the plantain tree, no bark or leaf is seen apart [from the fruit]."
"Thus, O Lord, no otherness of the universe from that which rests in You is perceived.
Also, in the first book of the Devībhāgavata:
"To Viṣṇu, who was in the form of a child lying upon the leaf of a banyan tree..."
Then, by means of half a verse, the Blessed One spoke that which bestows all purposes.
"Indeed, all this is only 'I'; there is nothing else that is eternal.

Alternatively, the state of being a living soul (jīva) is an extremely low form of Brahman itself; thus, it is equal to a dog. For this very reason, the livelihood consisting of service to the lowly is designated as "dog-like conduct" (śvavṛtti).

"Lower" means the state of being a mere animal; she by whose grace such a nature has departed is Viśvarūpā. Alternatively, it is undisputed that [she] is Tripurasundarī, who consists of sixteen digits (kalās). As it is said in the *Vāsanāsubhagodaya*:
"The fifteen digits (kalās) indeed begin with the new moon (darśa) and end with the full moon (pūrṇimā);
however, the sixteenth digit should be known as having the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).
For in the lunar orb, there is one digit called Sādākhyā, which is devoid of increase and decrease; the others [are otherwise].

Fifteen [deities] share in the process of coming and going. Of those, the single digit (*kalā*) of the venerable Goddess (*Śrīdevī*), who is non-different from them and whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is denoted by the term Tripurasundarī. The others, however, beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā, revolve according to the divisions of the lunar days (*tithi*). Within that which is non-different from them...
Even within these fifteen [syllables], there is one syllable that is to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru, which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa);
by virtue of this, she is given the name Śrīvidyā. The other fifteen syllables, which are heard by all practitioners, are of the nature of the Nityās. Thus...

The identity of the goddess Candramaṇḍalā with the fifteen [syllables] implies that there is likewise an identity between each of those digits (*kalā*) and their corresponding syllables. For this very reason, the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) and their syllables also possess a three-part structure (*trikhaṇḍatva*), as follows: Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Riktā.
By the repetition three times of the word "Pūrṇā," and by the distinction of the *vāgbhava* and other *kūṭas*,
they indeed recite the names of the fifteen nights of the bright fortnight according to the *Taittirīya* tradition through these very three sections: "Darśā, Dṛṣṭā, Darśatā, Viśvarūpā, Sudarśanā."

"Āpyāyamānā, Āpyāyamānā, Āpyāyasūnṛtā; Āpūryamāṇā, Āpūryamāṇā, Pūrayantī; Pūrṇā, Paurṇamāsī"—in this way, the names of these days are also traditionally taught through three distinct groups. "Saṃjñānam, Vijñānam..."
"Consciousness as knowing, fully knowing;
as intending, forming, fashioning; as fashioned, formed, better, best, coming into being, having come into being"—thus [it is said] in these two sections.

The fact that these are the names of day and night is also recorded in that very same [text]: "Consciousness (saṃjñānam), discernment (vijñānam), the new moon (darśa), and the seen (dṛṣṭa)"—these two liturgical formulas (anuvākau) are the names of the days and nights of the first fortnight (pūrvapakṣa). Here, although all three sections are indeed equal in number, [the distinction remains].

Nevertheless, when there is a *daśamī-vedha* (contamination by the tenth day) on the eleventh day, because it is [technically] the tenth day, the statement "one should fast on the pure twelfth day" applies;
and since the twelfth day itself constitutes the eleventh day, [the tithi] contained within the final segment [of the eleventh] is [to be excluded] from the middle segment.

Due to the entry [of the vowel], the second and third segments of the mantra consist of six and four syllables respectively. For this very reason, with the intention of the view that there is no piercing (*vedha*), the three *kūṭas* in other Vidyās such as Sūryā and others have exactly the same number of syllables. With this same underlying purpose—

In the *Subhagodaya-ṭīkā*, Lalla stated: "Even though the *kalā* being filled (*āpūryamāṇā*) resides within the lunar segment (*candrakhaṇḍa*), it is included within the solar segment (*saurakhaṇḍa*).
Because it is a specific division of the *irā-kalā*, one should contemplate the identity of the *irā* and the *āpūryamāṇā*. This was said in the aforementioned verse.

The term "darśādyāḥ" (beginning with the new moon) means beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), since the cited scripture states that the *pratipad* is named after the new moon (*darśa*). Regarding those lunar days (*tithis*) and the syllables of the mantra,
each possesses its own specific nature as being composed of the principles (*tattvas*) such as Śiva, Śakti, Māyā, and Śuddhavidyā.
The various methods of worship according to the different views of the Kaulika and Sāmāyika traditions should be seen in the *Candrakalā*.
And thus, due to their mutual non-difference, [this practice] is also known by the name of the night of the fourth day of the bright fortnight.

The term *viśvarūpāpada* signifies that which expresses both the fourth syllable of the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* and the *śuddhavidyā-tattva*; thus, the meaning is that it is non-different from these three. Alternatively, *viśvarūpa* is a neuter noun, and its feminine gender (*viśvarūpā*) is established by analogy with terms such as *mithyājagad-adhiṣṭhānā*. And that—
It denotes the fifth day of the dark fortnight. And so it is heard in scripture:
"The extolled, the praised, the highly praised, the auspicious, the universal-formed; the bright, the immortal, the radiant, the kindled light;
the ruddy, the luminous, the possessed of rays, the scorching, the glowing, the pressed, the pressing."
"Born, being born, being pressed; drinking, providing a source of drink, satisfying, gratifying;
beloved, desirable, born of desire, yours, the cow of plenty; prepared, extended, pressed, pressing"—these two sections [of the Veda] belong to the days and nights of the dark fortnight.

The phrase "names" means that it has that form. Thus, although by way of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) and with the desire for a pun (*śleṣa*), only one specific night and one specific day are mentioned, the meaning results in [the reference to] that which consists of all nights and that which consists of all days. Therefore...

Regarding such knowledge, a specific fruit is heard in scripture: "He who indeed knows these honey-makers and honey-bees—for him they produce honey in the fire; they do not consume his merit from sacrificial and charitable works. But for him who does not know them, they do not produce honey in the fire."

"They drink his *iṣṭāpūrta*," it says. Here, the word *madhukṛt* refers to the nights, and the word *madhuvṛṣa* refers to the days; for the supplementary passage states: "Those which are the nights of the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), they are the *madhukṛts*; those which are the days, they are the *madhuvṛṣas*. Madhu...

They perform [their functions] and they rain, by virtue of their individual powers. For one who knows these, these nights joined with days produce honey—that is, they cause it to flow—from the place of Bindu within the fire, through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
They do not consume his collection of works consisting of sacrifices and charitable deeds; having drunk them, they do not destroy them.

He states the undesirable consequence in the case of their absence with the words "Now, as for those... and so forth. Only when there exists the internal ritual—consisting of the arousal of Kuṇḍalinī, the flowing of nectar, and the flooding of the maṇḍalas of Ḍākinīs and the others—do external rituals such as sacrifices become fruitful. In the absence of that, however, at whatever time...
Actions are performed, and that very time becomes the form of death by means of those actions;
this is the resultant meaning. This has been further elaborated in the *Candrajñānatantra*:
"For those whose nature is cool, who cause the flow of honey within the internal fire..."
It is said that ritual acts such as sacrifices and charitable works bear fruit in due course of time.
For those devoid of internal flow and whose minds are constantly tormented,
their actions, even as they are being performed, are swallowed by Time in that very instant.
"The internal Kālakarṣaṇī alone causes [the breath] to rain nectar"—
he who knows this shall experience a flow of nectar from the *brahmarandhra*.
Vaidehī gave birth to Saraghā Kālakarṣaṇī;
she mastered this knowledge consisting of fifteen syllables in five days and nights.

Thus, the meaning of the third and fourth verses here is as follows: the goddess named Kālakarṣiṇī is the "honey-maker" (*madhukṛt*), being the form of night; and she is the "honey-rain-maker" (*madhuvṛṣā*), being the form of day.
In this manner, he who knows the Goddess as non-different from night and day, and so forth.

He whose body has departed is *videha*, namely *anaṅga* (the bodiless one), the Lord of Desire (*kāmeśa*). *Vaidehī* is she who belongs to him, the Mistress of Desire (*kāmeśvarī*). With fifteen letters that are non-different from day and night, she generated this fifteenth *vidyā*. And so says the Śruti: "Janaka, the Videha, by means of days and nights..."
"He came together" (samājagāma). And this very [earth] is called *saraghā* because she produces honey (*madhu*).
Amara states: "The *saraghā* is the honey-bee. The Śruti also says: "This earth, indeed, is the *saraghā*; her fire is the *sāragha* honey. Enough with further elaboration.
The definition of the state known as waking (*jāgarā*) is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"That creation which, by being within the range of all the senses, exists as external and stable,
and is common to all, this universal manifestation is waking."

Thus: the one possessing that [state] is the waking state, known as Viśva, the individual soul (jīva) who identifies with the gross body; the feminine form *jāgariṇī* is non-different from that [state], according to the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*. The definition of the dream state is also given in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"Because of the delusion [of perceiving] through the path of the mind alone as an object of direct perception..."
"The creation of objects with clear manifestation is considered the state of dreaming.

Thus, "svapan" means one who sleeps; it refers to the individual soul (jīva) known as Taijasa, who has entered the state of dreaming and identifies with the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra). The word "svapantī" (the sleeping one) is non-different from that [soul], according to the rule "ugitaśca" [Pāṇini 4.1.6].

The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied here]. "Taijasātmikā" means that whose nature (*ātman*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) is Taijasa—the individual souls (*jīvas*) characterized as described above, and Hiraṇyagarbha who is their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*). || 113 ||
The fourth state (*turyā*) is the sleeping state characterized by wisdom;

"sleep" (*suptam*) refers to the state of intoxication (*samādāvasthā*). Its definition is given in the *Śivasūtra*: "Non-discrimination is *māyā*; it is the state of deep sleep. [This is expressed as] "I slept happily; I was not conscious of anything."

The meaning is that deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) is that state in which there exist three modifications of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*), postulated because otherwise recollection would be inexplicable, having as their objects non-cognition (*ajñāna*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*), and bliss (*sukha*). One who possesses that [state] is called the *prājña* (the "intelligent" one).

The individual soul (*jīva*), which identifies with the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), is asleep. [The suffix] *ac* is applied according to the rule *arśa-ādibhyo 'c*. That [state] is non-different from that [soul], thus it is "asleep. The term *prājña* refers to the one characterized as previously described; the Lord (*īśvara*) is the soul (*ātman*)—the essential nature (*svarūpa*)—of those souls who constitute its collective totality (*samaṣṭi*). Thus, she whose nature is the *prājña* is "consisting of the *prājña*" (*prājñātmikā*). This pertains to these three states.

And for those who experience that [bliss], the state of *turya* (the fourth) is the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) known as the arising of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), which is produced by discerning [knowledge]. As it is said in the *Spandaśāstra*:
"That which is to be enjoyed in the three abodes, and he who is proclaimed as the enjoyer..."
"He who knows both of these, while enjoying them, is not tainted.
Varadarāja also says:
"The Fourth is the supreme abode; its full enjoyment is the aesthetic wonder (*camatkriyā*)."
"Even when there is a distinction between waking and so forth, that [state] is possible for the yogi.

Thus says the *Śivasūtra*: "Even amidst the distinctions of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the enjoyment of the Fourth (turya) is possible," and "The Fourth should be poured like water upon a surface into the three. One who possesses that [Fourth state] is the one who identifies with the great causal body (*mahākāraṇaśarīra*).
The individual soul (*jīva*) is the fourth state (*turya*). Its fourth state is non-different from it, both in its individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*) aspects.
Regarding the means for attaining the state of the Fourth, Śiva has said: "The mind should enter by means of one's own consciousness.
"Having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth, which are gross and conceptual means..."
By means of one's own mind, which is non-conceptual in form and self-aware,

and which consists of the essence of the aesthetic relish (*rasa*) of the wonder of inward-turned reflective awareness— by means of this "fourth" (*turya*) flavor of the mind— one [dissolves] the state of being a subject here, such as one's own body and so forth.
"Having pacified [the mind] with immersion, one should enter and become absorbed therein.

Alternatively, as stated in the *Śaktirahasya*: "They consider Śiva to be non-dual and the Fourth (*turīya*)," thus You are that certain Fourth Goddess whose nature is well-known from the scriptures. O Turīyā, You are indeed that certain [Deity].
This is also because of the statement by the venerable Ācārya [Śaṅkara]: "The greatness of which is difficult to attain and limitless. Furthermore, in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*, it is said:
"O fair-faced one, because of the grace of Turīyānandanātha, the name 'Turyā' became perpetually renowned for that Goddess."
The meaning is clear. || 14 ||

There is a fifth state of the individual soul (jīva). Since there is no other conventional name for it, and because it transcends the fourth state (turya), it is designated by the etymological term "turyātīta" (beyond the fourth); with this intention, he says:
—[it is] devoid of all states.
Regarding "all": since for a person who has transcended the fourth state (*turya*), the transcendence of the first three states is necessary, [it is devoid] of all four states.

Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva), being specifically devoid of and free from the absence of return, is "transcending the fourth" (turyātīta); because there is no distinction between its collective and individual aspects, this state is also free from all conditions—this is the meaning. And that [state] arises from the firm consolidation of the fourth state (turyāvasthā).
For there is the saying: "By the support of the fourth state (turya), the supreme station beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is attained.
Varadarāja also says:
"Through the excellence of the practice of the fourth state, the station consisting of that which transcends the fourth is reached."
The practitioner has directly attained [union] with the inner self of all the worlds.
"He is equal to Śiva, who abounds in pure consciousness, absolute freedom, and bliss.
There are three aphorisms for describing the true nature of one who has reached the fifth stage:
"The conduct of the body is the vow; discourse is the recitation; and self-knowledge is the gift."

Because maintaining the body serves as a means for the worship of Śiva, which consists of the contemplation of one's own true Self, such maintenance of the body in the form of a vow is not trivial. For this very reason, Bhaṭṭotpala has prayed for the preservation of the body:
"May this body of mine be nourished by the nectar of my own pure power, which has arisen within, for the enjoyment of your worship.
Recitation (*japa*) consists merely of such spontaneous utterances, because the mind thereby grasps the truth. As it has been said:

In the two *Yoga-sūtras*: "When there is proficiency in the state beyond reflection (*anirvicāra-vaiśāradya*), there is clarity regarding the inner self (*adhyātma-prasāda*); therein, wisdom is truth-bearing (*ṛtambharā*). This is stated because, according to the Śruti—"Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech"—everything spoken thereby possesses a true form and thus has the nature of a mantra. As it is said in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*:
"The virtuous should always be approached even if they do not instruct us;
for whatever casual conversation they may have, that becomes their instruction.
Giving instruction to others is itself the gift. As it was said by Kṛṣṇadāsa:

"The direct realization of the Self, whose nature is the consciousness described [in the scriptures], that indeed is knowledge; and that which is given by it is itself the gift. Thinking that these three aphorisms should be explained as being intended as illustrations (*upalakṣaṇa*), they have stated:
By the venerable teacher [Abhinavagupta]: "Recitation, speech, and all forms of craft are the fashioning of mudrās," and so forth.
Also in the Vārttika:
"Thus, performing the prescribed vow, maintaining the recitation (japa), and observing the conduct (caryā)..."
One's own self is always equal to Śiva, being ever intent upon the worship of Śiva.
"This very one is the great yogin, the bearer of the burden of the great mantra; he truly awakens his disciples to reality within.
Thus, having described the fivefold nature of the individual soul (jīva) who is under the sway of ignorance, [the text continues].
He states that the Lord, who is delimited by the *māyā* under His control, possesses such a nature through the differentiation of His functions:
"She is the creator of the universe in the form of Brahmā, and the protector in the form of Govinda. (114)

By the words "sṛṣṭi" and so forth, this meaning was elucidated by the venerable teacher (Ācārya Bhagavatpāda) in the verse beginning with "She who gives birth to the world and sustains it. Creation (*sṛṣṭi*) refers to the fashioning of the universe, which is the function of Īśvara when the quality of *rajas* predominates;
she is the agent of that act. Brahmā, the four-faced one, is such an Īśvara, and she has him as her very form.
This has been stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "O Brahman, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the primary powers of Brahman.
Preservation of the world is its maintenance, and that is the function of the Lord when the quality of *sattva* predominates. Of that [preservation]...
She is the "Protector" (*goptrī*) because she is the agent of protection; *Govinda* is the Lord Viṣṇu of such a nature, and he alone is her form.
Thus, there is a statement by Nārada in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"The illustrious goddess Umā is the first portion of Prakṛti."
"Viṣṇu, the manifest, who consists of all things and is the creator of the worlds, is designated as 'Strī' (Woman). Regarding the etymology of the word *Govinda*, it is stated in the Viṣṇubhāgavata:
"I am indeed Indra among the gods, and you have attained the state of Indra (*indra*) over the cows (*go*)."
"Men on earth shall sing of you by the name Govinda. Thus it is said. Also, in the Mokṣadharma section of the Mahābhārata:
"In former times, I indeed found the lost earth that had gone into a cave."
"Therefore, I am praised by the gods with the words, 'Govinda!
Also, in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"This cow is indeed speech (*vāṇī*); and you, sir, find her."

"O God, you are therefore called Govinda by the sages. [The suffix] *śa* is applied according to the rule "in the case of words such as *go* etc., when forming a name. Alternatively, he may be considered an embodiment of Bṛhaspati, based on the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon which states: "Govinda refers to Vāsudeva, the superintendent of cows, and Bṛhaspati."

She is the Withdrawer, whose form is Rudra, the Sovereign Lady who effects concealment. "Withdrawal" (saṃhāra) is the destruction of the universe down to its subtle atoms, leaving nothing behind; it is the function of the Lord (Īśvara), who is dominated by the quality of darkness (tamas). She performs that task, and thus she is the Withdrawer.
Rudra is such a Lord. He is so called either because he "drives away" (*drāvayati*) disease or because he "makes weep" (*rodayati*).
This is because the rain occurring at the time of universal dissolution (*saṃvarta-kāla*) takes the form of tears, being produced from the eye known as the sun.
As the Vedic scripture states: "He wept; because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra. Thus, he drives away disease.

For it is said in the *Śivarahasya*: "Therefore Rudra is remembered as Paśupati. And from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the Rudras, for they cause all this to weep (*rodayanti*). The suffix *rak* is derived from the root *rud* according to the rule "roderṇilukca" (Uṇādi Sūtra).
They also say that the suffix *rak* occurs even after roots that do not take the causative marker *ṇic*.

"For the sake of Brahmā’s satisfaction, the imperishable Lord of the universe himself arose from his forehead as a son and wept with a terrible yet melodious sound," so it is said in the *Mahābhārata*. However, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* it is stated:
"He who, as the Lord, causes that which is suffering or the cause of suffering to flee is called Rudra; therefore, Śiva is the supreme cause.
Thus it has been said. She whose form is that very [Rudra] is so described. Tirodhāna means concealment, [that which is] without remainder.
Destruction. Even the dissolution of atoms and the like into their primal cause is similar to the extinguishing of a lamp;

she performs that which is the function of the Lord, who consists primarily of the most dense and pure *sattva*. Thus, she is the "Concealer" (*tirodhānakarī*). Alternatively, she is a specific power (*śakti*) known as the "Veil" (*tiraskariṇī*). As it has been said:
In the *Tripurāsiddhānta*:
"O fair-faced one, because she causes concealment for all those who are devoid of devotion, Śrī is therefore truly called Tirodhānakarī (the Concealer)."

Thus [it is said]. By the word *īśvara*, the Lord (*īśvara*) is denoted as one whose primary constituent is extremely dense, pure *sattva*. This is because the word *īśvara* has multiple referents, since both *māyā* and such a quality of *sattva* serve as the delimiters of its denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). She is *īśvarī* because she is non-different from him. [This is according to the rule] "vanoraca."

The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied]. In reality, however, the suffix *varaC* is added by the rule "stheśabhāsa... (Pāṇini 3.2.175), and because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Alternatively, from the root *aś*, the suffix *varaṬ* is added with the substitution of *iC* for the penultimate vowel; since the suffix is *ṭit*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The meaning is that she possesses sovereignty (*aiśvaryatva*) which is ever-shining. And it has been said in the *Viśvaśarīraskandha* section of the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"Sovereignty, agency, independence, and the nature of consciousness—these are said by the wise to be synonyms for the I-consciousness (ahantā). Thus [it is said].
She bestows the grace of Sadāśiva and is intent upon the fivefold cosmic function (pañcakṛtya). 115.

Īśvara is predominantly composed of extremely pure *sattva* and is Sadāśiva; because she is non-different from him, she is Sadāśivā (the feminine form is derived by adding the suffix *ṭāp* due to the absence of a final *t*). "Grace" (*anugraha*) refers to the return of the universe—which has undergone complete dissolution—to the state of atoms and so forth at the beginning of creation. And that [grace]...

Thus far, the function of the Lord (Īśvara) as described is that He "gives" and "effects"; this refers to grace (*anugraha*), which consists of concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace, or alternatively, bondage and liberation. In this view, the capacity to bestow these [states] belongs to Īśvara and Sadāśiva, who are characterized by the outward expansion (*unmeṣa*) and inward contraction (*nimeṣa*).

It is natural. It is the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇa*), that is, the support (*āśraya*) for the five kinds of activities described above, or it is that which is intent upon them. Or, it is that whose desired objects are those [five]. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *parāyaṇa* may mean 'desired object,' as well as 'intentness' and 'support. And it has been said:
In the *Mṛgendrasaṃhitā*:
"This indeed is the sole cause of the creation, maintenance, destruction, and concealment of the world,
as well as the regulator of all elemental and derivative entities."
Thus it is said. Also in another scripture:
"The fivefold activity of this [Lord], who is eternally risen, consists of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and likewise the bestowing of grace upon the world."
Thus it is said. Also in the fourth skandha of the Devībhāgavata:
"She creates the universe at will; she protects that which has been protected;
and at the end of the kalpa, she indeed withdraws it—she who possesses three forms and deludes the universe."
Joined with her, Brahmā creates; joined with her, Viṣṇu protects;
and joined with her, Rudra destroys the world at will.
O lord of men, she binds the entire world, which is deluded by the noose of illusion,
with the very firm noose of "I" and "mine."
"Yogis who are free from attachment, desiring liberation and seeking release,
worship that very Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe, the Auspicious One.
Thus it was also said by the venerable teacher [Śaṅkara] in the passage beginning with "The Creator produces the world, Hari protects it," and so forth.

In the *Śaktisūtra* it is also stated: "Nevertheless, like that [Lord], it performs the fivefold acts. The definitions of these acts are given in the subsequent sūtra: "They consist of manifestation (*ābhāsana*), coloring (*rañjana*), reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), stabilization of the seed-state (*bījāvasthāpana*), and dissolution (*vilāpana*). The meaning of this should be sought in the *Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya*.
Bhairavī Bhagamālinī resides in the center of the solar orb;

that is to say, she stands in the middle of the solar orb (bhānumaṇḍala), because at the time of twilight the Goddess is to be meditated upon there. As it is said in the *Antaradhikaraṇa*: "This which is within the sun..."

Furthermore, because of the determination that the form described in the Śruti passage, "The golden person is seen," is indeed the Supreme Lord; and likewise, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Hymn to the Goddess composed by Himavat:
"He whose nature is the entirety of the Vedas, who is the sole object of knowledge, and who has filled the various worlds with his own splendor."

"I bow to the form known as Parameṣṭhin, the cause of the three worlds, situated within the solar disc. Here, the solar disc may refer either to the orb of the sun or to the unstruck lotus (*anāhata-kamala*). Bhairavī is the consort of Bhairava, who is Paraśiva;
or else, Bhairavī is a collection of timid women, according to the rule "a group of those" (*tasya samūha*).

Thus, by the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Nor does there arise the contingency of neuter gender—as in the cases of *kākam*, *śaukam*, *yauvatam*, or *gārbhiṇam*—because when the word *bhairava* is connected with *vibhūti*, the application of *aṇ* again allows for the possibility of *ṅīp*. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "Śambhu is the meaning, and Śivā is speech."
Beginning with "Śambhu [is] by day, Śivā by night," and having specifically described Arundhatī, Anasūyā, Śacī, and others as being forms of Gaurī, it concludes:
"All those who are denoted by feminine nouns are the manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ) of Gaurī."
In the Tripurāmbā Cakreśvarī mantra, when the letter *ra* is extracted from the middle *kūṭa*, its name becomes "Bhairavī";
or it is of the nature of that mantra; or she has the form of a twelve-year-old girl. For it is said: "A [girl] of twelve years..."

This is because of Dhaumya’s statement regarding the maiden [Kātyāyanī]: "She is Bhairavī. She is called Bhagamālinī because she wears (malati) or bears (dhārayati) *bhaga*, which consists of the sixfold attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*). The verbal root is *mala* or *malla*, meaning "to bear. while five other external contentments are declared to arise from the cessation of the objects of the senses.

"Reasoning (ūha), oral instruction (śabda), study (adhyayana), the three types of removal of suffering (duḥkhavighāta), association with a friend (suhṛtprāpti), and charity (dāna)—these are the eight means of attainment (siddhi). Prior to attainment, the curb (aṅkuśa) is threefold.
This is the meaning: prior to liberation, there is a threefold obstacle that acts as a restraint.

[The obstacles] are incapacity, contentment, and attainment. Among these, incapacity (*aśakti*) refers to the inability of the sense organs to perceive their respective objects, caused by defects such as blindness, deafness, and so forth.
This [incapacity] is of eleven kinds, corresponding to the eleven sense organs. Contentment (*tuṣṭi*), moreover, is of two kinds—
[Contentment is] divided into internal and external. Among these, the first [internal contentment] is fourfold due to the distinctions of *prakṛti* (nature) and so forth.
The satisfaction consisting in the thought "I am liberated" because the mind has dissolved into the eightfold *prakṛti* is called *prakṛti-tuṣṭi* (contentment with nature).
The satisfaction consisting in the thought "I have achieved my goal" merely by adopting the outward garb of renunciation is called *upādāna-tuṣṭi* (contentment with acquisition).

The contentment called "Time" is the thought, "It will be accomplished through time alone; what is the use of the hardship of meditation? The contentment called "Fortune" is the thought, "It will be accomplished solely through the rise of destiny. These are internal (ādhyātmika) because they pertain to the self. The external ones, however, are distinguished by the fivefold objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth.

The five kinds [of contentment] consist of the state of having enough regarding various objects, arising from perceiving the defects such as the acquisition, preservation, expenditure, and loss of wealth, as well as certain defects inherent in sound and other sense-objects. Thus, there are nine contentments. Of these—

The names beginning with *salila* and ending with *uttamāmbhas*, as well as those beginning with *tārā* and ending with *samudita*, should be understood as the names of the *siddhis* (accomplishments) themselves. Accomplishment (*siddhi*) is of eight kinds, according to the distinctions of *ūha* (inference/insight) and so forth. *Ūhasiddhi* is the deduction of meaning independently of instruction.
From the incidental hearing of words comes the knowledge of their meaning, which is the accomplishment of the word (*śabdasiddhi*).
From the teacher’s instruction alone, the knowledge of the meaning through discernment arises, which is the accomplishment of study (*adhyayanasiddhi*).
There are three [accomplishments] consisting of the destruction of the threefold suffering—internal, celestial, and elemental.

The accomplishments (*siddhi*) are as follows: there is one accomplishment of wealth through the acquisition of friends, and one accomplishment of wealth obtainable through service to the learned and ascetics; thus there are eight accomplishments and nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*). The opposite of these seventeen is also seventeenfold.
The names beginning with "astu" and ending with "pramuditā" are to be found in the original source (*ākara*).
These too are denoted by the terms "incapacity" (*aśakti*) and "intellect" (*buddhi*); thus, there are seventeen [defects].
Together with the eleven capacities of the sense organs (*indriya-śakti*), there are twenty-eight types of bondage (*vadha*). And of these...
The systematic classification is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "The eighth is the Anugraha creation; it is established as fourfold:
through error (viparyaya), incapacity (aśakti), attainment (siddhi), and contentment (tuṣṭi)."
In stationary beings it arises from perversion; in the animal realm, by its own power; among humans, through the nature of accomplishment; and among the gods, entirely through contentment.
This is the general direction. She is served and worshipped by Hari, Brahmā, and Indra—that is, by Viṣṇu, Vidhi, and Śakra.
In the city of Śrīnagara, she is situated between the eighteenth and seventeenth walls for Viṣṇu;
between the seventeenth and sixteenth for Brahmā; and between the fifteenth and fourteenth for [Indra].
Because it is remembered as the dwelling place for the purpose of serving the Goddess by the world-protectors, Indra and the others;
and also in the Devībhāgavata:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu, Vāsava, Varuṇa, and Yama..."
Vāyu, Agni, Kubera, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Bhaga.
"The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts—
all meditate upon that Goddess who effects creation, maintenance, and destruction.
By this [it is shown] those who perceive the scriptures concerning Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others alone...
Because of the absence of knowledge regarding the true nature of Viṣṇu and others, even though there may be engagement in their worship,
those who perceive the Devyāgama do not engage in that worship due to their specific insight. For a beggar does not deserve to beg from other beggars when a non-beggar is present.
This is implied by the phrase "because it contradicts logic. This very point was stated by us in the *Śivastava*:

"O Supreme Śiva, how could I—a beggar—beg from other mortals, such as Indra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu, who are themselves beggars [for favors], saying 'Give! when I am already a partaker of the sovereignty bestowed by you?"
"Even though the *ukthya*— which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of a hundred *ukthya*s— is ignorant [of them],
it desires the properties of the *ukthya* of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, but not the properties of the *ukthya* of the twelve-day sacrifice. || 120 ||
She is Nārāyaṇī, whose form is sound (nāda), and who is devoid of name and form (nāma-rūpa).

In the sense of "the offspring of Nara," the suffix *phañ* is applied according to the rule for the *naḍādi* group, resulting in *Nārāyaṇa*; this refers either to Śiva or Viṣṇu, and she belongs to him, hence she is Nārāyaṇī. Regarding the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the word *Nārāyaṇa*, it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*:
"Water is called *nārāḥ*, for water is indeed the offspring of *nara*;
since it is his place of resort (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Thus it is said. Also in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "Since he is the resort (*ayana*) of *naras* (men), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the word *nara* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*). This is because, with reference to the verbal root *nṛ* (to lead), the *Devībhāgavata* states: "He is called *nara* because he leads; the eternal Supreme Self is so designated. Furthermore, the etymological derivation is possible as *nārāḥ* being "those belonging to *nara*. In the *Mahābhārata*, however—
"The wise know that the principles (tattvas) born from Nara are called 'Nārās'; since He has them as His abode (ayana), He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Of this Nārāyaṇa, who is Paramaśiva, the female consort is Nārāyaṇī. With reference to the Fourth State (turīya):

"He is the Lord of Śrī, and he is also the Lord of Pārvatī," according to the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*. This statement is made with the intention of asserting the non-difference between [the Goddess] and Lakṣmī. In reality, however, in the rule "puṃyogādākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.48), the term "puṃyoga" (connection with a male) does not refer exclusively to the relationship between a bride and a groom.

It is intended [to include such cases], for an example of the relationship consisting of the father-daughter bond is also seen there. Therefore, in this case, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied to the masculine connection (*puṃyoga*) in the form of the brother-sister relationship; the meaning is "the sister of Nārāyaṇa.
For this very reason, they explain it in exactly the same way in the verse: "Salutation to Śiva, who has Nārāyaṇī as his companion."
She is also called Nārāyaṇī because of her non-difference from Nārāyaṇa along with Gaurī. This was stated by Guṇi-Śiva in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"I am Nārāyaṇa, and Gaurī is the eternal Mother of the World."
The Supreme Lord, the God, having divided himself, remains established as his own self.
"The gods and others, as well as the great sages, do not know my supreme reality;
I alone, the Soul of the Universe, know it—namely Bhavānī and Viṣṇu.
Thus [it is said]. But in the Devīpurāṇa:
"One should perform [the rite] at Jalāyanānala, or else at Samudraśayana;
she is celebrated as Nārāyaṇī, for she brings about both men and women.
And this [site] is well-known in the Supārśva region. It is also stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
In the Devīkṣetrādhyāya it is said: "Nārāyaṇī is at Supārśva, while Bhadrasundarī is at Trikūṭa.
In the Hrīṃkāra-mantras and others, above the Bindu (the point) are the Ardhacandra (half-moon), Rodhanī, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, and Vyāpikā.

There exist eight phonemes known as Samana and Unmanā, which take on subtle, subtler, and most subtle forms; among them, the third phoneme is called Nāda. Its essential nature is described in the Mahāsvacchandatantra:
Regarding that which was called Rodhinī by you, its Nāda is situated above it;
it resembles the filaments of a lotus and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
"Surrounded by innumerable cities... and so on, up to:
"The supreme Śivā, who ascends upward, seated upon his lap..."
"One should meditate"— ending thus— [she] is she whose form is such a resonance (*nāda*), or else she whose very form is resonance itself.
For there exist [in the world] appearances that, through mutual differentiation, take the form of a knot between consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*).
There are five forms:
"It exists," "It shines," "It is dear," "Name," and "Form"—this is the pentad of aspects.
The first three are the form of Brahman; the latter two are the form of the world.
Thus have the learned analyzed [the matter].

In that regard, because name and form—which constitute the nature of the world—are false, she is devoid of them. Furthermore, since the relationship between the unreal and the real is itself false, her true relationship is with the Real alone.
That which exists is "bhāva. And the Chāndogas record: "Ether, indeed, is the name;

it is the bringer-forth of name and form; that which is within these two is Brahman. Ether, whose nature is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), is itself the bringer-forth of name and form, [existing] without those two.
The meaning of that [scriptural passage] is that whatever remains as mere substratum is indeed Brahman.
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Bhāskararāya, the fourth digit named Marīci has arisen from three hundred names. (300)
Thus ends the fourth ray, the third hundred [of verses], in the commentary on the *Lalitāsahasranāma* composed by the venerable Bhāskararāya, author of the *Padavākyapramāṇa* and other works. 4.
The fifth digit, named the Fourth Hundred, is Jvālinī.
She is Hrīṃkārī and Hrīmatī.

She is called Hrīṃkārī because she produces shame (*hrī*); [this is formed] from the root *hrī* with the suffix *aṇ* (denoting agency) and the feminine suffix *āp*, with the elision of the second case ending (*aluk*).

Alternatively, *hrīṃ* is an indeclinable because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *svarādi*. For this very reason, in the *Triśatikā*, the usage for the ninety-ninth name in its dative case is simply *ahrīṃ namaḥ*.
Its meaning, however, is stated in the *Svatantratantra* by means of a verse containing scrambled syllables: [The verse follows here.]
"You are not to be questioned regarding the recitation of the Kāma-mantras; you have not bowed before Agni, nor have you studied the Veda.
You are like a blind man who has fallen into a hundred-cubit-deep pit.
Thus [it is said]: "He who knows the deity, the chariot, and the horse, but not the sequence..."

"Though possessing a divine chariot and horses, he is mute with jumbled syllables"—such is the sequence of the statement. Since creation, maintenance, and destruction culminate in having Him as their purpose, He is the "performer of those" (tatkārī);
thus He is Hrīṃkārī. Alternatively, this suffix *kāra* is applied to the syllable (*varṇa*).

Because [the class] beginning with *gaura* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The meaning is that she is the very essence of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśvarī. She is called *hrīmatī* because she possesses modesty (*hrī*); and thus it is heard in scripture: "She is Lajjāvatī, Tuṣṭi, iṣṭā, and Puṣṭi."
—It is heart-pleasing and free from anything to be rejected or accepted. || 121 ||
She dwells in the heart (*hṛdya*), residing within the hearts of sages; or she is delightful (*ramaṇīyā*).

She is devoid of both the rejectable and the acceptable (*heyopādeya*), which are fit for being abandoned or acquired, because scriptures that teach engagement and withdrawal have as their object only those possessed by ignorance (*avidyāvat*). || 121 ||
The Queen is worshipped by the King of Kings (Rājarāja), is delightful, and has lotus-like eyes.
She is honored and served by both Manu and Kubera, the King of Kings;
or alternatively, she is the embodiment of the knowledge (vidyā) of Kubera and others. For this very reason, [she is] the fourteenth—
Describing the ground between the fifteenth and sixteenth walls, the sage Durvāsas said: "In the eastern part of that world, I meditate upon Dhanada, the Lord of the family of treasures,
as well as upon the Yakṣas headed by Maṇibhadra, who take refuge at the feet of the Mother."

Thus: in the phrase "talloke," the meaning of the word *tat* (that) is Vāyu. She is a *rājñī* (queen) because she is the principal consort of the Lord of the Kings of Kings (*rājarājeśvara*). She is *ramyā*, meaning beautiful. By the word *rājīva*, either a lotus (*padma*), a deer, or a fish is understood; she whose eyes are like those is *rājīvalocanā*.
"Rājīvā refers to a deer, a fish, a lotus, or one who lives off a king," according to the Viśva lexicon.
She is called *rājopajīvinī* because she looks upon [the king] or because she lives off the king.
She is the delighter (*rañjanī*), the beautiful one (*ramaṇī*), the delightful one (*ras yā*), and she possesses a girdle with tinkling bells (*raṇatkiṅkiṇimekhalā*). || 122 ||

She is called *rañjanī* because she delights her devotees; or alternatively, because she colors the Supreme Śiva—who resembles pure crystal—by her mere presence, like the *aruṇā* goddess or the hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*).
She is called *ramaṇī* because she causes her devotees to rejoice and sports with them, as it is said: "Eating, playing, and rejoicing."

According to the Śruti, "rasya" means fit to be tasted or relished, for it is said in the Śruti, "He is indeed rasa. She is one who possesses a girdle or waist-belt (*mekhalā*) upon which small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*) are tinkling. || 122 ||
She is Ramā, whose face is like the full moon, who is the embodiment of Rati, and who is beloved by Rati.

According to the statement in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*: "She shines like a dancer in the form of Lakṣmī, Vāc, and so forth," she is Ramā because her essential nature is that of Lakṣmī. Furthermore, when [the moon] is deficient in its digits she is Anumati, and when it is full...
By the authority of the lexicon found in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, which states "rākā [means] the moon," she is one whose face is like the full moon (*rākendu*), like the full moon itself.
Her form is Rati, because she is the wife of Kāma. *Ramā* is the vowel *ī*. Thus, she is *rākenduvadanā*.

If accompanied by the *anusvāra*, it becomes the *Kāmakalā* in the form of *Rati*; this is the extraction (*uddhāra*). *Rati* is the consort of Kāma, or she whose delight (*rata*) is what is dear to her.
She is the protector (*rakṣākarī*), the slayer of Rākṣasas (*rākṣasaghnī*), the beautiful woman (*rāmā*), and one who is devoted to pleasure (*ramaṇalampaṭā*). || 123 ||
She is the *rakṣākarī* (protector), because she performs protection (*rakṣā*), which is the act of guarding, or because she is the ash; she is the agent of preservation and dissolution.

She is the *rākṣasaghnī* (slayer of demons), for she slays those who are indeed *rākṣasas* (demons). She is *rāmā*, whose nature is that of a woman in general; or alternatively, she is so called because yogis delight (*ramante*) in her, according to the rule "after roots ending in *jvaliti*, *ka*, and *saṃt*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied."
[The word "Gaurī" is] feminine because of the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*, which states: "Everything is feminine, Gaurī. In another passage of that same work, it says:
"All males are Śaṅkara; all females are Maheśvarī. Those who are denoted by masculine words are proclaimed to be Rudras."
"All those things denoted by feminine words are manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ) of Gaurī;
likewise, men and women are said to be manifestations of those two [Śiva and Śakti].
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa as well:

"Among gods, animals, humans, and so forth, the Blessed Lord Hari exists in that which bears a masculine name, and Lakṣmī exists in that which bears a feminine name, O Maitreya; beyond these two, nothing else exists.
Thus it is said in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa as well.
"Whatever feminine form is seen in the three worlds, O Goddess, all that is your own form; such is the certainty in the scriptures.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bṛhatparāśarasmṛti*:
"Women when pleased, women when angry, and even deities when pleased or angry—
when pleased they cause a lineage to flourish, but when insulted they destroy it.
Because she is the embodiment of all women, [she acts thus] toward her own husbands, who are her lovers, during dalliance or sexual union.
Or she is one who is addicted to, longing for, and thirsty for play. || 123 ||
She is *Kāmyā*, whose form is the aesthetic power of desire (*kāmakalā*), and who is fond of the *kadamba* flower.

She is called *Kāmyā* because she is desired by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) as something to be attained through knowledge (*jñāna*). Alternatively, she is the form of the night of the twelfth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa-dvādaśī-rātri*). In this context, she consists of the three *bindus* and the half-moon digit (*hārdhakalā*).

The first *bindu* is called *kāma*, and the final *kalā* is [also] called *kāma*; thus, by the principle of *pratyāhāra* (synecdoche), they are referred to as *kāmakaletā*. Her essential nature begins with the passage: "The Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), whose form is the sprout of the seed of the manifest union of Śiva and Śakti."

The meaning is "having that form," as determined in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa* by the passage ending with: "Kāma is [the letter] due to its desirability, and Kalā is the [letter] *i*; the two dots (*bindu*) are the forms of fire and the moon. Alternatively, "Kāma" is the womb (*yoni*) and "Kalā" is the [vowel] *a*.
As it is said in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*:

"O Pārvatī, she who is known as Kāmeśvarī and [her consort] Kāmeśvara—she who is called Kalā and is full of grace—is renowned as Kāmakalā. Alternatively, it may mean "she who is desire (kāma) and whose form is Kalā. This refers to her being denotable by the word *kāma* alone.
Because it is established in the *Kālīpurāṇa*:
"Since she came to the great mountain with me for the sake of love (*kāma*),
the Goddess is called Kāmākhyā, having gone to the interior of Nīlakūṭa."

"She is called Kāmākhyā because she is the bestower of desires (kāmadā), the passionate one (kāminī), the desirable one (kāmyā), the beloved (kāntā), the giver of the limbs of desire (kāmāṅgadāyinī), and the destroyer of the limbs of desire (kāmāṅganāśinī). She is she for whom the *kadamba* flowers— the blossoms of the *nīpa* tree— are dear.
She is auspicious, the root of the world, and an ocean of the essence of compassion. || 124 ||

She is Kalyāṇī because her very nature is auspiciousness (maṅgala). Furthermore, in the *Pādma Purāṇa* and the *Devīpurāṇa*, she is enumerated as one of the specific forms [of the Goddess] under the name "Kalyāṇī of the Malaya Mountain. Alternatively, she is Kalyāṇī because she causes that auspicious speech (kalyā) to resound; she makes it vocalize. She is the bulbous root (kanda) of the world, its fulfillment.
Or, she whose root is that [compassion]. Yādava states: "The word *kanda* may mean filling, the root of a plant, or even a cloud.

She is one in whom the oceans consist of nothing but the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of compassion; that is to say, her nature is characterized by a compassion even greater than that of the oceans. This refers to the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
In the case of the words *kanda* and *sāgara*, there would be the occurrence of the masculine gender due to their taking the gender of the following word (*paravalliṅga*). || 124 ||

Kalāvatī, Kalālāpā, Kāntā, and Kādambarīpriyā. She is called *kalāvatī* because the sixty-four arts (*kalā*) exist within her. She is *kalālāpā* because her speech (*ālāpa*) is soft (*kala*), or because her speech is soft and melodious (*mañjula*). Regarding "in sound" (*dhvanau*): [the following applies].

"Madhura-asphuṭe" (sweet and indistinct). According to Amara, "kala" means this. Or, it may mean that from whose presence the attainment (*āpa*) of *ka*—that is, Brahman—is exceedingly easy, by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as if it were saliva (*lālā*). Or, it may mean that she whose speech (*lālāpa*) consists primarily of saliva-like water (*āpa*). The word *āpam* refers to a collection of waters (*apām samūhaḥ*), according to the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ... [Pāṇini 5.4.74].

Or [the suffix] -a is used as a compound-ending. She is "Kāntā" because she is desirable (*kamanīyatva*). Or, she is so called because her final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is *ka*—that is, Brahman itself. Or, she is in the form of the night of the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*). Or, she is one for whom *kādambarī*—the most excellent wine—is dear. For this very reason, the Śruti says:
"By offering to the Great Goddess wine, fish, choice meat, and well-prepared grains—the very sources of nourishment—and by making these his own, the virtuous man attains perfection. Thus it is said.
She is the granter of boons, with beautiful eyes, and intoxicated by the wine of Varuṇa. (125)
She is the "Bestower of Boons" (Varadā) because she grants boons to her worshippers, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others.
As it has been stated by Nārada in the *Mātsya* and *Pādma* Purāṇas: "And as for what I said regarding her hands being perpetually turned upward..."
This hand of the Goddess, however, is always turned upward and granting boons.
"It shall become that which grants boons to the hosts of gods, asuras, and sages.
In this context, it is said that "the hand is the granter of boons" because, for the most part, the act of giving is performed by means of the hand.
In reality, however, the intent lies merely in fulfilling the desires of the deities, and not necessarily in the assumption of the *varadamudrā* (the boon-granting gesture).
