By the venerable teacher Bhagavatpāda:
"The host of deities, with their two hands, bestows the gestures of fearlessness and boons; you alone are not thus, for you have manifested the gestures of both the boon and fearlessness."
When this was said,
the Sovereign fulfills the desires of the gods and others who seek boons;
since the root *vṛñ* is declared to mean "choosing," she is therefore remembered as the Giver of Boons (*Varadā*).
Thus it is stated in the Devībhāgavata; and in the Vārāha Purāṇa, in the section concerning the slaying of the demon Vetrāsura, it is said:
"On the ninth day, this Goddess should always be worshipped with meditative concentration;
she will become the bestower of boons upon all the worlds, of this there is no doubt."
Thus: she whose beautiful (*vāma*) eyes or glances are lovely;

or, she who leads (*nayati*) toward the left-hand path (*vāma-mārga*); or else, the fruit produced by action is called *vāma*. This is seen in the Śruti passage, "He indeed is Vāmanī," and in the Śruti concerning the Saṃyadvāmas and so forth.
Because the left foot is seen to be explained in that manner, she is "Vāmanayanā" (she who leads or brings [one] by means of that).
She belongs to Varuṇa, thus she is Vāruṇī; he who possesses her is Vāruṇīmān, namely Śeṣa, who has a thousand hoods.
Regarding Śeṣa, it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "He who is himself worshipped by his own splendor and by Vāruṇī..."
According to the reading "mūrtaye," she is "unperturbed" (avihvalā) just as the Earth does not become overwhelmed when bearing the weight [of the world].

Alternatively, *vāruṇī* refers to the wine produced from the date-palm (*kharjūrī*); she is "intoxicated" (*vihvalā*) by its exhilaration—the bliss born of drinking—and is thus characterized by a forgetfulness of external objects.
This means: "the singular savoring of the bliss of one's own Self. Alternatively, they are called *vāruṇīmantas* because they are not agitated (*avihvalā*) within [that state].
Or, those who have conquered the channel named *vāruṇī*, which has Vāyu as its presiding deity, are called *vāruṇīmantas*. And it is said in the Yogaśāstra:
"The channel situated below and above, which goes everywhere, is Vāruṇī;
she is declared to be the deity of the direction [South], while Vāruṇī is the deity of the Wind. Thus [ends verse 125].
She who is superior to the universe, who is to be known through the Vedas, and who dwells on the Vindhya mountain;

she is superior and more exalted than the entire universe, from the earth up to Śiva, according to the Vedic revelation: "Rudra, the great seer, is the lord of the universe. She is to be known—that is, understood—through the Vedas: the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharvaṇa. And by the Vedas...

This is because of the Śruti and Smṛti texts stating, "I alone am to be known by all. Alternatively, the four doors of the Cintāmaṇi palace are the four Vedas; since there is no vision of the Deity without entering through the doors, [the Lord] is to be known solely through the Vedas. And thus says the Śruti:
"The eastern direction is said to belong to the Ṛks; they say the southern, which is boundless, belongs to the Yajus;
the western belongs to the Atharvans and Aṅgirases; and the northern, the great direction, is said to belong to the Sāmans.
Thus [it is said] by means of Śuddhavidyā and the others.

The meaning is also that she is to be known through Saubhāgyā and others, Lopāmudrā and others, Turīyāmbā and others, as well as the deities of the Ṛg, Yajus, Atharva, and Sāma Vedas. She dwells on the mountain named Vindhya;
thus it is said in the *Pādmapurāṇa*, in the enumeration of the Goddess’s sacred sites: "And likewise Sītā on Trikūṭa, and [she] on the Vindhya..."
"the dweller of the Vindhya mountains. Also, in the *Pāñcarātra-lakṣmītantra*:
"In the Vaivasvata interval, those two, Śumbha and Niśumbha, shall again be born, intoxicated by boons and causing affliction to the gods."

"Born in the family of Nanda the cowherd, originating from the womb of Yaśodā, I, known as Nandā and dwelling in the Vindhya mountains, shall destroy them both. This same matter is well-known in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as well.
The ordainer, the mother of the Vedas, the illusory power of Viṣṇu, the playful one. || 126 ||

She is called *vidhātrī* because she creates, sustains, or nourishes the world; for the *Devīpurāṇa* states: "A *dhātrī* is declared to be a mother, and she is so praised because of her act of supporting. Alternatively, she is the wife of Vidhātṛ (Brahmā). Or, she is one whose *dhātrī*—the *āmalakī* tree—is especially dear to her.

The "mother of the Vedas" means their progenitor; for there are such scriptural passages as, "This Rigveda, Yajurveda, and so forth, are the breath of this Great Being," and "From her were born the Ṛks and the Sāmans. Furthermore, in the Devīpurāṇa:

It has been said: "Because the vowels and consonants have emerged from the Kuṇḍalinī, which is shaped like a *śṛṅgāṭaka* (a triangular or cross-shaped object), she is therefore known as the Mother of the Gods (*Devamātṛ*). [Furthermore,] although Viṣṇu, whose nature is all-pervasive (*vyāpanaśīla*), is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, his *māyā*...
It is that which creates an obstruction; that is to say, it is that which delimits, or it is the *māyā* associated with that [obstruction].
For it is said in the words of the Blessed One: "For this divine *māyā* of mine, consisting of the *guṇas*, is difficult to overcome.
It is also stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"She who, having divided herself through the qualities of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* in the form of the unmanifest and the manifest, effects the purpose [of the world], is called Viṣṇumāyā.
Thus it is said. She is so called because she possesses *vilāsa*, which is the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*); or else, she is the specific form of the *pīṭha-śakti*.

She is called *vilāsinī* because she is enumerated among them in such passages as "the eternal, the playful (*vilāsinī*), the milch-cow," and so forth; or alternatively, she is *vilāsinī* because she resides (*āste*) in the *bila*, the aperture of Brahmā. As it is stated in the *Svacchandatantra*, introducing the subject: "There, the aperture of Brahmā is to be known as surrounded by billions of Rudras."
"Another power is Brahmāṇī, who rests upon the lap of Brahmā;
she stands having blocked the gateway to the path of liberation. (126)
She is the very nature of the field (*kṣetra*), the Mistress of the field, and the protectress of both the field and the Knower of the field.

The "field" refers either to the body—consisting of the thirty-six principles beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva—or to [the realm] such as Kāmarūpa and others. That is her own, her innate nature.
She whose form is such [is she]. And so it is said in the *Laiṅga*:
"The Goddess, beloved of the Destroyer of Tripura, maintains the state of the Field (*kṣetra*);
the unborn Lord, the Slayer of Death, maintains the state of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)."

Thus, Śiva is the Lord of the field (kṣetra), which is the body; she is his Kṣetreśī. The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the individual soul (jīva); because she protects both that Knower of the Field and the field, she is called Kṣetrakṣetrajñapālinī. And so it is stated in the Viṣṇusmṛti:
"O Earth, this body is designated as the field."
Those who know this declare that he who understands this is the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).
"Know Me also as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) in all fields, O Bhārata"—
even in the Gītā, it is constructed in this very same way with the two addresses, "O Kaunteya" and "O Bhārata.
Also in the Laiṅga [Purāṇa]:
"The wise have declared that the twenty-four principles are designated by the term *kṣetra*, and likewise, the experiencing person (*puruṣa*) is designated by the term *kṣetrajña*.
However, in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*, it is stated: "The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is indicated as the *kṣetra*, and Brahmā is called the *kṣetrajña*."

Thus it has been said. Also in the Brahmapurāṇa: "The bodies are called fields (kṣetra); he who knows them, as well as their respective pleasures, by means of his yogic self, is therefore called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)."
Thus it is said; however, in the *Manusmṛti*:
"That which causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field);
but that which performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise."
There is another internal self, distinct from the body, known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
by means of it, one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births.
Both of these—the Great One (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they remain pervading that which dwells within high and low beings.
"Countless forms issue forth from His body, which constantly set various beings in motion"—so it has been said.
She is free from decay and growth, and is worshipped by the Kṣetrapālas. (127)

Although it is the presiding controller over decay and growth—which are themselves modifications of the states belonging to the field—it is nevertheless free from them; for so says the Smṛti: "Weapons do not cut this," and so forth. Or rather, it is free from those two as produced by karma. "This..."

"The greatness of a Brāhmaṇa is eternal; it does not increase by action, nor does it become less," according to the Kaṭhaka Śruti; and "He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action," according to the Vājasaneyi Śruti. For the sake of slaying the demon Dāruka, Kālī [was created] by Śiva...
Having been created, she killed Dāruka.

Thereafter, observing that the world was being thrown into turmoil by her unappeased fire of wrath, Śiva became a child and wept. She suckled that child at her breasts; through the milk, he [quenched] hers.

The story that this very Kṣetrapāla even drank the fire of his own wrath—being a particular incarnation of Śiva—is well-known in the Laiṅga Purāṇa and other texts. The etymological derivation is: he who protects (pālayati) the field (kṣetra), which is the sacrificial ground (yāgāyatana).
By him [the goddess] was properly worshipped. 127.
Vijayā is stainless, venerable, and affectionate toward those who bow before her;
she is called Vijayā because her victory (*jaya*) is preeminent, or because she is the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpā*).
She is counted among the sixty-eight Śiva-tīrthas in the *Devīpurāṇa* as "Vijaya and Kāśmīra."
Or she is of the very nature of Śiva. In that same work, in the chapter on etymologies (Nirvacanādhyāya), it says:
"Having conquered the exceedingly powerful Daitya king named Padma, she became renowned throughout the three worlds as Vijayā and Aparājitā."
Thus [it is said]. Or, it may take the form of a specific house known as Vijaya, well-known in the *Viśvakarma-śāstra*.
The moment (muhūrta) called Vijaya is described in the *Cintāmaṇi*:
"On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, at the rising of the stars..."
"That time should be known as Vijaya (Victorious), which grants success in all undertakings.
In the Ratnakośa, however, it is said:
"When the twilight has slightly passed and the stars have just begun to appear..."
This time is called Vijaya; it accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
"The eleventh *muhūrta*, which is proclaimed as *Vijaya* (Victory),—in that [time] a journey should be undertaken by all who desire victory.
This means she has such a time as her form. She is *vimalā* (pure), meaning that from her the impurity consisting of ignorance (*āvidyaka*) has departed.

In the *Pādma-purāṇa*, she is described as "Vimalā in Puruṣottama," meaning she is either a specific form included among the sacred sites (*devītīrtha*) or a specific type of house. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Viśvakarma-śāstra* concerning houses:
"Dhruva, Dhānya, Jaya, Kānta, Vipula, and likewise Vijaya..."
"Sumukha, Vimala, Nanda, Nidhana, and Manorama.

Thus [it is said]. "Vandyā" means worthy of being saluted. He states that very worthiness with the word "vandāru": those who salute are "vandāravaḥ"; the suffix *āru* is applied according to the rule "śṝvandyorāruḥ. Such [people]...
She draws people toward her like a cow its calf and favors them; or [the name] "Vatsālā" is derived with the suffix *la* according to the rule "vatsaṃsābhyāṃ kāmabala.
She is the speaker of speech (*vāgvādinī*), the mistress of the left (*vāmakeśī*), and the dweller within the circle of fire (*vahnimaṇḍalavāsinī*). || 128 ||

She is called *Vāgvādinī* because she utters speech, or because she is a certain deity in the form of speech; or alternatively, because she causes speech to be uttered. This etymology is stated in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*:
"And for all her own devotees, [she exists] always in the form of speech."
"Or rather, because of her steadfastness, she is renowned in the world as Vāgvādinī.

And also in the *Laghustava*: "In this world, you alone are the mother of all sounds; you are called Vāgvādinī. She is one whose hair (*keśa*) is beautiful (*vāma*). Or, [she is] simply beautiful (*vāmā*).

Vāmeśa is Śiva, the lord of those [deities] on the left. Or, it refers to his consort, as he is established in the *Devīpurāṇa* among the sixty-eight Śiva-tīrthas with the statement, "One should know Vāmeśvara at Jaṭe. Alternatively, it is the *Tantra* spoken by Vāmakeśa; that is, either the *Tantra* taught therein, or that which is related to him by virtue of being its subject matter.

She is so called because she dwells there in the fire-mandala (vahni-maṇḍala), which exists either at the mūlādhāra or in the supreme space (paramākāśa). Alternatively, the word "fire" (vahni) may refer to the number three;
thus, the meaning is that she resides in the triad of the lunar, solar, and fiery mandalas. || 128 ||
She is the wish-fulfilling creeper (*kalpalatikā*) for those possessed of devotion, who releases the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu*).

She is like a wish-fulfilling creeper because she grants the desired objects to people who possess devotion. Alternatively, by using the suffix *kalpa* in the sense of "slightly incomplete," those whose devotion is not yet perfect are called "those who are almost devoted" (*bhaktimatkalpāḥ*); [the goddess belongs to them].

Like a creeper (*latikā*), she is expansive; like musk (*kastūrikā*), she is fragrant—according to the *Rabhasa* lexicon, "the word *latā* refers to the *mādhavī* creeper, dūrvā grass, and musk"; she is the one who satisfies those who have offered half their portion of food by granting them the fulfillment of their devotion. As it is said in the *Śaktirahasya*:
"Is worship performed for Bhavānī through non-sequential means or with half-faith intended to result in the attainment of sequential [practice] and full faith in another birth?
Thus it is said. Those devoid of the knowledge (*vidyā*) whose nature is the realization of non-duality (*abheda*) are *paśus* (bound souls). This is stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*:

"He who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know, like a beast," [it says]. Here, "another" means the triangular wheel (*trikoṇacakra*), according to another scriptural passage: "In that golden sheath, which has three spokes and is threefold-supported. For such beasts, who are devoid of knowledge—

It is so called because it specifically liberates one from the thirst for food; thus, there is a designation by the word *pāśa* (bond) for the two verbal roots *pibati* (to drink) and *aśnāti* (to eat). By adding the *kvip* suffix to *pā* (from *pā*) and *aś* (from *aś*), and then applying the feminine suffix *ṭāp* to those consonant-final forms, the compound form *pāśam* arises through their combination. It is precisely because it possesses only that much [quality] that it is so designated.
For those who have become weary of the state of being cattle (*paśutva*), it is heard in scripture: "Now, as for other cattle, hunger and thirst alone are their distinguishing mark;
they do not speak what is known, they do not see what is known, they do not know the morrow, nor the worlds of light and darkness. Or else, [the term] *paśu*...

This is because such an interpretation is seen in the Śruti: "Thinking him to be a beast, they lead him away with the indeclinable *samyañc* in the sense of 'correctly' (*samyagarthe*). Thus, [the mantra means] he releases the bonds—the bonds of Varuṇa—in such a way that he becomes a beast; or alternatively, he causes the bonds to fall away correctly. Together with Śiva...
It means that in the game of dice, having correctly cast the dice-pieces (*pāśas*) upon the board, one conquers Śiva.
Alternatively, *paśupāśān* refers to those whose desire (*āśā*) is for Paśupati, the Supreme Śiva; he specifically liberates them and extends [the state of] having attained Śiva to them. Or else:
From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, they are called "bound souls" (paśu) because their nature is identical to that of cattle;

since it is the means for their bondage, ignorance itself is the "fetter" (pāśa). This has been stated in the *Saurasaṃhitā*, in the section defining the names of ignorance: "Because it is the support of all, it is the Support."

Regarding the phrase "by means of the cause of the bond of *pāśa*": the *pāśas* are the principles (*tattva*) and so forth, which are its modifications; he liberates them through devotion to Śiva. As it is said in the *Laiṅga*:
"From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, [all belong] to the trident-bearing God of gods."
All those who abide in the state of a bound soul (paśu) are proclaimed to be "beasts" (paśavaḥ).
The twenty-four principles consist of Māyā, Karma, and the Guṇas;
they are also called "objects" because they bind the individual soul (pāśajīva) through fetters.

"Bound by these, all embodied beings are liberated through devotion to Śiva alone. Alternatively, the afflictions (kleśa) are fivefold: ignorance (avidyā), egoism (asmitā), attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa), and the clinging to life (abhiniveśa). Ignorance is the absence of discrimination between the Self and the non-Self; [it is] regarding that which is not the Self...

The misconception of the body and so forth as the Self is *asmitā* (egoism). From that arises *rāga* (attachment), which is the longing for garlands, sandalwood, and other objects used for the body’s enjoyment. *Dveṣa* (aversion) is anger toward that which obstructs the attainment of those objects. *Abhiniveśa* (clinging) is the failure to relinquish them, even after knowing them to be harmful, like an ignorant person. This, then, is...

Having provided a mere enumeration in the penultimate sūtra of the first pāda of the *Yogasūtra*, [ignorance] is described with its defining characteristics by means of five sūtras in the second pāda. As it is stated in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"Delusion (moha) is the failure to distinguish between darkness (tamas) and discernment; it is a delusion of the internal organ."
Great delusion, moreover, should be understood as the longing for the pleasures of vulgar enjoyment.
"Death is called *andhatāmisra*, and *tāmisra* is said to be anger;
this fivefold ignorance has manifested from the Great Self.
In that context, *tamas* and the others are merely synonyms for ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest. The word "death" (*maraṇa*)...
Devoted to false attachment, it is said in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "O best of bipeds, he bows to ignorance, egoism, passion, hatred, and attachment— these afflictions that have become like fetters."
O wise ones, they say that the afflictions exist in five forms: darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and blinding gloom (andhatāmisra).
They say that ignorance is darkness (tamas), and egoism is delusion (moha);
passion is indeed great delusion (mahāmoha), and hatred is gloom (tāmisra).
"And they declare that *andhatāmisra* is false attachment.
Furthermore, the subdivisions of these five afflictions (*kleśas*) are also mentioned in that same work:
"The division of *tamas* is eightfold, and *moha* is likewise declared to be eightfold."
The wise have considered the divisions of great delusion to be tenfold.
"The wise have likewise declared eight varieties of *tāmisra*, and eighteen divisions of *andhatāmisra* are proclaimed;
thus, taken together, there are fifty-two. Thus, by relying on the eighteen-fold nature of *tāmisra* as well, [the total is calculated].

Some say there are sixty-two bonds (*pāśas*). Furthermore, these afflictions (*kleśas*) are distinct for each of the three types of bound souls (*paśus*)— namely, those devoted to sense objects, those devoted to yoga, and those who know reality—
as stated in the *Devībhāgavata*:
For those who know reality, the afflictions are as if asleep; for yogis, they are like burnt bodies; but for those attached to sense objects, the afflictions remain in their unbroken and noble form.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the Kulārṇava:
"Compassion, doubt, fear, shame, and disgust as the fifth;
family, conduct, and caste—these eight are proclaimed to be the fetters."

Thus, this is a partial restatement by way of extraction (*avayuti-anuvāda*) from among the fifty-two divisions already mentioned for the five afflictions (*kleśa*), beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*). Those divisions have not been stated here for fear of prolixity.
And so, in the root text, the word *paśu* (the bound soul), according to the previously stated technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), also refers to the number fifty-one.
By means of the relationship of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the word] "fifty-two" is intended;
for in the verse from the *Śāradātilaka*, "by the fifty letters flowing incessantly in succession," it is precisely by such a secondary indication that the word "fifty" is used.

This is because Harṣadīkṣita and others have explained it as referring to fifty-one; thus, the meaning is that he liberates the fifty-two bonds of the bound souls (paśu). As it is said in the Śivarahasya:
He who binds the bound souls with the five afflictions and the fifty-two nooses is himself their liberator when he is properly worshipped with devotion.

This, however, is the summary according to the tradition of the Paurāṇikas. Alternatively, there are three fetters (pāśas): the atom (aṇu), differentiation (bheda), and action (karma). Among these, ignorance (ajñāna) is the atom (aṇu). And that consists of both the absence of the knowledge of selfhood in the Self, whose nature is consciousness, and the knowledge of selfhood in what is not the self, such as the body and so forth.

It is twofold; both of these together are called the atomic impurity (*aṇavamala*). And its designation by the term "atomic" (*aṇu*) is because it delimits the Self, even though that Self is unlimited.
As it is said in the *Saurasaṃhitā*: "Because it is the cause of the atomization of the Self, it is 'atomic' (*aṇu*) due to its being a stain (*mālinya*)."

Regarding the term "impurity" (*mala*): the multiplicity of the one Self alone is "division" (*bheda*). In this context, there are two kinds of that which pertains to *māyā*: first, the single root cause called the principle (*tattva*) known as *māyā*, which is the sixth among the principles;
and second, the group of principles beginning with the seventh and ending with the thirty-sixth, which is produced from it. Both of these are of the nature of *māyā*.
Impurity (*mala*) is defined as follows: *karma* is the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by actions prescribed or prohibited, which has the capacity to grant a body.

That too is twofold, distinguished as merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*); both together are called the *kārmaṇa-mala*. Among these various categories of atoms and *karma*, each subsequent one is pervaded by each preceding one.
All of this has been stated in the Pratyabhijñā-śāstra:
"The loss of freedom of consciousness, and the lack of consciousness even in that which is free—
this is the twofold atomic impurity (*āṇava-mala*), arising from the concealment of one's own true nature."

That which consists of the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is the power of *māyā*, which bestows birth and experience; that which consists of the awareness of what is to be done is the power of *karman*. Thus, these three [powers] arise through the power of *māyā* alone.
Thus it is stated even more clearly in the *Śaivasūtravārttika*:
"Now, if the body of this universe of such a nature is consciousness, then how can there be a connection with bondage? It is in order to dispel this doubt [that the following is said]."
Through both the reading with and without the elision [of the *a*], Maheśvara states the aphorism:
"Ignorance is bondage. Regarding that term "ignorance," the first [definition] is as follows: it is that which consists of the expansion of consciousness.
The knowledge that the self is not-self is ignorance; conversely, the knowledge regarding what is not-self is true knowledge.
The conceit of selfhood regarding the body and so forth—both of these constitute the *āṇava* impurity. It is imagined by oneself within oneself, manifested through one's own will as bondage.

It is stated that this bondage is not solely of the nature of the *āṇava* impurity; rather, the group of *yoni*s constitutes the body of *kalā*. The category of *māyā*, which arises from that, is the cause for the manifestation of differentiation (*bheda*).
The aggregate of principles (tattva-rāśi), beginning with Time and ending with the Earth, has that [consciousness] as its essence.
The impurity known as *māyīya* consists of the manifestation of various distinct objects of knowledge; having entered the body, it is called *kalā*, which effects limitation for human beings.
Furthermore, that body whose nature consists of merit and demerit is the *kārmaṇa* body;
in these two, bondage continues to persist.

Thus, among these three bonds (*pāśas*), living beings (*jīvas*) who are bound by one, two, or even all three are also designated by the term "bound soul" (*paśu*), being of three kinds. Although, when the permutations of the three are calculated, there are seven types of souls— three with one bond each, three with two, and one with all three— nevertheless...

Nevertheless, because there is a rule that each subsequent division of the subtle actions (*aṇukarma*) is pervaded by each preceding one, there are exactly three types of bound souls (*paśu*). These bound souls are designated by the terms "pure," "mixed," and "impure" in the *Nityāhṛdaya* and other texts such as the *Svacchandatantra*.
However, those who possess only consciousness are designated as *pralayākalas* and *sakalas*. Thus it has been said:
"The bound souls (*paśus*) are of three kinds; among them, some are considered *sakalas*, while others, O Great Goddess, are known by the names *pralayākala*."
"But others are *vijñānakevalas*; hear their nature in due order.
Among them, the *sakala* is bound by all three fetters (*pāśa*). As it has been said:
"The omnipresent one is covered by beginningless impurity (*mala*) and enveloped by *māyā* and *karman*."
One who knows the Śiva-principle within the body, whose sole delight is in non-duality, is light.
One who always acts as the agent of karma, who experiences the fruits of one's own actions,
and who is eternally attached to sense objects, is called a "complete beast."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the words *mala* (impurity) and *māyā* refer to the specific types of limited souls (*aṇu*). These bound souls (*paśu*) are of two kinds, according to whether their impurity has ripened or not. Among them, those whose impurity has ripened are three;
within that group, there are one hundred and eighteen who have attained perfection (*siddha*).

By virtue of the complete grace of Śiva, they have attained the status of Mantreśvaras. These consist of the eight known as the Śatarudras, the hundred Maṇḍalins, the eight Krodhabhaṭṭārakas and others, Vīreśvara, and the two beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha. Furthermore, Śiva [establishes] others also in the form of Ācāryas.

In this way, He bestows grace; however, toward those whose three impurities (*mala*) are not yet matured, He assigns them to various states of existence (*yoni*) through experience for the sake of maturing those impurities, and that too is indeed a form of grace. As it has been said:
"But when the impurities and so forth have not yet matured, there occurs a general grace."
The sovereign power pertaining to office arises solely through the grace of Śiva.
But the sacrificial animals, O Supreme Goddess, shall be of three kinds.
Thus [it is said]: "Out of a desire to show grace, He impels them toward ripening within various wombs.
Furthermore, those bound by the two fetters known as *aṇu* and *karman* are the *pralayākalas*.
They too are of two kinds, based on the presence or absence of the ripening of those two [fetters]. Among them, the latter...

By the power of karma, they are born in the highest wombs; in the primary [realms], wherever there is the grace of the Lord, they become lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*). As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Those known as *pralayākala*s are of a mixed nature, having the form of subjects (*pramātṛ*)."
And they possess bodies composed of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), O beloved, according to their respective karmas.
Having entered all wombs and experienced the enjoyments and so forth resulting from their respective karmas,
Śiva himself [manifests] when those karmas reach equilibrium.
Having slightly favored those whose impure karma has been well-matured,
the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) appear in three ways within the midst of the principles beginning with the water-principle (jalatattva).
Thus: those bound by the *āṇavamala* alone are the *vijñānakevalas*. As it has been said:
"Bound by *mala* alone, the bound soul (*paśu*) is the *vijñānakevala*;
when his *mala* is fully ripened, O Dear One, he is himself the *vijñānakevala*."

Thus, they are also of two kinds: those whose impurities are exhausted (*samāptakaluṣa*) and those whose impurities are not yet exhausted (*asamāptakaluṣa*). Among these, the former are the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s). The latter, however, consist of the seventy million great mantras (*mahāmantra*s). Nor should it be suspected that they are insentient; for although their bodies are of the nature of sound (*śabda*), they are nonetheless sentient.
Because it is established that embodied beings like ourselves possess consciousness; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Mṛgendrasaṃhitā*:
"Then Śiva, who is free from beginningless impurity, the all-doer and all-seer, removes the net of bonds from the individual soul (aṇu) who was previously cast into bondage."
Thus it is said. Those who follow the scriptures also say:
"Śambhu, the benefactor of all, ordains enjoyment and liberation for individual souls (aṇu) that are capable of their own functions, as well as for the insentient category."
Thus, because they possess the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) characterized by unripened *āṇava* impurity, even mantras are designated as "atomic" (*aṇu*).
In this way, due to the infinite gradations in the ripening of the impurities of all six types of bound souls (*paśu*), there are infinite divisions.
And for them, through their experience (*bhoga*), there are also the bestowals of sovereignty (*aiśvaryadāna*) that lead them to various births appropriate to those respective gradations.
Because its purpose is the ripening of impurity (*mala*), it consists precisely of the forms that liberate from bonds.

And thus, it is called *paśupāśavimocinī* because it specifically liberates the bonds—that is, the impurities—of the bound souls (*paśu*) who possess the aforementioned nature, according to their respective capacities. Nor is there [any contradiction] regarding this liberation...
It should not be asked how the Goddess can possess agency therein since it is Śiva’s work;

for, since that [work] is impossible for Śiva without the power of liberation (*mocakatva-śakti*), it is more appropriate— based on both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)— to accept the agency of liberation as residing in the Power alone.
As it has been said by the learned:
"I bow with my whole being to that primordial Power, whose nature is consciousness, by whom Śambhu is capable of bestowing both enjoyment and liberation upon this multitude of bound souls."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, agency (*kartṛtva*) is indeed autonomy (*svātantrya*), according to Pāṇini’s sūtra: "The agent is one who is independent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*). And that [autonomy] consists precisely in power (*śakti*). Accordingly, the *Śaktisūtra* states: "Consciousness (*citiḥ*) is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe. As for the *Śivasūtra*: "The Self is consciousness" (*caitanyam ātmā*).

Because its sovereignty is not explicitly specified [in that context] and by virtue of the neuter gender, it refers to the absence of attributes such as agency. As for the statement found in the Śakti-śāstra: "Consciousness is sovereign, the cause of the manifestation of the universe," and so forth—this is indeed a sūtra.
In the Śaiva scripture, however, it is held that consciousness is the Self; for both Śiva and Śakti are indeed nothing but consciousness.

Thus it is stated by the learned; however, the definitive conclusion of the Śaiva secret (rahasya) is that this is intended with the view that [the power] is non-different from the possessor of power (śaktimān).
It has destroyed all heretical systems and promotes the practice of the virtuous way of life. (129)
She is so described because she has withdrawn—that is, destroyed—all heretics (pākhaṇḍas) without exception. And the nature of a heretic is described in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
"Those whose vows and conduct are outside the Vedas, and who are excluded from the Śrauta and Smārta rites..."
Known as heretics, they are not to be conversed with by those of the twice-born caste.
Thus it is said. Also in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]:
"The Vedas, together with the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of dharma."
Thus, with reference to the enumerated branches of knowledge:
"This is the truth; anything other than this is heresy conceived by the intellect, created by the Great Delusion for the purpose of deluding the Daityas."

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the word *pāśa*, its etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is that the meaning of the Veda is the "rope" (*pāśa*), and the heretics (*pākhaṇḍas*) are its "fragments" (*khaṇḍakas*). For this very reason, it is called "the promoter of right conduct" (*sadācārapravartikā*). Right conduct (*sadācāra*) is the conduct of the "good" (*sat*), meaning either the best, or the cultured (*śiṣṭa*), or the existent (*sat*), namely Brahman; it is that which promotes such conduct regarding the dharma described in the *Karmakāṇḍa*.

Furthermore, he teaches and causes others to practice the various means for attaining that non-dual Brahman described in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*, preceded by a deep delight in it; that is to say, he instructs them in the Purāṇas and other texts.
And it has been stated by the Blessed One herself in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
O King, eighteen Purāṇas were indeed narrated by Vyāsa at the command of Brahmā; in them, Dharma is firmly established.
Furthermore, other Upapurāṇas were expounded by his disciples;
indeed, in every age, the author of all these is one who knows the treatises on Dharma.
Grammar, ritual, etymology, prosody,
astronomy, and logic— these are the supplements for all [the Vedas].
Thus, O best of men, these fourteen branches of knowledge are declared along with the four Vedas; dharma is not found elsewhere.
Thus, by my command, Manu, Vyāsa, and others establish this supreme dharma of the Grandfather until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus [ends the section]. || 129 ||
She is the moonlight that brings complete refreshment to those scorched by the fire of the threefold suffering (*tāpatraya*).

For those people thoroughly tormented by the fire characterized as *saṃsāra*— namely, the triad of sufferings known as the internal (*ādhyātmika*), the external (*ādhibhautika*), and the celestial (*adhidaivika*)— she is the cooling light.
Or like moonlight, which brings joy by first removing [darkness] through its perfect refreshing [of the world].
She is a young woman to be propitiated by ascetics, slender-waisted, and the dispeller of darkness.
She is "Tarunī" because she possesses eternal youthfulness, according to the Vedic revelation that she is "ageless and immortal.
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied here by the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) stating, "There is an addition [of the suffix] for the words *taruṇa* and *taluna*.
She is "to be propitiated by ascetics" (*tāpasaiḥ ārādhyā*), meaning she is the essence within *tāpa*, which is the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) that produces such suffering.
Or, she is so called because her meditation (*dhyāna*) is extensive (*ādhi*) on all sides. She is one whose waist (*madhya*) is slender (*tanu*).
In the region of Kāñcī, there is a well-known goddess named Tanumadhyā. As it is said: "May the goddess Tanumadhyā, the beloved of Bilveśvara, who dwells on the bank of the Nīvārī, protect me."
Or, it may take the form of a specific type of even meter (samavṛtta) called *tanumadhyā*. Accordingly, the *Piṅgala-sūtra* states:
"*tanumadhyā* consists of *ta* and *ya*. By the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "per foot" from the sūtra on *padacaturūrdhva*, [it applies] to each foot.
The meaning of the rule is that if the *tagaṇa* and *gaṇa* follow [the *na-gaṇa*], it is called *tanumadhyā*.

The previously mentioned example— “Among meters, I am the Gāyatrī”— is cited because this meter possesses the same structure as the Goddess’s own statement from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, and thus it takes on that form.
It is called *tamopahā* because it dispels the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus it is heard in the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*:

"Into blinding darkness they enter who worship ignorance. The reading here is *avidyām*, according to the authors of the Padapāṭha. In this way, the *Āraṇyaka* scripture censures any form of meditation other than true knowledge (*vidyā*).
And this is the corroborative statement (upabṛṃhaṇa) found in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. || 130 ||
Consciousness (citi) is the meaning indicated by that word (tat), and its nature consists of the single essence of consciousness.

For this very reason, it is said: "Consciousness is of the nature of knowledge which is the adversary of ignorance. The meaning is that its nature is as described in the *Śaktisūtra*: "Consciousness is independent and the cause of the manifestation of the universe. This indeed is what is called "Consciousness."
"From life for those who desire life"—thus it is said in the *Mahāvāsiṣṭha*.

Regarding the word *tat* (That) within the great Mahāvākyas such as *Tattvamasi*, its primary denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) is the variegated Brahman (*śabala-brahma*) characterized by being the agent of the creation and so forth of the universe. That very same [Brahman], when praised here, is the mere substratum (*dharmimātra*).

Pure Brahman is the indicated meaning (*lakṣya-artha*). The relationship between these two—the qualified and the absolute—is identity (*tādātmya*). This is what is stated: by the word "that" (*tat*), that which is the indicated meaning with which [the word] has attained identity is "that whose indicated meaning is the referent of the word *tat*. However, if it were intended to refer merely to the substratum (*dharmin-mātra*), then—

By the rule that "a *tatpuruṣa* compound takes the gender of its final member" (*paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*), there would follow the consequence of it being masculine; however, since even the form alone is qualified by attributes such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, it should simply be stated as such—therefore, he says: "one with consciousness. (*citā saha ekaḥ*)

Those whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is *rasa* (flavor), and for whom consciousness alone is the primary *rasa*, are those whose forms consist of the single flavor of consciousness (*cidekarasa*). Since she possesses attributes such as bliss and consciousness, she is "she whose form consists of the single flavor of consciousness" (*cidekarasarūpiṇī*). This means, in effect, that she possesses attributes non-different from herself. And it has been stated in the *Pañcapādikā*: "Bliss..."
The experience of objects and eternity— these attributes, though not distinct from consciousness, appear as if they were separate from it. And thus,
regarding the attributes such as being the creator of the universe, which serve as the delimiters of the capacity [to denote Brahman]:

The sense is that since [the Lord] is not included within His own nature (*svarūpa*), and because the attributes (*dharma*) included therein cannot serve as the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) due to their absolute non-difference [from Him], the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) known as "partial abandonment" (*bhāgatyāga*) is necessary. Alternatively, it is stated [that way] because of the difference between the two, insofar as pure Brahman is not the substratum (*dharmī*) of the Lord.

Since the relationship [between them] is not tenable, he says: "The meaning is that her very nature consists solely of the single essence of consciousness (cidekarasa) and is non-different from pure consciousness (cinmātra). Even though there is a difference between those two, because non-difference also exists, [it is] precisely the non-difference that has the same locus as the difference.
The sense is that, because it consists of identity (*tādātmya*), the aforementioned relationship is indeed possible. Now, one might object:

even if attributes such as being the creator of the universe are not included within the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the deity], they can still serve as the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); therefore, it is precisely that which is qualified by those attributes that is conveyed by the word "That" (*tatpada*).

Let the meaning of the sentence be precisely that non-difference; for by the force of the scriptural statement, it is possible to accept identity even between two things qualified [by different attributes]. This is because statements such as "He who has faith in what, he is that very thing" establish non-difference precisely between those qualified by attributes such as the state of being the object of meditation and the meditator.
Not so, because it lacks intrinsic necessity (*svārasya*).
By this, even that which is postulated through the impossibility of any other explanation (*anyathānupapatti*)—namely, the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) [Brahman]—is refuted;
thus, although a relationship between the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) and the absolute (*kevala*) is possible, it is simply not the operative factor. Therefore, he says:
The continuous stream of bliss beginning with Brahmā has become but a mere fragment of the bliss of one's own Self. || 131 ||

Regarding the term "one's own self" (*svātman*): the bliss that constitutes one's own nature (*ātmarūpa*)—when considered through the lens of the drops of bliss belonging to Indra and others, it becomes like an ocean; thus, although they are not drops themselves, they become drops within the ocean of the Goddess’s bliss for those beginning with Brahmā.
She is the one whose "streams"— meaning perfect collections— of blisses are the Brahmas, Viṣṇus, and Rudras, who are distinguished by attributes such as being the creator of the universe;
for the Śruti says, "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss."
In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], among the joys described with progressively increasing degrees starting from human joy, there are also enumerated the joys of Prajāpati and others.
Because that which is limited is inferior to the unlimited bliss of Brahman,
it cannot function as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); and since the unlimited bliss of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman is thus established,
there would be a contradiction with the authoritative means for determining the intended meaning, such as the opening statement regarding the knowledge that is the means to that human goal.

The intention is that it is only logical for the word *tat* to denote a Self devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*). According to the *Viśvakośa*, the word *lava* means "a small portion" (*leśa*) and "sport" (*vilāsa*). || 331 ||
The supreme Goddess, Paśyantī, is the nature of inward-facing consciousness. Now,

since the very identity of word and meaning constitutes the category of "power" (śakti), why would words such as "Truth" (satya) and so forth not apply to Brahman— even though it is devoid of qualities— given its non-difference from Śabdabrahman?

Anticipating the objection that [the words] consisting of *vaikharī* speech cannot possess identity with pure Brahman because they already possess identity with the Virāṭ Puruṣa, the author analyzes speech with the desire to provide a resolution.
Here, this should be understood: during the dissolution (*pralaya*).
In the state when the karmas of the beings being created have not yet reached maturity,
Brahman— delimited by Māyā which is non-different from such karmas— is said to be "condensed" (ghanībhūta).
When, through the power of time, the karmas reach maturity, it is in a state of dissolution.
The prior absence of ripening is called the desire to act (*vicikīrṣā*). Thereafter, at the moment of ripening, the activity of *māyā* arises;
such [Brahman], characterized by *māyā* which is reckoned according to the form of the ripened karma, is denoted by the term "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*).

For this very reason, its origination is also recorded in the Smṛti: "From that, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest (avyakta) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa) was produced. Because it is the hollow interior of the sprout of the universe, it is designated by the term *kāraṇabindu* (the causal drop). As it is said in the *Prapañcasāra*: "Desiring to manifest the world, that consciousness (cit), having become condensed, approaches..."

Regarding the phrase "bindutām iti": from this causal *bindu*, there sequentially arises the triad consisting of the effect-*bindu*, then the *nāda*, and then the *bīja*. This very [triad] is also expressed by the terms "supreme," "subtle," and "gross."
Their forms are the conscious portion (*cidaṃśa*), the mixed conscious-unconscious portion (*cidacinmiśra*), and the unconscious portion (*acidaṃśa*). As it is stated in the *Rahasyāgama*:
"When that *bindu* is divided by time, it becomes threefold."
Its threefold nature is accepted according to its gross, subtle, and supreme aspects.

"It is described through the distinctions of Bindu, Nāda, and Bīja. And these four— the Kāraṇabindu and the others— are, from the perspective of the presiding deities (adhidaivata), the Unmanifest (Avyakta), Īśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Virāṭ.
They possess the forms of Varuṇā, Śāntā, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā, and they consist of the forms of Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), and Action (kriyā).
As for their objective sphere (adhibhūta), they consist of the forms of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) of Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, and Oḍyāṇa; thus it is stated in the *Nityāhṛdaya*.
This is clear. Internally, however, the causal bindu (kāraṇabindu)—which is denoted by such terms as *śaktipiṇḍa* and *kuṇḍalī*—resides in the *mūlādhāra*.
It is said: "The power (*śakti*) is Kuṇḍalinī, who has bound her efforts to the activity of generating the universe."

"Knowing this, men do not enter again into the womb of a mother to attain childhood"— in such a manner has this very *kāraṇabindu* (causal point), existing in a state of non-differentiation, been treated by the Teachers (*ācāryas*). And it is precisely this [bindu] which, when it becomes intent on generating the triad beginning with the *kāryabindu* (effect-point), undergoes differentiation.
In that state, an unmanifest sound, designated as Śabdabrahman, arises there.
As it has been said:
"From that Bindu, as it was being differentiated, the unmanifest sound came into being."
That sound, by those perfected in hearing, is sung as the Śabdabrahman.
Thus, although this sound (rava) is omnipresent because it has attained identity with the causal bindu,
it is manifested for living beings specifically in the mūlādhāra due to the influence of the vital air refined by the manifesting effort. As it has been said:
Within this body, at the mūlādhāra, the vital air arises,
well-refined by the effort born from the desire of one who wishes to speak.
"He manifests even the all-pervading Śabdabrahman right there.

Thus, this Śabdabrahman, which consists of the causal *bindu* and has been manifested, is motionless due to its self-established nature; that very same [reality] is called *parāvāk*. Now, that very same...
When that wind reaches the region of the navel, it becomes manifest through the mind in the form of reflection (*vimarśa*);

joined with the mind, consisting of the *bindu* which is the effect in the form of the light of general vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*), it is called the speech of *paśyantī*. Then, that very same *śabdabrahman*, by means of that same wind—
Manifesting as far as the heart, joined with a determinative intellect, and consisting of *nāda*—

the nature of which is the manifestation of specific vibrations— it is called the "intermediate speech" (*madhyamā-vāk*). Then, that very same [speech], by means of that same vital air, [manifests] as far as the mouth.

That which is manifested in the locations such as the throat and so forth, consisting of the forms of the phonemes beginning with *a*, capable of being grasped by the ear, having the nature of a very clear manifestation, and being of the essence of the seed-syllable (*bīja*),
is called the *vaikharī* speech. As it has been said by the Teachers:
The state known as Parā first arises from the Mūlādhāra; thereafter, that which resides in the heart and is joined with the intellect is called Paśyantī and Madhyamā;
then, when the individual being desires to weep—that is, to manifest speech—it becomes Vaikharī within the Suṣumṇā.
Therefore, being bound by that, the designations of phonemes arise when impelled by the vital air (pavana).
158) Thus it is said. Also in the *Nityātantra*: "That which arises in the *mūlādhāra*, born from the sound known as *parā*, is led upward and unfolds within the *svādhiṣṭhāna*."
In that same way, moving gradually upward, it attains the state called Paśyantī;
then, joined with the principle of the intellect (buddhi-tattva) in the Anāhata [cakra], it is designated as Madhyamā.
Likewise, being impelled by those two, it becomes purified at the region of the throat;
[there it is] that which is called Vaikharī.

And so forth. Thus, among the fourfold *mātṛkās*, those of gross vision who do not know the triad beginning with the *parā* consider only *vaikharī* to be speech. Accordingly, the *Śruti* states: "Therefore, humans subsist upon that which is unattained by speech. "Unattained" (*anāpta*) means incomplete.
"In the Vedabhāṣya, the meaning is that [speech] is devoid of three [parts]. Also in another Śruti: 'Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech humans speak.'"
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The stateless has attained the state, and the state becomes stateless;
he who perceives the distinction between state and statelessness, he truly sees."
Thus: "The footless" means devoid of movement, the motionless Śabdabrahman itself has become the fourfold set of states beginning with the "Beyond" (para).

The meaning is that when this very same fourfold set of states is known, it becomes the footless Brahman itself. Thus, because the word *tat* (That) possesses these four aspects according to both Śruti and Smṛti, [it is so].

Since the suffix *sup* and other elements included within the definition of a "word" (*pada*)— as established by Gautama’s sūtra, "A word is that which ends in an inflection," and Pāṇini’s sūtra, "A word is that which ends in a nominal or verbal suffix"—
are themselves fourfold, the supreme *tat-pada* likewise possesses identity with the unmanifest (*avyakta*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
Furthermore, since there is no identity with the Supreme Brahman devoid of attributes (nirguṇa-brahman), the identity of the word *tat*— which consists of *vaikharī* speech— with that [Brahman] is,
by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*), even further removed; thus,
even in the view that the power (*śakti*) is the very identity between word and meaning, the term *tat* possesses only secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the Absolute.
The sense is that she is to be accepted [as such]. She is called *Parā* because she transcends the three [other] divisions of the *Mātṛkās*.
However, in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*, her etymology is stated through other methods as well:
"She is *Parā* because of the grace of Śrī Parānandanātha."
And because she is well-known in the tantra named Parānanda, she is called Parā.
And she who has the form of a palace is that supreme Śāmbhavī, the highest.
Thus: that which moves toward its own self in a contrary direction is *pratīcī*; and that which is both *pratīcī* and *citī* (consciousness) is *pratyakcitī*.

It is Brahman, known by the name *avyakta* (the unmanifest), which has that very [consciousness] as its form. From the root *cinoti*, with the suffix *ktic*, and according to the rule *kṛdikārād aktyarthāt ṅīṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. That which sees is *paśyantī*. Of this very [speech], there is also the state called *uttīrṇā* (the transcended).
This is *saṃjñā*. And it is said in the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*:

"Because she perceives everything within her own self and has transcended even the path of causal factors, this Mother is called 'the Perceiver' (*paśyantī*) and is also proclaimed as 'the Transcendent' (*uttīrṇā*)."
Thus: She is both supreme (*parā*)—meaning most excellent—and a deity (*devatā*), hence the "Supreme Deity" (*paradevatā*);
the meaning is that she is the essential nature of the Lord who is to be worshipped.
The intermediate form (*madhyamā*) consists of the *vaikharī* speech, which is like a swan upon the minds of devotees. (132)

The Madhyamā resides in the middle. As it has been said: "The Madhyamā, being of the nature of speech, is distinct from these two; for it is not merely transcendent like the Paśyantī, nor is it external like the Vaikharī, since all its parts are more clearly manifest."

Thus: specifically, *khara* means hard; this [speech] belongs to that, and it is its form (*vaikharī*). That is to say, it has attained a state of density (*ghanabhāva*). The etymology stated in the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya* is: "It certainly (*vai*) goes to (*rāti*) the void (*kham*), namely the cavity of the ear. It is [also] by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) known as *vikhara*.
Furthermore, according to the statement in the Yogaśāstra, "The *vaikharī* [speech] is impelled [by the breath]," she is so called because she is led forth by the *vikhara* wind.

She is a *haṃsikā* (swan-maiden) like a swan in a particular lake within the minds of devotees, through the superimposition of non-difference based on the foundation of word-play (*śleṣa*). The suffix *kap* is used because she is unknown to others. (132)
She is the life-channel of Kāmeśvara, the grateful one, and the one worshipped by Kāma;
she is like the life-channel, the channel of vitality, for Kāmeśvara, the Śiva of desire.
As it was said by the venerable Ācāryapāda:
O Mother, that the Lord Śiva— who swallowed the terrible poison— was not subject to the reckoning of Time is due to the power of your earrings.

Thus: she is "grateful" (*kṛtajñā*) because she knows what has been done, whether good or evil. "The sun, the moon, Yama, time, and the five great elements—these nine are the witnesses here of one's auspicious and inauspicious actions."

Or, [the name] may mean "she who is divided by the nine thus described. Or, she is the one who returns a favor through the knowledge of a favor already rendered. Or, she is the one whose knowledge (*jñāna*) is like that of a doer (*kṛtavat*). Or, because knowledge also diminishes progressively in each successive age—just as Dharma does—in the Kṛta age, there is full knowledge as before.
The meaning is "possessing such knowledge. Alternatively, in the science of gambling (*dyūta-śāstra*), four types of dice-games are well known, designated as Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.
These are composed of four, three, two, and one [sides] respectively, and take the forms of ten, six, three, and one.
Because each preceding game of dice is included within each subsequent one; and thus it is heard in scripture:

"Those five and these other five, being ten, constitute the *kṛta*"; thus, the name *kṛta* is applied to ten. For this very reason, by one who has won the *kṛta* game, the three games beginning with *tretā* are also won.

"Thus it happens" is also the established rule (*maryādā*) of the treatises on gambling (*dyūta-śāstra*). And it is heard [in those texts]: "When the *kṛta* die has been won, the lower dice (*ayāḥ*) follow along.
*Ayaḥ* refers to the form of the die used in the game of gambling; for one by whom the *ayaḥ* has been won, the "lower ones" (*adhare*) are those situated below it.

The meaning is that the *ayāsa*, *tretā*, and other dice-games come together, approach, and are won; thus, she is one whose knowledge is "made" (*kṛtam*)—that is, it is all-pervasive and encompasses all objects—or alternatively, she is one who knows what has been done (*kṛtam*). In the game of dice with Śiva, [she is] necessarily...
Because of her gratitude, it is implied that victory belongs to the Goddess alone. She is worshipped and served by Kāma, the god of love. Therefore, in the Vāruṇopaniṣad it is said:
"O Vaideha, the son of Nirṛti is both the insentient and the sentient."
He found that jewel.
Thus it is heard: the meaning is that Anaṅga, the son of Lakṣmī, obtained the jewel of knowledge. Jayā, who is filled with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), resides in Jālandhara. 133.

It is completely filled with the aesthetic flavor (rasa) known as the erotic (śṛṅgāra). Alternatively, since the Jālandhara and Uḍḍiyāṇa seats are mentioned later on, one should maintain—according to the principle of "part standing for the whole"—that these two names refer respectively to Kāmarūpa and Pūrṇagiri. Completely...

"Full" (*sampūrṇā*) means "it sits full" (*pūrṇe āste*); this is derived from the root *ās* with the suffix *kvip*, followed by the substitution of *ru*, *yat*, and the elision of *y*. By the word "horn" (*śṛṅga*), the number two is indicated; by the word "wheel-rim" (*arara*), a petal (*dala*). "Flavors" (*rasāḥ*) are six. Thus, "six pairs of petals" refers to the twelve-petaled Anāhata-cakra. This is the well-known [Anāhata] in its objective aspect (*adhibhūta*).

Because the Tantras state that the four seats (pīṭhas) reside internally in the Mūlādhāra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā, the term "twelve-peaked" (dvādaśaśṛṅga) is an epithet for Pūrṇagiri. Alternatively, it refers to that [city] whose "peak" (śṛṅga)—
meaning its primary element— is the "door-leaf" (arara), that is, the door-panel, which is ignorance (avidyā) as a concealer.
She is Śṛṅgārarā (the embodiment of erotic sentiment). She is Sasampūrṇā, being accompanied by the complete Brahman.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound of these two, she possesses both the variegated Brahman (*śabalabrahman*) and the pure Brahman (*śuddhabrahman*). She is Jayā because her very nature is victory; in the *Pādma-purāṇa*, she is enumerated as "Jayā on the Varāha mountain."
She resides in Jālandhara, a particular sacred seat (pīṭha). As stated in the Pādya: "In Jālandhara she is Viṣṇumukhī," thus she is known by the name Viṣṇumukhī. || 133 ||
Now, in the mandala of definitions of names, he divides the forty-four terms:
"By means of two, two, two, two, existence (*bhava*), longing (*dohada*), earth (*bhuvi*), a portion (*leśa*), character (*śīla*), water (*jala*), and delusion (*moha*);
we are those who go through two, a half, and four existences; on earth there is the beauty of water, and in the sky the sphere of the Lord (*bhagola*). (17)

In this context, the third word "dve" (two) refers to two names consisting of six syllables each, while the others refer to [names] consisting of eight syllables. The four-word [set] refers to a group of four names consisting of four syllables each. || 17 ||
She whose abode is the sacred seat of Oḍḍiyāṇa, who dwells in the circle of the Bindu.

Her abode—that is, her place of residence—is the sacred seat known as Oḍḍiyāṇa itself. She dwells there in the circle of the Bindu, which is the mandala consisting of universal bliss. [The word] *bindu* [means "drop"].

Her white *maṇḍala* is, according to others, the *brahmarandhra*; for it is said by the Teacher: "In the thousand-petaled lotus, you sport in secret with your Lord. She is to be worshipped through the sequence of the secret sacrifice, and she is gratified by the secret libation. 134.

The *rahasya-yāga* (secret sacrifice) consists of eight oblations of merit and so forth, performed in secret and in solitude within the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*), which is presided over by *Anackakuṇḍalinī*. She is to be propitiated through the sequential practice of this sacrifice.

According to the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), the root *yaja* is used in the senses of "worshiping a deity," "forming an alliance," and "giving"; thus, it refers specifically to a solitary union.
Or it is the sacrifice in secret; therein, she is to be worshipped and attained by means of the sequential stepping of the feet.
As Āpastamba said:
"Liberation is not for one devoted to the science of grammar, nor indeed for one who is fond of beautiful dwellings."
Not for one intent on food and clothing, nor for one delighted in winning the hearts of the world.
For one who is exclusively devoted to moral conduct, firm in his vows, who turns away from worldly pleasures,
and who is intent upon the yoga of the inner self, there shall be perfect liberation, provided he is always non-violent.

Thus [it is said]. The Aruṇopaniṣad also states: "If one should enter, one should enter after having moved about in secret. The meaning of this is that one should enter only after having accomplished the secret [practice] on the path of the worship of Śrīvidyā;
for the lexicon [Amara-kośa] defines *mithas* as "mutually" or "in secret."
Grasping with both hands of light and awareness the sacrificial ladle of *unmanī*,
I offer the clarified butter of the portions of merit and demerit into the full fire.
Thus: the contemplation of the meaning expressed by the mantra—
into the fire of consciousness, which blazes within without external fuel, which is the adversary of the darkness of delusion,
and which is the ground for the expansion of some wondrous radiance, I offer the entire universe as an oblation.
Beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva.
Thus, by means of the illumination of the meaning of the mantra and the secret libation, she is satisfied by him. || 134 ||

She is "one who is immediately propitious" (*sadyaḥprasādinī*), meaning she becomes gracious at once, in that very moment, through such sacrifice and libation. She is the "witness of the universe" (*viśvasākṣiṇī*), meaning she is the direct seer of the universe through an unmediated awareness that is her own essential nature. She is "devoid of witnesses" (*sākṣivarjitā*).
The suffix *in* is applied in the sense of "one who sees directly. Since the witness of all things has no other witness, she is "devoid of a witness" (*sākṣivarjitā*).
The six constituent limbs are the heart, head, crest-lock, eyes, armor, and weapons. Of these—
She is surrounded by and joined with the deities who are her powers. As stated in the *Jñānārṇava* and other texts:
"Then one should perform the enclosure of the limbs arising from the Śrīvidyā mantra;
one should worship them in sequence near the outer enclosure of the six limbs."
"O Dear One, the worship of the retinue comes later, while the enclosure of the limbs comes first"—

from seeing such usage, these [limbs] also possess the status of deities of the enclosure (āvaraṇadevatā), and because it is possible for the count of nine enclosures to be completed only together with them.
She is endowed with the six-limbed deities and is perfected in the six qualities. || 135 ||
The presiding deity of the six limbs is Maheśvara himself, or else she is joined with him. And it is said in the Devībhāgavata:
"Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, absolute sovereignty, and eternally undiminished power..."
And infinity—those who know the ritual rules say these are the six limbs of Maheśvara.

Thus, the meaning is that it is of the nature of Śruti because it is accompanied by the presiding deities of the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga), such as Śikṣā and Kalpa; or [it refers to] the six measures of statecraft— peace, war, marching, halting, duplicity, and seeking refuge— as taught by Kāmandaka, and the six qualities of sovereignty, virtue, fame, prosperity, knowledge, and dispassion.
Or, *ṣāḍguṇya* is the collection of the six qualities well-known from the Purāṇas; she is completely filled with that. || 135 ||
Nityaklinnā is incomparable and bestows the bliss of nirvāṇa;
she is eternally moist with compassion, hence "sārdrā" (wet). She is called Nityaklinnā because she is the Nityā of the third lunar day.
Regarding this, it is said in the Garuḍa Purāṇa: "Now I shall describe Nityaklinnā Tripurā..."
Or, she is of that nature as elaborated by the passage beginning with "bestowing enjoyment and liberation" (*bhuktimuktidām*).
She is "beyond comparison" (*nirupamā*), meaning she whose likeness (*sādṛśya*) has departed; for the Vedic scripture states, "There is no image (*pratimā*) of Him.
It is "bodiless" (*aśarīram*), meaning that from which the *bāṇa*—the body—has departed; as in the Vedic text: "Having supported this *bāṇa*... (*etadbāṇam avaṣṭabhya*).

This is because the Vedāntins explain the word *gīrvāṇa* as referring to the gods, while the Mīmāṃsakas explain the word *bāṇa* as referring to the body, based on Amara’s lexicon supplement (*Amara-kośa-śeṣa*) which states: "In the sense of 'body,' [the words] *bāṇa* and *udgala* [are used]. Thus, it is so called because it bestows the bodiless bliss known as liberation (*mokṣa*), which is not limited by any measure (*iyattānavacchinna*). As stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
The Goddess’s words to Himavat:
"O Lord of Mountains, the supreme, stainless state of Nirvana is not attained by disregarding me; therefore, come to me for refuge."
"O Great King, by worshipping me as one, as distinct, or even as both, you shall thereafter attain that state. [Thus it is said].
She is the form of the eternal Ṣoḍaśī, whose body is half that of Śrīkaṇṭha. (136)
She is she whose forms are the sixteen Śoḍaśikās, who are both eternal and sixteen-fold, beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Tripurasundarī. And it is said in the Tantrarāja:
Of the first, Lalitā, the other fifteen are her limbs;
by virtue of having Lalitā as their principal body, they all constitute her own form.

Thus, it is the *ṣoḍaśī* itself, or the *ṣoḍaśika*. It is the eternal, free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and all-encompassing (*āsamantāt*) specific practice of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup-offering within those sacrifices; by them, it is manifested on all sides, or it is pleased. Even though the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is optional in the *atirātra*, it is drawn on the following day of the two-night rite (*dvirātra*).

Because of such statements, [the practice] is obligatory in the subsequent sacrifices. And it is said in the *Śaktirahasya*: "Just as Ambā is pleased by ten million Vājapeya sacrifices or sixteen crores [of them], so too is she pleased by a single utterance of the *Ṣoḍaśī*."

Thus: "Śrīkaṇṭha" is Śiva, he whose neck bears the *śrī* (poison); she whose body is for his sake is [Śrī]. Alternatively, she is one who possesses a body that is the object (*artha*) of Śrīkaṇṭha; that is to say, she possesses a half-body that is non-different from him. For this very reason, there is a dual nature within a single entity.

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad it is heard: beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," it continues, "He split this very Self into two; from that, there arose the husband and the wife.
Alternatively, she has half of her body like Śrīkaṇṭha; just as [half the body] belongs to Śrīkaṇṭha.
That is to say, the body is of a dual nature, being partly blue and partly white. As it is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"In that regard, she who is the illustrious one, forming half the body of Śaṅkara..."
Her right half of the body is white, and likewise, her left is white.
When addressed by Svayambhū, "Divide yourself," that goddess,
O twice-born one, became twofold at that very moment as Gaurī and Kālī.

Thus [it is said]. Or alternatively: according to the *Mātṛkā-kośa*, "Aḥ is Śrīkaṇṭha and Sureśa; the forehead is Keśava; Amṛta..."—the meaning is that the letter A is Śrīkaṇṭha, and he constitutes half the body of her whose form is Speech (*vāk*). And so it is heard in scripture: "The letter A is indeed all speech; this [Speech] is she..."

The essential meaning is that [the power], being manifested by the touch and heat [of the breath], becomes manifold and assumes various forms; thus, the first speech, known as Parā and consisting of the letter *a*, indeed arises in the form of Vaikharī. And it is said in the Sūtasamhitā:
I perpetually worship with devotion that Supreme Power who is Speech, whose nature is consciousness, who is designated as the Supreme (Parā), and who shares half the body of Śrīkaṇṭha.

Thus it is said. Alternatively, it means that Śrīkaṇṭha is the other half of the Goddess who consists of one half, and he is that which effects her completion. That too has been stated in that very same [text]: "The power known as Icchā is complete within the belly of Śiva. In the Śaiva Mātṛkā-nyāsa, one half [of the body] is [assigned] with the powers beginning with Pūrṇodarī and so forth.

The realized meaning is that she is filled by Śiva, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha. Alternatively, it means that at the time of writing the letter *a*, she possesses a body non-different from that half which is of the same nature as the *kāmakalā*. || 136 ||
Prabhāvatī is the well-known Supreme Goddess whose form is light (*prabhā*).

"Light" refers to the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatāḥ*) beginning with *aṇimā*; for it is stated [in scripture] that she is "surrounded by rays such as *aṇimā*. She possesses these, meaning she is surrounded by them. Rays, moreover, are not merely of the nature of qualities (*guṇasvarūpa*).

The view of the ancients is that rays are distinct substances (*dravyāntara*). This has been set forth by Jaina masters such as Haribhadra in works like the *Dharmasaṃgrahaṇī*: "Rays are qualities (*guṇa*), not a substance; among them, whiteness is a quality, not that [whiteness] is a substance. Rays are qualities, not a substance; among them...
The statement "a quality is not a substance" is merely a reflection of that [reality]. Consequently, because of the non-difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality, it is said:

she whose very nature consists of the deities such as *aṇimā* and others, which are of the form of light. This is according to the Vedic revelation: "Consisting of mind, having light as its form. She is well-known because she is perceived by all as "I". And thus, the Goddess.
In the *Bhāgavata*, [it is said] under the pretext of providing proof: "All living beings know Her.
In that very work, at the beginning of the First Skandha, it says: "We meditate upon Her, the primordial Vidyā, whose nature is all-consciousness.
She is supreme (*paramā*), most excellent (*utkṛṣṭā*), and the sovereign mistress (*seśvarī*) along with the Lord (*sā īśvarī*).
The primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) is unmanifest, possessing the essential form of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
The "Root" (mūla) refers to the Śrīvidyā mantra, whose nature consists of two syllables known as Prakāśa (Light) and Vimarśa (Reflective Awareness), which serve as its causal basis;
or it may refer to the Mūlaprakṛti (Root Nature) well-known in the Sāṃkhya system, as they say:
Root-nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolution;
the group of sixteen is only evolution; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolution.

Thus [it is said]. However, in the *Mṛgendrasaṃhitā*, it is stated that the Kuṇḍalinī itself—encircled by the sevenfold Suṣumṇā consisting of Mahat and the other principles—is called the Mūlaprakṛti (Root Nature) as the eightfold Prakṛti; therefore, she may be of that form.
Alternatively, among the elements beginning with Earth and ending with Ākāśa, for each preceding one...

For that which has become a modification (*vikṛti*), each subsequent element is the material cause (*prakṛti*). However, for space (*ākāśa*), Brahman alone is the material cause, according to the Vedic scripture: "From the Self, space was produced. Since there is no other material cause for that [Brahman], it means that it is the first material cause, standing as the root. For this very reason:
In the *Pañcarātrāgama*, there is a statement of Śiva:
"The Mother of the World, Sarasvatī, the Mother of the Vedas, appeared;
she who has no primal nature (prakṛti) is this one known as the Root Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*)."
"I was born therein from those principles, beginning with Mahat.

Here, this should be understood: for among the karmas whose ripening is fixed in time, there is the exhaustion of those that have ripened through experience, and [the remaining] others that have ripened...
Because the creation intended for that purpose is no longer useful due to the exhaustion of enjoyments, the dissolution of primordial nature (*prakṛta-pralaya*) occurs.
At that time, Māyā, having swallowed the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), becomes dissolved within the partless Supreme Śiva, who is established in Himself.

It remains exactly as it is until the ripening of the remaining karma. As it has been said: "At the time of dissolution, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by her. Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"O divine sage, the earth, which is the foundation of the world, dissolves into water."
Water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into air.
The wind dissolves into space; that [space] dissolves into the unmanifest (avyakta);
the unmanifest, O Brahmin, completely dissolves into the partless Puruṣa.

Thus: the unmanifest is *māyā*. And its dissolution does not mean absolute destruction as in liberation (*mokṣa*), but rather—like the dissolution of the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in deep sleep—the non-arising of the functions of *māyā* within the light of the Supreme Self, which is absolutely free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).

Even if there is manifestation by force, it is as if there were no manifestation at all; for if there were a total absence of manifestation, it would follow that the object itself does not exist. If one were to accept this consequence, the subsequent process of creation could not be explained. Furthermore, the remaining karmas of living beings must first dissolve into that very *māyā* before [creation can proceed] in due order.

When those [souls] have reached full maturity, the function of Māyā consisting of the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) is produced by Paraśiva in order to bestow their respective fruits. This very state of Māyā is expressed by such terms as "looking" (*īkṣaṇa*), "desire" (*kāmatas*), "will" (*upavicikīrṣā*), and so forth. As it is said: "He looked: 'Shall I now create the worlds? (*sa īkṣata lokānnu sṛjā*)."
In the *Aitareya*: "Then it thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate. In the *Chāndogya*: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. In the *Taittirīya*: "Brahman is built up by austerity.
Such is the manifestation of Māyā through conceptualization (*savikalpaka*), as it is the object of such mental modifications (*vṛtti*).

This is the first creation from *tamas*, which is not preceded by conscious intention. The Vedic scripture beginning with "There was neither non-existence nor existence" and ending with "In the beginning there was darkness, hidden by darkness" has this as its purport; likewise, the Smṛti passage beginning with "From that, the unmanifest was produced" is directed toward this very same point.

From this state, which is designated by the term *avyaktatama* (the most unmanifest) and in which the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) have not yet attained differentiation, there arises the second creation: that of the *mahat*, which consists of the three qualities and is slightly manifest due to its internal differentiation. As it has been said: "From the unmanifest arises that which consists of the grasping of the threefold internal divisions."
That which is called "Great" (mahat) would be the reality, and likewise, the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) arises from that Great One.

Thus, the third creation is that of the ego (ahaṅkāra), which exists as the three qualities (guṇas) in an external state of differentiation. This threefold ego— namely, the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi* which is *tāmasa*— is born from the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*).
Because of this statement, the fact that the other two [forms of ego] are characterized as *sāttvika* and *rājasa* is indicated by qualifying the *bhūtādi* as *tāmasa*. Therein,
from the *tāmasa* ego named *bhūtādi*, when it is pervaded by *rajas*, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise.

The fourth creation is that of the [tanmātras]. The fifth creation is the production of the group of eleven organs from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*) known as *vaikārika*, when it is dominated by *rajas*.

From the *rājasa-taijasa* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), there is the sixth creation: the emanation of the presiding deities of both [the internal and external senses], namely the directions, wind, sun, Varuṇa, Indra, and the others. As the Sāṃkhyas say:
"The group of eleven, characterized by *sattva*, proceeds from the *vaikṛta* ego."
From Bhūtādi arises the tanmātra; that is tāmasa, while from Taijasa arise both.

Thus [it is said]. However, in the Śaiva system, the distinction is that from the *ahaṃkāra* characterized by *sattva* arises the mind (*manas*), and from the *ahaṃkāra* characterized by *rajas* arise the ten sense organs (*indriya*). As the Śaivas say:
"It (the *ahaṃkāra*) is born again threefold, through the divisions of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*."
And it manifests under the names of Taijasa, Vaikārika, Bhūtādi, and so forth.
From the Taijasa [ego] arises the mind there, and from the Vaikārika arise the sense organs;
from the Bhūtādi [ego] arise the subtle elements (tanmātras)—from these, this creation proceeds.
