Thus [it is said]. These six creations are primary (prākṛta). The three secondary (vaikṛta) creations consist of: the upward-streaming form consisting of trees and so forth; the transverse-streaming form consisting of animals and so forth; and the downward-streaming form consisting of spirits, ghosts, and so forth.
The Kaumāra creation is one that consists of both primary and secondary types. This is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:

The first creation is that of the Great Principle (mahat), arising from the imbalance of the qualities (guṇas) of the Self; the second is that of the I-sense (ahaṃkāra), wherein the emergence of substance, cognition, and action occurs.
The third is the creation of the elements (bhūta-sarga), which consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and possesses the power of substance;
the fourth is the creation of the senses (indriya-sarga), which consists of both cognition and action.
The fifth is the divine creation, known as the *vaikārika*, of which the mind (*manas*) is composed;
the sixth, however, O Lord, is the creation of darkness (*tamas*), which is characterized by a lack of discernment (*abuddhi*).

"These six are the primary creations; now hear from me the secondary ones as well," and so forth. Here, the statement that the creation called *avyakta* (the unmanifest), which is characterized by *tamas*, is the sixth is according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). However, according to the logical sequence (*ārthakrama*), it is indeed the first.
On this very point, other texts such as the Vāyu Purāṇa may also be cited.
Thus, among the creations beginning with the unmanifest (avyakta), each subsequent one has the preceding one as its material cause (prakṛti);
however, Brahman alone is the material cause of the unmanifest, because it is the root of all creations.
And because there is no other root, the meaning is "the root-nature" (mūlaprakṛti). For this very reason, it is stated in scripture:
beginning with "Objects are indeed superior to the senses," and continuing, "The unmanifest is superior to the Great One; the Puruṣa is superior to the unmanifest."
There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal.

Thus it is said. Alternatively, the letter *m* signifies the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), while the letter *l* indicates the triad consisting of the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Therefore, the meaning is that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is eightfold. Accordingly, the summary aphorism states: "The eight are the primary natures."

Now, he begins to praise her sequentially through all her forms: "The Unmanifest" (Avyaktā) means she whose nature is the manifestation of primordial *māyā*; or, according to the Sāṃkhya system, she is that which is denoted by terms such as *pradhāna* and *prakṛti*. As it has been said:
In the *Sāṃkhyasaptati*: "Subtle, without marks (*aliṅga*), insentient, without beginning or end, likewise characterized by productivity,
partless, indeed one, and common to all— this is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*)."

Thus it is said. The teacher Pañcaśikha also stated: "The wise declare the Pradhāna to be without beginning or middle, beyond the Mahat, eternal, and unmanifest. And that [Pradhāna] consists precisely of the aggregate of the three *guṇas*;
therefore, according to the *Sāṃkhya-prapañca-sūtra*, qualities such as *sattva* and the rest do not belong to it [the Puruṣa], because they are of the nature of that [Pradhāna].

This is clear. Alternatively, Brahman itself is denoted by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). For this has been determined in the section beginning with "He says that it is unmanifest" (*tad-avyaktam āha hi*) through such scriptural passages as, "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other gods; neither by austerity nor by action. Or, the meaning may be that it is the very nature of Viṣṇu.

"Pradhāna, Avyaya, Yoni, Avyakta, Prakṛti, and Tamas—these are the names of Viṣṇu, who is eternally characterized by the power of manifestation. Thus it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*. "Vyakta" refers to the principle of Mahat (the Great), because it is manifested from what precedes it and because of its magnitude.

"Āvyaktā" means that which is unmanifest all around; "tad-janya-ahaṅkāraḥ" refers to the ego born from that [unmanifest]; thus, "tadubhayasvarūpiṇī" (she whose nature consists of both) constitutes a single compound word. Alternatively, by accepting "vyaktā" as a separate word, it is also appropriate to treat the subsequent two names, "brahma-jananī," as a single unit, since this avoids defects such as tautology.
On the contrary, it is also because this conforms with the predominant reading of names beginning with the letters *va* and *ba*.
In this view, the construction should be understood as: "she whose manifest nature (*vyakta-svarūpa*) consists of the Great I-consciousness (*ahantā*).
This is because the Supreme I-consciousness (*parāhantā*) is the very form of Tripurasundarī, and she is manifested within the category (*tattva*) known as the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*).
Or, it means that its own nature consists of both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
The sense is that it possesses both association with and dissociation from the modifications of the states of the elements. This too has been stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"By the second [category], namely the modification of the states of the elements, it is called 'Being' (*sat*)."
It is evident that because it is devoid of that [manifested form], the unmanifested is also non-existent.

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, the meaning is "in the form of the perishable and the imperishable. For it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "The imperishable is declared to be the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the manifest (*vyakta*) is the perishable (*kṣara*). Or, it means "in the form of the aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*).
For it is stated in the *Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa*: "O lords of sages, the wise know the unmanifest to be the aggregate and the manifest to be the individual."
Or rather, she is of the nature of the twenty-three principles (*tattva*).
The wise say that the twenty-three principles are denoted by the term "manifest" (*vyakta*),
and likewise, the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is denoted by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).

Thus, from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*. Alternatively, by means of another *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term) applied to "the manifest and the unmanifest" (*vyaktāvyakte*) and "the manifest-unmanifest" (*vyaktāvyaktam*), the meaning is that it takes the form of three types of *liṅgas*: the manifest, the unmanifest, and the manifest-unmanifest. Their characteristics are described in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*:
The Bāṇaliṅga is of three kinds— Svāyambhuva, Śaila, and Liṅga—
and these are proclaimed as manifest (vyakta), unmanifest (avyakta), and both manifest and unmanifest (vyaktāvyakta) respectively.
The manifest is said to bestow enjoyment, while the unmanifest bestows liberation;
the linga that is both manifest and unmanifest is proclaimed to bestow both enjoyment and liberation.
That which, when mounted upon two or three scales, increases in weight and does not decrease, is declared by the wise to be a *bāṇaliṅga*; all others they know to be *śaila* (stone).

Thus it is said. Alternatively, her essential nature (*svarūpa*) is clearly manifest in those whose impurities (*mala*) have been ripened, yet remains unmanifest in those bound by fetters (*pāśa*). This has been stated in the *Śaktirahasya* on the occasion of defining the meaning of the term "descent of power" (*śaktipāta*):
How can the all-pervading supreme power be said to have "fallen"? Falling is the movement from above to below, which belongs only to that which has form and is not omnipresent.
It is true that she is all-pervasive, eternal, innate, and established like Śiva;
however, she remains concealed within those bound by the fetters of impurity, karma, and the rest.
"When the humors have been ripened, she is clearly perceived as having fallen," so it is said.
Vyāpinī:

She is called Vyāpinī because she is all-pervasive due to her transformation into the threefold primordial creation (prākṛta-sarga), which consists of the remaining effects of the three types of ego (ahaṅkāra); or alternatively, because she pervades the entire universe.
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Bhāskararāya, the fifth digit, Jvālinī, has been completed with the four hundred [verses]. (400)
Thus ends the fourth century, the fifth digit (kalā),
named Pañcamī; and the fifth century, the sixth digit, named Ruci,
which possesses diverse forms and has the nature of both knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā).
She is she whose various forms consist of primary creations, modified creations, and the creation of Kumāra.
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—him I call a knower of the Vedas; he who does not know these two together is called ignorant.
Having crossed over death through ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge.

Thus, *vidyā* and *avidyā* are well-known in the Śruti. *Vidyā* is knowledge whose nature is one's own Self; *avidyā* is knowledge whose nature is the final mental modification (*vṛtti*). Both of these constitute her essential form. And it has been said in the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
The supreme power of Viṣṇu, capable of accomplishing the work of the universe, is that which consists of the nature of both existence and non-existence; it is celebrated as both Vidyā and Avidyā.

Thus it is said. In the *Devībhāgavata* as well, it is stated that Brahman itself is that exceedingly difficult-to-attain [Devi] whose nature consists of both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). In another passage of that same work: "O King, know that knowledge and ignorance are the two forms of the Goddess."
By one [path] a living being is liberated; by the other, he is bound once again.

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively: *vidyā* (knowledge) is knowledge in the form of the final mental modification (*caramavṛtti*). *Avidyā* (ignorance) is knowledge in the form of the delusion of duality. *Svaḥ* (the self) is knowledge whose essence is the Supreme Brahman;

for the word *sva* denotes the Self (*ātman*), according to the lexicon: "The word *sva* refers to one's own, a relative, and the Self. These three—[knowledge, ignorance, and the self]—are as follows.
This is its nature. And it is said in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"Error (*bhrānti*), knowledge (*vidyā*), and the supreme (*para*)—these three constitute the form of Śiva.
Among objects that possess distinct forms, cognition is called error."
"Cognition in the form of the Self is called *vidyā* by the wise;
that reality which is free from conceptual construction is designated as the Supreme. Thus [it is said].
She is the moonlight that delights the night-lotuses of Mahākāmeśa’s eyes. || 138 ||

Or, he is the Great Lord of Desire (*mahākāmeśa*); or, he is the Great Desirer (*maheccha*), the Great-Intented (*mahāśaya*), and the Lord (*īśa*). His eyes are like night-lotuses (*kumuda*) or white water-lilies (*kairava*), or like red lotuses (*raktapaṅkaja*). Their "delight" (*āhlāda*) refers to their blossoming, or, in the case of the lotuses, their closing, which brings about an excess of pleasure.
*Kaumudī* is like moonlight, or it is like the full moon of the month of Kārtika.
*Kumuda* refers to the white water-lily (*kairava*) and the red lotus (*raktapaṅkaja*); *kumuda* also refers to a monkey. *Kaumuda* refers to the month of Kārtika; *kaumudī* refers to moonlight.

Thus says Yādava. Alternatively: those for whom joy (*mud*) is contemptible (*ku*), being blameworthy due to reasons such as its perishability and its being mixed with excessive suffering—they are *kumuda*s, meaning those attached to sense-objects (*vaiṣayika*s). Precisely because they are objects of compassion, [the term] *kṛpaṇa* is used for the *kumuda*.

*Kumuda* is defined as "eternal" (*śāśvata*) by Śāśvata; Viśva also states, "The word *kumut* may mean 'miserly' or 'other than that'. The joy (*hlāda*), which is an excellence of bliss in the form of liberation, pervades them on all sides.
And that [joy] is [attained] by means of leading—that is, bringing—[the soul] toward Mahākāmeśa; thus it is a compound with the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*).
It is the moonlight that illuminates the worldly pleasure arising from the attainment of Śiva, which is centered upon sense objects.
It has been heard that the succession of rays of the Sun-like One is for the purpose of shattering the darkness within the hearts of devotees;
"darkness" here refers to those states of ignorance in the hearts of devotees which possess the power of obscuration.
Upon their breaking and destruction, there is a succession of rays from the sun,

like a continuous stream of light from the sun; for the word *hṛdaya* undergoes the substitution *hṛt* before suffixes such as *lekhā*, *daṇḍa*, and *lāsa*, and the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "being therein."
Śivadūtī, she who is worshipped by Śiva, the embodiment of Śiva, and the bestower of auspiciousness. || 139 ||

She whose messenger is Śiva, who conveys her message in a manner that is "alpa" (small or limited), is Śivadūtī. [The root] *dū* means "to afflict. Even a messenger, by acting according to his instructions, becomes an afflictor (*upatāpaka*). According to the lexicon, "dūtī" and "sañcārikā" are synonyms; thus, the word *sañcāra* also refers specifically to the transmission of a message.
In the *niṣṭhā* [suffix -ta] following the roots *du* and *tan*, there is lengthening according to the rule *dutanibhyāṃ dīrghaśca*.

The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ktādalpākhyāyām*. The meaning of this is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added to a feminine *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *kta* and terminating in *a*, when "smallness" is indicated. And it has been stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
Since Śiva himself was appointed as a messenger by that goddess,
she consequently attained renown in this world as "Śivadūtī" (the Goddess of Śiva’s Messenger).

Thus [it is said]. However, the commentators on this [text] state that she is called Śivadūtī because she delivers a message from Śiva; they further claim that the suffix *īp* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *gaura*-class of the *ākṛtigaṇa*, whereas in a *bahuvrīhi* compound the suffix would be *ṭāp*. This [view] is to be considered. Moreover, she resides at the sacred site (*tīrtha*) named Puṣkara. As it is stated in the *Puṣkarakhaṇḍa* of the *Padmapurāṇa*:

"Now I shall describe to you others who are established at Puṣkara," having thus introduced the subject, [the text mentions] Śivadūtī, Vedī, Kṣemā, Kṣemaṅkarī, Sadā, and so forth. She is to be propitiated and worshipped by Śiva.
This is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Even Śiva, having propitiated her through the power of meditative yoga,
became the Lord of all supernatural attainments (siddhis) and the Lord whose body is half-female (Ardhanārīśvara).

Thus [it is said]. Or, she is the very nature of the four-syllabled *vidyā* worshipped by Śaṅkara. She is that whose form (*mūrti*) is Śiva himself, because of the non-difference between Śiva and Śakti. As it has been said:
"Rudra is one, hidden within all beings; Rudra is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), being Māyā."
She alone is the Goddess and not distinct from Him; indeed, knowing this, they attain immortality.

Thus [it is said]. Or, she whose form (*mūrti*) is auspicious (*śiva*), consisting of well-being; or, she whose very nature (*rūpa*) is liberation (*śiva*). For liberation has the nature of the Self alone (*ātma-mātra-svarūpatva*). As it is stated in the fourteenth chapter of the *Saurasaṃhitā*: "Now I shall explain to you, in brief, the true nature of liberation."
Beginning from this point:
"Therefore, O sinless one, supreme liberation, which is of the very nature of the Self, though obstructed by ignorance,
is manifested through knowledge for one who is purified."

Thus far. She makes the devotee Śiva himself; that is, by removing the bonds of ignorance (avidyā-pāśa), she makes him like the Brahman attained by the liberated—this is a figurative expression. Alternatively, she is "Śivaṅkarī" because she brings about auspiciousness (maṅgala). According to the rule *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied [to the root *kṛ*]. By the rule *śiva-śam-ariṣṭasya karaḥ*, the augment *muṭ* is added. 139.
She who is dear to Śiva, she who is devoted to Śiva, she who is beloved by the disciplined, she who is worshipped by the disciplined;
she who is the beloved of Śiva, or she for whom Śiva is beloved;
she who is beyond Śiva, because her very existence is dependent upon his power (śakti), or she for whom Śiva is supreme.

Alternatively, she is "devoted to Śiva" (śivaparā) because she teaches Śiva; for in this very context, we see such an interpretation when it is said that "this word 'Śiva' has him as its referent. She is "beloved by the disciplined" (śiṣṭeṣṭā), meaning she for whom the prescribed rites taught by the disciplined (śiṣṭa)—that is, those things enjoined—are desired (iṣṭa), being objects of her will and dear to her. This is derived from the verbal root *iṣ*, meaning "to desire."

The form *iṣṭam* is derived from the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) with the suffix *niṣṭhā*, involving vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of *ṣ* according to the rule *vraśca*. Alternatively, it means "worshipped" (*iṣṭā*) by the learned (*śiṣṭaiḥ*) through the performance of prescribed duties (*vihita-karmabhiḥ*). [She is worshipped] by the dharmas of one's own respective caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), when these are properly offered unto the Lord.
That which is true worship is not accomplished by the offering of perfumes, garlands, and the like.
Because of this statement; and because of the statements in the *Mahābhārata* and the *Bṛhannāradīya*: "Dharma originates from conduct (*ācāra*), and Acyuta is the lord of Dharma. Or else:
"One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes."
Nor is one who is fickle in speech and limb within the sphere of the refined.
Those for whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been handed down through tradition,
are to be known as cultured Brahmins, who are the authorities for the direct perception of the Śruti.

She is one for whom the "learned" (śiṣṭas)—those possessing the characteristics described in the Vasiṣṭha-sūtra—are beloved; or rather, she is "worshipped by the learned" (śiṣṭaiḥ iṣṭā), meaning honored by them. He clarifies this very point: "Honored by the learned.
She is immeasurable, self-luminous, and beyond the reach of mind and speech. (140)
She is *aprameyā*, meaning that which is fit to be measured (*pramātum yogyā*) is *prameyā*, and she is not so; thus, she is *aprameyā*.

Alternatively, she is *prameyā* by means of the meanings of the letter 'a', such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others. Or, she is *prameyā* within the waters (*apsu*), according to the Vedic revelation: "My womb is within the waters, in the ocean. She is she whose light (*svaḥ*) is non-different from the Self (*ātman*).

Because it lacks the quality of being an object of sight, it is not illumined by another, according to the Vedic scripture: "In this regard, this person is self-luminous. Or, it is that in which there is light even during deep sleep (*suṣupti*). It is beyond the range and outside the domain of both minds and words; for from it, words turn back.
This is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "not attained by the mind, together with speech. And there is the statement of Prahlāda in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"I bow to that Supreme Goddess, who is beyond the range of words and minds, who is without distinctions, and who is to be discerned by the knowledge of the wise."

Thus [it is said]. In passages such as "The triple Veda (trayī) is not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and the offspring of the twice-born," the word *gocara* takes the feminine gender. Alternatively, it may mean "that in which no range exists. That is to say, there is not even a single object that falls within the domain of speech or mind in her.

The intended meaning is that even their qualities are infinite, and thus they transcend both speech and mind. As for the two *chalākṣara* sūtras recited under the heading "the last ones" (*antyā*), namely *nirman dve ktiṣṭhe*:
there are exactly four names ending in these syllables—*niḥ*, *man*, *ktiḥ*, and *ṣṭhā*.
The meaning is that they consist of two words;

it refers to two words possessing the same case-ending. This is because, according to the maxim "a sentence is purposeful where [the meaning] is not otherwise obtained," such instances alone serve a purpose by dispelling the misconception of there being two distinct names. For example:

"Supreme light, supreme abode, supreme power, supreme goal"—this is a single name composed of two words with different case endings, so there is no fault. Although "manas" and "vāk" form the compound *manovāc*, and these, being raw (*āma*) and unrefined (*apakva*), constitute *manovācāme*; this is an adjective [qualifying the preceding].

Because it is stated that [the word] is frequently placed after the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), there is no prior placement [of *amanas*]. Thus, they do not occur as *amanas-vācau*. It is easily explained that this name is indeed a single compound: "within the range of those two" (*tayor-gocara*). This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture stating "from which words turn back," the scriptural statement regarding being knowable through the Vedas alone, and the scripture stating "it is to be perceived by the mind alone," and so forth.

The contradiction has been resolved in the *Bhāmatī* by establishing a systematic distinction based on whether [the words] refer to primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and based on whether they refer to minds that are matured or immature. Nevertheless, [the statement] "one should fill the *ga-svi-ya-dṛ-ḍhī-ṭha-kāṃ-pṛṇ*" contradicts the *Chalākṣara-sūtra*. And its shadow-text (*chāyā*) is as follows:
The commentator has stated that there are eleven names beginning with "pṛ" and ending with "dṛḍhīṭhakāmpṛ.

Among these, fourteen names are set forth, starting from the name under discussion and ending with "pañcakośāntarasthitā. These include two eight-syllable names beginning with a letter of the *pa*-class.

The meaning is that twelve names are encapsulated (*saṃpuṭīkṛta*). However, if one were to conjoin (*praśleṣa*) a single syllable with the name under discussion, there would be nine syllables and it would begin with a vowel. In such a case, because there would be an absence of encapsulation by such [a syllable], there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra.

Even regarding the Sūtras, since they consist merely of the presentation of means observed [in the world], if one considers that the means taught therein do not invalidate other means, then that position also is indeed correct. This should be understood in the same way in other cases as well. || 140 ||
The power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) has the nature of sentience, while the power of insentience (*jaḍa-śakti*) consists of the insentient.

The power of consciousness is the power of comparison; for there is the traditional teaching of Yāska that "the word *cit* is used in the sense of comparison," and also the traditional rule of Pāṇini that "the word *cit* is employed in the sense of comparison."
Two syllables, supreme in Brahman, infinite, wherein knowledge and ignorance lie hidden;
the perishable is indeed ignorance, but the immortal is knowledge. He who rules over both knowledge and ignorance is another.

Thus, that which is indicated by the term *vidyā* in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* is spoken of; and the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is synonymous with pure intelligence (*caitanya*) and whose efficacy consists in its nature as the remover of ignorance, is described in the fifth book of the *Devībhāgavata*:
O King, power exists within all beings by means of the universal self;
however, a living being devoid of power is in every respect like a corpse.

"The power of consciousness (cicchakti) exists in all beings, for that alone is its form. Thus he says: "It has the nature of consciousness. The teachers of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* state: "The pure power of consciousness of the Supreme Lord is called consciousness itself. It has the essential nature of consciousness.
And there is the Gauḍapādīya-sūtra: "She is Śakti. Also, in the opening verse of the Devībhāgavata:

"We meditate upon that primordial Vidyā, whose form is all-consciousness; may she impel our intellect. This is a Gāyatrī consisting of three quarters (pādas). Therefore, it is said in the Mātsya-purāṇa: "And by means of the Gāyatrī..."

"Those who know that undertaking [of action] as belonging to the Bhagavān—this, indeed, is the inquiry into bliss," so says the Śruti. This means that this very power of bliss, which is Brahman, is of the nature of consciousness;
it is the inquiry, consisting of reflective awareness (vimarśa).

As seen in the commentary on the *Vidyāratna* by Śaṅkarāraṇyacaraṇa, the "insentient power" (*jaḍaśakti*) is a specific transformation of *māyā* whose counter-correlate is the capacity [to create] the world that is to be created; this is an indication of the power of the object of creation alone. And it has been stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
The powers of all entities fall within the scope of inconceivable knowledge;
indeed, hundreds of such powers of being, beginning with creation, belong to Brahman.
O best of ascetics, just as heat belongs to fire,
he is merely the instrumental cause in the act of creating those things to be created.

Since the powers of the objects to be created have indeed become dependent upon the Pradhāna as their cause, it requires nothing else whatsoever, except for the One who acts merely as the instrumental cause.
"O best of ascetics, she is led by her own power, though in reality [it is otherwise]. Thus,
that Māyā whose very nature (svarūpa) consists of the insentient (jaḍa) alone— that which is merely the visible—
is "insentient-natured" (jaḍātmikā).
The *gāyatrī* is the *vyāhṛti* of the twilight (*sandhyā*).

The *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables. This is stated in the *Gītā*: "I am the *gāyatrī* among meters" (*chandāsām asmi gāyatrī*), and also in the *Devī-stava* of the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "You are the *gāyatrī* among meters. Alternatively, it is that which is called by the name *gāyatrī*.
The cowherd girl was the youngest wife of Brahmā. It is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* that while Brahmā was performing a sacrifice at the sacred site of Puṣkara, Sāvitrī was summoned;
she replied, "Lakṣmī and the others have not yet arrived, so I shall come along with them. Because of that—

Enraged by these words, Brahmā summoned a certain cowherd girl from Śakti’s hand and spoke to Viṣṇu; having introduced the matter thus, Brahmā said to Hari: "For the sake of our sacrifice, act with haste."
And this, O illustrious Lord, is divine by name, known as Gāyatrī.
When this had been said, Viṣṇu then spoke this to Brahmā: "Therefore, O Lord, marry her today; she is given by me to you."
Do not hesitate for long regarding the Gāndharva form of marriage;
take the hand of this cowherd maiden without agitation.

"Then the Grandfather (Brahmā) married the cowherd girl by the Gāndharva rite," and so forth. By this, the meaning is "having the form of such a cowherd girl. Alternatively, according to the *Gāyatrī-kalpa*, she is called Gāyatrī because she protects (*trāyate*) the one who sings (*gāyan*).

The word *gāyatrī*, well-known as the Mother of the Vedas (*vedamātṛ*) due to the etymological definition stated in the *Bhāradvāja-smṛti*, also denotes Ambā because of her non-difference from her. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*;
the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added because she belongs to the *gaurādi* group. This has been stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Having bathed specifically at Puṣkara, one should mutter me, the Mother of the Vedas;
I abide as the eight-syllabled [mantra], and by me indeed is this entire world pervaded.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the Devīpurāṇa it is stated: "Gāyatrī is worshipped by the thirty gods, whether through singing or even through going [to her]."

The *Chāndogya* states that it is called *gāyatrī* because it both sings (*gāyati*) and protects (*trāyate*). The *Mahāvāsiṣṭharāmāyaṇa* also states that it is *gāyatrī* because its nature is singing. It is of the form of a *vyāhṛti*, meaning utterance or pronunciation; or it is of the form of a specific mantra. However, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Because you have appeared before me as soon as I uttered these words,
therefore this name 'Vyāhṛti' shall attain fulfillment for you."

Thus it is explained in the *Nirukta*. The meaning of the term *sandhyā* is the contemplation of the non-difference between one's own consciousness as delimited by the sun and [the universal] Consciousness; this is also because of its etymological derivation: "that in which they meditate perfectly" (*sam-yak dhyāyanti asyām*). As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:
The Sandhyā is Brahman residing in the sun, due to its non-differentiation from the resonance of the Sandhyā;
it is the Saccidātman, whose parts consist of all beings beginning with Brahmā.
"The thought of the worshiper should be: 'I am his servant,' and 'I am he'—thus indeed do those who know the Vedas understand."
Thus it is said. Because of that non-difference, this [Gāyatrī] is also the *sandhyā*. And so Vyāsa says:
"One should not perceive Gāyatrī as distinct from Brahman;
one should meditate upon her with the thought 'I am she,' by whatever means prescribed."
Thus it is said. Also in the Bhāradvāja-smṛti:

"The radiant power of the Lord (Īśvara-śakti), which is divided according to the different forms of Brahmā and the other [deities] and which is the witness of all actions—that is designated as Sandhyā by the wise."
"O Tripurā, you alone are declared by the Āgamas to be the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras and the fourth [Veda], consisting of the Sandhyā, the bestower of the fruits of great rites"—
such is the statement of the learned. Therefore, this word refers to the deity to be worshipped at the time of the Sandhyā.

Mādhava: She is called *Sandhyā* because she is to be properly meditated upon (*samyaṅ-dhyeya*). The author of the *Pārijāta* states that the suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. Furthermore, she is the mind-born daughter of Brahmā.
As it is said in the *Kālikopapurāṇa*:
Then, from his mind, there arose a woman of beautiful form and excellent limbs;
she was renowned by the name Sandhyā, known as the evening twilight and Jayantikā.
Since this excellent woman was born perfectly while Brahmā was meditating,
she shall be known in this world by the name Sandhyā.
Thus it is said. Also in the Bhagavatī Purāṇa: "She who was formerly Sandhyā, the daughter of Brahmā born from his mind, having performed penance and cast off her body, became Arundhatī."
Thus it is said. However, in the *Reṇukā-purāṇa*:
"Iḍā is Mahākālī, Piṅgalā is Mahālakṣmī, and this Suṣumṇā is Ekavīrā; thus she consists of the three junctions (*sandhyā*)."

Thus it has been said. According to the statement of Dhaumya in the section concerning virgins (*kanyā-prakaraṇa*), the twilight (*sandhyā*) may be a virgin of one year’s age, or she herself may be one year old.
She is served by throngs of the twice-born. (141)
She is indeed the Sandhyā (the Twilight Deity) because she is served and worshipped by throngs of the twice-born and by assemblies of those belonging to the three higher castes.
And it is said in the Reṇukā Purāṇa:
"The single Sandhyā is always to be saluted by the gods, the twice-born, and the high-souled ones."
On the seat, on the bed, on the carriage, and at the meal—she was indeed like Reṇukā.
Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, the triad of names beginning with *vyāhṛti* refers to the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep].
*Vyāhṛti* is the activity of speech, which indicates the waking state.
The word *sandhyā*, by the etymological derivation "born at the junction (*sandhi*) of two states," expresses the creation in the intermediate state (*sandhya*).

Furthermore, because of its usage in the *Vyāsasūtra*, the word "she" (*sā*) refers to the state of dream; it is feminine in gender both with the intention of denoting a specific state and with the intention of denoting the Goddess delimited by that state. The phrase "served and connected by the multitude of *dvijas*" is a statement from the perspective of deep sleep (*suṣupti*); for just as birds are *dvijas*, so too are living beings (*jīvas*) *dvijas*, and she is served and bound by their host with complete non-differentiation.

Just as birds, exhausted by their movement, fold their wings and settle into their nests, so too do living beings, when weary, withdraw from the states of waking and dreaming and dissolve into the Supreme Brahman;
for thus it is said. As it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Just as in this space..."
"Just as a hawk or a falcon, having flown around and become weary, folds its wings and holds itself steady for the sake of settling down,
even so this person hastens toward that end where, when asleep, he desires no desire and sees no dream. At that time, my dear, he is with Being."

And because of the scriptural statement, "He becomes complete"; and because of the determination made in the third chapter's section (Tārtīyīkādhikaraṇa) that "the absence [of dream-experience] occurs in the channels and in the Self," as stated in the scripture. || 141 ||

*Tattvāsanā* means "she whose seat consists of the *tattvas*. Her seat, known as the *yogapīṭha*, is the thirty-six *tattvas* themselves, beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, which reside within the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*). Alternatively, it means "she who casts forth or projects the *tattvas*. This refers to the word *tatpada*.

Power resides in the object that revolves within the intellect (*buddhi*). Since even the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) indeed revolves within the intellect of all, He becomes denotable by that word [“That”]. This is exactly what was stated by the venerable teacher Ācārya Bhagavatpāda in his *Viṣṇusahasranāmabhāṣya*: “That which is the unsurpassed ‘That-word’ (tat-pada). And therefore, therein, that which...
The construction of a mantra ending in the dative case, such as *namastade namaḥ*, proposed by some, is to be reconsidered;

for since [the word *tat*] applies to Brahman without abandoning its delimitor (*avacchedaka*)—that is, its denotable property—it lacks the status of a proper name, and thus its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is not lost. Furthermore:

Even though the word ends in any one of the four letters of the *tavarga* (dental class), because of the rule of *cartva* (the substitution of *c*, *ch*, *t*, *th*, or *n* for *s*), the formation of the *saṃhitā* as *yattatpadaṃ* is possible; however, [the claim] that these two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) end in the letter *d* is difficult to justify.
Therefore, the correct usage is simply *yasmai namastasmai namaḥ*.

The use of the neuter gender is justified by the intention that Brahman is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In exactly the same way, since the Blessed Lady is also denoted by the word *tvam*, the correct usage is "namas tubhyam" (salutations to you). However, when the words *tat* and *tvam*—as in the case of "tattvam asi"—indicate the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma*), then too [the same applies].

Because it does not lose its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), the application [of the rule] is exactly as previously stated. For even when its scope is restricted—as in the case of the word *viśva-* in *viśvedevāḥ* and similar expressions—it does not forfeit its status as a pronoun. The particle *ayi* is an indeclinable used for gentle address. This form arises from the addition of the suffix *ṅīṣ* due to the fact that the *gaura-* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

The meaning is that she is to be addressed by people because she is the mother of all beings (*janamātṛ*). Alternatively, *ayaḥ* refers to a destiny (*vidhi*) that brings about auspiciousness, and she is of that nature.

Or, the word *ayi* may express the identity of the referent of the word *asi*. Since the root *i* (as in *aya-paya-gatau*) is listed in the Dhātupāṭha with the sense of "going," and since that sense culminates precisely therein, the usage *ayyai namaḥ* [is justified].

The reasoning is that the authors of the Sūtras devised this designation out of a desire to avoid the redundancy of having two names for the same person within the final century [of the Buddha’s era]. This should be inferred in other cases as well. The term "pañcakośāḥ" (the five sheaths) is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*), meaning "sheaths numbering five. And these...

The specific mantras well-known for the fivefold worship (*pañcapañcikā-pūjana*) are [as follows]; by virtue of their non-difference from those [mantras], their deities are likewise [non-different]. And these are stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Śrīvidyā, Paraṃjyotis, Parā, and Niṣkalaśāmbhavī."
The Ajapā and the Mātṛkā—these are proclaimed as the five sheaths (kośas).

Thus, when these five deities are being worshipped in the Śrīcakrarāja, the four deities beginning with Paraṃjyotis are worshipped on all sides within the cakras of emanation (sṛṣṭi) and the rest, according to the distinction between the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective (samaṣṭi). Śrīvidyā, however, resides in the center as the Bindu; such is the established state. Therefore—
The meaning is that it resides within, in the midst of the five sheaths (pañcakośa). Alternatively,
there exist within the bodies of ourselves and others, arranged in successive inner layers, those known as the annamaya, prāṇamaya, manomaya, vijñānamaya, and ānandamaya.

The categories denoted by the term "five sheaths" (pañcakośa) are as follows: among these five, the innermost is the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa), wherein [the Self] abides non-differently. Regarding this, the commentators on the *Ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa* [cite] such scriptural passages as, "There is another inner self consisting of bliss," and so forth, concerning the *ānandamaya*.

Because the nature of Brahman has been stated [in that passage]. However, since the venerable teacher Śaṅkarācārya includes the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) among the elements to be purified, its impurity is established; with the intention that its status as Brahman would therefore be untenable, he maintains that the designation of Brahman occurs specifically in the statement regarding the "tail which is Brahman" (brahmapuccha). According to that view:

Since the expression "if this bliss were not in space" (yadayamākāśe ānando na syāt) is used in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it follows that the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*) has the nature of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) which constitutes the body of Brahman, whose essence is the supreme space.

This meaning is clear in the Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya and its commentaries. However, according to the view that the tail is Brahman, the meaning is "situated in the midst, within the five. And this is appropriate, because such an expansion is seen in the Brahmagītā in exactly that manner. As it has been said:
Likewise, even the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is complete through the Witness-Brahman, which is supreme over all;
Brahman is not [complete] through anything else whatsoever.
O best of gods, that which is known as the tail of Brahmā, consisting of the non-dual nature of truth and knowledge, is always directly present; it is not otherwise.
Thus say even the venerable Krodhabhaṭṭārakas:
"By means of the words of the great Upaniṣads— made famous as manifesting the head, the two wings, the tail, and the self through food, breath, mind, awakening, and supreme bliss— "
"He who knows that you, though dissolved within these very five sheaths, are a radiant light, blazing and flickering by nature—he is a knower of Brahman. Thus [it is said].
She possesses boundless majesty, is eternally youthful, and is full of intoxicating charm. (142)

"Niḥsīma" means that whose greatness (mahiman) has gone beyond the boundary (sīmā), or from the boundary, or is without boundary, or is limitless. Because of the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] by the rule *manaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.11), the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply; rather, the optional suffix *ḍāp* is used. Therefore, the usage is either "niḥsīmamahimne namaḥ" or "niḥsīmamahimāyai namaḥ."

Because she is never separated from passion (*rajas*) throughout the three periods of time, she is eternally youthful. *Mada* is a particular state of mental modification whose sole object is bliss and which is devoid of contact with any other sense-objects; she "shines" or "glitters" (*śālate*) by means of that, and thus she is so described. 142.

"Her eyes were red and rolling with intoxication, and her cheeks were rosy with wine. This means: she whose eyes were red and rolling with *mada*; "rolling" (*ghūrṇana*) refers here to turning away from external objects. She whose cheeks—the surfaces of her temples—were rosy (*pāṭala*), that is, white-red, due to the intoxication.

*Mada* means intoxication, characterized by the drinking of liquor; alternatively, *mada* refers to musk (*kastūrī*). *Pāṭala* is a specific kind of flower. The suffix *ac* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
She is one whose cheeks are variegated by the application of that [musk] and adorned with ear-ornaments.
*Mad* is declared to mean semen, musk, pride, joy, the ichor of an elephant,
and also liquor.
Thus says the Viśvakośa:
"She whose limbs are smeared with sandalwood paste and who is fond of campaka flowers. (143)
Her limbs were smeared—that is, anointed—with the liquid essence of sandalwood produced in Malaya;
she for whom the *cāmpeya* flower—the *nāgakesara* blossom or the flower associated with Campā—is dear. 143.

Kuśalā, Komalākārā, Kurukullā, Kuleśvarī. She is *kuśalā* because she possesses skill (*kauśalya*) in the creation of the world and so forth; or else, she is so called because she takes (*lāti*) or receives (*ādatte*) the water (*kuśam*). [The suffix] *ka* is applied here because the root ends in a vowel (*ādantatvāt*). Alternatively, she is *kuśalā* because the moon (*śala*), which is "wicked" (*kutsita*) [in its waxing and waning], is before her.

Or rather, it is because she possesses even greater splendor than that. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *śala* refers to the hair of the *śallakī* tree, while *śala* also denotes a swarm of bees and the Creator. She is one whose form—that is, the arrangement of her limbs—is tender and delicate.
The goddess named Kurukullā resides in Śrīpura, situated between the two walls consisting of ego and mind.
She is presiding over the pond consisting of discernment (*vimarśa*). As it is said in the *Lalitāstavaratna*, concerning that pond:
"Residing upon the sun-like ruby, with a waist that causes the mountain ranges to tremble in rivalry with her breasts..."
We constantly meditate upon Kurukullā, her limbs smeared with saffron.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the twenty-second chapter of the *Tantrarāja*, she is described as having that very form: "She is the Sovereign (*Īśvarī*) of the *kula*—the collection of the cognizer, the means of cognition, and the object of cognition, which are of the same nature.
She dwells in the *kulakuṇḍa* and is served by those devoted to the path of the *kaula*. (144)

The *bindu* situated in the center of the pericarp of the *mūlādhāra* is the *kulakuṇḍa*, which is like a cavity located in the middle of the lotus-root; she whose abode (*ālaya*)— her place of sleep—
is that very [place], or rather, she in whom there is a dissolution (*laya*) on all sides (*ā*) like deep sleep (*suṣupti*), is what is meant by *kuṇḍalinī*.

As it has been said by the venerable Ācārya Bhagavatpāda: "Having reached your own ground, coiled like a serpent with your middle encircled, you, O hollow one, lie asleep within the hollow of the Kula-kuṇḍa, making yourself your own self."
Thus [it is said]. The path obtained through one's own respective ancestral lineage is called *kaula* because of its connection to the family (*kula*).
As it is stated in the *Vrata-khaṇḍa*:
"Whichever goddess resides within whichever person's path according to the family tradition (*kulamārga*)," [she is their deity].
And she should be honored with various offerings of oblations, perfumes, and ointments.

Thus it is said: "And one should worship according to the Kula path with various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*). Alternatively, regarding the worship of the *Vidyā*, there are three systems of doctrine: the *Samaya-mata*, the *Kaula-mata*, and the *Miśra-mata*.
The first is that which is intermingled with the Vedic path and is taught in the five *Saṃhitās* of Śuka, Vasiṣṭha, and others.

However, that which is taught in the eight tantras beginning with the *Candrakula* is the final [category], because it follows both the *kula* and the *samaya*. The Kaula path is that proclaimed in tantras distinct from these; the term *kaula* is derived in the sense of "sought by the Kaulas" using the suffix *ghañ* in the objective sense (*karman*).
The specific distinctions between those various modes of worship and the distinctions in qualification are clearly explained within those respective tantras themselves.
It was frequented by those who were devoted to it and attached to it.

Kumāragaṇanāthāmbā is Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Mati, and Dhṛti. Kumāra is Skanda; Gaṇanātha is Gajānana (the Elephant-faced one); their Ambā is the Mother. Alternatively, she is so called because she binds (ambate) those who are "Lords of the hosts of base Māras" (kumāragaṇanāthān), that is, those whose [afflictions] consist of a multitude of base passions (māragaṇa) such as the transformations of desire (smara).
The verbal root is *bandh* (to bind). By the word "Kumāra," either the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) presided over by that deity is intended.
As it is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa:
"Puruṣa is called Viṣṇu, or Śiva, according to his name."
The Unmanifest, however, is the goddess Umā, or Śrī, whose eyes resemble lotuses.
From that conjunction arises the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and it is Guha, the commander-in-chief.

Thus it is said: "The attendants do not bow excessively to the Lord because He is possessed by ego. The seven names beginning with Tuṣṭi (Contentment) are expressive of contentment, nourishment, knowledge, fortitude, tranquility, auspiciousness, and loveliness;
they denote her as well, intending to convey that she possesses the very nature of such a Goddess. And so it is said:
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Salutations to her who dwells within all beings in the form of contentment; salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again."
And so forth. Also, in the *Mallārimāhātmya*:
"To that God who dwells within all beings in the form of contentment—salutations to him, salutations to him, salutations to him, salutations again and again."
And so forth. In the third book of the *Devībhāgavata*:
"Intellect, fame, fortitude, fortune, power, faith, understanding, and memory—Sāmbā is the manifest evidence of these for all living beings."

Thus, in the *Padmapurāṇa*, during the enumeration of the sacred fields (*devīkṣetra*) of the Goddess, it is stated that Tuṣṭi is at Vastreśvara, Puṣṭi is in the Devadāruvana forest, and Dhṛti is in the Piṇḍāraka field; in this way, these are said to be the names of the Blessed Goddess presiding over those respective fields. As for Mati, she is mentioned in the *Vāyupurāṇa*.
It is explained as follows:
"He maintains the sense of 'I', he conceives [objects], and he also reflects upon distinctions;
the person is thus connected with experience, and for that reason he is called 'mati' (the intellect)."
And her nature as the Goddess is described in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:

"We praise that auspicious Śivā, who is the experience that has arisen as the supreme intellect, who is devoted to the Veda, who brings about welfare, and who bestows exceeding happiness; she is served by Keśava and the other gods," and so forth.
Śānti, Svastimatī, Kānti, Nandinī, and Vighnanāśinī. || 145 ||

Or, by the word *śānti*, a specific power (*kalā*) belonging to the wind element is expressed. As it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama: "That power by which the flood of impurities, *māyā*, and transformations is stilled for the person is called *śānti*; it is the state that serves as the locus for authority."
Thus it is said. Also in the Bṛhatpārāśara-smṛti:
"That which extends over fifteen fingers' breadth and is situated outside the nose, wherein the individual soul (jīva) becomes purified—that is known as the sixteenth digit (kalā)."

Thus, beginning with the words "iti prakṛtya" and ending with "sā ca śāntiḥ prakīrtitā," [the text continues]: "Suṣṭhu astiḥ" means existence (*sattā*); or, by virtue of possessing that, it is "possessing its own-being" (*svastimatī*). The excellence of existence consists in its being ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) and its superiority over empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattā*). For it is said: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed truth (*satyam*), and He is the truth of them."
And because of the Vedic revelation that it is "the truth of truths.
The *Ratnakośa* states: "The word *svasti* denotes well-being (*āśis*), security (*kṣema*), freedom from sin (*niṣpāpa*), merit (*puṇya*), and auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
And Yāska says: "*Svasti* is among the names for the imperishable. By the word "splendor" (*kānti*), the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is expressed.

She is Nandinī because she brings joy; she is either a specific type of cow born from the lineage of Kāmadhenu, or she is the very embodiment of the Gaṅgā. She is so called because it is her nature to destroy obstacles—those impediments to knowledge—which are termed "vighnas" because they strike (ghnantīti) with particular force. 145.

She is Tejovatī (the radiant one), Trinayanā (the three-eyed one), Lolākṣī (the one with tremulous eyes), and Kāmarūpiṇī (she who can assume any form at will). She is Tejovatī because she is the substratum of the splendors of the sun and other luminaries, according to the Vedic scripture: "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon are held apart. She is Trinayanā... [three eyes].
She whose eyes have the forms of the moon, the sun, and fire;

there is no substitution of *ṇ* for *n* because the word belongs to the *kṣubhnādi* class even though it is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*). Alternatively, she has the form of "Trinayana" (the Three-eyed One), as the name of the exclamation *vauṣaṭ* is well-known in the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*.

Alternatively, the word *nayana* refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), based on the etymological derivation: "it leads" (*nayati*) or "it brings about" (*prāpayati*) the means of valid cognition. Thus, there is a usage in the *Śāṇḍilyasūtra*: "These [deities] have three eyes, due to the distinction of word, mark, and sense-organ, like Rudra. Three.
She whose means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consist of perception, inference, and verbal testimony;
for the generation of valid knowledge regarding Her, there are only these three types of means:
hearing (*śravaṇa*), which is verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*); reflection (*manana*), which is inferential due to its logical nature; and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*).

It is indeed perception in the form of one's own direct experience; however, it is occasionally interrupted in the interim by heterogeneous cognitions. It is with this very intention that the sage Śāṇḍilya enumerated the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas) beginning precisely with verbal testimony (śabda). As for analogy (upamāna)...
Because it would be irrelevant to the present context as it would merely concern the apprehension of the expressive power [of words], it is for this very reason that it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*:
"Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions..."
One who desires purity of Dharma should thoroughly understand these three.
Thus [it is said]. The *Sāṃkhya* compendium-sūtra also states: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are threefold.
The *Yoga* sūtra also states: "Perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition.
Alternatively, it may mean that it leads those who are qualified toward the three paths; namely, the southern path and the northern path.
And the path of Brahman—these three paths will be analyzed further on. Thus it is said in the Devīpurāṇa: "The southern and the northern world, as well as the supreme path of Brahman."
The Guide is considered to be the Three-eyed One, who possesses the method and the class of the true path.

Thus: she is the embodiment of the desire—that is, the passion (manmatha)—of women with tremulous eyes (*lolākṣī*). The qualification "belonging to women with tremulous eyes" is used for the purpose of setting aside [the desire] of Śiva.
Alternatively, she is the form of Yogeśvarī, who presides over desire (*kāma*). As it is said in the Varāha Purāṇa:
Lust, anger, greed, pride, and delusion as the fifth;
they say envy is the sixth, and likewise malice is the seventh.
Envy is to be known as the eighth; these are the eight Mothers.
Know Desire to be Yogeśvarī, and likewise Anger to be Māheśvarī.
Lobha (greed) is said to be Vaiṣṇavī, and Mada (intoxication) is indeed Brahmāṇī;
Moha (delusion) is Svayambhū Kalyāṇī, and they know Mātsarya (envy) to be Indrajā.
"The goddess Yamadaṇḍadharā, Paiśunya herself, Asūyā, and she named Varāhā—these are thus proclaimed. Mālinī, Haṃsinī, Mātā, and Malayācalavāsinī. (146)

She is called Mālinī because she possesses a garland (*mālāvat*); the suffix *-in* is applied according to the rule for the *vrīhy-ādi* group. Alternatively, "Mālinī" is the name of the presiding deity of the fifty-one *mātṛkās*, and she is of that nature.
Or else, the Goddess has a female companion named Mālinī, and she is of her form. As it has been said:
In the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, in the section concerning the marriage of Pārvatī, regarding the taking of the seven steps (*saptapadīkramaṇa*), it is said:
"Then the foot of Hara was grasped by Mālinī for the purpose of receiving [the bride].
'What do you ask for? I shall give it; let go! thus spoke Hara."
Mālinī said to Śaṅkara: "O Śaṅkara, grant to my friend the auspiciousness belonging to your own lineage; from that, you shall attain liberation."
Then Mahādeva said, "O Mālinī, I have given [you my word]; release me," and so forth. She was either in the form of a specific meter (*vṛtta*) or in the form of the Mandākinī river.
*Mālinī* may refer to a variety of meter, or also to the wife of a garland-maker.
In the city of Campā, at Gaurī, and at Mandākinī and Mālinī.
Thus says the *Viśva* lexicon. A girl of seven years is called *Mālinī*, or she may be so named because she possesses that form;
for in the section on girls, there is a statement by Dhaumya: "She who has seven [qualities] would be *Mālinī*.
She is *Haṃsinī* because the *haṃsas*—a specific class of ascetics—exist within her without distinction, or because the *haṃsa* is the *ajapā* mantra.

She is called "Mother" (*mātṛ*) because she gives birth to all beings, or because she is the form of the *mātṛkās*. According to the *Skānda Purāṇa*, "The Supreme Goddess is the *mātṛkā*, who has become the mother of the mantras. Alternatively, the masculine form [of the word] signifies the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Here, "Light" (*prakāśa*) is the substantive. Or else, she is the "mother" of the mantra of the *nityā* of the tenth lunar day.
This is the name. The meaning is that she is of such a form, as seen likewise in the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*.

This Mother is the presiding deity of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) called Kāyāvarohaṇa, according to the *Padma Purāṇa*. She is also known by the name "Mother" (*Mātā*), which is a seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Lakṣmī. [Her names are] Śrī, Mā, Ramā, and Kamalā.

She is the Mother, Lakṣmī, and Maṅgalā, according to the statement in the Viśva lexicon. She is the Goddess whose abode is Malaya, well-known in the Śābaracintāmaṇi; because she is of that nature, she dwells on Mount Malaya, and is thus so called. (146) She is Sumukhī, Nalinī, Subhrū, Śobhanā, and Suranāyikā.

She whose face is beautiful is *sumukhī*. This is because the splendor of her face excels through [her] knowledge, according to the Vedic revelation: "The face of one who knows thus shines," and also from the Vedic revelation: "O gentle one, your face shines like that of a knower of Brahman. Alternatively, she may be a specific deity to be meditated upon as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice.

Sumukhī: Because her limbs—hands, feet, face, eyes, and so forth—are like lotuses, she is Nalinī according to the logic of creation; or because she is of the nature of the Bhāgīrathī, for she is counted among its twelve names as "Nandinī, Nalinī, Gaṅgā. [She is also] King Nala.

Or, she is "Sā" because she is entered into through identity by means of that worship. She is "Subhrūḥ," one who possesses beautiful eyebrows; she is beautiful due to her nature of loveliness. The lexicon states: "Suṣumam, sādhu, and śobhanam [mean beautiful]. She is the supreme leader and sovereign of the gods, whose greatness is most exalted.
According to the scripture, "of the deities," [they are] Kālakaṇṭhī, Kāntimatī, Kṣobhiṇī, and Sūkṣmarūpiṇī. || 147 ||
She is the wife of that Lord whose throat is Time (Kāla). And it is said in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"While the hosts of gods, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rakṣasas were looking on, I held the terrible poison in my throat; therefore, I am Kālakaṇṭha."

Thus, in the Devīpurāṇa, within the section on the sixty-eight Śiva-tīrthas, she is remembered as Kālakaṇṭha at Kālañjara. By this, the meaning is that she is the presiding deity of that sacred field (kṣetra). Alternatively, "kala" refers to a sweet and indistinct sound; "kāla" is that same [sound] with the suffix *aṇ* added in its own sense; thus, she is "Kālakaṇṭhā," one whose throat (*kaṇṭha*) possesses such a [sweet] sound.

Or [the suffix] *ṅīp* is applied after *aṅga*, *gātra*, and *kaṇṭha*. Alternatively, she has that form because of the well-known story in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "The Enemy of Kāma (Śiva) created Kālī, who has a dark throat (*kālakaṇṭhī*) and wears matted hair (*kapardinī*), for the sake of slaying the demon Dāruka. Or [the suffix] *aṇ* is added pleonastically to the word *kala* itself; thus, she is one whose sound is charming (*mañju*).

That is its meaning: she possesses beauty, thus she is *kāntimatī*. She agitates the two Supreme Lords by means of their orientation toward creation, thus she is *kṣobhiṇī*. As it is said in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Having entered both Prakṛti and Puruṣa by His own will, Hari..."
At the time of creation, the Blessed One, having taken recourse [to it], caused it to vibrate.

Thus [it is said]. Or else, she is called *Kṣobhiṇī* because she generated certain *Gaṇas* from the agitation of the mind (*manaḥkṣobha*). This is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa regarding the three forms:
"The Goddess Vaiṣṇavī who went to Mount Mandara to perform penance..."
As she was performing those austerities, after a long time, her mind became agitated.
From that agitation arose maidens of serene appearance,
with dark curly hair, lips like the *bimba* fruit, and lotus-like eyes.
Resembling blue lotuses, richly adorned with necklaces and anklets, and full of splendor—
such were the goddesses as soon as their minds were agitated.
"Hundreds of thousands, by the millions, with various faces, arose," and so forth. Her form is subtle and difficult to perceive;
for the Śruti declares, "Subtler than the subtle, eternal, smaller than the smallest. Furthermore, "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is a designation for a specific type of oblation (*homa*).
In the *Tantrarāja*, beginning with the passage "In the center of the *mūlādhāra* there is fire, arising eternally and non-eternally," and ending with "Thus,
the oblation (*homa*) shall be performed twelvefold by means of the uttered syllables," that very form is described as belonging to her; or rather, the Goddess herself also possesses three forms.
It is quite evident that they truly exist through the divisions of gross, subtle, and supreme. || 147 ||
Vajreśvarī is Vāmadevī, free from the limitations of age;

she is the Nityā of the sixth lunar day (Ṣaṣṭhī) and the presiding deity of the Jālandhara-pīṭha. Alternatively, the twelfth enclosure wall of Śrīpura is composed of vajra-jewels, and [she resides] within that eleventh [wall].
The river named Vajrā is its presiding deity. And it was said by Durvāsas:
"May that river called Vajrā, which flows there eternally, be long victorious—nourished by the sweet warbling of flocks of kalahamsa swans dancing amidst the network of her restless waves."
On its beautiful banks dwells Vajreśī, victorious and richly adorned with vajras;
her conduct is praised by the gods, and she has gratified the face of the Vajrin (Indra) through the offering of the vajra.
Thus it is said. Even the thunderbolt was given to Indra by the Goddess alone. This is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa* concerning Śakra’s penance in the water:
"The Goddess, having arisen from that water, gave the thunderbolt to the enemy of Bala."
Having accomplished his purpose, he too vanished and went to heaven.

Thus: Vāmadeva is the desirable (vāmanīya) god. Regarding him, the gods said, "He is indeed the desirable one (vāma) for all of us"; therefore he is called Vāmadeva, according to the Aitareya Śruti. Alternatively, Vāmadeva is the Lord who sports with the left (vāmena) portion, that is, the Ardhanārīśvara.
Resembling powdered saffron, wearing the garb of a forest-dweller,
the face called Vāma belongs to the Supreme Lord and is established in Pratiṣṭhā.

Thus, according to the Śiva Purāṇa, Vāmadeva is a specific form included within the manifestation (vyūha) of Sadāśiva; she is his consort, Vāmā, who is beautiful. Alternatively, she is the presiding deity of "vāmas," meaning the fruits of actions. Those who delight in the left-hand path (vāmācāra) are called vāmas.
"Even the worshipper may be Vāma, being constantly devoted to that path," according to the statement in the *Kālikā-purāṇa*;
thus, they may be called "Devīs" (the Left-hand ones). And it is said in the *Devī-purāṇa*:
"Vāma is of a contrary nature; indeed, it is sung as being the reverse."
The goddess who bestows happiness with her left [hand] is therefore known as Vāmadevī.
Thus: she is devoid of the distinctions of age, such as childhood, youth, and adolescence, because she is eternal.
She is the Sovereign of Siddhas, the Knowledge of the Siddhas, the Mother of the Siddhas, and the Illustrious One. 148.

She is the sovereign mistress (*īśvarī*) and queen (*svāminī*) of the Siddhas headed by Gorakṣa, and is renowned in Kāśī by this very name. She is both a Siddha and a Vidyā; thus, she is called *Siddhavidyā*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kādimata* regarding the Nityās that there is no purification of the circle of enemies (*aricakra-śodha*) for the *Pañcadaśī*.

Because her mantras are perfected (*siddha*), you need not consider [her] *aṃśaka* and so forth; she is the mother of the perfected ones (*siddhas*) because she protects them. She is "Glorious" (*yaśasvinī*) because glory (*yaśas*) belongs to her, according to the rule *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* and the Vedic scripture stating, "Her name is Great Glory. (148)
Then, by means of the sixty-two names according to the sequence of the Yoginī-nyāsa,
he begins to praise the Blessed Lady, who is the embodiment of the seven Yoginīs beginning with *ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-ha-yā*, presiding over the seven cakras starting from Viśuddhi.
"Residing in the wheel of purification (viśuddhi-cakra), red in color, and three-eyed"—by these words [the text describes her]. Herein is the meditation on Ḍākinī:
in the throat-pit, within the lotus of sixteen petals belonging to the wheel of purification, she is white and red, and possesses three eyes.

I bow to Ḍākinī, who is worshipped by heroes, whose body is surrounded by Amṛtā and the other goddesses, who dwells within the skin, who is intent solely upon milk-rice (pāyasa), who inspires fear in the ignorant masses, who possesses one face, and who holds in her hands a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a sword, a trident, and a great shield.
Thus: "She whose abode is the very pericarp of the sixteen-petaled lotus of the Viśuddhi-cakra;

she whose color is reddish"—this is her five-syllable name. The prefix *ā-* is used in the sense of "slightness. Therefore, the meaning is that her color is like that of the *pāṭalī* flower, which is described by the definition: "white and red is *pāṭala*."

And because there is no tautology with the name found in the *Lākinīprakaraṇa*, [she is] she who has three eyes; she whose weapons are the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and so forth, and who is endowed with a single face. 149.

A *khaṭvāṅga* is the leg of a bed, or alternatively, a skull-staff (*naraka-pāla*) mounted on a handle. She is the one who possesses these weapons—among which are those beginning with that [khaṭvāṅga]—within her four [hands]. As for the term *vadana-eka*, it is a compound formed according to the rule *pūrva-kāla-eka-*; however, because the rule is not mandatory (*anityatva*), the word *vadana* does not necessarily take the first position. Therefore...
Endowed with; joined. || 149 ||
She who is fond of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), who resides in the skin, and who causes fear to the world of cattle:
*pāyasa* is a transformation of milk, and that food is *paramānna*; she for whom that is dear is [Pāyasānnapriyā]. She resides in the skin-element (*tvak-sthā*) because she takes pride in it.

Those devoid of the knowledge of non-duality (advaita-vidyā) are indeed like cattle; for them, [this world] is terrifying. According to the Śruti: "He who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know, being like a beast. For from duality, fear arises; "for him who perceives even a slight difference in this [Reality], there is fear."
And because of the scriptural statement, "fear arises," the Mistress of the Ḍākinīs is encompassed by the great powers such as Amṛtā and the rest. 150.

She is surrounded by those sixteen great powers beginning with the one called Amṛtā— namely Amṛtakarṣiṇī, Indrāṇī, and so forth, ending with Akṣarā— each residing upon an individual petal. And it is said in the Svacchandatantra:
Therefore, above one finger-breadth is the pure sixteen-syllable [mantra];
the Ḍākinī resides in the center, while the Supreme Goddess is on the outer petals.
"From Amṛtā to Akṣarā, and above that is the lunar disc.
Thus [it is said]. He indicates the substantive for the nine adjectives by its name:
"the Sovereign Lady of the Ḍākinīs" (Ḍākinīśvarī). The meaning is: the Sovereign Lady known as Ḍākinī. || 150 ||
Residing in the lotus of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), dark-complexioned and possessing two faces,
the Yoginī named Rākiṇī dwells in the heart within the twelve-petaled lotus known as the *anāhata* wheel. Her meditation is as follows:
In the heart-lotus with twelve petals, one should visualize her who is dark-complexioned, possessing two faces,
fangs, and three eyes, holding a rosary, a trident, a skull-cup, and a hand-drum in her hands.
We meditate upon Rākinī, who dwells in the blood, surrounded by Kālarātri and others, solely devoted to affectionate food, worshipped by the illustrious Vīrendras, and the bestower of desired fruits.

Thus: she whose abode is the pericarp of that unstruck lotus (*anāhatābja*); *śyāmābhā* means she who resembles a sixteen-year-old girl (*śyāmā*), or else she whose radiance (*ābhā*) and beauty (*kānti*) are dark-blue (*śyāmā*);
she who possesses a pair of faces.
She possesses fangs, radiant eyes, a rosary, and other attributes, and she stands amidst blood.

Resplendent and shining with tusks resembling those of a boar, she is the bearer of four weapons, the first of which is a rosary (*akṣamālā*). [The suffix] *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*), whereas if the suffix *aṇ* were applied according to 3.2.1 (*karmaṇyaṇ*), the form would have been *dhārā*. In the aforementioned verse, if it had simply said "the discus" (*cakra*) and "the trident" (*śūla*), [the intended meaning would be lost].

In that context, the term *akṣamāla* should be understood as "the wheel" (*cakra*), because it takes (*lāti*) or assumes the beauty (*śobhā*) of the axle (*akṣa*) and the chariot-felly (*rathāṅga*). She is established in blood—that is, in the vital fluid (*rudhira*)—by virtue of identifying with it. 151.
Enveloped by the flood of powers such as Kālarātri and others, she is fond of smooth rice porridge.
There exists a certain power named Kālarātri. This is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa concerning the three forms:
O Earth, hear now the vow of that Raudrī Śakti, born of darkness, who went to Mount Nīla with a mind resolved upon asceticism.
Beginning thus: "The goddess Raudrī, devoted to austerity, is the supreme tamasic power;
she is known by the name Kālarātri as the bringer of dissolution."

Thus: she is surrounded by the flood—that is, the assembly—of the twelve Śaktis, those whose first is [the aforementioned] and whose last is Ṭhaṃkāri; she is encircled upon the petals. She for whom rice mixed with ghee and smeared with oil is dear;
she who, with a single face, grants boons to the great lords of heroes.

"Vīrāḥ" refers to those for whom there is various "īrā" (food or refreshment); that is to say, panegyrists whose speech causes wonder on both sides [of the debate]. Alternatively, "mahāvīram" refers to a specific sacrificial vessel used in the Soma sacrifice, as is well known from Vedic texts such as: "But the mahāvīra is free from dispute and pure."
And by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to those devoted to the drinking vessel; therefore, the suffix *ac* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
This means they are those whose habit is the drinking of the nectar of the essence of Brahman. For this very reason, they are "Indras," that is, knowers of Brahman (*brahmavidas*).
They are witnesses who perceive "this" (*idam*) through direct immediacy (*āparokṣyeṇa*), [realizing] "I am Brahman," which is their own self.

They are the Indras who directly realize [this]. Thus it is heard in scripture: "Because they say, 'I have seen this, I have seen this,' therefore he is named Indra. Alternatively, the one who does not experience the triad is the Vīreśa; according to the definition stated in the *Śivasūtras*, even while in states such as waking and so forth, he remains intent upon the contemplation of the Fourth State (*turya*).
The lords of heroes (vīrendra). And it has been said by Varadarāja:
"The Lord of Heroes (vīreśa) is the sovereign of the senses—which cause the affliction of duality for heroes—whether they are spreading internally or externally."
Thus it is said. Alternatively, Mahāvīra refers to Prahlāda and Indra to Śakra.

In the fourth book of the Devībhāgavata, when a battle between Śakra and Prahlāda had lasted for a hundred divine years, the Blessed Goddess was subsequently praised by both of them and granted a boon to each.
Because he grants a boon to them by recollecting their past narratives, it is so called.
Rākiṇī is the one whose nature is that of the Mother (Ambā). || 152 ||
Her essential nature is that of the Mother named Rākiṇī. || 152 ||
Residing in the lotus of Maṇipūra, she is endowed with three faces.
The lotus called Maṇipūra has ten petals and is located at the navel; therein resides the Yoginī known as Lākinī. As it has been said:

In the lotus of the navel, within the petals of the directions, [one should meditate on] the fierce Mahogrā, red in color, possessing three faces and sporting fangs, holding in her arms a spear, a thunderbolt, a staff, and the gesture of fearlessness.

We meditate upon Lākinī, who is surrounded by Ḍāmari and the others, who brings fear to the ignorant masses, who is solely intent on flesh and blood, whose mind is attached to molasses and food, yet who bestows all happiness.

Thus: she whose abode is the lotus called Maṇipūra; she who is endowed with three faces; she who is equipped with weapons such as the vajra; and she who is surrounded by Ḍāmari and the others. || 153 ||
She is endowed with the four weapons beginning with the vajra, and is surrounded by the ten Śaktis beginning with Ḍāmari and ending with Phaṭkāriṇī.
"Red-colored and abiding in flesh"—
she whose color is red; she who dwells intensely within the flesh by virtue of identifying with that constituent element (*dhātu*),
and thus so described.
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by the illustrious Bhāsurānanda, the sixth digit named Ruci was completed with five hundred verses. || 500 ||
Thus ends the sixth digit, named the Five Hundred [Verses], in the commentary on the *Śrī Lalitāsahasranāma*.
Now begins the seventh digit, named the Six Hundred [Verses], the Suṣumṇā digit, whose mind is delighted by sweetmeats (*guḍānna*).
Food mixed with jaggery is *guḍānna*. This is a compound meaning "the act of mixing with an edible.
She whose mind is pleased by that [food] is Lākinyambā, who exists in her own essential nature as the bestower of happiness upon all devotees. || 154 ||
She is so called because she bestows happiness upon all devotees; her essential nature is that of the Mother known as Lākinī. 154.
Residing in the lotus of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, she is enchanting with four faces.
The Yoginī named Kākinī dwells in the six-petalled lotus known as the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
As it has been said:
In the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, which shines with six petals, she has four faces and three eyes;
she holds in her two hands a trident, a rosary, a skull-cup, and the gesture of fearlessness, and is full of pride.
She is established in the fat-element, delighted by the intoxication of wine, and is accompanied by Bandhinī and the other [consorts].
We meditate upon the yellow Kākinī, who is fond of curd-rice and bestows desired fruits.
Thus: she has gone to—that is, reached—the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna; she is charming and beautiful with four faces;
she is endowed with weapons such as the trident; she is yellow in color and exceedingly proud. || 155 ||
She is endowed with the weapons previously enumerated, such as the trident and others. She is one whose complexion is yellow (*pītavarṇā*).

She is one who possesses excessive pride (*garva*) produced by her beauty and other qualities; she is "extremely proud" (*atigarvitā*), formed from the root *gṛ* (pride) with the suffix *niṣṭhā*. 155.
She whose final abode is in the fat, who is delighted by honey, and who is endowed with Bandhinī and others;

that is, she whose *niṣṭhā*—her state of being or residence—is in the specific bodily element (*dhātu*) of fat (*medas*). She is pleased by *madhu*, whether it be wine or honey. And thus says the Śruti: "In that one offers with honey, [one offers] this very great..."
"It gratifies that deity" means it gratifies Mahādevī. She is endowed with the six [goddesses] beginning with Bandhinī and ending with Lamboṣṭhī;
she has her heart attached to curd-rice and assumes the form of Kākinī. (156)

"Dadhyanna" is a compound meaning "food with curd," specifically rice sprinkled with curd; she is one whose heart is attached to that. She is so called because she assumes the form, that is, the very appearance, of a *kākini*. 156.
Seated upon the lotus of the *mūlādhāra*, she resides within the bones and possesses five faces.

The Yoginī known as Śākinī dwells in the four-petalled lotus called the *mūlādhāra*. As it has been said: "In the lotus situated at the *mūlādhāra*, which is adorned with four petals, [she is] five-faced and three-eyed."

She has a smoky luster and stands upon a skeleton; she holds in her long arms a goad, a lotus, a book, and the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā), and is surrounded by the beautiful primary Śaktis beginning with Varadā.
We meditate upon the Ḍākinī, whose mind is not attached to food and who is delighted by the intoxication of honey.
Thus: she is mounted upon the lotus known as the *mūlādhāra*, situated in its pericarp;
she whose faces are five in number; she who is established within the bones or among the bones;
she whose weapons are the elephant-goad and others, and who is attended by [the gestures] such as the boon-granting (*varada*). || 157 ||
She who possesses four weapons, beginning with the goad; she who is attended by the four Śaktis, beginning with Varadā and ending with Sarasvatī. 157.
Sākinyambā is one whose nature is characterized by a mind attached to *mudgaudanā* (rice mixed with mung-bean soup).
Regarding her characteristics, it is stated in the *Kumārasaṃhitā*: "She whose mind is attached to rice mixed with *mudga* soup..."
One *prastha* of well-husked rice, half of that [measure] of split mung beans,
four *palas* of jaggery, and a coconut of the same measure are prescribed.
One muṣṭi of black pepper should be used, half of that amount of rock salt, half of that again for cumin;
and they know that one kuḍava of cow’s ghee is required.
Having combined it with an equal measure of cow’s milk,
this excellent prepared food is perfected simply by cooking over a gentle fire.

Thus [it is said]. This is the nature of Sākinyāmbā: in the center of the eyebrows is the lotus called the Ājñā-cakra, which has two petals; there resides the Yoginī named Hākinī. As it has been said:
"In the center of the eyebrows, in the lotus of the Bindu, which is endowed with a pair of petals, [one should meditate on her] white in color, with [her] lotus-hands..."
We meditate upon Hākinī, who holds the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), a *ḍamaru* drum, a stainless rosary, and a skull-cup;
who stands within the center of the six chakras; who is radiant with three eyes; who is joined by Haṃsavatī and others;
who is devoted to many kinds of turmeric-colored food; and who bestows all happiness. Thus.
Residing in the lotus of the ājñā-cakra, she is white in color and has six faces. || 158 ||
She whose abode is the lotus of the *ājñācakra*; she whose complexion is white; she who has six faces. 158.
She who dwells within the marrow (*majjā*) like a swan, endowed with her primary power (*mukhya-śakti*).

The word *majjā* ends in the letter *n* and is masculine; according to the *Amara-kośa*, "marrow (*majjā*) is the essence (*sāra*). Following that, by eliding the vowel *ā* and prefixing *ā*, the analysis of the compound is: she who stands perfectly (*samyaṅ*) and completely (*āsamantāt*) within the marrow (*majjñi*).

The meaning is that she is one who takes pride in the marrow-element (*majjadhātu*). Alternatively, the word *majjā* may end in the vowel *-ā*.
