This is because of such usages in the *Jñānārṇavasiṣṭha*: "This is the marrow of the *cidbilva* fruit," "Everything whose form is the marrow of consciousness is the wonder of one's own marrow," and so forth; [and because] *majjā* can be used as *majjayā*.

And because of the *kośa* [lexicon] stating "saha," it is indeed a word ending in *ṭāp*; therefore, there is no elision (*praśleṣa*) of the nasal *ṇ*. She is endowed with those two powers, Haṃsavatī and Kṣamāvatī, both of which have as their primary [aspect] that which exists in the mouth (*mukhya*), namely the Haṃsavatī itself.
She who delights solely in turmeric-colored food and assumes the form of Hākinī. || 159 ||
She whose primary taste is the perception of deliciousness and her delight lie in food mixed with turmeric;
she is thus one whose nature it is to assume the form of the goddess named Hākinī. 159.
Residing upon a thousand-petaled lotus and adorned with all colors;
in the *brahmarandhra* there is a thousand-petaled lotus where the yoginī named Yākinī resides.
As it has been said:
I meditate upon Bhavānī, who is of all colors, seated upon the moon at the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus situated in the hollow of the *muṇḍa*;
she is established in the seminal essence (*reta*), her hands are adorned with all weapons, her lotus-face is turned in every direction,
and she is surrounded by a multitude of powers consisting of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.
We meditate upon Yākinī, whose mind is unattached to all food and who delights in the supreme Śiva.

Thus [it is said]. She "dwells" (tiṣṭhati) upon a thousand-petaled lotus; thus she is so called. She is "adorned with all colors," such as pale-red, dark-blue, red, yellow, and so forth—that is to say, she possesses variegated colors.
Alternatively, she is one whose "colors" (varṇāḥ)—meaning syllables—are all those beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.

She is adorned and surrounded by those fifty powers, beginning with Amṛtā and ending with Kṣamāvatī, situated upon the petals nearby; that is to say, she is encircled by those hundred-fold powers—numbering one hundred—abiding on the petals ten times each, according to the method of direct and reverse order. This is because of the technical definition provided for the prefix *upa*.
Furthermore, it is because it is impossible for [the word] to denote the number ten. For this very reason, some desire that their placement (nyāsa) be performed ten times in the Yoginī-nyāsa.
She holds all weapons, is established in whiteness, and has faces on all sides. || 160 ||

She is the support (*dhārā*) and the sustainer (*dhārayitrī*) of all weapons, according to the Vedic revelation: "Thousands upon thousands are the missiles in your two arms. In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, she is described as being perfectly established within the pure element called *vīrya* (virility/semen) by virtue of presiding over it.
The specific meditation during the time of enjoyment is called "white" (śukla), or she who abides therein.
She is one whose faces are on all sides, in all directions, according to the scriptural statement: "On all sides are her eyes, heads, and mouths. 160.

She whose mind is pleased by all kinds of cooked rice— from milk-rice and the like, down to turmeric rice, and including other varieties without distinction— is Yākinyambā, who possesses the form of a mother known as Yākinī.
This is her essential nature.
Having thus described her as being the very nature of the Yoginī, he begins to describe her by other modes as well:
Svāhā, Svadhā, Mati, Medhā, Śruti, and the unsurpassed Smṛti. || 161 ||

By [the words] "svāhā," "svadhā," and so forth: according to the lexicon (*kośa*), the words *svāhā* and *svadhā* denote the relinquishment of a substance intended for a specific deity, used respectively in the offering of oblations to the gods (*devahavirdāna*) and in the context of *śrauṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *vaṣaṭ*. The Goddess herself is also of the nature of that meaning. As it has been said:

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "O Goddess, the seven types of rites— the Soma-saṃsthās, the Havis-saṃsthās, and the Pāka-saṃsthās— are performed by the exponents of the Veda through the mere utterance of Your name."
Thus it is said elsewhere as well:
"O Goddess, she whose utterance brings satisfaction in all sacrifices, wherein all forms of delight are contained..."
Since you are indeed the cause of satisfaction for the host of ancestors, you are therefore addressed by people as both "Svāhā" and "Svadhā."
In this view, because these two are indeclinables (*avyaya*), the usage is *svāhā namaḥ* and *svadhā namaḥ*.
Their etymological explanation is given in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The word *sva* is taught to mean heaven and the self; *hi* should be understood as 'because' and 'going'."
And the Sāma-branch, whose self is heaven, is offered by one's own self into the fire, wherein everything is sacrificed.

Thus it is said; "That very speech of yours," she replied—so the *Taittirīya Śruti* explains that the word *svāhā* means "one's own speech. In the *Sāmabrāhmaṇa*, questions such as "How many syllables does *svāhā* have? and their respective answers are heard. Regarding these etymological explanations:

The only recourse is its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular words]. This should be understood similarly in Yāska’s *Nirukta*, in such passages as *su āha iti* or *svam āha iti*. Others, however, say: the etymology is "that by which one is well called" (*suṣṭhu āhūyate 'nayā*). The suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well. It approaches (*ājihīte*) its own people (*svān*).

She is called *svāhā* because she goes as her own (*svīyatvena*) or because she knows correctly; or alternatively, because she well (*suṣṭhu*) approaches (*jihīta*) the Grandfather (*āṃ*). She is the wife of Śiva in his form as Fire and the mother of Skanda. As it is said in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*:
The syllable *svāhā* is declared to be dear to Paśupati, whose nature is fire;
the divine Lord Ṣaṇmukha is designated as his son by the wise.
Thus it is said. Also in the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]: "That body of Paśupati which is remembered by the twice-born as Agni, his wife is remembered as Svāhā, and Skanda is also remembered as his son."

Thus [it is said]. And she is the presiding deity of the Māheśvara-pīṭha. According to the *Padma-purāṇa*, "Svāhā is in the Pūra [pīṭha] of Māheśvara. Alternatively, she is called *svāhā* because by her [offerings] are well (*su*) placed (*ādhīyate*). Or, she is *svadhā* because she well (*su*) bestows (*dadhāti*) or nourishes (*poṣayati*) Viṣṇu (Aṃ) or herself. In this latter sense, [the mantras are] "Salutation to Svāhā" and "Salutation to Svadhā."

Such is the application [of the term]. In the *Ātharvaṇa-śruti*, regarding the statement "that which does not pass away (*na vyeti*) is the indeclinable (*avyaya*)," the explanation is that "does not pass away" means it does not assume the properties of existence (*sattva-dharma*), such as gender, number, and case-role (*liṅga-saṃkhyā-kāraka*). This is because, in the context of offering oblations (*havir-dāna*), those two [gender and number] have no referent in reality (*asatvārthakatva*). "Amati" is a name consisting of three syllables.

The meaning is "ignorance" (avidyā). Alternatively, by relying on the negative particle *nañ* having the sense of "slightness," it may mean "that which consists of functional knowledge" (*vṛttyātmakajñānarūpā*). This word *amiti*, found in the Vedic glossary (*nighaṇṭu*), was explained by Durgabhaṭṭa in his work on etymology (*nirukta*) as referring to the realization of one's own self (*svātmavijñāna*). In another passage of that same work, it is stated as referring to "form" (*rūpa*). Or else:
In the previously mentioned order of creation, the initial creation was either without prior intelligence or of that nature;
however, because it follows the sequence [of creation], the Goddess herself is also the form of the creation preceded by intelligence. Thus he says:
"O Goddess, you are Medhā (Intelligence), you who have understood the essence of all the Śāstras," and "The Goddess who [resides] in all beings..."

Because of the statement, "She is established in the form of *medhā*," and because of the *Āgneyapurāṇa* statement, "Medhā is wisdom (*dhī*) endowed with retention (*dhāraṇā*"), she is either of the nature of a specific type of intellect. Or, she is of the form of the Goddess mentioned in the *Padmapurāṇa*: "Medhā [is located] in the region of Kāśmīra. The Vedas...

The Śruti declares that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are of this very same nature: "The Ṛg-veda, Yajur-veda, Sāma-veda, and likewise the Atharva-veda—this is the innate form of Brahman; it is His eternal, imperishable power."
Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*. Alternatively, it consists of knowledge in the form of hearing and recollecting. However, in the *Vāyu Purāṇa* it is said:
"Because it remembers all tasks—those present, those past, and likewise those yet to come—it is called *smṛti* (recollection)."

Thus it has been said. In the *Devīpurāṇa*, however, it is stated: "She is the Goddess (Devī) because she is remembered (*saṃsmaraṇāt*). She is the unsurpassed (*anuttamā*), for there exists no other object superior to her; as the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) declares: "Neither one equal to Him nor one greater than He is seen," and "There is none equal to You, nor any greater."
And because of the traditional teaching (smṛti), "Whence could there be another?"; and also in the third book of the Devībhāgavata:
"People do not speak of one who is devoid of Rudra or devoid of Viṣṇu in the same way as they all speak of a base man who is devoid of Śakti."
Thus: "She whose intellect or sovereignty is not *nutta*—meaning not impelled by another;
that is to say, she whose intellect is independent and whose sovereignty is innate. (161)
Her fame is meritorious, obtainable through merit, and consisting of the hearing and chanting of merit;
her fame is itself meritorious and bestows merit, and it is obtained through past merits. And it is said in the third book of the Devībhāgavata:
Those who possess a mass of merit and those ascetics who have realized the Vedāntas behold her;
but those possessed by passion do not at all behold the Goddess, the Blessed Śivā.
Thus: she whose hearing and chanting consist of merit in the form of prescribed actions; the genitive sense here denotes a relationship mediated by her conduct.
She is the daughter of Puloman, worshipped, the liberator from bondage, and possesses dark, curly hair. 162.

She was worshipped by Indrāṇī, who was born from Puloman; thus the story is recorded in the sixth book of the Devībhāgavata: while Nahuṣa was ruling the sovereignty, Indrāṇī propitiated the Goddess in order to regain the status of Śakra.
Thus addressed by him at that time, Śakra’s wife Sumānasā duly received from her guru the mantra for the excellent accomplishment of the Goddess.
Having received the vidyā from her guru, the goddess thoroughly propitiated the goddess Tripurasundarī with auspicious offerings of oblations and flowers.
And so forth. She liberates one from bondage born of ignorance; she liberates one even from prison. This was said by Aniruddha in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"O Śāṅkarī, you are indeed celebrated by these names and others."
Through your grace, may I be swiftly released from bondage without obstacle.
Look upon me, O large-eyed one; I seek refuge at your feet.
You ought to grant liberation from all bonds indeed.
Having begun thus, the goddess Durgā, whose prowess is difficult to overcome, being praised in this manner,
then liberated the heroic Aniruddha who was imprisoned in the city of Bāṇa.

Thus far. Likewise, in the sixth book of the Devībhāgavata, there is recorded the story of how the princess named Ekāvalī, having been bound by the demon Kālaketu, was liberated by her friend Yaśovatī through the power of the mantra of the Goddess she herself worshipped; that story too should be cited here.

She whose curls (*alakāḥ*), which are *cūrṇakuntalāḥ* (powdered locks), are wavy (*bandhurāḥ*) and undulating (*unnatānatāḥ*). However, the reading transmitted through tradition is *barbarālakā*; the word *barbara* is conventionally used for hair that is short and curled at the tips, as seen in the usage in the *Lalitāstavaratna*: "of those with dark-blue, glossy, and *barbara* hair."

Even if the reading is *barbareti*, the meaning remains the same; furthermore, because the vernacular form *bābara* is observed, this very reading is in fact the one most widely accepted, rather than *bandhureti*. || 162 ||
Vidyā is of the nature of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) and is the progenitor of the world beginning with space (*viyat*).
*Vimarśa* is said to be the natural vibration (*sphuraṇa*) of the Supreme Brahman, whose essence is light (*prakāśa*). As it is stated in the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*:
He possesses an innate power of vibration whose nature is self-reflective awareness (vimarśa);
that very power generates this entire world of the moving and the immobile, and it likewise withdraws it.

Thus it is said: "That very [consciousness] is her form and her power. Or rather, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—the expressive word—is her very form, being both the defining agent (*nirūpaka*) and the object to be defined (*nirūpya*) of this [power]. As it has been stated in the *Mātṛkā-viveka*:
"Without the expressive reflective awareness, what indeed could be manifested?"
Or rather, what could even be reflected upon without the manifestation of the expressible?
Therefore, reflective awareness requires manifestation for its vibration;
and manifestation, in turn, requires reflective awareness for its own cognition.

Thus, it is called *vidyā* because its essential nature is the knowledge that bestows liberation; for the *Devīmāhātmya* states: "She is indeed that blessed one, the supreme goddess, who is *vidyā*. Likewise, there is the *Gauḍapādīya-sūtra*: "That very [power] is *vidyā*.
Here, by the word *tat*, the power (*śakti*) whose nature is consciousness is referred to, as it was introduced in the preceding sūtra.
It is discernment (*parāmarśa*), or it consists of a specific aspect of the power residing in *tejas*. Its definition is given in the Śaiva Tantra:
"That by which one knows the state of *vidyā* through the discrimination of the effects of *māyā*."
That supreme digit (kalā) is to be known as Vidyā, whose nature consists of knowledge and action.
Thus [it is said]. That from which the world—of which ether (viyat) and space (vyoman) are the first—is produced, according to such Vedic texts as "From the Self, space was born.
It is the pacifier of all diseases and the warder-off of all death. 163.

It is the pacifier and the cause of destruction for all diseases, such as fever and the like; it wards off all forms of death, including untimely death and death at the appointed time. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "Having known the God, one is liberated from the jaws of death. || 163 ||

Foremost, of inconceivable form, and the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age. She is "foremost" (agra-gaṇyā) because, being the root cause of the entire universe, she is worthy of being reckoned first;
that is, she is to be counted at the beginning. Alternatively, she is "foremost" and she is "to be reckoned" (gaṇyā), meaning she possesses the status of being counted.

The suffix *pratyaya* is used here in the sense of "having obtained" (labdha) a multitude of riches (*dhanagaṇa*). Because she is devoid of contact with [worldly] qualities (*guṇa*), her form is inconceivable (*acintya*), meaning it is impossible to conceive. Since the excess of impurity (*kalmaṣa*) is inevitable in the Kali age, she alone effects its destruction, which cannot be accomplished by any other means.
Thus it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Water is sufficient for the quenching of fire; the rising of the sun is for the dispelling of darkness;
and the chanting of the names of the Goddesses is for the pacification of the flood of sins in the Kali age."
For every sin committed, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
the remembrance of the feet of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) is declared to be the supreme expiation.
Thus it is also stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Kātyāyanī is the destroyer of Time (Death) and is worshipped by Kamalākṣa. (164)
*Kata* is the name of a sage; his female descendant is *Kātyā*, formed by the suffix *yañ* according to the rule for the *garga*-class.
From that, the suffix *ṣpha* is applied according to the rule "after *lohita* and those ending in *kaṇṭha*," etc. Because it has the marker *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added.
This is the name of the Goddess, who consists of the aggregate of the splendor of all the gods. As it has been said:
In the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"And that great, excellent, and supreme splendor became renowned on earth by the name [of the goddess];
she then shone as Kātyāyanī, and by that very name she became famous throughout the world."
Thus [it is said]. And she is the one who presides over the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Oḍyāna. As it is stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Kātyāyanī is in Oḍḍiyāna; Kāmākhyā is in Kāmarūpaka;
Pūrṇeśvarī is in Pūrṇagiri; and Caṇḍī is remembered as being in Jālandhara."
Thus it is said. However, in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Ka is declared to be Brahman, Ka is the head, and Ka is considered to be iron;
because of her bearing [these] or because of her dwelling [within them], she is therefore regarded as Kātyāyanī."
Thus it has been said. She is the destroyer of Time (Kāla), that is, Death; for the Śruti declares: "The Knower is the Time of time, the possessor of qualities, the all-knowing.
She is constantly served and worshipped by Kamalākṣa, Viṣṇu. And it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Viṣṇu always worships the Goddess made of sapphire (indranīla)."
By that, he attained the state of Viṣṇu.
And so forth. || 164 ||
Her mouth was filled with betel, and she possessed the luster of a pomegranate flower.

"Whose mouth is filled with betel" (*tāmbūlena pūritaṃ mukhaṃ yasyāḥ*). There exists a particular kind of tree, devoid of fruit and possessing only flowers, which possesses the genus-property (*jāti*) pervaded by the state of being a pomegranate (*dāḍimītva*).
She whose radiance is like that of a flower;

Mṛgākṣī (deer-eyed); Mohinī (the Enchantress), who is preeminent; Mṛḍānī (the Consort of Śiva)—she whose eyes are like those of a deer. She is called Mohinī because she deludes [the mind]. As it has been said:
In the *Laghunāradīya Purāṇa*:
"O beautiful one, because this entire world has been deluded by you,
your name shall be 'Mohinī' (The Enchantress), arising from your own quality."

Thus it is said. Alternatively, that form of Mohinī which Viṣṇu assumed during the churning for the nectar (amṛtamathana) has manifested here through the contemplation of non-difference from her, residing in Nivāsapura on the bank of the river Pravarā. As it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
In the beginning, Śakti appeared from the meditative yoga of Brahmā;
she is known by the name Prakṛti, the bestower of desired success upon the gods.
A second form appeared as the churning for the nectar of immortality proceeded—
a form that produced universal delusion and was beyond the reach of speech and mind.
"By the sight of which even the Lord, though omniscient, was deluded," and so forth.
In that very same work, in another chapter, introducing the form of Mohinī:
"The non-dual and wonderful form which was obtained through the power of meditation..."
Having meditated upon her alone with undistracted mind, he smiled slightly.

And so forth. "Mukhyā" means that which exists at the very beginning, at the mouth [of creation]; for the Śruti says, "I am the first-born of the Cosmic Order (Ṛta). From the *Śivarahasya*: "Obeisance, obeisance to Mṛḍā, who brings happiness to beings when there is an abundance of Sattva; she is the wife of the supreme Śiva, who is Mṛḍa, the bestower of happiness. Thus is the meaning.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied when distinguished by a subsequent vowel (*ānugāgama*), as in *mitrarūpiṇī*. || 165 ||
Her form is like that of the suns of Mitra; or, she is the very embodiment of a friend. 165.
Eternally satisfied, a treasure-trove for devotees, the controller, the sovereign of all;

eternally—that is, at all times—satisfied, or satisfied by the bliss of her own essential nature. She is like a treasure-trove for devotees because she fulfills their desires. Here, there is not even a partial [lack of fulfillment]; salutations to the Treasure-trove.
Such is the application [of the term]. She is the Controller because she governs the world;

she is the Sovereign (Īśvarī) of the entire, complete phenomenal universe (prapañca). She is attainable through the latent impressions (vāsanā) of friendliness and other virtues, and she is the witness of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). || 166 ||

There are four latent dispositions (*vāsanās*), namely: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Loving-kindness is established toward those who are happy, compassion toward those who suffer, sympathetic joy toward those who are meritorious, and equanimity toward those who are wicked;
these are well known in the *Viṣṇubhāgavata*. These [four] are the purifiers of the mind.
As it has been said by the learned:
"Those who know how to cultivate the mind through friendliness and so forth, having abandoned the afflictions here and attained yoga with its seed,"
And having attained the discernment of the difference between the intellect (*sattva*) and the person (*puruṣa*),
those who maintain meditative absorption desire to suppress even that [discernment].

Thus it is said. And likewise, the *Yogasūtra* also states: "The clarification of the mind results from cultivating friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward those who possess happiness, suffering, virtue, and vice.
Here, according to the *Rājamārtaṇḍa*, words such as "happiness" and so forth denote those who possess such qualities.

She is attainable through the four latent impressions beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Since even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others are destroyed during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) in the cosmic dance of Paramaśiva, she alone is the witness thereof. And it has been said:
Of the Lord Khaṇḍaparaśu, the Supreme Bhairava, who performs the cosmic dance fashioned by the withdrawal of the aeons,
[who is armed] with noose, goad, sugarcane bow, and flower-arrows;
That singular form of yours stands as the witness to your victory.
Thus, even in the *Gurukalā*:
"Even those such as Surendra, Rudra, Padmaja, and Acyuta are subject to death; their wives do not even touch the status of a married housewife (*suvāsinī*)."
Behold this bride, most auspicious, who is the witness to Maheśvara, the devourer of death; come together and look upon her.
Thus [ends the section]. 166.
The Supreme Power (Parāśakti) is the ultimate goal, whose form is a mass of pure consciousness.
Within the body, the tenth constituent element (dhātu) is called the Supreme Power. As it is stated in the Kāmikāgama:
"The elements of skin, blood, flesh, fat, and bone have their root in Śakti."
The elements of marrow, semen, vital breath, and life-force have Śiva as their root.
This body consists of nine elements and arises from nine sources;
the tenth element alone is declared to be the Supreme Power (Parāśakti).
Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, "parā" means the most excellent power (*śakti*). Its excellence arises precisely from its nature as pure power (*śaktimātra-svarūpatva*);
the lengthening of the vowel [in *parā*] is observed even in other cases. As the Śruti states: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold. It is also stated in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
Whatever power is proclaimed to belong to whichever object, that very power is the Goddess Viśveśvarī; every capable being is Maheśvara.
Those entities that possess power are indeed all manifestations;
the wise know those various powers of entities to be Gaurī.

Thus, the supreme culmination (*parā niṣṭhā*) is the highest completion, consisting of a specific form of knowledge (*jñānaviśeṣarūpā*), because all actions and the entire world find their completion in this alone. And it is said in the *Gītā*: "O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge. And that specific knowledge—
It is stated in the Sūtagītā:

"Having firmly ascertained the Self through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, and by means of reasonings that conform to the scriptures, as the witness of all, one becomes perfectly steady."
Having realized that everything appearing as something other than one's own self is, in fact, without distinction,
and is nothing but one's own self, one then realizes one's own non-dual self.
Having ascertained for oneself through one's own experience that Brahman is pure,
one should dissolve that very ascertainment into one's own non-dual, changeless pure consciousness.
Having realized that the process of dissolution is itself the nature of consciousness,
this preeminent sage, a knower of Brahman, should abide as the manifest reality in its absolute state.
Such is this supreme culmination of the Vedic path, consisting of one's own direct experience.
Thus: "Salutation to Parā Śakti," and "Salutation to Parā Niṣṭhā"—such is the formulation.

This is because, as in the case of "To Agni Pavamāna, this [offering]," the use of the dative case in both instances is established by logical rule (*nyāya*). As it is said: "We bow to the friend of Parā Śakti, the five-faced one."

According to the application [found] in the works of the venerable Bhagavatpāda, if there is only one word, then "parāśaktyai namaḥ" (salutation to the Supreme Power) should be employed. The meaning is that she is of the nature of that power which belongs to the mantra. She is dense (*ghana*) with supreme, eternal knowledge that is distinct from the [ordinary] functions [of the mind].

Its nature is untouched even by a trace of ignorance, without interruption. And thus it is heard among the Kaṇvas: "Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a single mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a single mass of consciousness."
She is intoxicated and languid from drinking honey-wine, and her form is composed of the letters of the alphabet. || 167 ||

The word *mādhvī*, like the word *paripanthin*, is used even in common parlance despite being Vedic; [thus it is said]: "Alas, O dull-witted ones, how can you resort to both the *mādhvī* and the *gauḍī* intoxicants—delusive, censured by the virtuous, and destroyers of one's own nature as Brahman—as if they were a path?"
Thus, by this [rule], just as in the case of *paripanthi* and *pariparin*,

the portion of the sūtra stating "the words *ṛtvyavat*, *vāstvyavat*, *vāstvam*, *mādhvī*, and *hiraṇyaya* are used in the Veda" (*chandasi*) should also be interpreted as referring to a combination with the common language (bhāṣā) based on usage, even though it is a part of a single sūtra.

Or, even if this is Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), it is not faulty here. She is languid from drinking *mādhvī*—wine produced from grapes—and cool due to her exclusive focus on the inner self; for this very reason, she is as if intoxicated (*matteva*), or else, the word *mat* signifies "I," and *mattā* is the state of that.
The meaning is that her form is the supreme *ahantā* (I-consciousness) established in Paraśiva. *Mātṛkā* refers to the letters from *a* to *kṣa*;

their "colors" (*varṇa*) are forms such as white and so forth, and these alone constitute her form (*rūpa*), that is, her essential nature (*svarūpa*). And those [colors] are described in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*:
The vowels beginning with *a* are smoke-colored; those beginning with *ka* have the luster of vermilion; those from *ḍa* to *pha* are fair-complexioned; the five beginning with *ba* are reddish;
those beginning with *la* have the luster of gold; and the two ending with *ha* resemble lightning.
Thus it is said. However, in another tantra:
"The vowels are said to have the luster of crystal; the *sparśa* consonants resemble coral;
the nine letters beginning with *ya* are yellow; and the letter *kṣa* is considered to be reddish."

Thus [it is said]. In some places, it is also stated that "all phonemes (varṇas) are white. However, in the *Mātṛkā-viveka*, specific colors for each individual phoneme are described, beginning with: "The letter 'A' belongs to all deities and is red, bringing everything under control," and so forth. Alternatively, there are simply fifty-one phonemes of the Mātṛkā.
"Her form is this. Alternatively, it means that phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves are her forms, as they are the defining and expressive [elements] of her.
As it is said in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*:
"Just as Śambhu, the Supreme, is twofold by way of the nature of Śakti and Śiva..."
In that very same way, the goddess Mātṛkā herself became divided into two.
The Vācikā of Śakti consists of a single form, whereas that of Śiva consists of the other; this is the Vidyā belonging to Śiva, which directly leads to the state of the Padas.
Thus, the meaning that the letters beginning with *a* denote Śrīkaṇṭha and others, as well as Pūrṇodarī and others, has been stated in its commentary.
Alternatively, she is of the nature of the rosary (*akṣamālā*). And it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
The letter *a* is the first goddess, and the letter *kṣa* is the last thereafter;
she is renowned as the "Garland of Letters" (*akṣamālā*), having the form of the phonemes of the Mātṛkā.
"This [reality], whose nature is the Śabdabrahman, is chanted as that which transcends sound.
Thus, it is called *mātṛkā* because it measures (*mimīte*) or generates (*janayati*) the phonemes.
This is the manner in which the phonemes arise through the sequence beginning with yoga, by means of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) of Śiva, who is known as Anuttara.

This should be seen in the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*. That the phonemes of the *mātṛkā* themselves constitute the nature of the *śrīcakra* has been explained in detail in the sixth chapter of the *Mātṛkāviveka*.
For this very reason, the realization of the identity between the *mātṛkā* and the *cakra* is taught in the *Sanandanasaṃhitā*.
The two names "Kailāsaprastāra" (meaning "having such a form," as it is so designated) and "Pracaṇḍājñā" (the fierce command)—

accepting the identity between these two names which will be mentioned later— and also because of the etymological definition found in the *Devīpurāṇa* stating that she is the "Mātṛkā" due to the birth of Skanda, [the text] provides the two names "Mātṛkā" and "Avarṇarūpiṇī" (she whose form is the letter 'a').
Easy to speak with. || 167 ||
She whose abode is Mahākailāsa, and whose creeper-like arms are as soft as lotus stalks.
"Mahākailāsa" is the name of a world situated far beyond Kailāsa, renowned in the Śiva Purāṇa and other texts as the dwelling place of Paramaśiva.

Kailāsa is the specific state of meditating on non-difference as previously described by name; or, according to the *Tripurāsāra*, Kailāsa is the thousand-petalled lotus located at the *brahmarandhra*, for it is said there: "The God of gods resides in this station named Kailāsa, which is the partless station (*akalapa-da*), whose nature is the *bindu*."

She is "Great" (*mahān*) because she is superior to other arrangements (*prastāra*), namely those known as identity with all thunderbolts and so forth, and non-identity with the eternal. She has that very [Great One] as her abode (*nilaya*). Her creeper-like arms are as soft as a lotus fiber (*mṛṇāla*), which is a lotus stalk.
She is the venerable embodiment of compassion, endowed with a great empire. || 168 ||

She is "mahanīyā" (worthy of worship) because she is to be honored; she is one whose very form and nature is compassion itself; she is "tacchālinī," endowed with that great sovereignty which is the lordship over Mahākailāsa. 168.
Ātmavidyā (the knowledge of the Self) is Mahāvidyā (the Great Knowledge), the Śrīvidyā, which is served by Kāma.

It is called Ātmavidyā because its nature is the knowledge of the Self, or because it takes the form of the eight-syllable mantra of the Self. These indeed are the Mahāvidyās; they are both great and knowledge.

Its greatness arises from its being the warder-off of all misfortunes. Furthermore, the name "Mahāvidyā" (Great Knowledge) applies to the Navadurgā-vidyā as well, or it refers to that very form. Śrīvidyā is the essential nature of the Pañcadaśī.
And it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:

O beautiful one, you are the science of sacrifice, the great science, and the secret science; O Goddess, you are the science of the Self that bestows the fruit of liberation. You alone are Ānvīkṣikī, the Triple Veda, commerce, and the science of government.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding this, the commentators state: the meaning of the four terms for "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is as follows: the knowledge of ritual action (*karma-vidyā*), the worship of Viśvarūpa and others; the knowledge of mantras (*mantra-vidyā*); and the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-vidyā*). "Trade" (*vārtā*) refers to the sciences of crafts, medicine, and so forth; "the science of government" (*daṇḍanīti*) refers to royal policy. "Desire" (*kāma*)...
She is the Mahākāmeśvarī, served and worshipped by him; or rather, she is the one sewn (sevitā) by Kāma, the bodiless one (*anaṅga*).
For the lexicon states: "Serving (*sevana*) is sewing (*syūti*). And it is heard in the Āruṇika Upaniṣad: "The son of Nirṛti was the Vaideha; he who was both mindless and conscious found that jewel."
He was without fingers because he lacked limbs; he was without a neck because he could not turn his head; he was without a tongue because he could not speak.

One should not enter a city having failed to recognize this seer (ṛṣi). If one should enter, one should do so by moving about in secret. This is the vow of Saṃbhava. He was the son of Nirṛti and Lakṣmī, the Videha from Videha, the bodiless one.

Manmatha, being bodiless (*anaṅga*), was indeed insentient and devoid of eyes, fingers, neck, and tongue; yet, though blind, he found the jewel that is the treasure of knowledge (*vidyāratna*). Then he joined it together, sewed it, and subsequently wore it upon his neck and tasted it. Because he perceived this mantra, he alone is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Of him—

In the city of Jñānottara, there is entry into the external wheel (*bāhyacakre*). Since the ostentation of worship is useless and because the task has already been accomplished, it need not be performed. If, however, there is a desire for worship in every respect, then one should perform it after realizing the state of union (*mithunībhāva*), which consists of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti.

The meaning of the scripture is that this very state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) is the most profound vow for the god of love (*manmatha*) who arises from the mind. The intended sense is that worship performed without realizing the equilibrium of Śiva and Śakti does not bear fruit in such a manner.
The venerable sixteen-syllable vidyā is the Trikūṭā, the pinnacle of desire. || 169 ||

The collection of sixteen syllables is the "sixteen-syllabled" (*ṣoḍaśākṣarī*). It is "endowed with Śrī" (*śrīyuktā*) and it is also that "Vidyā," hence [the term] *tathā*. Although the *Gauḍapādīya-sūtra* is also read as being characterized by twenty-eight syllables including the *avidyā*, [this refers to a different recension].

Nevertheless, there is no contradiction, as the intention is to count by dividing the three peaks (*kūṭa*) therein according to their form as fifteen syllables. Alternatively, it may mean "that which possesses the sixteenth syllable, *Śrī*," and is thus the *vidyā*. [This refers to] that which is included within the *Gaurī* group and so forth.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because the *pippalyādi* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). It is that in which there is a *kūṭa*, meaning a collection or aggregate, of the three—namely Brahmā and the others, or of the states (*avasthā*), seats (*pīṭha*), worlds (*loka*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth;
or it is non-different from the three *kūṭas* beginning with Vāgbhava. *Kāma* is indeed Paraśiva himself.
That which has the "peak" (koṭi) as its one part is indeed the Kāmakoṭikā, because it is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, the state of essential identity between Śiva and Śakti. || 169 ||
Served by millions of Lakṣmīs who have become her maidservants through her sidelong glances;

that is, she is served by millions of Lakṣmīs who have become servants of her glance—the casting of a portion of the eye—by which even a slight look [is bestowed]. Upon whomsoever there is such a slight look...
The intended meaning is that the Lakṣmīs choose [him] beyond the highest limit (parārdha).
She who resembles the moon is situated on his head; she whose splendor is like Indra’s bow is situated on his forehead. (170)
She resides in the form of the Guru at the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā) on the head.

With the intention that there is a moon below the *brahmarandhra* and that it consists of the third peak (*kūṭa*) of Vidyā, he says: "The streak on the forehead, resembling the moon, abides in the form of a point (*bindu*)."
She resides on the forehead; to indicate that she stands above that in the form of a half-moon, it says:
"having the radiance of a rainbow. And it is said in the *Nityāhṛdaya*:
"The form of a lamp, consisting of a half-measure, is desired as being circular on the forehead."
Its form is like a half-moon, and above that, it measures one foot.
Thus [ends the section]. || 170 ||

"Abiding in the heart" (*hṛdayasthā*) means she dwells in the heart as the object of meditation; or else, the supreme seed-syllable (*parābīja*) is called the "heart. For one who knows the heart of the Lord, there are joys at every step.
This is because of its usage in the *Kalpasūtra*. Alternatively, she is called "Hṛdaya" (Heart) precisely because of the Upaniṣad named *Parameśvarahṛdaya*;

therein she abides either as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) or as the object to be realized. Or else, since the Heart is the seed of the entire universe, she resides there in the form of the universe itself.
As it is said in the *Anuttara-triṃśikā-śāstra*:
"Just as the great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of the banyan,
so too does this entire world of moving and non-moving beings exist within the seed of the Heart."
"Resplendent like the sun, a lamp within the triangle.

With the intention that there exists a solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*) in the heart, and that this is the second peak (*kūṭa*) of the Vidyā, he says: "resplendent like the sun. The words *nibha* and *prakhya* [are used here].
Furthermore, here the third and second peaks also refer to non-difference because of their non-distinction from that [first peak];

for we observe the conventional usage, "A person like me," with respect to oneself alone, or as in the expression, "possessing a luster equal to the sun. [This occurs] in the center of the pericarp of the *mūlādhāra* lotus.
There is a triangle; within that is the circle of fire (agnimaṇḍala), and that has the nature of the first *kūṭa*.
This he states: "In the interior—that is, in the middle—of the triangle is the lamp-like [light], meaning it is non-different from that.
As it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
In the center of the *mūlādhāra* of all living beings, there is the fire that has arisen as both eternal and non-eternal; likewise, in their hearts, there is the sun.
The moon is situated at the crown, below the aperture of Brahmā;
that which consists of these three is indeed the primordial Nityā, the Trikhaṇḍā.

Thus [ends the previous point]. Alternatively, he points out the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), unifying— by means of an identification based on *śleṣa* (punning coalescence)— the two properties residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), which are in fact distinct, with the aforementioned state of being equal to the sun.

Regarding the term "triangle" (*trikoṇa*): in the case of the Goddess, the application is exactly as previously stated. In the case of the Sun, it is as follows: while circumambulating Meru, the Sun illuminates only three corners at a time of Meru, which consists of eight corners. For instance, when the Sun is at midday in the city of Indra (Indraloka).

The setting and rising [of the sun] occur in the northern and southern cities respectively. Thus, it illuminates precisely these three cities situated as the three corners. As for the northeast and southeast corners, since they fall within the middle of the line of the triangle, their illumination follows by implication. At that time, it is the third watch (yāma) in the northeast; however, in the southeast—

The first watch [of the night]. In this way, it illuminates the three cardinal directions and, by virtue of being situated in the center, the two intermediate directions as well. When it is midday in the city of Agni (the southeast), there is sunset in that very place and sunrise in the city of Nirṛti (the southwest).
In the cities of Indra (the east) and Yama (the south), it is the third and first watches respectively. Thus, it exists as a configuration of three hexagons.

It illuminates the three intermediate directions and the two cardinal directions situated at the positions of their respective lines. In this manner, it should be understood for the cities of Yama and the others during the time of midday. As it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Abiding in the city of Śakra and the other gods, he touches three cities."
Two triangles are situated within a hexagon, and likewise three triangles are within two squares.
Thus: there is one corner situated at its own [center], two corners—its own right and left—and likewise three corners;

and within them, in the middle thereof, it illuminates—that is, makes manifest—the five cities consisting of its own right and left lines situated in that center. Therefore, it is called the *Trikonantaradipika* (the Illuminator of the Interior of the Triangle).
The daughter of Dakṣa, the slayer of the Daityas, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. || 171 ||

She is the daughter of Dakṣa, hence *Dākṣāyaṇī*; the suffix *ṣpha* is applied here because she belongs to the *lohita*-class. Alternatively, she takes the form of Aśvinī and the other lunar mansions; for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *dākṣāyaṇī* refers to Aparṇā, Rohiṇī, and the stars.
Or, she is of the nature of the *Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña*, which is the term used for the repeated performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
She is the slayer of the Daityas, such as Bhaṇḍāsura and others. Dakṣa is of two kinds:
one is well-known as a Prajāpati, and the other is a human king, who is a specific incarnation of the former.
It is her nature to destroy the sacrifice of both; the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

Even though the destruction of the sacrifice was brought about by Śiva, the Goddess is designated as the agent because she served as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*). This is stated in the *Brahma-purāṇa* and the *Vāyu-purāṇa*:
"Having addressed the Seven Sages, he then cursed Dakṣa."
"You shall become a human king in the lineage of Cākṣuṣa."
"You shall be born as the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of Pracetas,
by the name of Dakṣa, in the womb of Māriṣā."
When the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara arrives, during the reign of Kanyā and the presence of the Śākhins,
I shall likewise destroy your sacrifice there out of a desire to do what is pleasing to the Goddess.

Thus: if the penultimate vowel here is read as *a*, then [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is added to the word *vināśana*, which ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*; however, if the reading is *i*, it is from a word ending in the suffix *ṇini*. In this same manner, it should be inferred in other cases as well. || 171 ||
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Bhāskararāya,
the seventh digit, Suṣumṇā, was completed with the six hundredth verse.
Thus ends the seventh digit, named the sixth century, in the commentary on the *Lalitāsahasranāma* entitled the *Śrīsaubhāgyabhāskara*. 7.
The eighth digit, named Saptakaśataka, bestows enjoyment; her long eyes tremble slightly, and her face is radiant with a gentle smile—
where "dara" means slightly, such that they are thus slightly trembling and restless.

She whose eyes rest as far as the tips of her ears; or rather, she whose long eyes have dispelled— meaning shaken, made unstable, and destroyed— fear (*dara*), such that fear is eliminated by the mere casting of a sidelong glance.
She whose face shines with a radiant, gentle smile;
she who is the venerable form, a treasury of virtues, the mother of the cows (Gomātā), and the birthplace of Guha (Guhanmabhū). 172.
The Guru is her very form—that is, her body. Therefore, it is heard in the *Sundarītāpinī*:
"Just as 'ghaṭa', 'kalaśa', and 'kumbha' are synonyms denoting the same object, so too are the mantra, the deity, and the Guru synonyms denoting the same reality."

Thus [it is said]. The etymology of the word *guru* is also given in the *Śaktirahasya*: "The letter *gu* signifies darkness (*andhakāra*), and the letter *ru* signifies that which removes it. It is stated elsewhere as well:
"The syllable *gu* is declared to mean 'existent' (*sat*), and the syllable *ru* denotes knowledge (*jñāna*)."
Because his nature is solely that of the knowledge of Brahman, he is designated as a guru.
Thus, it is stated in the *Nityāhṛdaya* as well: "One should contemplate that Goddess, whose form is desire, in the form of the Guru.

[The term] *śevadhiḥ* means a treasure-store of qualities (*guṇānām*). The suffix *ki* is applied here according to the rule "after a verbal root, when denoting the object or the location" (*karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca*).
Although the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth are threefold by virtue of their universals (*jāti*) such as *sattvatva*, there is an infinity of individual instances (*vyakti*).
This is according to the Sāṃkhya tenet. For this very reason, the Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra states:
"The mutual similarity and dissimilarity of the *guṇas* is established through their qualities such as lightness and so forth; and although *sattva* and the others are substances (*dravya*),..."
They are called "qualities" (*guṇa*) because they are the instruments of the Person (*puruṣa*). She is either the treasury of such qualities;

or rather, she is one whose number of treasuries consists of the qualities in the form of the manifestations (*vyūha*). That is to say, she possesses the quality of having the nature of the ninefold manifestation. As they say: "The [Lord] consists of the ninefold manifestation."
"The God is supreme bliss, whose nature is the Supreme.
Likewise, there is the array of time (kālavyūha), the array of the Kula (kulavyūha), and the array of names (nāmavyūha);
thereafter, there shall be the array of knowledge (jñānavyūha) and the array of the mind (cittavyūha).

The array of sound (nādavyūha), then the array of the point (binduvyūha), followed by the array of the ritual procedure (kalpāvyūha) and the array of the individual soul (jīvavyūha); thus, these are the nine.

And so it is said. These characteristics were explained at length by Lalla on the occasion of commenting on the verse beginning with "situated in your *ājñācakra*," in his *Saundaryalaharī*. Alternatively, *guṇa* means a rope;
here, it refers metaphorically to the boat-tether known as a *vaṭīrikā*. That [rope] is thoroughly...
It is called a "treasury of qualities" (guṇanidhi) because all things are deposited within it. Indeed, this story is recorded in both the *Matsya Purāṇa* and the *Kālī Purāṇa*:

at the time of universal dissolution (pralaya), Manu, following the command of the Blessed Lord, placed all the seeds and the sages upon a boat, and [the boat] was [secured] to the horn of the Blessed One in his Fish-incarnation (matsyāvatāra).
The boat was bound with a rope; that rope, being presided over by Ambā, attained firmness. As it has been said:
"It was nine yojanas long and well-spread across three yāmas."
Quickly prepare a large pit for the hide with bricks.
The sustainer of the world, the Great Illusion, the Mother of the World, who is identical with the universe—
she will make that rope so firm that it shall not break.

Thus, by the words of Viṣṇu addressed to Manu; and in another passage of that same work: "Yoganidrā, the sustainer of the world, sat upon a banyan tree. She is the mother of cows and milch-cows, appearing in the form of Surabhi. Other meanings of the word *go*, such as speech (*vāk*) and so forth, which are possible, should also be understood. And so it is said:
The word *viśva* is recorded as meaning heaven, a bull, a ray of light, a thunderbolt, and the moon;
while *gauḥ* is considered to mean collyrium, an eye, a direction, an arrow, the earth, speech, and water.

Thus [it is said]. And the *Anekārthadhvanimañjarī* states: "The word *go* denotes an arrow, speech, an animal, the earth, a direction, a ray, water, the eye, heaven, a mother, a thunderbolt, fire, a mouth, and truth."

Thus [it is said]. "The birthplace of Guha" means the place of origin of Skanda; or alternatively, from the verbal root *guh* (to conceal), "guhā" refers to living beings (*jīva*) who are concealed by ignorance (*avidyā*), and it is their place of birth, according to such Vedic texts as: "Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire," and so on. The *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* also states:
Just as sparks fly forth from a glowing mass of iron,
even so do selves indeed emerge from the Self.
Thus [ends the verse]. || 172 ||

The Goddess is the sovereign (īśī) and mistress (īśvarī) of the gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; she abides in the science of governance (daṇḍanīti), that is, in the treatises on statecraft (arthaśāstra). Thus, she is the very Goddess who makes known the principles taught in the science of ethics (nītiśāstra).
To that effect, it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Because it establishes people who have strayed into right and wrong courses within non-discrimination,
and because it punishes or subdues them, it is traditionally known as Daṇḍanīti (the Science of Punishment)."

Thus [it is said]. The small (dahara) space residing within the cavity of the heart is her very form. This is established in the section of the Uttara-mīmāṃsā [Brahma-sūtra] beginning with "The small [space], because of the subsequent [texts]" (1.3.14), which states: "Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus..."
For the Śruti states, "In this small abode is the inner space; that which is within it is to be sought," thereby establishing that the *daharākāśa* (the small space) alone is the Supreme Brahman.
She is worshipped by the assembly of lunar days (*tithi*) presided over by the primary moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight.

She is worshipped in that cycle of lunar days— that collection of fifteen tithis— in which the primary day is the first (the new moon) and the final day is the full moon (rākā). Since the tantras state that there are different modes of worship according to the specific lunar day, the meaning is that she is honored through such particular varieties of ritual.
Alternatively, the words *pratipad* and *rākā* refer to Kāmeśvarī and Citrā respectively, while the word *tithi* refers to Nityā.

Thus, she is worshipped by the circle of Nityās and surrounded by the form of the three lines of the triangle. Or else, it refers to those deities whose lunar days (*tithis*) begin with *pratipad* and end with *rākā*.
She was worshipped by the *maṇḍala*, that is, by the assembly. And regarding them, it is said in the *Varāha Purāṇa*:
"O great sage, how did the birth of Agni, or of the two Aśvins, or of Gaurī, Gaṇapati, the Nāgas, or Guha come about?"
And [the worship] of Āditya, of the Mothers, or likewise of Durgā, of the Quarters,
as well as of Dhanada, Viṣṇu, Dharma, or Parameṣṭhin.
O Sage, how did these deities come to possess embodied forms within the body of Śambhu, or of the ancestors, or likewise of the Moon?

Furthermore, O Sage, what is their food, what are their names, and what is their lunar day? To this question, the origins of Agni and the others are described in sequence as the presiding deities of the lunar days (tithis), beginning with the first day (pratipad), across sixteen chapters. Here, the word *parameṣṭhin*— [The text continues: ...refers to Brahmā. Furthermore, regarding the question "What is their food?", it is said that their food consists of the oblations offered by those who perform sacrifices according to the rules. Regarding the question "What are their names?", they are known as the *Tithidevatās* (deities of the lunar days). Regarding the question "What is the lunar day?", it is explained that each deity presides over a specific lunar day in succession. Thus, the generation of Agni and the other deities is recounted through these sixteen chapters. In this context, the term *parameṣṭhin*...
It is merely a qualification. For this very reason, it is also stated in the *Kādima-tantra*:
"Fire, the two Aśvins, Umā, Vighna, Bhujaṅga, Ṣaṇmukha, Ravi, the Mothers, as well as Durgā, the Quarters (the Lokapālas), Dhanada, and Keśava."
"Yama, Hara, and Śaśin are proclaimed as the lords of the lunar days (tithīśas).

In that [system], the new moon (amāvāsyā) is counted in the fifteenth position and the full moon (pūrṇimā) in the sixteenth; however, here the distinction is that the full moon alone (rākā) is the fifteenth. But in the present context, there is no such distinction.
All sixteen deities mentioned by Vārāha are concealed. || 173 ||
She whose nature consists of the arts (kalā), who is the mistress of the arts, and who delights in poetic discourse;
here, by the word "arts" (kalā), there are the ten arts of Fire, the twelve arts of the Sun, and the sixteen arts of the Moon, according to their enumeration as sixty-four.
These are well-known. Other arts (kalās) are also included: "Arising, waking, awareness, and the constant withdrawal of the mind—this fourfold set of arts is established in the waking state."
"When awake, she is said to possess all qualities, yet she is purely of the nature of power (śakti). Likewise:
"Death, forgetfulness, fainting, and sleep are likewise enveloped by it."
In the state of deep sleep, these digits are to be known; they are all essentially composed of the Śrī-kalā.
Likewise: "Desire, delusion, anxiety, and recollection regarding sense objects—
this group of four arts, O Goddess, is designated as the state of dreaming."
Those digits (kalās), whose nature is Śiva and whose nature is Śakti, are of the essence of Tripura.
Likewise:
detachment, the desire for liberation, and the mind purified by meditative absorption (samādhi).
The determination of existence and non-existence, and these states of the fourth (turya)—these are the kalās.
In the section on the *dūtī-yāga*, sixteen *kāmakalās* are mentioned;

in the section on the *antaradūtī*, the sixteen *kalās* of the Śrīvidyā are mentioned. Likewise, there are certain *kalās* belonging individually to the *bindu*, *ardhacandra*, *rodhinī*, and so forth.
The meaning is that she possesses the nature of all such *kalās* as described in the *Svacchandabhairava* and other scriptures;
she is the mistress and sovereign of these *kalās*. Alternatively, since the lunar orb is of the nature of the *Śrīcakra*, the meaning is that she is "in the form of the Moon. Of poems...

He especially rejoices through the recitation of specific compositions created by great poets such as Vālmīki, which are characterized by the eighteen marks of poetic excellence and distinguished by various types of dramatic forms (rūpaka); thus he is described.
Furthermore, he is served on his left and right sides by Sarasvatī, who holds a fly-whisk. 174.

He was served and fanned on his left and right respectively by Ramā and Vāṇī—that is, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī—who were accompanied by chowries, being thus possessed of those two types of chowries. || 174 ||
The Primordial Power (Ādi-śakti) is the immeasurable self, the supreme and most purifying form.
Because she is the producer of all the worlds, she is the "first" (ādi), that is, the causal source; and she is power (śakti).
She is "immeasurable" (ameyā), meaning she cannot be measured, or alternatively, she is that for whom no object of measurement exists.
The meaning is that there is no object of knowledge (*meyam*) existing apart from that [consciousness]. As it is stated in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*:

"Within the eightfold covering of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), including the worlds of heaven and the subterranean realms (*pātāla*), every object of knowledge is the form of Umā, and the knower (*mātā*) is the Lord Maheśvara."

Thus, by the word *ātman* the individual soul (*jīva*) is denoted, and following the word *parama*, the supreme self (*paramātman*) is also expressed through the application of the word *ātman*; thus it is spoken of by these two names. And it is said in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"Just as the marks of Viṣṇu are remembered in many ways within fire..."
All individual souls as well as all Śivas are remembered as that Supreme Self.
Thus it is said. Also in the Śiva Purāṇa:
"The Self is his eighth form, the supreme body of Śiva;
it pervades all other forms, and therefore the universe has Śiva as its essence."

Thus, in this view, there is the employment of two names: "Salutation to the Self" (ātmane namaḥ) and "Salutation to the Supreme Self" (paramāyātmane namaḥ). Even in the case of mantras such as "Salutation to Bhava and Rudra," where the salutation occurs on both sides, [the mantra] is recited only once.

The word *ātman* functions by repeating [its application] to both the word *namaḥ* and the word *rudra*, just as it does for the word *sarva*. Alternatively, by the word *ātman*, Brahman itself is meant—
that which one attains, that which one takes, and that which one eats here among sense-objects.
And because it exists as his constant state, it is therefore proclaimed as the "self."
Because of this statement, the word "self" (ātman) refers to the body alone. And so it is stated in the Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga:
"All bodies of embodied beings are forms of Gaurī;
likewise, all embodied beings are established as portions of Śaṅkara."

Thus, other meanings stated in the *Viśvaprakāśa*—namely, that the self (*ātman*) [is so called] in relation to the body, the mind, Brahman, inherent nature (*svabhāva*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—should also be applied here, based on such statements as: "The Goddess who resides in all beings in the form of intellect. Furthermore, [the term *ātman* may be derived from] "that which measures" (*māti*) or "that which delimits" (*paricchinatti*) the Supreme Brahman.

*Paramā*: either the *mā* (splendor) of the supreme *para* (Śiva), or else, because the Supreme Brahman possesses four forms, she is *paramā*, meaning most excellent. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"O twice-born ones, the first form of the Supreme Brahman is Puruṣa..."
Likewise, others are the Manifest and the Unmanifest, as well as Form and Time as the supreme.
That which is indeed the supreme among primordial matter, the individual soul, the manifest, and time—
that pure state which the wise perceive is the highest step of Viṣṇu.
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Vyakta, and Kāla, according to their respective divisions,
are the causes of the existence of the forms of persistence, creation, and dissolution.
Thus [it is said]. Her form—whether her body, her conduct, or her knowledge—is purifying (*pāvanī*), that is, a purifier (*pāvayitrī*).

And so says the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*: "Austerity (*tapas*) is the purification of the elemental self (*bhūtātman*); knowledge (*vidyā*) is the purification of the intellect (*buddhi*); and wisdom (*jñāna*) is the purification of knowledge."
The purification of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) through the knowledge of the Lord (īśvara) is considered supreme.
The mother of many millions of cosmic eggs, possessing a divine form.
She is the mother, the progenitor, of those many infinite millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*);
or alternatively, she is the one for whom there are many millions of cosmic eggs.
The meaning of the genitive case here is a relationship characterized by such things as being identified with them. Of those...
She is the mother of Virāṭ and the others.
For the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is the effect of the gross elements produced by quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), which reside within the sixteen transformations;
the one who identifies with that is called Virāṭ.
The one who identifies with the collective subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) existing within the cosmic egg is the Svarāj;
the one who identifies with the unmanifest (avyākṛta), which is the cause of both, is the Samrāj. As it has been said:
"Primarily, the Virāḍ-self identifies with the cosmic egg."
The Śruti declares that both the self-ruling (svarāṭ) and the essential nature (svarūpa) belong to the sovereign ruler (samrāṭ).

Thus: she whose *vigraha*—that is, her body (*deha*)—is divine (*divya*) and beautiful (*ramaṇīya*). Or, she whose *vigraha*—meaning battle (*raṇa*)—takes place in the divine space (*divi*, i.e., the atmosphere). Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "There too, that Caṇḍikā fought with him without support," the meaning of the word *vigraha* is either expansion (*vistāra*) or division (*pravibhāga*).
According to the Medinīkośa: "Vigraha means battle, body, expansion, and the division of two. (175)
She is *klīṃkārī*, the solitary (*kevalā*), the secret (*guhyā*), and the bestower of the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).

She is called *klīṃkārī* because she produces the seed-syllable *kāma* (the syllable *klīṃ*), or because her nature is that of the *kāma-bīja*, or because she is the consort of *klīṃkāra*, who is Śiva-Kāma. She is *kevalā* because of her solitude due to the absence of all attributes (*dharma*).
One who is liberated from that [bondage] is a *kevalin*. Alternatively, a *kevalin* is one who possesses a specific type of knowledge well-known from the *Śivasūtras*.

"Kevala" means entirety (*kārtsnya*) and the determined meaning; in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), it refers to that which possesses such [knowledge], or that which is non-different from it.

The term *kevala* occurs in the sense of a distinction of knowledge, as "the absolute" (*kevala*) in the sense of the one and the whole; it is declared as "decidedly" (*nirṇīte*) when used as an adverb, and in some cases as "deceitful" (*kuhane*).

Thus [says] the *Viśva* lexicon. Alternatively, "kevalatva" (isolation) refers to the absence of consonants consisting of the letters *ka* and *la* within the previously mentioned *kāmabīja* (seed-syllable of desire). Therefore, the meaning is that the *kāmakaletā* (the digit of desire) has the nature of the isolated *turya* (the fourth state). "If he hears this, he hears it as one devoid of form; for he does not truly know the merit of good deeds."

This is because of the Vedic revelation: "the path" (*panthām*). As for the hearing of only the vowel *ī*, it refers to hearing [the word] devoid of the letters *l* and *k*; therefore, he possesses that [path]. He does not lead one to the paths of good deeds—that is, to the worlds resulting from virtuous actions—but rather attains the world of the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*).

The ultimate meaning is that the three aims of life (*trivarga*) are attained through the mere seed of desire (*kāma*), while liberation (*mokṣa*) is attained through the mere art of desire (*kāmakalā*). He explains this very point by means of two names: *guhāṃ praviṣṭā* (entered into the cave) means "secret" (*guhyā*), which signifies that its meaning is extremely esoteric. *Kaivalya* is the state of being alone (*kevalasya bhāvaḥ*), wherein only the substratum remains.

The fifth [chapter] bestows that very state of liberation; or rather, it is her nature to bestow isolation (*kaivalya*), states, and stations. By the word *kaivalya*, one refers to the final sūtra of the Yoga Śāstra: "Isolation is the establishment of the power of consciousness in its own nature."

Liberation is said to be the nature [of the self] as it has been established. In the *Bhojarāja-vṛtti*, it is stated that "isolation (*kaivalya*) is the abiding in its own essential nature alone upon the cessation of the conformity of the cognitive power (*citiśakti*) with the fluctuations [of the mind]. By the word "state" (*pada*), the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya* is meant, because these consist of specific locations.
In this regard, the following should be understood: through meditation on symbols (*pratīka*), one attains *sālokya* (residing in the same world).

Through [meditation] without a symbol, there is *sārūpya* (attaining a similar form), which is the identity of form between the deity—distinguished by specific sovereignty as distinct from one's own self—and the worshiper. This very state is called *sārṣṭitā* (attaining equal power).

The meaning is "having attained equality. By means of the *ahaṃgraha* (the method of identifying oneself with the deity), one attains identity with the deity whose form possesses qualities (*saguṇa*) and who is the object of worship. This very state is *sāyujya* (union) for those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) who practice the duties appropriate to their own stage of life (*āśrama*).
"Proximity": "He attains union with these very deities, equality of power, and residence in the same world"—this Taittirīya Śruti is the authority for the three aforementioned types of liberation.
Regarding the fourth [type], however, there is the Maṇḍūka Śruti:
Those who dwell in the forest with austerity and faith— peaceful, wise, and practicing the way of subsistence on alms—
go, free from passion, through the gate of the sun to where that immortal Person of imperishable nature resides.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the phrase "by way of the sun," the meaning is that having traveled by the path beginning with light (*arcis*) as indicated by the sun, they go to where that Person, who is Brahman, resides in Satyaloka.
These are liberations consisting of the fruits of karma; they are impermanent and characterized by gradation. For this very reason, [the text] uses a term denoting a location...

These have been pointed out here word by word. As for liberation, known as *kaivalya*, which is the fruit of knowledge characterized by unsurpassed bliss, the *Taittirīya* Śruti itself is the authority regarding it: "He who, knowing this, dies during the northern course of the sun, having gone to the greatness of the gods, [attains] that of Āditya..."
He attains union [with them]. Now, he who dies in the south, having gone to the greatness of the ancestors, attains union with the moon and the state of being in its world.
Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa who knows this conquers these two greatnesses of the sun and the moon; therefore—

"He attains the greatness of Brahman. Here, by the phrase "by mere ritual acts," the attainment of the world of the moon is meant. By the words "he who knows thus"—referring to one who possesses the three types of meditation on the symbols and so forth denoted by the term "knower"—the phrase "the greatness of the gods" signifies the triad beginning with *sālokya* (residing in the same world). [The word] *brāhmaṇaḥ*...

By the word "the wise one" (vidvān), it is meant that one who possesses the knowledge of Brahman, having understood that these two glories of the sun and moon—attainable through ritual action and meditation—are subject to defects such as being surpassed by others, overcomes them; that is, he completely transcends them. Beyond that is the unsurpassed Brahman.
The meaning is that one attains greatness. This very point is elaborated upon in the *Śaktirahasya*:

"By worshipping [the Lord] with the intellect identifying Him as the Self, with the intellect regarding Him as a symbol (*pratīka*), with the intellect of 'I', and even through ritual action, a mortal attains the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*)."
Tripurā, who is praised by the three worlds, the embodiment of the triple form, and the sovereign of the thirty gods. || 176 ||
She is called Tripurā because she is more ancient than the three forms (*mūrti*). As it has been said:
"Because she is more ancient even than the triad of forms, the name of that Mother is Tripurā.
The Gauḍapādīya Sūtra also states: "The division [of Brahman] occurs through the three principles. Brahman is indeed one.

The meaning is that she is differentiated by means of the three principles (*tattva*). However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the word *tattva* has been explained in many ways as referring to the qualities (*guṇa*), the forms (*mūrti*), the seeds (*bīja*), the worlds (*jagat*), the seats (*pīṭha*), the sections (*khaṇḍa*), and so forth;
thus, the meaning is "in the city [located] beyond the qualities and the rest. In the *Tripurārṇava*, however—
The three channels are Tripurā—namely Suṣumṇā, Piṅgalā, and Iḍā; likewise, mind, intellect, and consciousness are declared to be the "three cities."
She dwells in each and every place; therefore, she is considered Tripurā.
Thus it has been said. Also in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, having introduced the passage beginning with "Her mandala is a triangle," it states:
"Because everything is threefold, threefold, therefore she is known as Tripurā.
[She is] the triad of the gods, the triple Veda, the three fires, the triad of powers, and the three vowels.

The three worlds, the three cities, the three Puṣkaras, the three Vedas, the three castes, and the three— the whatever in the world is regulated in a threefold manner and consists of the three aims of life—
all that truly follows the name "Tripurā" in you, O Blessed One, according to reality.

Thus it is stated in the *Laghustava*. Furthermore, in the fourth chapter of the *Pūrvacatuḥśatī*, beginning with the words "Tripurā is the supreme Śakti" and ending with "she has attained the name Tripurā," other etymologies for this name are also explained; these, however, are as follows:
Since these will be explained in this very commentary (*ṭīkā*), they should be looked for there.
Or, she is "one by whom the three worlds are to be worshipped" (*tribhir jagadbhir vandyā*); thus she is *trijagadvandyā*.
Alternatively, because she has the form of a three-year-old girl, she possesses a triple nature (*trimūrtitvam*). For it is said: "A three-year-old girl is indeed *trimūrti*."
This is because of the words of Dhaumya in the section concerning the maiden (*kanyāprakaraṇa*).
Alternatively, she may be in the form of the three *mūrtis* (embodiments) whose feet consist of the red, white, and mixed [energies].
The extraction of their respective mantras and their essential nature and so forth are clearly explained in the Tantras. Or else:

The triad of forms beginning with Brahmā, the triad beginning with Vāmā, and the triad of forms beginning with Icchā belong to her alone; thus she possesses the nature of the three forms (*trimūrtitva*). As it is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa:
"Having spoken thus, Brahmā himself gazed upon the wielder of the Pināka bow."
And the Supreme Lord remembered Nārāyaṇa in his mind.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa stood between the two;
thereafter, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara became one.
Filled with joy, they gazed at one another with subtle vision;
thereafter, their gaze indeed became threefold.
Having described her with the words, "In that vision, a maiden of divine form arose," and so forth—
then, having gazed upon that girl, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [said]:
They said, "Who are you? Tell us, O lady of pure smiles, what is your purpose?"
To this question,
that girl of the three castes— black, white, and yellow— replied:
"O best of beings, it is by the grace of the Blessed One's vision that I have been born."
"Do you not know me, O lady of beautiful hips, as your own power, the Supreme Goddess?
When this was said, Brahmā and the others were highly pleased with her and granted her supreme boons.
O Goddess, you are known by the name Trikālā; protect the universe at all times.
O sinless one, O highly fortunate lady, there will also be other names for you, arising from your qualities, which shall grant all accomplishments.
Having said this and more, he declared: "Furthermore, O Goddess, listen to that other cause which I shall speak:
O lady of beautiful countenance, you possess three colors—white, red, and black."
"O Goddess, fashion the three forms within your own body by means of the three syllables.
Thus addressed by the gods, she then assumed a threefold form.
"Having become white, red, and likewise black, she indeed attained the state of the triple form (trimūrti).

Having stated this and other such things, the performance of penance and so forth by Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī on the White Mountain, Mount Mandara, and the Blue Mountain is described. In another place as well:
This is declared to be the triple form (trimūrti), which conforms to the established conclusions of the systems;
this is the supreme Śvetā-śakti, the sattvic state of abiding in Brahman.
This very same goddess, when red, is proclaimed as Vaiṣṇavī in the quality of passion (rajas);
this very same goddess, when black, is proclaimed as Raudrī in the quality of darkness (tamas).
Just as the Supreme Self, O Lord, though one alone, exists in a threefold manner,
so too the single Power becomes threefold according to its purpose.
Thus it is said. The *Gauḍapādīya-sūtra* also states: "The *Śāmbhavī-vidyā* is dark blue (*śyāmā*). Furthermore, in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"The *Śāmbhavī* is white in form, and the *Śrīvidyā* is red in form."
Śyāmalā shall be of dark form; these are the powers of her qualities.

Thus: [it refers to] the thirty-three groups (trayastrimśad-gaṇāḥ), by way of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇayā), through the number thirty— whether of the thirty-three gods (tridaśānām devānām), or of the three times ten states (tisṛṇām vā daśānām avasthānām), or of the thirteen [states] joined with three (triyuktadaśānām trayodaśānām), or of all the gods (viśveṣām devānām) whose number is ten multiplied by three (triguṇitadaśānām).
She is the sovereign mistress. || 176 ||
*Tryakṣarī*:
the collection of three syllables consisting of the seeds of Vāk, Kāma, and Śakti.
And it is said in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*:
Vāgīśvarī is the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), the embodiment of liberation in the Vāgbhava [bīja];
Kāmeśī is the power of action (kriyāśakti), the embodiment of desire in the Kāmarāja [bīja].
Within the seed-syllable of Śakti, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) is indeed Will (Icchā) in the form of Śiva;
thus, the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī consists of three syllables.
Thus, *śuddhavidyā* is either in the form of the *kumārī-mantra*. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Gauḍapādīya*:

"The three-syllabled *śuddhavidyā* is the *kumārī*. It is of the nature of the heart (*hṛdaya*) or of the nature of truth (*satya*). This very [mantra] is the three-syllabled heart, and this very [mantra] is the three-syllabled truth, according to the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*. Ā.
Or, it is the collection of the syllables *ī*, *pa*, *lla*, *vi*, *ta*, *yu*, *ga*, *akṣara*, *māsa*, *akṣara*, and *nityākṣara*.
She is enriched with divine fragrances and adorned with a tilaka of vermilion.
"Divine" (*divya*) refers to those things pertaining to heaven—gods and so forth—the entire multitude of objects consisting of both sentient and insentient natures.

It is richly endowed and filled with their fragrances and associations; that is to say, it is not surrounded by earthly objects like a king or others. It is enriched by divine fragrance, such as the scent of *hari-candana* and the like, according to the Vedic text: "She whose door is fragrance, who is invincible. Alternatively:

Regarding the Yoga Sūtra statement, "Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, [the divine ear arises]," it is said that for a yogin who has performed *saṃyama* on the connection between the auditory faculty and space, a divine ear comes into being, by which the hearing of divine sounds occurs. By the same logic, [the following applies].

This is an indication of all the sense faculties. Therefore, the meaning is: "by which," that is, by whose grace, [the goddess] became enriched and perfected with divine fragrances; [this is expressed] by means of a tilaka made of vermilion (sindūra)—that is, red powder—or of gorocanā.
"Adorned with *citraka*" means joined with it. Alternatively, the word *tilaka* refers to a mole (*tilakālaka*). In that case, the analysis of the compound is "by means of the *sindūra-tilaka*s.

According to the *Rabhasa* lexicon: "The word *sindūra* is used for red chalk, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), red powder, and the *dhātakī* flower. Furthermore, they say that *tilaka* refers to a speckled mark (*citraka*) or a forehead mark (*lalāma*).

"Regarding *tilakālaka*: [it means] 'a mark'—thus the *Viśva* lexicon. Or, she is surrounded by *nāgas* (elephants) and women; for the *Viśva* states: 'The term *sindūratilaka* refers to an elephant, and *sindūratilakā* refers to a woman. Hemacandra states: 'A female elephant is a *sindūratilakā*, and a woman is a *sindūratilakāṅganā*. Alternatively, she moves with the gait of an elephant. Or, she is honored by women; for the root *añc* signifies 'motion' and 'worship.'"
This is because it is established by the *dhātupāṭha*. Likewise, in the *Viṣṇubhāgavata*,
beginning with the description of the young maidens of Nandavraja whose sins were shaken off by the intense suffering of their unbearable separation from their Beloved:
O Kātyāyanī, O Mahāmāyā, O Sovereign of the Great Yoginīs!
O Goddess, make the son of Nandagopa my husband; salutations to you.
"Reciting this mantra, those young maidens performed the worship," and so forth. Also, in the section concerning the marriage of Rukmiṇī, there is a statement made after the delay in Kṛṣṇa’s arrival:
For the Creator Maheśvara is not favorable to me, an unfortunate woman;
and the goddess Gaurī, Rudrāṇī, Girijā, and Satī has turned her face away from me.
Having spoken thus,
the maiden, protected by guards, went from the inner apartments to the temple of Ambikā;
she departed on foot to behold the sprout-like feet of Bhavānī.
By these and other verses, the fulfillment of desires and other benefits resulting from his worship are described.
Umā, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, Gaurī, is served by the Gandharvas. (177)

The syllable *u* denotes Śiva; *mā* is Lakṣmī. Alternatively, she is *Umā* because she measures (*māti*) or defines (*paricchinatti*) *uṃ*, the Supreme Śiva. Or, she is *Umā* due to the metaphorical identification [of her] with the flax flower (*atasīkusuma*) because of her similar color, or likewise because of her turmeric-like hue, or because her nature consists of fame and splendor. She who is the Goddess...

This is because of such statements as "in all beings, by way of beauty" (*sarvabhūteṣu kāntirūpeṇa*).
