According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *umā* refers to flax (*atasī*), the daughter of Himavat (*haimavatī*), turmeric (*haridrā*), fame (*kīrti*), and beauty (*kānti*). Furthermore, *u* is used as a form of address, and *mā* is used in prohibition. Alternatively, she is called *Umā* because, while performing austerities in her childhood, the Blessed One addressed her mother and forbade [her from doing so].
As it is stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Because she was sent away by Menā to go to the forest for asceticism,
the virtuous lady then received the names Umā and Somā."
Thus it is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"But Aparṇā, being without food, her mother addressed her;
though forbidding her with the word 'Umā', she then became known as Umā."
Having spoken thus, that goddess, who had performed difficult austerities,
became renowned in the worlds by that very name, honored by the gods, through her mother.
Thus it is said in the Puṣkara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:
"Then, from the sky, a divine voice spoke throughout the three worlds:
'O Umā, that which was spoken by you regarding your daughter has indeed been understood.'"
"Because of this, her name shall be 'Umā' in the worlds," it is said.
Or, she is "Uḥ" because she is both supreme (*uttamā*) and the mental faculty (*mā*). This has been stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"She is the supreme experience that destroys the bonds of worldly existence, and she is exceedingly beautiful even for Sadāśiva."
I bow to Umā, whose mental disposition is supreme and who possesses manifold worldly splendors.

Thus. Alternatively, since it is composed of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*—which constitute the *praṇava* and denote Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Brahmā respectively—it is of the nature of the three forms (*trimūrti*);
these and other meanings of the *praṇava* should be applied here. For this very reason, of this word...
Those who know the secret tradition state that "Devīpraṇava" is its name. And it was said by Paraśiva himself to the Blessed Lady in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
"The letters A, U, and M reside within my Praṇava."
The syllable *u*, the syllable *ma*, and the syllable *a* are uttered in succession.
"Know your own *praṇava* to be the three-measured (*trimātra*), the supreme protracted (*pluta*) sound.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Mahāvāsiṣṭha*: "Because it is the essence-power of the syllable *Oṃ*, it is celebrated as the Supreme (*Parā*), known as *Umā*. In that same work:
"Then, for those whose intellects are dormant, by the utterance of the *Amātra* [the measureless] within the heart..."
This is eternally said to be the digit of the moon that rises for all beings in the three worlds.

Thus, whether all living beings are asleep or awake, there exists within the heart the Śabdabrahman— the nature of which is the sound of the *praṇava*— consisting of the portion of sound that is devoid of the three measures (*mātrās*) beginning with the letter 'A', and whose essence is the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*).

In its commentary, it is stated that through constant recitation, the digit of the moon (indukalā) in the form of a point (bindu) resides upon the head of Śiva— the space within the cavity of the heart-lotus, which is the "small space" (daharākāśa).
Furthermore, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, beginning with the statement "The syllable Om is Brahman," it says:

It has been stated that after the parts [of the breath] have ceased, the sound (*nāda*) consisting of half a *mātrā* is heard at the top of the *liṅga*. Furthermore, in the *Haṃsopaniṣad*, after describing the different states of consciousness through the piercing of the petals of the heart-lotus and the abiding of the *haṃsa*, it is said that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) occurs at the *liṅga* and the fourth state (*turīyā*) upon the abandonment of the body.
It is said that when the Goddess, residing at the top of the *liṅga* of the *haṃsa*, merges [therein], it is the state beyond the fourth (*turyātītāvasthā*).

Alternatively, she is of the nature of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), for in the *Śivasūtra* it is stated that "Umā-Kumārī" refers to the will of yogis as being named "Umā"; she is that very form. And it has been said by the venerable Kṛṣṇadāsa:
They declare that Umā is the power of will (icchā-śakti) belonging to that very yogin who is perpetually swallowing the state of supreme Bhairava that has been described.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, according to the *Padma Purāṇa*, this Goddess Umā is the presiding deity of the Vināyaka-pīṭha, as she is called "Vināyakī.

She is also remembered in the *Padma Purāṇa* itself by the name "Umā in the Sindhuvana forest. Alternatively, Umā is six years of age, for in the section concerning maidens, the words of Dhaumya state: "Umā is considered to be six years old. [She is the daughter] of Śailendra...

She is the daughter (*tanayā*) of Himavat, the king of mountains; "she was born in the house of the lord of mountains, therefore she is the daughter of the king of mountains"—this is the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) in the *Devīpurāṇa*. She is *Gaurī* because of her fair complexion (*gaura-varṇatva*). According to the *Mahāvāsiṣṭha*: "She is Gaurī because of her fair-limbed body. The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca*.

In the *Pādya*, it is said: "Gaurī is the beloved of Varuṇa. Furthermore, in the lexicon (*kośa*): "Gaurī may also refer to a particular river, or to a woman who is ten years of age. Therefore, she is [the Goddess] in those respective forms. However, in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"She who was consumed by the fire of yoga was born again from the Himālayas."
Because her color is like that of a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon, she is remembered as Gaurī.

Thus it has been said. And she is the presiding deity of the Kānyakubja-pīṭha, for it is stated in the Pādya that "Gaurī is likewise in Kānyakubja. She is served by Gandharvas such as Viśvāvasu and others; or she is the goddess known as Aśvārūḍhā (Mounted on Horses), being served by Gandharvas in the form of horses; or "gandharva" refers simply to divine song. || 177 ||
She whose womb contains the universe; she whose womb contains gold (*svarṇa*); she who is the bestower of boons; she who is the sovereign of speech.

"She whose womb contains the universe" means that the entire manifested world (*prapañca*) is within her womb. "She whose womb contains gold" means that gold is within her womb, or else she is born from the womb of gold. As it is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
He was the embryo within the Golden Egg (Hiraṇya), and he was born from the embryo of that Golden Egg;
therefore, he is designated as Hiraṇyagarbha in this Purāṇa.
Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, she is "Svarṇā" because she possesses an auspicious womb (*garbha*) of *arṇas*, meaning letters or *mātṛkās*;
that is to say, she is the one expounded by the *mātṛkās*. This is based on the usage: "a word pregnant with many meanings.
Or, she is "Svarṇā" because she has within her womb (*garbhe*) mantras consisting of beautiful letters (*śobhanārṇā*). "Avaradā" consists of four syllables.

She is so called because she tears asunder—that is, cuts to pieces—the lower, ignoble, and demonic beings. Alternatively, she is "Avantī" because her teeth (rada) possess luster (ava); the suffix *ac* is applied to the root *ava*, which here signifies luster.
She is the sovereign mistress of speech.
Accessible through meditative absorption, she is indefinable, the giver of knowledge, and the embodiment of wisdom. 178.

She is to be reached and known through meditation and the dissolution [of mental constructs], for the scripture states: "Those who have attained the practice of meditation perceive the power of the Self of the gods, which is concealed by its own qualities. She is "unlimited" because she lacks that state of being the counter-positive of non-existence, which constitutes limitability.

For spatial limitation is indeed absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); temporal [limitation] consists of destruction and prior non-existence (*dhvaṃsa-prāgabhāva*); and substantial [limitation] is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), such being the established state. She is the "Giver of Knowledge" (*jñānadā*) because she bestows that knowledge which is intended as the grantor of liberation (*kaivalya*). Thus it has been said:

In the *Talavakāra Upaniṣad*: "Into that space he came upon a woman, Uma Haimavatī, shining most brightly; he said to her, 'What is this spirit? She replied, 'It is Brahman,' and so forth. Also in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
Such is this supreme Śāṅkarī Vidyā, which destroys worldly existence;
indeed, it arises for living beings solely through the grace of Śakti herself.
Thus it is also stated in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"The form of knowledge which is Śivā, who is to be known through the Vedas, whose nature is truth, bliss, and infinite consciousness— of that Ambikā,
the sole mother of all worlds, there shall be speech only through the grace [obtained] by devotion."

Thus [it is said]. It either bestows knowledge or it shatters it. As for the statement "knowledge is bondage," this is one sūtra in the first unmeṣa of the *Śivasūtra*; however, it is stated there that the letter *a* is also to be elided (*praśleṣa*).
This is possible because, in the continuous recitation (*saṃhitā-pāṭha*), it follows the preceding sūtra: "Consciousness is the Self" (*caitanya-m-ātmā*).

In the third unmeṣa as well, there is another such sūtra, but in that case, a [grammatical] elision (praśleṣa) is not possible; for [the word "citta" follows] from the previous sūtra, "The self is the mind. And that has been explained in the Vārttika:
"It possesses internal functions such as happiness, objects of enjoyment, determination, and so forth."
It is directed outwardly toward objects such as the body and blue color, which are suitable for that [perceptual] engagement.

And for this [individual], whose nature conforms [to that state], knowledge consisting of the appearance of difference is bondage; because he has not realized that [non-difference], he certainly wanders in transmigratory existence as an *aṇu*.

Thus, the meaning is that this very knowledge which brings about the state of pure consciousness destroys [the previous state]. For this very reason, in the second *unmeṣa*, there is another *sūtra*: "Knowledge is food. And the *vārttika* states:
"That which was previously called bondage is said to be knowledge for the supreme yogin."
Because the perception of selfhood in that which is not-self consumes the food, [it is called the eater].
Thus: she whose very form or body is knowledge (*jñāna*), because the entire world consists of the nature of knowledge. As it is stated in the second book of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Knowledge alone is the supreme Brahman; yet knowledge is also considered the cause of bondage."
This universe consists of knowledge; nothing exists beyond knowledge.
O Maitreya, understand that both knowledge and ignorance are indeed nothing other than cognition itself.
Thus; or, she from whose presence there is the manifestation—that is, the expansion—of knowledge. || 178 ||

She is to be served by all the Vedāntas and is the very nature of Truth and Bliss. She is to be correctly known through all the Vedāntas, that is, through the entire collection of Upaniṣads. And it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa: "This is declared to be the Triśakti (the Triple Power), which conforms to the conclusions of the Naya school."
This power, whose essence is knowledge, pervades all the Vedāntas.

Thus [it is said]. She whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is truth (*satya*) and bliss (*ānanda*). Here, by relying on *satya* as a separate word, it is possible to form the single compound *ameyātma*. She is "truth" (*satyā*) because of the Vedic scripture: "It became both the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*tyat*). Or, she is "truth" because her forms are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), food (*anna*), and the sun (*āditya*). Thus, "the existent" (*sad*)...

This is because of the Vedic revelation: "The vital breath is 'iti' (it is), the food-sheath is 'anna-maya', and this is the sun. Furthermore, although there is a three-syllable count due to the protracted pronunciation of "ye" (in *sati ye*), it should be understood that through their combination, it remains a two-syllable word.
This point was established in the *Chandobhāskara* during the commentary on the *Chandaḥsūtra* rule regarding the filling of syllables such as "iy".

This has been explained by us [elsewhere]. She is "Satyā" because she is virtuous toward the good, or because her own nature (*svarūpa*) is truth (*satya*). She is "Ānandarūpiṇī" because bliss (*ānanda*) is her own nature.
For this very reason, in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*, in the third chapter's section (*tārtīyīkādhikaraṇa*), it is stated: "Bliss and other [attributes] belong to the Pradhāna (the Principal)."
It has been established that attributes such as bliss (ānanda) and others are to be combined in other meditations precisely because they constitute the very nature [of Brahman].
She is worshipped by Lopāmudrā; she who fashioned the entire sphere of the universe through her divine play. (179)
She was worshipped and propitiated by Lopāmudrā, the wife of Agastya. As it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "Her wife, named Lopāmudrā, worshipped me with devotion, saying, 'Worship me.
It is also stated in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*:
Because this Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, was pleased with the mudrā known as Lopā, the wife of Agastya,
she is celebrated as Lopāmudrā.

Thus it is said. For this very reason, it is also well-said that she is both Lopāmudrā and Arcitā. She is worshipped either by means of the *vidyā* named Lopāmudrā or as the instrument [of worship]. According to the *Kādimata*, "One should perform all the ritual services (*upacāra*) with the third section of the *vidyā*. These [services] were fashioned effortlessly, as a mere play (*līlā*).

She whose [form] consists of the spheres of the universe; as it was said by us in the *Devīstava*: "O Mother of the World, even Śiva is not the master over the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the gods headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
for you, however, this sequence is like the plucking of *uddālaka* flowers for a mere moment."
Thus, the nine-syllable name *Uddālaka* and so forth refers to a particular kind of play (*krīḍā*). The *Śaktisūtra* also states:
"By its own will, it unfolds the universe upon its own screen. (179)

Invisible, devoid of visibility, the knower, and free from the knowable—she is invisible because she is distinct in nature from the visible, or because she is not an object fit for the senses such as the eyes, according to the Vedic scripture: "One cannot see the seer of seeing. And it is said in the *Devībhāgavata*:
In the Third Skandha, beginning with the statement, "The form of the Sage who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) cannot be within the range of vision," and concluding with,

"The power (śakti) devoid of qualities is difficult to fathom, and the Supreme Person (para-pumān) is likewise devoid of qualities," [it is established that] the visible is merely phenomenal (vyāvahārika).

Because it possesses ultimate reality, it is devoid of the visible; or rather, it is consciousness without an object. It is the "knower" (*vijñātrī*) because it knows specifically, according to the Vedic scripture: "O, by what means could one know the knower? Because there remains no other object of knowledge (*vedya*) whatsoever, it is "devoid of the knowable. [Regarding] the knowable...
Or she who possesses ultimate non-existence;
she is Yoginī, the Giver of Yoga, the Worthy One, the Bliss of Yoga, and Yugandharā. || 180 ||

Yoga is the cultivation of oneness; because she possesses that, because she bestows it, and because she is fit for it, she is the Yoginī, the Giver of Yoga, and the Fit One. The suffix *yat* is used here in the sense of "that which arises from yoga" (and so forth). As it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Having restrained all the organs of perception along with the mind..."
The yoga of meditating on the unity of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman).
Thus it is said: "One should know that as the separation from the union with suffering, which is designated as Yoga"—so in the *Gītā*.

And the *Pātañjala-sūtra* states: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. Furthermore, that [Yoga] is fourfold: Mantra, Laya, Haṭha, and Rāja. Rājayoga is also threefold, through the divisions of Sāṃkhya, Tāraka, and Amanaska.

Their respective characteristics are not stated here for fear of prolixity. Alternatively, she has the form of the eight Yoginīs— beginning with Maṅgalā and ending with Saṃkaṭā— who revolve repeatedly through the twenty-six-year cycle according to the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), as well as the seven [Yoginīs] beginning with Ḍākinī who are well-known in the science of mantras (mantraśāstra).

Alternatively, *yoga* means attachment to objects, which is to say enjoyment (*bhoga*). Thus, the meaning of the three names is that [the Goddess] consists of the triad of the enjoyer, the giver of enjoyment, and the object of enjoyment.
As it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller, all..."

"It has been stated that this Brahman is threefold. Herein, this should be understood: the Sāṃkhyas hold that *māyā* is *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and independent; the Vedāntins hold that it is simply the power (*śakti*) of Śiva;
and the Vivaraṇācāryas state that by the term "power," its dependence [on another] is expressed. It consists of the three *guṇas*.
And the qualities (guṇas) are mutually suppressive. O Bhārata, when sattva overcomes rajas and tamas, it prevails;
likewise, rajas overcomes sattva and tamas, and tamas overcomes sattva and rajas.
Thus it is stated in the *Gītā*. Consequently, she is established as being of three kinds:
one consists of pure *sattva* due to the absolute suppression of *rajas* and *tamas*;
the second consists of impure *sattva* due to the slight emergence of *rajas* and *tamas*.
The third [nature], consisting solely of *tamas* and being for the most part non-existent, is that in which *rajas* and *sattva* are utterly overwhelmed.

Among these, consciousness (*cit*) delimited by the first is called by the name Īśvara; it is the bestower of enjoyment and is termed the *yogadā*. Consciousness delimited by the second is called the *jīva*; it is the enjoyer and is termed the *yoginī*. Consciousness delimited by the third—

The distinction is that she who is named the insentient object (*jaḍavastu*) is called the "enjoyable" (*bhogyā*) and the "suitable" (*yogyā*). Yoga is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti, which is itself bliss (*ānanda*); since sleep (*nidrā*) is characterized primarily by bliss, it is also termed "Yoga-sleep" (*yoganidrā*). And she is none other than this Goddess. Thus it is said:
In the *Harivaṃśa*, beginning with the statement, "That which is established in the world as yogic sleep (*yoganidrā*), dense with bliss," it says:
"Even among the gods, no one other than Nārāyaṇa can sustain her;
she is the companion of Sadāśiva, the illusory power (*māyā*) born from the body of Viṣṇu."
O lotus-eyed one, this very same highly deluding woman, through her persistence in the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, will intensely enjoy the worlds in a short period of time.

Thus [it is said]. She is either Nṛsiṃha, known as Yogānanda, or she whose form is that [of Nṛsiṃha]. By accepting "mohinīmukhyā" as a single compound, it is easy to explain two names here: "Ayo" and "Ānandā. "Ayo" means she in whom attachment (*yoga*, i.e., *saṅga*) does not exist, according to the Vedic scripture: "The unattached one indeed does not cling. Alternatively, "ayo" means she who has the form of a mountain (*parvata*). She is "indestructible" (*abhedyā*).
This is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*): either it means that one goes to *Um*, the Supreme Śiva, by means of the auspicious method (*ayena*);
or *Nandā* refers to the Gaṅgā in the form of the Alakanandā; or she is the lunar days (*tithi*) consisting of the first, sixth, and eleventh;
or she is the Goddess named Nandā who will be born as Nandajā.

Alternatively, she is the specific form of the deity described in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*; or, due to her association with a particular location, Sarasvatī herself is designated by the name Ānandā, as stated in the *Pādya*: "Nandā is on the back of the Himavat.
Or, she is a specific river situated at the edge of Puṣkara; this too is stated in the *Pādya* itself.
In the *Puṣkara-māhātmya*:
"This meritorious river, endowed with holy waters, is the daughter of Brahmā;
known by the name Nandā, she flows extensively toward the south."
Even if he does not go there, the man who utters her name attains happiness while living and becomes a sky-walker after death.
Thus [it is said]. The etymology of the name is given in the Varāha Purāṇa:
"Having installed the Goddess on the snowy mountain, they departed as they had come;
because she was established there and brought joy, she became known as Nandā."
Thus it is said. However, in the Devīpurāṇa:
"She rejoices among the worlds of the gods, or dwells in the Nandana grove; because she resides on the highly meritorious Himācala, she is therefore remembered as Nandādevī."
Thus it is said. Regarding her essential nature, the Vārāha Purāṇa states:
"She who, as Gāyatrī with eight arms, fought against the demon Caitra—she herself became the goddess Nandā out of a desire to accomplish the work of the gods."
On Mount Mandara, during the era of Svāyambhuva Manu, the Daitya known as Mahiṣa was slain by Vaiṣṇavī;
later, he became the Asura Caitra.
On Mount Vindhya, she who possesses great strength and prowess was slain by Nandā;
for that goddess is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), while Mahiṣa is the embodiment of ignorance (ajñāna).
"Ignorance is indeed destroyed by knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
*Yuga* means a pair, as well as the four [ages]; *yuga* also refers to the pole and the yoke of a chariot.
Furthermore, *yuga* denotes the Kṛta age and other ages, a pair, and also a medicinal herb named Vṛddhi.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Viśvaprakāśa*, since horses and bulls— which bear the parts of a chariot or a plow— are seen to be the ones that pull the chariot or the plow, the term *yugandharā* is used here with the intended meaning of merely "that which sustains the entire universe.
Alternatively, it is called *yugandharā* because it supports the pair of Śiva and Śakti, or the Kṛta-yuga and the others.

In the case of *saṃjñā*, the suffix *khac* is applied by the rule "after the roots *bhṛ*, *vṛj*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, *tap*, and *dam*. Then, the augment *mum* is added by the rule "after *aruṣ*, *dviṣat*, and words ending in a short vowel, [the suffix *ka* takes the augment *mum*]. (180)

She is the very nature of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). The triad of qualities consisting of will, knowledge, and effort constitutes her essential form. And it is said in the *Sanketapaddhati*:
Will is the region of the head, and Knowledge is situated below it; Action resides in the feet. Thus, her body consists of the three powers.
Thus it is said. Also in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
"The Goddess Tripurā is threefold, having the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa;
she consists of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the power of will (icchā-śakti), O Dear One."

Thus [it is said]. Here, although there is no mention of a triad of powers (*śakti*) corresponding to the sequence of the well-established causality where each preceding factor—knowledge, desire, and effort—is the cause of each subsequent one, the word *kriyā* (action) refers to effort precisely because the root *kṛ* (to do) has the power (*śakti*) to denote effort. And it is stated in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*:
This resolve (dhṛti) commanded by me is considered the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) and action (kṛti);
likewise, it has the form of will (icchā) and knowledge (jñāna), and these two are undoubtedly the two Vidyās.
Thus [it is said]. Or rather, they are solely actions characterized by movement. And it is stated in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa* that this [action] is fivefold:
"Vibration (*spanda*), oscillation (*parispanda*), commencement (*prakrama*), and repeated practice (*pariśīlana*)."
These five activities are called "the movement" by the wise.

The long vowel [in "sarvāsām"] is due to the elision of the prefix *ā*. It is the continuous stream of all the *jagatīs* (worlds), because of the non-difference between the produced and the producer. As stated in the *Mālinīvijaya Tantra*:
"That which is called the supreme power (*parā śakti*) of Brahman, the creator of the world..."
That goddess assumes the nature of desire for him who wishes to create.
"It is thus, it must be known; it is not otherwise"—this is perfectly certain.
That which makes this known instantaneously within is called the power of internal knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
When, having understood that "let this object become such-and-such," they bring about that very object, that is what is called "action" (kriyā) in this context.
Thus, in the Vāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa:
"The wise know Śiva as the peaceful Brahman, ineffable even to those who master speech;
it is his power of vibration (spanda-śakti) that extends this appearance of the visible world through its own will."
"The desire of a person possessing form is like a city of imagination.
Thus it is said. And it is called "action" (*kriyā*) because it brings about the experience of the appearances of objects.
Regarding the appearances of objects, there are four types [of action] characterized by production, acquisition, transformation, and refinement.
"But it is for the sake of the *halā*s," as explained in that respective commentary:
"The All-Sustainer (*sarvadhārā*), the Well-Established (*supratiṣṭhā*), who bears the form of both the existent and the non-existent. (181)
Or, it means "she whose support is everything. That is to say, she exists as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) within all things;
or, she is the form of the substratum for all. As it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Those objects which are eternal, those others which perish, and those objects which are gross and those which are subtle..."
Subtle;
whatever is formless and whatever is formed, everything in its entirety, and whatever exists as even a single part among the elements.
"O Goddess, whatever objects exist on earth, in the intermediate space, or elsewhere, their attainment comes from you alone.

Nor is there any inconsistency regarding the feminine gender in this view, because of the grammatical rule: "The gender of a dvandva or tatpuruṣa compound follows that of the final member," and because [the word *devī*] functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the rule: "The substratum is the locus."
It should be stated that the masculine gender of the word *ādhāra* (substratum) is determined in accordance with the Sūtra;
for when the qualityless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahman*) is to be described, that [masculine form] alone is indeed appropriate. To explain:
masculinity is the increase of the three qualities, such as *sattva*; femininity is their decrease; and [neutrality is their] equilibrium.

The state of being neuter [is untenable], because those [categories] consisting of the absence of both gender and the female organ are not applicable to insentient things; furthermore, since the entire universe is established in works such as the *Devībhāgavata* as being composed of the three *guṇas*, they are possible everywhere.

Since accumulation (*upacaya*) and so forth are established as having limits, accumulation and the rest certainly exist in relation to something else; thus, because all three logical marks (*liṅga*) are purely positive (*kevalānvayin*), their application is determined by convention according to the speaker’s intention.
With all this in mind, it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and production (*prasava*)."
"The gender should be determined according to one's own established doctrine:
*saṃstyāna* (contraction) from the root *styai* with the suffix *ḍraṭ* is the female (*strī*); *sap* (bringing forth) from the root *sū* is the male (*pumān*);
and that which is the interval between these two, in the absence of both, is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*)."

And thus: "The gender is not to be taught" (liṅgamaśiṣyam), and "the relationship will follow" (sambandhamanuvartiṣyate); as well as the usage "what indeed is this called inference? (ko'sāvanumāno nāma), and the Vedic usage in the sūtra "in a bahuvrīhi [compound] when it denotes a kinsman" (bandhuni bahuvrīhau). This being so, lest there should arise a lack of systematic order (avyavasthā).

The application of the rules governing gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) has as its sole purpose the attainment of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) through restrictive injunctions. However, in the case of sentient beings, rules such as *ajādyataṣṭāp* are intended precisely to express the combination of both types of gender.
Therefore, for one who seeks to prove that gender is indeed intended—just as the number "one" is intended in the case of an animal sacrifice—it follows accordingly that...

The term *liṅga* signifies the cessation of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Consequently, with respect to Tripurasundarī— the Mother of the entire universe, who is the power of consciousness transcending the three *guṇas*— the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) of both kinds exists by virtue of its uncontracted function, following upon the qualified consciousness (*saguṇacetana*).

Intending to convey the sense of being unobstructed, the goddesses of speech employ only the feminine gender; however, for the sake of following established convention, we demonstrate there and there a conformity with the rules of gender grammar.

Furthermore, this is merely a direction for the purpose of dispelling the charge of being an incorrect word (*apaśabda*). "Supratiṣṭhā" means the beautiful foundation or the substratum of the universe;
alternatively, it refers to a specific twenty-syllable meter named *supratiṣṭhā*. "Sat" is Brahman.
"Asat" is the world, which is distinct from Being. Even though the world, being indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), is characterized by being neither existent nor non-existent, [it is so described].

The term "non-existent" (*asat*) denotes [the effect] merely by its being distinct from the existent (*sat*), because in such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning this was non-existent; how could the existent be born from the non-existent? we observe the usage of the term precisely through its distinction from one of the two.
Thus, it is so because it maintains the form of those two. Alternatively, "existent" refers to the conventional (*vyāvahārika*).

It maintains and illuminates those two very forms—truth (satya) or the ultimate (pāramārthika), and non-existence (asat) or the void (tuccha). The meaning is that its nature consists of two cognitions whose objects are existence and non-existence respectively;
[it is like] a final mental modification (vṛtti) having pure existence as its object, as well as one having pure non-existence as its object.
Because of the existence of the mental modification known as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And thus says the Pātañjala Sūtra:

"Conceptual construction is that which follows mere words and is devoid of a real object. The Gautama Sūtra also states: "That which is established by the intellect is non-existent (*asad*). Alternatively, the words "existent" (*sat*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) refer to presence and absence; and these two...
By virtue of their fitness, they should be understood as having the nature of truth and non-sublatability;
for truth and so forth are not distinct from the substratum,
and because a property in the form of a negation, such as non-sublatability, is identical with the nature of its locus.
Or rather, it is the substratum of the mere existence and non-existence of things. As it is said in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Whatever appears as existing, and whatever also appears as non-existing..."
All of that was fashioned by the illusory power (māyā) of Mahādeva.
Thus [ends the section]. || 181 ||
The eight-formed, unborn, conqueror, who ordains the course of the world;
as stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "Lakṣmī, Medhā, Dharā, Puṣṭi, Gaurī, Tuṣṭi, Prabhā, and Dhṛti."
With these eight forms, O Sarasvatī, protect me.
Thus, she is the one whose eight forms are to be understood through the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras. Or, as stated in the Yogaśāstra:
"Due to the distinction of the qualities (*guṇa*), the form of the Self (*ātma-mūrti*) is proclaimed to be eightfold:
the individual self (*jīvātman*), the inner self (*antarātman*), and the supreme self (*paramātman*), which is stainless."
The pure self (śuddhātman), the self whose nature is knowledge (jñānarūpātman), and the great self (mahātman) are remembered as the seventh;
the elemental self (bhūtātman) among them is the eighth—thus the eight selves are proclaimed.

Thus: she whose eight forms consist of the five great elements (pañcamahābhūtāni), the sun and moon, and one among those initiated for heaven (jīvātmasvargadīkṣitānām)—namely, the individual soul—making an eightfold number of forms. For it is stated in the *Śaktirahasya*: "The elements, the two luminaries (puṣpavantau), and heaven (svar) are the eight forms of the Goddess."
In the first book of the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well, it is stated: "The Sun, water, earth, fire, wind, ether,
the initiated Brāhmaṇa, and the Moon— these are considered the eight forms."
Their wives were, in due order: Suvarcalā, Sukeśī, the other Śivā, Svāhā, Aditi, Dīkṣā, and Rohiṇī.
Śanaiścara, Śukra, Lohitāṅga, Manojava,
Skanda, Svarga, Santāna, and Budha were the sons born in successive order.
Thus it is said; however, in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* it is stated:
"The eight *prakṛtis* are proclaimed as the forms (*mūrtis*) of the Goddess; likewise, her bodies, which possess boundless manifestations, are the *vikṛtis*."
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is my nature divided eightfold.
Thus [it is said]. Or, it means that she whose forms are the Gītās as taught by the Blessed One. Alternatively, it means she whose nature is the eightfold *kula*.
And that is stated in the *Samayācārasmṛti*:
"The courtesan, the liquor-seller, the fisherwoman, and likewise the washerwoman..."
A weaver woman, a leather-worker, a woman of the outcaste class, and likewise a prostitute.

Thus it is said. Alternatively, the characteristics of the eight [Śaktis] are stated in the Rudrayāmala: "She who has very small limbs and long hair is considered Anaṅgakusumā," and so forth. Their manifestations, however, are well known in the third enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) as being of the nature of that group of eight; or they are of the nature of Brāhmī and the others, as well as Vaśinī and the others.

She is the conqueror of the "Unborn One" (ajā), who—well-known from such Vedic scriptures as "The one unborn female, red, white, and black"—is of the nature of ignorance; that is to say, she is the destroyer of ignorance because her nature is knowledge. She is the one who ordains the maintenance, dissolution, or preservation of the fourteen worlds.
This is her nature.
"Alone" (*ekākinī*) means being devoid of a second; the suffix *ākinic* is applied in the sense of "without a companion."

"He was afraid; therefore, one who is alone is afraid. He looked for a companion [and thought], 'Since there is nothing other than myself, from what should I be afraid? Then his fear departed. Thus says the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti.
In the Devīpurāṇa:

"Alone she swallows the worlds, alone she establishes them as well; alone she creates the universe; therefore she is considered solitary. Thus, she is of the nature of plenitude (*bhūma*), non-dual, and devoid of duality. (182)

The form of the *bhūman* (the Infinite) is that which has been determined in the *Bhūmādhikaraṇa* as being none other than Brahman, based on the scriptural passage beginning with "where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else," and ending with "that which is the *bhūman*, that is bliss. Alternatively, it is the form of the *bhūman* derived from the grammatical rule: "there is the elision of the final syllable of *bahu*, and *bhū* is substituted for *bahu*."
The word *bhūman* has many meanings; therefore, the sense is that although she is solitary (*ekākinī*), she possesses manifold forms (*bahurūpā*). As it is said in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"Though she is one, through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) she is *bhūman*; Śivā is renowned everywhere."
Just as a crystal gem is colored by various hues according to what it reflects.
Likewise, the Goddess Umā is described as attaining the names of the various elements through the power of her qualities;
just as a single cloud exists both as one and as many,
so too does Umā exist through the power of her qualities in terms of color and form.
Just as water fallen from the sky may come to possess various tastes.
Just as Umā [appears differently] through the specific quality of the earth's essence and likewise through the power of its attributes,
so too does the single wind become manifold through the specific nature of substances.
Whether it be foul-smelling or fragrant, Uma likewise [assumes] qualities according to her influence,
just as the Gārhapatya fire may take on another name.

In the same way, that Goddess is proclaimed through illustrative examples as being both one and manifold, existing in the form of the Dakṣiṇa, Āhavanīya, and other fires, as well as in the forms of the Brahmā and other priests.
"Therefore, supreme devotion should be practiced for the sake of attaining the state of being all-pervasive.
Also, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The one Śakti, the Mistress of Desire (Kāmeśvarī), through association with manifold limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),"
In his presence, he sports with forms both supreme and inferior.

Thus, by the passage beginning with "where one sees nothing else" and ending with "what is small is mortal," the Śruti establishes that dualistic perception has impermanent objects; because such perception is to be abandoned, that state in which duality has departed is "nondual" (nirdvaitā). It does not mean, however, that duality previously existed there.
It has emerged subsequently; however, he says "devoid of duality" to show that it does not exist even from the very beginning.
The sense is that because difference is unreal, there is an absence of it at all times. || 182 ||
She is the giver of food, the giver of wealth, the aged one, whose essential nature is the unity of Brahman and the Self.

She bestows food upon people; she bestows *vasu*—meaning both wealth and jewels. And so it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "That indeed is this great, unborn Self, the eater of food and the giver of wealth; he obtains wealth."
"Thus he knows. Regarding this, the traditionalists have explained it as "he bestows food on all sides. "Vṛddhā" means aged; for the Śruti says, "Thou, being worn out, totterest with a staff";
"vañcasi" means thou goest.

She is called *Vṛddhā* because she is the eldest of all, or because she has grown through the form of the universe; alternatively, the suffix *kta* is used in the active sense derived from the causative (*ṇijanta*) root, meaning "she causes the universe to grow. Her own, innate nature (*sva-rūpa*) is the very identity of the individual selves (*ātman*, i.e., the *jīvas*) with Brahman, which is consciousness (*caitanya*). Or else, [it refers to] the identity of Brahman and the self.

Her form is the *haṃsa* mantra, which establishes that the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) is one's own very self and all-in-all. As it is stated in the *Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Alternatively, this *jīva-mantra* is the expounder of the individual soul."
Because the word "I" (ahaṃ) is conventionally established in common usage as referring to the entity of the individual soul (jīvātman).
The Śakti-mantra, known as the letter *sa*, denotes the Supreme Lord;
because it is well-known in its primary sense, the Supreme Lord is [here] the established meaning.
The entire universe, from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the atom, including all that is moving and unmoving,
is born, exists, and dissolves within the Supreme Lord.
I who appear as a transmigrating being am that very Supreme Lord;
I am indeed He, there is no doubt, according to the authority of my own direct experience.

Thus, by this [verse], the name "Haṃsamantrārtharūpiṇī" (Embodiment of the Meaning of the Haṃsa-mantra) from the Triśatī is explained. [She is] Bṛhatī, Brāhmaṇī, Brāhmī, Brahmāṇḍā, and Balipriyā. (183)

She is called *bṛhatī* because she is greater than the great, or because she takes the form of a specific meter consisting of thirty-six syllables. Nor is there any contradiction with the statement in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* that "Gāyatrī is not among the meters," for such a contradiction would not exist if one accepts her dual nature. For this very reason, it is said: "The *Bṛhat-sāman* is likewise among the *sāmans*."

There is no contradiction between the statement in the *Gītā* regarding the description of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) of the Blessed Vāsudeva and the description of the universal form by the Blessed Goddess, because of the *Kūrma Purāṇa* statement: "and the *jyeṣṭha-sāman* among the *sāmans*. In the *Talavakāra* recension, [the verse] begins with "udutyaṃ..."

The *sāman* sung upon these two verses beginning with "citram" is called the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, according to the statement of Haradatta in the *Ujjvalā*. The *Bṛhatsāman*, however, is well known as being sung upon the verse beginning with "sattvaṃ naḥ citre. This is also because the words *bṛhat* and *jyeṣṭha* can be considered synonyms. Therefore...

The explanation is either "she who has the form of the *jyeṣṭhasāman*" or "she who has the form of the *bṛhatsāman*. According to the *Viśvakośa* and other lexicons, *brāhmaṇī* refers to the plant *phañjikā* or *spṛkkā*, renowned among the wives of the twice-born (*dvija*); thus, she may have the form of a specific medicinal herb, or the form of any woman of the twice-born caste, or the form of a particular state of consciousness (*saṃvit*). And it is said:
In the *Samayācārasmṛti* it is said: "The Brāhmaṇī is rich with white flowers; she is consciousness, whose essence is the deity.

Alternatively, she is called Brāhmaṇī because Śiva possesses the caste (*jāti*) of a Brāhmaṇa. Thus it is heard in the *Chāndogya*: concerning Śiva, [it says] "You are Virūpākṣa, whose radiance is in the teeth," and [continues] "among the gods..."
"I am a Brāhmaṇa among men; as a Brāhmaṇa, I seek refuge in a Brāhmaṇa;
I seek refuge in you"—so it is recorded in the *Parāśara*, *Āditya*, *Kaurma*, *Vāsiṣṭha*, and *Laiṅga* [Purāṇas].
"The venerable Sāmba is a Brāhmaṇa, for he is indeed the deity of Brāhmaṇas."
Out of a sense of distinction, one should go for refuge to Rudra, the Lord, who is superior even to Brahmā.

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, in the *Viṣṇubhāgavata*, beginning with the words "O Brahmin, do not cast this [child] into my womb," the fact that Ādityā was afraid of Śiva’s wrath makes his Brahminhood manifest;
this should be seen in the *Śivatattvaviveka*. There is no evidence for the existence of any insentient genus (*jaḍajāti*) other than ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, he says "brāhmī. It is correct by virtue of the grammatical irregularity (nipātana) in the rule *brāhmo jātāv*. Alternatively, she is of the nature of speech (*vāgātmikā*).

Or, for her who possesses attributes (*saguṇā*), Brahman itself is bliss; thus, by means of the possessive suffix *ac*, she is "possessing the bliss of Brahman" (*brahmānandavatī*). Those who are powerful are capable of dispelling ignorance and are conquerors of the enemies such as desire.
She for whom compassion is dear; or she who is identical with that Vāmana for whom King Bali is dear; or she for whom offerings of worship are dear. 183.
Bṛhatsenā is of the nature of speech, devoid of existence and non-existence;
she whose form consists of languages such as Saṃskṛta and Prākṛta, or who is described by means of languages. As it has been said:
Some speak of you in Sanskrit alone; some in the languages of the mlecchas and others; some in a common tongue, while others indeed in Prakrit.
Thus: she possesses a vast and boundless army consisting of the fourfold forces;
or, she is the specific form of the king named Bṛhatsena. She is devoid of both existence—such as substances and qualities—and non-existence—such as prior non-existence and the rest.

But surely, since the non-existence of both [existence and non-existence] is itself a non-existence, if [the ultimate reality] possesses that, how can it be said to be "devoid of non-existence"? Furthermore, even antecedent non-existence, destruction, absolute non-existence, and so forth, have only substances, qualities, and the like as their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).

They must be stated [as distinct categories], because no other alternative is possible. If it is argued that "thereby, in the absence of the non-existence of a substance, there would follow substantiality (*dravyatva*), and in the case of the absence of a substance, there would follow the state of being the non-existence of a substance (*dravyābhāvatva*); so how can there be freedom from both existence and non-existence?", we reply: No, for this has already been resolved by Vyāsa himself.
This has been stated in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The destruction of an imagined object is indeed the remaining of its substratum;
for the non-existence of an entity is its destruction, while the existence of an entity is its [true] being."
For the destruction of the substratum is indeed imagined as something distinct from both existence and non-existence;
it never truly occurs, precisely because of its reality.
Thus: the absence whose counter-positive is an entity possessing the same level of reality as its substrate exists in that substrate as something distinct from it;
however, the absence of an entity possessing a different level of reality from its substrate is not distinct, but is the very nature of the substrate itself.
The collective meaning is that the foundation, being itself real, does not perish.
It is a state of existence that is easy to attain, auspicious, beautiful, and easily accessible. (184)

She is to be propitiated even without bodily afflictions such as fasting and the like, or without the rigorous constraints of fixing the mind upon the nature of the object of meditation. Thus, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the Blessed Lady spoke these words to Himavat: "If one is unable [to practice] me..."

By the passage beginning with "one should meditate on the immutable form of the Lord," there is an instruction on increasingly accessible methods. And they say that one should not fear sin on account of this much;
for it is auspicious, meaning it produces only merit (*puṇya*).

Because it consists of the goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha) such as liberation (mok�ṣa), the goal (gati)—that is, the state to be attained—is "excellent" (śobhanā) and "easily accessible" (sulabhā). It is called a "goal" (gati) because it is gone toward (gam-yate); it is the fruit. Or, "goal" refers to knowledge or the means; for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "In the context of the path and its stages, 'gati' refers to knowledge and the means of travel. This very [state] is...

"Because it is the supreme goal among all goals of beings," according to the *Kūrma Purāṇa*. The application [of the mantra] is with three instances of the dative case: "Obeisance to the auspicious goal (śobhanāyai), to the easily attained goal (sulabhāyai), to the goal (gatye). Here, the two names are easily expressed by attaching the word "goal" (*gati*) to each: "the auspicious goal" and "the easily attained goal. By that much alone, [the purpose is fulfilled].
Because it is possible to avoid redundancy, for here three words beginning with "śobhanā" (beautiful) are recited:
"sumukhī nalinī subhrūḥ śobhanā" is one name as it stands;
and in "suvāsinyarcanaprītāśobhanā," the four-syllable word "aśobhanā" is the second.

In the present case, since the elision of the vowel *a* (praśleṣa) is impossible and its separation is likewise untenable, the established position is that the tautology is resolved by assuming syntactic unity with the subsequent word,
following the pattern of "matir amatir" and so forth.
This very same reasoning is the basis even for the analysis of word-divisions (*padaccheda*),
because the Blessed Pādas (Śaṅkarācārya) have determined the word-divisions in the *Viṣṇusahasranāmabhāṣya* by means of such reasonings alone. For example, in the case of [the name] *nidhiravyayaḥ*:

The two words [“the Imperishable” and “the Person”] share a single name in order to avoid redundancy with the phrase "the witness. This applies similarly to such terms as "the Great," "the Firm," "the Eternal," "the Pillar," "the All-knowing," "the Radiant One," "the Lord of Speech," and "the Noble-minded One," and so forth. Thus...

In order to avoid the redundancy of the phrase "the birth and so forth of people is terrifying" (*jānanō janajanmādir bhīmaḥ*), the letter *a* has been elided in the expression "the incomparable Śarabha is non-terrifying" (*atulaḥ śarabho 'bhīmaḥ*). Likewise, [the terms] "desired" (*iṣṭaḥ*) and "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭaḥ*) are to be understood in this manner.
Consequently, since even the *chalākṣara-sūtras* (puzzles based on syllables) are rooted in such logical justifications, they should be interpreted according to that very method.

One should not pay excessive attention to the division of words (*padaccheda*). By this very principle, those well-versed in the Vedas maintain that even the *Ūha* texts, though recited by them in accordance with Vedic boundaries, are merely human compositions because they lack a foundation in logic; thus, they hold that such works are non-authoritative when they contradict logical reasoning.
The followers of Jaimini [hold that]: since it is possible to avoid redundancy in both ways regarding the subject at hand,
one should accept "jñā" as a separate word within the sequence of names beginning with the letter *pa*, such as "Prasavitrī," "Pracaṇḍājñā-pratiṣṭhā-prakaṭākṛti."

Due to the inconsistency in the purity of the textual context (*sandarbha*), it is appropriate here to accept two names by appending the word *gati* to the phrase *pracaṇḍājñā*, with the desire to treat it as a single compound word; such is the direction [of the argument].
If, however, there is insistence that the name must be one and only one, then it can easily be stated that it is indeed a single word.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *śobhanā* (excellent) and *sā* (that), combined with *avasulabhā* (difficult to obtain), yields the meaning "very difficult to obtain" (*sudurlabhā*). That by which the coming back—that is, rebirth—is very difficult to obtain; in other words, that which cuts off birth.
[This applies] to one whose final birth has occurred, or else to Śaṅkara himself.
By that very means, the glorious fifteen-syllable Vidyā is obtained.

Thus from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*. Alternatively, the meaning is: "That by which the goal is difficult to attain—that is, birth as a human being and so forth, which is hard to obtain—is rendered auspicious. And it is said in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"By whom the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* has not been heard, and by whom the ancient Prakṛti has not been worshipped..."
"The oblation was not offered into the mouths of those gods and mortals; thus the birth of those men has gone in vain.

In the Viṣṇubhāgavata, however, there is a distinction here, as the second quarter is read as: "by whom the Ancient Person (Puruṣa) was not worshipped. Regarding the phrase "the beautiful leader of the Asuras":
Having observed that this applies to the auspicious asuras, such as Prahlāda and others, it is easy to explain all three names in the present context as well. 184.

She is the sovereign of the kings of kings, the bestower of sovereignty, and the beloved of sovereignty. She is the mistress even of those who are kings among kings— namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— as well as of the king of kings, Kubera.

It is her nature to bestow sovereignty over Svārājya, Vaikuṇṭha, Kailāsa, and so forth; she for whom the aforementioned kingdoms are dear and beloved. By the word "kingdom" (rājya), their lords—the kings—are also meant. For this very reason, their residence in Śrīnagara is recorded in tradition, as it has been said:
O Dūrvāsas,
we praise again and again the kings who are accompanied by slender-waisted women, as well as the lakes consisting of great sapphires upon this central earth of theirs.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning of "of these two" is "of the thirteenth and fourteenth types. Her compassion shines, having seated her own dependents upon the royal throne. 185.
She whose compassion shines and is beautiful; she by whom her own [devotees] have been seated upon the thrones and lion-seats of kings, of princes, and of Indra and the other gods. 185.

Rājyalakṣmī is the mistress of the royal fortune, the sovereign of the fourfold army, and the Lakṣmī who takes pride in sovereignty; she whose mantra is well-known in the *Tantrarāja*. She is the mistress of the treasury—the divine storehouse—or of [the wealth] consisting of food and so forth.

The Mistress: She is the sovereign of those children who possess four limbs in the form of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. Or, "aṅgabala" refers to military arrays (*vyūha*) whose strength consists solely of their constituent parts;
she is either the mistress of those arrays consisting of four components, or the term "aṅgabaleśvarī" itself [denotes her].
It denotes a manifestation (*vyūha*). Because it is a *dvigu* compound, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied; thus, the meaning is "whose self consists of the four manifestations.

These [manifestations], such as Vāsudeva and the others, are well-known not only in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas but also in the Śaiva and Śākta Purāṇas, and they are to be cited here. [The types of Puruṣa are: the Body-Puruṣa (*śarīra-puruṣa*), the Metre-Puruṣa (*chandas-puruṣa*), and the Veda-Puruṣa (*veda-puruṣa*).
Or she is the one described in the Bahvṛca-Upaniṣad as the "Great Person" (Mahāpuruṣa);
she bestows sovereignty, is true to her promise, and has the ocean as her girdle. 186.
One who has sacrificed with the Rājasūya is either a lord of a circle [of kings], a king over kings, or an emperor;
his state is sovereignty (sāmrājya), which he bestows.
"He by whom the Rājasūya has been sacrificed and who is the lord of a circle..."
And he who rules by the command of the king is the sovereign emperor (samrāj).
Thus, from the *Agnipurāṇa-kośa*: she whose alliance—that is, her vow and boundary—is true and not to be transgressed; she is the Earth, whose girdle is the oceans themselves.
The *dīkṣā* is the subduer of the Daityas and the bringer of all worlds under control.

It is called *dīkṣā* because it "destroys" (*kṣiṇoti*) and "attains" (*prāpayati*) wisdom and knowledge (*dhī-jñāna*). Thus, beginning with the passage, "Now, therefore, concerning *dīkṣā*: for what reason indeed is one called 'initiated' (*dīkṣita*)?", [the text continues] up to, "Him, indeed, being thus initiated (*dhīkṣita*),..."
This is according to the *Atharvaveda Brāhmaṇa*, ending with the passage: "They call him *dīkṣita*.
Alternatively, he is so called because he destroys evil by bestowing mantras upon his disciples;
for [the mantra] is given out of compassion to the disciple, and the accumulation of sin is destroyed.
"Therefore, it is called initiation (*dīkṣā*)...

[as stated] from the *Parānandatantra*. She has arisen within him; thus he is "initiated" (*dīkṣita*), being non-different from her. She is the pacifier—that is, the destroyer—of the Daityas, such as Bhaṇḍa and others. She brings all the worlds under her own control. "Under control" (*vaśam*) means...
The indeclinable ending in "mān" is the absence of opposition;
she who bestows all objects is Sāvitrī.
She is the bestower of all four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

Since the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* prohibits only the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in connection with words ending in the suffix *tṛn*, the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix remains;

thus, even though the compound is prohibited by the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* regarding the agentive genitive, the compound is formed with the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). And it has been said:
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"She bestows upon all worlds whatever objects are desired, such as dharma and the rest;
therefore she is celebrated by all as the Goddess who accomplishes every purpose."

Thus [it is said]. This *sāvitrī* belongs to Savitṛ, the Supreme Śiva, who brings forth the universe. According to the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, he is called "Savitṛ" because he causes the procreation of living beings (*prajā*). Furthermore, she is designated as *sāvitrī* because she effects the manifestation of the light of Savitṛ.
Or also by this reason: "She is the progenitor of the world."
Thus it is from the Bhāradvāja-smṛti; and also from the Vāsiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa: "Sāvitrī [is so called] because she presides over procreation. Furthermore, in the Devī-purāṇa:
"The Goddess is worshipped by the thirty gods and honored in the Vedic conjunctions."
And because her essential nature is pure existence, she is therefore celebrated as Sāvitrī.
Thus it has been said. However, in the Devībhāgavata:
"The root *sru* is here used in its causative sense (*syandana*);
because light is produced through this flowing (*sravaṇa*), she is therefore called Sāvitrī."

Thus it has been said. And she is the presiding deity of the Puṣkara Tīrtha. As it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa: "The auspicious Sāvitrī is present by name at Puṣkara, the most excellent of sacred fords."
She whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss. || 187 ||

Existence (sattva), consciousness (cit), and bliss (ānanda) are her form (rūpa) and essential nature (svarūpa); for this very reason, these are to be integrated from other Vidyās into this one, and thus she is "she whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss" (saccidānandarūpiṇī). || 187 ||
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Bhāskararāya, the eighth digit (*kalā*), which bestows enjoyment, was completed with the seventh hundred [verses]. (700)
Thus ends the eighth digit, named the seventh century, in the commentary on the *Lalitāsahasranāma* titled *Śrī Saubhāgyabhāskara*.
The ninth [chapter], named the Eight Hundred, is the universal *kalā* (power), which is unlimited by space and time, all-pervading, and the deluder of all.
It is "unlimited by space and time," meaning it is devoid of any limitation produced by them. And it has been said:

In the *Yogasūtra*: "He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time. This means that Īśvara is the teacher and father even of the ancients, such as Brahmā and others, because he is not delimited by time. Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is the object of the cognition "it does not exist here."

Limitation by space (*deśataḥ pariccheda*) refers to [the absence of a thing] in a particular location. Limitation by time (*kālataḥ pariccheda*) consists of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), which are the objects of the cognitions "it did not exist previously" and "it will not exist hereafter," respectively. The cognition "it does not exist now," however, refers exclusively to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). [In this context,] there is a restriction of time upon the occurrence in space, and a restriction of space upon the occurrence in time.

Furthermore, due to the rule regarding delimitation (*avacchedakatva*), there is a detailed discussion in other treatises stating that the usage of "now" (*idānīm*) and "here" (*iha*)— as in the cognition "the cow is now in the cow-pen, not in the stable"— is intended to express one as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the other as the delimiter (*avacchedaka*). Such an absence of delimitation is what is meant [by the term].

The meaning is that it possesses the absence of being its counter-correlate, or rather, the absence of those two [the self and the world] in relation to it by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*). As it is stated in the *Saurasaṃhitā*:
"The Person (*pumān*) is all-pervading like space, because whatever is distinct from Himself is illusory (*mṛṣā*)."
For it is remembered as being infinite in terms of space, time, and substance.

Thus [it is said]. The word *ananta* (infinite) means that which possesses the absence of limitation (*paricchedābhāva*). Now, it may be objected that even here the absence of limitation in reality (*vastutaḥ*) is recorded in the Smṛti; for there exists a real limitation called mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), which is the object of the cognition "this is this, not that."

If it is asked, "Why is the absence of its counter-correlativity not mentioned?"—understand that this is because it is not to be pointed out separately, as it is the subject of disagreement among disputants and will be supported by many names. That very point is stated by the verse beginning with *sarvagā*: "It goes to all things (*sarva*)," meaning it pervades every mere object (*vastumātra*) through non-difference.
She is called *sarvagā* because she "reaches" (*prāpnoti*) [everything]. The suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule *anta-atyanta-adhvā* and so forth.

This is stated in the *Varāha Purāṇa*, where Brahmā says to the Goddess—who is named Sṛṣṭi among the three forms (*trimūrti*) and is performing penance on the White Mountain (*śvetaparvata*)—"Let a boon be chosen. To this, the Goddess replied:
"O Blessed One, I am unable to remain in one place for long;
therefore, desiring omnipresence, I beg this boon of you."
Thus addressed then by the Goddess for the sake of creation, Brahmā, the Lord of Progeny, said: "You shall be all-formed; you shall become omnipresent."

Thus [it is said]. Here, because the vocative "sarvarūpe" (O you who are all forms), which serves as an exposition of omnipresence, has the meaning "in that which is non-different from all," there is the figure of speech *parikarāṅkura* (the sprout of poetic embellishment). Furthermore, since non-difference from all is already established, the word "asi" (you are) is used. For this very reason, [there is no need for] that which indicates something yet to be proven (*sādhyatva*).

The statement "thou shalt be" has the sense that "in all fields (kṣetra) there shall be thy qualified forms (saguṇamūrti). Therefore, the meaning is also "existing in all fields," or "the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all. Intending these three meanings, it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
O Mahāmati, this is the established conclusion and the ultimate truth of the Goddess;
she is the Vedas, the sacrifices, and even heaven itself—of this there is no doubt.
This entire world, both stationary and moving, is pervaded by the Goddess;
she is praised and worshipped as the very essence of food and drink.
The Goddess Śāṅkarī is omnipresent; she exists everywhere through her forms and her names—in the trees, on the earth, as well as in the wind, in the sky, in the waters, and in the fire.
For this goddess of such a nature should always be worshipped according to the prescribed rites;
he who knows her to be such indeed merges into her alone.
Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object:

"Since contradictory attributes such as eternity and non-eternity, insentience and sentience, coexist [in the world], how can there be an absence of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) in Brahman? To this, he says: "She who deludes all."
It is so called because it deludes all ordinary people— who, perceiving duality, consider it to be real—

and renders them devoid of knowledge regarding non-duality; for since the appearance of duality between Brahman and the world is merely an illusion, there is no harm whatsoever to its actual indivisibility.
This is the state of being. And it has been said by Śiva in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"This is that supreme power, consisting of me, whose form is Brahman;
she is Māyā, my beloved and infinite, by whom this world is deluded."
By means of this [māyā], O best of the twice-born, I delude this entire world— including gods, asuras, and humans— and I create and dissolve it.
Thus [it is said]. In this very context, the Goddess spoke these words to Himavat:
"Whatever various scriptures are seen in this world that contradict the Śruti and Smṛti, and which are devoted to dualistic discourse..."
The Kāpāla, the Bhairava, the Śākala, and the Gautama—
these and other such [tantras] are intended for the purpose of delusion.
Those who, through their application to false scriptures, seem to delude human beings—
these very scriptures were created by me for their delusion in another life.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*:
"People who are devoid of grace, most sinful, deluded by *māyā*, and afflicted by birth, death, and so forth, do not know the Lord of Gods at all."
Thus; or, it means she deludes the entire three worlds. That is to say, she is the embodiment of both the Trailokyamohana-cakra and the Vidyā.
Sarasvatī, whose nature is the Śāstras, is Guhāmbā, who possesses a secret form. (188)

[Objection: But surely, by the same logic, even the appearance of difference between a jar and a cloth is merely delusion; therefore, let there be non-difference even between those two. To this, [the author] says: Sarasvatī. This means the deity presiding over knowledge, whose nature is an ocean of knowledge—that is, whose nature is knowledge unconditioned by objects.

Up to this point: although delusion (*moha*) is logically untenable in the determination of insentient objects such as jars, nevertheless, because of the scriptural statement, "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance;
by that, living beings are deluded," the obscuration of knowledge is necessary regarding the subject of non-dual knowledge; therefore, in its determination—

The sense is that for sinners who are deprived of your grace, delusion is inevitable, even regarding that which is the supreme human goal consisting of the removal of all misfortunes. Alternatively, having introduced the subject of virgins with the statement, "Sarasvatī [is a virgin] at two years of age," [the text proceeds].
The meaning is also that she possesses such a form of a maiden according to the words of Dhaumya. Furthermore, in the Bharadvāja-smṛti it is said:
"Because she always dwells upon the tongues of living beings through the movement of speech, she has been designated by the great seers by the name Sarasvatī."
Thus it is said; and in the *Vāsiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa* it is stated: "Because she causes all views to flow away, she is called Sarasvatī.

Now, one might object: "This delusion is not like the confusion of directions and the like, because difference is inferred through thousands of arguments such as the coexistence of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma-samāveśa*)," and so forth. To this [the author replies]:

He said: "Consisting of scripture" (*śāstramayī*). The suffix *-maya* here has the sense of "predominance. It means that this [knowledge] has scripture as its primary authority, such as in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman," and so forth. This is the intended meaning: in this context, scripture alone is the primary means of comprehension, and not inference or other means of knowledge, because those are weaker than scripture. Therefore...

Thus, the *Brahma-sūtra* states: "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*). Furthermore, there are scriptural passages (*śruti*) that indicate that [Brahman] is known solely through the Veda, such as:

"I ask you about that Person who is known from the Upaniṣads" (*taṃ tv aupaniṣadaṃ puruṣaṃ pṛcchāmi*). Consequently, when the scripture has taught the non-difference of the entire multitude of entities from Brahman, [this applies] to the mantra.
Even when [the object] is restated by the third peak (kūṭa), because it contradicts that [other means of knowledge], the erroneous nature of the inference itself must be postulated;

for the Vedāntas are engaged in determining Brahman as the sole reality with absolute intent. For this very reason, due to such a contradiction with the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra), [the cognition] regarding the moon's being the size of a thumb [is sublated].
Even that which is perceived by all people may be considered an error;
thus, because his body possesses limbs consisting of the scriptures themselves, it also means he is "one whose transformation is the scripture.
As it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
With the winds of his breath, he created the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas,
as well as the great mantras of the Atharva, through his own self-conception.
Sarasvatī, the mother of all, created the ornaments of poetry, drama, and the like through her sweet expressions, and she produced them from her tongue.
From his thumb, the fair-eyed one created the six Vedāṅgas,
as well as Mīmāṃsā, the Nyāya-śāstra, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmasaṃhitā.
By means of the thread-like line above her throat, the Mother of All created the Āyurveda; by the line situated in the middle of her throat, she created the Dhanurveda.
He produced the sixty-four sciences from the hollows of his knees,
all the Tantras from his limbs, and the Madanāgama from the base of his arms.

And so forth. Now, one might object: "The appearance of difference is not merely worldly—like the cognition that the moon is the size of a thumb—but is indeed scriptural. To this, he replies: *guhāmbā* means the Mother situated within the cave; that is to say, she whose form is shadow (*chāyā*). This is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*).
Drinking the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest part of the supreme,
those who know Brahman— and those who have thrice performed the *Nāciketa* fire-sacrifice— call them shadow and light.

The meaning is that, because shadow and light are described in the Śruti as having entered the cave and being mutually distinct, their difference is established both by this description and by the force of the dual number. Alternatively, "Guha" refers to Skanda; his mother is Ambā. For her sake—specifically for the purpose of the task of slaying the demon Tāraka and so forth—...

Then follows the prayer by the gods, the union of Śiva and Śakti there, the creation of obstacles by him, and the resulting anger, curses, and so forth; thereafter, the birth of Skanda through the conjunction of Agni, Gaṅgā, and the reed-cluster (śarastamba), and other such stories accessible only through the scriptures.

The meaning is that because they establish difference (*bheda*), the non-dualistic scriptures (*advaita-śruti*) themselves must be said to have a figurative meaning (*upacaritārthatā*), just like the scripture stating "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), due to contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). True, this entire empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) relies upon conventional reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*); however, non-duality...
With the intention that she takes ultimate reality as her object, he provides the following resolution: "She whose form is secret" (*guhyarūpiṇī*).

That which is situated in the cave (*guhā*) is the "secret" (*guhya*), the supreme mystery; her very form is knowledge (*jñāna*) itself, which is unfit for the conventional perspective. And it is said in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
We praise her who assumes the form of the Guru, the secret one whose nature is secret wisdom,
who is pleased by those devoted to the secret, and who is established within the cave of the heart.

Thus, the sense is that the scripture, being twofold, is rendered consistent by relying upon two forms of the one and the same Brahman; or alternatively, it means that the Guhyopaniṣad itself is its form.
This has been stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa, during the description of the yoga of manifestations (*vibhūti-yoga*), regarding all the Upaniṣads, O Goddess: [text follows].
"You are called the Secret Upaniṣad," thus [it is said]. || 188 ||

Now, one might object that because of the authority of two [conflicting] scriptures, the consequence would be both difference and non-difference, and thus non-duality (advaita) could not be established; to this he says:
"She who is eternally devoted to Sadāśiva, being completely free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi)."

It is completely liberated from and abandoned of all attributes— whether delimited or undelimited, such as the state of being a producer of the aggregates (*skandha*), shadow, heat, and so forth— and is thus devoid of any connection with attributes. Consequently, it exists in a state where there is an absence of any relation to its own attributes.
Since the relationship appearing [in cognition] is indeed false— just like the identity of silver with mother-of-pearl—
it is for the sake of establishing the validity of the scripture, which consists in its revealing the truth,
that all Vedāntas [point toward] the non-dual, ultimate Supreme Brahman.
Since the intended meaning must be stated either directly or indirectly, a scripture that teaches duality exists only from the perspective of conventional reality,
just as an eclipse-treatise that reports the consumption of five or six finger-breadths exists only from a conventional standpoint.

The meaning is that "manifestation" (*pravṛtti*) does not stand on the same level as difference and non-difference; or rather, it is devoid of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) well-known to logicians and is accessible through such valid reasons (*saddhetu*). But if this is so, since Tripurasundarī is of the nature of power (*śakti*), and since...

Since there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence of [the Goddess] being false, as there is no distinction in her being of the nature of the attribute of the Supreme Ego (parāhaṃtā), he says:
"always" (sadā). She whose vow—her observance—is that Śiva alone is the Lord, and which is "always," meaning perpetual;
that is to say, her status as the consort of Śiva is eternal, just like Śiva himself, uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time. But others...
Objects are imagined; since there is no distinction in their being objects of perception, even their "property-ness" (dharmatva) is merely imagined.

However, in the case of *śakti*, it is only the property-ness that is imagined, but *śakti* itself is not imagined. Therefore, the sense is that she belongs to the category of Brahman. Alternatively, she is the devoted wife (*pativratā*) of Sadāśiva. Now, [an objection]:
How is this understood—that only those attributes distinct from the supreme *ahantā* (I-consciousness) are imagined?
On the contrary, due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*), it might follow that all attributes whatsoever are either false or unreal; therefore, he says:
She is the mistress of the tradition, the virtuous one, whose form is the circle of gurus. || 189 ||

It is called *sampradāya* because it is correctly handed down to disciples. In this context, the term "Ishvari" means capable or able to provide support; the meaning is that this is understood through both reasoning (*nyāya*) and tradition (*sampradāya*).
For instance, just as space and other attributes are superimposed upon Brahman, which is devoid of all attributes (*nirdharmaka*).

Furthermore, just as properties such as being an object of a word, substantiality, and being a quality are superimposed upon consciousness delimited by space and so forth— and likewise, properties such as being a quality are superimposed even upon those very consciousnesses delimited by them— so too is the state of being a quality [superimposed] just like the state of being a substrate.

The sense is this: since the relationship of attribute and substratum (dharmin-dharma) is established by logic alone for the one [Brahman]—even though Brahman is devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka) with respect to the visible world—it should be understood from the tradition that, in that case, Śiva alone is the substratum and Śakti alone is the attribute. Brahman itself...
The traditionalists maintain that it is called "power" (*śakti*) because it is the counter-correlative to the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) that is capable of being negated.

Furthermore, the meaning of the mantra known as the "Tradition" (*sampradāya*) is well-known both in the *Yoginīhṛdaya* and in the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*; and this [meaning] is naturally inherent precisely in the *Kādividyā*.

This has already been established by us in the *Varivasyārahasya*. Alternatively, it means "the Mistress" (*īśvarī*). He states that this is appropriate: "It is fitting" (*sādhu*), meaning suitable. The sense is that since in the world the power of burning and so forth is observed to be a property of fire alone, it is fitting to say that the power of supreme subjectivity (*parāhaṃtā-śakti*) is likewise a property [of the Goddess].

This name is neuter; therefore, the usage is *namaḥ sādhune*. Consequently, there is no redundancy with the phrase "the virtuous one who bestows the supreme goal" (*sādhvī sadgatidāyinī*). He states that this Dharma has two forms:
*Ī* is the nature of the fourth state (*turya*), a single syllable known as *Kāmakalā*; this is the name.
From the syllable *a*, which is the first vowel and the form of Viṣṇu's supreme [seed-syllable], [the word] "his sister" (*asya bhaginī*) is analyzed;

when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for feminine derivation through connection with a male (*puṃyogalakṣaṇa*), and the *a* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the case-ending (*sup*) that would have been obtained after the remaining suffix alone is [elided].

The formation of the word is established by the elision [of the feminine suffix] according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). The usage *yainam* does not refer exclusively to the relationship between wife and husband; for the relationship between father and daughter is also accepted under the term *puṃyoga*. [Example: Subhadrā.

It should be "Vasudevī. Furthermore, in the expression "namo śivāya nārāyaṇīsahacarāya," she is explained as simply being the sister of Nārāyaṇa. Likewise, the name "Jayantī" is well-known precisely through the etymological derivation that she was the sister of Jayanta, the daughter of Śakra. [This applies] to a single substratum possessing attributes.
Because it is only logical for two coexistent entities to be siblings;

the literal meaning of the phrase "qualified by being the sister related to Viṣṇu" is that she is both the form of Viṣṇu and the form of his sister. That is to say, the one and only Brahman possesses these two forms: as Dharma (the attribute) and as Dharmī (the possessor of the attribute).
