It attained [that state]. Therein, Dharma again became twofold—as male and as female. Of these two, the female became the consort of Paraśiva, while the male became Viṣṇu, who attained the status of being the material cause of the entire universe.
This triad, when united, is the one undivided Brahman; such is the method of the Śaiva doctrine.

The followers of the *Kūrma Purāṇa* and other texts should study this matter in detail as it has been expounded by the initiated (*dīkṣita*) in the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā*. Furthermore, the essential nature of this *kāmakalā* is described [in the *Śrīvidyārṇavatantra*] by the passage beginning with "from the consciousness of the vibration of the *bindu*, which arises from the form of the void up to the end of the *visarga*," and so forth.

This has been elaborated upon in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* with the words, "From the letter *ī* [comes] this beloved Māyā, the creator of the universe, whose nature is the fourth state (*turyātmikā*)," and so forth; in the *Jñānārṇava*, with "The letter *ī* should be known as having the *Samanu* [meter], red in color, and full of majesty," and so forth; and in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, as well as in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa* and other works.

In the *Saundaryalaharī*, in the verse beginning with "Having made the face the dot" (*mukhaṃ binduṃ kṛtvā*), the venerable Śaṅkarācārya has explained it quite clearly. However, he says that the definitive extraction of its true nature (*svarūpa*) should be sought from his own mouth alone, because of its being the most profound secret. [The term] "the gurus" refers to those starting from Paramaśiva down to one's own respective guru. Their...
The maṇḍala is that very lineage; this is its form and its definition.
The sense is that this secret has come down through an uninterrupted succession of gurus and is not written in books.
For this very reason it is said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "By means of instruction from ear to ear..."
"He has reached the surface of the earth. || 189 ||
He declares its very secret nature through four [epithets]:

*kulottīrṇā*, *bhagārādhyā*, *māyā*, *madhumatī*, and *mahī*. *Kulottīrṇā* means she has transcended or gone beyond the *kula*, which is the aggregate of the senses; for she is inaccessible to them. *Bhage*... [The text continues: ...in the *bhaga*.

She is to be worshipped and meditated upon within the solar orb (*savitṛmaṇḍala*), because the solar orb serves as the secret locus for meditation. Alternatively, she may be worshipped in the form of the *bhaga*, according to the statement: "The seed-syllable that is the eleventh support consists of three corners."
Māyā is the power that is conducive to the non-manifestation of even that which is most well-known. However, in the Devīpurāṇa it is said:
"Because it performs diverse effects, bestows inconceivable fruits, and is like a dream or a magician’s trick in the world, it is therefore proclaimed as Māyā."
Thus it has been said. And this very point is stated in detail in the Varāha Purāṇa, in the words of Viṣṇu addressed to the Earth: "Parjanya rains there, and a flood of water arises."
The quarters of the sky become devoid of water; this, my dear, is my illusory power (māyā).
The moon wanes day by day and likewise waxes day by day;
it is not seen at all on the new-moon day—this, O beautiful one, is my illusion.
This is indeed the power of my illusion by which I abide upon the water;
it is by this that I create and withdraw both Prajāpati and Rudra.

By these thirty-seven verses ending with [the word] *iti*, it is established that the agency of performing diverse effects belongs to Māyā alone, which serves as its own delimiting factor (*avacchedikā*). Furthermore, such an effect itself constitutes the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the term "Māyā. In the Bhaktitantra, however, that power (*śakti*) is Māyā.

In the sūtra beginning with "jaḍasāmānyāt" (due to the commonality of being insentient), it is stated that the power (*śakti*) of the Blessed One is indeed *māyā*. [The word *madhumatī* means] possessing honey, wine, nectar from flowers, or bee-honey at the time of worship and so forth; for there is a Vedic revelation stating, "This form which is honey belongs to this great deity. Alternatively, [it refers to] "the sun is indeed the honey of the gods."

It is of the nature of a specific meditation known as Madhumatī, which is enjoined in the Śruti; or alternatively, it refers to the fourth among the four types of yogis mentioned in the Yogaśāstra, who is said to have "transcended all movement" (gatikrāntābhāva).
He is superior to the preceding types, yet even for him there are seven stages (bhūmikās) that must be transcended. Among these—
The final stage is called "Honeyed" (*madhumatī*); the meaning is that it possesses that nature.

Because the knowledge arising in such a stage is a deliverer, it is termed "the deliverer from saṃsāra. This very deliverance is all-encompassing in its objects and complete in its sequence of objects.
It is clear from the *Yogasūtra-bhāṣya* and other texts that she is "knowledge born of discernment" (*vivekaja-jñāna*). Alternatively, she is a specific river.

Although she is of such a secret nature, he says she is as manifest as the earth itself; or she is the earth, taking the form of a specific river named Mahī. In the *Devīpurāṇa*, however, it is said that she exists pervading the Great One (*mahat*).
It has been stated that "All is Earth" is considered the primordial nature (prakṛti).
She is Gaṇāmbā, the one meditated upon by Guhyaka, the one of delicate limbs, and the beloved of the Guru. || 190 ||
The Mother (Ambā) of the Gaṇas, such as the Pramathas, or of Gajānana;

she who is to be worshipped by the Guhyakas—beings of a specific divine class—or in a place where secrets are unknown; she whose limbs are tender and delicate; she for whom her Guru is dear; or she who is non-different from the wife of her Guru.
Or she is the wife of Śiva, the teacher of the world. || 190 ||

She is independent, the sovereign of all tantras, and possesses the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti. She is "independent" (svatantrā) because she is the agent of all things even without dependence on causal factors;
or she is the embodiment of the eternal tantra called *Svatantra*; or she is one whose own tantras are her very self.

The sense is that because the very same manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of this [Śakti] are expounded even in the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Gāṇapatya, and other Tantras, they belong to her own nature. "Sva" means one's own, dependent on oneself;
*paraśiva* is "tattantra" or "tadadhīna," meaning dependent upon her. The meaning is that they are mutually dependent.
Thus it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, in the section on the majesty of the sacred field of Kāmarūpa: "He dwells there eternally with Pārvatī in playful dalliance;
in the center is the temple of the Goddess, and Śaṅkara is subject to her."
In the northeast, on Mount Nāṭaka, there is the eternal abode of Śaṅkara;
the Lord dwells there perpetually, and Pārvatī is dependent upon him.
Thus, he establishes that all the sixty-four tantras are contained within the *Iṣṭa*. The form of Śiva facing south is renowned as the teacher of Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and others;
the mantras well-known in the tantras are indeed her very form.
She is the one worshipped by Sanaka and others, and the bestower of the knowledge of Śiva. || 191 ||
She is to be properly propitiated and worshipped by Sanaka, Sanandana, and the others; for this very reason, they are included in the lineage of her gurus. As it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"You alone are beginningless, the entirety of all things, both cause and effect."
For indeed, yogis such as Sanaka and others seek you alone.
Thus [it is said]. It bestows knowledge concerning Śiva in its highest degree. As it is stated in the Vāsiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa:
"The wind is obtained through vibration; fire is obtained through heat."
That which is pure consciousness alone, stainless and tranquil, is indeed declared to be Śiva.
"It is indeed perceived only through the power consisting of vibration, and not otherwise.
Or, Śiva is the bestower of knowledge upon her. For this very reason, the Varāha Purāṇa, referring to the Trimūrti, states:
"These three also attain perfection for him who knows Rudra according to reality. (191)
The bud of bliss of the digit of consciousness (cit-kalā-ānanda-kalikā), whose form is love and who acts for the beloved's welfare.

She is that in whom the digit of consciousness (cit-kalā)—that is, consciousness itself—is as if a single part of Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss; or alternatively, she is that in whom the consciousness conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is a single part of the unconditioned consciousness.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti): "In the world of living beings, He alone exists as the eternal individual soul (jīva), being a portion of My own Self. Furthermore, in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the section enumerating the forms of the Goddess, it says: "In the minds of all embodied beings, there is the power named Citkalā.
Likewise, she is one whose single portion is bliss itself; the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for optional derivation from a root ending in a long vowel (*śoṣāt vibhāṣā*).

Or, she is one whose nature consists of a single portion of the bliss residing within living beings; the suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), according to the Śruti: "Other beings subsist on a mere measure of this very bliss. Or, she is the *ānandamaya-koraka*, for the lexicon states: "The word *kālikā* means a bud (*koraka*) or a man (*pumān*). She is one whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is love, affection, and devotion itself.
Just as the word "ghee" (ghṛta) is used for that which produces the manifestation of color (rūpa)—as in the expression "longevity is ghee"—the term "form" (rūpa) is likewise applied here.
She who acts kindly is Priyaṅkarī. She is Nandividyā, pleased by the recitation of names, and Naṭeśvarī. || 192 ||
Beginning with *a ā i ī* and ending with *kṣaḥ kṣā*, these are the names of the Bhagavatī. There is one letter *a* and thirty-five beginning with *ka*; thus, there are thirty-six letters.
These correspond to the forms of the thirty-six years; when each of these is joined with the sixteen vowels in sequence, [the following occurs].
There are that many months. Thus, there are five hundred and seventy-six syllables.

These are the initial letters. Having made each one of these the first [syllable], one should sequentially place thirty-six [syllables] in the position of the second letter. And at the end, the sprout is *ā ī*.
One should join them. Consequently, there are twenty thousand seven hundred and thirty-six names.
As it has been said:
"By joining the vowels *ā* and *ī* with the consonants in pairs and triplets, respectively, [the names are formed]."

O Bhairava’s consort, salutations to those twenty thousand names of Tripurā that arise from the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, combined with the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *au*, which are indeed extremely secret. Salutations to those beyond them.
Thus it is said. Also, in the third book of the Devībhāgavata:
"O descendant of Raghu, when joined with the vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', as well as with the consonants, the names [of the Goddess] become innumerable."

Thus it is said. And their complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) is stated to be fivefold in the *Kādima-tantra*: "By day, by weekday, by fortnight, by month, and by thirty-six days," and so forth. This is the rite known as the *nāma-pārāyaṇa*; and the same applies to the recitation of the *Sahasranāma* (Thousand Names).

Because both [words] are present through etymological derivation (*yaugika-vṛtti*)— the former by way of *yoga* (etymology) and the latter by way of *rūḍhi* (conventional usage)— she is pleased by them.
Whether she worships me or not, whether she recites the mantra or not.
One should always recite this Thousand Names for my pleasure.

According to this statement: the *vidyā* of Nandin, that is, the *vidyā* worshipped by him, belongs to Naṭeśvara, the dancer of Citambara; this [present work] is an imitation of it. As the learned have said:
"The shanks, thighs, and stalks [of his legs], formidable with rows of filaments shimmering from the rays of his toenails..."

Victorious is the fresh, upright foot of Bhavānī during her imitation of her Lord’s dance— a foot whose sprout-like toes spread the luster of fresh lac-dye, upon which the humming bees of her tinkling anklets settle, and which creates the beauty of a lotus born from the pond of the natural, transparent loveliness of her own body.
Thus [ends the section]. || 192 ||
The substratum of the illusory world—the locus of the appearance of the world that is illusory in nature, just as mother-of-pearl is the locus for [the appearance of] silver.
"This duality is mere māyā; from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is non-duality. It does not exist here..."

This is because of such scriptural passages as "There is no plurality whatsoever," and from the *Devībhāgavata*: "All this indeed is only Me; there is no other eternal reality," and from the *Viṣṇubhāgavata*: "In which the threefold creation is unreal. This is stated with the intention of expressing the dissolution of the three qualities (*guṇa*).

It is feminine gender. Alternatively, the word *adhiṣṭhā* itself means "the substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Consequently, the analysis of the compound is: Brahman, who is the substratum of the universe, is the *anaḥ* (vital breath) of whom [she]. Or else, the word *adhiṣṭhāna*—by means of the suffix *ac* in the sense of possession—refers to that which is supported. By that [analysis],...

The grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) is: "she whose substratum is the illusory world. However, in reality, according to the view of the Tantrikas—who accept that the world is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman—the world is indeed real;
for, due to the absolute non-difference between Brahman and the world, as in the case of clay and a pot, [the world is not distinct from] Brahman.

Since the world must necessarily be real if it possesses reality, all the non-dualistic scriptures (*advaita-śruti*) are fully accounted for by accepting that difference alone is false. Precisely because difference is false, even the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*), which is constituted by difference, is itself false.

If there is no contradiction with that much alone, then the Vedāntins' postulation of the entire world as being illusory is indeed purposeless; this is explained in detail in the *Śāmbhavānandakalpalatā*.
Consequently, the substratum of the world is itself illusory.
The feminine gender is justified by the analysis of the compound as "that in which there is a subsistence through a relation constituted by difference."
She is the giver of liberation and is the very embodiment of liberation.
She is called "muktidā" because she bestows *mukti*, that is, liberation. And so it is said in the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa: "Therefore, one seeking liberation [should worship] Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess."
One should take refuge in that which is the self of all beings, whose nature is auspiciousness.
Thus it is said. Also in the Śiva Purāṇa:
"Even for those who utter the names of Maheśa out of ignorance, Śiva grants them liberation; what more than this can be said?"
Thus it is said. Also in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:

"Those who worship the Supreme Śakti, whether according to the prescribed rule or even without it, are certainly not subject to worldly existence; they are truly liberated, of this there is no doubt."

Thus, liberation alone is its form. For if the cessation of ignorance were of the nature of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) or of a fifth category (*pañcamaprakāra*), it would fail to constitute the supreme human goal;
therefore, it must be stated that liberation is precisely the bliss of one's own self as characterized by that [cessation]. And it has been said:
In the fourteenth chapter of the Saurasaṃhitā:
"Now I shall describe to you in brief the true nature of liberation,
by the knowledge of which supreme liberation is accomplished for all embodied beings."

Having begun thus, and having refuted the status of knowledge as a causal factor (*kāraka-hetu*) therein by stating, "Knowledge is not a causal factor; indeed, for the wise, it is merely a revealer," and so forth, [the author concludes] that it cannot possibly exist as a produced substance (*kārya-dravya*), and so on.

Having refuted even the view that liberation consists of the nature of substance, quality, action, generality, and so forth, and having established the final conclusion with such statements as "Therefore, supreme liberation is directly one's own self alone," [the author states]:
"Therefore, supreme liberation is indeed the very nature of the Self, [obscured] by ignorance."
O sinless one, though it has become concealed, it is manifested by knowledge for the pure one.
Because of this conclusion:
"She who loves the *lāsya* dance, who causes dissolution, modesty itself, and she who is worshipped by Rambhā and others. (193)

Lāsya is dancing, which is dear to her. *Laya* is a particular state of the mind, according to the statement: "Laya is equal to the ten stages of meditation. Alternatively, *laya* is the synchronization of dance and song by means of rhythmic beats (*tāla*). She is the one who performs it, the agent thereof. She is the Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of modesty (*lajjā*).
She is modesty arising from remembrance, or she whose essential nature is the *hṛllekhā* seed-syllable;
she is saluted by the Apsarases, such as Rambhā and Urvaśī. || 193 ||
Existence is a rain of nectar for the forest fire of the wilderness of sin;
existence is indeed *saṃsāra*, and it is like a rain of nectar because it extinguishes that forest fire (*dāva*). Existence is indeed *saṃsāra*.
*Dāva* means forest (*araṇya*). According to Amara, *dava* and *dāva* refer to the fires of a forest or a jungle.

Alternatively, because she revives [the world] by raining arrow after arrow upon that [fire], she is like a rain of nectar (*pīyūṣa-vṛṣṭi*). Or, her name consists of three words: a rain such as this which *bhava-datte*—gives *bhavam*, the Supreme Śiva—and *vasu*—possesses *vasu*, jewels and wealth.
That is to say, she is the bestower of both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). And it is said in the *Maṅgalarājastava* of the *Rudrayāmala*:
"Where there is enjoyment, there is no liberation; where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment.
But for the preeminent practitioners of Śrī Sundarī, both enjoyment and liberation are held right in the palm of their hand."

Thus, the "forests" (araṇya) are indeed sins, because they produce suffering; she is so named because she is like a forest fire (davānala) that destroys them, or because she is the forest-fire for the forests of sin. As it is said in the Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa:
The supreme name of Gaṅgā is a forest fire to the wilderness of sin;
Gaṅgā removes the disease of worldly existence, therefore she should be served with diligent effort.

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, the word *dava* refers to forest fires; those who take away (*lāti*)—that is, sustain—the lives (*prāṇān*) of the fires of the forests of sin, which serve as the means for their destruction through practices such as worship, are so called.
The meaning is that they expand the rites that destroy sin. As it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
For every sin committed, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
the supreme expiation is said to be the remembrance of the feet of Parāśakti.
Thus it is said. In that very same other chapter:
"And hear this, O Lord of the Gods, which is a supreme and great secret, the simultaneous destroyer of all sins."
Endowed with devotion and faith, having bathed and remaining within the water,
one should recite the fifteen-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times.
"By propitiating the Supreme Power (Paramā Śakti), one is liberated from all sins," and so forth.
She is a whirlwind for the cotton of misfortune and the radiance of the sun for the darkness of old age. (194)

"Daurbhāgyameva tūlam" means that misfortune itself is the cotton; she is like a "vātūla," meaning a whirlwind (vātyā), which drives it far away. According to Amara, "vātūla" refers to a male [whirlwind] or a gale.
Alternatively, those for whom misfortune is the cotton are "daurbhāgyatūlāḥ"—[those characterized by] misfortune.

The specific qualities [of this goddess] are dispellers of cotton-wool, as it were. For this very reason, those very qualities are "winds" (*vātūla*) through a figurative application (*gauṇyāvṛtti*); thus, the analysis of the compound is: she from whose presence there is "cotton-wool of misfortune" (*daurbhāgyatūla*) by means of those winds. From her presence arise the ritual acts that dispel misfortune.
Or rather, it means "she whose [attributes] are connected [to it]"; that is to say, old age itself is the darkness, and she is like the light of the sun because of her power to destroy it. || 194 ||
She is the moonlight for the ocean of fortune; she is the rain-cloud for the peacocks that are the hearts of devotees.
She is like the moonlight (kaumudī) because she causes the ocean characterized by good fortune to swell;
she is like a rain-cloud (ghanāghanā) because she causes the peacocks that are the hearts of devotees to rejoice.

She whose very nature is like a cloud; or rather, by the word *ghana* itself, clouds are expressed. Since the deeds performed by the Goddess take the form of clouds for the peacocks that are the hearts of her devotees, her deeds are figuratively denoted by that word.
The meaning is that she is "dense" (*ghana*)—that is, continuous and uninterrupted—on all sides by the clouds that are the peacocks of the devotees' hearts.
It is the thunderbolt against the mountain of disease and the axe for the wood of death. || 195 ||
Since diseases themselves are mountains due to their bulk, [the Lord] is like a thunderbolt (*dambholi*) or *vajra* to them;

for according to the Śruti, "I hear of You as the best of physicians among physicians," this word is used exclusively in the masculine gender. Therefore, the usage must be *rogaparvatadambholaye namaḥ* (Salutation to the thunderbolt of the mountain of diseases) alone, and not optionally otherwise.

"Salutation to Dambholī. Alternatively, since the *Agni Purāṇa* states, "The word *svaru* means a hundred-fold [thunderbolt], while *śamba*, *dambholi*, and *aśani* apply to both genders," it is easy to explain that the word *dambholi* is also feminine due to its association with the word *śamba* as well as the word *aśani*. What...?
Having thus prepared the ritual for the successful execution of the practice pertaining to the *Mokṣadharma*, [the author]—

by the mere force of association with the word *niyati* in the phrase "fate (*bhāgya*), woman (*strī*), necessity (*niyati*), and destiny (*vidhi*)"— [refers to] that which is well-known in the masculine gender.

Because we observe the explanation that the word *vidhipada* is in the feminine gender, the occasional usage *dambholaye namaḥ* is consistent with this position. Previously, twenty-eight types of killing were mentioned, distinguished by the divisions of incapacity (*aśakti*), attainment (*siddhi*), and contentment (*tuṣṭi*). Those...

They are called by the term "wood" (*dāru*). Since the term "wood" (*dāru*) has the conventional meaning of the number twenty-eight, they are so designated. By way of punning (*śleṣa*), pieces of wood are also implied; because they cut those [twenty-eight], they are like axes, with the suffix *ka* added in its own sense (*svārthe*).

The *Amara-kośa* states that "an axe" (*kuṭhāra*) refers to two things; and there is the Vedic scripture stating, "Death is its condiment. In these eight names, there is the poetic figure of metaphor (*rūpaka*). || 195 ||
Maheśvarī, Mahākālī, Mahāgrāsā, and Mahāśanā.
Furthermore, "Mahatī" and "Seśvarī" constitute the name "Māheśvarī," as previously explained.
There is no tautology between these two [names] due to their possessing short and long vowel qualities respectively. She is both Mahatī and Kālī.
She is called Kālī because she "drives on" (kālayati). Her greatness in driving on is due to her driving on even Death itself.
And thus says Kālidāsa:
"O Mother, this is so, but that is not"—such doubts characterized by mental constructs remain in our hearts.
He who is indeed Yama, skilled in the sport of restraining living beings, is being driven away by you.

Thus [it is said]. Or, she is the consort of Mahākāla, the lord of the seat (pīṭha) of Ujjayinī. She is one whose "mouthful" (grāsa)—that is, the morsel—is great and immeasurable; for according to the Śruti, "Brahman and Kṣatriya, both of these become her rice-offering.
Alternatively, she is one whose "eating" (aśana) is great because it has the mobile and immobile universe as its object. In this [verse], the third consonant is palatal (tālavya).
Since her name ending in the third syllable was explained previously, there is no tautology. Aparṇā, Caṇḍikā, the destroyer of the Asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa. (196)

She from whom debt has departed is Aparṇā. As it was said by us in the *Devīstava*: "O Śivā, how does the conventional name 'Aparṇā' (debtless) not become a burden to you, while my own debt remains even as I chant your name?"

Thus [it is said]. According to the etymologists (*nairukta*), *parṇa* means "falling"; hence, she is "one who is devoid of falling. Alternatively, it refers to her who, while performing penance, did not possess even leaves (*parṇa*) as food. As it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"Because the daughter of Himavat abandoned leaves (*parṇa*) regarding food, she became [known as Aparṇā]."
Therefore, she was called Aparṇā by the gods upon the surface of the earth.

Thus it is said. In the *Brahma Purāṇa* as well, in the verse: "But Aparṇā was without food; her mother addressed her," this very etymology is suggested by the first quarter-verse. She is *Caṇḍikā* because she is prone to anger (*caṇḍi*) toward those who do not revere her. In the *Devī Bhāgavata*: "Caṇḍikā [was] seven years old."

The word *syāt* refers to the name of a particular maiden. She is so called because she destroys (*niṣūdayati*) those two Asuras, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa; by this, it is indicated that her very name is Cāmuṇḍā. And it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
And because you have come here having seized Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa,
you shall therefore become known in the world as the goddess Cāmuṇḍā.
Thus [it is said]. In the Varāha Purāṇa, however, it is stated:
"And in battle, the Goddess struck that Ruru with her trident;
when the auspicious eyes of that Daitya were struck by her..."
The hide and the head of Ruru, the lord of the Dānavas, both became completely separated from one another at the very moment the hide and the head were beheld.
"Having carried [the head] away, the Goddess practiced [it]; therefore she became Cāmuṇḍā.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, from the lexicon *Karmamoṭī*, which states "Cāmuṇḍā, Carmamuṇḍā, and Carcikā," the name *Carmamuṇḍā* is also seen as a designation for a particular goddess. Therefore, in the *Vārāha[-purāṇa]*—

It is inferred that the reading should indeed be "carmamuṇḍeti sābhavat"; this is another matter. Alternatively, it may mean "the destroyer of those Asuras whose heads (muṇḍa) were fierce (caṇḍa), extremely violent (pracaṇḍa), or possessed of such traits as the redness of the eyes which are signs of extreme anger. [This refers to] those being slain.
By the natural force of the qualifier "possessing such skulls," there is an implied suggestion (*dhvani*) of the form of Kālikā as one who wears such a garland of skulls. || 196 ||
She whose nature consists of both the perishable and the imperishable, the sovereign of all worlds, the sustainer of the universe;
she whose self (ātman) is her own form (svarūpa), consisting of perishable elements of indefinite number and imperishable phonemes (varṇas).
The meaning is that her form comprises both one and many syllables. And it is said in the Varāha Purāṇa:
Renowned as the "Single Syllable," she is auspicious and composed of all syllables;
she alone is the Goddess Viśveśvarī, and she alone is the immeasurable syllable found somewhere beyond reach.
Thus it is said. Alternatively, "the Perishable" (kṣara) refers to all beings, while "the Imperishable" (akṣara) is called the Unchanging (kūṭastha).
She whose nature (svarūpa) consists of both of these is [Māyā]. As stated in the Mahābhārata: "The existent and non-existent, the Perishable and the Imperishable. And likewise in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
Those who know that Viṣṇu has three forms designated as Puruṣa—
the first being the creator of the Mahat, and the second residing within the cosmic egg— [attain liberation].
The third [form] resides in all beings; by knowing these, one is liberated.

Thus she is the sovereign (Īśī) and the mistress (Īśvarī) of all worlds. She is so called because she sustains the universe. She is the bestower of the three aims of life (Trivargadātrī), the auspicious one (Subhagā), the three-eyed one (Tryambakā), and her nature consists of the three qualities (Triguṇātmikā). || 197 ||

The *trivarga* is the group or aggregate of the three—dharma, artha, and kāma; as Amara states: "The *trivarga* consists of dharma, kāma, and artha, while the *caturvarga* includes those [three] along with liberation (*mokṣa*). She is the giver (*dātrī*), devoted to bestowing it. A maiden of five years is called *subhagā*. In the section concerning maidens:
According to the words of Dhaumya, "She should be auspicious (*subhagā*) and five years of age," she is non-different from that [auspiciousness]. Alternatively,
she is one in whom the qualities denoted by the word *bhaga*— such as fortune, majesty, heroism, effort, and fame— are beautiful (*śobhanā*).
[The term *bhaga* is used] in the sense of sovereignty, majesty, knowledge, dispassion, and source;
as well as in fame, heroism, effort, desire, fortune, dharma, splendor, and liberation.

Thus says the *Viśva* lexicon. Or, it is that by which auspicious fortune (*bhaga*)—that is, the Sun—is attained; for in all solar activities, this very power residing within him is the instrumental cause. As it is stated in the second part of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
The entire supreme power of Viṣṇu is known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
this very Trayī blazes away evil and destroys the suffering of the world.
Wherever the sun is month after month,
there indeed that supreme power of Viṣṇu, consisting of the three Vedas, establishes her presence.
The *ṛc* verses scorch in the forenoon, the *yajus* formulas indeed at midday,
and the *sāman* chants, such as the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, when the sun is setting at the close of the day.
This triad known as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman is the embodied form of Viṣṇu;
it is that power of Viṣṇu which eternally abides within the sun.
That Vaiṣṇavī power, consisting of the three Vedas, resides not only in the Sun;
for Brahmā, Puruṣa, and Rudra—this triad is likewise composed of the three Vedas.
Bearing the form of Śakti, Viṣṇu never rises nor does he ever set;
even this group of seven elements is distinct from that Viṣṇu.

Just as a mirror situated on a pillar, when it comes into proximity with someone, attains a connection with that person through the perception of their reflection, so too does the self attain its own [reflection].
In this way, O twice-born one, that Vaiṣṇavī Śakti never departs from there;
month after month, she dwells within the sun situated therein.

Thus: the gods, sages, gandharvas, apsarases, yakṣas, serpents, and rākṣasas—this group of seven is divided according to the sun, which is differentiated month by month, since they serve as its instruments; however, the Power (Śakti), being the primary essence, is not divided.

The collective meaning [of the name] is as follows: Alternatively, she is called *Subhagā* because whatever auspiciousness (*saubhāgya*) exists within the three worlds—whether mobile or immobile—is her very form. Regarding that which is immobile, it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
Sugarcane, the king of trees (mango), flat beans, and quick-growing grain;
likewise, cow's milk that has undergone transformation, safflower, and its flower.

"And salt—this is called the eightfold auspicious stationary [substances] (*sthāvaram-aṣṭakam*). As for the mobile [substances], they are well-known as the *suvāsinīs*. It is stated in the *Pādma* itself:
"The goddess Umā, who consists of the auspiciousness of the three heavens and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation..."
What indeed does one not obtain by devotedly propitiating a fortunate woman?
Thus [it is said]. Here, the first two qualifiers also suggest the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the word *subhagā*.
She is she who has three eyes (*trīṇy ambakāni*). As it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*, in the chapter on etymology (*nirvacanādhyāya*):
"She whose three eyes are the Moon, the Sun, and Fire is [Ambikā]."
Therefore, the goddess is celebrated by the sages as Tryambakā.
Thus, by the rule *pratyayasthātkātpūrvasya*, the penultimate vowel does not become *i* because *āp* follows *sup*. Alternatively, she is the mother (*ambikā*) of the three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
The absence of the substitution of *i* is due to the rule *abhāṣitapuṃskācca*. For this very reason, he says that she consists of the three qualities (*triguṇātmikā*).
Her form consists of the equilibrium of the three qualities (guṇa) whose nature is sattva, rajas, and tamas. || 197 ||

Pure, bestowing both heaven and liberation, and resembling the japa flower in appearance— that happiness which is unmixed with suffering, not immediately swallowed by it, and brought about by desire, is the locus of the term "heaven" (svaḥ).

Thus, the category of pleasure well-known in the scriptures is perishable, whereas liberation (*apavarga*) is eternal pleasure. She bestows both of these. She is pure, devoid of the impurity of ignorance (*avidyā*). Her form and nature are like the *oḍra* flower, resembling the hibiscus; for "form" (*ākṛti*) is said to mean "appearance" (*rūpa*).

The *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon states: "Even for those whose forms are common [to both genders]. Here, by eliding the vowel 'a' (*praśleṣa*), one may also readily accept *ajapā* as a separate word and *dharādharasutā* as a single compound; in that case, *ajapā* refers to a specific type of mantra. Its etymological definition is given in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
O Goddess of the gods, even without recitation, the mantra-practitioner performs recitation;
therefore, this is called Ajapā, which severs the bonds of worldly existence.

Thus: "Puṣpa" means blooming, the menses, the celestial chariot of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), a flower, and also eye-disease—so says the Haimakośa. The meaning is: she whose form is like that [flower].
She is full of vigor, possessing luster, having the form of sacrifice, and devoted to her vows. 198.

"Ojas is the eighth element," according to the Vedabhāṣya; others say it is the capacity of the sense organs. *Ojas* [is used] in the senses of the brilliance of the elements, their support, and their manifestation. "Ojas means strength and luster," according to the Viśvakośa. That which possesses these is *ojovatī*. It is called *dharā* because it supports (*dharati*), formed with the suffix *pacādyac*. From the root *dyut*...
She is the support of splendor. According to the Vedic revelation, "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice," the Goddess is non-different from him and thus has the form of sacrifice;
or rather, sacrifice itself is her form. This is stated in the *Harivaṃśa* and *Padma Purāṇas*, concerning the Lord:
The Vedas are his feet, the sacrificial posts are his fangs, the rituals are his hands, and the fire-altars are his mouth;
Agni is his tongue, Dharma is the hair of his body, Brahmā is his head, and he is possessed of great ascetic power.
The divine one has day and night for his eyes, is adorned by the hearing of the Vedānta,
has the sacrificial ladle for his snout, clarified butter for his nose, and the sound of the Sāmaveda chants for his great voice.
Consisting of the truth of Dharma, glorious, performing the noble acts of successive strides,
having penance for his claws, steadfast, with sacrificial animals for his knees and mighty arms.
The Audgātra is his anus; the signs of the oblation are his great medicinal herbs;
the Vāyu is his inner self; the Mantras are his buttocks; and Soma is his blood.
The altar was his shoulders, the fragrance of the oblation was his scent, and he possessed great speed in carrying the offerings to the gods and ancestors;
the eastern hall was his body, radiant and adorned with various initiatory rites.
The yogin has the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as his heart; he is great, consisting of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*);
he is the Upākarma rite with eight chins, adorned with the whirlpools of the Pravargya ceremony.
He whose path of movement consists of various meters, who is seated upon the secret Upaniṣads,
and who is accompanied by his consort Chāyā, stands as lofty as the peak of Mount Meru.
Or rather:
having propitiated the deity that is the Self by means of the objects such as fragrance, which are apprehended through the doors of the senses,
in their true nature— this is the great sacrifice for the knower.

Thus, she is non-different from the sacrifice taught in the secret teachings of the primary tradition (*mukhyāmnāya*). She whose beloved vows relate without distinction to all the deities. As it is said in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
Whatever vow a man performs dedicated to the God and the Goddess,
all that is for the gratification of Śiva and Śivā, who are by nature the progenitors of the universe.
"No distinction is to be conceived there; the world consists of Śiva and Śakti.
Or [she may be] in the form of the king named Priyavrata. || 198 ||

She is difficult to propitiate, difficult to overcome, and fond of the *pāṭalī* flower. She cannot be propitiated with ease by those whose senses are fickle; "impossible" is the ultimate conclusion. As it has been said: "She is not easily obtained by those of restless faculties. This is of the nature of suffering.

She whose subduing is brought under her own control; she for whom the white-and-red flower named *pāṭalī* is dear. And it is said in the *Pādma Purāṇa*: "Lord Śaṅkara resides in the *śrīvṛkṣa* tree, while Pārvatī resides in the *pāṭalā*."
She is the great one, whose abode is Mount Meru, and who is fond of mandāra flowers.

Because it possesses the dimension of the supremely great (*paramamahatparimāṇa*). Śākapūṇi explains that "great" (*mahat*) is so called because it leaves behind (*jahati*) other things by its measure (*mānena*); however, Yāska’s etymological interpretation is that it is "to be honored" (*mahanīya*). Furthermore, the *mahatī* is a specific type of lute belonging to the sage Nārada, or it may be of the same nature as him.
She whose abode is Meru itself. In the twenty-eighth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*,
beginning with "Now I shall tell you the nature of the sixteen Nityās as the world," and after describing the earth together with its oceans and continents, it is said:
The highly effulgent Lalitā always resides on Mount Meru, situated in the center;
surrounding her, within the limits of the ocean of water, lie the remaining fourteen [lands].

"Outside of that, in the supreme void (parame vyomni), the variegated [wheel] is situated at the end," and so forth; many such specific details have been stated, which are to be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone. Alternatively, there are three expansions (prastāra) of the King of Wheels (cakrarāja), distinguished by the divisions of Bhūmika, Kailāsa, and Meru. Among these:
The Bhū-prastāra consists of the contemplation of differentiation together with the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī.

If it is with the letters of the Mātṛkā, it is the Kailāsa-prastāra. If it is with the sixteen Nityās, it is the Meru-prastāra; indeed, the Meru-prastāra is simply the contemplation of identity with the Nityās.

The meaning is "that which has [this] as its abode. Furthermore, the method of meditation (bhāvanā) is set forth in three ways, respectively, in the three Saṃhitās of Sanatkumāra, Sanandana, and Vasiṣṭha. Alternatively:
Bhūmi, Candra, Śiva, Māyā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇa, Adhva, and Mādana.
The half-moon and the bindu—these nine syllables are called Meru.

Thus, in the *Jñānārṇava*, the nine-syllable mantra has been extracted; it is designated as "Meru," and she whose abode (*nilaya*) is that very mantra—the source from which all mantras arise—is so described. As it is said: "The mantras of Mahātripurasundarī originate from Meru," and so forth. *Mandāra* is a celestial tree or a white *arka*. Of that...
She for whom flowers are dear. || 199 ||

Worshipped by heroes and possessing the form of Virāj— bringing about the dissolution of the "this" (idam) which is the counter-correlate of the "I" (aham), the Supreme One enjoys His own supreme valor, which destroys all inauspiciousness.

She is to be propitiated by the heroes (*vīra*) whose characteristics have been described in such passages as "and so forth. Her nature is that of the *virāja*, whose characteristics were previously stated;
she is the stainless (*virajā*) one who faces in all directions (*viśvatomukhī*).

She from whom dust and evil have departed; the application [of the name] is "Salutation to Virajā. She is the presiding deity of the sacred field named Virajā, located in the region of Utkala. As it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
In Virajā, the mother Virajā was established by Brahmā;
by the mere sight of her, a mortal purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation.

Thus [it is said]. However, the etymologists (nairuktāḥ) maintain that light, water, and the worlds are denoted by the word *rajas*. She whose face is on all sides—that is, without any limitation—according to the Vedic scripture: "She who has eyes on all sides and faces on all sides. It is precisely there that a form is conceived as an object of meditation by the practitioners.

With the intention that [the Lord] manifests right there, there is no contradiction between the statements such as "having hands and feet everywhere; having eyes, heads, and faces everywhere," which refer to His ultimate form, and those such as "handless and footless, yet swift and grasping," which refer to His conventional form. That which moves toward [objects] in opposition [to the senses] is *pratyak*.

Such is her form. The outward orientation of the senses—being directed toward objects, being turned outward, and being averted—is so called. By abandoning that, there is the inward orientation of the inner self—being turned within and facing inward.
It is said: for this very reason it is heard in scripture—“The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self.
She is the inward form, the outward light, the giver of life, whose nature is breath. (200)
The phrase "whose essential nature is perceived inwardly" means, in short, that very thing.
It is the *parākāśa*—the supreme (*para*) and most excellent (*utkṛṣṭa*) space (*ākāśa*). It is in the feminine gender because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatvāt*).
Its meaning is the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*). [As the scripture says: "He said it is space; for space indeed [is superior] to these."

In the *Chāndogya*, in the passage "The greater [than this] is space, the ultimate resort," it is the Supreme Brahman alone that is denoted by the word "space" (ākāśa), not the elemental space (bhūtākāśa);
for this has been determined in the *Brahmasūtra* by the aphorism: "Space [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks. Furthermore, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Of whom that is the supreme..."
"The Goddess Śakti is situated in the ether.
For thus she is the single source of the universe, the soul of all, and the ruler of all;
the power of Maheśvara, established from beginningless time, designated as the Void, shines as if in the heavens.
And thus it is said. Alternatively, she is of the nature of that supreme ether (*parākāśa*), which is established in the "supreme firmament" (*parame vyoman*) as proven by such scriptural passages;

this ether is twofold, distinguished as the macrocosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and the microcosmic egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*), and it is the locus for the manifestation of Brahman. And it has been stated in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*:
O Mother, reveal that Śiva who moves through the sky, situated between the moon and sun of the heart’s activity, whose abode is the vision of fire,
and who is the supreme sky with its upward-pointing peak.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
"The End of the Twelve (*dvādaśānta*) is above the forehead, terminating at the top of the skull;
two finger-breadths above the region of the head, it is proclaimed as the Supreme Space (*paraṃ vyoma*)."
Thus it is said. Alternatively, *parākāśa* is the space beyond the seven oceans.
Therein resides Lalitā, who, being established in her sixteenth year, is metaphorically described as having that form. As it is stated in the *Kādimata*:
"Beginning from the Kṛta age and so forth, she is established in this manner for each successive year."
In the second and subsequent years, those [periods] occur in sequence through revolutions.
In the sixteenth year, Lalitā is in the supreme sky, while Citrā is in the ocean of water;
thus indeed do they undergo their cyclic transformation.

Thus: on the sixteen locations—Mount Meru, the seven continents, the seven oceans, and the supreme ether—in the first year of the Kṛta Yuga, the sixteen Nityās, beginning with Lalitā, Kāmeśvarī, and Bhagamālinī, and ending with Citrā, reside in sequence. But in the second [year],...

In the [first] year, Lalitā descends into Jambudvīpa; Kāmeśvarī, however, proceeds to the salt ocean; and Bhagamālinī, residing there, advances to the region further north than that. In this manner, Jvālāmālinī remains in the supreme ether (parākāśa), while Citrā stays on Meru. In the third year, [she resides] in the salt ocean.

The meaning is that, according to the sequence beginning with *lalitā* and so forth, one should infer that she abides as *citrā* in Jambudvīpa by following the order of the successive locations. Alternatively, the word *parāka* denotes a specific type of *kṛcchra* penance, and by extension, it indicates austerity (*tapas*) in general; its *āśā* (direction) is the goal.
That is to say, the path is to be attained through austerity (*tapas*). Alternatively, it means she "consumes" (*aśnāti*) exertion;

the sense is that she is the enjoyer of the fruits produced by exertion and the like. Or, she "consumes" (*aśnāti*)—that is, destroys—the supreme (*para*) evils (*aka*) and sufferings (*aka*); for the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon states: "The word *aka* refers to both evil and suffering."
The meaning is "incomparable" (anupamā), derived from words such as *upama*, *arthaka*, *pratīkāśa*, *pratispardhin*, and *parākāśa*.

Or, it means that he takes away the fivefold vital breaths (*prāṇas*) or the eleven sense organs; or, he pierces and shatters the vital breaths. [He says: "I am the vital breath, the self of wisdom (*prajñātman*); meditate upon me as life and immortality."
In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, it is established in the Prāṇādhikaraṇa that the word *prāṇa* has Brahman as its ultimate referent.
Therefore, the phrase "having *prāṇa* as her form" means "having Brahman as her form. [As stated: "Prāṇa is Brahman; Kaṃ is Brahman."

And because of the Vedic scripture, "The ether is Brahman. Furthermore, from the verbal root *pṛ* (to fill), by applying the rule *saṃyogāderāto dhātoryaṇvataḥ* which changes the *t* of the past passive participle to *n*, the meaning is "Brahman is full" (*pūrṇam*). This is confirmed by such scriptural passages as, "That is full, this is full," and so forth. And it has been said:
In the *Manusmṛti*: "Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati;
others [call him] Indra, others the Supreme Prāṇa, and still others Maheśvarī."

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, in the *Nityātantra*, starting from the statement "Now, the time of the sixteen Nityās is declared as breath," and so forth, the arrangement of days, months, and so on is taught beginning precisely with the time known as breath (*śvāsa*). This is further stated in such passages as: "Twenty-two and a half breaths correspond respectively to the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*)," and so on.

A unique methodology has been shown, such as the conception of the zodiac signs, the moon, the sun, and so forth, which consists essentially of the vital breath (*śvāsa*). According to that system, the fact that Lalitā is the very self of the vital breath (*prāṇātmatva*) becomes manifest; this is the meaning of the phrase "of that form" (*tadrūpā*). || 200 ||
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to Mantriṇī, he was devoted to the worship of Mārtāṇḍabhairava.
In Śrīpura, within the ground between the twenty-second and twenty-third enclosures, there resides the deity Mārtāṇḍabhairava, a devotee of the Goddess.
And so it was said by the preeminent teacher Dūrvāsas on the occasion of describing that [deity]:
"I consider Mārtāṇḍabhairava to be within my heart— resplendent with a crest of rubies, and performing his play through the shadow of the power that illuminates the eyes."

Thus, it is well known in the Mahārāṣṭra region and in the tantra named *Tantracintāmaṇi* that Śiva, having descended to earth mounted upon a horse for the purpose of slaying the demon named Maṇimalla, is designated by the term Mallāri and is also referred to by the title Mārtāṇḍabhairava.

The propitiation of the Goddess performed by him is also well-known in the *Mallārimāhātmya*. Alternatively, *mārtāṇḍa* means the Sun; for it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Because he was born from a dead egg (*mṛte'ṇḍe*), he is Mārtāṇḍa, and therefore Bhāskara. The change to the single form [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule for *śakandhu* and similar words. The secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix indicates that he was born there. [He is] Bhairava.

The *baṭuka* and others are of many kinds. Regarding that, the fact that [the Sun] is worshipped by the Sun-god is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Having daily worshipped with devotion the gem-like image of the Goddess, Divākara attained the divine and most auspicious state of Sūryatva."
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the fact that Bhairava is the one to be propitiated is established many times in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*.

Alternatively, "Bhairava" means a collection of those who are fearful (*bhīru*). This is supported by the *Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa* in the section on the praise of the Goddess: "O Durgā, when remembered, you take away the fear of all living beings."

She is to be worshipped by all of them through the grammatical principle of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of several identical items). Alternatively, as established in the *Śivasūtra*, "Bhairava is exertion" (*udyama*);
thus, effort is called Bhairava. He alone is the Sun (*mārtāṇḍa*) because he destroys the darkness of delusion.

As it was stated by the authors of the *Vārttika* in the *Sūtra*: "From the victory over delusion, through infinite expansion, there is the innate victory of knowledge. Regarding this, [they explain]: "Delusion (*moha*) is darkness (*tamas*), which is the non-manifestation of one's own nature; from its victory, that is, from its subjugation..."
Arising from the sun of effort, it is infinite, lasting until the complete subsiding of all latent impressions.
For that yogin whose expansive scope is such as has been shown by this [teaching] regarding the self,
there shall be victory and the attainment of innate knowledge.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that she is to be attained by worshipping with a specific exertion [of effort] equal to that of Mārtāṇḍa, [namely] Bhairava.

Mantriṇī is Śyāmalāmbā. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied because the word ends in *n*, following the rule for the suffix *ini* which denotes a mantra expressing deliberations useful for governance (*rājya*). Of her—

She by whom the burden of sovereignty—the weight of the kingdom—has been laid down and cast aside; concerning her, it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* while introducing Rājaśyāmalā: "Whatever deliberations regarding the kingdom were held by the supreme sovereign Lalitā..."
He is under the sway of every discourse concerning even the various powers (śaktis).
Thus it is said. Alternatively: *mantriṇaḥ* (practitioners of mantra) are those who worship mantras;
or, because they possess the nature of protecting through reflection (*manana-trāṇa-dharmavattvāt*), the stainless mind itself is the *mantra*, and those possessing it are the *mantriṇaḥ*.
She leads them—that is, causes them to attain unity with the Blessed Lady—therefore she is the *Mantriṇī*, a specific form of spiritual effort.

In that [state], the secret of the unity of the kingdom— which is of the nature of one's own sovereignty— has been entrusted and established by the minister, such that she possesses the specific property that constitutes the cause of producing that unity.
Furthermore, there is the attainment of unity for practitioners and yogins through a particular kind of effort.

The realized meaning is that [the universe] is dependent upon the Goddess. This very point has been stated in three Śiva-sūtras: "The mind is the mantra; effort is the practitioner; the radiance of the body of the Vidyā is the secret of the mantra.
And it has been said by the blessed Kṛṣṇadāsa:
That by which the supreme reality of one's own self is perceived and contemplated is called *citta*; it is the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the palace of one's own radiance and so forth.
That very [reality], which is the inner Lord, is secretly recited without distinction;
because one's own true nature is recited by means of this, it is therefore called a *mantra* by the teachers.
Because its nature is a surging contemplation whose essence is the continuous connection with full self-identity,
and because its nature is protection that brings about the destruction of saṃsāra, it is called the Sun.
The mind of the worshiper attains identity with that deity through the contemplation of its mantra; and because it is joined with those attributes, the mind itself is the mantra.
And of this aforementioned mantra, whose nature consists of both reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*),
there arises a state characterized by the exertion of support through the continuous contemplation of the mantra as it has been taught.
Effort is indeed an internal exertion, and that alone is truly the means of accomplishment;
for through it, the mantra of the practitioner becomes equal in luster to the deity itself.
By a yogi joined with such a practitioner, the vitality of the mantra— consisting of the contemplation of the fullness of I-consciousness— is attained as it first arises.
Vidyā is that which consists of the supreme realization of non-duality;
he whose body is the Lord Śabdarāśi is so called.
The very radiance of that [consciousness], whose nature is the perfectly complete and all-encompassing I-consciousness throughout the entire path,
is precisely what constitutes the essence of mantras, which possess the characteristics of both contemplation (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*).
"The concealment of meaning from people is called a secret.
For further detail on this, one should consult Kṣemarāja’s commentary (*vṛtti*).
Tripureśī, Jayatsenā, Nistraiguṇyā, and Parāparā. (201)

The name *Tripureśī* belongs to the Sovereign Lady of the Wheel that fulfills all desires; because she is non-different from that [Wheel], this Mother is also called by that name. She is *Jayantī*, meaning she whose army is a multitude of powers (*śakti*) that conquers the demon Bhaṇḍāsura and others, or she who has the nature of a specific king named Jayatsena. [The word] *nirgatam*...

*Traiguṇyam* means the state of possessing the three *guṇas*. She is *parāparā* because her essential nature is expressed by the word *para*, the word *apara*, or the word *parāpara*. Here, *para* means "other," while *apara*—being distinct from that—means "one's own. Alternatively, *para* means "superior" and *apara* means "inferior."

"Brahma-dāsas, Brahma-dāśas, these gamblers are indeed Brahma"—so says the Śruti. "The enemy is one, the friend is another"—this is not so; "to me there is none hateful and none dear"—so says the Smṛti. "Another is far away, another is near"—this is not so; "that [Brahman] is both far away and near"—so says the Smṛti. Another... [is he].
According to the *Viśva* lexicon, the term *kevala* may refer to the Supreme Self (*uttama-ātman*) or to those who are far from it.

Generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). There is also a third, called the intermediate (*parāpara*). Brahman is twofold—distinguished as *kevala* (pure) and *śabala* (variegated)—and is respectively called the higher and the lower. "This indeed, O Satyakāma, is the higher... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.31].
This is because of the Vedic revelation: "Two Brahmans are to be known—the higher and the lower.

And from the Smṛti: "The higher Brahman is the supreme qualification, which is Śakti; the lower is the primary qualificand, which is Śiva. Indeed, it is Śiva alone who is qualified by Śakti through the relationship of essential identity (sāmarasya)."

The Supreme Brahman. By the Śruti text, "I yoke for you both the ancient Brahman with prostrations" (*yuje vām brahma pūrvyaṃ namobhiḥ*), it is stated that among the two of you, I yoke with prostrations the Brahman which is the primary object to be qualified (*viśeṣyabhūta*).
Since there is the designation *pūrvyam* for Śiva—the one who possesses prostrations (*namaḥ-śiṣin*)—the suffix *-yat* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). This is indeed Uṣas.

"In the Vedic revelation, [it is said] 'the beloved of heaven dawns as something unprecedented' (*apūrvyā*); by the Goddess's own designation, *apūrvyā* means distinct from what preceded (*pūrvasmādbhinnā pareti*). This is because here the power that assumes the form of time (*kāla*), consisting of the creative glance at the beginning of creation, is being praised; such is the detailed explanation in the *Śivānandalaharī*. Space (*vyoma*) also..."

It is of two kinds: supreme (*para*) and non-supreme (*apara*). As stated in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, "Knowledge is twofold: supreme and non-supreme. Also, in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "Two Brahmans are to be known: the supreme and likewise the non-supreme."
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda are also there.
Likewise, the Sāmaveda and the Atharvaveda, which accomplish all aims;
as well as phonetics (śikṣā), ritual manuals (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), and prosody (chandas).
And Jyotiṣa is the lower knowledge; it is established that the Supreme Syllable (Parākṣara) is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, and without color.
And so forth, ending with: "That which is unconditioned (*asaṃvṛta*) is the supreme knowledge (*parā vidyā*) itself, and not otherwise.
The *praṇava* is of two kinds: the supreme (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). This has been stated in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa* of the *Skānda*:
The Praṇava is considered to be of two kinds through the division of the higher and the lower:
the higher is the supreme Brahman, characterized by consciousness, bliss, and so forth.
Because it is supremely new by its very nature,
the Supreme Brahman is the other Praṇava, which is directly the form of sound and perfectly pure.
It is remembered as *praṇava* because it is the cause of excellence (*prakarṣeṇa navatva*),
or alternatively, because it is the cause for attaining the supreme *praṇava*.
Thus [it is said]: the meaning of the Veda is twofold, namely the higher (para) and the lower (apara). As it has been stated in that very same work:
"The meaning of the Veda is traditionally held to be twofold through the division of higher and lower;
the higher meaning of the Veda is directly the Supreme, which is higher than the highest."
"Another may possess the notion of Dharma, which is the means for attaining that [higher state].
Thus, in the Yogaśāstra, threefold knowledge is taught—namely, the higher (*para*), the lower (*apara*), and the both-higher-and-lower (*parāpara*)—as follows:
"That knowledge should be known as threefold, according to the distinction between the higher and the lower."
Among these, the first is the supreme knowledge: the vision of the self as distinct from the fetters of the bound soul (paśu).
The second is the supreme knowledge, which is the exclusive vision of the bonds (pāśas),
just as there is a difference in vision at night between the eyes of a human and a cat.

"Thus, knowledge characterized by such distinctions is declared to be supreme (parā), non-supreme (aparā), and both supreme and non-supreme (parāparā). Worship is likewise threefold: supreme, non-supreme, and both supreme and non-supreme. As it is said in the *Nityāhṛdaya*:
'Your eternally manifest worship is established through these three divisions.'"
Gaurī is both supreme and non-supreme, and the third is both supreme and non-supreme.
The first state is abiding in non-duality, which is the sphere of all activity;
the second is the wheel-worship, which is always performed by me.
"Thus, the third Goddess consists of knowledge and consists of her own self-manifestation.
In this way, speech (*vāk*) is twofold: *parā* (the supreme) and *parāparā* (the intermediate). Furthermore, the *aparā* (the inferior) is threefold due to the divisions of *paśyantī* and so forth.
The states (*avasthā*) are likewise twofold: *parā* and *parāparā*. Among these, *parā* is the fourth state (*turyā*). The *aparā*, however—
It is threefold due to the distinctions of waking and so forth. As it has been stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava:
"O Dear One, wherever the mind goes—whether externally or internally—therein the state of Parā is established because of its all-pervasiveness."

Thus, there are two kinds of oblation (*homa*): the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). Among these, the lower is further divided into two types based on the distinction between the gross (*sthūla*) and the subtle (*sūkṣma*). This very point has been stated in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"The well-known gross oblation has its locus in the fire of the *mūlādhāra*."

Having established the subtle fire-sacrifice (sūkṣmahoma), which shares the same characteristics as the Prāṇāgnihotra, at the conclusion of that [treatise] it is said: "The supreme sacrifice (homah) is the abiding state of the objects of speech— the entire range of the known, the knower, and the Self of the giver— resulting from the dissolution of all dualities."
Always within the form of the great flames of the fire of one's own nature,
which, from the perspective of ultimate reality, are stable in the supreme self where the form of fuel has been extinguished.
"But the *parahoma* is proclaimed as that which is without emergence or elaboration.

Thus, a specific mantra included within the *mantrapārāyaṇa* is called *parāparā*. The Goddess is also threefold: *parā*, *aparā*, and *parāparā*. This is stated in the *Varāhapurāṇa* regarding the *trimūrti*:
By nature,
the supreme creation there is said to have the form of the color white;
that which belongs to Viṣṇu is large-eyed and has the form of the color red.
That other one is declared to be Raudrī, who is both supreme and non-supreme;
all three of these are mastered by him who knows Rudra according to reality.
Thus, by dividing the terms *parā* and *aparā* and adding the seventeen meanings, there are five;
thus, [the total] is twenty-two. Others should also be joined according to what is available. || 201 ||

She whose form is truth, knowledge, and bliss, who is devoted to the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*). According to the Vedic revelation: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite; Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss. She is the Real (*satī*).

Those who are ignorant—that is, lacking knowledge—regarding that subject of the sixfold science (sadvidyā), for them it manifests as, or bestows, nothing but suffering, which is distinct from bliss. This is because of the scriptural declarations in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣads: "They enter into blind darkness who worship ignorance. Thus, [the word] "avidyām" [is used].

The *padapāṭha* belongs to the authors of the *padas*. Furthermore, there is corroboration in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, where the *Āraṇyaka Śruti* thus censures the worship of other sciences (*vidyā*). Alternatively, "those whose knowledge is truth" (*satyajñānāḥ*) refers to those for whom ignorance regarding the Goddess Satyavidyā exists.
Because it is heard in the *Āraṇyaka* itself that he "fashions those worlds called Bliss," and because it is heard likewise further on:
"Those worlds named Bliss are enveloped in blind darkness."
To those [worlds] go after death those people who are ignorant and lacking in wisdom.

Thus [it is said]. *Sāmarasya* is the state of Śiva and Śakti, whose essence (*rasa*) is equal—neither deficient nor excessive—and this very state of equilibrium is her supreme resort or abode. And it has been stated by the learned:
"The two are each other's fruit, having become the perfection of each other's asceticism."
We praise the ancient parents of phenomenal proliferation, the husband and wife.

Thus [it is said]. And there is the statement by Kālidāsa: "Śiva is she who yields the essence of *sāmarasya* (cosmic harmony) when the waves of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the instruments have subsided. And there is the Śruti: "He who is equal toward them, whose sattva is equal, and who is the same [in both]. Or, it is the ultimate resort or the support for the world of *sāmarasya* together with the immortals (*amaraiḥ sahitasya*).

The *rasyas* are those which are tasted and sung; they are the *sāmans*. She whose desired goals (*parāyaṇāni*) are those *rasyas*—or rather, she whose desired goals are those [goals]—[is so called]. Due to the inclusion of the term "bahula" (in the rule), there is no obligatory prior placement of the qualifier. According to the *Viśva*, "the word *parāyaṇa* means 'desired' (*abhīṣṭa*), and it also applies to 'supreme' (*para*) and 'refuge' (*āśraya*). [The form] *kaparda*...

This [epithet] signifies abundance, praise, or excellence, based on the traditional rule cited by the commentators of the *Sūtasamhitā*: "The suffixes *matup* and others are used in the senses of abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, and intensity.
Alternatively, she is adorned with a string of cowrie shells (*varāṭaka-mālā*). She is the consort of Śiva in his descent as Mairāla.

The name Mahālasā is derived from the root *pṛ* (to fill) with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), followed by the elision of *r*, resulting in the word *pūrti*, which signifies "filling. Alternatively, when the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is implied and the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), it signifies "one who fills" (*pūra*). Thus, she causes the flow (*pūra*)—the stream—of the Gaṅgā water to be given (*dāpayati*). She is adorned with cowrie shells (*varāṭaka*).

She is called Kapardī because she purifies; from the root *daip* (to purify), with *sup* as an upapada, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto dhātoḥ supi sthaḥ* through a split of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*).
She is the wearer of matted hair, the garland of digits, the cow of plenty, and the one who assumes forms at will. || 202 ||

The meaning is that her matted locks are purifiers even of the Gaṅgā. According to the *Viśvakośa*, "kaparda" refers to the mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭa*) of the one whose axe is broken (Śiva), or to a cowrie shell.
Alternatively, she possesses the form described in the *Laghustava*: "one whose mass of matted hair is adorned with the crescent moon," by way of her majestic power (*ārbhaṭyā*).
Or she is the wife of Śiva, named Kapardin;

for it is recorded in the *Devīpurāṇa*, during the enumeration of the sixty-eight sacred sites (*śivakṣetra*) of Śiva, that "at Chagalāṇḍa [is] Kapardin. She is the garland, the succession, of the arts (*kalā*) in their forms as sixty-four and so forth.

Or, she is so called because she takes (*lāti*) a portion (*kalām*) of beauty (*lāvaṇyam*), splendor (*śobhām*), and me (*mām*). She is the "Cow of Plenty" (*kāmadhuk*) because she milks out desires; the meaning is that she fulfills one's heart's wishes. Or, she has the nature of the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*). For the Śruti says: "May she, the cow who is Speech, yielding for us gentle food and strength, come to us well-praised."

Desire (*kāma*) is indeed the very form of this [Goddess]. The Lord (*īśvara*), who possesses the desire to emit the universe as established by the Śruti—"He desired: 'May I become many; may I procreate'"—is Kāmeśvara. With reference to him, the followers of the Kāṇva school recite: "This person who consists of desire, he is the divine Śākalya; his..."
"Is it a deity? "It is a woman," he said. "Or rather, its forms are according to one's desire. || 202 ||
He is a treasury of arts (*kalānidhi*), a connoisseur of poetic art (*kāvyakalā-rasajña*), and a storehouse of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-śevadhi*).
He is a treasury of the various arts previously described;
for it is stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* that "the sixteenth part is the Self itself," referring to the selves, which are the individual souls (*jīvas*).

Or it is a treasure-trove (*nidhi*). Or it has the form of the lunar disc. In the *Śivasūtra*, "the class of wombs (*yonivarga*) is *kalā*, the body," the word *kalā* is explained in its commentary as referring to karma.
Thus, it is so called because "karmas are deposited (*nidhīyante*) in this"; the suffix *kvip* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Everything...
"O Pārtha, all action culminates in knowledge," according to the Smṛti. The work of a poet is *kāvya*;
and that is of many kinds—such as the *nāṭaka*, *śāṭaka*, *bhāṇa*, *ḍima*, *prahasana*, and so forth—as described in the *Agni Purāṇa* and other sources.
Such a collection of arts is indeed the very form of the Mother. And it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Whatever poetic discourses there may be, and all songs whatsoever—these constitute the body of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears sound as his form."

Thus [it is said]. Or rather, the *kalā* (art/skill) of poetry is simply the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) that produces poetry, for it is frequently described in the *tantras* as bestowing the capacity for poetic composition through a specific form of meditation. Alternatively, it is the *kalā* known as "Reviving the Dead" (*mṛtasañjīvanī*), which is the semen (*śukra*) of poetry; [it consists of] the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) distinguished by the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth.

She is called *rasajñā* because she knows the ten kinds [of flavors], or because her essential nature is the sense-organ of taste (*rasanendriya*). She is the treasure-trove (*śevadhi*) or storehouse (*nidhi*) of *rasa*, which is the nectar of Brahman. For the Śruti declares: "He is indeed *rasa*; for having obtained *rasa*, one becomes blissful. Also, in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
Rasa alone is the supreme Brahman; rasa alone is the highest goal.
For rasa bestows beauty upon men, and rasa is traditionally known as semen.
Indeed, it is said that by attaining rasa, one becomes blissful.
Through the establishment of the authority of the Vedas, the aesthetic flavor (rasa) exists as the vital breath (prāṇa).
"Who indeed could breathe or live if he were other than this?"—thus it is declared in the Śruti.
O Agastya, the essence consisting of the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be the giver of life.

Thus [it is said]. "Nidhi and śevadhi" [are synonyms], according to Yāska. From the *Kośa* (lexicon), the words *nidhi* and *śevadhi* are masculine; therefore, the correct usage is *namaḥ kalānidhaye* ("salutation to the storehouse of arts") and *namaḥ rasaśevadhaye* ("salutation to the storehouse of aesthetic essence"), and not the optional forms *namo nidhyai* or *namaḥ śevadhyai*. [This applies] to the arts (*kalā*) and aesthetic essences (*rasa*).
In the analysis of the compound *nidhiḥ śevadhir yasyāḥ* ("she whose treasure is a hoard"), that [interpretation] is also possible.
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Śrī Bhāsurānanda,
the ninth digit named Viśvā has been completed with the eight hundred verses.
Thus ends the ninth digit (Kalā), named the Eighth Century, in the commentary on the Śrī Lalitāsahasranāma. 9.
The tenth digit, named the Ninth Century, is nourished, ancient, venerable, lotus-born, and lotus-eyed. || 203 ||

She is "Nourished" (*puṣṭā*) because her body consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). She is nourished by many qualities, by the essence of Brahman (*brahmarasa*), or by the Brāhmaṇas. This is according to the Smṛti: "Brahman is nourished by the Brāhmaṇas," and also according to the Śruti: "The lifespan of Brahman is long; it is made long by the Brāhmaṇas."

Because she is the primordial source of all things, she is "purātanī"; the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. Alternatively, it may be derived from the word *purātana* with the possessive suffix *ac*, meaning "she in whom ancient qualities reside," followed by the suffix *ṭāp*. For this very reason, she is "sarveṣāṃ pūjyā"—worthy of being honored by all—or "pratīkṣyā," worthy of being awaited. *Puṣkam* means nourishment (*poṣaṇam*).
She is Puṣkarā because she takes away [sins] at night; or because she is in the form of the holy place (tīrtha) named Puṣkara;
or because she is pervasive (vyāptā), since *ra* and *la* are interchangeable; or because her eyes are like lotuses (*puṣkara*), that is, like water-lilies.
The word *puṣkara* denotes a lotus, the sky, water, the tip of an elephant’s trunk,
a medicinal herb, a continent, a bird, the king of holy fords (Prayāga), and a species of serpent.

"Puṣkara [is used] for the mouth of a wind-instrument, for a reed, and also for the blade of a sword," according to the Viśva lexicon. Likewise, the yoga known as Puṣkara is well-known in the Padma Purāṇa:
"When the Sun is situated in Viśākhā and the Moon is in Kṛttikā..."
This conjunction, named Puṣkara, is extremely rare even at the Puṣkara tirthas.
Thus [it is said]. The word *puṣkara* also refers to the earth. As it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* itself: "O gods, that which is the pericarp of the lotus they call the earth;
those which are the heavy piths within the lotus are the divine mountains here."
Those leaves which belonged to the lotus became the lands of the Mlecchas; those leaves which were on the lower part became the abodes of the serpents, the enemies of the gods.
Thus, for the sake of Nārāyaṇa, the earth was born from the lotus;
because of that manifestation and its arising, it is known by the name Puṣkara.

Thus, the meaning is that she possesses a *kṣaṇa*—meaning either a festival or a state of inactivity—regarding the earth and other objects as far as possible. Regarding the state of inactivity, Amara states: "The word *kṣaṇa* denotes a particular time and a festival.
[In this compound] there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending. Furthermore, the word *puṣkara*, though seen as referring to the *nyagrodha* tree, is also observed here.
For the term *puṣkaradvīpa* is seen to have its etymological derivation based on that very fact in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"In Puṣkaradvīpa there is a banyan tree (*nyagrodha*), and therefore it is remembered as Puṣkara. Also in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"In Puṣkaradvīpa, the banyan tree is the supreme abode of Brahmā. He [the Lord] is the one Prajāpati.
The Śruti also states, "She was born upon a lotus leaf.

Here, Viṣṇu is understood by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) because of his habit of reclining on a banyan leaf. Alternatively, it may mean "she whose glance is a compassionate look. As it is said in the Devībhāgavata:
Then, for Viṣṇu in his infant form reclining upon a banyan leaf,
the Blessed One spoke a half-verse that bestows all goals.
Or, it means "she whose gaze is upon the waters. For there is a Vedic revelation: "These indeed are the four waters—the gods, humans, ancestors, and asuras. (203)

The supreme light, the supreme abode, the supreme atom, higher than the high—the light whose nature is Brahman, which is the highest and most excellent. Regarding this, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* states: "The gods worship that light of lights as life and immortality. There, the sun does not shine... [nor does the moon].
The supremacy [of this light] is established by the Śruti passage, "Neither the moon nor the stars shine, nor these lightnings, much less this fire," and by the Śruti passage,
"By whose splendor the sun shines, kindled with heat. There is also the Śruti passage, "Having reached the highest light," and "May he enjoy the mind as his light through speech."

From such usages as "jyotiṣāsta" (be seated with light), it follows that *jyotis* denotes mere illumination; the sense is that among those [lights], the Self-light (*ātmajyotis*) is supreme. Furthermore, the eight-syllable mantra taught in the fifth chapter of the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* is also called the Supreme Light (*paraṃ jyotis*). It is the Supreme Abode (*paraṃ dhāma*).
It is supreme splendor. Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that;
that is my supreme abode, having gone to which they do not return.
Thus, in the Gītā, the word *dhāma* refers to a state; that which transcends those states is the supreme *dhāma*.
And it has been said by the Teacher: "That which is to be enjoyed and the enjoyer, as proclaimed in the three *dhāmas*..."
But he who knows both of these, while enjoying them, is not defiled.
Thus it is said; and also in the Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa:
"He who is the three abodes of the Veda known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—he alone is the Self, not that which is seen; the visible world is merely imagined within him."
Take refuge in the supreme abode, the witness of the three states, characterized by truth, knowledge, bliss, and the like, which is the referent indicated by the words "thou" and "I."

Thus, the word *dhāma* may refer to the *pada* (the supreme state); that is, the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*). This is according to the Śruti: "That is the supreme state of Viṣṇu. Also, in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "This very Gaurī, the power of Maheśvara, is stainless, peaceful, true, eternally blissful, and the supreme state."

The Śruti as well provides the usage: "Obeisance to the supreme light (parasmai jyotiṣe), obeisance to the supreme abode (parasmai dhāmne). They say that *param* is an indeclinable ending in *m*. Furthermore, because there is an option regarding the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to various rules—such as "and [the word] *aṇu*" (*aṇvī*) from Pāṇini 4.1.44, "from a word denoting a quality" (*guṇavacanāt*)—there is an absence of *ṅīp*. This is seen in the expression "smaller than the small" (*aṇoraṇīyān*).
