The Śruti says: "Durgeya" means difficult to understand. Or, it may mean that even the *pīlava* meters imagined by the logicians (*tārkika*) are merely her form.

Or, she is the supreme, most excellent *aṇu* (atom) or mantra. She is higher than the highest—that is, more excellent even than Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. Alternatively, the measure of Brahmā’s lifespan is called *para*.

Therefore, it is supreme (*parā*), being devoid of such limitation by number. In this regard, its nature as the supreme abode (*paramadhāmatva*) and its nature as the supreme atom (*paramāṇutva*) are the reasons. And it has been shown exactly thus in the *Kālīpurāṇa*:
"Whatever day and night there may be for that which is of the nature of Brahman..."
The square of that is called *tatpara*; half of that is designated as *parārdha*.
That is said to be a day of Īśvara, and his night is of the same duration;
he is considered the coarsest among the coarse and the subtlest among the subtle.
For her there is no distinction between day and night, nor is there a year;
she holds a noose in her hand, is the slayer of nooses, and the shatterer of supreme mantras. 204.

She who has a noose (*pāśa*) in her lower left hand; this is an exception to the rule of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*), as it occurs after a word ending in the locative case or a past passive participle used in the sense of an instrument (*praharaṇārthe*). Alternatively, she "nooses with the hand" or "casts [things] with the hand.
She is the destroyer or the annihilator of nooses. And it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*:
To that hero Aniruddha, who was bound by the serpent-noose with his mind overwhelmed,
she spoke after tearing apart with her hands the serpent-cage which was like a diamond fortress,
while he remained imprisoned in Bāṇapura.
And then that queen, seeking to appease him, became inclined toward favor.

And so forth. [The text] distinguishes the mantras of others—namely, kings who hate one's own worshippers—from the specific powers included within the triad of powers known as *prabhu* (sovereignty), *mantra* (incantation), and *utsāha* (enthusiasm). Alternatively, [it refers to those mantras] employed by others for the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and the like.

*Manuḥ* refers to a supreme mantra employed by an enemy, or a mantra for a weapon (*astra-mantra*). As it is stated in the *Harivaṃśa*, in Indra’s message to Pradyumna: "In order to counteract that weapon, you ought to remember the Goddess here. Alternatively, *para* means the most excellent mantra, which is the form of the *Pañcadaśī*.
He causes division:
Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, and Manmatha;
Agasti, Agni, Sūrya, Nandin, Skanda, and likewise Śiva.
The Lord Krodhabhaṭṭāraka and the Goddess—these twelve are the lay practitioners (*upāsakas*).

Thus, according to the method taught in the Tantra, he performs it in twelve ways. Alternatively, he shatters—that is, destroys—the sins (*avī*) of those who are supreme (*parā*) and most excellent (*utkṛṣṭa*) thinkers (*mantāraḥ*), that is, those who perform reflection.
In the Vedas, the twice-born declare that the word "avi" refers to sins;
since [this place] has not been abandoned by me even though it was freed from them, it is therefore remembered as Avimukta.
Thus, in the Liṅga Purāṇa, it is stated that the word *avipada* has the sense of "sin. || 204 ||
The swan of the mind of the sage is never satisfied with the manifest and the unmanifest.

"Manifest" refers to that which possesses form, such as earth and so forth; "unmanifest" refers to that which lacks form, such as air, space, and so forth—this is the meaning of the two names. Alternatively, the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) composed of the fivefold combination (*pañcīkṛta*) are "manifest."

But the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) that have not yet undergone quintuplication (*apañcīkṛta*) are formless (*amūrta*). For in the Śruti passage, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman, the formed and the formless," two interpretations are observed:
either [the gross elements and the unevolved matter] are the formed and the formless, or the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Brahman are the formed and the formless.
That Brahman has two forms, both manifest and unmanifest;
these two, consisting of the perishable and the imperishable, abide within all beings.

"Brahman is the immutable, the peak, while this entire world is the mutable"—as seen in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*. Since the logical construction of the Naiyāyikas—that "embodiment" (*mūrtatva*) consists in possessing action characterized by motion—is baseless, it is not to be trusted. [The Lord] is satisfied with transient offerings alone.

It is called "five-syllabled" because it is dear solely through devotion. Alternatively, the meaning of the word *aniti* is "the living being," as it breathes (*aniti* = *śvasati*). Although the rule *ikśtipau dhātunirdeśe* prescribes the suffix *tip* when indicating a verbal root, in this context the term *animiḥ* refers to the meaning of the root. [As in the Vedic injunction: "In sacrifices, [one recites] *ye yajāmahe*..."

For we see the usage of the verb even when its object is expressed, as in the Vedic text *karoti* ("he does"), in Jaimini’s sūtra *itikartavyatāvidher yajateḥ pūrvavatvam*, and in Vyāsa’s sūtra *īkṣaternāśabdam*.
Therefore, the meaning is that [the Lord] is not satiated by the individual souls (*jīvas*). This is shown in the passage: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kshatriyahood are the rice."

Because, according to scripture, it consumes everything. Or rather: "in this manner" (*iti evamprakāreṇa*), she is not unsatisfied—that is, she does not fail to be satisfied. Two negatives convey the original affirmative meaning.
There is no such manner by which she would not be satisfied; on the contrary, she is indeed satisfied by every possible manner.
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water— that offering made with devotion by one of purified soul, I accept.
By this statement, it is declared that even whatever is given with mere devotion serves to bring about satisfaction.
The mind of the sages is itself called "Mānasa" through a pun; there she is like a female swan (*haṃsī*).

[The suffix] *ka* is used in the sense of the base word itself. Alternatively, she is like one accompanied by a swan (*sa-haṃsikā*)—that is, as if equipped with anklets (*pādakaṭaka*)—in the honor (*māna*) of the sages, which is the object of their great respect. The intended meaning is that she dances, as it were, due to the joy they feel because of her honor.
The *Haṃsaka* lexicon states that *pādakaṭaka* means "anklet.
She is Satyavratā (she whose vow is truth), she whose form is truth (*satyarūpā*), the inner controller of all (*sarvāntaryāmiṇī*), and the virtuous one (*satī*). || 205 ||

Truth is indeed the vow (*vrata*); she for whom that [truth] is dear is, by figurative usage, one whose vow is truth. This is because we see the word "vow" used in the sense of something to be consumed in the Vedic text: "The milk-vow belongs to the Brāhmaṇa. Alternatively, she is one who is attainable through a vow consisting solely in the observance of truthful speech.

Up to this point: [it refers to] the truths or the vows that yield fruit quickly; for it is described in the *Viṣṇu-bhāgavata* that the vows to Kātyāyanī performed by the gopīs for the sake of attaining Kṛṣṇa bear fruit very swiftly.
To one who has surrendered even once and entreats me, saying "I am yours," I grant fearlessness in every way; this is my vow.

Or, it means that for her, the vow spoken by the Blessed One is unfailing. Alternatively, according to the *Śivasūtra*, which states that "the function of the body is the vow" (*vrataṃ śarīravṛttiḥ*), even the maintenance of the body is indeed the vow.
[The name refers to] that which has its function within a body filled with the nectar of devotion to Śiva.
"This vow is to be performed; that maintenance [of the body] is not trivial," according to the *Vārttika*. That such a vow is true and necessary—she [is she] by whose devotion it is so.
For this very reason, the maintenance of the body was requested by the venerable Bhaṭṭotpala:
May this body of mine, nourished by the nectar of my own pure power that wells up within, be for the enjoyment of Your worship.

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, there was a Brahmin named Satyavrata who, out of fear of a boar, uttered "Ai Ai! and by that much alone, through his austerity, became a great poet and a devotee of the Goddess; because of his non-difference from her, she is called Satyavratā.
This is stated in the third book of the Devībhāgavata:
There was a twice-born man named Satyavrata, who was illiterate and a great fool;
having heard a syllable from Kola’s mouth, he then uttered it himself.
Due to the omission of the nasal drop (bindu), he was born as that most excellent of the wise;
however, at the mere utterance of the vowel 'ai', the Blessed Lady was then pleased.

"The Supreme Goddess, moist with compassion, made him a king of poets," and so forth. "Satyam" means she whose form is unimpeded throughout the three periods of time. Alternatively, by adding the possessive suffix *ac* to the word *rūpa*, it may mean "she who possesses a true form. Or, she is the "protector of truth."
...up to this point. And thus the Bahvṛcas recite: "Truth and falsehood contended as two words;

of these two, that which is truth, whichever is more upright—that indeed Soma protects; he slays the untrue. The meaning is that Soma is accompanied by Umā. He is the regulator of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of all. This is for you.

From the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa: "The Self is the inner ruler, immortal"; and from the Māṇḍūkya Śruti: "This is the inner ruler; this is the source of all. Alternatively, [the compound] may mean "she who is both all and the inner ruler. The meaning is that she is the essential nature of all things and has entered into all as their infinite self.
For the Śruti says: "Having created that, He entered into it; having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat). And the Smṛti says:
"Because of His knowledge of everything at all times, He is the origin and the dissolution of everything."
It creates both the existent and the non-existent; therefore, it is called "all."

Thus [it is said]. She is Satī because of her devotion to her husband and because of her virtuous nature; this is the name of the daughter of Dakṣa. Regarding Haimavatī, it is stated in the Brahma Purāṇa:
"That goddess was formerly Satī, and afterwards she became Umā."
"Bhava himself shares the same vows; Bhava is not released by her alone. || 205 ||

Brahmāṇī, the mother of Brahmā, multiformed, and worshipped by the wise; she is of the nature of Brahman. *Aṇī* refers to the tail. The name *Māṇḍavya* is applied to the sage Māṇḍavya merely because he was marked by the tip of a stake (*śūlāgra*). *Aṇi* means the small peg at the end of an axle.
"Āṇī occurs in the sense of 'tail' and 'the boundary of fire,' according to Śāśvata.
This means she is the form of Brahman that serves as the tail within the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*).

There is also a scriptural text stating, "The two *āṇīs* of Brahman. Alternatively, she is called *brahmāṇī* because she brings forth or gives life to Brahman; she is *brahmāṇī* because she gives birth to Brahman.

"Or by the life of Brahmā," according to the *Devīpurāṇa*. The word "Brahmā" refers to Pitāmaha (the Grandfather), or it may refer to his wife. Or, "Brahman" is that knowledge distinct from one's own self which is to be attained by the liberated. This has been stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
That knowledge which is designated as Brahman is that in which all distinctions have subsided, which is pure existence alone, beyond the reach of words, and to be realized by the self.

Thus [it is said]. She is the "Mother" (*jananī*) because she brings forth the entire manifold of phenomenal existence (*prapañca*). Here, in accordance with the natural flow of the primary recitation beginning with the letter *va* and with the desire to maintain consistency with the aforementioned *Devīpurāṇa*, the single compound *brahmajananī* is to be understood as being intended to provide an etymological definition (*nirvacana*) of the term *Brahmāṇī*.

It is proper to accept this. In this view, in the phrase "the inner ruler of all" (*sarvāntaryāmiṇī*), the word *sarva* (all) must be understood as a separate term. Nor does this lead to a contradiction with the context of the section on names beginning with the letter *sa*, such as *antaryāminī*, because the state of being the inner ruler of all follows from the term *antaryāmin* itself without further qualification.

Since the position that [the name] consists of a single word has been established, it is appropriate to describe its meaningfulness by avoiding the consequence of rendering all the other words useless and by not contradicting the context of the recitation (*prāyapāṭha*). This is because we observe such names as *Viśvamātā*, *Jagaddhātrī*, *Viśālākṣī*, and *Virāgiṇī* within that same context; therefore, the name to be cut off should be understood as being at the very beginning of that group.

And because the rule is not eternal. He says "multiform" (*bahurūpā*) precisely because she is the progenitor of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). She is one whose forms are many. As it is said in the *Devīpurāṇa*: "She is multiform because she is beyond form and other states, and her nature is action. This is so even though she consists of the contemplation of the Supreme Brahman.

The meaning in this context is that she possesses "multiformity" (*bahurūpatva*) because she performs various actions, such as the slaying of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, and thus assumes those respective forms. Accordingly, there is a sūtra by Gauḍapāda:
"For the purpose of slaying the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, she who is one indeed becomes many. Furthermore, in another section of the Devīpurāṇa:
She who possesses many forms, both stable and moving—
divine, human, and animal— is therefore Śivā, the multiformed one.
Thus it is said; and in the Sūta-saṃhitā: "I bow to Her who is higher than the highest, who exists as one, as two, and likewise as sixteen, or divided into thirty-two forms."
Thus [it is said]. It is twofold, consisting of vowels (*svara*) and consonants (*vyañjana*). Due to the sixteen distinctions of the vowels beginning with *a*, it is sixteenfold.

Due to the distinctions of the consonants beginning with *ka*, it is thirty-two-fold. The commentators on that [text] state that this is because *la* and *la* are not distinct, and because the letter *ha*—being the root of all—is not counted among the individual [consonants].

By proximity, it is also easy to say that this consists of thirty-two words, intended to describe the letters that constitute the beginning of the *Sahasranāma* (Thousand Names), with thirty-three being the maximum. In the *Bhāgavata* as well, it is said: "She who shines like a dancer in the form of Lakṣmī, Vāk, and others. And in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:
The universe is to be known as manifold, and she exists everywhere;
therefore, because of her many forms, the auspicious Śivā is considered to be multiform.
Thus [it is said]. She is Bahurūpā (the Many-formed) even as the consort of those Rudras celebrated in the Śruti as "the countless thousands of Rudras who are upon the earth.
As it is stated in the Vārāha Purāṇa:
That fierce, tamasic power is proclaimed as Cāmuṇḍā;
she exists divided into nine crores of distinct forms of Cāmuṇḍā.
That which is the Rājasa power and the Vaiṣṇava power of protection has eighteen crores of divisions proclaimed.
O Earth, that power of Brahman which abides in the quality of purity (sattva) is proclaimed to be infinite;
within all its various divisions, it exists individually and one by one.
The Blessed Lord Rudra is the husband of all [the goddesses] because he is omnipresent;
as many great powers (mahāśaktis) as there are, Śaṅkara has assumed that many forms and always dwells with them in the form of their husband.
And Rudra becomes gracious toward those whom he propitiates.
"Then those goddesses grant success to the practitioner; there is no doubt in this.
With all this in mind, it is stated in the *Nārasiṃhopapurāṇa*: "Umā herself exists in many forms as the wife [of Śiva]. And likewise in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*:
Lopāmudrā, Saubhāgyā, and Mahāvidyā Ṣoḍaśī—
these, O fair-faced one, are said to be the wives of Paraśiva.
Śyāmalā, Śuddhavidyā, Hayārūḍhā, and Parāpriyā—
these are to be known as the consorts of Sadāśiva, O Supreme Goddess.
O Śivā, Vārāhī is of great significance and twelvefold;
Bagalāmukhī is the fourth; and Śrīparā is Bhuvaneśī and Śāmbhavī.
Listen to the truth regarding the wives of that very Rudra; there is no doubt about it, O beloved:
they are Śrī, Tiraskariṇī, Lakṣmī, Miśrā, and Kāmakalā.
Annapūrṇā is known as the wife of Viṣṇu,
and Vāgvādinī and Bālā are the two wives of Śiva and Brahmā, O auspicious one.
The nine messengers, Hasantī, the nine Siddhas, and these other deities— O beautiful one, these and many other forms are yours.

Thus, even the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the term *bahurūpā* is found in various forms in every Mahāpurāṇa, Upapurāṇa, and Tantra; however, it is not written here for fear of prolixity. She is "honored" (*arcitā*), meaning worshipped by the wise who possess knowledge.
O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me:
the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom.
Thus, from the statement in the Gītā:

"The progenitor" (prasavitṛ) means she who has brought forth, or given birth to, the manifold world consisting of ether and the rest, or the subjects (prajā), in an eminent manner; hence she is the progenitor.
Thus it is said in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "And because he causes the procreation of living beings, he is called Savitṛ. Also in the Bhagavatī Purāṇa:
"From her alone have emerged all beings, from Brahmā down to the immovable [plants]."
From whom the world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), has emerged.
We praise that very Supreme One, the progenitor of all things. Thus [it is said].
In this context, the words "third" and "fourth" refer to the number eight syllables, while the other two refer to the number four syllables. || 29 ||
She is Pracaṇḍā, the Command, the Foundation, and she of manifest form. || 206 ||
She whose messengers are exceedingly fierce and wrathful; [the root] *caḍi* means "to be angry. For this very reason, the Śruti says: "From fear of him the wind blows.
No beings are afraid of him whose anger is not even the slightest.
How can one protect this policy for a ruler whose subjects do not fear him?

Thus says Kāmandaka. Indeed, because it possesses the characteristic of instilling fear, the word *vajra* (thunderbolt) in the Śruti—"A great fear, a raised thunderbolt"—is stated in the *Kampa-nādhikaraṇa* to refer to Brahman. And *caṇḍā* is the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* plant, so called because it is the object of intense (*prakṛṣṭā*) affection.
Or [the name] *yasyāḥ*; or *pratāpaśīlā*.

*Caṇḍā* means "wealth-stealing" and refers to the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* plant; *caṇḍa* means "extremely irascible. *Pracaṇḍa* means "difficult to bear" and refers to the white oleander (*śvetakaravīra*); *pratāpinī* means "glowing with majesty."

Thus says the Viśvakośa. *Ājñā* (the command) is, in the Veda, the will of the Blessed Lord, synonymous with impulsion (*pravartanā*) and prohibition (*nivartanā*). For this very reason, there is the statement of Śiva in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
For, upon investigation, this is neither the primordial nature nor the individual soul, nor is it a modification;
rather, it is my eternal command that issued from my mouth in the past.
The five-faced one, highly fortunate, bestows fearlessness upon the worlds.
Thus [it is said]. In the Śiva Purāṇa as well, it is stated: "This command of Rudra is established; indeed, by this Mother (Ambā), liberation is attained.
Therefore, even the single syllable "Jña" is well-spoken. Its meaning is "the nature of the Puruṣa who experiences the guṇas.
This is because the Laiṅga Purāṇa states: "By the word 'jña', they speak of the Puruṣa who enjoys the guṇas. Furthermore, "jña" refers to Viriñca (Brahmā).

Regarding "Budha," according to the lexicon (*kośa*), it means "gentle" (*saumya*); or else, it refers to the essential nature of the ordinance of Budha. Furthermore, the Śruti states: "The Knower (*jña*) is the Time of time, the possessor of qualities, and all-knowing. It is called *Pratiṣṭhā* because the entire universe is established within it due to its being the substratum of the whole world;
for the Śruti says, "It is the support (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the entire universe. And it has been said:
In the *Brahmagītā*: "This supreme Goddess Prajñā is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of all things.

The *chandas* consisting of sixteen syllables is also *pratiṣṭhā*. Furthermore, a specific *kalā* (phase) residing in the water-element (*jalatattva*) is also *pratiṣṭhā*. And its definition is given in the Śaiva Āgama:
That by which the self, colored by passion for Śiva, is established in the state of the Puruṣa,
should be known as the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā.

Thus [it is said]. [The word *pratiṣṭhā* means] merely a place of establishment; according to the *Viśva* lexicon, it also means respect, the completion of a sacrifice, and a four-syllabled verse (*padya*). Here, we have determined in the *Chandobhāskara* that the word *padya* should be explained as referring to a foot [of a verse]. *Prakaṭā* (manifest) means being experienced by all.
Such is her form. It is stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"All living beings know Him through the guise of the notion of 'I';
nevertheless, due to *māyā*, they do not know Him in His true nature as Śiva."

Thus: the Yoginīs called *Prakaṭā* (Manifest) are those situated in the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*), or they possess that form. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *aprakaṭā* (Unmanifest), meaning "of secret form. Or [it may be read as] *apsu prakaṭā* (Manifest in the waters);
for according to such Vedic texts as "She alone sustains the greatness of the waters" and "The waters indeed are all this," [she is manifest within them]. || 206 ||
She is the Mistress of Life (Prāṇeśvarī), the Giver of Life, and the embodiment of the fifty sacred seats (pīṭhas).
She is the "Mistress" (Īśvarī) because she presides over the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the sense organs (indriyas);
for it is stated in the aphorism *jyotirādyadhiṣṭhānaṃ tu tadāmananāt* [Brahma Sūtra 2.4.13] that the light and other elements have her as their presiding deity.
This is because the existence of a presiding deity for that [prāṇa] has been established;

or rather, it is the sovereign lord of the fivefold vital breath (prāṇa), according to the Śruti: "The breath of the breath. Or, "pra" means preeminent and "aṇa" means sound in the form of the Veda; its mistress is the deity who is the object of its exposition. All the Vedas...

This is because of the Vedic revelation: "They reach that state. She is the giver of life-breaths (*prāṇa*), the sustainer of the entire world, or the giver of the eleven sense organs; for in the scripture, "When the life-breath departs, all the *prāṇas* depart after it," the word *prāṇas* refers to the sense organs. Thus [it is so].

This is because it is seen in the commentaries, because the seven courses have been specifically distinguished, and because such a determination was made in the second section (adhikaraṇa). This word "fifty" refers here, by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), to fifty-one, due to the proximity-based relationship with its primary meaning. For this very reason:

In the verse from the *Śāradātilaka*, "The body of eternal bliss [flows] by means of the fifty phonemes flowing without interruption in succession," the word "fifty" (*pañcāśat*) is explained by Harṣadīkṣita as referring specifically to fifty-one; this is generally the case.

In common usage, the application of words such as "ten," "twenty," and so forth, as well as "hundred" and "thousand," is frequently observed even when there is a deficiency or excess of one, two, or three units, and also when there is a desire to express merely a plurality. Alternatively, it may be an elliptical restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*) based on the principle that "a hundred is [contained] within a thousand."

For instance, we observe that regarding the Lord of the World, there is the usage "the nine incarnations" (*navāvatāra*) and "the ten incarnations" (*daśāvatāra*), which occurs by taking some intermediate limiting condition (*upādhi*). What more need be said? Even the word "thirty-two" (*dvātriṃśat*) [is used] for thirty-five consonants in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*.

This has already been explained previously. Here, however, because the *antarmātṛkā* nyāsa employs only fifty *mātṛkās*, or because of the non-distinction between *la* and *la*, or because of the absence of the letter *kṣa* as a separate entity, it is placed only on the *meru* of the rosary (*akṣamālā*).

Even if it is conventionally referred to as the "fifty mother-letters" (*pañcāśanmātṛkā*) because there are fifty jewels (*maṇi*), its status must still be stated as being beyond fifty-one. For this very reason,
even in the section concerning the external placement of the mother-letters (*bahir-mātṛkā-nyāsa*):
"His face, arms, middle, and chest are divided by the fifty letters," and "His face, arms, feet, belly, and chest are fashioned from the distinctions of the fifty phonemes"—
such are the usages of poets.

Having stated the assignment (*nyāsa*) of the fifty-one [phonemes], at its conclusion, the applications found in tantras such as the *Jñānārṇava*— namely, "this one whose form consists of the fifty letters, adorned by Kandarpa and the Moon," and so forth— are also rendered consistent.

Precisely because they share the same security and well-being (*yogakṣema*) as the *mātṛkā*, the fifty [deities] beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, as well as the fifty-five [deities] beginning with Keśava and so forth, are also exclusively focused on the fifty-one [energies] in their applications in the *Tantrasārasaṃgraha* and other works. Therefore—

The meaning is that her form consists of the fifty-one sacred seats (*pīṭhas*), beginning with Kāmarūpa and ending with Icchāchatra. For this very reason, within the *Ṣoḍhā-nyāsa*, there is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the fifty-one sacred seats. And it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:

More clearly: from "Then one should place the fifty seats and the one wheel" up to "one should install them in the locations of the letters, conjoined with the sequence of the letters. Also in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"O Goddess, O Beloved, one should install the seats in the locations of the Mātṛkās," beginning thus, [it continues] "these are the seats."

By the statement "they are designated as abiding in the form of the *mātṛkā*," the fact that there are exactly fifty-one [phonemes] is made manifest through the mention of the locus of the *mātṛkā*. In its commentary as well, [it states that] for each one from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*...

It has been stated that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) by first uttering the individual phonemes and then [placing them] in their respective locations. By this, due to the inherent force of such names, even in the *pīṭha-nyāsa*, there are exactly fifty [phonemes], excluding the position of the letter *kṣa*; such is the view of the authors of the *Sundarīmahodaya*.

The *lekha* (written text) is not to be respected because it consists of mere audacity; for this name does not have the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), by which there would be an exclusive restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) to a single seat (*pīṭha*) in the ritual placement of seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*). Nor [is it authoritative], as it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"From the collection of fifty seats... [and so forth].
One should place the arrangement of the fifty seats (pīṭhas) upon the site in the manner of the Mātṛkās.

Thus, it must be stated that the conclusion is established by both the opening and the closing statements, because it has been stated that the term "fifty" refers to fifty-one; otherwise, the enumeration of fifty-one in that very context would be untenable. For this very reason, [the text mentions] Kāleśvara...
To claim that the reading "mahāpīṭhaṃ praṇavaṃ ca jayantikā" is imaginary and to assert that only the reading "mahāpīṭhaṃ jayantikā" is authoritative is sheer audacity;
for the reading with "praṇava" alone is supported by the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, which states: "oṃkāraṃ ca jayantikā."

Because it is authoritative. In reality, however, one must accept that in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the word "mountain" (*giri*) is enumerated separately from Meru, as in the passage: "The mountain is Meru, and from that, the mountain [is others]. This is because the clear opening statement, "the fifty-one seats," would otherwise be untenable through any other interpretation. Therefore...

And because there is an intervention by a word; for thus it is said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Then Jaleśa, the Malaya mountain, Meru, and likewise Girivara," and in the *Jñānārṇava* as well: "Malaya is the great pīṭha, Śrīśaila, and Meruka the mountain. Due to the agreement between these [texts] and the natural sense of the distinct words, [it refers to] Mount Meru.

And because the natural force (*svārasya*) of this non-statement [indicates otherwise], it must be accepted exactly so; and it has been established in that very way in the *Subhagārcā*, the *Ratnasubhagārcā*, the *Pārijāta*, and other manuals (*paddhati*). Furthermore, the seat (*pīṭha*) known as Girinātha is well-known among the Easterners. By this, [the reference to] the *Jñānārṇava*...
Just as it is said, "O Goddess, O Beloved, at the end of each of the fifty-fold Gaṇeśa-nyāsa,

one should perform this [nyāsa] like the Mātṛkā-nyāsa," and as it is also said, "O Goddess, O Sinless One, at the end of the Kāmarati-nyāsa, one should always perform [the nyāsa] with the letters of the Mātṛkā,
just like the Mātṛkā[-nyāsa]," so too, at the end of the Pīṭha-nyāsa, one should always [perform it] like the Mātṛkā[-nyāsa].

The uniformity [of the procedure] is established by the statement "one should perform the nyāsa," because since fifty-one [syllables] are specifically mentioned for the external mātṛkā-nyāsa, it is proven that the same applies here as well to achieve parity with that;
furthermore, since consistency with other tantras is possible, it is improper to abandon it. In the present case...

If there is such insistence that exactly fifty-one words are required, then let the word *rūpa* be explained as referring to the number one; for this is seen to be the interpretation given by Halāyudha and others in their commentary on the Piṅgala-sūtra, where they state "there is a zero in *rūpa*. This is the general direction [of the argument].
Unfettered, dwelling in solitude, the mother of heroes, and the progenitor of the sky. || 207 ||

The "chain" (śṛṅkhalā) is the bondage of karma and so forth, because it serves as a means of confinement like an iron fetter. For this very reason, it has been said by the learned: "O Lord, cut away even my heap of merit, just as you have [cut away] my mass of sins."
Whether the chain for the feet be made of gold or of iron, there is no difference between them.
Thus: she whose fetters have departed, because injunctions and prohibitions pertain only to those possessed by ignorance;
or, "the naked one," because such forms of the Goddess are seen in the sacred seats (pīṭhas) such as Alampura and others.
One should thus remember her, who causes the class of bound souls (paśus) to be deluded upon seeing their own [limited] nature.

Furthermore, because of the visualization of the *tiraskariṇī* (the veil), it is appropriate that such meditation does not depend on another curtain; for the *Viśva* lexicon states that *śṛṅkhalā* refers both to the girdle-fastening of a garment and to a chain. A secluded place (*vivikta*) is a location devoid of people, and it is also pure (*pavitra*). This applies everywhere.

"Where the earth is pure, the world is not seen"—so says the Hārīta-smṛti. According to the Amarakośa, "vivikta" means both "pure" (*pūta*) and "solitary" (*vijana*); thus, both a place that is solitary—whether its people be pure or impure—and a place that is pure—even if it is not solitary—are called *vivikta*. However, in this context, what is intended is solitude (*vijanatā*) accompanied by purity. In such a place...

She remains present; that is, she remains present through the experience of her manifestation even amidst the oppression of impure people, or among those whose nature is the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self. Or, "vīrāḥ" refers to the foremost of practitioners who have been slain facing the enemy in battle; their mother is the progenitress, for she is the bestower of benefit, [the source] of the heroism of the wine.

Regarding the word *bhājane*, according to the *Viśvakośa*, it means a drinking vessel; thus, she is "the mother of that" (*tanmātī*). Alternatively, she is the "Mother of Vīra" (*vīramātā*), because the lord of the Gaṇas named Vīra was accepted as a son by the Mother. Accordingly, in the *Padmapurāṇa*, concerning Vīraka, there is this statement of Śiva:
O Goddess, this very Vīraka is always dear to my heart;
at the gateway of the various wonders, he is worshipped by the hosts of the Lord of Ganas.
After hearing such praise of him,
the Goddess said:
"O Destroyer of Cities, I have long felt a longing for such a son."
When shall I behold such a son, the giver of joy?
Śiva said:
"O slender-waisted one, let this very boy be the cause of joy to your eyes;
through you, even Vīraka shall have his purpose fulfilled as a son."
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the daughter of the king, eager for joy, dispatched her friend Vijayā to quickly bring Vīraka.
And so forth. She is the progenitor, the mother, of the sky (viyat), that is, of space (ākāśa), according to the Vedic scripture: "From the Self, space was produced. || 207 ||
She is Mukundā, the abode of liberation, whose form is the primordial body (*mūlavigraha*).
She is called *Mukundā* because she bestows liberation (*mukti*); this is according to the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular formations]. Alternatively, it is because she is the very form of Viṣṇu.
As it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*, at the beginning of the section on the various mantras of Gopāla:
Sometimes the primordial Lalitā, assuming a male form with a body like that of Kṛṣṇa,
rendered the world helpless by beginning to play her own flute.
Then he was surrounded by his own powers known as the Gopīs;
at that time, for their diversion, he divided his own body into six parts.

And so forth. Or, she is in the form of various jewels and the like. According to the *Viśvakośa*, "Mukunda" refers to Puṇḍarīkākṣa (Vishnu) and also to a type of gemstone, as well as to mercury (*pārada*). She is the *nilaya*—the source or repository—of the fivefold liberations (*mukti*).
She is the embodiment of Rājarājeśvarī, who is the fundamental ground of the powers (*śakti*) such as Bālā, Bagalā, and others.

That very [form] is her form. Thus, the ten sūtras of Gauḍapāda, beginning with "She is indeed Vidyā" and ending with "she herself in an upward form," establish that the single Vidyā has a threefold nature through the distinctions of Śāmbhavī-vidyā and Śyāmā; and regarding each one of those...
Those who know the true nature of existence specifically demonstrate that she is the producer of manifold powers:
"She is the knower of existence, the destroyer of the disease of existence, and the one who sets in motion the wheel of existence. (208)
She is called *bhāvajñā* because she knows the *bhāvas*.

Regarding the word *bhāva*, Amara states: "The word *bhāva* [is used] in the senses of existence (*sattā*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), intention (*abhiprāya*), gesture (*ceṣṭā*), soul (*ātman*), and birth (*janman*).

Furthermore, the *Amaraśeṣa* states: "The word *bhāva* [is used] in the senses of source (*yoni*), intellect (*budha*), purpose (*artha*), compassion (*kṛpā*), play (*līlā*), and manifestation (*vibhūti*). Of that...

In the rule *bhāvas-tvatal-au*, *dharma* is also considered *bhāva*. In the traditional maxim *bhāvapradhānam ākhyātam*, *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is also *bhāva*. The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in its absolute, pure state is designated as *bhāva*.
Furthermore, the modifications enumerated by Yāska—such as "it exists," "it is born," "it grows," and so forth—are also [included].

There are six types of *bhāva* (entities/manifestations). *Bhāva* refers to existence, devotion, or that which is to be worshipped; it is also the state of being. Furthermore, the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) accepted by the logicians (*tārkika*) are also called *bhāva*. *Bhava* is *saṃsāra* (the cycle of existence), and that itself is *bhāva*;
those things related to it, the worldly phenomena, are also *bhāva*. *Bhava* is also Śiva, and those belonging to him, the Śaivas, are likewise *bhāva*.

The *bhāvas*. *Bhava* is devotion (*bhakti*), for its state (*bhāva*) is that which is to be worshipped; thus, by the Pāṇinian sūtra [Pāṇini 5.1.119], the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Alternatively, the sun and other luminaries also go toward (*vānti*) or move toward *bhā*, which is splendor (*kānti*); they too are *bhāvas*. Devotion (*bhakti*) is also a *bhāva*. This is stated in the sixfold meaning of the mantra described in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.

The primary meaning is also "existence" (bhāva). According to the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "Existence—that is, saṃsāra—is itself the disease; I see no other medicine for it than the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva).
Just as there is a remedy for diseases by virtue of its being an opposite nature, [so too is this the case].
In the same way, the auspicious path is the antidote to the diseases of saṃsāra.
Thus it is stated in the Śiva Purāṇa. It sets in motion the *bhavacakra*, the wheel of worldly existence;
or rather, it sets [it] in motion like the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*). As it is said in the Manusmṛti:
"This [Prakṛti], having pervaded all beings with its five forms..."
It perpetually causes one to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Viṣṇubhāgavata*:
"You alone are the Lord of all worlds regarding bondage and liberation;
the wise worship you as Hara, the remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge."
Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, it is the *bhavacakra* or the *anāhatacakra*, because Śiva resides therein. Now, one might object:

according to the established tenets of the Tantras, the term "cakra" (wheel) applies only to a collection of spokes (*koṇa*) and petals (*patra*); since there are no spokes in the *anāhata*, how can the word "cakra" bring that [center] to mind?

For this very reason, the formulation "residing in the unstruck-lotus" (*anāhatābjanilaya*) is used. If it is argued that this is incorrect because the established doctrine holds that "lotus-ness" resides only in a collection of petals and "yantra-ness" resides only in a collection of corners, we say no; for with the intention of referring to the corners, the conventional designation "cakra" (wheel) is applied even to the *mūlādhāra* and other centers.

Some maintain that this is the intention of the authors of the *Vidyāratnabhāṣya*, who, being thus concentrated, employ figurative usage by superimposing "corners" (*koṇa*) upon the petals (*patra*). That is not correct;
for if there is an intention to express "corners," there is an absence of the intention to express "yantras."

Since this would result in the mere application of the term "yantra" (mechanism/diagram), we consider it appropriate that the intention of the Commentary is simply that there exists a triangle upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that [lotus].
[The components are: the point (*bindu*), the circle (*cakra*), the eight-petaled lotus, the sixteen-petaled lotus, the three circles, and the three earth-houses (*bhūgṛha*).

Or, it refers to the wheels of worldly existence contained within the Śrīcakra; or, it is so called because the mind sets in motion the wheel of Bhava (Śiva). For in the Viṣṇupurāṇa, it is stated that the mind alone is indeed the wheel: "Its nature is exceedingly mobile, surpassing the wind in its speed."
"And Viṣṇu holds the wheel, which is the very nature of the mind, in his hand. Thus [it is said]. (208)
She whose essence is the Vedic meters, whose essence is the scriptures, whose essence is the mantras, and who has a flat belly.

The word *chandas* refers to the Veda, or to the *gāyatrī* and other meters, or to the *Paiṅgala-tantra*. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *chandas* [denotes] a lotus, the Veda, one's own conduct, and desire. *Para* means an opponent or disputant.
The word *sāra* is not exclusively masculine; it is that very state which is the essence (*sāra*) in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
This is because of usages such as *tāntavī* (a weaver’s wife).
The word *sāra* is used for strength, the marrow, the solid part, what is right, water, and wealth;
they cite the Veda as another example of *sāra*.

And thus says the *Viśva* lexicon. Here, the word *sthirāṃśa* (stable portion) refers to the extracted essence (*niṣkṛṣṭāṃśa*), because that which is not extracted is unstable. Consequently, in the Veda, her essential nature is extracted in the portion consisting of the Upaniṣads. The analysis of the compound is: "she whose essence—the extracted core—is within the meters (*chandaḥ*)."
The extracted form from among the *gāyatrī* and other meters is the *gāyatrī* mantra; the extraction of even that is the *pañcadaśī*. This has been stated by us in the *Varivasyārahasya*:
"For the sake of knowing That, fourteen sciences are proclaimed in the world as the means."
And among those, the Vedas are the essence; and even among them, the Gāyatrī is the essence.
Of her two forms, one is clearly proclaimed even in all four Vedas, while the other is most exceedingly secret.

Even the Veda-Purusha does not openly employ that Vidya which is designated by such conventional terms as "Kama," "Yoni," and "Kamala. This is also stated in the Atharvaveda, in the sixteen-verse Traipurasūkta: kāmasya yonir asi kāma tvayi saṃbhavati | kāma tvayā jīvati kāma tvām prapadye || 1 || kāma tvam eva sarvam idam tvayi sarvam idam jagat | tvayi bhūtam bhaviṣyac ca tvayi sarvam pratiṣṭhitam || 2 || kāma tvam eva pūrvasmāt parasmād api cottaram | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protam sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 3 || kāma tvam eva prathamā kāma tvam eva cottarā | na tvatparaṃ vidyate kiṃcit tvayi sarvam pratiṣṭhitam || 4 || kāma tvam eva sarvajñā kāma tvam eva sarvavit | kāma tvam eva sarvasvaṃ tvayi sarvam pratiṣṭhitam || 5 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 6 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 7 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 8 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 9 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 10 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 11 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 12 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 13 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 14 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 15 || kāma tvam eva sarveṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ kāraṇottamam | tvayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva || 16 ||
Kāma, Yoni, Kamalā, Vajrapāṇi, Guhā, Hasā, Mātariśvan, Abhra, Indra;
again Guhā, Sakalā, and Māyā—this Purūcī is the Mother of the Universe and the Vidyā.

Thus, in this *ṛc*, there is the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the *Kādividyā*. For in the *Paiṅgala-tantra*, the "Great Array" (*mahāprastāra*) is set forth by the two sūtras: "Two *k*s are *glau*" and "And the mixed ones. This is the means for the complete knowledge of the infinite web of words. And that [work] is the *Chandobhāskara*.
Thus has it been made manifest by us in the treatise on prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*). "Whose power" means whose greatness belongs to Vaikharī Sarasvatī. Or alternatively:
"Wherever there is satisfaction of the mind, one should fix the mind right there."
In each and every instance, the nature of supreme bliss shines forth.

Thus, according to the method taught by the venerable Vijñānabhairava, for the foremost of practitioners, that which is desired is itself dharma, and that which is not desired is itself adharma. And it is said in the Śākuntala: "For in matters that are subjects of doubt, the inclinations of the inner organ (the heart) are the authority for the virtuous."

Even persistence enjoined by the mindfulness of conventional conduct (*samayācāra*) extends only up to the stage of maturity (*prauḍha*), for the *Kalpasūtra* states that conventional conducts end at maturity. With all this in mind, it is heard in the *Kaulopaniṣad*: "Dharma is adharma; adharma is dharma."
Also in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Drinking, dancing, embracing, and eating, devoted to his own spontaneous conduct,
he should wander happily while contemplating the identity of 'I-ness' and 'this-ness'."

According to the manner thus stated, the intended meaning is that for those possessing such mental concentration (*manaḥsamādhi*), an object that is the focus of their desire necessarily becomes *dharma*. This is also supported by the Smṛtis, which list among the authorities for *dharma*: "The Śruti, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and one's own satisfaction."
The counting of the activity of the mind is precisely that of one whose mind is thus concentrated;

otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the definition]. The meaning is: "that which has such unrestrained conduct as its essence" (sāra) is what is logical. Or alternatively: "that which has longing—that is, desire—as its extracted essence" (sāra). [This refers to] the Goddess.

Because it has the nature of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). As for the word *sāra* meaning "excellent," since it is dependent on the gender of the noun it qualifies (*viśeṣya-nighna*), there is no inconsistency in its being feminine.

The same applies to the two subsequent names [in the verse], because [the Lord] is the source of the scriptures (*śāstrayonitvāt*). From this sūtra, the scripture concerning rice (*vrīhi-śāstra*) [is derived].

Regarding the phrase "the scripture of barley" (*yavaśāstra*) and so forth: from the technical usage of the Tantrikas, the word *śāstra* refers either to the Veda or to the Mīmāṃsā and other systems that follow it. As it is stated in the *Bhāmatī*:
"Activity or cessation [from activity] is brought about by that which is eternal or that which is produced."
That by which men are instructed is called a śāstra.

Thus [it is said]. The word *mantra* also refers to the Veda, as seen in usages such as "the *liṭ* [perfect tense] after a verbal root ending in a *kāspratyaya*, except for *ām* in a *mantra*" (*kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi*), or it may refer to the Tantras, either those belonging to the Tantric system or the sixty-four Tantras that expound them. Her abdomen is thin and even like the palm of the hand (*tala*), and not otherwise.

She whose belly is bent and swollen like a kettle-drum (bherī) and so forth; or, by eliding the vowel 'a', she whose belly is the very world known as Atala—this is also easily explained as referring to her in the form of Virāj. She is of noble fame, of unrestrained majesty, and is the embodiment of the letters. 209.

She whose fame is noble (*udārā*) and most great (*mahattarā*); or, she whose worship results in fame that is excellent (*utkṛṣṭā*), all-pervading (*āsamantād-vyāptā*), and swift to be accomplished (*arā*). According to the *Agnipurāṇa* lexicon, *laghu*, *kṣipra*, *aram*, and *druta* are synonyms for "quickly. The syllable *ṛ* denotes the Mother of the Gods. Thus: *ā arau araḥ*.

The *rūpas* (phonemes) are: *uḥ*, *apatyāni*, *arāḥ*, *devāḥ*. She is so called because her fame (*kīrti*) has transcended these, or because she has transcended *āram* (auspiciousness). That is to say, her glorification (*kīrtana*) dispels the defects of evil planets and the like, beginning with misfortune. She resides within the solar orb (*ādityamaṇḍala*).
Qualified consciousness is denoted by the word *utpada*. This is because of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which, referring to "this golden person within the sun," states:

"His name is *ud*. [The term *utpāda*] may also mean one whose fame (*kīrti*) possesses *ārā*—a specific type of weapon—or, according to the lexicon (*kośa*), a leather thong; thus, it refers to one whose fame is like that. [The prefix] *ut* belongs to the person (*puruṣa*).
The meaning is that her fame brings about suffering; the intent is that her fame is "conquering" (jetrī), meaning it arises through the worship of her.

Alternatively, she is one whose fame is as excellent as the lake of nectar (sudhāhrada) known as Ara, which is pervaded on all sides. [She resides] in the city of the Supreme Brahman called Aparājita, which is difficult to attain even for those who worship the Brahman with attributes.

It is well known in the Śrutis that the two [spheres], Ara and Ṇya, exist like two lakes of nectar (sudhāhrada) equal in color. Furthermore, in the Sūtra "Non-return, on account of the word" (anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt), the venerable Ācārya Bhagavatpāda also stated: "Dāma means a binding rope, that which delimits."
Her majesty is such that it has transcended [all limits] and is not delimited by measure.
Her form consists of sixty-four phonemes (varṇas). As it is stated in the *Pāṇiniśikṣā*:
"Sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes are considered [to exist] according to the doctrine of Śambhu; they were proclaimed by the Self-born One himself for both Prākṛta and Saṃskṛta. (209)
Bestowing rest upon people tormented by the heat of birth, death, and old age,
she clearly grants the bliss of one's own self through rests that remove suffering for those people scorched by the triad beginning with birth.
Proclaimed by all the Upaniṣads, she consists of the aspect that transcends tranquility (śāntyatītākalā). || 210 ||

In all the Upaniṣads, such as the Aitareya and others—which are secret in nature and constitute the crest-threads of the Vedas—this [knowledge] is proclaimed with preeminence as the subject to be established. This is evident from the passage: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣad, that alone becomes more powerful. Herein lies the significance of the term *upaniṣad*.

This is because it is observed that [the term] is explained as being primarily concerned with the secret [teachings]. Its etymological derivation has also been shown by the Teachers: "Having led this Self to Brahman, which is devoid of duality, it destroys ignorance along with its products; therefore, it is considered an *upaniṣad*."

Thus [it is said]. Here, "exaltation" (utkarṣa) means uniformity (aikarūpya), because the quality of being high-pitched (uccais-tva) is obtained by the verbal root itself; for the *Kośa* states that "highly proclaimed" (*uccair-ghuṣṭam*) means "proclamation. And this uniformity refers to the absence of difference among the meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahmopāsti*) enjoined in each Vedānta. This, then, is the principle of "cognition based on all Vedāntas" (*sarvavedāntapratyaya*).
This is clear from the section beginning with "codanādyaviśeṣāt. The *kalā* residing in Ākāśa is called Śāntyatītā. Its nature is described in the Śaiva Āgama:
"The Śāntyatītā-kalā consists of non-duality, liberation, bliss, and consciousness. She is of that nature and non-different from it. (210)
She is profound, situated within the limits of the sky, proud, and eager for song.

She is "profound" because of her infinity; the meaning is that she has the nature of a great lake. And so it is stated in the *Śivasūtra*: "From the contemplation of the great lake comes the experience of the potency of mantra."
The supreme Goddess Śakti is called the "Great Lake" (mahāhrada);
"contemplative inquiry" (anusandhāna) is said to be the reflective awareness of identity with that [Śakti].
The "potency of mantra" is said to be the reflective awareness of the fullness of I-consciousness;
its experience is the clear manifestation of one's own self.
"Dancing within, eating whatever comes his way, and himself intent on his own spontaneous conduct.
Also elsewhere:
"The Supreme Goddess is consciousness, preceded by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)."
Emitting the entire internal universe up to the limit of gross objects of cognition.

[The senses] possess the nature of external forms distinct from other subjects, due to their qualities such as being the instigators [of activity], transparency, and depth, with respect to the objects of the sense organs.
"The great lake pervades the world, beyond the reach of space, time, and so forth.

Here, "gaṃ" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Gaṇapati; by it, Gaṇapati himself is expressed. Alternatively, its meaning is that he bestows (*rāti*) or takes away (*ādatte*) fear (*bhī*), or casts it out (*nirasyati*). [It is the seed of] the sky (*gagana*), the small space (*daharākāśa*), and the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*).

"He stands within the midst of the supreme space," according to the Śruti: "Like a tree, He stands alone, fixed in heaven. Or, "He stands at the end of the sky" means even at the time of destruction; for "sky" (*gagana*) is the syllable *a*, and "end" (*anta*) refers to the semi-vowels *ya, ra, la, va*—this is the extraction of the seed-syllables of the five elements. *Garva*...
The supreme *ahantā* (I-consciousness) regarding the creation of the universe has arisen within her. [The suffix] *-itac* is applied here because it belongs to the *tārakādi* group.

"Gāna" consists of the fourfold collection of stringed, percussion, wind, and solid instruments, or musical instruments such as drums and the like, or the body of music (*gāndharva*), or the *sāman* chant; she is *lolupā*, meaning full of longing or craving for these.
She is free from conceptual construction, the ultimate limit, unloved by the passionate, yet possessing a body half-formed by her beloved.

It is free from the waves of the visible world, which consist of conceptual constructions and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), precisely because those [waves] are merely imagined. Alternatively, it is beneficial even during the *kalpa*—for the *kośa* states that *saṃvarta* means dissolution (*pralaya*) and *kalpa*. [This is derived] from the root *nṛ*, meaning "to lead": he who leads is called *nara*, the eternal Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

And according to the Smṛti: "The *nārāḥ* are these living beings (*jīvāḥ*) of *Nara*. This means that she is the benefactor who, even at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) which effects the destruction of everything, places the living beings within her own belly in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); how much more so during the periods of creation and maintenance? As it is said in the *Aṣṭāvakragītā*:
Within me, the infinite ocean of consciousness, the waves of living beings arise, subside, sport, and enter by their very nature— a wondrous spectacle.

Thus: a period of time consisting of eighteen *nimeṣas* is a *kāṣṭhā*. The term *kāṣṭhā* also refers to the plant *dāruharidrā*. For it is said in the *Mairālatantra* that because it consists of the transformation of the trunk, navel, and stalk [of the cosmic tree], it is non-different from the Śakti of Śiva. [The lexicon states: "The word *kāṣṭhā* is used for the plant *dāruharidrā* and for a specific division of time measurement."
Rabhasa: That which possesses both forms is the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*), even the definitive extraction of the true meaning of the Vedānta statements.
As it is said in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"Whether perceived or unperceived, existent or non-existent, the Supreme Śiva [is all]."
Thus, the final culmination of the Vedānta statements is called the "ultimate limit."

Thus [it is said], and the Śruti also states: "She is the limit, she is the supreme goal. Alternatively, she is the consort of the Supreme Śiva named Bhīma, whose nature is the ether; as the mother of heaven (Svarga), the Goddess is called *kāṣṭhā* because her form is the cardinal directions (*dik*). And so it is stated in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
The Lord, the divine one whose self is space, who provides room for all beings, both moving and unmoving, is called Bhīma by the wise.
The tenfold-formed quarters are the wives of the Greatly Glorious God Bhīma, the Supreme Self; and Heaven is their son, according to the wise.
Thus it is said. Also in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The sixth body of his, named Bhīma, is said to be the ether;
the quarters are remembered as his wives, and heaven is remembered as his son."

Thus [it is said]. The etymologists (nairuktāḥ) say that she is called *kāṣṭhā* because "she stands having traversed" (*krāntvā tiṣṭhati*). The Śruti says, "She stood transcending by ten fingers' breadth" (*atyatiṣṭhad daśāṅgulam*). And the Smṛti says, "Having pervaded this entire world, I stand with but one part" (*viṣṭabhya idam kṛtsnam ekāṃśena sthito jagat*).
*Akāntā* is a three-syllabled name; *aka* refers to sin and suffering, and she is so called because she is the end—the destruction—of those two.

She is she whose half-body (*ardhavigraha*)—that is, half of the body (*vigraha*)—is the beloved Supreme Śiva himself. This is a compound formed according to the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*. Alternatively, it may mean she whose body (*vigraha*) consists of half of her beloved (*kāntārdha*). In this latter case, it does not mean "half-beloved" (*ardhakānta*).
Thus is the application of the form. Since the term *ardha* occurring here is accepted as having a fixed gender (*niyataliṅga*),

and because the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) applies only to those words that have a fixed neuter gender, this [term]— in the *Mahābhāṣya*, which consists of questions and answers such as "But what is the masculine?"— is understood as referring to a word of fixed gender, like the masculine.
This is because of Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. And thus the venerable Piṅgalanāga employed [the expression]:
"The vowels [constitute] half, and that is half of an Āryā. In reality, however, in the compound *ardhavigrahāḥ*, the compound is indeed a *karmadhāraya*.
For if it were a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, the form would necessarily result as *vigrahārdham*. Precisely for this reason...

It is another matter that in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *paravalliṅga* sūtra, the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* is rejected. Consequently, even in the compound *kāntārdham*, it should be understood that the word *ardha* denotes an equal division; [it means] "the end of the letter *ka*."

The letter *kha* signifies the sky (*dyu*); the word *ardha* refers merely to a portion. Thus, the meaning is "she whose body has the sky as one part," according to the Vedic mantra: "All beings are one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6). || 211 ||
Free from cause and effect, yet rippling with the play of desire;

"effects" refers to greatness (*mahat*) and the rest, while the "cause" is primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*); she is free from these because, in reality, they do not exist within consciousness. For her, there is neither effect nor instrument.

According to the scripture, she is so called because the waves—the successions of playful pastimes (*kelī*)—of Kāma, the Lord of Desire, have arisen within her. She wears shimmering golden earrings and possesses a body that assumes various graceful forms. 212.

She whose earrings—specific ornaments for the ears made of gold—are shining and radiant; she who effortlessly and with ease bears various bodily forms through her divine play; she is Queen Līlādevī, the consort of King Padma.

Or she may assume that very form; and she is well known in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*, beginning with the passage: "O protector of the earth, in this lineage there was a blooming lotus named Padmā; she had a fortunate wife named Līlā, devoted to her husband. (212)
She is the Unborn (Ajā), liberated from decay, innocent, and swiftly gracious.
She is called "Unborn" because she is devoid of birth, according to the Śruti: "The one Unborn," and also according to the Śruti: "She was not born, nor will she be born.
This is also stated in the Mahābhārata:
I have not been born, I am not being born, nor shall I ever be born;
as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of all beings, I am therefore remembered as the Unborn.

Thus [it is said]. For birth is co-extensive with death; for according to the scriptural statement, "For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain. Therefore, in this context, he states the point established by the perception of something incompatible with the pervader, which is the absence of birth: she is "freed from decay," that is, from death. Specifically, "decay" refers to the house itself.
Or, it may mean "by which one is liberated. Those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) abandon their homes out of fear of sense-objects;
however, the intended meaning is that for the worshippers of Sundarī, liberation is attained right here in the home.
This very point was stated by us in the *Śivastuti*: [The Sanskrit verse would follow here.]
If you desire the supreme abode, abandon even your own name;
remember in your heart the name of the Enemy of Kama, which is the tether that binds one to the highest state.

Thus it is said. Dūrvāsas also says in the *Śaktimahimnastotra*: "She is *mugdha-saundaryavatī*—one who releases attachment (*saṅga*) and possesses beauty (*saundarya*). By eliding the vowel 'a' (*akārapraśleṣa*), it can also be well-explained as 'she for whom there are no deluded ones (*na santi mūḍhā yasyāḥ*).
According to the *Viśvakośa*, the word *mugdha* refers to both 'beautiful' and 'deluded. She becomes gracious very quickly, in just a few days."
Likewise, for this very reason it is stated in the Saura Purāṇa:
"O twice-born ones, liberation is attained by others only gradually through worship;
however, through the worship of Umāpati, one is liberated in that very birth."

Thus [it is said]. However, this refers specifically to the foremost among men who possess the most intense devotion. For others, it is recorded in the Śiva Purāṇa: "Even that mortal who possesses only a slight degree of devotion, after three more births,"
There will be no pain from the pressure of the birth canal; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, with this established rule in mind, it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Otherwise, the recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth performed according to the tradition will,
in another birth, lead to the attainment of the authentic tradition."
She is to be propitiated by those who are introverted; she is very difficult to attain for those who are extroverted.
She is perfectly propitiated by those whose mouths, which are the fluctuations of the mind, have the *praṇava* of their own inner self as their opening;

she is very difficult to attain for those whose mouths are directed solely toward external objects. Thus it is said in the *Ānandalaharī*: "She is not easily obtained by those whose senses are fickle. (213)
She is the Trayī (the threefold Veda), the abode of the three goals of life (trivarga), she who exists in the three states, and the garlanded one of the three cities (Tripuramālinī).
According to the lexicon, "striyām ṛksāmayajuṣī" refers to the three Vedas; thus, Trayī is the embodiment of the three Vedas.
Likewise, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, the Goddess spoke these words to Himavat:
My own supreme power, known as the Veda and ancient,
proceeds at the beginning of creation in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "O Goddess, Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, and Daṇḍanīti are spoken of.
Also in the *Devī Purāṇa*:
"Since she exists within the Vedas along with their limbs (Aṅgas) through the divisions of Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman..."
That which is recited in the world as the "Trayī" (the Triple Veda) is the means for accomplishing both the seen and the unseen.
Thus it is said. However, in the Nityātantra:
"The Sāmaveda begins with the letter 'a', and the Ṛgveda begins with that [same letter];
the Yajurveda begins with the letter 'i'; through their conjunction, one becomes pure."
O wise one, listen to its accomplishment as it has been explained according to the sequence of the preceding and following [sections].
Having first written it down, one should apply it in accordance with the rules of grammar.
The twilight of the qualities (guṇasandhyā) is the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda; by that, another [twilight] arises likewise.
One should join the twilight of increase (vṛddhisandhyā); thus was the pure body produced.

"Therefore, the knowledge consisting of the three Vedas [is established] through the connection of cause and effect"—thus it has been said. Here, by the word *śuci*, the seed-syllable *vāgbhava* is expressed; or else, the meaning is "having that as its form. According to the lexicon, *trivarga* consists of dharma, kāma, and artha. She is the one in whom that *nilayaḥ*—the abode or locus—resides.
She is *tristhā*, meaning she whose abode (*sthā*) is in the three times—namely the past, present, and future—or in the three syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*;
or alternatively, she who dwells without distinction throughout the three worlds and so forth. As it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"The three worlds, the three gods, the triple Veda, and the three fires."
There are three lights, the three castes, and likewise the three qualities beginning with dharma.
There are three qualities, three sounds, three defects, as well as the stages of life;
there are three times, as well as the states, the ancestors, day and night, and so forth.
"And your form consists of three measures; O Goddess, you are Sarasvatī abiding in the three.
Thus [it is said]. The deity presiding over the inner ten-spoked wheel is Tripuramālinī—free from affliction, without support, delighting in her own self, and a stream of nectar. (214)

That by which diseases and ailments have departed is [the state] free from illness. It is "without support" (*nirālambā*) because it is impossible for that which has everything as its object to have another object; for if it did, an infinite regress would result. Furthermore, the fact that such a state "destroys the root" establishes precisely its lack of any objective support.

She whose delight and play are in her own self alone; that is to say, she who, having divided her own self into two parts, sports with the other. Thus the Mādhyandinas recite: "He indeed did not find delight; therefore, one who is alone does not find delight. He desired a second; for he was as great as this... [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.2.3.1].

"The woman and the man embraced; he caused this very Self to fall into two parts, and from that, there became a husband and a wife. Or [it means]: she whose "garden" (*ārāma*) is her own Self, which is the manifold world in the form of an artificial grove. [This refers to her] at the times of the creation and dissolution of the world.
Because nothing remains but his own self. And so it is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"The Lord, who is indeed one, becomes manifold through the power of his sovereignty;
and having become manifold, he becomes one again."

Thus [it is said]. Or, it may mean that her *ārāma*—her play, sport, or mode of existence—is both "herself" (*sva*), meaning her own self, and the "world" (*jagat*), which is Brahman. As it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"O Goddess, you are the supreme imperishable (*akṣara*) in whom everything is established."
The imperishable Brahman is supreme, while this world consists of the perishable.
Just as fire resides within wood and the atoms of the earth reside therein,
so too does Brahman abide within you, as does this entire world in its entirety.
Thus: she is the Kuṇḍalinī by whom there is a flow, a streaming forth, of nectar situated at the moon in the pericarp of the Sahasrāra; or rather, she is simply the flow of nectar itself.
The meaning is that she, the Goddess, is indeed Action (Kriyā), nourishing the maṇḍalas of Ḍākinī and the others. Or else:
"This very [nectar] is a rain of ambrosia that produces satisfaction for the fire, the sun, and others, even from the well-known lunar orb"—
thus, by drinking from the ten and five streams of flowing nectar-ambrosia,
the gods always become full-bodied during the dark fortnight.

"All that is the Māyā of Śambhu"—thus it is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*. Furthermore, in the *Jñānārṇava*, regarding the practice of the seed-syllable of Śakti, the following visualization is described: "She who rains down streams of flowing nectar and is the destroyer of poison."
Or, [it means] "possessing such a form. || 214 ||

She is skilled in lifting up those submerged in the mire of saṃsāra; she is expert and proficient in the complete rescue of people who are entirely sunk in the mud characterized by worldly existence. Therefore, it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Those who, seeking refuge, remember Śarvāṇī even for a moment, do not fall into the ocean of saṃsāra, which is difficult to cross and shoreless. Thus [it is said].
She is fond of sacrifice, the performer of sacrifice, and the very embodiment of the sacrificer. (215)
She for whom sacrifices are dear; or, according to the Vedic scripture stating "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice," she is his beloved.

She is the wife of Paramaśiva—who is the performer of the sacrifice, whose essence is the sacrificer, and whose form is the initiated one (*dīkṣita*)—and she is known as *Dīkṣā*, the mother of the lineage. As it is said in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
The Lord Mahādeva, whose essence is the sacrificer,
is called "Ugra" by the wise and "Īśāna" by others who are virtuous.
The wise have declared that initiation (dīkṣā) is the wife of the Lord known as Ugra, who is the sacrificer himself; their son is called Santāna.

Thus it is said. Also in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "The seventh form is the fierce one (Ugrā); initiation (dīkṣā) is remembered as his wife, along with the initiated Brāhmaṇas; their offspring is called the son."

Thus it is said. Among the eight forms of Śiva, the last is sometimes described as the *yajamāna-mūrti* (the sacrificer’s form) and sometimes as the *ātman* (the self); he mentions both of these: *yajamānaśca svaśca yajamānasvau*, meaning "the sacrificer and one's own [self]"; these two are its two forms (*rūpe*). The rule regarding the prior placement of the word with fewer syllables is not absolute.

This is because of the grammatical rule "etattadoḥ" and so forth. And it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "O best of sages, the five elements, the moon, the sun, and the self—these eight they call the forms of the wise Śiva, the God of gods."
"The Self is its eighth form, the supreme one called the sacrificer. || 215 ||

The substratum of Dharma, the presiding deity of wealth, and the increaser of riches and grain— those actions which have come down through the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) in various regions and are not contrary to the Vedas are denoted by the term "Dharma. And so says the *Saṃvarta-smṛti*:
In whatever region a particular custom has been handed down through successive tradition and is not contradicted by the sacred scriptures (āmnāya), that is proclaimed to be dharma.

Thus [it is said]. For them, the *dhārā* is an unobstructed flow in all directions and in all places; or, it is so called because Dharma is its support (*ādhāra*), or because it abides in Dharma by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), according to the Vedic scripture that "everything is established in Dharma"; or, it is that by which Dharma is supported. Of Dharma...

That is to say, she is that by whom the state of being the support of all is established. She is the presiding mistress (*adhyakṣā*) of wealth, because of the non-difference between the object of worship and the worshipper; or alternatively, she has the form of Kubera. She causes wealth and grain to increase specifically.
She who is dear to the Brahmins, who takes the form of a Brahmin, and who causes universal delusion. || 216 ||
Brāhmaṇas who possess knowledge of the Vedas, the Śāstras, and other sciences are called *vipras*. As it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"One is known as a Brāhmaṇa by birth; he is called a *dvija* (twice-born) through sacramental rites (*saṃskāras*);
he attains the status of a *vipra* through learning (*vidyā*); and by all three, he is called a *śrotriya*."

Thus [it is said]: she for whom those [brahmins] are dear and beloved. For, by the Lord’s own statement, "Whether ignorant or learned, the brahmin is My body," affection for brahmins is established through the logic of the *kaimutika* (how much more so) argument.
Precisely from that stated word, such brahmins constitute her *rūpa*, that is, her true nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore...
It is heard [in scripture]: "As many deities as there are, they all dwell in a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda. The Parāśara-smṛti also states:
"Brāhmaṇas are a moving shrine, renowned throughout the three worlds."
By the water of whose words alone do defiled people become pure.
Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, it is so called because it "transforms" (*rūpayati*) the Brahmins—making them possess their former form—or because it "satisfies" (*āpyāyayati*) them;
that is to say, by means of the recitation of mantras and other rites, the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of the Brahmins occurs through it.
As it has been stated in the *Āpastamba-smṛti*:
Through insult, asceticism increases; through honor, asceticism is diminished.
A Brahmin who is honored and worshipped perishes like a cow that has been milked dry.
Just as [the moon] swells during the days with blades of grass born from nectar,
so too does the twice-born swell again through recitations and burnt offerings.
Thus, He causes all the universes to revolve, effecting their coming and going in the form of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
Some poets call this inherent nature (*svabhāva*), while others, being utterly deluded, call it time (*kāla*).
But this is the majesty of the God in the world, by which this wheel of Brahman is made to revolve.
Thus says the Śruti. The meaning is that the greatness residing in the gods is indeed the power (*śakti*) that causes delusion.

And there is a Smṛti: "Causing all beings, mounted upon a machine, to wander by means of Māyā. Alternatively, the word *viśva* refers to Viṣṇu, because it is said, "Viṣṇu is the universe, Viṣṇu is the vaṣaṭ-call"; [the power] is that which effects the wandering of Him.

This historical account is recorded in the Tāṇḍava-Kālikā-Purāṇa: once, while Viṣṇu was traveling through the sky mounted upon Garuḍa, he passed below the region of Kāmarūpa; although the goddess Kāmākhyā, who dwells on Mount Nīla, was nearby, he disregarded her and departed without even bowing before her.

Then, under the influence of that anger, he fell into the middle of the ocean and remained wandering right there. After some time, Lakṣmī, while searching for him, heard this account from the mouth of Nārada;
she propitiated Kāmākhyā through ascetic penance and made Viṣṇu attentive.
He liberated her from wandering; thereafter, having propitiated her, he too dwelt in the world of Vaikuṇṭha. || 216 ||
She who devours the universe, resembling coral, belonging to Viṣṇu, and having the form of Viṣṇu.
She is called *viśvagrāsā* because she swallows the entire universe, including all that is moving and stationary;
the meaning is that she is the destroyer of all things mobile and immobile. And thus it is heard in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad:
He for whom both the Brahmin and the Kshatriya are the rice,
and for whom death is the condiment— who truly knows where he is?

Thus [it is said]. Here, with the intention that by the statement of death being the "sprinkling" (upasecana), there is the perception of the moving and non-moving world as its object of withdrawal, the Brahma-sūtra states: "The Eater [is Brahman], because of the mention of both the moving and the non-moving. Coral (vidruma) refers to red coral; "coral-like" means reddish like that. Knowledge itself is the tree (druma).
Or, it may mean "equal to that" because of the similarity in being extended one after another like arrow-shafts (*puṅkhānupuṅkha*). This [goddess] belongs to Viṣṇu, thus she is *Vaiṣṇavī*.
And so it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"The mother of Viṣṇu likewise wields the conch, the discus, and the mace, and is the destroyer of enemies."
Or rather, because she is of the form of Viṣṇu, the Goddess is celebrated as Vaiṣṇavī.

Thus it is said. Here, four etymological derivations (*vyutpatti*) are indicated. For instance, the meaning of *ariha* is "one who slays enemies (Daityas) like Viṣṇu. The meaning of *viṣṇurūpā* is "one who is non-different from Him. Therefore, the [latter] meaning is not already covered by the first derivation. He states this very point: "Viṣṇu alone is her form."

This has been stated in the *Lalitopākhyāna* of the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* itself: "My own form as a man is that which deludes the Gopikās," according to the words of the Goddess. In that very same work, there is the speech of Viṣṇu addressed to Vīrabhadra:
The primordial power of Maheśa, whose form is divided fourfold,
assumes the form of Bhavānī in the enjoyment of worldly pleasures and the form of Durgā in battle.
"In anger she takes the form of Kālikā, and in intoxication my very self takes the form of a man.
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the hymn to the Goddess composed by Himavat:
"The ancient Puruṣa, who has a thousand heads, infinite power, and a thousand arms..."
I bow to that form of yours known as Nārāyaṇa, who lies upon the charming ocean.
Thus, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* itself, when Śiva had manifested his universal form (*viśvarūpa*) to Maṅkaṇaka, [Maṅkaṇaka asked]:
"O Blessed One, what is this most terrible form of yours, with faces on all sides? And who is she, shining resplendently, stationed by your side?"
Thus, being questioned by him, Śiva described the power and nature of his own essence and said:
"That supreme Māyā of mine, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), is called Prakṛti;
it is declared by the sages to be the eternal Śakti, the womb of the universe."
He alone, the knower of all, deludes the universe through his illusory power (māyā);
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme unmanifest one whose form is māyā—so says the Śruti.
Thus it is said in the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā, after describing the devotion to Viṣṇu of King Prabhākara and the devotion to Pārvatī of his queen named Padminī:
"In this way, Janārdana exists both as the Goddess and in his own form."
Because the couple constitute a single body, he is worshipped as one, though in two forms.
Thus it is said; and also in the Bṛhatpārāśara-smṛti:
