"By worshipping Durgā, Kātyāyanī, and Vāgdevatā with a perfectly serene mind, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu."
Thus it is said. Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"He who bathes Caṇḍikā with sugarcane juice rejoices together with Viṣṇu, traveling in a celestial vehicle drawn by Garuḍa."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in both the Āditya Purāṇa and the Śiva Purāṇa: "The young woman who stands by his side is Hari, born from a portion of Pārvatī. Also, in the Vāmana Purāṇa: "He who worships Śivā according to the prescribed rites on the full moon day of the month of Māgha..."
He obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Vishnu. Thus it is said.
She is without origin, yet her abode is the womb; she is immutably established, yet possesses the form of the lineage.

That which has no *yoni*—that is, no cause—is "without origin" (*ayoni*). Alternatively, the word *yoni* signifies a place, as according to the Vedic scripture: "O Indra, a seat (*yoni*) has been prepared for you to sit upon. Thus, the meaning is: "O Indra! A place has been made by me for your sitting (*niṣada*)."
Therefore, it means "without a location" (sthānarahitā), that is, "unlimited" (aparicchinna). Or, it is the "womb" (yoni)—the source or mother—of this Viṣṇu.

It is the "abode" (nilayā) because the world dissolves within it; thus, it is both the womb and the abode. The word *yoni* refers here to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), as seen in the Vedic usage: "the agent, the Lord, the Person, whose womb is Brahman."

This is because of the explanation: "By means of meditation, one beholds the agent, the Lord endowed with the power of action, the controller, the Person, the inward-facing, the full Brahman, the source (yoni). Furthermore, there is the *Brahma-sūtra*: "And it is indeed sung as the source. Or else, as in the Śruti: "He who alone presides over every source (yoni)."

Since there is also seen an explanation of *yonipara* as being "supreme over *māyā*," [the compound] means: she whose abode (*nilaya*), that is, her defining limit (*paricchedikā*), is *māyā* itself, which is the *yoni*. Alternatively, it means: she in whom there is the ultimate dissolution (*nitarāṃ laya*) of the *yoni*s—that is, the causes of the world such as Brahmā and others. Or, it means: she whose abode is the *yoni*, which is the triangle (*tryasra*) wheel itself.
Or, it refers to the Goddess whose form is the *bindu*. For this very reason, it is heard in the Atharva Veda, in the Śaunaka recension:
"In that golden casket, which consists of three syllables and is established on three supports..."
Whatever in that [body] possesses consciousness, that indeed the knowers of Brahman understand to be Brahman.
Thus [it is said]. Prior to this verse:
"The eight-wheeled, nine-gated Ayodhyā of the gods;
within it is a golden treasure-chest, heaven itself, enveloped in light."

Thus it is heard. The meaning of these two verses is as follows: even for the gods, *Ayodhyā* is an unachievable and difficult-to-attain city; by this, the *Śrīcakra* is meant. For the word *cakra* signifies "city," "abode," "dwelling," and "chamber" (used for a woman), according to the *Viśva* lexicon cited by Śaṅkara Āraṇya.

The city of Ayodhyā, which is the abode of the Lord (Īśvara), is indeed "unconquerable" (ayodhyā) for mortals; however, this [city] is so even for the gods—this is the meaning. Of what nature is it? It has eight wheels (*aṣṭācakrā*):
eight wheels consisting of an eight-spoked [wheel], two ten-spoked [wheels], a fourteen-spoked [wheel], and the three circuits within the eight-petaled and sixteen-petaled lotuses.
That [city] which possesses three subterranean chambers (bhūgṛha), and that in which there are nine doors—
triangular in shape like the doors of the womb (yonidvāra)—
is described in the *Nityāhṛdaya* as "the arising of the wheel (*cakra*) from the conjunction of five powers and four fires."

According to the technical terminology of the mantra-śāstras, a triangle with its apex facing oneself is *śakti*, while a triangle with its apex facing away is *vahni*. Within that [triangle], in Ayodhyā, there is a golden, radiant treasure-chest (*kośa*) in the form of a triangle; that itself is heaven (*svarga*), because it is of the nature of bliss.

The reading "svargo lokaḥ" found in the *Taittirīyas* has this very same meaning. In that [context], the group of five words ending in the locative case, beginning with "tasmin hiraṇmaye," are in grammatical apposition and their meaning is clear. Within the triangle, there is a wheel in the form of a *bindu*; in that [wheel] resides the Yakṣa, who is to be worshipped.

The knowers of Brahman recognize that [Bindu] as well-known, just as they recognize the Self; the meaning is that they consider Brahman to be non-different from Bindu, just as they consider it non-different from the Self. It is called *kūṭa* because it deceives (*kūṭayati*), deluding the Self by veiling its bliss and other qualities, and thereby casting it into the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

It stands there as the presiding witness over that deceptive ignorance (*kūṭamajñānam*), according to the traditional teaching: "It is immovable, unchanging, and eternal" (*kūṭasthamacalaṃ dhruvam*). Or, it is that in which the station (*sthā*)—the abiding (*sthitih*)—of deceptive ignorance resides. Or, it stands like a peak (*kūṭaḥ*), such as a mountain summit, due to its state of being devoid of action (*niṣkriyatayā*). [As used by] blacksmiths...
A *kūṭa* is a specific piece of iron fixed in the ground as a boundary marker for a blow or conflict;

she is like that, being changeless (*nirvikārā*). Alternatively, it is that in which the stability (*sthiti*) of all *kūṭas*—that is, the multitudes of the universe—resides. Or, she dwells within the three *kūṭas* beginning with *vāgbhava*. [The word] *kūṭa*...
Or, it means that [the deity] resides there at the city gate, which is a triangle situated within the circle of women (strīcakra).
290) *Kūṭa* refers to a mechanical device (*yantra*), falsehood (*anṛta*), a zodiac sign (*rāśi*), an immovable object, an iron mallet,
the peak of a mountain of illusion (*māyā*), something trifling, a part of a plow (*sīra*), and deceit (*dambha*).
And at the city gate they praise her—thus says the Viśvaprakāśa. "Kula" means the Kaula path, external worship, lineage, or conduct; she is of that nature.
She who is fond of assemblies of heroes, she who is herself a hero, and she who is beyond ritual action (*naiṣkarmya*).

An "assembly of heroes" (*vīragoṣṭhī*) refers to a gathering, a council, or a conversation among heroes, which she loves. She is also a "heroine" (*vīrā*) because of her own possession of valor. According to the *Nāmamālā*, however, a "heroine" is one who possesses a husband and sons. [The word] *nirgatāni* means "gone forth."

Because he is devoid of actions (*niṣkarma*), his state is *naiṣkarmya*; that which possesses this is *naiṣkarmyā*. The suffix *-in* (forming *naiṣkarmya*) is used here in the sense of possession according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*, or it is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) as the feminine suffix *ṣyaṅ*. The meaning is "one who is free from the taint of action. This is supported by the Smṛti: "He is not tainted by sin," and thus there is neither merit nor demerit.
And because of the scriptural statement, "It is mine. The Yoga Sūtra also states: "Īśvara is a distinct Puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or their latent impressions."
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Bhāskararāya, the tenth digit, the *Bodhinī*, was completed with the ninth hundred [verses]. (900)
Thus ends the tenth century, named the Tenth Kalā, in the illustrious commentary on the *Lalitāsahasranāma*.

The eleventh digit, named the Hundredth, is the sustaining power (*dhāriṇī*) whose form is sound (*nāda*). Sound resides at the head of the *praṇava*; she has that as her form. Thus it has been said by the learned:
O Sovereign Lady, Your form, characterized by bliss, has transformed into the nature of resonance (nāda) within the region known as the Unstruck (anāhata);
it is perceived by the inward-turned mind and proclaimed through tears and horripilation.
Blessed are they!

Thus [it is said]. Or rather, its form resides within the *nāda*. This has been stated in the *Svacchandatantra* with the passage beginning, "That which was called *rodhinī*, the *nāda* is situated above it," and ending with, "One should meditate on the supreme Śivā, who is seated upon its lap and moving upwards."
The movement of consciousness is auspicious, skillful, and seated upon the lunar seat (baindavāsana).
The conceptualization (*kalanā*) of consciousness—that is, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—is the direct realization of one's own self;

for the retention of the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) is indeed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in its true sense. Or, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) may be understood as that which is stated by Kūrma: "one should know that [is] consciousness. One who is proficient in the arts (*kalā*) is "skilled" (*kalyā*). Alternatively:
She is worthy of being contemplated as the auspicious dawn in its personified form, or in the form of the *Kādambarī* and other such works. For it is said:
"The word *kalya* denotes creation and morning; *kalya* refers to one who is healthy and capable;
*kalyā* signifies auspiciousness and is also remembered as the name of the *Kādambarī*."

Thus says the *Viśva* lexicon. She is "erudite" (*vidagdhā*), meaning she possesses a clever nature. She is one whose seat is the "Bindu" (*baindava*), which is a circular configuration in the upper portion of the eyebrows. And it is said in the *Svacchandatantra*:
"Above the mandala of Hākinī, there is a circle in the form of a Bindu," and so forth. Therein—
Having described the lotus and Śiva, she is seated on his left side; she is Śāntyatītā, Manonmanī, and so forth, or she is one whose seat is the wheel associated with the *bindu*,
known as Sarvānandamaya, which is a collection (*samūha*) of *bindus*.

Or rather, it is that whose support and designator is that very seat (*āsana*) called *bindava*, which is the substratum for the meanings of the terms to be expressed. And so it is said in the *Jñānārṇavatantra*:
"O fair-faced one, I shall explain the arrangement of the *bindu*, which is the form of the seed-syllable (*bīja*)."
O Pārvatī, know that the letter *ha*, in the form of a bindu, is Brahmā.
O Goddess of the gods, Hari and I [Śiva] are the letter *sa* together with the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the visarga;
in this world, Hari and Hara are thus inseparably connected.

By such statements as these, having declared that the triads of Vāmā and the others, Icchā and the others, Bhūḥ and the others, and Jāgrat and the others, are each of the nature of the *bindu*, [the text] concludes:
"Thus, through union with the three *bindus*, she is named Tripurā and possesses form. Alternatively, by eliding the vowel *a* (in *ap*), [it refers to] the waters (*apsu*).

When that lunar [light] resides in that cluster of living beings (jīvakadamba) as a collection of moons, it exists as a single entity itself without distinction within the many reflections, because it has the nature of a reflected image; for the Śruti declares: "It is seen as one and as many, like the moon in water. || 218 ||
She is superior to the principles (*tattva*), consists of the principles, and has the nature of the meaning of the word *tattva*.
The principles are indeed thirty-six in number, being entities that persist until the time of dissolution;
for objects such as jars do not possess the status of being denoted by the term "principle. And it has been said by the learned:

That which remains until the dissolution of the universe and bestows enjoyment upon all beings is declared to be *tattva* (the ultimate reality); therefore, the body, a jar, and the like are not *tattva*.

Thus [it is said]. She is superior to those [other powers] because she persists even when they have perished. She consists of the *tattvas* (principles), meaning she is abundant in *tattvas*. Alternatively, the meaning of the two names is that she is superior to the *tattva*—namely the Śiva-tattva—and she is composed of consciousness (*cinmayī*).
This amounts to saying she is of the nature of both *samprajñāta* and *asamprajñāta* samādhi. As it has been said:
In the Jñānārṇava:
"That which is known as *svayaṃprajñāta* arises through the preponderance of Śiva;
that which is named *asamprajñāta* indeed becomes the very essence of Śiva (*śivatattva*)."
Regarding those very characteristics, it is said in that same [text]: "The distinction of self-awareness (saṃprajñāta) may be intense or more intense;
likewise, the distinction of non-awareness (asaṃprajñāta) is mild or milder."
O Goddess, samādhi characterized by laughter, weeping, horripilation, trembling, perspiration, and so forth, is observed to be intense and even more intense.
Her eyes were devoid of blinking, and her body remained fixed with those characteristics;
O Goddess, her meditative absorption (samādhi) was observed to be exceedingly slow and steady.

Thus it is said. And this dyad arises through the fixing of the mind upon a particular radiance (*tejas*). That radiance is to be understood from the mouth of one's own master. Alternatively, it consists of the threefold reality (*tattva*): the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), the reality of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), and the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*).
The meaning is that it is "superior to the threefold reality" because its nature consists of the totality of all principles (*sarvatattva*) as their collective whole (*tatsamaṣṭi*).
The nature of the fourfold reality has been stated by the elders: "The *ātmatattva* extends up to *māyā*, and the *vidyātattva* should extend up to *sadāśiva*."
Śakti and Śiva are the Śiva-tattva; the Turīya-tattva is their combined offering (samiṣṭi).
Thus, the nature of the triad consists of the principle of Being (*sattattva*), the principle of Consciousness (*cittattva*), and the principle of Bliss (*ānandatattva*).
Among those entities beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth that are born from Brahman— which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*)—
the aspect of bliss (*ānandāṃśa*) of Śiva and Śakti remains unobscured, as does that of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā.
The aspect of consciousness (cid-aṃśa) is unobscured; however, from Māyā down to the earth (kṣiti),
only the "space between" (sandaṃśa) is unobscured,
due to the absence of successive veils over existence (sat), consciousness (cit), and bliss (ānanda).

Due to the rule that each preceding [category] is necessarily pervaded by the absence of the subsequent veil, all three are unobscured in the *śiva-tattva*. In the *vidyā-tattva*, the aspects of existence (*sat*) and consciousness (*cit*) are unobscured, whereas in the aspect of bliss (*ānanda*), there is only slight obscuration. However, in the *ātman-tattva*, the aspects of consciousness and bliss remain fully obscured.

The word *ātman* is well-known in usages such as "attainment of self" (*ātmalābha*) as referring merely to existence; the word *vidyā* refers to consciousness (*cit*) in the form of knowledge; and the word *śiva* is well-known as bliss in the form of liberation (*mokṣa*).
Thus, by these three words alone, the possession of the aspects of existence (*sat*), consciousness (*cit*), and bliss (*ānanda*) is obtained.

The secret of the three principles (*tattva*). Alternatively, because the path of the thirty-six principles (*tattvādhvan*) also possesses limbs within the body of the Supreme Self—which consists of the six paths—it is composed of principles (*tattvamayī*). As it is said in the *Kāmika*:
The thirty-six principles beginning with earth have been taught by those who know the Āgamas;
this path of principles (tattvādhvan) of his assumes the form of semen, marrow, and bone.

Thus: the meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam* contained within the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) are Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*). Her essential nature is this: she is fond of the chanting of the Sāmaveda, she is gentle, and she is the consort of Sadāśiva. (219)
She for whom the singing of the *sāman* is dear; or, she for whom the *sāmagās*, that is, the *chandogas*, are dear;

or, she for whom that which is "anavat," meaning "possessing breath" (*prāṇavat*), is dear. According to the rule "one who deserves *soma* takes the suffix *ya*," the word *somyā* means one who is worthy of the *soma* sacrifice. Alternatively, in the sense of "she whose constituent part is *soma* accompanied by *umā*," the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to the rule "in the case of *mayat*... (Pāṇini 4.3.82).

Or it is that which has the suffix *ya* by virtue of a [specific] rule (*sūtra*). Alternatively, "Soma" refers to camphor and the moon; in the sense of "delighting like the moon," the suffix *ya* is applied according to the *śākha*-class (Pāṇini 5.3.103). Or, in the sense of "one who is proficient therein," the suffix *ya* is applied. However, in the reading with the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) as in *saumya*, the suffix is applied in its own sense according to the *cāturvarṇya*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.124).
The suffix *ṣyañ* [is applied]. This means that Sadāśiva’s wife (kuṭumbinī), Śyāmalā, is one whose form is mounted upon a horse and is Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). || 219 ||

"Abiding in the paths of the right and the left"—the right path (*savya*) and the left path (*apasavya*), these are the "paths of the right and the left"; she is established in, or presides over, them. That is to say, she is capable of granting authority such as the power of bestowing and protecting. Of those...
Or, it is that in which the station (*sthiti*) of three [paths] is situated. For there are indeed three paths for the solar disc, distinguished by their northern, southern, and middle portions.
Each path (*vīthī*) consists of three constellations each, beginning with Aśvinī.
Each individual path consists of three such triplets of lanes. This has been explained in detail in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and Bharaṇī (Yāmyā) are designated as the Nāga-vīthī."
Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, and Mṛgaśiras are designated as the Gaja-vīthī (the Elephant Path).
Puṣyā, Āśleṣā, and Ādityā are known as the Airāvatī path;
these three paths are called the Northern Course.
Likewise, the two Phalgunīs, Maghā, and Ārṣabhī are considered [the second path];
and Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī are designated as the Govīthī.
Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā are considered the Jāradgavī path;
these three paths are called the middle course.
Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Uttarāṣāḍhā are designated as the Ajavīthī;
likewise, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and Mārgī [are the next].
Vaiśvānarī is proclaimed in Bhādrapada, and Revatī likewise;
these three paths are called the southern route.
Thus: Bharaṇī belongs to Yama; Punarvasu has Aditi as its deity (ādityā); Mārgī is the path of Mṛga.
The rest is clear. Here, each of the three terms beginning with *savya* can individually denote all three paths. For instance, the left side of the body—

According to the *Kośa*, "savya" means "apasavya," which is the south; thus, in the present context, by the word "savya," the northern path consisting of the Nāga-path, Gaja-path, and Airāvata-path is intended.
By the word "apasavya," however, the southern path consisting of the Aja-path, Mṛga-path, and Vaiśvānara-path is intended.
The path (*mārga*). By the word "path," which denotes a general category, the middle path—consisting of the Ārṣatavīthī, Govīthī, and Jāradgavavīthī—is indicated by process of elimination.
Alternatively, it is the northern path (*uttaramārga*), called the path of the deer (*mṛgamārga*) because of its connection with Mṛgaśīrṣa (the constellation).

Thus, by this etymology, it is designated by the term *mārga* (path). The middle [path], however, is called *savya* because, relative to the path of birds (*pakṣimārga*), it stands on the left (*savya*). The *apasavya*, meanwhile, remains as it is [on the right]. Alternatively, according to the lexicon which states that *savya* refers to both the right and the left, it refers specifically to the right and the middle paths.

The [terms] *savya* and *apasavya* denote two paths, while the term *mārga* denotes the northern path; thus, the description of the three paths is accomplished in a counter-clockwise sequence. Alternatively, the southern path itself—due to its connection with the *mṛgavīthī* (the deer-path)—is designated by that etymological derivation.

Let it be stated by the term *mārga* (the path). But the middle [path] is designated by the term *savya* (right), because it is to the right of the path, or because it is on the right side relative to the northern path. For this very reason, the northern path is *apasavya* (left) due to its opposition to that. Alternatively, the middle [path] itself may be designated by the term *apasavya* in relation to the northern path.

One interpretation is that because the right side is the position [of honor], the word "left" (*savya*) refers specifically to the north; thus, even according to the sequence of right-to-left orientation, the designation is appropriately established.
Or alternatively: the "left" (*savya*) is the path of the gods (*devayāna*), such as the path beginning with light (*arcis*), which is to be attained by those intent on cessation (*nivṛtti*).
The *apasavya* path, beginning with smoke (*dhūma*) and leading to the ancestors (*pitṛyāṇa*), is attained by those intent on worldly activity (*pravṛtti*).

The word "situated on the path" (*mārgastha*)—derived from the etymology "that in which there is standing (*sthā*, i.e., *sthiti*)"—refers to the world of Viṣṇu, characterized by eternal stability. [It refers to] the respective paths of the planets, such as the Sun and others.
Because establishment depends upon stability; the meaning is that it consists of these three paths. The detailed account of this is found in the second book of the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"That which is north of Agastya and south of the Ajavīthī..."
That is indeed the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa), which lies outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
There sit the high-souled sages who maintain the sacred fire,
praising the Brahman as the source of all created beings, while the officiating priests stand ready.
But for those worlds that undertake [new actions], the path is indeed the southern one;
they, however, establish the Brahman again and again in age after age.
Through the performance of intense austerities, by means of established boundaries, and through sacred learning,
those who were born previously indeed entered the houses of their descendants.
And here, those of the west are born from the deaths of those of the east;
thus revolving, they remain steadfast in their fixed vows.
"For they remain on the southern path of the Sun as long as the moon and stars exist.
Thus it is said. The northern peak of the Lokāloka mountain is the abode of Agastya. This is stated in the *Agni Purāṇa*:
For these world-protectors stand at the Lokāloka mountain in the four directions;
to the north of that is the peak of Agastya, worshipped by divine sages.
Thus: from the Ajavīthī (the path of the goats), consisting of the three constellations beginning with Mūla,

and from the Vaiśvānarapatha (the path of fire), consisting of the final three constellations, [arises] that portion of the Veda consisting of the Karmakāṇḍa, which brings about the elements and indicates the path of the activity of Brahman.
The collective meaning is that even those considered "being born" are born again and again within their own family; likewise, in that very same [text]:
"That which is north of the Nāgavīthī and south of the Seven Sages..."
The northern path of Savitṛ is known as the path of the gods.
There, those perfected ones (siddhas) are self-controlled, stainless, and celibate;
they loathe progeny, and therefore they have conquered death.
Eighty-eight thousand sages of sublimated vital energy remain on the northern path of the Sun until the dissolution of all beings.
Through the avoidance of attachment to sensual union and sexual intercourse,
through the non-occurrence of desire and aversion, and through the refraining from the destruction of living beings;
Furthermore, because they perceived the defects of desire and the like through their association with the unattainable,
they became pure by these very causes and indeed attained immortality.
Indeed, the state that lasts until the dissolution of all beings is called immortality;
this duration of the existence of the three worlds is termed "no-more-death."

Thus [it is said]. "Beyond the Nāgavīthī" means beyond the triad beginning with Aśvinī. "Due to the avoidance of the commencement of elemental existence" means due to the abandonment of the path of worldly activity (*pravṛttimārga*). Lest it be thought that there is an identity of fruit with the third path, he says: "until the dissolution of all beings" (*ābhūtasaṃplavam*). Likewise, in that very same [text]:
Above the Ṛṣis, where Dhruva is established,
is this divine third station of Viṣṇu, radiant in the sky.
O Brahmin, that supreme state belongs to those ascetics who have shaken off the mire of defects, whose selves are fully restrained, and for whom merit and demerit have been exhausted.
When merit and demerit have ceased and all causes of suffering are exhausted,
that supreme abode of Viṣṇu is reached, where having gone, they do not grieve.
Like an eye stretched across the sky, it is seen by yogis whose selves are absorbed in That; and that supreme abode of Viṣṇu is perceived through the vision of discriminative knowledge.
And so forth. This is another explanation.

Or rather: in the sequence of spiritual practice (*upāsanā*), two paths are observed—the Left Path (*vāmamārga*) and the Right Path (*dakṣiṇamārga*). Among these, the so-called Left Path consists of those [duties] prescribed for one's own respective caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
In all those rites— whether Vedic such as the Agnihotra and others, Smārta such as the Aṣṭaka and others,

or Tantric such as the accomplishment of mantras and so forth— whatever deities are present, whether as primary or as subsidiary, [one should worship] one's own chosen deity in each of their respective places.

One should perform this everywhere. The method consists of inserting the word denoting one's own deity as the predicate after each word denoting a specific deity within all mantras. In such a path, there is the sin arising from the failure to discharge the debts owed to the gods, sages, and ancestors.

On the path of the Right (dakṣiṇamārga), however, there is no strict requirement that one must meditate upon one’s own chosen deity (svopāsyadevatā) in the place of the respective deities of the limbs of the rites prescribed in the Śrauta and other traditions; rather, it is precisely as an ancillary to those rites which are enjoined in the Tantras concerning those respective deities.

Because there is no obstruction to any actions on this path, such a sin does not exist here; thus, liberation is instantaneous. On the Vāma path, however, it is delayed due to the absence of the clearing of debts, which causes an impediment for some time. And even so, [liberation is not difficult] despite the practice being arduous.
It must be explained how the learned (śiṣṭas) engage in the Left-hand path (vāmamārga) even when the means for the portion of liberation (mokṣāṃśa) involve delay;

[the answer is] because they must endure a slight delay in liberation due to their desire to enjoy various high and low fruits of this world right here in this very birth, since [this path] bestows both enjoyment and liberation.

This is because activity is possible for those refined individuals (*śiṣṭa*) who are attached to sense objects; however, for those refined individuals who are detached from worldly enjoyment, since delay in liberation is intolerable, their engagement occurs only on the southern path—this is the distinction.
This very point has been explained in detail in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
In all mantras of the Goddess, as well as in Vedic ones, one should always meditate upon Bhairavī and Tripurā according to the sequence of the Vedic mantras.
Among all the names of the goddesses, one should always use the word "Bhairavī" as a constant qualification;
one should never utter [the name] without a qualification.
Having recited "May the waters purify the earth" and the Tripurabhairavī mantra,
the Brahmin should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) and likewise practice the Drupadā rite.
"This Viṣṇu, indeed Bhairava, strode across"—thus it is said;
one should employ this mantra for the purpose of handling clay.
Uttering the Gāyatrī mantra beginning with "Tripurā" and the auspicious Bhairavī mantra, one should offer the arghya water to the Sun, saying: "To Mārtāṇḍabhairava."
The rays bear aloft that god Jātavedas, Sūrya, so that all may behold him; but when he lies down, one should utter the Bhairava [mantra].

One should employ [the mantra] at the beginning of the libation (tarpaṇa) and so forth, saying: "May Brahman-Bhairava be satisfied. And during the invocation, one should satisfy one's own ancestors as Bhairavas, saying:
"O Mother Bhairavī, may you be satisfied; O Bhairava, may the ancestors be satisfied."
At the beginning, one should first employ Tripurā even in the rite of libation (tarpaṇa).
Wherever one worships [the deity] in rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma or Aśvamedha,
there one should worship both the Goddess and Bhairavī in the form of Bhairava.
In this way, one should worship Tripurabhairavī with a left-handed disposition;
she is to be worshipped by the left path, devoid of the right-hand manner.
He who worships the sages, the gods, the ancestors, humans,
and the multitudes of beings with the five sacrifices that purify one’s debts.
Whatever worship is performed according to the rules through ritual bathing and giving,
along with its secret aspects, that is here called *dākṣiṇya*.
Because he is skillful (dakṣiṇa) in all matters, such as toward the ancestors and the gods,
and because the goddess Dakṣiṇā belongs to him, he is therefore called Dakṣiṇa.
That goddess who, when worshipped by gods and others without exception,
herself enjoys the sacrificial portions, is proclaimed as Vāmā.
The worshipper may also be one who is constantly devoted to that left-hand path;
he need not perform the five great sacrifices, nor need he perform the worship of the left-hand path.
Since the woman takes a share of the worship belonging to another,
there can be no clearing of debt for him who worships with the dispositions of a woman.
For one who travels by that path, the yoga of Tripurā arises at all times and in every respect for the sake of the ancestors, gods, humans, and others.
When this arises in the wise man, then he shall attain liberation;
however, a man of the Traipura school attains liberation through the left-hand path only after a long time.
O Bhairava, because he is overcome by the sins born of failing to repay debts,
he is endowed with happiness and sovereignty in this world and is beloved everywhere.
Shining with a body as beautiful as the god of love,
he brought the king, along with his entire kingdom, under his control on all sides.
He deluded all the women and rendered them overwhelmed with passion; he likewise deluded lions, tigers, hyenas, and the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
Moving with the speed of the wind and unimpeded,
he wanders while bringing under his control either the youthful Goddess Tripurā, or the middle-aged Bhairavī.
He who, being skillful and like the five-arrowed god of love, should worship with supreme devotion Kāmeśvarī known as Kāmā, may worship her according to his desire.
Whether through courtesy or through charm, one shall attain success in every way;
[one should worship] Mahāmāyā, Śāradā, and likewise Śailaputrī.
In whatever manner, one should worship with courtesy alone;
he who worships Mahāmāyā and the others without courtesy and devotion [is at fault].
That sinner, fallen from all the worlds, becomes a bearer of disease;
as for the other goddesses previously mentioned, such as Śivadūtī and the rest—
Those [deities] should be worshipped by practitioners either from the right or from the left out of courtesy;
however, that worshipper who is on the left side is one who causes the destruction of other directions.
"Because it fulfills all desires, the right [path] is therefore supreme.

This is Śiva’s speech addressed to Vaitāla and Bhairava. According to this interpretation, "savyāpasavyau ca tau mārgau" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "those two paths, the left and the right"; she is situated upon those two.
The meaning is that [the deity] is to be worshipped by both paths.

This refers to those deities such as Tripurabhairavī who are to be worshipped exclusively by the Vāma path; those such as Śāradā who are to be worshipped exclusively by the Dakṣiṇa path; and those who may be worshipped by either way as an option.
In the ultimate sense, there is non-difference between the goddesses such as Śivadūtī and Tripurasundarī;
this is another interpretation.
What is the point here? [The answer is that] in the *Śivasūtra*, in the passage beginning with "in the left, right, and suṣumṇā," the terms *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* are employed.

Another interpretation is that, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the words "left and right" actually refer to the Suṣumṇā itself through the term "path. In this second interpretation as well, since the path of the Pole Star (*dhruvamārga*) is understood through the term "path" alone by way of elimination and through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the same conclusion follows].

There are four words: three words consisting of compounds of two pairs of three-footed terms, and one word consisting of a *karmadhāraya* compound containing two two-footed terms; these four words are then further combined by means of a *dvandva-apavāda-ekaśeṣa* (a single-remainder compound that sets aside the *dvandva*).
The synthesis of the four commentaries is to be understood.

Now, those who do not know these two paths— those who have fallen away from the two paths according to the manner stated in the Śruti, "They become worms, moths, and whatever this [is] that has bristling hairs," and so forth— [are as follows].

It is said that he compassionately wards off even the calamities of those who have fallen into painful distress merely through the means of recollecting his name and so forth, without any effort on their part: kaṣṭamāpadaṃ prāptāsteṣāmapyāpadamanāyāsanāmasmaraṇādisādhanamātreṇa dayayā nivārayatītyāha— (He says that he compassionately wards off even the calamities of those who have fallen into painful distress merely through the means of recollecting his name and so forth, without any effort on their part.)
—The warder-off of all calamities.
Regarding "all calamities": she wards off all calamities specifically and most effectively. And thus, in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, there is this statement of the Goddess:
But those who, having abandoned all attachments, have come to me alone for refuge and always worship with devotion, relying upon the sovereign yoga;
Compassionate toward all beings, peaceful, self-controlled, free from envy,
humble, wise, ascetics whose vows are firmly restrained.
With their minds fixed on Me, their lives surrendered to Me, and delighting in the discourse of My knowledge—
whether they be renunciants, householders, forest-dwellers, or students.
And those who, though lacking the aforementioned characteristics, chant my name—
those who are constantly devoted to it— even mountains of calamities [shall not overwhelm them].
"I shall utterly destroy [these] here before long by means of the lamp of knowledge.

Thus, in the *Harivaṃśa* as well, Viṣṇu speaks these words to the Goddess, having set forth a succession of calamities for men, beginning with: "bondage, execution, imprisonment, loss of sons, and loss of wealth," and so forth.
"In all calamities, you protect [us], of this there is no doubt"—thus it ends. Also, in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*, at the conclusion of the hymn to the Goddess composed by Brahmā and others:
"O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, those who take refuge in You..."
No calamities whatsoever arise for them, nor do any perils occur anywhere.
And so forth. Even those who are learned have said:
"In times of distress, what is to be done? One should remember the pair of feet of the Mother.
What does that remembrance accomplish? It makes even Brahmā and the other gods her servants."
Established in her own state, sweet by nature, steadfast, and honored by the wise. || 220 ||
Because of the absence of agitation caused by suffering, she is "svasthā"—either established in her own self or remaining in herself.
This is according to the Śruti: "O Blessed One, on what is he established? [The answer is: "In his own majesty," it is said.
The indeclinable *svar* denotes heaven; she either stands there as the presiding overseer, or she is a beautiful abiding (*śobhanā asthā*).

That by which there is an absence of staying—that is movement—or rather, she is sweet and desirable to all by her very power alone, even without contact with external conditions. "Madhura" means flavorful, delicious, or dear; it is called "madhura" like anything else that is so.

"Madhurā" refers to *śatapuṣpā*, "Madhūlī," and "Nagarī," according to the *Viśvakośa*. For this very reason, it may also be understood as "the city of Madhurā which possesses its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) or state of being. Furthermore, it is the abode of Mīnākṣī and the field of Hālāsya (the dance of Śiva).

Up to this point: or rather, those who are foremost—that is, to be counted as first—among the wise regarding their own self, namely those who are supreme among the knowers of the Self; of them, the "dhur" (burden/forefront) is like the pole of a chariot.
The word *dhur* takes the feminine suffix *ṭāp* according to the opinion of Bhāguri because it ends in the consonant *r*, just as the pole (*dhur*) of a chariot.

The meaning is that, likewise, this [practice] is the most excellent limb (*sarvottamamaṅga*) for those possessing self-knowledge, as it is what carries them to liberation (*nirvāhikā*). Nor should one be deluded into thinking that the word *avama* refers only to something inferior; for we observe the usage of the words *avama* and *uttama* to refer respectively to the first and the last, as in: "Agni is the first among the deities."
Viṣṇu was the foremost among those who have gone together; thus [it is said] in the mantra of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the *Āgnāvaiṣṇava* sacrifice,
regarding the mention of Agni and Viṣṇu as the first and last among all the deities.

In the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa*, in the passage explaining how the inclusion of all intermediate deities is accomplished through the principle of "collective withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) in the *Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* sacrifice, it says: "Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods, Viṣṇu the highest."

Since it is observed that the first word is explained by the latter word, their synonymy is established. Alternatively, [the compound may mean] "among those who vomit—that is, emit, create, or accomplish—[their own] light, there is the highest burden. Therefore, the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) based on the rule "there is no [compound] when there is a selection" (*tena na nirdhāraṇe*) does not apply.

There is a contradiction; for here, as in the case of *puruṣottama*, it is understood as a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*). "Beautiful non-existences" means intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). By qualifying non-existences with "beauty," the ugliness of their counter-correlates—the positive entities—is thereby expressed. Consequently...
Or she is "Madhurā" because she is free from the absence of qualities such as the imbalance of passion and hatred or cruelty;

or she is "Madhurā" because she abides with affection (*bhāva*) toward her own devotees (*sveṣu*); or she is so called because she bestows the honey of excellent fruit (*satphala*) through her own disposition of devotion (*bhāvena*), for it is stated in the Śruti: "Moving about, he indeed finds honey."

This is because we observe the explanation of the term *madhu*. In this way, the meanings of the abstract nouns (*bhāvapadārtha*) for both *abhiprāya* (intention) and *avatāra* (descent/incarnation) should also be applied as appropriate. *Dhīrā* means the wise or those possessed of fortitude;
or it means she who bestows (*rāti*) wisdom (*dhī*), that is, the realization of non-duality (*advaitabuddhi*).

According to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*), the latent impression of non-duality (*advaitavāsanā*) arises in men solely through the grace of the Lord (*īśvarānugraha*). Alternatively, she is *irā*—the tenth lunar day (*daśamī tithi*)—which bestows intelligence (*dhī-pradā*). She is honored by the steadfast (*dhīraiḥ*), meaning by the wise (*paṇḍitaiḥ*), as the Veda states: "The steadfast poets (*dhīrāsaḥ kavayaḥ*) draw him forth. For this very reason, those of auspicious conduct [manifest] their own steadfastness (*dhairya*).
It has been made manifest:
"O Mother, whether you cast me into the netherworld or establish me in the sovereignty of all the worlds, I shall not let go of your pair of feet; indeed, I shall never let them go."

Thus, she is either worshipped with intent directed toward that which is designated as "intellect" (dhī)—which is non-different from knowledge—and which consists of aesthetic flavor (rasa) and bliss (ānanda). || 220 ||
She is to be perfectly propitiated with the *arghya* of consciousness; she is fond of the flower of consciousness.

According to the *Śivasūtra*, "Consciousness is the form of *cit*, the self-consciousness is the Self," that very consciousness is the *arghya*—water and so forth—which is fit for worship, and by means of it she is to be properly propitiated.

Because the worship known as "without support" (nirādhārā) consists of the contemplation of non-difference from consciousness, it is said in the Bhāvanopaniṣad that "knowledge is the water-offering" (jñānam arghyam). And it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"By one's own experience, [one realizes] Maheśvarī herself, who is directly one's own self..."
One should worship with sincere reverence; such worship bestows the goals of human life.

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, the meaning is "by means of knowledge," which is the *arghya* (offering) of the conscious Self—that is, by means of one's own experience. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *arghya* is used in the context of a ritual of worship (*pūjāvidhi*), as well as for 'price,' and for the root of a tree of knowledge. The suffix *-ya* in *arghya* is used in the sense of "suitable for" (*sādhu*). Or, because the group beginning with *cāturvarṇya* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, it may be used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*).

The suffix *ṣyañ* [is applied]. The word division is simply "ārghyam. Alternatively, it may mean that the *manu* (sacred syllable) which denotes consciousness is the deity of the *vidyā* (knowledge-mantra) and the goddess. For there is the statement: "By means of that *bhuvaneśvarī* mantra, the female deities are to be propitiated; the *vidyās* are goddesses, while the *mantras* are considered male deities. This is stated in the *Sūtasamhitā*: [The text continues: "In the *Sūtasamhitā*—"
Having recited ten thousand times the mantra that expresses consciousness,
one is liberated from the multitude of great sins as well as other transgressions.

Furthermore, in this verse, the mantra-word denoting consciousness (*caitanya*) is explained as referring to the *bhuvaneśvarī* mantra. Alternatively, *caitanya* is consciousness itself—the essence (*rasa*) whose nature is pure awareness (*saṃvit*). According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *cetanā* is said to mean consciousness (*saṃvit*), and it is remembered [also] as meaning a sentient being, like its referent. That very thing is the *arghya*.

That is to say, the worship materials have been rendered fit for worship by means of consecrations through the filling of the special *arghya* vessel. By that [means], she is to be propitiated through perfect libations and so forth.
According to the *Rudrayāmala*, among *saṃvit* (consciousness) and *āsava* (liquor), consciousness alone is more important; thus it is held by the Tantrikas.

The fifth element (pāñcamika-rasa), which is conventionally designated by the term *kuṇḍagola-udbhava*, is consciousness (*caitanya*), because it arises from living beings. And consciousness is indeed the "flower" (*kusuma*), because it brings forth the great fruit.

This is seen in such passages as "the stream of nectar flowing from the cluster of flowers that is consciousness for the insentient," where there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) of consciousness with a flower.
Because it is established by the tradition of the poets; she for whom that [eightfold path] is dear.
This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the eight flowers:
"Non-violence is the first flower, as is the restraint of the senses."
Patience is the flower; compassion is the flower; and wisdom is considered the supreme flower.
As stated by the learned: "Austerity is its flower, truth is its flower, and then feeling is the eighth flower.

Accordingly, the two positions beginning with *saṃvit* (consciousness) should also be extended here. Since flowers exist in both of those [positions], the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) for both positions is simply "the flower of consciousness" (*caitanyasya kusumam*).
Ever-arisen, ever-contented, and as rosy-red as the rising sun. || 221 ||

She is always (*sadā*) and eternally (*nityam*) risen (*uditā*), because she possesses self-luminosity; or alternatively, she is risen in every way (*āsamantāt*) and with excellence among the virtuous (*satsu*). In this very manner, there are two meanings for the term *sadātuṣṭā*. She is pale-red (*pāṭalā*)—white and red—like the young sun (*taruṇa*) at the time of midday; yet she is not fair-complexioned (*gaurī*).

An objection based on contradictions such as [the description of the Self] as "dark-complexioned" and so forth must be raised; however, this is resolved because the arrangement is logically consistent through differences in form or differences in meditative visualization. For it is heard in scripture:
"Just as a garment dyed with saffron, or like white wool, or like the indragopa insect"; and it is likewise remembered in the Smṛti:
Śāntā, appearing white in color, is for the formulation of the dharma of liberation;
Pāṭalā is for subjugating women, subjugating kings, and subjugating people.
Yellow [sandalwood] is for the attainment of wealth; black is for the rite of killing;
brown is said to be for causing enmity; and the pale-red form is for the erotic sentiment.
"Comprising all colors, she is to be meditated upon as consisting of light, supreme in every attainment. || 221 ||
She is to be propitiated through both the right and the left; her lotus-face is radiant with a gentle smile.

She is to be propitiated by the right-hand path (dakṣiṇā) and by those who are skillful (dakṣiṇaiḥ kuśalaiḥ); or alternatively, by the "right" (dakṣiṇaiḥ) learned ones and the "left" (adakṣiṇaiḥ) fools. [She is to be worshipped] by a follower of the right-hand path (dakṣiṇāmārgopāsakena).

Or alternatively, by one who follows the left-hand path; or else, those who seek to know mere ritual action are called "right-handers. By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where all desires have ceased.
Neither sacrificial gifts nor ignorant ascetics go there.
Since such an interpretation is seen in the Śruti, those who know Brahman are to be worshipped by those two even without sacrificial fees (adakṣiṇā).
"O Arjuna, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me... [Bhagavad Gītā 7.16].
The afflicted, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom, O bull of the Bharatas.
According to this statement: she whose lotus-face is *smera*—that is, smiling slightly (*daram īṣat*) in such a manner;
or alternatively, that whose lotus-face is *smera*, meaning shining like a conch (*śaṅkha*), with its neck curved like a conch. Thus, it is she whose lotus-face is thus radiant.

"Kambukaṇṭhī" means up to that point. Alternatively, it means she whose lotus-face is ever-smiling even in *dare*, that is, at times of fear. For others, their faces turn pale from fear even during occasional times such as the end of a kalpa;
however, for the Mother, her face is always smiling—this is the meaning. In *dare*...
"Smiling" means gracious or pleased regarding the honoring of devotees.
Here, this should be understood: in the second half of this verse, four names appear;
among them, three—excluding the third—are redundant.
The Kaulinī is exclusively the bestower of the fruit of priceless liberation. || 222 ||
She is the noble woman dwelling within the lineage, the Kaulinī, the Yoginī of the Kula;
she is the one who utters *klīṃ*, the absolute, the secret, and the bestower of the state of liberation.

In this context, because three [names] have been explained, and with the desire to avoid that [consequence], the authors of the *Chalākṣara-sūtra* accepted *kaulinī-kulayoginī* as a single compound; thus, in the present case, they recognized two names: the one remaining, *kaulinī*, and the other, *kulayoginī*.

As it has been said: *ḷyḷdḷkhḷrīḍṛkikoṭapatī | ḷyāyūṭāṭkhṛrīḍṛkīkorīyṝphī*—this is the *chāyā* consisting of thirteen syllables. According to the method beginning with "three names of eight syllables each," there are twenty-one names starting from *sadāśivakuṭumbinī*.

In that context, [the names] ending with "mānavatī" are described. Therein, by means of the two syllables *ki* and *ko*, there are two names: one consisting of three syllables and one consisting of thirteen syllables.
This is explained as describing the two names under discussion, in the sense that their initial syllables belong to the *ka*-group (the gutturals).

[The word] *sthitiḥ* [is used]. For here, since it has already been stated that the aphorisms of the *Chalārṇa* are rooted in observed logical justification (*dṛṣṭopapatti*), it is appropriate to describe the division of words (*padaccheda*) as referring to four names, rather than three, in consideration of the formation of three names from six [individual] names.
Our venerable teacher, the author of this work, considering that one name remains while another is required, has accepted two names here: *Kaulinī* and *Kulayoginī*.
In this view as well, the avoidance of redundancy is exactly the same. It is not [otherwise].

And thus there is an excess of names; for although the authors of the *Chalākṣara-sūtra* accept two names in the case of "Prasavitrī," "Pracaṇḍājñā," "Pratiṣṭhā," and "Prakaṭākṛti," [the list remains excessive].

Because the feet of the Guru accept the status of being a single name (*ekanāmatva*), that [objection] does not apply. Therefore, in this context, *kaulinīkevalā* is a single name. Nor is there an impossibility of composition (*samāsa*) in this view;

for in a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*), the words "pūrvakāla" (prior time), "eka" (one), "sarva" (all), "jarat" (old), "purāṇa" (ancient), "nava" (new), and "kevala" (exclusive) [precede the other member].
It should not be argued that, because of the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.49] stating "with a word in grammatical apposition," the single word *kevala* would necessarily take the first position;
for in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *kaulinī* would likewise incur the status of being treated as masculine (*puvadbhāva*).
This is because, as in examples such as *paraṃjyotiḥ*, it is possible for two distinct words to function as a single name.

The meaning is that she possesses the Kaula dharma and possesses the knowledge known as Kevala. The knowledge of the Lord (Īśvara) is denoted by the term *kevala*, as such usage is frequently seen in the Jaina Tantras.
Alternatively, *kevalā* means "freed from all attributes" (*sakala-dharma-vimuktā*), or "freed from pleasure and pain. One who is freed from those [is *kevala*].

This is because the term "kevalī" (the isolated one) is seen as a designation in the *Śivasūtra*; furthermore, by the word "tat" (that), there is a reference back to the pleasure and pain mentioned in the preceding sūtra— namely, "external mentalization of pleasure and pain"— and even though the possessive suffix *-in* (*ini*) is absent here, [the meaning is still conveyed].
Because such a suffix *ac* can easily be applied [to form the word *ekakṛtsna*], three meanings—namely *eka*, *kṛtsna*, and *nirṇīta*—should be described here. And thus the *Viśva* lexicon states:
"The word *kevala* may denote a distinction in knowledge (*jñānabheda*), and it also occurs in the senses of 'alone' (*eka*) and 'entire' (*kṛtsna*)."
It is said that when [the matter] is determined, it is merely [that]; and "kevala" is sometimes used in the sense of "deceit."

Thus, the actual meaning is that she possesses only the Kaula dharma; for there is a rule that two distinct words are a single name only when they are mutually connected through a relationship such as qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Alternatively, as in the case of the expression *dattābhārya* ("one whose wife has been given"), [the compound is formed].

Just as grammarians accept that even the word *dattā*, which is derived from the cause of the act of giving (*dāna-kriyā-nimitta*), is a proper name (*saṃjñā*) and thus rely on the rule *saṃjñā-pūraṇyoś-ca* to prohibit its transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*),
so too here, because the word *kaulinī* is also a proper name, [the feminine plural] is *kaulinyah* alone.

The compound *jñānavatyaḥ* can also be understood as a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "those by whom [the truth] was known. Alternatively, it may be a third-case (*tṛtīyā*) tatpuruṣa compound, meaning "determined by the *kaulinīs*," according to the rule *tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena*. This is because, in that sūtra, the term *guṇavacana* is explained as referring primarily to words denoting substances (*dravyavacana*), with the quality (*guṇa*) being subordinate.

One who speaks of a quality (*guṇa*) is called "quality-expressive" (*guṇavacana*). According to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113), which allows for the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) as well as the past passive participle, even the word expressing the object of that [action]— namely, the state (*pada*) called liberation (*kaivalya*),
which is priceless, beyond measure, and unlimited— is also termed "quality-expressive."

Its nature is to bestow that which is the fifth liberation (pañcamamukti). Alternatively, if the reading is *anarghyā* with a long final vowel, it may be explained as "that which is completely pervaded by absolute isolation (*kaivalya*)" (*āsamantād vyāptam yat kaivalyam*). Or, it may be interpreted as "that state (*padam*) in which there is no non-isolation (*akaivalyam*)," meaning that from which isolation is not absent. || 222 ||
She is fond of hymns, possessed of praise, and her majesty is extolled by the Vedas.
A hymn (*stotra*) is a worldly recitation of qualities (*guṇānuvāda*), which is sixfold: salutation (*namaskāra*), benediction (*āśis*), statement of tenets (*siddhāntokti*), and valor (*parākrama*).
Manifestation and prayer: these are the six characteristics of a hymn of praise.
Thus it was said by the learned: "She who is worthy of worship by the three worlds, the auspicious one, the substratum of the illusory world;
she who showers back the rain of weapons released by the demon lord Bhaṇḍāsura with counter-weapons;
she whose very nature consists of the power of will, the power of knowledge, and the power of action."
She who bestows sovereignty—[and so forth].

She for whom the Vedic hymn (*stotra*) is dear, which consists of names and forms such as these, and which is the designation of qualities residing in the substrate (*guṇin*) to be accomplished by means of chanted mantras. Furthermore, those waters are themselves worthy of praise; thus, they are "the praised waters" (*stotrayas*).

Or [the word "priya"] belongs to that which is dear to her. There is a masculine transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the word *stotrī*. Gods, humans, ancestors, and asuras are denoted by the term "waters" (*āp*), according to the Śruti: "These indeed are the four waters," and "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man' (*puruṣavacas*)."

Furthermore, because the Śruti declares that water itself has transformed into the forms of humans and so forth, as in the passage beginning, "Water indeed is all this. It is called *stutimatī* because it possesses praise through its connection with the status of being an object of action;
or alternatively, it is so called because it possesses both wisdom (*mati*) and sovereignty (*īś*) through such praise. It is that [state] by whose praise wisdom and sovereignty are obtained.

...up to: she whose majesty (*vaibhava*) and sovereignty (*vibhutva*) have been correctly praised or familiarized by the *śrutis*. According to the lexicon, "familiarization" (*paricaya*) means "praise" (*saṃstava*).
Alternatively, the word *śruti* may refer to the number four; for "Yugas and oceans" [are four], and the *śrutis* are four.

Thus, from the *Chandaḥsudhākara*: the analysis of the compound is "she whose majesty is familiarized in four ways. The meaning is that she is the nature of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) as stated in the *Bahvṛca-upaniṣad*—namely, the Body-Person (*śarīrapuruṣa*), the Meter-Person (*chandaḥpuruṣa*), the Veda-Person (*vedapuruṣa*), and the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*). Also, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
The four powers of the Goddess are established as her very nature;
hear from me, O best of sages, how they function through her presiding influence.
Peace, Knowledge, Foundation, and Cessation—these are remembered as such;
therefore, the Supreme Lord, the God, is said to consist of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
"By means of this, the Supreme Lord enjoys the bliss of His own Self;
and among the four gods, Maheśvara is the one who possesses the four forms. Thus [it is said].
She is the wise one, the proud one, the Great Goddess, whose form is auspicious. (223)

She is called *manasvinī* because her mind (*manas*) abides in independence rather than in a state of dependence on others; [the suffix] *viniḥ* is applied after the words *asmāya*, *medhā*, and *sraj*. She is so named because she possesses *māna*—which is either the loftiness of the mind, or respect, or an action indicative of a lover’s transgression, or a standard of measure, or cognition.
She is possessed of pride (*mānavatī*). She is the wife of Maheśa, thus *Maheśī*. And it is said in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"Because she was born from Mahādeva and because she is honored by the great ones, and because she is the bride of Maheśa, she is therefore remembered as *Maheśī*."
Thus, she is one whose form is auspicious in nature. || 223 ||
Viśvamātā (the Mother of the Universe), Jagaddhātrī (the Sustainer of the World), Viśālākṣī (the Large-eyed One), and Virāgiṇī (the Passionless One).

She is the mother of the universe, of the world, or of Viṣṇu, according to the Vedic revelation beginning with "Soma purifies" and continuing with "and he was born from Viṣṇu. She is called Jagaddhātrī because she sustains the world in the form of the earth, or she is the foster-mother.
Because he is the protector; for the *Kaṇva-śruti* states: "He is the guardian of beings, he is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded. Also, in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"Since he sustains the worlds and provides their livelihood..."
The root *ḍudhāñ* means "to sustain," and she who sustains the world is thus regarded by the wise as the *Dhātrī*.
Thus: she whose eyes are *viśāle*, meaning broad and expansive. She is the one who identifies with the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of Vārāṇasī;

for it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* that she is "Viśālākṣī" in Vārāṇasī. Furthermore, although the word *viśālā* denotes Badarikāśrama, it refers here to the Nepāla-pīṭha by virtue of the common characteristic of being situated upon the Himavat.

Furthermore, in the section concerning the ritual placement (*pīṭhanyāsa*), the placement at the location of the eyes is prescribed in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa* and other texts; thus, she is "she whose eye-location is indeed a vast seat. She is "possessing detachment" (*virāgiṇī*) because she has detachment (*vairāgya*).
She is confident, supremely generous, the highest delight, and composed of mind.

She is *pragalbhā* (bold/competent) because of her proficiency in acts such as creation; she is *paramā* (supreme), *sodārā* (noble), and *mahatī* (great). The meaning is that she possesses greatness in terms of both space and time. According to Amara, *udāra* refers to one who is generous or great. This is supported by the Vedic scripture: "And like the ether, it is all-pervading and eternal. She is *paraṃ* (the supreme).

Alternatively, it is so called because it bestows (*rāti*) supreme joy (*moda*) and bliss (*ānanda*) on all sides. Or, *paramoda* refers to the ocean (*samudra*) in which the waters (*uda*) are supreme; and in the present context, that ocean takes the form of the ocean of worldly existence (*bhava*). Its *ārā*, a specific type of weapon, is the nose.
Or, by eliding the letter *a* (in *aparamā*), those from whom *ramā* (wealth) has departed are *aparamāḥ*, meaning the poor;
[the name] means "generous" (*udārā*) toward them, bestowing sovereignty upon them. Or, *para* means excellent, and *āmodaḥ* means fragrance, that is to say, fame;
or it is that in which there is joy (*modaḥ*) or satisfaction (*santoṣaḥ*) on all sides (*ā*). Of the pure Brahman...
Because it has the mind as its locus, it is "consisting of mind" (*manomayī*). As it is said in the *Mahāvāsiṣṭharāmāyaṇa*:
"That Bhairava, the space of consciousness, is designated as Śiva;
know that his non-different power of vibration, consisting of mind, is that [same thing]."

Thus, it is "consisting of mind" (manomayī) because the mind is predominant; for, as in the statement "it is to be perceived by the mind alone," the mind alone is primary in the production of self-knowledge. || 224 ||

Vyomakeśī, Vimānasthā, Vajriṇī, and Vāmakeśvarī. She whose hair is the sky itself is Vyomakeśī, referring to her Virāḍ-form; or she is the consort of Śiva, who is Vyomakeśa (Sky-haired). Alternatively, "vyomaka" means a small portion of the sky, the suffix *ka* being used in the sense of diminution; she is the mistress (*īśī*) of that as well.

Or she is the pervasive one. Or Ambikā is the female form of the Lord whose nature is space (*vyomakara*). Or she is the female form of the directions (*dig*). A *vimāna* is a celestial vehicle; the gods reside therein, and because of their non-difference [from her], Ambikā is also so called. Or, she is one whose *sthā* (standing/place) is characterized by *viśeṣamāna* (special honor/respect). Or, *vima* refers to that which possesses a distinguished luster (*mā*).
Or, it may mean that such a cart (*anaḥ*)—a chariot consisting of wheels made of stone and so forth—is situated there.

Alternatively, it refers to Brahman, which is "devoid of measure" (*vigata-māna*), meaning it is unlimited; or it refers to those who are established in that Brahman. Or, it may mean that in which the "standing" (*sthā*, i.e., existence) within "measure" (*māne*, i.e., limitation)—that is, the state of being delimited by measurement—is gone.

"Vimāna" refers to the Veda because it measures (māti) by distinguishing (viśiṣya) and extracting (niṣkṛṣya), thereby generating valid knowledge (pramā); or alternatively, it is so called because [the subject] stands therein as that which is to be established. The form "vimāna" is derived from the root *mā* with the prefix *vi-* and the suffix *śānac*. It refers to specific means of knowledge (*māna*) that are not contradicted by the Vedas.

Or, it may mean that he abides in the form of the Brahman that is Dharma; or, it may mean that he abides within those very fourteen seats of learning (vidyāsthānas) which are specifically enumerated as such by their individual forms through the categories of Purāṇa, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and so forth.

This has been stated by the venerable Jaimini: "If it be argued that [the Smṛti] is contradicted when there is no conflict with the learned (śiṣṭa), we say no, because the scripture has a fixed measure. [The word *vajriṇī* refers to] Indra’s wife in the form of Śacī, or the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajra*), or she who is adorned with jewels called *vajras*. For in the Śruti it is said: "The raised thunderbolt is a great terror."
Alternatively, it is that which possesses [the Vajrapada], because the Vajrapada culminates in Brahman through the relationship of being its defining delimiter;

or it is the form of the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, that which is to be propounded by the *Vāmaka* tantra. Or, "Vāmaka" refers to those who delight in the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*); they are called "Vāmakas" because they are contemptible due to their destruction of the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*).
Or, she is Vāmakā because she emits or creates the world; or she is the sovereign (Īśvarī) of Dakṣa and the others.
She is fond of the five sacrifices (Pañcayajña-priyā) and reclines upon the couch of the five spirits (Pañca-preta-mañca). || 225 ||

The fivefold sacrifices are the *pañcayajñas*. This is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*). Consequently, according to the rule for *dvigu* compounds, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. She whose beloveds are these [sacrifices], and who is this very sacrifice itself—fivefold, consisting of the *agnihotra*, the *darśa*, and the *pūrṇamāsa*.

The Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice are mentioned in the Śruti; or, as they are well known in the Smṛtis, the Devayajña, Brahmayajña, Bhūtayajña, Pitṛyajña, and Manusyayajña.
In the Pāñcarātra Āgama, these are stated as abhigamana, upādāna, ijyā, svādhyāya, and yoga.
Or, according to the Kulāgama, there are five kinds of worship:
the solitary (kevala), the paired (yāmala), the mixed (miśra), the wheel-conjoined (cakrayug), and the hero-combined (vīrasaṅkara). Thus is the fivefold worship.

Or as it is stated [in the *Nityātantra*]: beginning with "The first [mandala] should be with weapons in the center, the second among the nine *yonis*," and ending with "thus the fivefold worship has been declared, which grants the accomplishment of all aims. Or as it is stated in the *Bṛhattantrakaumudī*, which is based on that [source].

And in the *Mantramahodadhi* it is said: "The waters in the form of milk and so forth, being offered in the *agnihotra*, are repeatedly offered again and again into the five sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) consisting of the moon, heaven, earth, the male, and the female. When this occurs—whether it be the practice of the sick, the impure due to death, the ignorant, the terrified, or the one seeking accomplishment—it is thus described.

That these very waters assume the state of a body is a matter clearly established in the Upaniṣads and in the *Rahasyādhikaraṇa* and other sections. Alternatively, these are the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*). Since the root *pac* means "to expand," by the rule allowing the suffix *ka* in the sense of *ghañ*, "five" (*pañca*) here signifies the expanded sacrifice, such as the *Viśvasṛjāmayana* and others.
There is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) for all of these. The four *pretas*, beginning with Brahmā, are the feet.
The *preta* named Sadāśiva lies upon such a plank—a couch or bedstead (*mañca-paryaṅka*).
And it is said in the *Bhairavayāmala* and in the *Bahurūpāṣṭakaprastāra*:
Upon the great couch whose essence is Śiva, with Maheśāna as its pillow,
the four quarters are the attendants and Sadāśiva is the bed-covering.
"In that [state] rests the Great Sovereign, Mahātripurasundarī.
Thus it is said. And it has also been stated by the venerable Ācārya-pāda:
"Brahmā, Hari, Rudra, Īśvara, and Bhṛgu have become the supports for her couch."
Śiva has a deceptive coverlet fashioned from his own pure radiance.

The fifth [form] is the mistress of the five elements, who moves about by means of the number five; she is the consort of Sadāśiva, the fifth among the five beginning with Brahmā, for it is stated in
