Among the three, Rudra is the most excellent; among them, the supreme Śiva is the possessor of *māyā*.
From that omniscient one distinguished by *māyā* arises Sāmba, whose characteristics are truth and the like.
"Sadāśiva shall be the most excellent; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

Thus, the word "fifth" (pañcamī) is established in reference to Vārāhī—just as she is the fifth among the deities of the five jewels (pañcaratna), such as Brāhmī and the others, or as she is the final deity among the deities of the five sheaths (pañcakośa) and so forth.
Although that [deity] appears in her [form] as a purely derivative (yaugika) one, nevertheless, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* it is said:
"One should worship the Son of the Fifth;
having touched the jar and meditated upon the Supreme Goddess, the Fifth, within the heart."

"The fifth is the cart-mechanism (śakaṭayantra), difficult to obtain in the three worlds"—since such usage is seen extensively in the *Vārāhī* [Tantra] and elsewhere, it should be understood as a term based on both etymology and conventional usage (*yogarūḍha*). Alternatively, because the fifth among the letters beginning with *ma* is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), she is of that form. And thus says the *Kalpasūtra*:
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is established within the body;
its manifesters are the five *makāras*, and with them, one performs worship.
"By way of concealment...

and so forth. For this very reason, the compound *pañcamī* may refer to the collective totality (*samāhāra*) of the five measures (*māna*) or the five *makāras*. And these are described in the *Traipurāsūkta*: "The flowing liquor (*parisruta*), the fish (*jhaṣa*), and the meat (*pala*)."
These [elements] are well-known from this verse. Purity through generosity (*dāna-śuddhi*) and the others are to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.

In the fifth oblation, "the waters become human speech"—this is well-known from the Śruti. The woman is the oblation of the seed-offering (*reto-havis*) into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); she is the fifth among the aforementioned sacrifices, or she takes that form. She is called Kaivalya.

The fifth [syllable] is liberation, or inseparable from it. It is the mistress (*īśī*) of the five elements, earth and the rest; or else, it is that which has become fivefold, or has arisen in five ways. Or it is the Vaijayantī garland, consisting of the five great elements, or consisting of the five jewels.
She is its mistress. And it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O twice-born one, that Vaijayantī garland of five forms belonging to the Wielder of the Mace is the 'Garland of Beings' (Bhūtamālā), consisting of an aggregate of the causes of all beings."
Thus it is said. Here, they explain the term "five-fold form" (*pañcarūpa*) as being of colors equal to those of pearl, ruby, emerald, sapphire, and diamond.
It is also stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
From the earth came the perception of the color blue; from the waters, pearls;
from fire, the Kaustubha gem was born; and from the wind, that which is known as lapis lazuli.
"From Puṣkara comes Puṣparāga; these belong to Hari by way of Vaijayantī.

Thus, its fivefold services—consisting of fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings—are eternal, belonging to her who possesses eternal sovereignty, bestowing happiness and enchanting Śambhu. (226)

"Śāśvatī" means constant repetition; that is to say, it is connected with being practiced again and again, or it is eternal (*nityā*). According to Amara, "śāśvata," "dhruva," and "nitya" are synonyms. Likewise, it is "śāśvata" because of the Vedic scripture which states, "The attainment is eternal, not that of others."

She whose sovereignty is eternal; or, by eliding the vowel *ī*, she is *Īśā*: one who possesses such sovereignty as that by which the five *pretas*—the lords of the world (*jagadīśāḥ*)—are made *aśvat*, meaning they are rendered steeds, serving as her vehicles.
The resultant meaning is that she is seated upon the thrones of the five *pretas*. She bestows *śarma*, which is happiness. *Īśam*... [text truncated]

Śambhu brings about existence (bhāvayati) or exists (bhavate); the suffix *ḍu* is applied according to the rule for the *mitadru* group. Alternatively, it is "the deluder" (*mohinī*) of him; or, she is Śambhumohinī because she deludes Śambhu. || 226 ||
The daughter of the mountain is blessed, righteous, and the increaser of dharma;
she is *Dharā*, whose nature is the earth (*pṛthvī*), because she supports the entire world, or because her form is the letter *la*.
The letter *la* is the goddess Earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves.
She is endowed with the fifty sacred seats (pīṭhas), consists of all holy fords (tīrthas), and is the supreme.

Thus it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*. She is the daughter of Dharma, the Himavat mountain; she is blessed (*dhanyā*), one who has accomplished her purpose, or one beneficial for wealth (*dhana*). Alternatively, she is "one who obtains wealth" (*dhana-labdhṛ*), where the suffix *-yat* is applied in the sense of "having obtained a mass of wealth.
Or, she may be the specific form of a Yoginī renowned in the science of astrology as Maṅgalā, Piṅgalā, and Dhanyā.

Alternatively, there are four types of final thoughts described in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, categorized as afflicted (*ārta*), cruel (*raudra*), meritorious (*dhanya*), and pure (*śukla*), as follows:
[regarding] the enjoyment of sovereignty, beds, seats, and vehicles...
When excessive desire and longing arise through delusion for women, perfumes, garlands, jewels, garments, and ornaments, those who know the truth declare that such meditation is "afflicted" (ārta).

They say that one for whom passion arises here toward those who undergo cutting, burning, beating, and torment, as well as blows to the body, subjugation, and dismemberment, and who feels no compassion, possesses "fierce meditation" (*raudra-dhyāna*).
The peaceful ones.
The investigation of the meaning of the Sūtras, the cultivation of the great vows, reflection on the causes for the departure from and arrival at bondage and liberation,
the pacification of the five senses and so forth, compassion toward living beings, and meditation— these are indeed auspicious.
The virtuous declare that.
Those whose senses are not agitated by sense-objects through the fluctuations of conceptualization, the destruction of mental constructs, and the expansion of discursive thought;
whose inner self is sustained by the yoga of steadfastness fixed solely on reality— the perfected ones declare that to be "white" meditation (śukla-dhyāna).
Thus it is said. The distinction in the fruits of these [meditations] is also stated in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"In the meditation on the Fierce (raudra), a miserable state among animals or a downward rebirth is certain;
in the Auspicious (śubha), the fruit is a fortunate birth as a god; and in the Pure (śukla), there is the destruction of rebirth."

Therefore, the wise person should exert effort in that meditation which removes the disease of birth, is more beneficial, sustains one through cyclic existence, is whiter than white, and crushes the dust of passion.

Thus [it is said]. In that context, "of the nature of the meditation called Dhanya" means: she is *dharmiṇī* because her character is righteousness (*dharma*), or because she is the substantive locus for attributes such as the experience of bliss and eternity. She is *dharmavardhinī* because she increases righteousness. As it is stated in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
Control of the senses, purity, auspiciousness, and devotion—
this is considered the duty of human beings toward Śaṅkara, Bhāskara, and the Goddess.
When meditated upon, Sāmba brings these dharmas to growth for embodied beings.
Or, from the root *vṛdh* meaning "to cut," it means that which cuts away the entire collection of visible phenomena— which are mere dharmas presided over by Brahman—
or that which transcends and passes beyond the worlds, beginning with the world of Indra and ending with the world of Viṣṇu, [reaching] the place known as Mahākailāsa.

She resides in Paraśivapura. Regarding the transcendence of Paraśivapura over all worlds, it should be understood from the *Śivadharmottara*, which, after describing the lower worlds, begins: "Above the station of Viṣṇu is the great, divine Śivapura," and so forth.
Thus, this other great Śivapura has been declared to you;
for embodied beings devoted to ritual action, a return [to rebirth] is prescribed.
Having thus described Śivapura, which is attainable through ritual action (*karma*),
[the text continues]: "Above Śivapura, one should know three unsurpassed abodes,
which are eternal, supremely pure, and consist of Skanda, Umā, and Śaṅkara."
Beginning with these words:
"Those men who have reached the supreme state, being devoted to the yoga of meditation,
there is no returning for them to the terrible ocean of saṃsāra."
"Omniscient, all-pervading, pure, perfected, and great lords, endowed with power equal to Śiva, they have gone to the supreme city of Śiva. Thus it ends.
Transcending the world, transcending qualities, transcending everything, her very nature is peace. (227)

She has transcended the worlds or the individual souls; for this very reason, she has transcended the qualities (*guṇas*), or she has transcended everything, or she has transcended all sounds. And it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The Supreme Brahman is always beyond sound and devoid of calculation."
Know the true nature of the self.

Thus: *Śama* refers to that whose very self (*ātman*) or essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the cessation of phenomenal expansion (*prapañcopaśama*). As stated in the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya*: "They consider the fourth state to be the cessation of phenomenal expansion, auspicious, and non-dual. Alternatively, it means that whose self is *śam*, which is happiness (*sukha*). || 227 ||

The young woman, who delights in playful pastimes, resembles the *bandhūka* flower. The *bandhūka*, also known as *bandhujīvaka*, is a large tree famous in the region of Vaṅga; her splendor is like its flower, or rather, she possesses a splendor that is exceedingly crimson.
She is the young maiden (*bālā kumārī*), according to the Śruti: "Thou art a youth, or indeed a maiden.

Also, in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*: "O Dear One, she is called 'the Child' (*bālā*) because she is distinguished by her child-like play (*līlā*). Her play is the worldly sport itself, which is her diversion. She is the wife of Padyarāja, named Līlā.
Or rather, it means that she, being well-known in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*, specifically impels one toward virtuous deeds;

for there is a detailed description in the narrative of how Sarasvatī was propitiated by Queen Līlā through her penance, and being pleased, she granted her both knowledge and the restoration of her husband's life.

In the *Devīpurāṇa*, in the chapter on the etymological derivation of names (*nāmanirvacanādhyāya*), since the etymology "Līlā" is seen in the sense of "being cherished by Lakṣmī" (*lakṣmīlālana*), it is equally plausible to accept that "Līlā" alone constitutes one distinct name, while "Brahmajananī" (the Mother of Brahman) and [the other] constitute another single name.
She is highly auspicious, a bringer of happiness, richly adorned with fine attire, and a virtuous matron. || 228 ||

The term *suvāsinī* (married woman) is derived from the fact that she possesses auspiciousness (*śobhanaṃ maṅgalam asyāḥ*). Because it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *kevalamāmaketyādinā*. Alternatively, the suffix *ṅīṣ* may be applied according to the sub-rule of the *gaurādigaṇa*, namely *sumaṅgalī saṃjñāyām*. Or again, it may mean that her auspiciousness is the auspicious Brahman itself (*śobhanaṃ maṅgalaṃ brahmaiva*).

Thus it is said in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "That which dispels inauspiciousness and expands the continuity of auspiciousness for men by its mere hearing— that they know to be Brahman, that is the auspicious."
Thus [it is said]. But in the Atri-smṛti:
"The constant practice of what is praiseworthy and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—this indeed is declared as auspiciousness by the sages who discourse on Brahman."

Thus it has been said. She is "one who brings happiness" (*sukhakārī*) because she is the agent of happiness; the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action according to the rule *kṛño hetu-tācchīlya-anuvamśyeṣu*. She is "endowed with" (*āḍhyā*) a beautiful appearance. A "married woman" (*suvāsinī*) is one whose husband is alive at all times, or she is non-different from the class of married women. || 228 ||

Delighted by the worship of married women, she is beautiful and pure-minded. "Delighted by the worship of married women" means she is pleased by the honoring of *suvāsinīs*. "Āśobhanā" is a four-syllabled name; she possesses beauty on all sides. She is one whose mind (*mānasa*) is pure.
Tripurāmbikā, the ancestor, was satisfied by the libation of the drops.

She is perfectly satisfied by the libation offered in the *bindu*-wheel, which consists of universal bliss and is performed by the four castes beginning with the Brahmins, using drops of milk, clarified butter, honey, and fermented liquor;
she is satisfied by the gratification of those knowers who understand the term *bindu* as it is etymologically derived from the root *iṣ* (to desire).

Or she was born satisfied previously; for there is the Vedic revelation: "She who first shone forth—she is indeed this one," and "I am the first-born of Cosmic Order (ṛta). Or she is of the nature of that first creation which occurred without prior conscious deliberation. Or she is the form of the deity known as Tripurāmbā, who presides over the eighth wheel (cakra).
Ambikā is either the progenitor or the sustainer of the three cities, which are the forms of the states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep].
Or she is the mother of that Jīva who possesses the three cities, according to the Śruti: "He who sports in the three cities is the Jīva.
This is also supported by such Śruti passages as, "Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire," and so on. [She is the source] of Vāma and the others.
Or she is established by the scriptural statement as Tripurāmbikā, the mother of the ancient ones. || 229 ||
Tripurāśrīvaśaṅkarī is to be propitiated by means of the ten mudrās.
These ten mudrās, beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Trikhaṇḍā,
serve as the instruments for her proper worship in accordance with the mental impressions (vāsanā) described in the *Nityāhṛdaya*.
The goddess named Tripurāśrī is the presiding deity of the fifth wheel; she brings [all] under her control,
or she is so called because she possesses that which brings [all] under control, or she is the form of the Jñānamudrā consisting of the union of the index finger and the thumb.
She is the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā), accessible through wisdom, and her essential nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge. || 230 ||

Or, it is so called because she bestows joy (*muda*) through knowledge (*jñāna*). Or, she causes the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) and the aspect of bliss (*ānandāṃśa*) to melt away—that is, she removes their obscuration—by means of knowledge. Or, she is the object to be reached by knowledge; or, she is that which is to be attained through knowledge. And it has been said by the Goddess herself in the *Kaurma Purāṇa*:
That which is my partless form— pure consciousness alone,
auspicious, liberated from all limiting adjuncts, infinite, immortal, and supreme.
That supreme state is attainable through knowledge alone;
those who perceive only knowledge enter into me alone.
Thus, its own nature consists of knowledge and the object of knowledge, the seer and the seen. || 230 ||

Yonimudrā is the mistress of the three divisions (trikhaṇḍeśī), the mother of the three qualities (triguṇāmbā), and she who resides in the triangle (trikoṇagā). She bestows joy (mudaṃ rāti) within the womb (yonau); or she is the form of the ninth mudrā. Alternatively, she is the form of that drop (bindu) for whom the womb itself is the concealing mudrā (ācchādikā). Or else, [it refers to] the space between the anus and the penis.

It is called the *yoni*. The method of sealing it, intended for the removal of defects in the mantra, is to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru; or [the *yoni*] is of that nature. She is the mistress (*īśī*), the sovereign (*svāminī*), of the tenth mudrā called *trikhaṇḍā*. Of the three...

Or she is the sovereign of the mantra-sections known as Soma, Sūrya, and Anala. She is "Triguṇā," meaning she in whom the three qualities (guṇas) reside; that is to say, she is the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) as accepted by the Sāṃkhya school, being the substratum of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
As it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
The Mistress of Yoga creates and transforms bodies by her own play, assuming various forms, actions, appearances, names, and functions.
"Because it exists in the world in three ways, it is therefore called *triguṇā* (threefold).
Also, in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"O Soul of all, that other power of Yours which resides in all beings..."
O Goddess of the gods, salutations to you, the eternal refuge of all virtues.
Thus it is said. In the Devīpurāṇa, however, the synonymy of Trivikrama, the tripathagā (the river flowing through the three paths), and the triple-fold exploits is suggested. As it is stated:
"By three steps Bali was bound; [by them] the tripathagā [river] proceeded from heaven and the other realms."
It is called the "three qualities" (triguṇa) because it consists of the three—sattva and the others—and of origination, maintenance, and destruction.

Thus: Ambā is the mother, the causal source, even of such a triad of qualities (guṇatraya), which is called the "life-force of mantra" (mantrajīva) in the Tantras. And so it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"She is the cause of the luminous forms of power (śakti) and of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca)."
And the three qualities which have been declared to be the cause of these [elements]—
The accomplishment of the contemplation of its true nature is declared to be "perfection" (samyaktva);
that is designated as the potency of the mantra, and it is said to be the very life-force of mantras.

Thus; or, because she is without distinction, she is the Mother of the entire universe. She is called "Trikoṇagā" (she who goes to the triangular womb-circle) because she enters the triangular *yonicakra*;
or she is the one whose conduct is faultless and wonderful, and who bestows desired objects. || 231 ||
That which is free from *aṃhas* (sin), suffering, calamities, and evils is *anaghā*.
That whose conduct (*cāritra*) consists of wonders (*adbhuta*) that cause amazement;
or, those which move among wonders—such as earthquakes and other portents—and produce evil results are called *adbhutacārīṇi*.
Or, she protects from them; or, it is her nature to bestow desired objects upon them. 231.

"Known through the excellence of practice, having a form that transcends the six paths"—she is known through the excellence of the repeated contemplation (*anusandhāna*) on the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*), as enjoined by the instruction: "One should spend one's time in the reflection upon Vedānta again and again, from birth until death. And thus:
The *Vyāsasūtra* and the *Kapilasūtra* state: "There is repetition because of the repeated instruction. And it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"She who is to be seen solely through meditation, whose limb is knowledge, whose self is wisdom, and whose abode is the heart..."
Through identity with the Self and the weight of long-standing practice, it attains manifestation.

Thus [it is said]. The paths are six: the path of words (*padādhvā*), the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvā*), the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvā*), the path of principles (*tattvādhvā*), the path of energies (*kalādhvā*), and the path of mantras (*mantrādhvā*). Among these, three are aspects of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and three are aspects of luminosity (*prakāśa*). As it has been stated in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
A single atom of that reflective awareness becomes threefold— consisting of word, mantra, and phoneme—
which is the nature of the subject, the light itself, as its essence of word, reality, and energy.

Thus it is said. And in the *Jñānārṇava*, beginning with "In this wheel, O goddess worshipped by heroes, the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) exist," and ending with "one should thus contemplate the Śrīcakra, pure with its six paths," they are described along with their characteristics. Also, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:

Now, starting with the words "O Mistress of Yoga, hear now the form consisting of the six paths," and ending with "one should thus contemplate the Śrīcakra filled with the six paths," her form that transcends those has been described— that which transcends the six paths of worship such as the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava systems.
Or rather, its form is such because it is the means for attaining those [goals]. And it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"By those originating from Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, the Sun, Gaṇapati, and the Moon..."
For one whose mind is purified by mantras, the knowledge of the family (kula) is revealed.

Thus [ends the section on] the Jaina system, which originated from the Moon. Its meaning is that those who were the six kinds of lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) in a previous birth obtain the practice of the Beautiful One (*Sundarī*) in this present life.
She is the embodiment of sincere compassion and the lamp for the darkness of ignorance. (232)
She whose form (mūrti) and essential nature (svarūpa) is compassion that is sincere and free from ulterior motives—she triumphs.
This is because of the statement by the learned: "There is a certain Compassion who is Aruṇā (the Dawn). For this very reason, he says: "Ajñāna...
Ignorance itself is the darkness (dhvānta), and she is like a lamp for it, because she destroys it.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the radiant lamp of knowledge.
Thus, from the words of the Blessed One. || 232 ||
She is known by everyone from children to cowherds, and her command is not to be transgressed by anyone.

She protects (gopayati) the children (bālān), beginning with Brahmā and the others; thus she is the "child-cowherd" (bālagopa). He is both a child and a cowherd, hence "child-cowherd" (bālagopa). Including both such "child-cowherds" (bālagopau)—that is, extending to them—[she is known].
She is one by whom such knowledge is known even to children and cowherds (*ābālagopam*). Here, one of the two words *bālagopa* refers to Sadāśiva or to the incarnation as Kṛṣṇa;
the other is an indicator for the common folk (*pāmara*). The meaning is that she is known by everyone from Hari and Hara down to the lowliest commoner.

And it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "All living beings know Him under the guise of the notion of 'I'. Now, one might object that if this were so, then according to the maxim "familiarity breeds contempt," He would be disregarded by all; therefore, [the author] says:
"He is unfit—that is, impossible—for even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others to transgress or surpass."
And she is the one whose teaching is this. As it was said by the venerable teacher Bhagavatpāda:
"The Creator (Brahmā) procreates the world; Hari protects it; Rudra destroys it;
and the Lord (Īśa), casting this aside, conceals even his own form."
"Always prior, she bestows all this by relying upon the command of Śiva’s praise, through her two creeper-like eyebrows that quiver in an instant. Thus [ends the verse].
The venerable Tripurasundarī, whose abode is the Śrīcakra, [is the sovereign]. 233.
She whose abode or dwelling place is the Śrīcakra, which consists of the bindu, the triangle, and other forms.

As it has been said: "The Śrīcakra is the body of Śiva and Śivā. The meaning is that just as the individual soul (jīva) resides within the body, so do Śiva and Śivā reside within the Śrīcakra. She is the beautiful consort of Tripura, who is Paraśiva.

She is both Śrīmatī and Tripurasundarī; likewise, "Tripura" refers to Paraśiva, in whom there are three cities (pura), namely the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. As it is stated in the Kālikāpurāṇa:
By the power of the Supreme Lord’s will, Śambhu’s body became threefold;
therein, the upper portion became five-faced and four-armed.
In Maheśvara, the body of Brahmā has limbs as white as the filaments of a lotus;
its middle portion is blue-limbed, with one face and four arms.
That Vaiṣṇava body, with conch, discus, mace, and lotus in its hands,
became below that [head] five-faced and four-armed.
"That body of the moon-crested Lord is white, consisting of crystal and clouds;
thus, through the union with the three cities, the supreme Śiva is Tripura. (233)
The Mother Lalitāmbikā, whose form is the unity of Śrī Śiva, Śiva, and Śakti.

Endowed with Śrī, she is Śivā; thus she is Śrīśivā. Her very form is the unity and aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti. And it is said in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*: "By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Śakti has attained oneness with the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*)."
Then, at the beginning of creation, it vibrates forth like oil from sesame seeds.
Thus it is said. Here, *sāmarasya* (equilibrium) is the state of being of one flavor (*samarasatā*), the supreme equality, which is indeed absolute non-difference.
And so it has been stated in the *Saurasaṃhitā*:
"The power that is non-different from Brahman is indeed Brahman itself, and not something else."
If that were so, it would be stated in vain by the undiscerning that there is "power" (śakti).
O learned one, the relationship of both difference and non-difference between power and the possessor of power is difficult to establish.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Vāsiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa*:
"Just as the wind and its movement are one, and just as heat and fire are one, so too pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and the power of movement are always of a single nature."
Thus [it is said]. Or rather, her form is the unity of the Śiva-cakras and the Śakti-cakras.
As it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, beginning with: "The Bindu is joined within the triangle; in the eight-spoked [wheel] is the eight-petalled lotus," and so forth.
He who understands the relationship of inseparable concomitance between the Śaivas, the Śāktas, and the Cakras, is a knower of the Cakra (cakravid).
By this much [of the preceding], that *haṃsa*-mantra in which the unity of Śiva and Śakti is established is her form. And it is said in the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*:
"That which ends with the letter *śa* (Śānta) is called her Śakti; that which ends with that [letter] is called the seed-syllable (*bīja*)."
The power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) is the seed-syllable; it is Śiva himself and nothing else.
Therefore, this supreme mantra is traditionally held to consist of the essence of Śiva and Śakti.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that in the sequence of the phonemes *śa-ṣa-sa-ha*, the letter *ṣa* comes at the end of *śa*, the letter *sa* at the end of that, and the letter *ha* at the end of that. Alternatively, Śiva has five powers (*śakti*), such as Dhūmāvatī and the others;
their unity—that is, their collective totality—is her very form. And these have been described.
In the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"Dhūmāvatī is the power for concealment; Bhāsvatī is the power for the illumination of the paths; Spandā is for agitation; Vibhvī is for pervasion; and Hlādā is mine for nourishment."
Dhūmāvatī prevails upon the earth, Hlādā in the waters, and Bhāsvatī shines in the fire;
Spandā is in the wind, Vibhvī in the ether, and the universe is pervaded by them.
Thus, within this extensive framework, the universe [is characterized] by the first three names.
Having characterized the Deity by her agency in creation, maintenance, and dissolution,

and because the domains of concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*) are infinite, [the text] elaborates upon the very scope of those two from the passage beginning with "born from the fire-pit of consciousness" up to this point; thus, she is the agent of these fivefold cosmic functions.

He designates the deity by means of her uncommon, qualifying name, "Lalitāmbikā. The analysis of the compound is as follows: she who sports (*lalate*) is *Lalitā*, and she is also *Ambikā*; thus, she is *Lalitāmbikā*. And it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Because she sports (*lalate*) transcending the worlds (*lokān*), she is therefore called *Lalitā*. [The word *loka* is derived from] *lokyante*...
The meaning is that it shines exceedingly upon the forehead—that place of the bindu situated above those locations—having transcended the worlds, which are the rays, and the deities of the veils.
[Its qualities are: splendor, grace, sweetness, profundity, stability, and brilliance.
Elegance and likewise nobility—these are the eight qualities of manliness.

Thus, "lalita" is well-known among the learned as gracefulness, and it is also established in the treatises on erotics (*kāmaśāstra*) as the graceful movements of sexual play. Furthermore, "saukumārya" (tenderness) is well-known as *lālitya* (loveliness).
Since she possesses all of these qualities, she is called *Lalitā*. And it has been said:
The name "Lalitā" (the Graceful One) is indeed fitting for you, for your garments are divine and fresh; your bow is made of sugarcane, your weapons are flowers, and everything about you is graceful.

Thus [it is said]. According to the *Śabdārṇava*, "lalita" means "beautiful. This is also the name of the presiding deity of the Prayāga-pīṭha, for it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* within the section on the enumeration of the Devī-pīṭhas that "at Prayāga is Lalitā-devī.
Thus ends the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Bhāskararāya.
With the tenth hundred, Dhāriṇī became the eleventh digit.
Thus ends the eleventh part, named the Tenth Century, in the *Lalitāsahasranāmabhāṣya* composed by Śrī Bhāskararāya. 11.
In the latter portion of the *Lalitāsahasranāma*, there is the declaration of the fruits [of recitation].
The twelfth digit is named Kṣamā;
thus, having established the thousand names suitable for recitation as a means to attain the fruit of devotion, [the text proceeds].
Concluding that [section] and desiring to analyze the fruits [of the recitation], the venerable teacher Hayagrīva begins the subsequent composition of the text:
"Thus, O Pot-born One (Agastya), this Thousand Names has been told to you. (234)

By the words "ityevam" and so forth: the word *iti*, signifying completion, suggests that the number one thousand is neither deficient nor excessive. Thus, in the manner described—that is, as correctly set forth—in the *Sarasvatī-gaṅgā-sahasra-nāma* and other such works.

Because there is no completion of the number one thousand, it is implied that the term "Sahasranāma" (Thousand Names) here is either meaningless or used in a figurative sense; for "sāhasra" means simply a thousand names, with the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) added in its own primary sense, as in the words *rākṣasamānasa* and others. [The epithet] "Ghaṭodbhavā" refers to Agastya.
Perfect enlightenment. || 234 ||
Now, one might object that even in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* and other texts,
the *Devīsahasranāma* and similar works also consist of exactly one thousand names, neither more nor less; therefore,
he says:
It is the secret of secrets and bestows the pleasure of Lalitā;
a hymn like this has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again.

Regarding the phrase "of the secrets" (*rahasyānām*): the genitive case here is used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), meaning "among the secrets" consisting of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), recitation (*japa*), and so forth. Therefore, the word "secret" (*rahasyam*) means "the most secret" (*rahasyatamam*). Now, one might object that there are indeed other most secret [texts], such as the *Gaṅgāsahasranāma* and others.
Since [these mantras] are indeed found in the *Skānda* Purāṇa and other texts, he says "lalitā" (the charming one).

The meaning is that, because those [other mantras] produce less satisfaction for the deity than Lalitā, this [mantra] alone produces the highest degree of satisfaction for the deity. Now, even such [a mantra as this]—

Thinking that something might be possible [here], he says "by this" (*anena*). "Similar" (*sadṛśam*) means possessing a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), namely the state of being most secret while simultaneously being pleasing to Lalitā. "Hymn" (*stotram*) refers to another hymn; for the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) cannot exist within a single thing. It is not [already] existent (*na bhūtam*).

"Prior to this moment" means it will not exist at a time subsequent to this; "it will exist" is either the locative case of a present participle (*śatṛ*-anta) or [the third person singular future]. Since the present moment is unfit for the arising of such a hymn and lacks connection with the three periods of time, such [an object] is simply non-existent.
This is the state of affairs. The entire subsequent textual corpus is devoted to explaining these two qualifiers in order to demonstrate their non-existence elsewhere. || 235 ||
Therein, he analyzes the state of being the ultimate secret by means of two [verses]:
according to the principle that "the gradation of results follows the gradation of effort," [he discusses] the difficulty of accomplishment involved in achieving an abundance of results.

Because it is most well-known, this practice—which achieves great fruit with little effort—is the most profound secret. Since the extent of the exertion required for the chanting of the Name is so evident therein, [the author] explains only the abundance of its fruit: "All diseases..."

[These are] divided into categories such as incurable and manageable. Since poverty is also presented as being equivalent to disease, he states that even the increase of prosperity, which is invariably linked to the absence of that [poverty], is a fruit:
"It pacifies all diseases and increases all prosperity."
It pacifies all untimely deaths and wards off death at the appointed time. || 236 ||

"Complete prosperity" (sarvasampat): Alternatively, since health and prosperity are mutually exclusive (parasparābhāvavyāpyatva), one might fear that poverty would necessarily follow even when health is present; thus, to dispel this doubt, he conjoins health with prosperity by saying "complete prosperity."

The meaning is: of prosperities distinguished by various differences such as abundance of elephants and horses. "All untimely deaths" refers to those caused by snakes, tigers, and so forth. He says "at the time" because this [description] is stated too briefly; "at the time" means when the measure of one's lifespan has reached its completion.

Therefore, it is indicated that untimely deaths occur precisely in the midst of one's lifespan, even when accompanied by factors such as ghee or oil, just like the extinguishing of a lamp caused by a violent wind. || 236 ||

It pacifies all afflictions caused by fever and bestows long life. "All fevers" refers to those beginning with the quotidian (aikāhika) and ending with the complex (sānnipātika). "Affliction" (*ārti*) is the pain consisting of headaches and other symptoms produced by them; "pacification" (*śamana*) means their destruction. Alternatively, for all [fevers]...

The four words beginning with "ye rogāḥ" (those diseases) should be explained in this manner. By this, even the lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the result and the means—such as in the case of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice—is established.
Consequently, it is logical that in this context, one may engage in a means belonging to one locus for the sake of a result residing in another.

It should be understood as follows: although [the afflictions] are already included among "diseases" (*roga*), the separate mention of "fever" (*jvara*) and "distress" (*ārty*) is according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Alternatively, the distinction is made in accordance with the optional rites (*kāmyaprayoga*) to be described hereafter.
In that context, after the description of the four-limbed rites whose sole fruit is the pacification of disease and so forth, [the following occurs].

This is because the applications (prayoga) that have as their result merely those respective individual limbs will be explained later. For this very reason, the meaning of the term *dīrghāyuṣya* is also established here: *āyuṣya* is the state of life (*āyuṣaḥ bhāvaḥ*), which is "long" (*dīrgha*)—that is, complete;
it is longevity, specifically a lifespan of one hundred years, and [the mantra] is the bestower of that.

It dispels afflictions such as those caused by malevolent planets, poisons, and the like. Alternatively, *āyuṣyam* refers to longevity itself; it is the bestower of pills, medicinal formulations, and perfected substances that grant a lifespan exceeding the standard measure of one hundred years.
It brings about the attainment of that [state] by accomplishing the unprecedented (apūrva); therefore, its purpose is not exhausted merely by warding off untimely death.
It bestows sons upon those who are childless and grants the goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha). || 237 ||

[It is said] "for those without sons who are bound by the desire for a son. [The text says] "for those with sons" because, once that goal is accomplished, they are free from desire; since the desire for a son is generally observed only among those without sons, it is stated thus. For this very reason, in the Smṛtis, those who have only one son or whose children have died are counted among the barren women (*bandhyā*). Therefore—

Even for those who already have sons, there is eligibility here when there is a desire for another son; likewise, it is established that even for those who are childless, there is no eligibility for the performance of the rite for a son in the absence of a desire for a son.
By this, it is indicated that each specific desire serves as the delimiting factor for eligibility for the performance of its respective fruit. Not...

Nor should it be argued that because one who possesses a desire consisting of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) directed toward multiple fruits has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for all ritual performances (*prayoga*), there is a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to which specific performance should be undertaken first; for [the result follows] through *tantra* (simultaneous performance), whereby a single performance alone bestows all the fruits.

Because the performance of the ritual application is possible; and this being so, there is no contradiction with the fourth-book topic (the *cāturthika-adhikaraṇa*) which states "all [are included] because there is no distinction," for in that context,
[the rule applies to] sacrifices such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma, which grant all desired objects.

It should not be argued that "only a single result arises from a single performance," because that is established as the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) only for minor rites (*alpapradakarma*), since the principles of those specific sections (*adhikaraṇanyāya*) are restricted to them;

furthermore, the satisfaction of the deity (*devatāprīti*) is of a nature distinct from the world. For this very reason it has been said: "Transcending the world, transcending the qualities (*guṇātītā*)."
"Transcending all, it is of the nature of peace.

This is because other sages also accept such a principle regarding ritual actions (*karman*). As it is stated in the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*: "In a single performance, one may desire all desires; [but] when there is a separation of performances..."

Regarding the phrase "and each one": he says "puruṣārtha" (the goal of man) to show that even one who lacks the general desire for sense-objects has the qualification for this [practice]. Liberation (mokṣa) is the "goal of man" because it is sought after by wise persons.
The point is that even one who is free from desire is qualified for the performance of that which has liberation as its fruit.
In reality, the meaning is simply that it bestows the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*), as there is no evidence for a restrictive interpretation.
And it is stated in the *Puṣkarakhaṇḍa* of the *Padmapurāṇa*, in the section on daily rites (*āhnika-prakaraṇa*):
"After this, the wise man should cause the worship of the gods to be performed."
Whoever worships Gaṇeśa, no obstacle shall afflict him.

"One should worship Sūrya for the sake of health, Mādhava for the sake of dharma and liberation, Śiva for the sake of dharma, wealth, and liberation, and Caṇḍikā for the sake of the four aims of life. Thus [it is said]. (237)

Surely, while yielding abundant fruit, the quality of being achievable with little effort exists indeed in the *Sahasranāma-navaka*; likewise, the quality of bestowing pleasure upon Lalitā also exists therein by way of generating pleasure for Gaṅgā, Śyāmā, and others.

Dispelling the doubt that other hymns whose sole subject is Lalitā—such as the *Pañcamīstavarāja* and others—possess an unimpeded capacity to please Lalitā, [the author] now analyzes the quality of bestowing pleasure as it follows in the sequence: [He states: "In other hymns whose sole subject is Lalitā, such as the *Pañcamīstavarāja* and so forth, the capacity to please Lalitā is indeed unimpeded.
Thus, he analyzes the quality of bestowing pleasure as it follows in the sequence.
This particular hymn of praise to the illustrious Goddess bestows great joy;
one who is intent upon the worship of Lalitā should recite it daily with diligent effort. (238)

"This" means that, compared to the joy produced by reciting other hymns, the joy produced by this [hymn] is superior. Thus, the intended meaning is that its status as the most secret [teaching] lies precisely here, insofar as it generates a particular kind of joy.

By this very reasoning, since rites such as the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Jyotiṣṭoma, and the Viśvajit— which are accomplished through varying degrees of effort— cannot logically have a single type of heaven as their fruit, one cannot postulate a gradation among the heavens; this follows precisely from the logic established in the Pūrvatantra (Mīmāṃsā) regarding the satisfaction of the deities as well.

The objection— "What is the distinction [in the phrase] 'due to the excellence' (viśeṣāt), since the attainment of gradation is produced by individual hymns of praise?"— is refuted. For even in the case of the deity's satisfaction produced by another rite accomplished through greater exertion than this, that same logic would result in an even greater degree of satisfaction from this [present rite].

Because the inclusion of the qualifying term is purposeful with the intention that this [practice] should not be subject to common application, for this very reason its status as the "most secret" is also established. Therefore, the meaning is that a worshiper of Lalitā should recite this throughout their life, even while performing the most excellent sacrifice. || 238 ||
He states the procedure for the time of recitation in two verses:
"Having bathed in the morning according to the rule and having completed the twilight rites (saṃdhyā-karma), one should then go to the house of worship and honor the King of Wheels (cakrarāja). (239)
By the two [verses] beginning with "at dawn" (*prātar*), [the worship is performed] according to the rule in both Vedic and Tantric modes.

By the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākakṣinyāya*), this [phrase] is connected to both the bath and the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*). "Going to the house of worship" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the worship of the door and so forth. "The King of Wheels" (*cakrarāja*) refers to the Śrīcakra. "One should worship" (*samarcayet*) is used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*).
The causative suffix *ṇic* [is applied] when there is incapacity, or it refers to the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). 239.
A person should recite the mantra one thousand times, or three hundred, or even just one hundred;
thereafter, he should recite this *Rahasyanāmasāhasra*.
[One should recite] the fifteenth or the sixteenth *vidyā*, but not any mantra or *sāman* whose deity is a woman. In expressions such as "a thousand," the remainder is "one hundred and eight.
In "three hundred," it means three hundred, not one hundred and three. This is not an option of equal force (*tulyabala-vikalpa*), but rather...
The particle *eva* is used to indicate that the latter is an alternative (*anukalpa*) in the event that the former is impossible.

It occurs after [the recitation] and before the offering of the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). For this very reason, it is stated that "having recited, one should offer the handful of flowers"; the sequence between these two is not separated by anything, but rather—

The meaning is that [the recitation of the Thousand Names] is separated [from the preceding acts] by the recitation of the *Sahasranāma*, just as the performance of the *vedī* is separated from the *veda* by the sipping of water (*ācamana*) after sneezing, or as the study of *Mīmāṃsā* is separated from the study of the Vedas and the ritual bath (*snāna*). Here, the entire passage beginning with "having bathed in the morning" (*prātaḥ snātvā*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established by other injunctions. Regarding the recitation of the *Sahasranāma*:

However, only the time is to be enjoined. For this very reason, there is no relationship of mutual subsidiary and principal between the recitation (*japa*) and the reading (*pāṭha*). Since both possess their own results through their respective individual injunctions, even the chanting of the Thousand Names is [enjoined] by another injunction alone.

Since it is understood as being for the sake of the fruit, as in the case of "Having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma," the connection is determined to be solely for the purpose of time.
Alternatively, the sequence itself, in the form of an extension, of the five principal acts beginning with bathing is what is to be enjoined.
Therefore, even if one of the principal [factors] is not performed, the non-arising of the fruit due to deficiency is refuted by the principle that "there is no lapse in the case of time. || 240 ||
Since it has been stated that this specific kind of joy— which is distinguished from others— is something to be cultivated,
yet remains almost entirely uncomprehended due to a lack of knowledge regarding its particulars, he describes its magnitude, which is denoted by the word "specific," in eleven and a half verses:
O Pot-born One, listen as I describe the fruit of the merit for that wise person who recites this even once during their lifetime. (241)

By the words "in the midst of one's life" and so forth: according to the manner described, from the recitation of even a single name among the thousand names recited once during the course of one's life, there arises this heap of merit which is about to be described; and that, moreover—
If the fruit of reciting the hymn once were multiplied by a thousand,

then the measure of the deity’s satisfaction produced thereby would be the product of that fruit multiplied by as many repetitions as would occur if the hymn were recited throughout one's entire life.

The summary of the collective meaning is that this must be inferred by the wise. Precisely because the matter about to be explained is difficult to grasp, the teacher first makes a formal promise with "I shall speak" and then issues the command "Listen," thereby ensuring the student's attentiveness. || 241 ||
"Whoever should bathe in all the holy fords (tīrtha), such as the Gaṅgā and others, throughout ten million births"—

by the phrase "Gaṅgā and others," there is the inclusion of Puṣkara and so forth; even though in passages such as "Puṣkara and other holy fords," Puṣkara alone is well-known as the foremost of all holy fords.

Furthermore, the mention of the Gaṅgā first is for the purpose of including the holy sites (tīrthas) located in those respective worlds within the scope of the word "all" (sarva), since the Gaṅgā is present in the three worlds and is thus immediately brought to mind by the term "Gaṅgā. For this very reason, the word "Gaṅgā" is used in that same manner in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
It is explained:
"O Goddess, because Bhagīratha brought you from heaven here to the earth (gāṃ),
you are celebrated by all the sages as Gaṅgā."

Thus [it is said]. However, if other sacred sites (tīrtha) were included, then only those sacred sites existing on the earth would be manifested. Here, the four words beginning with "every day," "with supreme faith," and "for a thousand years"—which are recited later—should be applied to the preceding [passage].
This must be understood as applying everywhere. The phrase "throughout ten million births," however, applies to all subsequent instances as well.
Thus, among all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) contained within the three worlds, by bathing according to the prescribed rite with supreme faith at even a single sacred ford every day—
The merit produced by bathing at a single sacred site for as long as it takes to complete a thousand years— or even for as long as ten million such births— is equal to a single unit. Likewise,
the merit produced by bathing at all sacred sites constitutes a single aggregate of these units.
Furthermore, whoever should perform the consecration of ten million liṅgas at Avimuktaka, [attains the supreme goal].

Considering the superiority of the installation of Śiva over the installation of other deities based on such scriptural statements as, "When one *liṅga* is installed, the entire universe becomes installed," he says: "*Liṅge* [in Kāśī]... In Kāśī...

In the *Bṛhajjābāla* and other texts, four locations are traditionally taught: Kāśī, Vārāṇasī, Avimukta, and Antargṛha. Among these, each preceding one is pervaded by each succeeding one—just as the five-krośa area is pervaded by the inner sanctum—and each subsequent location is increasingly meritorious.
Among those, the inner chamber is most excellent; for it is indeed the very body of Paramaśiva.
And because there is no difference between the body and the embodied one, and because of its eternality—O best of the twice-born, by the word *avi* (non-being), sins are meant.
Because it was not released by them, and because it was not released by me, it is therefore known as Avimukta.

Thus, although both types of etymological derivation stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* are primarily applicable to the "interior of the house" (*antargṛha*) alone, due to the frequency of usage— whereby the term functions through a conventional metaphorical extension (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) to encompass specific locations— it applies universally to both scholars and commoners as "the interior of the house."

The primary state of non-liberation (avimuktatva) is unknown due to the absence of knowledge; thus, indicating that it is indeed "unliberated" as long as it remains within the house, he says: "in Avimuktaka. The suffix *ka* is used in the sense of something unknown. The meaning is "within the house" (*antargṛhe*). Within the house...
This non-mention [of the specific number] is for the purpose of highlighting the excellence of his merit by reminding one of the definition already stated;

consequently, the merit produced by him in a single lifetime— that person who, within his own home, installs ten million *liṅgas* every day with supreme faith for the duration of a thousand years— is [immeasurable].
The second heap is produced by multiplying by the number ten million (koṭi). || 242 ||
If one were to give ten million times [the gift] at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse,
or ten million bhāras of gold to learned brahmins, [it would not equal the merit of this].

Drawn by compassion, the region situated between Tarantuka and Kārantuka is called Kurukṣetra. During a solar eclipse— that is, when the sun is eclipsed— one who grasps everything, everywhere, and at all times, might perhaps be liberated.
A Brahmin who accepts [a gift] at Kurukṣetra during an eclipse is not released [from sin].

By such statements in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, which declare the absence of penance for the recipient, the infinity of the fruit of giving is established. Although the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti* states: "They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and knowledge (*sarasvatī*)," nevertheless, even among those...

Intending to emphasize the superiority of that very gift because it is accomplished through gold, he says: "sauvarṇa" (made of gold). A *bhāra* consists of twenty *tulās*. A *tulā* consists of one hundred *palas*. This is according to the lexicon which states: "A *tulā* is one hundred *palas*; twenty *tulās* would be a *bhāra*. Among those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*), [the merit is increased] by virtue of birth, sacraments, and knowledge.
According to the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, one is called a *śrotriya* on account of three [qualifications] among the conditioned factors (*saṃskṛta*).

Since place, time, recipient, object given, faith, knowledge, and secrecy impart excellence to ritual actions, some of these— though not explicitly mentioned for every specific duty— should nevertheless be applied accordingly.

Furthermore, if at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse one gives ten million *bhāras* of gold to a worthy recipient with faith and other virtues, that constitutes one meritorious act multiplied by ten million;
when this is multiplied by the number of days contained within a thousand years, its [merit]—
The third is the mass of merit produced by multiplying [the merit] by ten million lifetimes. || 243 ||
One might perform ten million horse-sacrifices on the banks of the Ganges, or one might dig ten million wells upon a waterless desert plain. (244)

Regarding the rites of *iṣṭāpūrta*, he says: "He who performs the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin; he overcomes evil. Thus, the *hayamedha* is a specific sacrifice enjoined by scripture. "On the bank of the Gaṅgā" means on the shore connected to the Gaṅgā. And so, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, together with learned officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), [he should perform it].

The fourth quantity is produced by multiplying the merit generated from a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) complete with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*)—by the number of days as before, and again by the number of ten million (*koṭi*). The term "well" (*kūpa*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for ponds, tanks, and the like. "Maru" is the name of a specific region; therefore, [the merit] does not...

The futility of digging in waterless places: when the merit arising from digging millions of wells and the like in such a location is multiplied by the number of days as before and by the number of ten million births, the resulting total constitutes the fifth heap. || 244 ||
He who, during a famine, would with supreme faith provide food for ten million Brahmins every day for a thousand years; || 245 ||
A region where alms are difficult to obtain is considered a famine-stricken land in its entirety.

In such a place, by giving food endowed with the six excellent flavors to ten million preeminent Brahmins, the merit produced is multiplied again by ten million times the number of days [the gift was given]. From this multiplication, [the result is] born.

The *rāśi* (heap) is the sixth [case]. In the expression *parivatsarān*, the accusative case is used to denote continuous duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*); the meaning is "without interruption for twelve thousand years.
Regarding the words *saṃvatsara*, *parivatsara*, *idāvatsara*, *vatsara*, and *anuvatsara*: [they are explained as follows...]

Even though there are twelve specific twelve-year cycles for the Prabhava, Pramāthin, Khara, Śobhana, Rākṣasa, and so forth, they are mentioned here as indicators of the general category alone. || 245 ||
By chanting even a single name from this Thousand Secret Names, one shall obtain that unsurpassed merit multiplied ten millionfold. (246)

It is multiplied by those millions of heaps of merit arising from their bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), the consecration of Śiva, the gift of gold, sacrificial rites (iṣṭa), works of public utility (pūrta), and the feeding of Brahmins— these six.
The meaning is that because merit is present, one obtains that very same great heap of the sixfold merit. This is the intended sense:
having visualized a single great heap from among the six heaps of merit, and having made it twofold by depositing it in two places, [one should contemplate] one of those heaps between them.
Having multiplied by the number ten million (koṭi), one should multiply the subsequent heap by the number produced thereby.
In that case, if the heap to be multiplied were delimited by the number one, its multiplication would be useless.
Therefore, since another number must necessarily delimit it, and because the number ten million is what is immediately present [in the context], it is indeed of the form of ten million.

The number is to be expressed as the multiplicand. Consequently, having multiplied both great masses (mahārāśi) individually by ten million times ten million (koṭikoṭi), two numerical aggregates (saṃkhyāpiṇḍa) are produced; these should then be multiplied by each other—this is established.
And by that, having multiplied that great mass by the number ten million, what is produced is...

Furthermore, one should multiply the *piṇḍa* by the number *koṭi*; this is the resulting implication. The essential point is that one should multiply that great mass (*mahārāśi*) by the number *samudra*. *Samudra* is the even product known as *kṛti* of the number *koṭi*; that is, a *koṭi* multiplied by a *koṭi*.
To that extent, it is said in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "If a thousand is multiplied by a thousand, and then again by ten millions (koṭi),
people who know calculation call that number a 'samudra'."

330) Thus it is said. And this is understood from the double usage of the word *puṇya*—once in the sense of the multiplier (*guṇaka*) and once in the sense of the multiplicand (*guṇya*). Furthermore, by the force of the transposed expression *puṇyakoṭyā*, it is understood that the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with a plural ending: "multiplied by millions" (*koṭibhir guṇitam*). All of this [is established].
Lest the misconception arise that the fruit belongs only to the recitation of the hymn according to the specific ritual procedure (*upakrama*), he says:
"Even of a single name" (verse 246).
Whoever recites even a single name from the *Thousand Secret Names*, their sins are destroyed, even the greatest; of this there is no doubt. (247)

Now, he states that the destruction of a mass of sins, just like the generation of a mass of merit, is the fruit of each individual name. The word "api" (even/also) serves as a conjunctive particle, either by way of implication through the logic of *kaimutika* (how much more so), or by way of being explicitly stated, [to include] minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and the like. || 247 ||
Whatever sin arises for men from the non-performance of obligatory duties as well as from the performance of prohibited acts, all that is quickly destroyed.
And as for those evils, although it is said:
"By the non-performance of what is prescribed, by the practice of what is censured,
and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man incurs downfall."

Thus, although three types [of sins] are taught in the Smṛti due to the threefold nature of their causes, nevertheless, because the restraint of the senses and its absence are respectively enjoined and prohibited, the sins produced by them are included within the two aforementioned categories; with this intention, [the text] treats them as being of only two kinds.

He enumerates them: the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), ritual bathing during eclipses, and so forth, which—according to the distinctions of various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*)—are prescribed in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Tantra* scriptures and result in sin (*pratyavāya*) if not performed;
by this [category], the occasional rites (*naimittika*) are also included. Then there are the prohibited acts (*niṣiddha*), such as the eating of *kalañja* (poisoned meat) and the like.
Swiftly, without depending on other expiations. || 248 ||

With the intention that the magnitude of the mass of merit produced by this [practice], as well as the magnitude of the mass of sins to be destroyed by it, must be inferred by the wise alone, he speaks again in one and a half verses, further alerting the disciple:
What is the use of saying much more here? Listen, O son of Kalaśī: hear the power that resides even in a single name for turning back sins. (249)
The fourteen worlds are not capable of counteracting that evil.

Regarding the word *kalaśī*: the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for denoting a genus (*jāti*). "That which is to be counteracted by her" means the evil or sin (*agha*) that is to be destroyed by that power; "not capable" (*nālam*) means the fourteen worlds, that is, the people, are not able [to do so].
If all living beings— those dwelling in the fourteen worlds and those dwelling in all the worlds alike—

were to commit various sins, high and low, at every moment from birth until death throughout tens of millions upon tens of millions of lifetimes, then even greater than that immeasurable heap of sin would be the merit of each single name [of the Lord].
The sense is that it should be inferred that by repeating [the mantra] a thousand times, the fruit of reciting the complete hymn is attained; this is what must be understood.
|| 249-49 |1/2 | As for that devotee of Śrīvidyā who, disregarding such a means for the destruction of sin—

If one desires to perform the expiations prescribed by the Smṛtis, a mass of sin born from that very disregard falls upon him, which cannot even be removed by those [expiations]; thus, he becomes an object of ridicule, like one fleeing from the fear of a scorpion who proceeds to hide himself in the mouth of an enraged venomous serpent.
Expressing this through the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration), he says:
"He who, having abandoned the Thousand Names, desires the destruction of his sins... (250).
For he resorts to the snowy mountain for the sake of removing the cold;
"he who" means that, desiring the destruction of sin, he performs another penance. Alternatively, the meaning of "resorts to" (*niṣevate*) is "desires to resort to."
This is because it conforms to the superimposition of identity between the sentence and its meaning. Alternatively,
when one intends to perform another expiation, by superimposing identity upon the service of Mount Himavat,
the extreme foolishness of that performer is shown, since there is simply no action at all that is similar to the act of performing an expiation.
[This] is the essence. 250–250½. He who is devoted and constantly recites this thousand names, 251.

Anticipating the objection that "if this were so, the scriptures on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would be rendered purposeless," he concludes the measurement of the specific degree of delight while dispelling that doubt with the word "bhakta" (the devotee). "Bhakta" means a worshipper (*upāsaka*).
"Nityam" means throughout one's life (*yāvajjīvam*). This [devotion] is characterized by the aforementioned extensive mode of commencement.
Buddhist. || 251 ||
To him, the venerable Goddess Lalitā, being pleased—that is, being endowed with a particular degree of affection—bestows his desired object;
that is, she grants both forms: the generation of a mass of merit as previously described, and the destruction of a mass of sin.

In this regard, the following should be understood: regarding the phrase "especially by the venerable Goddess," four qualifiers are mentioned in the reading at the commencement of the ritual action that generates a special degree of devotion: (1) having a practitioner as the agent, and (2) having the complete hymn as the object of the action.
These include being performed for as long as one lives and the association with the four primary practices such as the morning bath;
these very same points are again referred to in this concluding verse. Due to the consistency between the introduction and the conclusion, these qualifiers are indeed intended [to be understood].

Because there is no evidence for the intention not to express [the meaning]. Among those [qualifiers], by the first qualifier, the futility of the scriptures on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is refuted; for since they find scope among those who do not practice [meditation], their application is established precisely as being directed toward that [expiation]. By the second...

Those who consider themselves to have accomplished their purpose merely by reciting each individual name are refuted; for there is no evidence that the separate application of reciting each single name produces such a great fruit, as there is a lack of proof for its generating such a result. Nor is it the case that even a single name...

The statement "from chanting" (kīrtanāt) itself serves as the authority for the separate performance [of the name], because— as in the case of the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice within the *rājasūya*— there is no evidence for its separate performance otherwise. Nor should it be argued that statements such as "he who recites even a single name" and "from the chanting of even a single name," which reside within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), serve as proof for a separate performance.
Once it is established that there is a single unified statement (*ekavākyatva*) by virtue of the opening and the conclusion, it follows—

by the logic of the sentences concerning the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*) found within the context of the *Jāteṣṭi* ritual— that such statements read in the middle of that [text] have their purport (*tātparya*) directed toward the whole itself through its parts.
Because of this accomplishment:

if such is the fruit of even a single name, what need is there to mention that the entire hymn yields such a fruit? Thus, the praise of the hymn is established by way of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument.

This is because such an understanding arises from the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "api" (also/even). Alternatively, the statement that this much is the fruit of a single name is intended to establish that the fruit of the hymn is a thousandfold, and not to establish that each [name] possesses its own separate fruit. This is because there would be a conflict of intent (*tātparya*) in both cases.

Because this would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). For this very reason, it is accepted that [the injunction] "he chooses one" and so forth serves as the basis for the subsequent statement "he chooses three.
Furthermore, it is impossible for names consisting of one syllable up to sixteen syllables to yield equal results; for if that were the case, [the injunctions would be rendered purposeless].

This is because defects such as the redundancy of other [qualifications] are evident. However, by the third qualification, the desire for such a fruit through recitation lasting only a few days—without restriction—is rejected by the words: "The wise person who recites thus even once during the course of a lifetime."

Since the word "api" (also) is read within the middle of a single sentence, the two-fold interpretation should be inferred according to the method already stated, based on the natural force of that term. By the fourth qualification, it is indicated that just as there is no production of the fruit for the six [offerings] beginning with the Āgneya if they lack mutual association, so it is here as well.

However, there is this distinction: since the Āgneya and other rites, when taken together with the injunctions for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), are understood to be means for achieving a single result, the result simply does not arise if even one of them is absent.
In this case, however, [the result arises] from others even in the absence of the recitation of the *Sahasranāma*.

It is indeed fitting that various fruits should arise from the respective principal acts. Nor should it be argued: "How can it be said that the recitation of the *Sahasranāma* is fruitless merely because of the absence of association with other principal acts? For there exists a specific fruit produced by such a performance.

Even if there is no production [of results] due to a lack of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not the case that this is fruitless, because other results—such as the recollection of names—which are understood from other scriptural passages, are possible; such is the direction of the argument.
Now, he states in a half-verse that this is also necessary because it constitutes part of the body of the meditation (*upāsti*):
How can one who does not recite this hymn be considered a devotee? || 252 ||

O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me:
the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom.

Thus, among the four types of devotees mentioned in the Smṛtis, [the Lord acts] for the sake of removing the sins of those who are distressed (ārta), for the sake of purifying the minds of those seekers of knowledge (jijñāsu) even though they are free from desire, and for the sake of accomplishing the goals of those who seek wealth (arthārthin).

For the sake of maintaining social order (*lokasaṃgraha*), the chanting of the Name is necessary for the devotees who possess knowledge; thus, the chanting of the Name is a constituent part of the very body that defines one as a devotee. This has been established in such scriptural sections (*adhikaraṇa*) as "But for those who have committed great sins, [it applies] in times of distress," and so forth.
This is clear in the Bhaktimīmāṃsābhāṣya. || 252 ||
Now, for those who are unable to observe the third of the four aforementioned qualifications, he provides an alternative course of action in two verses:
"One who is unable to perform the constant recitation should recite it on a meritorious day."
At the transit [of the sun], at the equinox, on the three occasions of one's own birth, and at the solstice; || 253 ||

"Always" means on meritorious days such as the *kapilā-ṣaṣṭhī* or *ardhodaya*, or generally on occasions like the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*) which will be described hereafter; "at the equinoxes" (*viṣuva*) refers to the days when the sun enters the zodiac signs of Aries and Libra; and "in one's own three births" refers to one's own [natal] day, as well as the seventh and thirteenth days from it.
On the birth asterisms (*janmanakṣatra*) of one's own wife and son,
or on the triad consisting of one's own birth asterism together with the two asterisms preceding and following it— counting starting from one's own birth asterism.
Or on the days of the three constellations—the first, the tenth, and the nineteenth;

or on the triad of days consisting of one's own birth day, the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and the day of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*). Thus, in cases where there is a diversity of interpretations, the determination is according to the specific tradition (*sampradāya*) of the Tantras.

Because of the statement, "It should be performed according to the approval of the Guru," [the rite is done] on the day the Sun enters the signs of Cancer and Capricorn during the solstices (*ayana*). Since this is already established by the term "transit" (*saṃkrānti*) alone,

the specific mention of the equinoxes (*viṣuva*) and solstices is either for the sake of illustrating their superior merit according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), or to indicate their extreme necessity.
A few days prior to each respective transition, that very period known as an *ayana* in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is intended here by the term *vaihāyana*. || 253 ||
On the ninth or the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, or on a Friday, one should recite the Thousand Names; especially so on the full moon day.

The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "on the ninth day or" is intended to include the eighth day as well. The term "in the bright fortnight" (*sitāyām*) applies to the three days beginning with the ninth. Alternatively, it means "on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight. Here, by the use of the particle "and" (*ca*), it is implied that this should be done every day for as long as one lives.
For one who is unable to perform *kīrtana* on all of these days, there should be a collective performance;

the word "or" (*vā*) is used here to indicate that if one is unable even for this, one may omit any one day. Even in the case of omitting one day, he says the following to indicate that the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) must not be omitted:

Regarding the phrase "especially": if, on the ninth lunar day and subsequent days, one's birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*), a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), and a Friday all coincide, then the recitation of the *Nāmasāhasra* and so forth should be performed only once by way of a single performance (*tantreṇa*).
This is to be inferred by those who know the principles of logic. || 254 ||

Having analyzed the two qualifiers— namely, "the state of being the most profound secret" and "that which causes the pleasure of Lalitā"— through this much of the treatise, and desiring now to analyze those same two qualifiers even more extensively, [the author] first addresses the fruits that constitute the components of the former.

Since the pacification of disease and so forth were mentioned first, he first describes the optional ritual application (*kāmyaprayoga*) which yields the fourfold fruit beginning with the pacification of disease, using two verses:
"Having meditated upon the venerable Mother Lalitā in the lunar orb on the full moon day"—

regarding the phrase "on the full moon day": the word *paurṇamāsī* refers to the final night of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), as seen from its usage in the *darśādṛṣṭa* section [of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā] where it denotes such a night.
Because of this calculation, it is established that in this particular application, the lunar day (*tithi*) that extends throughout the night is to be accepted.
This is because of the scriptural statement: "The lunar day that pervades the specific time of a ritual is the one to be used," and:
"The solar day upon which the sun rises having reached [the next lunar day]."
That lunar day (tithi) should be understood as complete for the purposes of bathing, giving gifts, vows, and so forth.

Although this statement applies even when [the time] exists for only a single *muhūrta*, it is not applicable in the present context because it is supplementary to other injunctions such as "the Gaurī-vrata on the day [of the lunar date], or on the following day," and so forth; therefore, when there is partial overlap in both cases, the later [time] is preferred. In reality, however, regarding the recitation of mantras and worship of the respective *tithi-nityās* and others...
The Tantrikas accept only that lunar day (*tithi*) which extends across the time of sunrise. A scriptural statement is also cited:

"The lunar day prevailing at sunrise is to be accepted for the daily worship of the *Nityās* and other rites. Therefore, when the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) concludes during the day itself, its status as a full-moon day is established because that lunar day has Citrā as its presiding deity.

Furthermore, since the *anuvāka* beginning with "darśādṛṣṭā" is intended to prescribe names for that very night associated with the guest (atithi) belonging to each respective deity, it is logical that only that night receives the designation "Paurṇamāsī.
This applies just as the statement "the lunar day on which" (*yāṃ tithim*) serves as an injunction regarding the time for the Gaurī-vrata, so too it serves as an injunction for this present rule.

Since it is easy to speak of [the lunar day] as being residual (*śeṣatā*), only the lunar day at sunrise (*audayikī*) is to be accepted here. However, when it spans two sunrises, both days constitute an optional time (*vaikalpikaḥ kālaḥ*), because that is precisely how it is accepted in the daily worship of the Tithinityās. For this very reason, where the fourteenth day is shorter at sunrise and the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) has already commenced [from the previous day], [the latter is taken].

If [the rite] is completed even before the next sunrise, then this ritual application must be performed on that very day, just like the worship of Citrā; such is the general direction. Regarding "in the lunar orb" (*candrabimbe*), it refers to the full disc of the moon.
For therein resides one eternal *kalā*, known as Sādākhya, which is the form of Tripurasundarī herself; the other fifteen *kalās* are...
They participate in increase and decrease,

and they consist of the fifteen *tithinityās* beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā. Therefore, upon their completion, [they are joined] by the sixteen *nityās*, who are the deities of their rays, and by the powers beginning with Aṇimā.
Through yoga, the lunar disc becomes directly manifest as the Śrīcakra;

it is with this very intention that names such as "situated in the center of the lunar disc" are used. For this same reason, [the deity is worshipped] in the Śālagrāma stone, the Bāṇaliṅga, and so forth.

Just as there is no invocation for Hari and Hara because of their constant and uninterrupted presence, here too, because Tripurasundarī is likewise ever-present, neither her invocation nor her mudrās should be displayed; rather,
one should meditate upon her according to the specific characteristics of her limbs described previously.

And because, having reflected upon her as transcending the world characterized by veils and forms, the action is designated by the very term "Lalitāmbikā," and because that term— according to the etymological definition consistent with the aforementioned Padma Purāṇa citation— finds its ultimate resolution in that very state.
Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings, one should recite the Thousand Names.

Having worshipped with the five-fold offerings—namely, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food—according to the manner taught in the Śruti, "He who is I, he is that; he who is that, he is I; thou art indeed That, Thou art indeed That," and so forth, by means of the perfection consisting in mutual correlative identity;

The identity of one's own self and the deity must be contemplated. For this alone is the primary factor regarding ritual observances: "A thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices are not equal even to a hundred-thousandth part of the worship of Lalitā."
He is a donor, he is a sage, he is a sacrificer, he is an ascetic,
and he is a pilgrim who always worships the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and unguents.
