Thus, since the connection with the fruit of worship is seen in this injunction from the *Padmapurāṇa*, the ritual services (*upacāras*) are subordinate to it according to the principle that "that which is without fruit is subordinate to that which possesses fruit. For this very reason,
the instrumental case is used in expressions such as "with perfumes, flowers, and ointments" and "with the five services."
Furthermore, those scriptural declarations regarding the fruits of various ritual services— such as "one who makes a fragrant unguent with lotuses shall obtain the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice"—
are merely explanatory praises (*arthavāda*) for the sake of another purpose, like the case of the *parṇa*-wood ladle. However, as for those [other passages]—
Having anointed Lalitā in this world with finely ground sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, a person shall dwell [in heaven] for ten million kalpas.
Statements such as these are intended to enjoin the connection between a quality and its fruit based on a subsidiary element, like the *godohana* vessel; or alternatively,
they mean that a householder should always perform both internal and external sacrifices, and so forth.

The internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) consists precisely in the cultivation of the realization of oneness through the understanding of the two-fold nature of worship. External worship, however, is merely a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) consisting of the offering of perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
In such cases, because perfumes and the like serve as instruments, they possess the status of auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), as seen in injunctions such as "one should offer perfumes and the rest."

There is a suspension of the application [of the primary rule] according to the principle of the *saktu* (barley-meal) offering. The offerings of scents and so forth into the mechanical devices (*yantra*) and other such objects are designated by the term "figurative" (*upacāra*); they are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the formal presentation (*nivedana*).
And these offerings, numbering sixteen and so forth, being equally principal, are to be performed together according to the scriptural injunction.

The status of being the instrument for the result (*phalakaraṇatva*) and so forth should be inferred accordingly. Among all forms of worship, *kramapūjā* is the archetype (*prakṛti*). From it alone, the extension of ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*) occurs in other types of worship, such as those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*) or on specific occasions (*naimittika*). This [present] worship, however, is entirely unprecedented (*apūrva*), because its auxiliary benefits (*upakāra*) have already been established.

Furthermore, because of the repetition of the five ordinary constituent offerings (*upacāra*), the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) is set aside according to the principle of the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice. Regarding these offerings, the ritual formula (*karaṇamantra*) is of this form:
"Obeisance to the venerable Mother Lalitā. This is due to the [presence of the] word of injunction.
If it is established by the principle of the *adhikaraṇa* that [the third syllable] possesses the nature of a mantra, this is because of the restrictive rule regarding Vedic terms.

Alternatively, the third peak (*kūṭa*) alone is the instrument-mantra (*karaṇamantra*), according to the statement in the *Tantrarāja*: "One should perform all the ritual services (*upacāra*) with the third section of the Vidyā. Nor is this [the case] in the context of the original form (*prakṛti*).

It must be stated how [the details] are obtained in a novel worship (*apūrvapūjā*) that lacks an injunction (*codaka*), since they are not obtained through the textual recitation (*pāṭha*) as parts of the sequential worship (*kramapūjā*). For even though the primary worship itself is novel, its constituent services (*upacāra*)— being subordinate to it— are [obtained].

Since there is no obstacle to the transfer of ritual properties (*dharma*) by means of transfer through name (*nāmātideśa*), which serves as a subsidiary to the procedure (*upacāra*) when there is an expectancy for the *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to" of the rite) due to its being a modification of the archetypal procedure (*prākṛtopacāra-vikṛti*),
how else could this be?

Thus, even in the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, the application of the mantras for the *ājyabhāga* offerings, including the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, is logically established. For this very reason, although the *avabhṛtha* is an original (*apūrva*) rite, since the archetypal selection of the *hotṛ*— which pertains to both the primary and subsidiary acts— is applicable here as an auxiliary to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one does not [select] the *hotṛ*.

The commentators have stated that the prohibition [of choosing] is appropriate because [the word] "vṛṇīte" [is used]. By this, the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and other such acts that are ancillary to the food offering (*naivedya*) are also explained. Through the suffix *-lyap* in the word "sampūjya," it is enjoined that the mental process (*bhāvanā*) whose instrument is worship is an ancillary to the mental process whose instrument is recitation.
By the word "should recite" (*paṭhet*), however, there is a primary efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) which has recitation as its instrument.

This is like the injunction in the sentence, "Desiring cattle, one should sacrifice with this [rite], having made the *vāravantīya* the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*," where there is an injunction of another efficient-force qualified by a prior efficient-force; likewise, here [there is] that which has worship as its instrument.

The meaning is that one should cultivate the desired result, such as the destruction of disease, by means of the recitation accompanied by the Thousand Names, which occurs subsequent to the limbs of the form of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). And here, because of the repeated connection of the word "having meditated" (*dhyātvā*), the suffix *-tva* there [in *bhāvanārūpa*] is used in the same way as in expressions such as "he sleeps with his mouth open" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*).
Since the suffix *śatṛ* ultimately conveys the sense of simultaneity, the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) is that "one who studies" means "one should recite. || 255 ||
All diseases are destroyed and one attains a long life;
this practice, named "Life-Producer," is proclaimed in the Kalpa. || 256 ||

He qualifies the desired object by saying "all diseases. Here, the verb "to perish" (naśyati) refers merely to non-existence in general, common to destruction, prior non-existence, and so forth. "Longevity" refers to the absence of both untimely death and death at the [usual] time. By the word "and" (ca), prosperity is included. Therefore—
The state of possessing a very long life, characterized by the absence of any common disease, is what is to be cultivated and is thereby accomplished.

Consequently, just as in the case of a sick person, the eligibility for this practice is established even for one who is currently healthy, with the aim of maintaining the prior non-existence of disease.
He demonstrates the name [of this rite] for its utility in the performance of rituals and so forth:
"This is the *āyuṣkara*. [The word] *kara* means "one who does," derived from the root *kṛ-* with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). An *āyuṣkara* is one who makes (*kara*) longevity (*āyus*).
The change of the visarga to *ṣ* occurs because the *kaska*-group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). The word *nāma* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

This is for the purpose of establishing what is produced by conventional designation (*saṃjñā*). "Proclaimed in the *Kalpa*" means proclaimed or indicated in the *Kalpasūtra* composed by Paraśurāma; that is, by collecting the various sets of auxiliary rites (*aṅga-jāta*) scattered here and there across all the *Kalpasūtras* and read in different branches (*paraśākhā*).

The meaning is that, because the purpose is to provide a conceptual framework for the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vidhi-kalpana*), by describing a few procedures such as the daily worship (*nityārcā*) therein, other procedures—even those not explicitly mentioned there—are indeed indicated. Alternatively, it means "not uttered" (*noditaḥ*)—that is, not stated explicitly—in Tantras that are equivalent to *Kalpasūtras*. Or else, it refers to the conceptualization (*kalpanena*) of the material cause (*bhāvya*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).

It has arisen—that is, been established—by means of the conceptualization of the relationship between cause and effect; or alternatively, it has not arisen—that is, has not been brought about—even in the *kalpa*, that is, even at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). This is because practitioners from the period immediately preceding the dissolution, even though they were certain of future re-aggregation and death, [acted] out of a desire for long life.

The meaning is that this application [of the names] protects them even at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*). Alternatively, "this application of names" refers to the state of being employed in the form "this bestows long life";

that is to say, it is a conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). This is done through conceptualization—that is, through the conceptualization of the power of the individual components and the conceptualization of their etymological and conventional meanings (*yogarūḍhi*).
It has been explained [previously]. By that same principle of parity, the subsequent applications named "Fever-remover" (*jvarahara*) and so forth are also to be inferred.
Their purpose, however, is established as being useful for the initial ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and other such acts.
Now, the procedure for its practice is stated more clearly: [it should be performed] when the moon, stars, and other [planets] possess strength.

On the day of the full moon that extends across both [the preceding and following days], having completed the daily Vedic and Tantric rites according to one's qualification, and having fasted, he should again bathe in the evening,
perform the evening Vedic and Tantric *saṃdhyā* rites ending with the daily recitation (*pārāyaṇa*), and then proceed.

When the eastern moon has duly risen, having spread out a seat with mantras in a pure place and sat upon it facing east, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), restrain the breaths (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra,
and announce the place and time: "For myself, or for another named so-and-so, of such-and-such a lineage (gotra)..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of attaining freedom from disease, prosperity, and the accomplishment of long life, I shall perform this longevity-inducing rite by reciting once the garland-mantra consisting of the *Śrī Lalitāsahasranāmastotra*," [one should visualize] the lunar disc.

Beholding with eyes wide open, having meditated upon Tripurasundarī within that [space]— along with her limbs, her enclosures, the daily deities, and the lineage of gurus— and having contemplated her as non-different from himself,
he [offers salutation]: "Obeisance to the venerable Mother Lalitā."

Having offered the services of visible perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings— characterized by the same essential features as in the primary rite— with mantras such as "I offer perfumes," and having also offered betel-leaf according to tradition even though it was not explicitly mentioned, [one should offer these] into the lunar disc.

Having beheld the Goddess, recited the first fifty verses, performed the three nyāsas beginning with that of the Ṛṣi, recited the verse of meditation (dhyāna), and uttered the Praṇava according to his qualification;

Having recited the mantra of the Thousand Names— beginning with "Śrīmātā" and ending with "Lalitāmbikā"— clearly articulating each syllable, preceded by a reflection on the meaning, and without haste; and having again uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ) at the end and performed the three nyāsas beginning with the *ṛṣi*, one should likewise recite the latter portion.
Having offered the *japa* into the left hand of the Goddess with the preceding sprinkling of water, saying "O Secret One" according to the specific *liṅga*,

and having assimilated the Goddess into one's own self, one should withdraw the gaze from the lunar orb, perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), rise, satisfy the *sāmāyika* deities, and [recite] this life-prolonging [mantra].

"May the ritual application (prayoga) be complete with all its parts, and may Tripurasundarī be pleased by it"— having thus accepted her blessing, one should eat oneself. Only those who perform the obligatory rites (nityakarman) possess the qualification for the occasional rites (naimittika).

However, one must not forget that the principle established in other systems— that eligibility for such optional rites belongs only to those who perform both [daily and occasional duties]— is well-founded. Furthermore, it has already been stated that even the repetition of this rite, when performed, does not constitute a fault.
Previously. || 256 ||
Having thus analyzed the four qualifiers, beginning with "the pacifier of all diseases," he now analyzes the practice that follows in order:
"Having touched the head of one afflicted by fever, one should recite the Thousand Names."
At that very moment, the pain in the head and the fever are pacified.

Upon touching one afflicted and tormented by fever, while simply placing his hand [upon them], at that very moment, immediately, there is a piercing pain in the head. This is merely an illustration of the affliction caused by fever.
As for the ritual procedure for the application: on the day the cause known as fever arises, having performed his daily rites, [the practitioner] in a pure place...

One should perform the ritual from the mention of the place up to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). In the resolve, the wording should be modified according to the specific characteristics of the case. The name of the practice should be mentioned as "the procedure for removing fever. Then, having seated the person afflicted by fever facing north on one's own right side, and having bathed them with ashes or with the mantra, [one proceeds with] the eastern portion...

Having recited [the first part], one should place the hand on the head of the person afflicted by fever; while still touching him in that same manner, one should recite the middle portion; then, withdrawing the hand, one should recite the final portion and perform the feeding of Brahmins and other rites. However, in a rite for one's own benefit, one should do so only upon one's own head.

The gift of the hand (*hastadāna*). Furthermore, repetition until the fruit arises is established by tradition (*sampradāya*) and is also established by the logic of the section [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*] stating, "Repetition [is required], because of the instruction more than once. In the case of this method of repetition, having recited the first part, one should repeat only the middle part according to one's resolve.
The specific instruction is that one should recite the final portion; in this manner, the ritual procedure for subsequent [sections] is to be inferred. || 257 ||
He states another application that removes all diseases in common with [the treatment of] fever and so forth:
"For the sake of curing all diseases, one should touch the ashes and recite this mantra;
by the mere wearing of those ashes, diseases perish in an instant. (258)

"All" (sarve) means all those diseases, or the diseases of all [beings]. "Having touched" (spṛṣṭvā) means while merely touching. By the mere smearing—that is, by the wearing—of that consecrated ash, simply through this thousand-name mantra... || 258 ||

Now, following the sequence, he describes two applications for the purpose of destroying the afflictions caused by planets and poisons, as mentioned in the passage "bestowing long life," using two verses:
"O Sage, having consecrated water placed in a jar [by reciting] the *Nāmasāhasra* a thousand times..."
One should consecrate those seized by planetary spirits; the spirits perish at that very moment. || 259 ||

Having consecrated [the water] by reciting the hymn, one should cast the hand into the mouth of the jar; then, O Sage Agastya, one should sprinkle—that is, bathe—the person with that very consecrated water (this is the implied sense). Those seized by the *grahas*—such as the *bālagrahas* and others—by the *piśācas*, those occupying malevolent positions, and by the nine *grahas*.
Those who have been made to die through torment. || 259 ||
Having meditated upon the venerable Mother Lalitā, who dwells in the midst of the ocean of nectar,
whoever recites this Thousand Names, his poison shall be destroyed.
Wherever Śrīpura exists, there is a single pool of nectar (sudhāhrada) in each such place.
In the city named Aparājitā, which is attainable by the worshippers of Saguna Brahman, there are two pools of nectar known as Araṇya; there is also one in the Brahma-randhra. Among these—
Having meditated upon [the deity] according to one's qualification by means of its presence, and while meditating, one should worship with the mind—this is the remainder [of the sense].

"Poison" refers to both stationary (sthāvara) and moving (jaṅgama) forms. Furthermore, this ritual application generally does not have a result that belongs to a different locus [than the agent]. || 260 ||
For barren women to obtain a son, one should give them fresh butter consecrated with the Thousand Names; thus, the attainment of a son will certainly occur. (261)

Regarding the term "of the barren" (*vandhyānām*): the plural number is used to include those who have no offspring, those whose offspring have died, those whose offspring are female, and those who bear only one child like a crow. In the phrase "for the sake of obtaining a son" (*putralābhāya*), the word "son" (*putra*) denotes offspring in general. This is seen in such passages as, "May male children alone be born to me as my sons."

This is because of the natural force of the qualification "males" (*pumāṃsaḥ*), and also because of the usage in the *Manusmṛti*: "The daughter's son [is purified] by the hand of the maternal grandfather. Furthermore, if the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) were accepted from the word *putrī*, the resulting form would be *pautreyī*.
Alternatively, in the analysis of the compound as "sons and daughters" (*putrāś ca duhitaraś ca*), the term *bhrātṛputrau* applies.

By the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term) in the compound "svasṛduhitṛbhyām" (by sisters and daughters), the form becomes simply "putrāḥ" (sons); the acquisition of these is "putralābhaḥ," and for that purpose [the rite is performed]. By this, even those who desire daughters have the right to participate in this ritual application.
In the phrase "pradadyāt tamasmai bhakṣam prayacchet" (he should give him that food, he should offer it to him), one should understand a restrictive determination (*vyavaccheda*).
Therefore, the statement "one should sacrifice with that" is merely explanatory (arthavāda); here too, the meaning is "the barren woman should eat [the seeds].
By this, it is established that upon obtaining the seeds from the guru of a barren woman, one may oneself also consume them after performing the ritual recitation.
The acquisition of sons and daughters will certainly and surely come to pass. || 261 ||

Now, wishing to analyze with thirty-five verses the qualification "bestowing the goals of human life" (*puruṣārthapradāyaka*) as it follows in due order, [the author] first addresses here the last of the three aims (*trivarga*) contained therein— the granting of a son— by means of a specific ritual application.
Because she stands at the door of the woman, he describes with one and a half verses the practice of attracting the woman, which has her attainment as its fruit:
"Bound by the noose of the Goddess and drawn in by the goad..."
Having meditated upon his beloved woman at night, he should recite this thousand-name hymn.

Regarding the word "devyā" (by the goddess): here, although by the constraints of grammar the word *devyāḥ* is construed as a subordinate element—just as in expressions such as "the king's man"—it is in fact predominant in meaning.
Thus, [one should visualize] the Goddess drawing toward her with a hook a woman who is her desired object and who is firmly bound by a noose.

The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] while meditating. Since meditation upon that deity is already established as a necessary requirement for the mere repetition (*japa*) of the mantra, this sentence serves only to enjoin a connection between a subordinate element (*guṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*), by taking that [meditation] as its basis. Nor is it the case that...

It should be stated that, by means of the recitation, the quality of the form of the woman visualized as being drawn in by the noose is enjoined for the sake of the fruit; nevertheless, since the meditation on the Goddess is already established by another injunction and is free from contradiction, it is the quality of the form of the object of meditation that is enjoined for the sake of the fruit.
This is because it is only when [the meditation] is based on the *dhyāna*— through the relation of being its object (*viṣayitā*)— that consistency is achieved;

for a remote relation such as occurring at the same time, which exists between the recitation of the *dhyāna* and the *pāṭha*, is not a sufficient cause, as it is unfit to serve as the relation of substrate and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*).
"Throughout the night," meaning pervading the entire night; "he should recite," meaning he should cause it to be heard. || 262 ||
"Even though she has gone to the inner apartments (antaḥpura), she comes into my presence"—this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).

Even though she has gone to the inner apartments—that is, the private quarters (*śuddhānta*)—nevertheless, she comes into my vicinity even from such a place. Now, one might ask: "Is the beloved woman here one's own wife?"

Or [the woman] may belong to another. In the first case, although it would contradict the statement that she "has entered the inner apartments"—since by that [statement], the queen of the king is understood—it cannot be maintained that this ritual application belongs solely to the king as the performer.
For, as in the case of the *rājasūya* and other such injunctions, no specific qualified performer (*adhikārin*) is heard of; therefore, [the qualification applies] to her within the inner apartments.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of difficulty in accomplishment, summoning would be futile. Nor can it be argued that the engagement [in this practice] is for the sake of mere curiosity; for while the word "even if" (*yadyapi*) naturally suggests the perception of difficulty in accomplishment, it does not suggest a lack of qualification for one who possesses curiosity, nor does it suggest a lack of qualification for one who lacks curiosity.

If it is argued that it is improper for the final dharma (antyadharma) to be prescribed by injunction, we say no; for this injunction is meaningful in cases where [the goal] is difficult to accomplish due to causes such as the forcible abduction of one's own wife.
Indeed, there is a historical account in the *Hanuguṇṭhapīṭhamāhātmya* concerning a sage named Nārāyaṇa.

The wife named Candravadanā was abducted by Seturāja, the son of Śakra; however, having propitiated the Goddess, she was brought back again by the sage. Alternatively, another result [of the abduction] must be postulated that is not in contradiction with dharma. Or let it be so.

Attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) is for the sake of enjoyment alone; nevertheless, because it is connected [to the ritual] solely as an object to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) within that cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it does not possess the status of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). As it has been stated in the *Tantravārttika*: "With respect to the factor of the fruit (*phalāṃśa*), the suffix of the *bhāvanā* is not injunctive."
And Jaimini will state here that its definition is the purpose of the eternal [Veda].

Thus, because it is not prescribed [by the Vedas], the desire for another's wife does not possess the nature of dharma (*dharmatva*). However, in the specific performance under discussion which serves as the means for that [desire], it does possess the nature of dharma, just like the Śyena sacrifice. As for those [statements] such as "the Kaulika is the first husband of all women," and so forth—
However, according to the manner in which the authors of the *Śyāmārahasya* have extracted the meaning of those statements,
the nature of Dharma is to be understood solely from the mouth of the Guru.

In this context, since the middle category [of the three goals of life] follows immediately after desire (*kāma*), the author describes the attraction of the king through two and a half verses regarding the numerous ritual applications that yield that result:
"If one desires to attract the king, [one should face] the direction of the king's residence... (363).

Regarding the word "rājā" (king): by the use of the particle *ced* ("if"), it is indicated that this fruit is accomplished only when the ritual performance is undertaken with the specific intention of attracting [the king], provided that such a desire for attraction exists. However, as for the six rites (*ṣaṭkarma*) to be described later, they are incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*) even when the performance is carried out with their respective specific purposes.

It has been indicated that [the results] are accomplished even for Satyakāma. "In the direction of the king's residence" means facing the direction in which the king’s dwelling—his house, including his seat and so forth—is located.
This is an exception to the general rule whereby facing either the east or the north would otherwise be obtained. || 363 ||
He who, intent on the meditation of the auspicious Goddess, recites this for three nights,
[shall obtain] a horse or an elephant through the subjection of a king.
Having ascended, he approaches his presence and prostrates like a servant;
having come under his control, he should indeed surrender both his kingdom and his treasury to him. (265)

In the expression "trirātram," the accusative case is used to denote continuous duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Furthermore, the word *trirātra* refers to a period of three full days and nights, as is seen in such usages as "impurity for three nights" (*trirātram āśaucam*). Consequently, even obligatory religious rites (*nityakarman*) must be curtailed, and one should perform only those worldly duties that are strictly necessary, doing this without interruption.

It is established that one should recite for a period of twenty-four hours; for this very reason, there is a fixed rule regarding the number of repetitions. In the meditation on the Śrīdevī, one should be intent upon the visualization of the Goddess as she was previously described—binding the king with her noose and drawing him in with her goad.

[The practitioner] is attached [to the practice]. Nor is the purpose already established by the previous application. In that case, the time is specifically the night consisting of four watches, and the rules regarding facing east or north are optional; here, however, it is three days and nights.

The distinction lies in the restriction of the direction facing Rājagṛha and so forth; however, in reality, the difference between these two is based solely on time (*kāla*). This is because another Tantra establishes that for one whose face is being turned toward a direction, it is necessary [to face] only the act of turning itself. And thus it is said in the Vāmakeśvara-tantra:
Facing toward that direction, having made his body threefold,
and having bound the Kṣobhiṇī mudrā, he should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times.
Beginning with "Thus, one should meditate on the woman wandering even hundreds of *yojanas away," and ending with that [verse].

Also, in the *Nityātantra*, in the *Kurukullā-paṭala*: "By means of the thirteen-syllable *vidyā*, facing that direction, one shall attract a woman within three days," and so forth. Also, in the *Jñānārṇava*:

"Facing toward that hope, he himself takes the form of the Goddess," and so forth. In this way, texts such as the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* may be cited. The meaning is that whoever is intended by one's mind, he alone is the King. The phrase "or a horse" and so forth is used to indicate that [the king] does not come alone, like a thief. To him...
Having come under the control of the practitioner, being entirely subject to his command. || 264-265 ||
Since the six rites, beginning with subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and including the attraction of wealth (*arthākarṣaṇa*), are present [in this context], he describes their application in seven verses:
"He who constantly recites the thousand secret names..."
O Sage, by the mere sight of his face, the three worlds would be infatuated.
Regarding the word "rahasya" (in secret): "nityaśaḥ" means without conflict with obligatory daily rites (*nityakarman*); "yāvajjīvam" means continuously for as long as one lives.

By the word "mātra" in the phrase "mukhālokamātreṇa" (by the mere sight of the face), the intention of causing delusion (*mohana*) is excluded from the performance of the rite. Therefore, one should not include the statement "for the purpose of deluding the three worlds" in the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
He would become deluded and fall under [her] control. || 266 ||
Desiring hereafter to describe the practices that require progressively less effort, he speaks first of the rite of slaying:
"But he who, full of devotion, recites this *Nāmasāhasra* even once..."
The Lord of Śarabhas is the slayer of those who are his enemies.

Regarding the phrase "He who": one recites it once daily, continuing this throughout one's life; that is, one recites it once every day for as long as one lives. Śarabheśvara is an incarnation of Śiva known by that name.
According to the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*, this was for the purpose of removing [the obstacles] of Viṣṇu in his incarnation as Nṛsiṃha.

This is well known from the *Kālikāpurāṇa* and other sources. In the Tantras, the application of the mantras known as Śarabha and Sāluva for the purpose of reversing the *Nārasiṃha* ritual is most renowned. Because he is the slayer even of Viṣṇu and is thus the foremost among slayers (*māraka*), he alone has been selected for this rite. Therefore, this...

This is what is implied: even such a powerful deity, though inclined toward other means of departure and though not exclusively worshipped by the practitioner of Śrīvidyā, and though unknown to him, exerts himself of his own accord for the destruction of this enemy. Therefore, [this is said] with reference to those who worship that [deity] alone.

The greatness of the Lalitopāsaka is thus limitless; otherwise, one would have said simply that his enemies perish immediately and of their own accord. In this way, even in the subsequent mention of the group of five beginning with Pratyaṅgirā, the underlying implication (dhvani) should be understood. || 267 ||
Or whoever performs malevolent magic against one who recites the *Nāmasāhasra*, Pratyāṅgirā herself shall turn back that rite and destroy him. (268)

"Yo vā" means: having warded off, turned back, or averted *abhicāra*—that is, a ritual action such as the *śyena*-sacrifice which has as its means the death of an enemy through an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) medium. *Pratyaṅgirā* is the deity Atharvaṇabhadrakālī; [she is found] in the *mantrakāṇḍa* of the *Atharvaveda*.

In the Śaunaka recension, there are thirty-two verses; however, in the Pippalāda recension, forty-eight verses belonging to it are handed down. And the ritual applications for those [verses] are well known in the Nārada Tantra. || 268 ||
Those who look upon the reciter of the Thousand Names with a cruel gaze are quickly rendered blind by Mārtāṇḍabhairava himself. (269)
With a cruel gaze, red with anger; he named Mārtāṇḍabhairava was indeed an incarnation of Śiva, born in Premapura in the Karṇāṭaka country,
who became extremely widespread in the Mahārāṣṭra country, and whose mantras are found in the Mairāla-tantra (the Rudrayāmala).
And the applications are well-known. || 269 ||
If wealth is stolen by thieves from one who has recited the Thousand Names, the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla) destroys that thief, regardless of where he may be situated. || 270 ||
He who is the lord of thieves, acting through the thieves as his instruments; he who is the guardian of the field (Kṣetrapāla);

and for the sake of slaying the demon Dāruka, after the descent of Kālikā, even upon her killing him, seeing that her anger had not subsided, Śiva himself became a child under the pretext of drinking from her breast.

He drank the fire of his own wrath. This very one is renowned in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* as an incarnation of Kṣetrapāla, and his mantras are preserved in the Tantras. By the destruction of that king of thieves, the eradication of thieves was achieved as a matter of course. || 270 ||
If a learned man engages in a debate on the sciences with one who merely mutters names,
the Mistress of the Nakuli instantly effects a paralysis of his speech.
Regarding the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), the term "topic of debate" (*vādapada*) is an elliptical expression for both *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).

In the *Āraṇyaka* of the *Ṛgveda*, the mantra of Nakulī Vāgīśvarī is recited; it was also extracted by the venerable Paraśurāma in his *Kalpasūtra*. The applications (*yoga*) of this [mantra] are found in the *Prapañcasāra* and other such works.
They are well-known. || 271 ||
If a king harbors enmity toward one who recites the Thousand Names,
his fourfold army shall be destroyed by Daṇḍinī herself.

The fourfold army consists of troops in the form of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. Daṇḍinī, the mistress of punishment, is Vārāhī as she is well-known in the Tantras. She should destroy [the enemy] by inciting mutual hostility among the soldiers, and by the expulsion or destruction of a few.
The withdrawal of power (*balasaṃhāra*) consists in the absence of acting toward a single goal by coming together; one should perform that.

Thus the six rites have been described, and they are stated in the *Śābaracintāmaṇi* as follows: pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), immobilization (*stambhana*), causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*).
In this context, other [topics] are indeed mentioned; however, their mutual inclusion must be understood according to their respective nature. As it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Protection, pacification, recitation, attainment, suppression, and likewise destruction."
The six rites exist as non-distinct from it, because they are its constituent parts.

Thus [it is said]. The manner of inclusion and their definitions are not stated here for fear of prolixity; they should be consulted in the twenty-third wave (*taraṅga*) of the *Subhāgyaratnākara*. || 272 ||
Now, he describes two applications that grant wealth with the following two verses:
"He who recites the Thousand Names for six months, endowed with devotion, in his house Lakṣmī shall always abide, free from fickleness. (273)

"Whoever should recite it"—the word "once" (*sakṛt*) is understood to carry over from the previous context. If one should recite it once every day for a period of six months, prosperity (*lakṣmī*) will always remain in that person's house for as long as they live. For fickleness is indeed the very nature of prosperity; it is a well-known saying that "nature is difficult to overcome. Even such [fickle] prosperity [remains].
The meaning is: "having abandoned the fault. || 273 ||
The man who recites this three times every day for one month—Sarasvatī dances perpetually upon the tip of his tongue, as if on a stage. (274)

"for one month" is an exception (*apavāda*) to "six [months]"; "three times," however, is an exception to "once. There is no distinction as to whether one should recite it three times all at once or according to the divisions of the *saṃdhyās*. *Bhāratī* is Sarasvatī.

Alternatively, *bhā* means creative intuition (*pratibhā*), while *rati* means inclination (*abhiruci*) and resolve (*āsthā*). From the root *ram* with the suffix *ktic*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, the form *ratī* is derived.
The metaphor that the tip of the tongue itself is the stage and the arena for dancing is intended to accord with the conventions of other forms of dance.

All branches of knowledge remain unobscured even without depending on public proclamations, rehearsals, preliminary inspections, or formal instruction; however, formal study (*adhyayana*) is indeed required for the acquisition of knowledge.
The meaning is that this is because the Guru alone is the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) cause. || 274 ||

By way of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokana), he again states the practice that grants desires: "But he who recites it once for a fortnight without weariness—the deer-eyed women, falling under the power of passion, become infatuated at the mere sight of him. (275)
"Half-month" is an exception to the [rule of] a month; "once" is an exception to the three repetitions;
"unwearied" means free from sleep, drowsiness, and so forth. And this [quality], while necessary in all cases, is stated here to emphasize that it is especially necessary in this particular practice.

By this, it is also indicated that this ritual application (*prayoga*) is to be performed at midnight. Since the word "only" (*mātra*) is absent here, it is implied that in the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one must state: "for the purpose of bringing women under control," whether the rite is performed by him [as the agent] or directed toward them [as the object]. || 175 ||
Having thus spoken of wealth and desire, and now beginning to describe the methods for the bestowal of dharma in many ways, he states the dharma that is accomplished by the first effort:
"The man who recites the *Nāmasāhasra* even once during the course of his life..."
All those who come within the range of his vision are liberated from all sins. || 276 ||

Regarding the word "ya" (who): by the phrase "in the midst of birth," there is an exception (*apavāda*) to the [rules for] lifelong practice, six-month practice, one-month practice, and the fortnightly practices.
Although [the frequency] is already established by the recurrence of the term "once," the term "three times" is supplied by means of the *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) method.
The word "once" (*sakṛt*) is used as a counter-exception so that the doubt regarding the [repeated] occurrence of the function [of the sense organ] may not arise.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "all living beings who fall within the range of his vision," meaning those who are the objects of visual perception produced by him as its agent. || 276 ||

Now, with four verses, he describes the quality of being a bestower of merit (*dharmapradata*) as an essential constituent of the recipient’s worthiness (*pātratā*), which is the culminating factor (*kāraka*) in the act of giving:
"To that twice-born man who knows the Thousand Names, [the gift] should be given."
Food, clothing, wealth, and grain should never be given to others [in this manner]. (277)
Regarding the word "ya" (who): in the phrase "it should be given," the ellipsis is "by the worshipper of Lalitā.

This is established by following the subsequent text, which says "desiring the pleasure of the Śrī Devī. Therefore, it is proven that even one who is not a regular worshipper should give it to others as well, since there is no difference in their status as recipients (*sampradāna*). When the *Śāmbhavīcakra* has been set in motion, all...

With the intention that the statement from the *Kulārṇava*, "The castes are the twice-born," is an extension of the duties of a Brāhmaṇa [to others] and does not concern their status as recipients (*saṃpradāna*) established by the Śruti and Smṛti— but rather refers only to duties such as untouchability at the time of sacrifice— he says "dvijanmanaḥ" (of the twice-born).
The meaning is "to a Brāhmaṇa. The phrase "food" (*anna*) and so forth is an illustration for all things that ought to be given.

The meaning is that one should never give to others—namely, to those who appear to be practitioners (*upāsakābhāsa*) but are Brāhmaṇas lacking respect for the *Sahasranāma*—even at times prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, such as during the performance of priestly duties (*ārtvijya*) or ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
In that regard as well, the intention is that those solely devoted to meditation are indispensable. || 277 ||
The wise know him to be a worthy recipient who knows the glorious King of Mantras, who worships the Śrīcakra, and who recites its names. (278)

The "King of Mantras" refers to the Śrīvidyā. Here, it is established by logic alone that when all three [qualities] are present, there is the status of being a worthy recipient (satpātratā); in the absence of any one of them, there is a gradation [of worthiness]; and in the absence of all three, there is a lack of eligibility as a recipient.
Therefore, this is the summary: among these three qualifiers that delimit the status of the recipient (*sampradānatā*),
there are three with each one of the qualifiers,
three with two of the qualifiers each, one with all three qualifiers, and another which lacks all three.
Thus, although the eight types of Brahmins appear according to the method of expansion (*prastāra*), nevertheless,

because the status of being a worshiper of the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*) is pervaded by the knowledge of the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*), one characterized by that specific mantra is not possible [among them]. Therefore...
And thus, even one possessing only the two qualifications other than being a mantrin is like a sky-flower.
Therefore, there are exactly six types of Brāhmaṇas. Among them, those with three qualities are the best; those with two qualities are middling. Between those two [types],...

Comparing one who possesses the two qualities of being a knower of mantras and being a worshiper of the *cakra* with one who possesses the two qualities of being a knower of mantras and performing the recitation of names (*nāmakīrtana*), the latter is superior; those possessing only one quality each are inferior.
Even between those two, the one possessing the single quality of merely knowing the mantras is the more excellent.

The lowest [type] has the mere chanting of the name as its quality; however, since there is no eligibility for the chanting of the name in the absence of the mantra, even the quality residing in one who lacks eligibility is ineffective, according to the principle of the Vedic sentences studied by Śūdras. But the one possessing the three absences is not [eligible] at all.
The discernment is that it is a vessel. || 278 ||
One who desires the favor of the Goddess Śrī should bestow [this] with effort upon him who recites the names but does not know the King of Mantras. (279)

To that worthy recipient, it should be given with great effort; even when a superior recipient is unavailable, it may be given to a mediocre one—such is the meaning, which, though established by logic, is indeed a scriptural injunction. As it is stated in the *Pulastya-smṛti*:
An injunction with an unseen purpose is declared as the first; the second has a seen purpose;
the third serves both purposes; and the fourth is based on reasoning.
Thus, explaining this very point, he clarifies the portion beginning with "but never to others":
"He who does not proclaim the names [of the deities] and does not know the King of Mantras should be known as equal to a beast; what is given to him is useless."

And here, by the phrase "those five who are distinct from the three qualities and the effects of the three qualities," those [who are like animals] are designated, and the intended injunction is their state of being equal to cattle; furthermore,
they are subsumed under the property of possessing an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the state of having the three qualities (*triguṇatva*).

For even in the case of those possessing one quality or two qualities, that [absence] is easily available as having a counter-positive delimited by a property that occurs distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti). And that absence, which serves as the delimitant of the objective referent (uddeśyatāvacchedaka), has been defined by the first half [of the verse]. Although in that context, the absence of only two qualities appears to be indicated;
Nevertheless, because three qualifications are employed in the definition of a worthy recipient (*pātra*), it is intended that, in accordance with those,
the absence of those same three is also meant in the definition of a sacrificial animal (*paśu*); however,
with the intention that the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) follows from the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), [the text mentions] the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*).
The portion "does not worship" has been stated explicitly; for the knowledge of the mantra is pervaded by the state of being a worshiper of the wheel. || 279 ||
He should be known as equal to a beast; what is given to him is useless.
A wise man, having examined those who are learned in knowledge, should give [gifts] to them. || 280 ||

In the analysis *paśutulya* as *paśuśca paśuśca*, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) compound meaning "equal to those two. Among them, one word *paśu* refers to a four-footed animal; the other, by means of conventional metaphor (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), refers to the well-known "animal" who is devoid of knowledge (*vidyā*). And that knowledge is...
It is indeed Śrīvidyā. As it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa itself:
"The term 'learned' (vidvat) is not applied to one who possesses knowledge of [mere] weapons and the like;
he alone is declared to be learned who possesses the Vidyā that is the sole cause of liberation."
"And Śrīvidyā is the sole cause of liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus, among the five [practices] mentioned, although three possess the nature of *vidyā* (knowledge), and although the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the worship of the *cakra* and the chanting of the name exists, they remain "non-knowledge" (*avidyā*) because they are not performed.

For them, knowledge consists primarily of pride; such is their similarity to beasts. The distinction is that those who merely recite names and possess the three states of being (bhāva) are equal to four-legged beasts.
"Given to him" means a gift having him as its recipient; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*). "Meaningless" means devoid of purpose.

The word *artha* (wealth/benefit), having entered into a state of degrees of intensity (*taratama-bhāva*), denotes specific instances of results. Therefore, both the absence of a distinguished result and the absence of a result in general must be connected with the gradations of worthiness (*pātra-tāratamya*). Thus, [the text sets forth] the punishment for the opposite of the aforementioned purpose.

Having introduced the subject with a nipāta (particle), he concludes it with the second half [of the verse]. The word "tasmāt" (therefore) is to be supplied as the remainder. In the domain of knowledge (*vidyā*), "learnedness" (*vidvattva*) consists in possessing worship according to reality (*yāthātathya*).
And that is accomplished only when there is the accompaniment of the worship, the name, and the chanting of Lalitā; thus, [the author] describes the nature of the three qualities.

The meaning is that one should give to them after having examined them. Alternatively, "tebhyaḥ" (to them) is in the ablative case. The meaning is: because they alone are worthy recipients (*satpātra*), while others lack that quality; because the injunction for giving is prescribed only for a worthy recipient, whereas elsewhere it is prohibited. In this interpretation, no word needs to be supplied to complete the sense.
The rule that the status of being a recipient belongs only to those who possess knowledge will be established by the very force of the fact that examination has a visible purpose. || 280 ||
O Pot-born One, just as there exists no mantra equal to the glorious King of Mantras, so too there is no deity equal to Lalitā. 281.

And by means of the mutual relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison among the three qualities, [the author] suggests their supreme excellence through the absence of any other standard of comparison, [thereby establishing] their status as the defining characteristics of being worthy recipients.
He dispels that doubt with two and a half verses.
Here, the connection between "yathā" and "tathā" should also be understood in their reverse order. || 281 ||
There is no praise equal to the Thousand Secret Names.
Whoever writes down this supreme Thousand Names in a book, [attains the highest merit]. (282)
Now he says that even for one who is not a lay devotee (*anupāsaka*), this hymn bestows the Dharma: "Whoever"— meaning anyone at all, whether a lay devotee or not a lay devotee—
even though one who is not a lay devotee lacks the qualification for the recitation of the name, they do possess the qualification for the worship of its book.
Because it is free from affliction. || 282 ||
One should always worship her with devotion; then Sundarī is pleased with him.
What is the use of saying more here? Listen, O Pot-born One (Agastya)! 283.
A hymn like this is not found in any of the tantras;
therefore, a practitioner should always recite this with devotion. (284)
The sense is: "always, for as long as one lives"—this applies even to one who is not a lay devotee (*anupāsaka*), let alone to a lay devotee (*upāsaka*).
Although by this same logic he is pleased even by the worship of a book, how much more so by its glorification;
thus, by the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"), the intended meaning lies precisely in glorification (*kīrtana*).
Therefore, it is easy to say that the concluding summary later on with the words "one should proclaim" is appropriate; nevertheless,

even though the word *adhyayana* (study) in the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" is capable of signifying the act of repeating after the utterance by the teacher's mouth, [the following applies].

Just as in the case of the injunction "one should perform the meditation" (*bhāvanā-vidhāna*), which is intent upon enjoining a meditation that has for its object the knowledge of the meaning of that [mantra] which serves as its instrument, so too here, the fact that the injunction "one should recite the names" extends up to the knowledge of the meaning is beyond dispute.
Therefore: "Even he who knows but a single name through the etymologies of the verbal roots, the traditional exegeses (*nigama*), and so forth..."
Such a person shall dwell in the world of Śrī Lalitā for tens of millions of kalpas.
Thus it is said in the Devīpurāṇa:
"That which is studied without being understood is recited merely by rote;
like dry fuel in a fireless place, it never truly blazes forth."

Thus, the statements in other Smṛtis concerning the praise of the knowledge of meaning and the censure of its lack of knowledge become consistent. However, in the absence of the capacity for the knowledge of meaning as the ultimate goal, that cultivation (bhāvanā) may even be directed solely toward the mere recitation (nigada). [This concerns] the meaning of verbs...

This is because of the logical principle that for those who speak, power (*śakti*) is a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). For this very reason, the Śruti states: "He who knows the meaning attains all auspiciousness; he goes to the heavenly world, his sins shaken off by knowledge. Here, by the qualification "all" (*sakalatva*) regarding the fruit obtained through the knowledge of the meaning, [it is shown that] it is not attained by the mere knowledge of the words.
It has been made known that there exists a fruit that is somewhat deficient; and by the same logic,
even for one incapable of reciting the words [of the scripture], the mere possession of a book is obtained through right principle (*nyāya*),
for [the merit of] the recitation will [bear fruit] in another birth.
It can be easily stated that just as one who bestows knowledge of the meaning [of a text] may, in another birth, become one who bestows the recitation of the book itself,

so too it is possible for one who has performed worship— even if lacking the [proper] lineage (*asampradāya*)— according to the *Tantrarāja* and other scriptures, to attain [the fruit] in another birth.

It has been stated that one prepares oneself for the purity of the tradition along with its constituent limbs (*sāṅga-sampradāya*). Therefore, even the mere worship of the book is indeed a religious duty (*dharma*). Furthermore, since this is not prohibited even for one who is not currently a practitioner (*anupāsaka*), it must certainly be performed so that one may attain the practice in a future birth. For the practitioner (*upāsaka*), however—

Even for one incapable of reciting the names, it is absolutely necessary to preserve one's capacity in accordance with the injunction that "one should recite the name"; nor can it be argued that this is impossible for one who is not a lay devotee (*anupāsaka*), as that would contradict the injunction stated in the *Kalpasūtra* that "one should conceal the family scriptures."
It should not be said that one has the qualification for the worship of the book;
for that [text] is intended for wicked people who disparage the knowledge of the meaning, and lacks any intent toward virtuous people who desire future worship.

Otherwise, it would follow that the purpose [of the rite] is not perceptible; this is another matter. However, for those devotees capable of reciting the names, the mere worship of the book is certainly indispensable.
And this is the underlying principle.
With the intention that this is equally true even for the study of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), which serves as a means to the knowledge of this meaning, we shall state at the end of the work:
"O Mother, this Commentary, which was caused to be composed by you, is now offered at your feet."

May this work, which unfolds the meaning of your name, lead to your delight. Now, for him who worships you but does not study this, nor reads it, nor even takes possession of the book, let his graceful worship become in vain.

Thus, with the intention that [this mantra] is a protector even for those who do not practice worship, let alone for those who do— thinking, "It will surely protect the practitioners"— he concludes at the very midpoint with two and a half verses (283–284).

Now, with four verses, he describes the yoga that bestows the most exalted dharma, which— according to the sequence of the six previously mentioned signs (rāśis) and so forth— yields a fruit that cannot be fully grasped even by the intellect: "Whoever should worship the Śrīcakra even once with these thousand names..."
Or with lotuses, or with tulasī flowers, or with white water-lilies, or with kadamba blossoms. || 285 ||

Regarding the phrase "by these": the plural number in "thousand names" (*nāmasāhasraiḥ*) is intended to indicate that each individual name functions as an instrument [of worship], and also to suggest the necessity of repeated recitation during rites such as the hundred-thousand-fold worship (*lakṣapūjā*). "Names" refers to the nominal stems (*prātipadika*); those among which there are a thousand [names] are the ones beginning with "Obeisance to Śrī Mātā."

In the case of the mantras ending with "Obeisance to Lalitāmbikā" and so forth, which conclude with the dative case and the word *namaḥ*, [the repetition] is performed with those thousand names; furthermore, according to tradition, there is a repetition of the act of scattering flowers. Therefore, as in the Vedic injunctions such as "He takes up the spade with four [verses]" (*caturbhir abhriṃ ādatte*), this constitutes a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the four hundred thousand [recitations].

Let it not be so. Here, the mutual distinction between the *padya*, *kahlāra*, and *utpala* lotuses is to be inferred from their differences as intermediate species. [The offering is made] with the blossoming clusters of *tulasī* flowers, and not with its leaves. Regarding the beautiful woman (*sundarī*)...
Because of this very [scriptural] authority, it is appropriate that the prohibition of *tulasī* refers specifically to its leaves. For this reason, it is clearly stated in the *Nīlātantra*:
"With various offerings and oblations, and with various beautiful flowers..."
With Apāmārga leaves and Bhṛṅga leaves, excluding Tulasī leaves.
"She should always be worshipped with devotion by men for the swift attainment of results.
And as it is said in that very same place:
"The worship of the Goddess is always praised, whether performed with water-born or land-born [offerings]."
Whether by means of prescribed or prohibited acts, with a mind endowed with devotion.

Thus it is said. In that context, the acceptance of what is otherwise prohibited is intended to suggest the necessity of devotion (*bhakti*). However, as for the statement in the *Kālīpurāṇa*—"If even flowers are unavailable, one should worship Śivā with their leaves"—this refers specifically to obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), because there is an absence of substitutes in optional rites (*kāmyakarman*).

Because it is established by the sixth section [of the *Tantravārttika*]: regarding Sundarī, the prohibition of *tulasī* must, by the force of this very [principle], appropriately refer to its leaves, and thus refers to other leaves. However, in the case of the lotus and so forth, because they are highly similar, it is appropriate to include *kahlāra* and other such flowers for the sake of completing the number. This is because Viṣṇu [is compared] to the lotus of his eye.

Because the *Liṅga Purāṇa* states that the material cause (*upādāna*) exists for the purpose of filling that [space], it follows from the mark (*liṅga*). This is because there is no distinction among the various types of *kadamba* clusters. (285)
With *campaka* flowers, *jātī* blossoms, *mallikā*, and *karavīraka*; or with blue lotuses, *bilva* leaves, or *kunda*, *kesara*, and *pāṭala* flowers. || 286 ||
In the phrase "with *jāti* flowers," the short vowel occurs by the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasorbahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.63).

*Jātī* is the *mālatī*. *Mallikā* is the *vicakila*. *Karavīra* is the *hayamāra*. *Kunda* is the *mādhyam*. *Kesara* is the *kāśmīram*. *Pāṭala* is white-red, resembling the flower of the sesame plant.
Maheśvara is not able to describe the fruit of the merit of one who offers other fragrant flowers, such as the ketakī, mādhavī, and so forth. || 287 ||
This is for the purpose of excluding fragrant substances such as camphor, opium, and foul-smelling flowers;
for even scentless items like *japa* beads are dear to the Goddess when they are red.
The suffix *a* is applied according to the rule *gandhasyedutpūtisusurabhibhyaḥ* to form the compound *sugandhi*. *Mādhavī* refers to the spring (*vāsantī*).
By the word "mukha" (face), the *punnāga*, *bakula*, and others are included;
the internal gradations among these should also be observed in the *Ādityapurāṇa* and the *Kālikāpurāṇa*. However, there is a specific distinction in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
A flower, leaf, or fruit should not be offered with its face turned downward;
that is declared to bring suffering. One should offer it exactly as it has grown.
Offering with the face turned downwards is not desired, except in the ritual of the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).

Furthermore, in rites such as the Lakṣapūjā, one should offer each flower individually; if the worship is performed by offering them all at once as a collective mass, that is not the offering of a hundred thousand flowers.
Thus [it is said]. For here, the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) compound, like the *dvandva* (copulative) compound which it supersedes, also signifies the sense of association (*sāhitya*).

This is because of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that in the statement "he performs eleven *prayāja* offerings," the number eleven is applied only to the offerings taken together, not individually. And therefore...

By means of "fragrant flowers" (*sugandhikusumaiḥ*), due to the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term from a class), there might arise the unintended implication that the jasmine (*mallikā*) and oleander (*karavīra*), as well as the *ketakī*, *mādhavī*, and others, function collectively through a *dvandva* (copulative) compound as the instrument;
therefore, the word "or" (*vā*) in the preceding two verses serves as an exception to that. And that [word "or"]...

The term is used twice or thrice to suggest that it should be applied to each individual flower; thus, even the instrumental case endings—which indicate independence as the instrument of action—are supported by the logic of the *vrīhi-yava* rule (the principle of optionality between rice and barley). Maheśvara is the fourth among the five *pretas*.
Since he too is not omniscient and thus lacks the capacity to speak,

it is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*) that human beings lack the capacity to know or speak [of such things], through the aforementioned method of multiplying by the sixfold group of qualities and so forth.
This is a suggestion that the fruit is limitless. || 287 ||
For this very reason, he says that she alone is to be discerned by the Omniscient One:
"The Goddess Lalitā knows the fruit born of the worship of her own circle;
how could others, such as Brahmā and the rest, who possess but meager intellect, know it? (288)

Thus it is said. Regarding the ignorance of Brahmā and the others, the epithet "of small intellect" (*svalpamedhasaḥ*) is a *hetugarbha* (causative) qualification by way of the poetic figure *parikara*. "Of small intellect" means those whose intellect—consisting of the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*)—is small. The compound ending *-as* is applied according to the rule: *nityamasic prajāmedhayoḥ*. Now, [an objection]:...

Considering that the practice of offering flowers is easier than the extremely difficult practice of realizing the fruits of the six zodiac signs, and given that it yields results that are likewise boundless,
no one would engage in the more arduous practice.
If you argue that because engagement is impossible, the lack of authority characterized by non-performance would follow,
you are mistaken;

for the performance of the most difficult practice is understood through injunctions containing words such as "until death" and "constantly," and thus [non-performance] would result from its failure to be carried out.

Because it is obligatory (*nitya*) due to the awareness of the transgression incurred [by its non-performance]; because it has been stated that there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform optional rites (*kāmyaprayoga*), such as the offering of flowers for longevity and the like, if an obligatory rite is not performed;

and because the fact that even an obligatory rite may be optional by the force of scriptural injunction—according to the logic of the *agnihotra* and similar rites—is not contradictory. Thus, it is not [the case that the two are incompatible].
The state of being sublated by the actual engagement [in practice].
Now, regarding the specific rule for the ritual application (*prayoga*), at the very commencement of the wheel-worship (*cakrārcana*), one should resolve:
"For the sake of attaining immeasurable merit, I shall worship the Goddess with such-and-such flowers."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and performed the *prasannapūjā*, having recited the introductory section (*pūrvabhāga*), and having performed the three types of ritual placement (*nyāsa*),

one should utter the *praṇava* (oṃ) and offer each individual flower at the end of each respective mantra— mantras consisting of the deity's name in the dative case ending with *namaḥ*, preceded by the two *tārās* (oṃ and hrīṃ), and in such forms as "hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīmātre namaḥ" and so forth.

Having cast them into the *bindu* exactly as they arose, one should complete the count using only flowers of the same kind, unmixed with those of a different species; then, having uttered the *praṇava* at the end, performed the three-fold placement (*nyāsa*), and recited the declaration of the fruit (*phalaśruti*), one should conclude the remainder of the worship. || 288 ||

Having thus explained, through this extensive composition, how [the mantra] bestows the three aims of life (*trivarga*), the author— desiring now to demonstrate in various ways its status as the bestower of the fourth aim of life (*puruṣārtha*) which follows in sequence—
first states, in two verses, the ritual application that bestows the fifth liberation known as *kaivalya*.
Whoever, on the full moon night of every month, should worship the Supreme Deity residing in the Wheel-King with these thousand names, || 289 ||

The term *pratīti* [is used] because, having set aside the expression *pratipaurṇamāsī* ("on each full moon"), the phrase *pratimāsam* ("month by month") is stated for the purpose of conveying the meaning "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*). The purpose of that [term] is also the recurrence of the word *pratimāsa* in its sense of "as long as one lives" later on. By means of any one of these aforementioned [terms].
With flowers. || 289 ||
He himself is the form of Lalitā, and Lalitā herself is that very form;
no distinction exists between the two, and one who creates such a distinction is a doer of evil.

He himself states that, while a single act of worship has as its fruit a state where only the *lalita* form is perceived, the fruit of repeated worship is naturally attained as being of the singular form of *lalita* alone;
this is expressed by reversing the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) in order to convey their mutual identity.

Regarding the phrase "that which has that form": he dispels the misconception that this statement is well-supported even by the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), despite the existence of a real difference, by saying "not of those two. This means "of the Goddess and the devotee"; the word "difference" is to be understood as "real. It is not so here.

The sense is that even the exclusion of a third similar entity is indeed identity itself. He punishes the one who insists that "let there be a real difference" by stating "the maker of difference. In devotion to the Goddess, the two possess a real difference characterized by mutual opposition.

The meaning is: one who employs an inference establishing difference, such as "because it is the locus of contradictory properties consisting of the states of being mortal and immortal, worshiper and worshipped, and so forth";
[this is refuted] by contradiction with the scripture that establishes non-duality (*advaita*).

He says "the evildoer" to indicate that [the opponent] is to be ridiculed like one who employs an inference of impurity based on the reason of being a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅgatva*). The meaning is that he is most wicked because he employs fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and because his position contradicts the scriptures. Furthermore, even the delusion of death does not occur for him; his vital breaths do not depart, but remain right here.
The sense is that this [objection] has been refuted by the scripture itself in the words "they dissolve. || 290 ||
Now, he states here a practice that is easily accessible even for this purpose, which yields the fruit of the fourfold liberation:
"For the devotee who worships the auspicious Goddess, situated in the center of the wheel, with the Thousand Names on the Great Ninth day, liberation stands within his grasp. (291)

Regarding the phrase "on the Mahānavamī": the terms "every month" and "night," which signify [the practice] for as long as one lives, are to be understood as recurring here. The final two days of the nine-night period (navarātra) are called Mahānavamī;
that [day] consists of the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti. In that [state], there is the worship of the Goddess by people of all castes.
There is no such authority. For instance, the Navarātra is of two kinds: the autumnal (śārada) and the vernal (vāsanta).

This is evident from the statement in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "In the autumn season, the Mahāpūjā is performed, which is the annual (vārṣikī) [rite]. In this passage, the word *vārṣikī* refers to that which occurs at the beginning of the year (*varṣa*).

It occurs during the rainy season (*bhava*), according to the explanation of the traditionalists; because the conjunction "and" (*ca*) naturally implies the combination of both [the rainy and autumn seasons]; because the interpretation that it occurs during the period called the four-month [retreat] (*cāturmāsa*)—which would entail that autumn is the rainy season—is strained; and because it is performed every year.

Furthermore, even in the commentary, the qualification would be redundant; and because the *Rudrayāmala* explicitly states that there are two types of Navarātra, saying, "One should worship Raktadantikā even during the Vāsanta Navarātra.
Also, in the third book of the *Devībhāgavata*, regarding Sudarśana, a practitioner of the Kāma-bīja:
The Goddess’s words:
"In the autumn season, my great worship must always be performed.
O King, arrange the Navarātra festival according to the prescribed rites."
O Great King, you must celebrate a great festival during the month of Caitra and the month of Āśvayuja,
specifically during Navarātra, which brings me great pleasure.
And so forth. In the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*, however, the Navarātra is also stated to occur in Āṣāḍha and Pauṣa.
Among those, for the autumnal Navarātra, the eighth and ninth days are the most excellent (*mahāpūrve*). This is stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
That lunar day which falls on the eighth of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is called Mahāṣṭamī; it is supreme and brings great delight to the gods.
Then, the ninth lunar day that follows is known as Mahānavamī;
that lunar day is dear to Śiva and is to be worshipped by all people.
Thus [he spoke]. Dhaumya also said:

"The eighth lunar day in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina which falls under the asterism Mūla should be known as the Great Eighth (Mahā-aṣṭamī); on that day the Goddess has made her abode."

In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa as well: "When the sun is situated in Virgo (Kanyā), that eighth lunar day which coincides with the Mūla asterism should be known as the Great Eighth (Mahā-aṣṭamī); it is not [the one] joined with the ninth day, O deluded ones."
The mention of the conjunction with Mūla is intended to indicate its possibility; therefore, even when joined with Pūrvāṣāḍhā,
it is indeed the Mahāṣṭamī itself—
"When conjoined with the Mūla asterism, it should be worshipped with great effort."
Even in the absence of the root [mantra], it should be performed if it is accompanied by water.

Thus it is stated. *Toya* refers to Pūrvāṣāḍhā. When this asterism is joined with either of these two [asterisms], there is also another designation: *Mahānavamī*. As it is said in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*:
"The eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja that is conjoined with Mūla..."
Or it may be joined with Pūrvāṣāḍhā, or even with two constellations.
"That [day] is called Mahānavamī, which is very difficult to obtain even in the three worlds.
Also, in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"When the sun has entered Virgo (Kanyā), [the day] joined with the eighth tithi of the bright fortnight..."
When conjoined with the Mūla lunar mansion, that day is known as Mahānavamī.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, by the teacher Viśvarūpa: "If the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja is conjoined with the Mūla asterism, even if it is pierced by the Sun [i.e., falls on a Sunday], it is remembered as Mahānavamī."

Thus it is said. Regarding this, some explain that the lunar day (tithi) conjoined with the eighth and the root (mūla) is the "Great Ninth" (mahānavamī), meaning that the ninth itself is the Great Ninth.
However, that view is to be rejected because it contradicts the statements in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa* and other texts.

Furthermore, this would result in the interpretation that the phrase *saptamīvedhabodhakaravividdhāpada* means "joined with a Sunday. Moreover, the mutual piercing (*viddha*) of these two [the seventh lunar day and the Sun] is also considered auspicious. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
The eighth lunar day joined with the ninth, and the ninth joined with the eighth—
this lunar day of Umā-Maheśvarī is like Ardhanārīśvara himself.
Thus it is said. Also in the work of King Bhoja:
"On the eighth day Rudra is to be worshipped; on the ninth day Śakti is adored.
The ninth is declared to be the day of Umā, and the eighth is the lunar day of Hara."
The lunar day (tithi) of Umā-Māheśvarī, occurring at the conjunction of two [days], is of great merit.
Regarding that very occasion, the reason for avoiding the piercing by the seventh (saptamī-vedha) when accepting an eighth (aṣṭamī) pierced by a ninth (navamī) is stated:
"Neither by day nor by night should it be struck by Viṣṭi, nor should the seventh be afflicted by even a fragment of a 'thorn' (śalya)."
Or rather, the ninth day, which arises as a remnant of the eighth, is most worthy of worship even by the wise.

Thus, [the eighth day] should not be performed if it is afflicted by a *viṣṭi* yoga, the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*), or even a fraction of the *śalya* yoga. If the ninth day occurs during the remainder of the eighth, it is worthy of worship even for the gods; the meaning is that it does not become a deficient day (*avamī*). This same method applies to the determination of the eighth and ninth days of the spring Navarātra as well. (From the *Navarātrapradīpa*)
Because it is so stated; for even the teacher Viśvarūpa, having introduced the two Navarātras, says:

"In a sacred field of Śiva, there is a great festival on the conjunction of the eighth and ninth [tithis], due to the state of essential identity (sāmarasya) of Śiva and Śakti, during both fortnights."

This is because of the statement: "The autumnal and the vernal [Navarātra]—in both of these two periods," which is the meaning of that [text]. Furthermore, the worship of the Goddess on the eighth day is mentioned in the Devīpurāṇa:
"The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, when the eighth day is conjoined with the Mūla asterism..."
That is Mahānavamī; on that day, one should worship the Mother of the World.
Thus it is said; and regarding the ninth day, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"On the ninth day, endowed with Śrī and well-worshipped by all the gods, she slew the wicked Mahiṣa, who was incapable of being slain by the gods and others."
Having received the empowerment, O Giver of Boons, during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja,
therefore that Caṇḍikā should be worshipped there on the ninth day by the wise.
Since the goddess Sarasvatī has attained greatness here,
for this reason this ninth [tithi] is always called "Mahatī" (the Great) by the wise.
Thus [it is said]. And this worship is to be performed specifically at midnight.
Having worshipped the Goddess, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, in the month of Āśvina at the end of the rains, those who do so at midnight on the eighth lunar days—

Thus it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa. Also in the Śaktirahasya: "When the sun is situated in Virgo, one should worship the Goddess on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, fasting and at midnight with extensive displays of great opulence."
Thus it is said. And by the teacher Viśvarūpa as well:
"Having reached the eighth night, Pārvatī accepts worship;
the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī, the destroyer of sins, is indeed worshipped at midnight."
"Therefore, with every effort, one should worship her at night on the eighth day.
As for that which is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"There, on the eighth day, is Bhadrakālī, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice."
She appeared, most terrible, together with ten million yoginīs.

"For this reason, she should be worshipped by men on that day"—in this statement, the word "day" (ahar) refers to a full day and night (ahorātra). On the strength of this, the claim that worship must occur on the eighth day during the daytime alone is the mere prattle of the blind. On the ninth day, however, [worship] occurs only during the day.
They also say that one should worship [her]. Furthermore, although these two types of worship arise individually, they produce their fruit only when they are mutually dependent.
And on the eighth and the ninth [lunar days], [one should worship] Ambikā, the Mother of the World.
Having performed worship in the month of Āśvina, a man becomes free from sorrow.

This is because the statement from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa* indicates a single performance (*ekaprayogatā*), and also because of the previously cited statement, "at the conjunction of the eighth and ninth [lunar days]. For this very reason, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this is a distinct ritual act from the *Navarātra*.
Furthermore, all castes (*sarvajātīya*) have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform this worship.
This has been stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara* at the very commencement of the ritual:
"The Goddess is to be worshipped by people in every temple,
in every city, in every house, in every village, and in every forest by those devoted to Śakti."
O tiger among the Kurus, listen to this procedure [performed] by bathed, joyful, and delighted Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, devoted Mlecchas, and other men on earth, as well as by women.
And so forth. [One may worship] with those devoted to Śakti and dedicated to Caṇḍī, such as Mlecchas, Śabaras, Kirātas, Pulindas, and others; or by others born of anuloma or pratiloma unions.
However, one should worship only while conforming to the traditional practices of one's own lineage. As it is said in the Vrata-khaṇḍa:
Whichever goddess is established according to the tradition of one's own family lineage,
she should be worshipped by that person with offerings, perfumes, and unguents.
And one should worship the Kula-mother with various kinds of food offerings.
Thus [it is said]. Now, even though the Mahānavamī has been thus determined, since that word refers to time, what specific time is denoted by the term "Mahānavamī" in the present injunction?
For, according to the reasoning stated, both the eighth and ninth days possess the status of Mahānavamī. Even when—

This term "Mahānavamī" is, like the words *darśapūrṇamāsa* or *navarātra*, primarily denotative of a ritual action (*karmapara*). Even though the two types of worship on the eighth and ninth days constitute a single ritual, since that ritual is twofold—distinguished as the spring and autumn varieties—which of these two rituals is intended to be adopted in the present context? It is not [the spring one].
