If it is argued that both [terms] should be included because the possibility of a word of specific distinction (*vaidha*) referring to multiple indefinite objects within a single substratum has already been refuted,
we reply: if the term *mahānavamī* refers to the ritual action (*karman*).

For there is no multiplicity of referents here, as in the case of the single *agnihotra* sacrifice where repetition occurs due to the distinction between morning and evening; rather, by accepting mere repetition according to the distinction between spring and autumn, [the injunction] does not involve multiple objects. However, if the reference is to time, then all four times are included within this injunction.

For, in the case of a single substratum, it is only that which has an indefinite single meaning that is excluded, and not that which has a definite multiple meaning; thus there is no fault. Otherwise, how could a single mantra be employed for multiple purposes? Nor is it the case that only a word occurring within an injunction may have multiple meanings.

There is no established rule that [a term] cannot have multiple meanings, for even in the injunctive sentence "One should not eat *kalañja*," we observe various explanations of the word *kalañja*: as referring to entrails,
as referring to hemp (*bhaṅgā*), and as referring to a digestive powder for cleansing the throat.

Therefore, as long as one lives, during these four days, [the breath] moves to the point of the *bindu* within the center of the wheel; for any devotee who, according to their own lineage, worships the venerable Goddess Tripurasundarī at midnight with the Thousand Names, for him—

The fourfold liberation is indeed situated within the hand; the meaning is that it is extremely easy to attain. In this regard, if one worships for a single day, there is merely *sālokya* (residing in the same world); if for two days, there is also *sārūpya* (having the same form); if for three days, there is also *sāmīpya* (proximity);
and if for all four days, there is *sāyujya* (union).

The gradation [of results], however, is obtained through logic alone; thus, it has not been explained in detail. Alternatively, although the ritual performed during the pair of lunar days—the eighth and ninth—is one and the same, the fourfold nature of liberation should be applied according to the fourfold nature of the Navarātra; this is the direction [for further inquiry]. || 291 ||

Having thus described the ritual applications that result exclusively in worldly enjoyment and those that result exclusively in liberation, he now describes the application that results in both enjoyment and isolation (kaivalya):
"But he who worships with the Thousand Names on a Friday..."
Listen to the fruit of the merit of that [person] who [worships] the Great Goddess in the Cakrarāja. || 292 ||
"By him who [recites] the names"—this consists of three words. "With a thousand names" (*nāmnāṃ sahasreṇa*) is a single compound.

*Nāma* is either an indeclinable used in the sense of "renown" or "fame," or it can easily be explained as referring to the "thousand-word [text]" (*sahasrapada*) itself, given the context of the section. [This should be done] on Fridays—that is, on every Friday.
Because it concludes in exactly that same way through the persistence of words whose meaning extends as long as life lasts. || 292 ||
Having attained all desires here on earth and being endowed with every form of good fortune,
he shall enjoy all desired pleasures, accompanied by sons, grandsons, and other kin.
"Here" means in this very world of mortals (*bhūrloka*). By this, it is indicated that the merit produced by this [act] is extremely intense;

for according to the scriptural statement, "One experiences the fruit of extremely intense merits and sins right here. He is perfectly endowed with all forms of good fortune, such as progeny, prosperity, health, learning, strength, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "sons, grandsons, and so forth," there is the inclusion of nephews, kinsmen, servants, and trusted associates.

Although these are already established by the term "all prosperity" (*sarvasaubhāgya*), their separate mention is for the purpose of indicating that they act as co-agents (*sāhityena kartṛtva*) with respect to the act of enjoyment. The meaning is: "having enjoyed pleasures together with sons and the others."
Before the goddess Śrī Lalitā, one attains that most difficult-to-attain state of union (sāyujya), which is sought even by Śiva and others; of this there is no doubt. || 294 ||
"Before the fall of the body," means after departing by the path of the gods (*devayāna-mārga*); this is the ellipsis.

The qualification "extremely difficult to attain" (*sāyujyātidurlabhatva*) indicates its nature as absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). The phrase "to be prayed for by Śiva and others" is intended to suggest that this is liberation together with Brahmā (*sāyujya-mukti*). Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
When the time for reabsorption arrives, all those perfected souls, at the end of the Supreme, enter the supreme state together with Brahmā.

Thus [it is said]. Here, the word "para" (beyond) in the phrase "of the other" (*parasya*) refers to the lifespan of Brahmā. That which is considered the full lifespan of Brahmā—consisting of one hundred years—is called *para*; half of that is designated as *parārdha*.
Because of this statement,

it is also appropriate to explain the word *anta* in the present context as "the end of the subsequent [element]," since there is no fault in a delay toward liberation for that long in a ritual application (*prayoga*) that yields both the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Because enjoyment in the next world is necessarily preceded by enjoyment in this world,
for that very reason the term "enjoyments" (*bhogān*) should also be explained as referring to both types of enjoyment— those of this world and those of the next.
It is only with respect to these two kinds of enjoyment that there is association with sons and others, and not even with liberation (*mokṣa*).
It should be understood that this is impossible because [the state] consists in abiding solely in one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*).

Now, since there is nothing superior to such a fruit, he describes another practice to be accomplished in fewer days than the previous one, with respect to this very fruit: [The text continues: "idānīmīdṛśaphalāpekṣayādhikasyābhāvādasminneva phale pūrvasmādalpadinasādhyaṃ prayogāntaramāha—" (Now, since there is nothing superior to such a fruit, he describes another practice to be accomplished in fewer days than the previous one, with respect to this very fruit—).
Whoever, having worshipped a thousand Brāhmaṇas with these thousand names, should devotedly feed them with milk-rice, cakes, and foods of the six flavors; || 295 ||

"Who [performs] a thousand," etc.—by these two verses. Here, there is the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) and so forth. Thus, by means of the injunctions obtained through the *codaka* (the general rule), such as "the man who performs this even once during his lifetime with devotion," he has rendered [the rite] free from further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣīkṛta*). [This applies to] the Brāhmaṇas.

This applies only to those who possess knowledge and not to others; for it is established as such by the suffix *aṇ* in the word *brahma* in the sense of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that. *Pāyasa* is rice-milk food consisting mostly of milk with very few grains of rice; it is supreme food (*paramānna*). *Apūpa*s are various kinds of flour-based preparations, such as *pūrikā*s and others.

By those [substances] such as sugar and nimba, which are described in detail in culinary treatises like the *Bhojanakutūhala* and others as possessing the six flavors (*ṣaḍrasa*), and by other items mixed with them;
for even bitter things such as the *kāravella* fruit are to be eaten, it is said "with the six flavors. || 295 ||
Lalitā is pleased with him and bestows her own sovereignty upon him;
"her own sovereignty" means absolute non-difference, which is to say, liberation (*kaivalya*). And this [sovereignty] is devoid of the activity of governing the world.
This was stated in accordance with the *adhikaraṇa* of the followers of the Upaniṣads, on account of the context and because [the Lord] is not proximate [to the world].

In reality, however, the word "sovereignty" (*sāmrājya*) conventionally denotes the very activity of governing the universe, and it is precisely the granting of that which is intended here; for there is no abandonment of what is heard in scripture nor the assumption of what is not heard. Therefore...

Thus, due to this prior application, there is also a preponderance of fruit. Indeed, such a fruit alone is appropriate from the mass of blessings of a thousand Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vidyās.
And this being so, even when many devotees perform such a practice simultaneously, [the result is the same].

One should not fear that the defect mentioned in that section— that because all [deities] must possess independence regarding the activity of the world at one and the same time, the world would necessarily perish due to mutual disagreement—
would apply here; for the Lord’s activity proceeds solely in accordance with the karma of the living beings being created.
This is because they themselves have accepted this; otherwise, the unavoidable consequence of partiality and cruelty would follow.
Accordingly, the Brahma-sūtra states: "Partiality and cruelty do not [apply to God], because He is dependent [on other factors];
for thus [the scriptures] show. Consequently, the activity arising in accordance with karma belongs to many.
Even for those endowed with minds, there would arise only a single form [of cognition], and thus no disagreement;

nor is there a loss of independence for those acting in accordance with one another's wills, because the independence consisting in the capacity for activity according to one's own will remains unimpeded in all of them. For this very reason...

In the *Vāsiṣṭharāmāyaṇa*, within the narrative of Kundadanta, it is consistent with the description that the eight brothers of Mathurā simultaneously obtained sovereignty over the single earth consisting of the seven continents through a boon granted by their mother.

Because the factual concurrence of wills that arises in accordance with the karma of the beings being created does not obstruct that [creation], and because the Lord’s sovereignty over the world is natural and not produced by karma like the status of Śakra and others, how could the nature of one thing affect another?
This must be stated: there is no contradiction in accepting that while [the power] of Īśvara is innate, for others it is produced by karma;
for such is observed in the case of fruits such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world). By this, [the claim that] Īśvara is eternally established...

The objection that the agency over the operations of the world is impossible for those who worship the Tantra— because the scriptures declare that the creation of the world and so forth belong to [the Lord] by His very nature, and because those worshippers are not present [at the time of such acts]— is refuted; for the qualification of the worshippers is adventitious.
In the section concerning the description of the eternally established authority, because it is both relevant and proximate [to the subject], it is heard [in scripture]:
"The meditators attain sovereignty; they attain self-rule.
All the gods bring tribute to him. For them, there is freedom of movement in all worlds."

In such scriptural passages as "He becomes," etc., this does not refer to a limited sovereignty, because there is no evidence for such a restriction. Nor should it be argued that the subsequent scripture, "He attains the Lordship of the Mind" (*manasaspati*),
serves as the proof for the remaining possibility that the Lord is the object to be attained.

Since the attainment of the unique attributes of the Lord in the form of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) necessarily entails the attainment of the substratum itself through non-difference, this scriptural passage also favors our position.
Likewise, there are such passages as: "He becomes the lord of speech, the lord of sight, the lord of hearing, and the lord of cognition."
All the Śrutis are indeed favorable to this very point, not merely those of the Upaniṣads;

for it is explicitly stated in the Atharvaṇa Śaunaka recension that the worshipper is the ordainer of the creation and so forth of the entire universe: "He is the ordainer of everything in the whole world."

"The sustainer and the destroyer attains the state of universal form. Now, is such a preeminent worshipper distinct from the Lord, or not? Even in your own system, is one who has attained the fourth liberation called *sāyujya* and desires to reach the fifth liberation called *kaivalya* distinct [from the Lord], or not? No.
Furthermore, it should not be argued that in our view there is a distinction based on the existence or non-existence of that [jagadvyāpāra],
because even in our view, despite the presence of jagadvyāpāra, a distinction is possible based on the possession or lack of a mind (samanaskatva and amanaskatva). Not so.

It should be stated that in the first half-verse of the Atharvaṇa mantra cited, when the *parisrut* offering has been purified, the mention of "being free from mental distress" (*vaimanaska*) refers to the practitioner whose attachment has contracted and whose mental agitation has dissolved. By the statement "when attachment and contraction have dissolved," [the absence of] loathing, doubt, and fear [is indicated].

Because the eight fetters (pāśas) mentioned in the *Kulārṇava*, beginning with "shame" (*lajjā*) and so forth—which consist of specific modifications of the mental state (*cittavṛtti*)—are characterized by their non-arising [in the liberated state], that statement is therefore figurative (*gauṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the scripture cited by them in the sūtra, "And because of the similarity of the mere experience of enjoyment," it is as follows: [they cite] this...
"All beings protect one who knows this; likewise, all beings protect that deity.

He wins union with and residence in the same world as that deity"—this statement, though intent on describing a distinction, establishes the very point already stated. Furthermore, is qualification a means to happiness or not?

In the latter case, there would be no possibility of engaging in those rituals that serve as the means for all people’s entitlement to heaven and other such goals. In the former case, since the activity of the world (jagadvyāpāra) would likewise not differ in being an entitlement,
[the result] would be identical merely by virtue of the experience consisting of the direct perception of bliss.

Consider this further: since sovereignty without restriction is established for the worshiper by virtue of the [Vedic] indicative mark (*liṅga*), how can that very reason be used to prove its absence? Nor should it be argued: "How could a single office serve the benefit of many simultaneously? For in the *sattra* sacrifice, it is indeed one person alone [who performs it].

For it is observed that an addition (prakṣepa) serves the benefit of many sacrificers, and that a single world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) simultaneously serves the benefit of many worshippers. Nor should it be argued that this results in the use of the genitive case; for that is acceptable, and it is indeed logical.

This is because its logical establishment is due to its nature as a higher stage succeeding those [others], such that liberation—ranging from *sālokya* up to *sāyujya*—possesses an increasing excellence in each subsequent state, and because it occurs immediately prior to *kaivalya*. If it is asked, "What is the status of the Tantric convention that there are five kinds of liberation? [the answer is that] it is found in the *Sūta-saṃhitā* and other texts.

If it is argued that the status of conventional expressions such as "liberation is to be known as fourfold" applies to both *kaivalya* and *sāyujya* in your own system because you do not intend to express any internal distinction between them, then the same would apply to the distinction between the limited (*sāvagraha*) and the unlimited (*niravagraha*).

The argument that "this is not intended to be expressed" applies equally [to our position]. Therefore, it is established that those who practice meditation (*upāsaka*) possess the agency of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. For this very reason, the author of the *Vārttika* stated in the *Śaiva Tantra* under the aphorism "In the body, the instruments, and the external, as in the state of the mind": [text follows].
Thus, the power of that whose nature is self-bliss, characterized by absolute freedom (svātantrya),
clearly becomes the cause for the manifestation of objects according to one's will.

Thus [it is said]. It is the same in the sūtra "Stability and Dissolution" (sthitilayau). Also in the sūtra "The universe is the accumulation of one's own powers" (svaśaktipracayo viśvam): "All this world is His powers, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power"—according to the direction of the Āgamas, the universe is thus the accumulation of one's own powers.

Intending all this—namely that for Śiva, for one equal to him, and likewise for this supreme yogin, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain—it is said: "For him, no object exists in the three worlds that is hard to attain. (296)

Regarding the phrase "not for him": even for one who is habituated to the supreme meditation taught in the Upaniṣads, and who enjoys various high and low fruits— such as the statement that "by his mere volition, his ancestors arise"— there is still one thing that is difficult to obtain.

The meaning is that the universal sovereignty desired by the Vedāntins certainly remains [as an object of aspiration], yet even that is easily attained by this [practitioner]. Precisely because it is an extreme secret, the procedure for this has not been specified in this section; rather, after describing the ritual rules (*dharmān*) in the section on the "Feeding of Three Hundred," they are [applied] here.

An explicit extension (atideśa) has been made [of these rules]. This is stated in that very section of the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* regarding the feeding of a thousand [deities] with secret names: "In this very manner, one should first perform the daily offering (*nityābali*) and afterwards the feeding of the Brahmins."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: just as the sequence of precedence and succession was previously stated for the two rites known as the daily offering (*nityābali*) and the feeding of three hundred, exactly the same applies to the daily offering and the feeding of one thousand.
Herein, this is considered: for indeed, it is recorded thus in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:

Having first prescribed the rite consisting of feeding sixteen Brahmins— stating that "one should feed Brahmins in the form of the Great Sixteen"— and having established its procedure with the words "having anointed their limbs with fragrant oil, bathed them with lukewarm water," and so forth, [the text continues] thus:

By the statement, "One should first perform the *nityābali* and then the feeding of Brahmins," the name of this rite is shown to be *nityābali*; subsequently, one should worship the Brahmins in order with three hundred names— this is another distinct rite known as the *triśatabhojana*.

Having performed that, one should thereafter offer an oil massage and so forth with devotion if one has the means; and having thus performed various subsidiary rites, high and low, according to the passage beginning "the man who performs this even once during his lifetime with devotion": [The result is as follows:]... [omitted] ...he attains the supreme state. Thus, the man who performs this with devotion even once in the course of his life—[attains the fruit].
His very birth is fruitful; liberation rests in his hand.

Thus, it has been concluded by way of an injunction regarding the result. In this regard, there is a doubt: are the daily offering (*nityābali*) and the eating of three hundred [mouthfuls] equally primary, or is the eating of the subsequent three hundred [mouthfuls] a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the daily offering? If they are equally primary, then in the archetype (*prakṛti*)...

From words such as "ādi" (and so forth), which denote merely a connection with time or purpose, there is no extended application (*atideśa*)— just as the *āgneya* sacrifice is not extended to the modifications of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, nor is the three-hundred-meal rite extended to the thousand-meal rite, nor the obligatory *nitya* offering to the modifications of the *agnīṣomīya*. However, when there is a relationship of subsidiary and principal (*aṅga-aṅgin*), extended application does occur.

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since no indicator of subsidiarity (*aṅgatā*)—such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth—is observed, it must be asserted that both [the feeding of Brahmins and the offering] possess equal primary status (*samaprādhānya*). Nor can it be argued: "One should perform the daily offering (*nityābali*) first, and the feeding of Brahmins at the beginning."

It should not be argued that the relationship of primary and subsidiary (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is established here because of the prescription of sequence— namely, "after [the performance] with three hundred names"— just as in the case of the rule "having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava";
for the Vājapeya, being possessed of a fruit, is the primary rite, and [the subsidiary status applies only to what is recited within its context].

Even though it is possible for the Bṛhaspatisava to be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice], in the present case, since neither of the two is connected with a specific fruit and there is no certainty regarding the primary rite (*prakaraṇin*), there is an absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) for determining the relationship of principal and subsidiary; therefore, by the logic of the Viśvajit sacrifice...

Since the assumption of a result is equal for both [the *bhakti* and *jñāna* paths] due to the specific nature of their mutual expectancy, it is established that their connection is for the purpose of time (*kāla*), just as in the case of the injunction: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma. Nor is this so by the sentence: "He who performs [it] with devotion..."

It must be stated that once it is understood— through the rule of immediate succession (*ānantarya*)— that the rite possesses fruit by means of the "three-hundred-meal" [offering], then the subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) of the *nāmana* and *homa* offerings is established according to the maxim of "the fruitful and the fruitless" (*phalavad-aphala-nyāya*), as in the case of the *nitya* [obligatory] *abalih*. For in that context,
in the very originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*)— "One desiring a village should offer the *vaiśvadevī sāṃgrahiṇī*"— [it is so established].

Although the status of the *āmāhoma* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice is established by hearing the mention of its fruit, there is nevertheless a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through a single-sentence unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*), because of the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the fruit mentioned in a separate sentence within the context of the primary rite.
Because the connection with the fruit is established for both through their mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*),
and because in the phrase "he who performs [it]," both can be referred to by that very word, since immediate sequence is weaker than mutual expectancy.
Furthermore, because speech necessarily proceeds in a sequential order, it has been stated: "There is no injunction for immediate succession.

Moreover, regarding the subsidiary elements prescribed in the context of the daily offerings (*nitya-bali*), which range from the anointing with fragrant oil to the presentation of milk-rice and fruit—

Since the injunction regarding the fixed rule (*vyavasthā-vidhi*) heard in the section on the "Feeding of Three Hundred" (*triśatabhojana-prakaraṇa*)— which is based on censure and intent toward worldly prosperity— is dependent upon another statement, for the sake of its fulfillment, one must assume a relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) between these two, whereby the properties of the permanent offering (*nitya-balidharma*) [are extended].

An extended application (*atideśa*) must be stated regarding the meal of three hundred [deities]. By that, the sublation (*bādha*) of the original names such as Kāmeśvarī and others by the modified names such as Kakārārūpā and others—according to the principle of the arrow (*śaranaya*)—is also logically consistent. For the subordinate (*aṅga*) is [subordinate] with respect to the principal (*pradhāna*).

Primordiality (*prakṛtitva*) is impossible in the case of *bhāvanā*, for after the connection with the object to be produced (*bhāvya*), there follows the connection with the cause; subsequently, when there is an expectancy regarding the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*), the connection of the ritual details (*dharma*) occurs.

Thus, the determination of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is posterior to the connection with the object to be produced, and even later than that comes the extension (*atideśa*). [Therefore, it is] an auxiliary.
The established position is that this is according to the maxim "that which is constant is extended [to others]. Consequently,

in the case of the mental disposition (*bhāvanā*) whose instrument (*karaṇa*) is the performance of three hundred feedings, after the connection between the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) and the instrument has occurred, at the very moment of the third instant when there is an expectancy for the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*), one who asserts the status of the *nityābali* as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) [must account for this].

The expectancy for what is to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) must be stated. In the subsequent moment, once the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva*) between the two has been established by means of *prakaraṇa*—characterized by mutual expectancy—the expectancy of the cultivation of the three hundred meals is satisfied;
therefore, how [could there be an expectancy] even after that for the *nityābalī* offerings, which are subordinate members (*aṅga*)?

The extension [of details] is established in relation to the primary [act]. For there is no cognition of the relationship between subsidiary and principal through another sentence— such as occurs in the case of the Paurṇamāsī and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, which are each complete with their own three constituent parts within their respective sentences— because such a sentence is not observed.
However, because the relationship of principal and subordinate (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is possible through the aforementioned method by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa),

it should not be argued that the status of being a subordinate is established for the feeding of a thousand in the modification (vikṛti) of the feeding of three hundred solely on the basis of the indicative mark (liṅga) of transference (atideśa).

Because a determination based merely on the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not definitive; for instance, in the case of the phrase "in the *sahasrabhojana*," the locative case indicates that it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*)— just as in the rule "one should offer the *jayā* oblations there"— and thus, even though the *nityabali* is a primary rite elsewhere, its status as a subordinate element is restricted solely with respect to that [specific occasion].
Furthermore, the extended application (*atideśa*) is established even by way of making something known, as is seen in the case of the *Bṛhaspatisava* sacrifice.

However, this is the distinction: in that case, there is a difference due to a separate context (*prakaraṇāntara*), whereas here, within the very context of the *Triśatī*, it occurs by means of a reference to what is situated at a distance.

Because the *nityābali* is enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*)—just as the twelve *upasads* are—there is no distinction [between it and the main rite] according to the maxim "But in proximity, there is no division. Therefore, the *nityābali* and the three hundred feedings have equal primary status (*samaprādhānya*). However, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that [the relationship between] the sentence enjoining the fruit and the sentence regarding the *nityābali*...

The connection with both [the *triśata* and the *bhojana*] should be stated based on mere mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*). However, because of the sentence regarding the *triśata-bhojana*, and due to immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) as well as mutual expectancy, there is an immediate connection with that very [sentence]; thus, by the principle of "the fruitful over the fruitless" (*phalavad-aphala-nyāya*), it serves as an auxiliary to the primary act (*pradhāna*) precisely through its constant efficacy.

Since the requirement for a further object of meditation (*bhāvya*) is satisfied, there is no syntactic connection with the sentence concerning the fruit; thus, the determination of the *prakaraṇa* (context) remains unassailable. And so, even the mention of the employment of other names such as Kāmeśvarī and so forth within the *Nāmatriśatī-prakaraṇa* is not inconsistent.

[The objection] is refuted; nor is it necessary for a weak woman to be the primary agent (*prakṛti*) even for the feeding of three hundred [brahmins]. This is because, in the statement "one should give oil-massage and so forth with devotion if one has the means," only the oil-massage and such are enjoined as constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the feeding of three hundred.

However, since sentences such as "those who have been anointed with oil" (*abhyaktānāṃ dhṛtatailena*) belong to a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), they are injunctions (*vidhāyaka*) specifically as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to the *Nityābalī*; therefore, it must be accepted that these sentences merely prescribe a regulation (*vyavasthā*) by way of restating (*anuvāda*) that [the *Nityābalī*] for the purpose of [determining] its distribution (*vibhava*).
Since there is no basis for the application [of the rule] regarding the oil-massage and other rites for three hundred Brahmins— because there is no source for its attainment—
and since the established rule (*vyavasthā*) is proven to be necessarily dependent on the preceding statement (*purovāda*), there can be no attainment from a general injunction (*codaka*),
as the relationship between archetype and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*) is not yet established. If one were to attempt to prove it by force of this very [argument], [it would be futile].

Otherwise, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor does this result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in the *vibhava* statement, such that one part would be an injunction for massage and the other an injunction for the regulation [of time] by way of restating it; for according to the maxim that "the potency (*śakti*) is a cooperative factor when verbal roots express their meaning," the capacity [to convey the injunction] exists only when the *vibhava* is present.

Because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding that portion [of the agent] as something already established by logic; and because even in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the ritual experts (*tāntrika*) accept the connection with "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*) as a means of regulating the gradation of results;

furthermore, even if the relationship between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) is accepted, we do not claim that there is a status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*) based on the context (*prākaraṇika*).

Otherwise, a contradiction would arise according to the manner stated above. However, there is no such fault, because the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is enjoined by the very sentence [beginning with] "āditaḥ paścāt," just as in the case of the *vaimṛdha* and the *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Therefore, the consumption of three hundred [grains] by one who is constantly strong is indeed merely an auxiliary. Nor is this so in the case of the sentence of extended application (*atideśa*).

Since the extension (*atideśa*) of all auxiliary parts is already established by the phrase "in this very same manner" (*evameva*), the statement "one should first perform the *nityābali*" would otherwise be redundant. This [reiteration] serves to dispel the misconception that the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) refers only to the proximate auxiliary parts that provide direct assistance (*sannipatyopakāraka*), such as the oil massage (*tailābhyaṅga*).
This is the general direction [of the argument], as it is for the purpose of explaining that.

Herein is the procedure for the performance (*prayoga-vidhi*): having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) and having proclaimed the place and time, [one should perform the rite] for so many days for the sake of pleasing the illustrious Mahātrisurasundarī.

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall worship and feed one thousand Brāhmaṇas with the thousand secret names (rahasyasahasranāma), and as a preliminary rite for that, I shall perform the daily offering (nityabali)," he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) to be recited and invite sixteen Brāhmaṇas. When they have arrived—
Having washed their feet, anointed them with fragrant oil, bathed them with warm water,
and seated them upon thrones, and having applied the *tilaka* marks,
[he should worship] with the two *tārā*s (OM ĀḤ) followed by "Namaḥ" and ending with "Kāmeśvarī."

Having invoked one Tithinityā in each Brāhmaṇa with each of the sixteen mantras— beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Tripurasundarī, using their names in the dative case— one should worship them according to the method of sequential performance (padārthānusamaya) by means of the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).

Just as in the first *brāhmaṇa* [it says]: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Kāmeśvarī; I invoke, establish, worship, and gratify the daily deity Kāmeśvarī on this lunar day; obeisance!"—having thus cast unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon the head—in the second *brāhmaṇa*, [it says]: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, to Bhagamālinī..."
"Oṃ, salutation! I invoke, establish, worship, and gratify Bhagamālinī, the deity of the second lunar day;
salutation!"—having thus offered unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should likewise [invoke] Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī for the third through the sixteenth days respectively.
Having invoked Vajreśvarī, Śivadūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā, Jvālāmālinī, Citrā, and Tripurasundarī,
situated either facing east or facing north, one should [proceed] again with this very [mantra].
Having prepared the seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the bath according to the sequence of ritual activity,
and having offered visible ornaments for the face, he should satisfy [the deity] with refined words accompanied by reasons, and then offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Having fed [the guests] with special foods such as soups, cakes, sugar, clarified butter, milk-rice, fruits, and so forth,

one should perform the offering of betel, the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), prostrations, prayers, and the dismissal. In all ritual services, beginning from the seat and so on, one should first utter the *dvitāra* (the two-syllable mantra), then the respective mantras for each item, and finally [the concluding mantra].

The ritual formulas for the performance should be inferred as follows: the respective names [of the deities] ending in the dative case with the suffix *-namaḥ*, followed by "I offer the seat, *namaḥ*. In this context, the application of oil massage (*tailābhyaṅga*) and other such rites are essential. Thus concludes the daily offering (*nityābali*).
Then, on the second, third, or subsequent day, one should likewise feed a thousand Brahmins. The mantras are: *hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīmātre namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīmahārājñyai namaḥ*, and so forth.

"I invoke Śrīmātā"—this and similar phrases constitute the remainder of the mantra for invocation (*āvāhana*). "I offer a seat; obeisance" (*āsanaṃ samarpayāmi namaḥ*) and so forth are the remaining mantras for the seat and other offerings, according to their respective characteristics (*yathāliṅga*).
Anointing with oil (*tailābhyaṅga*) and the like are mandatory for those possessed of wealth, but for others, they are optional.

The distinction is that it should be performed "according to one's ability. At the commencement of the worship, the recitation and so forth of the first part, and at its conclusion, the recitation of the second part, are to be done exactly as before; however, the *padārthānusamaya* (sequential performance of constituent elements) may also be carried out by reciting one hundred [verses] or fifty [verses] at a time, or by some other method.

For the sake of convenience, having offered the ritual services (upacāras) ending with libation (tarpaṇa) or ending with flowers (puṣpa) according to the order of practice, it is also appropriate to offer incense and lamps by the thousands.
This is likewise the case when there is an abundance of four-pot-sherd sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) dedicated to Varuṇa, occasioned by the acceptance of a horse.
Because of the observation [of this]. However, if one obtains a thousand Brāhmaṇas simultaneously, one should fulfill the number by feeding them over many days as soon as they are obtained;
for there is no contradiction in the fact that a number resides in distinct individuals.

Since this has been established by us in the commentary on the *Sahasrabhojana-khaṇḍa*, one should personally observe the restrictive vows until its completion. As for that which is recorded in the *Prakṛti*:
"Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon, in due order..."
Every day, twenty Brahmins should be fed.
O Brahmins, thirty, sixty, one hundred, or three hundred guests should be fed, respectively, in ten, five, three, or even a single day.
Thus it is said. In that regard, even if three hundred Brahmins are obtained simultaneously, the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*) is to feed only twenty of them every day.
On the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*), because each single syllable has the nature of a single lunar-day goddess (*tithinityā*), [one should perform] the *ghaṭī* for each single syllable...

Since each of those twenty names is associated with its respective deity, it is appropriate to worship that specific deity on its corresponding lunar day (*tithi*). If one lacks the leisure for the full fifteen days, there are other alternative methods (*anukalpa*). And thus:

Since there is no evidence that even a few [names] in the *Sahasranāma* correspond to the respective deities of the lunar days (*tithi*) and *nityās* due to the absence of the sequence of syllables, and since the identity of the lunar day, the syllable, and the deity— which is the operative factor in the primary natural ritual— is absent in the modified form (*vikṛti*), that which is prompted by it [the number of names] is established by fifteen alone.

There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the rule consisting in the completion of the ritual actions over the course of days. For this very reason, in the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), since there is an absence of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which is the motivator for the use of potsherds (*kapāla*), there is no extension of the potsherds.
Therefore, in this case, provided it is possible, because the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) cannot tolerate delay, [the rites] must be performed on a single day alone.

A meal for a thousand is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*). Regarding the secondary rules (*anukalpa*), since the number [of guests] is already established by the phrase "ten or five" in the case of ordinary people, the repeated mention of "thirty or sixty" is intended to exclude numbers both lower and higher; therefore, the number must be equal every day.

Since the portion stating "the Brahmins are to be fed" is understood as something intended to be enjoined, it lacks any independent purpose; thus, once the extension [of the rule] is established, the three-day option is set aside because it is impossible in the Sādyaska and Sārasvata sacrifices, just as the piling of the fire-altar is set aside.

However, even if one hundred Brahmins cannot be obtained, it should be inferred by those who have mastered the preceding and succeeding Tantras that alternative periods of twenty days and so forth— though not explicitly mentioned in the *Prākṛta* [Tantra]— are nonetheless available by virtue of logic, provided they do not contradict the stated rules. Regarding this:

However, it has been determined by us in the commentary on that very [work] that the procedure for the "Feeding of a Thousand" (*sahasrabhojana*) as stated in the *Baudhāyana-sūtra* is to be combined [with the present rite]. || 296 ||

Thus, having completed the discernment of its status as the supreme secret by demonstrating, through thirty-five verses, how it bestows the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha), [the author] now explains the meaning of that which was stated: "This particular hymn to the Śrī Devī, which follows in sequence, brings about delight. He does so as follows:
He who, free from desire, recites this supreme Thousand Names attains the knowledge of Brahman, by which he is liberated from bondage. (297)

"Free from desire" (*niṣkāma*) means devoid of longing for sense objects. "Knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmajñāna*) is that which removes the delusion of non-difference between the individual self (*jīva*) and Brahman;
it is produced by the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), has the Self alone as its object, and is known as "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*).

The final mode of existence is knowledge consisting of direct experience, by attaining which one is liberated from bondage—that web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) and possessiveness (*mamatā*) established since beginningless time. This is the meaning: at the commencement of the constant practice of chanting the Name.

If, instead of the mention "for the sake of exhausting accumulated sins," one were to mention "for the sake of pleasing Śrī Tripurasundarī," the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman would result from that alone.
Nor should it be argued: "How can there be a disinterested performance (niṣkāma-prayoga) when there is a mention of a desire?"

For the designation "having desire" (*sakāmatva*) occurs precisely when there is a mention of longing for an object. For this very reason, among the learned (*śiṣṭas*), the designation "desireless" (*niṣkāmatva*) is applied to an action when it is mentioned as being "for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord.
By this [definition], the efficacy of a ritual performance intended to remove evil is established by implication. [Thus, one may say: "For the pleasure of the Śrīmātṛ..."

By not stating "he who should recite the Thousand Names" but rather saying "one who is free from desire," it is implied that one who is habituated to such practice should never engage in the pursuit of sensual objects; as it has been said: "Only by performing obligatory and occasional rites does one effect the destruction of evil. (297)
Now, one might ask: "What would happen if even one who is habituated to desireless practice were to engage in practice with desire due to negligence and the like? To this, he says:
"One who seeks wealth obtains wealth; one who seeks fame shall obtain fame."
And a seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge by reciting the Thousand Names.

"Seeking wealth": this refers to one who seeks knowledge—that is, one desiring the immeasurable sciences such as the Vedas and Shastras—but not one desiring the *Śrī-vidyā*. This is because prior to attaining that [knowledge], there is a lack of qualification for this [practice]; thus, even a performance carried out by one who lacks qualification is tantamount to not having performed it at all, being fruitless, and moreover, scripture records that it leads to misfortune.

Indeed, freedom from desire (*niṣkāmatva*) is the general absence of longing for sense objects. If, however, longing for sense objects should arise even once in the interim, that very state of freedom from desire would be contradicted. Even if one performs the practice in both ways due to mental instability, it remains the practice of one free from desire (*niṣkāma-prayoga*).

The sense is that [the seeker] is exhausted merely by desire, and thus attains only those respective fruits, but not the knowledge of Brahman. Alternatively, the word *vidyā* refers exclusively to the knowledge of Brahman;
even when one mentions "for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman"—just as one says "for the sake of pleasing the Mother"—that [knowledge] is nonetheless obtained.
This is the meaning. The mention of wealth (*dhana*) and fame (*yaśas*) is for the sake of illustration;

the sense is that, for example, one who desires wealth obtains wealth, and so forth. By this, [it is shown that] in the context of introducing practices with progressively superior results, the statement of the practice for those desiring wealth and so on immediately after the practice that is the absolute best is not inconsistent.
Refuted. || 298 ||
This hymn is such that, once one begins its practice free from desire, even if one should fall away from it, one does not regress;
on the contrary, whatever one desires, that very thing one surely attains. Therefore, he says: how could there be another hymn equal to this?
O Sage, there is no hymn equal to this which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
therefore, this should be recited by men who seek enjoyment and liberation. (299)

"By this [it is meant]: for one who has fallen from the application (*prayoga*) of enjoyment (*bhoga*), it grants liberation; for one who has fallen from the application of liberation, it grants enjoyment;
and for one who desires both, it grants both. Even in that case, the meaning is that it first grants enjoyment and subsequently liberation. This is also stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
Therefore, for all people without exception, neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation can ever exist simultaneously anywhere except through the worship of Tripura.
With your mind fixed on That, your life-breath absorbed in That, performing sacrifices for That, and with your exertion directed toward That,
you shall attain liberation by performing actions through identity with That.
"This secret has been declared out of a desire for the welfare of all.

Alternatively, according to the interpretation of the preceding verse as providing knowledge of Brahman, this verse states that it provides the detachment (*vairāgya*) which is the means to that [knowledge]. From enjoyments...

The meaning is as follows: liberation (*mokṣa*) from desires for sense objects is their release, which is the abandonment of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) thereof; it is that which bestows this, and so forth. And it has been said in the *Aṣṭāvakragītā*: "O dear one, if you desire liberation, abandon sense objects like poison. (299)

What need is there for much? He says that this [work] is beneficial even for those who, due to a lack of capacity for the rituals taught in the Tantras, are habitually devoted exclusively to the performance of Śrauta and Smārta rites:
This should always be recited by those devoted to the four stages of life (āśramas) for the sake of fulfilling any deficiencies in the performance of their own duties. 300.

"O clever one": by those established in the four stages of life (*caturāśrama*), namely the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the ascetic (*yati*), along with their respective sub-divisions, through the correct performance of their own duties according to the scriptures.

The dative case in the phrase "for the sake of" (*samādhānāya*) denotes purpose; it refers to the fulfillment and rectification of whatever deficiency or defect (*vaiguṇya*) is inevitable when [the rites] are being performed. All those various actions prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* for members of the four stages of life (*caturāśramin*)—all of them [are included].
Only for one capable of performing all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) do [the rites] bestow the fruit;
and the performance of all the constituent parts is, for the most part, most difficult for modern people to accomplish.
This very point has been demonstrated by us in the *Śivastava*:
Even when all the limbs [of the ritual] have been perfectly arranged as non-different from oneself, the karmas yield only something trivial;
if not, they cause one to dwell in doubt within the difficult abyss of hell.
[One must attend to] the mantras, the understanding of the purpose of the yantras, the rules of the teacher's household, and the purification of place, time, and purpose.
How is it that our intellect, having reached such extreme hardness, fails to grasp what is both firm and hidden from reality?

Thus, since the omission of even a single limb is difficult to avoid, it is essential for all [practitioners] that this [rite] be performed in order to achieve perfection by means of dispelling the sin produced by such omissions; so is the sense. And it has been said in the third book of the Devībhāgavata:
To the gods, the Blessed One said: "O gods, by the utterance of my name, you shall indeed always remain satisfied and contented in all sacrifices and in every respect."

And thus, by the principle of "separateness despite connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*), its dual nature as being both for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is established. || 300 ||

Now, one might object: "Since expiations have been prescribed here and there for the rectification of omissions of auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), and since perfection (*sādguṇya*) is achieved by those alone, what is the use of this *Sahasranāmastotra*? To this he says:
"In the Kali age, which abounds solely in sin and is devoid of the performance of dharma..."
Except for the chanting of his names, there is no other refuge for men.
Regarding the word *kalau*: it refers to the Kali age, when three-quarters of the four-footed Dharma have been destroyed by sin.

Regarding the word *muktvā*: this is a separate, indivisible construction with the sense of "without," and not a form ending in the suffix *ktvā*; for such a usage would be impossible here due to the absence of another action performed by the agent of the act of releasing. Regarding the word *sthitānām* (of those who remain): [it refers to those remaining in the world].

This must be rectified either by completing the remainder [of the rite] or through the very act of performing the seasonal transits (*ayana*). The meaning is that for those who remain indifferent to their names [and castes] yet fall from their practice due to the performance of their respective *sāṅga* rituals, other expiations prescribed in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Tantra* are not the ultimate recourse, nor are they the refuge. Not...

This means that it fulfills all deficiencies. Furthermore, the recitation of its name occurs as follows: "Of all the various penances consisting of ascetic practices, the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is supreme among them all."
That which was to be done has not been done, and that which was not to be done has been performed as if it were duty;
O Śiva, the expiation for both is said to be the two syllables of Your name.
O best of sages, what need is there for any other rite of expiation or ritual act? The recitation of the names of the goddesses is itself the expiation for a multitude of sins.

Because of such statements as these. Furthermore, here in the third statement, by the qualification "by means of the rite" (*karmaṇā*) applied to expiation (*prāyaścitta*), this is indicated: since expiations are also a specific form of ritual action, it must be stated that even they produce their results only when accompanied by all their constituent parts (*sāṅga*).

Furthermore, completeness (*sāṅgatā*) is indeed difficult to achieve according to the method already stated; even in that case, if one were to search for further expiations (*prāyaścitta*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor can it be argued that because the recollection of the Name is also a ritual act in the form of an expiation, it requires completeness.
It should not be said that seeking another expiation is equivalent [to the recitation of the name],
because the mere remembrance of the Name alone— without depending on other difficult-to-master auxiliary factors—
is what removes sin. As it is stated in the Viṣṇu-bhāgavata:
Whether it be used conventionally, in jest, as a mere exclamation, or even with contempt,
they know that the utterance of the name of Vaikuṇṭha removes every single sin.
Thus [it is said]. "Conventional" refers to names such as those of one's sons. "Stobha" is a meaningless sound. Also in the *Śivarahasya*:
"Since a person is liberated by chanting even involuntarily the name [of Śiva], why is that Great God not served by those possessed of intelligence?"
Thus it is said in the third book of the Devībhāgavata: "Even a name that is indistinct, if uttered even incidentally,
bestows all desired objects, even those that are altogether difficult to attain."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śaktirahasya*:
"O Gaurī, your name has been uttered by me even out of intoxication, negligence, madness, from a bad dream, or even from a slip of the tongue, for the removal of the sins of men."

Thus: *mada* is that produced by the drinking of liquor and so forth; *pramāda* is lack of attentiveness; *unmāda* is possession by spirits and the like; *utsvapna* is verbal expression during the state of sleep; *skhalana* is the emission of a word other than the one intended when one has set out to speak something specific. Furthermore, there exists...

The maxim of the well-digger (*kūpakhānakanyāya*), well-known in the *Mahābhāṣya*, is as follows: even while digging a well—which results in the cessation of thirst and the removal of the coating of mud—thirst and the coating of mud certainly persist; yet once the well is completed, those two are destroyed by the water produced from it. Thus it is, O King.

This is because it is accepted that the sin produced by the use of the corrupt form *puruṣa su* is destroyed by the use of the fully established form *rājapuruṣa* produced thereby; by that same logic, in the present case as well, since there is no difference in being delimited by the nature of sin which is to be destroyed by the remembrance of the Name, [the Name] destroys... the remembrance of the Name.

Since even the sin produced by failing in one's duty on the battlefield is destroyed by that very same remembrance of the Name, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). With this very intention, we shall state at the end of the book: "Nevertheless, O virtuous ones, the greatness of the Name of those whose hearts are compassionate is such..."
"Therefore, for me, there is indeed no fear from the two-fold sin of the *khalas* (the wicked).

Here, "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) means having the nature of removing the sin produced by the loss of one's own limbs; its meaning is that it has not been established anywhere previously in rites such as penances (*prāyaścitta*). Nor...
It should not be said that the recitation of the Name serves for the sake of making expiations such as those prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti complete;
for that would contradict the maxim: "Let the cause itself be the cause [of the effect]; what is the use of an intermediate step? All of this has been stated in our *Śivastava*:
O Śiva, the Creator, in order to rectify even those various transgressions of his own ordinances,
has prescribed expiations that are easily accessible through wealth and yet possess a sense of incompleteness;
for when a deficiency occurs at the edge of the rite, or when there is an obstruction to a full sacrifice, the rite must be performed once again.
But that the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is made with only a small amount of clarified butter—this truth I do not understand, despite having heard it many times.

It has been stated in the Purāṇas and other scriptures that even for the non-performance of what ought to be done or the performance of what ought not to be done, the supreme expiation within the category of atonements is the devoted recitation of "Śiva, Śiva.
O Maheśa, if one remembers You after having committed an action, it serves as its complete restoration.
If that which was performed at the very beginning does not deliver me, why then should I abandon my ritual actions?
Thus, the meaning is that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is for the sake of rectifying an action, and that [expiation] itself is a "rectification" in relation to another subsequent rectification.
Therefore, the sense is that the mere recitation of the Name alone is the ultimate refuge. || 301 ||

Now, one might object: "If the general act of chanting the Name produces the destruction of sin, what relevance does that have to the present case? Anticipating this, [the author] replies: although all meritorious names are equally capable of destroying sin, there is a distinction among those that dispel darkness—such as fireflies, fire, the moon, the sun, and so forth.

Just as there is a gradation among various splendors, he describes the different stages [of excellence] using the *sārālaṅkāra* (the ornament of the essence) in order to state that this very [practice] surpasses all others:
"The primary [excellence] over ordinary speech is the chanting of the name of Viṣṇu."
And even from a thousand names of Viṣṇu, a single name of Śiva is superior.

Regarding the phrase "from the worldly": even when employing words such as "pot" or "cloth," which are worldly, there is indeed merit. This is because of the scriptural statement: "A single word, correctly understood and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty (kāmadhuk) in the heavenly world. Therefore, compared to the utterance of thousands of such [worldly] words, [the merit of the former is greater].
The utterance of even a single word denoting a man of virtuous fame, such as Vikramārka, bestows a distinguished fruit. As it is said in the *Viṣṇu-bhāgavata*:
"Certainly [one attains] the seven Brahman-sages and men of virtuous fame."
Having risen at the end of the latter part of the night, being purified and well-concentrated, they [should proceed].

"The meaning of the phrase 'from the worldly statement' is as follows: by reciting such a thousand names, beginning with 'Those who remember my forms are liberated from all sin,' one attains liberation. Regarding the compound *viṣṇunāma*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *viṣṇūnām nāma* (the name of Viṣṇus)."
The meaning is that even the singular name of any one whatsoever among the Viṣṇus who are infinite in number;
"anukīrtanam" (proclamation) here means "that which is being proclaimed"; [the compound] means "one whose proclamation has been followed."

From the *Vigraha*: this term also recurs later in reference to the names of Śiva and so forth. "The name of the Śivas" refers to the names of Rudra, Īśvara, Śiva, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva. In the *Tattvabhedapaṭala* of the *Vātulaśuddha*:
One should know Śiva as one; he becomes fivefold as Sādākhya.
Maheśvara and Mahāsena possess twenty-five divisions.

The various distinctions mentioned in this and other passages are to be understood as follows: the underlying sense is that although Viṣṇus are infinite, they occupy only a single stage; however, for Rudras and others, the stages differ progressively higher and higher. Furthermore, within each of those stages, there is likewise an infinity of Rudras and the rest.
For the sake of illumination, [the term] "Maheśvara" is used, which denotes one who possesses qualities equal in acquisition and preservation to Viṣṇu;

furthermore, his manifestations (vyūhas) are described elsewhere in such passages as "Mahāsena," "the divider of the twenty-five [principles]," and so forth. Without employing the word *rudra*, the word *śiva*—which is woven through all things—is used.
From that, the stages beginning with the name Viṣṇu, then the name Rudra, and then the name Īśvarī are to be inferred.
However, this much is the distinction regarding the Viṣṇus:

Because they are infinite due to being arranged in a hierarchy of degrees (taratamabhāva), the recitation of their names yields the same result regardless of how it is performed. However, for the Śivas,
because they are infinite even in their hierarchical gradation and because there is a mutual intermingling of their names, [the result would differ].

The name being proclaimed, preceded by a consideration of such and such levels and categories of objects, is "supreme" in each respective way. Alternatively, even Viṣṇu is indeed of infinite kinds, by virtue of his inclusion within the group of Ādityas and so forth; nevertheless...
In the case of a confusion of names, the distinction is to be understood solely through the investigation of their respective meanings.

However, those words that are unique to each [deity], even when recited in any manner whatsoever, are indeed supreme. For this very reason, it is stated in the Sūtasamhitā that words such as "Śiva" are primary when applied to the Supreme Śiva:
Indeed, all names are mentally constructed by one's own *māyā* within that whose nature is eternal bliss and the Self;
nevertheless, words such as "Śiva" and others become primary designations for Śiva through the process of conceptualization.
Thus, even the superiority of names such as Rudra over the names of Viṣṇu is established. In that very context, there is a statement by the sage Śatānanda to Yama:
"The man who knows the words Śiva, Rudra, and so forth to be distinguished [as superior]..."
Therefore, avoid addressing that Lord with names such as Nārāyaṇa and the like.
Thus it is said; and also in the Parāśara Purāṇa: "Among all the deities, the Creator Brahmā is remembered as the highest;
and Mahāviṣṇu is superior even to Brahmā, being the protector of all."
"Even beyond Viṣṇu is Rudra himself, the agent of dissolution.
Also, in the Sūtagītā:
"Among the three, Rudra is the most excellent; beyond him is Māyin, the Supreme Śiva."
From the omniscient Lord, who is distinguished by Māyā, Sāmba—whose characteristics are truth and the like—[is born].
O sages, Śiva himself is the most excellent; there is no doubt about this. There is nothing superior to Śiva; this truth has been uttered by me.
Thus [it is said]. Here, by the word "māyin," Īśvara, Śiva, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva are understood as non-different.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five great pretas are stationed at the base of the feet.
Thus, because Sadāśiva is mentioned in the middle as distinct from Īśvara,
there, upon that most beautiful surface— the great couch whose essence is Śiva, with Maheśāna as its pillow— Sadāśiva is the mattress.
There reside the hired servants, the four-footed creatures, Maheśa, and the cloud-bearer;
there dwells the Supreme Sovereign, Mahātripurasundarī.
Thus, because six [deities] other than Kāmeśvara are mentioned in the Bhairavayāmala— namely, Bhṛtaka,
Bhṛtya, Druhiṇa, Hari, Rudra, and Īśvara— the meaning is that it is exactly the same in the *Bahurūpāṣṭaka-prastāra* and other such works regarding the term “Sāmbā.”
The referent is Śiva as Kāmeśvara, non-different from Tripurasundarī, characterized by truth and the rest; and these [characteristics] are stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Truth is all-pervading, subtle, immutable, immovable, and eternal."
Yogis behold that supreme state of the Great Goddess.
The supreme Brahman is bliss, absolute, partless, and transcendent;
it is the reality higher than the highest, eternal, auspicious, and immutable.
The supreme state of the Goddess is merged within the infinite primordial nature;
it is radiant, stainless, pure, devoid of qualities, and free from all wretchedness.
"The supreme state of the Goddess is the object of the perception of the Self.

Even though this is the case, because there is no difference in reality (*tattvataḥ*) among these [deities] despite their internal distinctions of name and form, and because there is a commingling (*sāṅkarya*) even of their names, [the same applies to] the Purāṇas that expound them.
And because there is no distinction [between them], it is said that the name of Śiva is one alone. With this very intention, it is stated in the *Śaktirahasya* and other texts:
"A thousand cycles of the four yugas is said to be a single day of Brahmā."
A single ghaṭī of Viṣṇu is considered equal to thousands of Pitāmahas (Brahmās).
Twelve lakhs of Viṣṇu’s [years] constitute half a nimeṣa of Maheśvara;
ten koṭis of Maheśvaras constitute a single truṭi of Śrīmātṛ.

In such passages as these, Maheśa alone is declared to be between Viṣṇu and Devī. If it be objected that there are indeed many statements in the Viṣṇupurāṇa, the Viṣṇubhāgavata, the Bṛhannāradīya, and other texts that establish the superiority of Viṣṇu, [the reply is: it is true that they are seen.
However, there is no contradiction because those [other Purāṇas] are intended to convey an essential identity with the Supreme (Parā).
This has also been stated in the Parāśaropapurāṇa: "Whatever deficiency is observed in the Vāiṇava Purāṇas..."
This belongs solely to the sovereign power of this Rudra, this Hara.
Thus, likewise in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"Even Vedic statements appear as if they were proclaiming the superiority of Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Indra over Śaṅkara as well."
For those who uphold the truth proclaim the superiority of these beings according to their essential nature; indeed, the believers declare the superiority of Rudra over Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Indra.
O twice-born ones, all those words which are spoken express [their meaning] both by their own form and by their essential reality.
"The established order of reality is that it is not so for Viṣṇu and the other gods.
Here, by the word *rudra*, Sāmba Kāmeśvara is meant.
By the phrase "Viṣṇu and the other gods," the word "others" (*ādi*) includes all those who fall between Viṣṇu and his consort.

They are called *śivas*. Because their number is an extreme secret, it is to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru. And this being so, there is no contradiction with the class of scriptural statements that teach the indestructibility of Viṣṇu and others; for even those [statements] are made from the perspective of the ultimate reality (*tattva-dṛṣṭi*) itself, as in: "I became Manu..."

This is logical, as it is consistent with the statement of Vāmadeva beginning with "I am the Sun" (*sūryaścāham*), and because it is also logically consistent in terms of its essential nature due to having a lifespan much longer than that of people like us. As it is said in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"A man who lives for a hundred years is 'infinite' (*ananta*) to one of very short life."
He who is immortal even while living at the very outset is therefore called "immortal" (amara).
"Thus, Viṣṇu and the others are considered [to be such] regarding births and deaths that are unseen. || 302 ||

Thus, once the superiority of the Lord of Desire (Kāmeśvara) is established, the superiority of his Śakti—the Goddess—over the previous [deities] is established by that very non-difference from him. This is so because of such Tantric statements as: "Even among themselves, in the case of the subtle Śiva, no name or abode exists without Śakti."

In the *Saundaryalaharī*, it is stated: "If Śiva is joined with Śakti, he becomes capable of exercising power," and so forth. Thus, since it is established that the excellence of Śiva is rooted in Śakti—being proven by universal experience through the very fact of their union—it follows by the maxim "let the cause itself [be the object of praise]" that the Mother [is the supreme reality].
With the intention that [her] supreme excellence is thus established, he says:
"Even compared to the thousand names of Śiva, one name of the Goddess is superior.
O Pot-born One (Agastya), there are thousands of millions of names of the Goddess. (303)

"Śivā"—this uncompounded expression is the name of the Goddess Tripurasundarī, who is non-different from Paraśiva, intended to dispel the delusion that the Goddess is infinite. Thus, it is said in the Vātulaśuddha Tantra:
"The supreme power of Śiva arises as a thousandth part [of Him]."
From a thousandth part of Parāśakti, Ādiśakti originates.
The power of will (icchā-śakti) arises from a thousandth part of the primordial power (ādi-śakti);
the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) arises from a thousandth part of the power of will.

The mention of the names of Parāśakti and the others, as stated in passages such as "the power of action arises from a thousandth part of the power of knowledge," serves to proclaim the supreme excellence of the Goddess among the entire collection of Triadic Upaniṣads, for the sake of the Great Deity.
This is indeed clear from such repeated usage and from scriptural declarations that [Śiva] is the progenitor of Śivā and others.

Even in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, when there arises an occasion for the incidental mention of other deities, the fact that other gods are generally mentioned by their respective unique names in the extensive recitation [of mantras]— [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary Sanskrit commentary. The translation reflects the logical flow and the specific terminology used in the original.]
This is also evident from such usages as, "This is indeed the form of that deity; thus one pleases that very great deity. Furthermore, in the Rudrayāmala it is said:
"A man becomes initiated through the abundance of merits accumulated over many births."
Even there, by virtue of manifold fortune, he was devoted to Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Even there, through many floods of merit, the state of Śakti arises;
even there, by means of great awakening, one attains the state of Sundarī.
And even there, the state known as the Fourth (turyā) may enter within through one's good fortune;
yet even that, the chanting of its name, is exceedingly difficult to attain.
In that birth in which she, being eternally pleased by the chanting of her name,
grants liberation while living (jīvanmukti), nothing further remains to be done.
Thus it is said; likewise in the Smṛtis: "Viṣṇu is remembered as the heart of Brahmā, and Śiva is remembered as the heart of Viṣṇu;
the Sandhyā is the heart of Śiva, and therefore she is to be worshipped by the twice-born."
Thus, by the words of Kaśyapa and others, as well as in all the Purāṇas such as the Kūrma, Padma, and Skanda, and in various places therein,
as well as in the Brahmāṇḍa, Mārkaṇḍeya, and other Purāṇas, and frequently in the Śaktirahasya, the third book of the Devībhāgavata, and so forth—

Furthermore, since this has been described everywhere in an immeasurable way throughout the *Jñānārṇava*, *Kulārṇava*, and other tantras, it is clear to those who know them; therefore, it is not elaborated upon here. || 303 ||
Among those, the principal is said to be the ten-fold Thousand Names;
this Secret Thousand Names is praised as the best even among the ten.

Among those ten million [names], these ten praises (*daśastava*)— namely *Gaṅgā*, *Śyālakā*, *Bāla*, *Rāsabha*, and so forth— are included according to the authoritative tradition, possessing a set of ten types. Here, the ten syllables beginning with *gaṅgā* constitute the initial syllables of the ten names from the *Sahasranāma*.
The two *Mads*, the two *Bhads*, the three *Vrats*, and the four [sets],
as well as the *Anāpaliṅga* and the *Kūṣka*, and the various *Purāṇas* individually.

Thus, it is established by the maxim that a name may be referred to by mentioning a portion of it, as in the verse from the *Devībhāgavata*. The final letter *bha* is indeed short; the long-vowel reading, however, is prompted by the use of the plural number. And therefore—
Gaṅgā, Bhavānī, Gāyatrī, Kālī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rājarājeśvarī, Bālā, Śyāmalā, and Lalitā— these are the ten.

Such is its meaning. They also say that there are ten thousand-name hymns (*sahasranāma*) for Tripurasundarī alone according to the different tantras. *Śastam* means "praiseworthy" or "excellent. || 304 ||
He concludes:
"Therefore, one should constantly recite it for the removal of the defects of the Kali age;
yet those who are utterly deluded do not know that the name of the Śrī Mother is the primary [remedy]. (305)

"Therefore" [means]: the defect caused by the Kali age is the deficiency in the performance of one's respective duties; for the sake of its removal and for the fulfillment of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) and so forth. And this "deficiency" does not consist merely in the omission of an auxiliary part, but rather also in the omission of the principal act (*pradhāna*), because there is no distinction between them in terms of being a deficiency of the principal.

Furthermore, because there is no difference in the fact that they are equally subject to the defects inherent in the Kali age, this [practice] is generally unavoidable for all modern people who consider themselves performers of ritual action (*karmaṭha*). Since sacrifice (*yāga*), which consists of the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity, is essentially a specific form of mental resolve (*mānasa-saṅkalpa*), it does not depend on fire.

Because this [meditation] arises through mere verbal expression, such as the clear words "This salutation" (*idaṃ namaḥ*) and so forth; thus, the primary element denoted by the term "Sandhyā-vandana" (the twilight worship) is the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra,
"That sun is Brahman," regarding the consciousness delimited by the sun.

It consists of the contemplation of non-difference with one's own essential consciousness (*svātmacaitanya*). Furthermore, even among the learned who are conversant with the secret teachings, that [contemplation] occurs only occasionally and not universally; thus, a deficiency in the primary requirement is unavoidable for everyone. Nor is it the case that...

For these [rites], resolution is achieved through the performance of expiation caused by the deficiency of a subsidiary (aṅga), because their prescription is for the omission of a subsidiary alone; however, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), when there is an omission of the principal (pradhāna), there must simply be a repetition of the rite. But this chanting of the Name applies to both types of causes [for expiation].
Because it is "conducive to concentration" (*samādhāyaka*), its superiority even over that [other means] is established.

Now, raising the objection that if this were so, the scriptures on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) would be rendered useless, he says "principal" (*mukhya*). This is because for those whose minds are deluded by *māyā*, a sense of greatness arises toward only minor deities.

Engagement in the worship of this or that [deity] appears like a great painting to one whose eyes are obscured by the veil of *māyā*, as we have stated in our *Śivastava*: "Because of our slight anger... and so forth. Consequently, due to the infinity of such mental dispositions, those [forms of worship] are intended solely for whichever person has a preference for whichever [deity].

The various scriptures have been set forth. Indeed, it is observed even in the world that some people have an inclination for a means that is gross and heavy, while others have an inclination for one that is subtle and light.
Therefore, with the desire to favor all such people, those various scriptures were indeed [revealed] by the Blessed One herself.

[The objection that] these [recitations] are not rendered useless is answered as follows: even in the recitation of the *Sahasranāma*, they possess purpose because they indirectly generate interest; this, however, is the hidden intention (*gūḍho 'bhisandhiḥ*). For even when an easy means exists, the engagement of people in a difficult means arises solely from the delusion (*vyāmoha*) resulting from their respective past actions (*karma*).
The state of being. || 305 ||
Some are devoted to the name of Viṣṇu, and others are devoted to the name of Śiva;
yet there is not a single person in the worlds who is so intent upon the name of Lalitā.

With the intention that devotion to the names of Viṣṇu can arise for many people through the ripening of merit produced by such actions over many births—specifically for those devoted solely to the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti—he says: "Viṣṇu... and so forth.

With the intention that by chanting the names of Viṣṇu of such a kind, devotion may arise in some toward even a few of the names of Śiva after several births, he says, "devoted to the names of Śiva. For Śiva, however,
because he possesses many forms through the distinctions of two, three, four, and so forth, [there is a possibility] even for one who exists therein.
Because the relative gradations between them are difficult to fathom, even those who have ascended to higher levels through diligent effort over many lifetimes appear to remain at the very midpoint;
for the determination of the exact extent of the levels of Śiva is a secret that is not widely known. Therefore...

Because it is attainable only through many births and vast accumulations of merit, devotion toward the most secret names of the Goddess culminates as something even more difficult to obtain. For this very reason, it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
This glorious fifteen-syllable vidyā is obtained only by one whose birth is their last, or by Śaṅkara himself.

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the word "Śaṅkara," one who has attained identity with the final Śaṅkara through the practice (*upāsanā*) consisting of the sequential contemplation of non-difference (*abhedānusandhāna*) is meant. And such a state is indeed extremely difficult to attain; and that which is so difficult to attain—[is as follows:]
With the intention that [such a person] is generally as if non-existent, he says, "not even anyone at all. This refers to among the worlds—among humans, gods, dānavas, and so forth. || 306 ||
Now he reveals his hidden intention:
"He who has chanted the names of other deities throughout millions of births, for him alone does faith arise in chanting the name of the Śrī Devī. (307)
Regarding the word "by whom": for one who has recited the individual names of other deities such as Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and so forth, throughout millions of births— [that person],
by virtue of the sequence of stages (*kakṣyākrama*), attains identity with each successive deity and ultimately attains identity with Śiva.
