The sense is that the sprout of faith regarding the chanting of the name of the illustrious Goddess has arisen in some rare, preeminent person, but not in others.

Now, raising the doubt as to what could be attained even through a multitude of births distinguished by the chanting of the names of such goddesses, he refutes it by showing that another birth is itself impossible, using an illustration:
Just as one becomes a worshiper of Śrīvidyā in one's final birth, so too should the recitation of the Thousand Names be performed in that final birth. (308)

Regarding the word "carama" (the last): since there is no other analogy for this portion, it is with the intention that the mantra of the Goddess herself is the analogy for the name of the Goddess that it was stated, "just like a practitioner of Śrīvidyā.
The word "upāsaka" refers to the act of worship (*upāsti*). "Śrīvidyā" is a separate word.

The term *upāsaka* (worshipper) is a qualifier for that [attainment], intended to signify the perfection of the contemplation of the identity (*aikya*) between the guru, the deity, the mantra, and one’s own self; for such [identity] is attained only in one's final birth, according to the statement in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "For whom there is no further birth," and so forth. Alternatively, [it may be understood as follows:]

The term "nāmasāhasrasya pāṭhaḥ" (the recitation of the Thousand Names) is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound; alternatively, the final member (*uttarapada*) itself refers to the reciter. Furthermore, there is a simile between the mantra and the name, which serve as the delimitors of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) for the practitioner and the recitation, respectively.
The state of being the object of comparison does not bear fruit. || 308 ||
Just as those who know the practice of the Śrīvidyā are rare in the world, so too is one who recites the Thousand Secret Names rare. (309)
The mere acquisition of the Śrīvidyā mantra does not constitute worship, for that can be accomplished even through easily accessible means such as books and the like; rather,
it consists in the performance [of the ritual] preceded by a complete understanding of all the practices, distinguished by their external and internal varieties, pertaining to that [mantra].
Furthermore, that [attainment] is extremely rare. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śaktirahasya* that "the gurus in the Kaula tradition are infinite.
This is because, despite the availability of many treatises concerning the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, there are still many men who possess complete knowledge regarding those subjects.

The fulfillment of a disciple’s desire may be accomplished by a single teacher, or by two or three; however, these practices are not recorded in their entirety in any of the scriptures. On the contrary, it is taught that if they were so recorded, one would incur the curse of the Yoginīs. For this very reason, in the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*, it is said that [the transmission occurs] through oral instruction from ear to ear.
It has been stated that [the knowledge] was obtained on the surface of the earth, but not from one book to another.
Therefore, his intention is that the acquisition of the knowledge of all practices comes only from the mouths of the gurus.
It is precisely with this intention that—
Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to flower,
so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, should go from teacher to teacher.

Thus, the established rule—that the sandals belong only to that guru who performs the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*)—is consistent. Consequently, although the mantra alone may be rare, it is not even a point of comparison here; rather, it is the knowledge of the practice itself that is meant, because it is even rarer than that. With this intention, the very same point has been stated.
"He confirms it as it truly is" means that they are rare, even extremely rare. || 309 ||
The recitation of the king of mantras, the worship of the king of cakras, and the chanting of the secret names—the fruit of these is not for one who has performed only slight austerity. 310.

Thus, he states the meaning established by logic with the word "mantra": the meeting in one place of even three rare things individually is extremely difficult to obtain. Furthermore, the word "niravadhikasya" (of that which is limitless) is to be supplied as the remainder; this compound is formed with the particle *na* itself, meaning "not of the little," and not with the negative particle *nañ*. 310.
He of deluded intellect who seeks to please Maheśvarī without reciting the Thousand Names would indeed perceive forms without the aid of his eyes. (311)
He who, desiring spiritual accomplishment, abandons the *Rahasyanāmasāhasra* is surely like one who seeks to end hunger without food. (312)

Having thus stated, by way of positive concomitance (*anvayamukhena*), that this [mantra] brings delight to the deities and fulfills all desires, he confirms it by way of negative concomitance (*vyatirekamukhena*) through two verses employing the figure of speech *vidarśanā* (illustration). The meaning of "apaṭhan" and so forth is clear. || 311-312 ||
The devotee of Goddess Lalitā should constantly recite this;
otherwise, the Goddess is not pleased even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
He states, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that this alone is also the defining characteristic of being a devotee (*bhaktatāvacchedaka*):

"He who... The meaning is: he alone is a devotee, and no other. The connection between the relative and demonstrative pronouns (*yad-tad*) is inverted, as in the case of the statement, "Those who are sacrificers are the officiating priests. || 313 ||
Therefore, one should recite the secret names of the Śrī Mother with great devotion.
Thus has this secret hymn been told to you, O Pot-born One (Agastya). 314.

Concluding the procedure for reciting the *Nāmasāhasra*, he summarizes the statement of its fruit with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). [The practitioner should be] self-controlled (*prayataḥ*) and pure (*śuciḥ*). || 314 ||
Later, he instructs on the manner of transmitting the tradition:

"O Sage, one should never speak this to one who does not understand ignorance [or: the Veda], nor to one who lacks devotion; just as the Śrīvidyā is to be kept secret, so too must this be kept secret. (315)
"No. One should not speak [of this] even to a devotee who lacks the knowledge and realization of the Vidyā, nor to one who possesses that knowledge but is not a devotee.

The sense is: just as the Śrīvidyā is to be kept secret and is not revealed to one who lacks it, so too this [teaching] should not be revealed even to one who possesses it, much less to one who lacks it. || 315 ||
One should not utter this supreme hymn among people who are like beasts;
for that deluded soul who gives it to one devoid of the Śrīvidyā, [incurs great fault]. (316)
For this very reason, it is prohibited by the half-verse beginning with "paśu. Two kinds of *paśus* (bound souls) were previously mentioned.
He states the punishment for transgressing this prohibition in the verse beginning with "yaḥ": "And the meaning obtained from the word 'ca' (and) is 'he who takes [it]';
the Yoginīs become angry with him, and that is remembered as a very great misfortune."
Therefore, one should keep this Thousand Secret Names well concealed. || 317 ||
To that giver and to the recipient who is devoid of knowledge;
for those [roots] whose meaning is "anger," "malice," "envy," or "slander," the one toward whom the anger is directed receives the designation of *saṃpradāna* (recipient).
He concludes the necessity of concealment with the half-verse beginning with "in secret" (*rahasye*); "in secret" and so forth is the substantive.

It contains the core of the reason; by that, it is the ornament of the sprout of the preparatory rite (*parikāra*). Therefore, because it brings misfortune to both the giver and the receiver who lack the qualification, and because it is a secret, the meaning is that one should conceal it.
This was not spoken by me in my independent [work], O Agastya (*kalaśodbhava*), even for you.
It was solely through the inspiration of Lalitā that this supreme hymn was spoken by me.
Hayagrīva addresses Agastya, who might raise the doubt, "How is it that you have revealed to me that which ought to be kept secret even from one possessed of knowledge?
He does so with the words *svatantraṇa*. This means "independently," that is, without being prompted by another. The form *kalaśī* takes the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* as a marker of a genus (*jāti*).

And that application is through *śleṣa* (punning) for the purpose of awakening the Son of the Goddess (*devīputra*). That too is by the power of worship, in order to suggest the inevitability of Lalitāmbā’s impulsion once one has ascended to the state culminating in the nature of the Son of the Goddess through affection (*vātsalya*). "In the parrot, in the Kali age, in the decayed, in the sweet... [the pun continues].
The term *nāda* means "extremely charming," as in the case of the bird *kalaśuka*; or it refers to the goddess *Kalaśī*, who "lies within sound" (*nāde śete*).

Alternatively, it may be due to her being the most excellent of all. According to the lexicon *Rabhasa*, the word *kalaśa* denotes the sound [of a vessel] because it is the most excellent among all things, the head (the highest limb), and a water-pot.
She is *Lalitā* because, through her mere impulsion, the activity of [the world] proceeds in a way that cannot be transgressed.

Furthermore, since such an impulse arises only toward those who possess the requisite qualification (*adhikārin*), the sense is that it should not be revealed to one who is a mere pretender to the status of a practitioner (*upāsakābhāsa*). || 318 ||
O Pot-born one, this should be recited with devotion continuously;
by that, the Great Goddess will be pleased and shall grant you your desired wish. (319)

But he proceeds [to speak] in order to suggest that you are not merely a semblance of a lay devotee (*upāsakābhāsa*), but rather a fully qualified practitioner; the word "by you" (*tvayā*) is to be supplied as the subject. This is to be done continuously, preceded by the contemplation of non-duality. Nor is it the case here that the injunction for the chanting of names (*nāmakīrtana*), though heard repeatedly, constitutes a ritual action through mere repetition.
It should not be argued that it is improper to describe the fruits as belonging to a single [act] alone, such that there are so many fruits;

for this is possible even through a mere difference in *bhāvanā* (efficient force). Since the fruit is not something to be enjoined (*anupādeya*), even if the ritual act itself is enjoined repeatedly with reference to specific fruits, [the text] remains focused on something else.

Furthermore, such repeated hearing lacks the nature of repetition (*abhyāsa*). Even though there is hearing six times for the sake of the variety of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) regarding the injunction "he carries forward the water" (*apaḥ praṇayati*), no distinction of ritual acts (*karmabheda*) is admitted. This is because, even when accompanied by non-essential qualities (*anupādeyaguṇa*), there is an absence of non-proximity (*asannidhi*).
And because it is also improper to suspect another context; such is the direction [of the argument]. || 319 ||
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hayagrīva meditated upon the venerable Mother Lalitā;
with his heart immersed in bliss, he was immediately covered in horripilation.

The venerable Sūta concludes what was begun with the words "He, being delighted, spoke these words," etc., in a single verse: he is one whose heart— that is, his mind— is immersed in bliss, meaning in the bliss of his own self, and is thus solely intent upon it due to the absence of wandering toward other objects.
"Pulakita" means one in whom "pulakas"—that is, horripilation born of bliss—have arisen;
the suffix *itac* is applied according to the rule beginning with "tārakādi. || 320 ||
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Hymn of the Thousand Names of Lalitā," in the *Lalitopākhyāna* of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya.
Thus, in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* composed by Bhāskararāya,
the twelfth digit named Kṣamā has been completed with these verses, concluding the declaration of its fruits.
The author’s eulogy:

In the lineage of the illustrious Viśvāmitra, there was Gambhīrarāja, a jewel among scholars in Kāśī, devoted to the worship of Śiva, a reciter of the Bhāratī [Veda], and a drinker of Soma; his son was Bhāskara.
In the autumn season, during the month of Āśvina when the time was auspicious,
on the bright and gentle ninth day, he composed this commentary on the *Lalita-sahasranāma*.

Although this commentary has been composed by me after ascertaining and churning the essence from the Śruti, Smṛti, Nyāya, Purāṇas, Sūtras, Kośas, Āgamas, and the tradition of the venerable Gurus, it must nevertheless be refined by the virtuous who possess a compassionate heart.
"Due to my dullness of intellect and laziness, negligence will surely arise in me, given that the principles of the nature of things are necessarily difficult to fathom;
however, may the virtuous within, with their compassionate hearts, [forgive] the greatness of my name..."
Therefore, for me, there is truly no fear of both the unprecedented and the evil consequences of sin. || 3 ||
O Mother, this commentary, dedicated at your feet and composed by you to illuminate the meaning of your name, may it lead to your delight; yet,
whoever worships you but does not study it, nor reads it, even from a book— [may that fault be mine].
He does not form any attachment; let there be no thought of him in you, O Lalitā.

Victorious are those feet of my guru, by whom— having led me from a single name to the further shore of the ocean of a thousand names— I have become but a drop of water in the ocean of worldly existence.

Thus [ends] the work composed by Bhāskararāya— also known as Bhāratī, son of the venerable Gambhīrarāya Dīkṣita Sūri, who was the foremost among those who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences (Padavākyapramāṇa), and who is independent in all systems (Sarvatantrasvatantra)—
and who bears the initiatory name Bhāsurānandanātha.
The commentary on the *Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma* from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, titled *Saubhāgyabhāskara*, is complete;
this work is finished.
